concepts.name: A* Search Algorithm
concepts.description: A best-first graph search algorithm that expands the node with the lowest cost-so-far plus heuristic estimate; with an admissible heuristic it finds a shortest path.
concepts.example: Driving across a city, A* ranks each junction by miles already driven plus straight-line miles left. A junction 10 miles in with 5 to go (15) is explored before one 4 miles in with 14 to go (18).

concepts.name: Abductive Reasoning
concepts.description: Reasoning from an observation to the most plausible explanation for it, as in diagnosis; unlike deduction its conclusions are not guaranteed to be true.
concepts.example: The lawn is wet this morning. It could be rain or the sprinkler, but the street is dry too, so you conclude the sprinkler ran. A doctor reading symptoms to pick the likeliest illness does the same thing.

concepts.name: AC-3 Algorithm
concepts.description: An algorithm for constraint satisfaction problems that enforces arc consistency by processing a queue of arcs and removing domain values that have no supporting value in a neighbor.
concepts.example: With X in {1,2,3}, Y in {1,2,3} and the constraint X < Y, AC-3 checks arc X→Y and deletes X=3 (no larger Y), then checks Y→X and deletes Y=1. Any arc pointing into a shrunken domain is re-queued.

concepts.name: ACT-R
concepts.description: A cognitive architecture developed by John Anderson that models human thought as production rules acting on separate declarative and procedural memory modules, used to simulate and predict human task performance.
concepts.example: To model someone solving 3 + 4, ACT-R retrieves the fact '3 + 4 = 7' from declarative memory if it is active enough; otherwise a production rule counts up from 3. It predicts how many milliseconds each step takes.

concepts.name: Action Schema
concepts.description: A planning operator that describes a family of actions with variables, listing the preconditions that must hold before the action and the effects (facts added or deleted) after it.
concepts.example: Move(b, x, y): precondition On(b,x), Clear(b), Clear(y); effect On(b,y), Clear(x), not On(b,x), not Clear(y). One schema covers every block-moving action by plugging in specific blocks.

concepts.name: Action Description Language
concepts.description: Action Description Language, a planning formalism that extends STRIPS with negative preconditions, conditional effects, quantified variables and typed objects, making domains easier to describe.
concepts.example: In STRIPS you can't say 'drive only if the road is NOT closed' or 'everything in the truck moves with it'. ADL allows both: a negative precondition and a conditional, universally quantified effect on all cargo.

concepts.name: Admissible Heuristic
concepts.description: A heuristic that never overestimates the true cost of reaching the goal from a state; with A* tree search it guarantees that the first goal found is optimal.
concepts.example: Straight-line distance is admissible for road travel: if two cities are 80 km apart as the crow flies, no road between them can be shorter than 80 km, so the guess never overestimates.

concepts.name: Adversarial Search
concepts.description: Search in competitive environments where an opponent's moves must be anticipated, typically by exploring a game tree with algorithms such as minimax and alpha-beta pruning.
concepts.example: In tic-tac-toe, before placing an X you imagine every reply O could make and assume O picks the one worst for you. You then choose the move whose worst case is best.

concepts.name: Agent Communication Language
concepts.description: A standard language such as FIPA-ACL or KQML that lets software agents exchange messages labelled with performatives (inform, request, propose) based on speech-act theory.
concepts.example: A buyer agent sends (request :receiver seller :content (price widget)). The seller answers (inform :content (= (price widget) 10)). The performatives 'request' and 'inform' tell each side what kind of speech act it got.

concepts.name: Agent Function
concepts.description: The abstract mathematical mapping from every possible sequence of percepts an agent has received to the action it takes; it specifies an agent's behaviour independent of implementation.
concepts.example: A vacuum agent's function could be a table: [A, dirty] → suck, [A, clean] → move right, [A, clean], [B, dirty] → suck, and so on for every possible percept history.

concepts.name: Agent Program
concepts.description: The concrete program running on an agent's physical architecture that implements its agent function, taking the current percept as input and returning an action.
concepts.example: The vacuum agent function could be an endless lookup table, but a 3-line program does the job: if the current square is dirty, suck; else if in A, move right; else move left.

concepts.name: AI Winter
concepts.description: A period of sharply reduced funding and interest in AI research after inflated expectations went unmet, notably in the mid-1970s and the late 1980s to early 1990s.
concepts.example: In 1966 a US report concluded machine translation was slower and costlier than human translators, and funding was slashed. Later, after the expert-system boom collapsed around 1987, many AI companies folded.

concepts.name: AND–OR Search Tree
concepts.description: A search over trees with OR nodes for the agent's choices and AND nodes for all possible outcomes of an action, used in nondeterministic environments to find a conditional plan; AO* is a heuristic version.
concepts.example: A vacuum whose suck action sometimes dumps dirt: OR node 'which action?', AND node 'handle both outcomes'. The plan becomes: Suck; if the square is still dirty, Suck again; otherwise move right.

concepts.name: Adaptive Neuro-Fuzzy Inference System
concepts.description: A hybrid neuro-fuzzy model that represents a Sugeno-type fuzzy inference system as a layered network and tunes its membership and rule parameters with backpropagation and least squares.
concepts.example: To predict room temperature, ANFIS starts with rules like 'IF humidity is high THEN temp = 0.5·humidity + 20'. Training nudges the fuzzy 'high' curve with backprop and fits the linear output coefficients by least squares.

concepts.name: Answer Set Programming
concepts.description: A declarative programming paradigm based on the stable-model semantics of logic programs with negation as failure; problems are encoded as rules whose answer sets are solutions, used for hard combinatorial search.
concepts.example: To 3-colour a map, write: each region gets exactly one colour; neighbours can't share a colour. A solver like clingo returns answer sets, and each answer set is a valid colouring.

concepts.name: Anytime Algorithm
concepts.description: An algorithm that can be stopped at any time and still return a valid answer, with solution quality improving the longer it runs; Anytime A* and real-time planners are examples.
concepts.example: A route planner returns a 50-minute route after 0.1 s, a 44-minute route after 1 s and a 42-minute route after 5 s. Whenever you press 'go', you get the best route found so far.

concepts.name: Arc Consistency
concepts.description: A property of a constraint satisfaction problem where for every value of a variable there is some compatible value in each neighbouring variable; algorithms like AC-3 enforce it by pruning domains.
concepts.example: With X in {1,2,3}, Y in {1,2,3} and X < Y, value X=3 has no supporting Y, so it is removed. Then Y=1 has no smaller X and goes too, leaving X in {1,2} and Y in {2,3}.

concepts.name: Arrow's Impossibility Theorem
concepts.description: Arrow's theorem that no rank-order voting rule over three or more options can satisfy unrestricted domain, Pareto efficiency, independence of irrelevant alternatives and non-dictatorship all at once.
concepts.example: Three voters rank A>B>C, B>C>A, C>A>B. Majority prefers A to B, B to C and C to A, a cycle. Arrow shows that every ranked voting rule, not just majority, breaks some fairness condition.

concepts.name: Artificial Bee Colony Algorithm
concepts.description: A swarm-intelligence metaheuristic inspired by honeybee foraging, in which employed, onlooker and scout bees exploit good food sources (solutions) and abandon exhausted ones to explore new areas.
concepts.example: Each food source is a candidate solution. Employed bees tweak their source, onlookers flock to the richest ones, and a source not improved after, say, 20 tries is abandoned while its bee scouts a random new spot.

concepts.name: Artificial General Intelligence
concepts.description: A hypothetical AI system able to understand, learn and perform any intellectual task a human can across domains, as opposed to narrow AI built for specific tasks.
concepts.example: A chess engine beats grandmasters but can't fold laundry or learn French. An AGI could do all three and pick up an unfamiliar task, like a new board game or job, about as flexibly as a person.

concepts.name: Artificial Intelligence
concepts.description: The field of building computer systems that perceive, reason, learn, plan and act to perform tasks that normally require human intelligence, spanning search, logic, probabilistic reasoning and machine learning.
concepts.example: A phone's map app finds the fastest route (search), filters spam (learning from examples), and guesses traffic delays (probability). Each is a task that would otherwise need human judgement.

concepts.name: Auction Theory
concepts.description: The branch of economics and game theory that studies how auction rules (English, Dutch, first-price, second-price) shape bidding strategies, revenue and allocation efficiency.
concepts.example: In a sealed second-price auction, you bid your true value: if you value a painting at $100, bidding $100 can't hurt, since you pay the second-highest bid. In a first-price auction you'd shade your bid below $100.

concepts.name: Automated Planning and Scheduling
concepts.description: The AI field concerned with automatically finding sequences or structures of actions that take an agent from an initial state to a goal, using representations such as STRIPS and PDDL.
concepts.example: A warehouse robot starts at the dock, must deliver box A to shelf 3 and box B to shelf 7. A planner outputs: pick A, go to 3, place A, go to dock, pick B, go to 7, place B.

concepts.name: Automated Reasoning
concepts.description: The area of AI and computer science devoted to programs that draw logical conclusions automatically, including theorem proving, SAT solving and model checking.
concepts.example: Give a program 'all humans are mortal' and 'Socrates is human', ask 'is Socrates mortal?', and it proves yes on its own. Chip makers use the same idea to prove circuits correct.

concepts.name: Automated Theorem Proving
concepts.description: The use of computer programs to prove mathematical or logical theorems automatically, typically by refutation methods such as resolution, tableaux or superposition in first-order logic.
concepts.example: To prove 'Socrates is mortal', the prover adds its negation, 'Socrates is not mortal', to the axioms and resolves clauses until it derives the empty clause, a contradiction, which proves the original claim.

concepts.name: Backjumping
concepts.description: A backtracking improvement for constraint satisfaction that, on reaching a dead end, jumps back directly to the most recent variable in the conflict set instead of the chronologically previous one.
concepts.example: Colouring a map, you assign WA, then NT, then Q, then a few unrelated regions, then hit a dead end at SA. If only WA and NT conflict with SA, backjumping goes straight back to NT, skipping the unrelated ones.

concepts.name: Backward Chaining
concepts.description: A goal-driven inference method that starts from a query and works backward through rules, trying to prove each rule's premises; it underlies Prolog and many expert systems.
concepts.example: Query: can Tweety fly? Rule: X flies if X is a bird and X is not injured. So try to prove 'Tweety is a bird' (a fact, yes) and 'not injured' (yes), and you're done. Only relevant rules get touched.

concepts.name: Backward State-Space Planning
concepts.description: Planning by regression: starting from the goal, repeatedly choosing relevant actions and computing the subgoal that must hold before them, until the initial state satisfies it.
concepts.example: Goal: have coffee. The relevant action is 'pour coffee', which needs 'coffee brewed', so that becomes the subgoal. 'Brew' needs beans and water, and you regress until the subgoal already holds in the start state.

concepts.name: Bayesian Game
concepts.description: A game of incomplete information in which players have private types drawn from a commonly known prior; players maximise expected payoff, leading to Bayesian Nash equilibrium.
concepts.example: In a sealed-bid auction, you don't know if your rival values the item at $50 or $100, only that each is 50% likely. You pick a bid that maximises your expected profit over both possible rival types.

concepts.name: Belief–Desire–Intention Model
concepts.description: An agent architecture modelling practical reasoning through beliefs about the world, desires (goals it would like to achieve) and intentions (plans it has committed to pursue).
concepts.example: A delivery-drone agent believes the road is jammed, desires to deliver a parcel and to save battery, and commits to the intention 'fly route B'. It sticks with that plan unless new beliefs make it pointless.

concepts.name: Blackboard System
concepts.description: An AI architecture in which independent specialist knowledge sources cooperate by reading and writing partial solutions on a shared data structure, the blackboard, as in Hearsay-II speech understanding.
concepts.example: Like detectives around a whiteboard: one writes 'sound = /k/', another turns sounds into 'cat', a third checks grammar and posts 'the cat sat'. No expert solves it alone; each adds to the shared board.

concepts.name: Blocks World
concepts.description: A classic AI planning domain in which a robot arm stacks and unstacks blocks on a table to reach a goal configuration, used to illustrate planning representations and algorithms.
concepts.example: Start: C sits on A, and B is on the table. Goal: A on B on C. Unstack C, put it on the table, stack B on C, then stack A on B. Facts like On(C, A) and Clear(B) describe each state.

concepts.name: Boids
concepts.description: Craig Reynolds's 1986 flocking model in which each simulated bird follows three local rules, separation, alignment and cohesion, producing realistic emergent group motion.
concepts.example: Each bird looks only at nearby birds: steer away if too close (separation), match their heading (alignment), and drift toward their centre (cohesion). With 200 birds following just these rules, a swirling flock appears.

concepts.name: Branching Factor
concepts.description: The number of successors generated from a node in a search tree; the average branching factor largely determines how fast the tree grows with depth.
concepts.example: In tic-tac-toe the first move has 9 options, so the branching factor starts at 9. In chess it averages about 35, so looking 4 moves ahead means roughly 35^4 ≈ 1.5 million positions.

concepts.name: Case-Based Reasoning
concepts.description: A problem-solving approach that solves new problems by retrieving similar past cases, reusing and adapting their solutions, revising them and retaining the result as a new case.
concepts.example: A help-desk system gets 'laptop won't charge'. It finds the most similar past ticket, 'laptop dead, faulty adapter', suggests swapping the adapter, and once that works saves the new ticket for future use.

concepts.name: Conflict-Driven Clause Learning
concepts.description: Conflict-Driven Clause Learning, the core algorithm of modern SAT solvers, which extends DPLL by analysing each conflict to learn a new clause and backjumping non-chronologically.
concepts.example: DPLL sets x=1 and y=0, and propagation then hits a clash. CDCL traces the clash back and learns the clause 'not (x=1 and y=0)', so it never tries that pair again, then jumps back past irrelevant decisions.

concepts.name: Certainty Factor
concepts.description: A number from -1 to 1 used in MYCIN-style rule systems to express how much evidence supports or refutes a hypothesis, combined with ad hoc rules rather than full probability theory.
concepts.example: A rule says 'gram-negative and rod-shaped → E. coli' with CF 0.6. If a second rule also gives 0.6, MYCIN combines them as 0.6 + 0.6·(1 − 0.6) = 0.84, so belief grows but never passes 1.

concepts.name: Chinese Room
concepts.description: John Searle's thought experiment of a person following rules to manipulate Chinese symbols without understanding them, arguing that running a program is not sufficient for genuine understanding.
concepts.example: You sit in a room with a rulebook: when you see these Chinese squiggles, copy out those ones. People outside get fluent replies, yet you understand no Chinese. Searle says a computer running a program is in your position.

concepts.name: Chinook
concepts.description: A checkers-playing program from the University of Alberta that won the human world championship in 1994 and was later used to prove that perfect checkers play is a draw.
concepts.example: Chinook used huge endgame databases of solved positions with few pieces left, so once a game simplified it played perfectly. In 2007 its team showed that with perfect play by both sides, checkers is a draw.

concepts.name: Chromosome (Genetic Algorithm)
concepts.description: The encoded representation of a candidate solution in a genetic algorithm, such as a bit string or vector of values, on which selection, crossover and mutation operate.
concepts.example: To pick which of 5 items go in a backpack, a chromosome could be 10110, meaning take items 1, 3 and 4. To tune a robot's gains, it could be a list of real numbers like [0.8, 2.1, 0.05].

concepts.name: Circumscription
concepts.description: A non-monotonic reasoning technique by John McCarthy that assumes the extension of certain predicates (such as 'abnormal') is as small as possible, formalising default conclusions.
concepts.example: Know: Tweety is a bird; birds that aren't abnormal fly. Circumscription assumes as few things are abnormal as possible, so Tweety flies. Learn Tweety is a penguin (abnormal) and the conclusion is withdrawn.

concepts.name: CLARION (Cognitive Architecture)
concepts.description: A hybrid cognitive architecture with an implicit, neural-network level and an explicit, symbolic-rule level that interact, used to model skill learning and the implicit-explicit distinction in cognition.
concepts.example: Learning to ride a bike, you first get better by feel (implicit neural level) and only later can say rules like 'lean into turns' (explicit level). CLARION models both levels and how rules can be extracted from the implicit one.

concepts.name: Classical Planning
concepts.description: Planning in fully observable, deterministic, static and discrete environments, where the task is to find a sequence of actions described by action schemas that reaches a goal from a known initial state.
concepts.example: Get a spare tyre on: start with the flat on the axle and the spare in the trunk. Actions: Remove(flat, axle), Remove(spare, trunk), PutOn(spare, axle). Every action's result is certain and the full state is known.

concepts.name: CLIPS
concepts.description: A rule-based expert-system tool developed at NASA that matches facts against production rules using the Rete algorithm and fires them with forward chaining.
concepts.example: Add the fact (temperature high). A CLIPS rule '(defrule fan (temperature high) => (assert (fan on)))' matches and fires, adding (fan on), which may trigger further rules until nothing new matches.

concepts.name: Closed List
concepts.description: The set of states already expanded during graph search, kept so that the algorithm does not expand the same state twice and avoids loops in the state space.
concepts.example: Searching a city map, once you've expanded 'Station Square' you note it as visited. When another route later reaches Station Square, you skip it instead of exploring it again and possibly looping forever.

concepts.name: Closed-World Assumption
concepts.description: The assumption that any fact not known or derivable from the knowledge base is false, as used in databases and in logic programming with negation as failure.
concepts.example: A flight database lists flights from Paris to Rome and Paris to Oslo. Asked 'is there a flight from Paris to Lima?', it answers no, because the fact isn't listed, not because it's stated as false.

concepts.name: Cognitive Architecture
concepts.description: A field and the theories within it that specify the fixed structures of a mind, such as memories, perception and control, to build agents and models of human cognition like Soar and ACT-R.
concepts.example: Like a blueprint for a mind: Soar says there is working memory, long-term rules and a decision cycle. Fill it with knowledge about algebra and it solves equations in human-like steps.

concepts.name: Combinatorial Explosion
concepts.description: The rapid, often exponential or factorial, growth in the number of possibilities as a problem's size increases, which makes exhaustive search infeasible.
concepts.example: A salesman visiting 5 cities has 4! = 24 possible orders from a fixed start. With 15 cities it's 14! ≈ 87 billion, and with 30 cities checking every order would take longer than the age of the universe.

concepts.name: Commonsense Reasoning
concepts.description: The study of giving machines the everyday knowledge and inference humans take for granted, such as naive physics, time, space and people's intentions.
concepts.example: If you put a glass of water in a closed cupboard, it's still there tomorrow; if you tip it, the water spills. People know this instantly, but a machine must somehow be given or learn such everyday physics.

concepts.name: Completeness (Logic)
concepts.description: The property of a proof system that every sentence logically entailed by a set of premises can actually be derived from them using its inference rules.
concepts.example: If 'all cats are mammals' and 'Tom is a cat' together entail 'Tom is a mammal', a complete proof system is guaranteed to have a step-by-step derivation of it. No true consequence is out of reach.

concepts.name: Computational Theory of Mind
concepts.description: The view that the mind is a computational system and that thinking consists of manipulating mental representations according to rules, like a program running on the brain.
concepts.example: On this view, deciding to take an umbrella works like code: the belief 'it may rain' and the desire 'stay dry' are symbols, and a rule combines them to produce the action, much like a program running on the brain.

concepts.name: Computing Machinery and Intelligence
concepts.description: Alan Turing's 1950 paper that asked whether machines can think and proposed the imitation game, now called the Turing test, as a practical criterion.
concepts.example: Rather than define 'thinking', Turing asked whether a judge chatting by text could tell a machine from a human. He also answered objections, like 'machines can only do what we tell them', in the same paper.

concepts.name: Conceptual Dependency Theory
concepts.description: Roger Schank's theory for representing the meaning of sentences with a small set of primitive acts (like PTRANS and ATRANS) so that paraphrases share the same representation.
concepts.example: 'John gave Mary a book' and 'Mary received a book from John' both become ATRANS (transfer of possession) of a book from John to Mary. So a program sees they mean the same thing.

concepts.name: Configuration Space
concepts.description: The space of all possible configurations of a robot, one dimension per degree of freedom, in which obstacles become forbidden regions and motion planning becomes path finding for a point.
concepts.example: A robot arm with 2 joints has a 2D configuration space: each point (θ1, θ2) is one pose. A table that the arm would hit becomes a blob of forbidden points, and moving the arm means drawing a curve around it.

concepts.name: Conflict Resolution (Production Systems)
concepts.description: The strategy a production system uses to choose which of several triggered rules to fire, for example by priority, specificity, recency or refraction.
concepts.example: Facts: it's raining and you're late. Rule 1 says take an umbrella; rule 2 says run. With 'specificity' the rule with more matching conditions wins; with 'recency' the rule matching the newest fact wins.

concepts.name: Conformant Planning
concepts.description: Planning without any observations, where the agent must find a plan that reaches the goal from every possible initial state by reasoning over belief states.
concepts.example: A robot vacuum doesn't know if it starts in room A or B and has no sensors. Plan: Right, Suck, Left, Suck. It works whichever room it started in.

concepts.name: Conjunctive Normal Form
concepts.description: A standard form of a logical formula written as a conjunction (AND) of clauses, each clause a disjunction (OR) of literals; it is the input format for resolution and SAT solvers.
concepts.example: (A or B) and (not A or C) and (not B) is in CNF: an AND of three ORs. 'A → B' becomes the single clause (not A or B), ready for a SAT solver.

concepts.name: Consistent Heuristic
concepts.description: A heuristic whose estimate never decreases by more than the step cost along any edge, h(n) <= c(n,n') + h(n'); it implies admissibility and makes A* graph search optimal.
concepts.example: Straight-line distance is consistent: if city A is 100 km from the goal as the crow flies and a 30 km road leads to B, then B is at least 70 km away, since the road can't beat geometry.

concepts.name: Constraint Graph
concepts.description: A graph representing a constraint satisfaction problem, with a node per variable and an edge between variables that share a constraint, used to guide propagation and decomposition.
concepts.example: For colouring Australia's map, draw a node for each state and connect WA–NT, WA–SA, NT–SA, NT–Q and so on. Tasmania has no edges, so you can see at once it can be solved separately.

concepts.name: Constraint Programming
concepts.description: A declarative programming paradigm where problems are stated as variables, domains and constraints, and a solver combines propagation and search to find solutions.
concepts.example: To schedule 4 exams in 3 slots, declare a slot variable per exam and 'Math ≠ Physics' wherever students overlap. The solver prunes impossible slots and searches; you never write the search loop yourself.

concepts.name: Constraint Propagation
concepts.description: Using constraints to repeatedly remove values from variable domains that cannot be part of any solution, shrinking the search space before or during search.
concepts.example: In Sudoku, placing a 5 in a cell removes 5 from every cell in its row, column and box. If a cell is left with just one option, fill it in and propagate again; often the puzzle solves itself.

concepts.name: Constraint Satisfaction Problem
concepts.description: A problem defined by variables, a domain of possible values for each, and constraints on combinations of values; a solution assigns values to all variables satisfying every constraint.
concepts.example: Colour three countries A, B, C with red or blue so neighbours differ, where A borders B and B borders C. Variables: A, B, C; domains: {red, blue}; a solution: A=red, B=blue, C=red.

concepts.name: Contingency Planning
concepts.description: Planning for partially observable or nondeterministic environments by building plans with branches that choose actions based on what the agent observes during execution.
concepts.example: Going to work: take the bus; if the bus is late, take a taxi, otherwise keep riding. The plan includes an 'if' because you'll only find out at the stop which branch you're in.

concepts.name: Contract Net Protocol
concepts.description: A multi-agent task-allocation protocol in which a manager announces a task, contractor agents submit bids, and the manager awards the contract to the best bidder.
concepts.example: A delivery manager agent announces 'parcel to Elm Street by 5 pm'. Three truck agents bid 20, 15 and 25 minutes. The manager awards the job to the 15-minute truck, which confirms and does it.

concepts.name: Cooperative Game Theory
concepts.description: The branch of game theory studying groups of players who can form binding coalitions, focusing on which coalitions form and how to divide their joint payoff fairly.
concepts.example: Three friends can share a taxi: alone each pays $30, but together the ride costs $40. Which groups form, and how to split the $40 fairly, perhaps by the Shapley value, is a cooperative game.

concepts.name: Crossover (Genetic Algorithm)
concepts.description: A genetic-algorithm operator that creates offspring by combining parts of two parent chromosomes, for example by swapping segments at a randomly chosen cut point.
concepts.example: Parents 11100 and 00011 are cut after position 2. Swapping tails gives children 11011 and 00100, so each child inherits the first part of one parent and the rest of the other.

concepts.name: Cyc
concepts.description: A long-running project begun by Doug Lenat in 1984 to hand-encode millions of commonsense facts and rules in a large knowledge base using the CycL logic language.
concepts.example: Cyc contains assertions like 'people can't be in two places at once' and 'once dead, people stay dead'. Given 'Lincoln was assassinated in 1865', it can infer Lincoln didn't vote in 1868.

concepts.name: D*
concepts.description: A family of incremental path-planning algorithms (D*, Focused D*, D* Lite) that efficiently repair a shortest path when edge costs change, widely used for mobile robot navigation.
concepts.example: A rover plans a route to a crater, then its camera spots a boulder blocking the path. D* Lite updates only the affected costs and repairs the plan in milliseconds instead of replanning from scratch.

concepts.name: Dartmouth Workshop
concepts.description: The 1956 summer research project at Dartmouth College organised by McCarthy, Minsky, Shannon and Rochester, where the term 'artificial intelligence' was coined and AI was founded as a field.
concepts.example: In summer 1956 a small group spent weeks at Dartmouth on the bold proposal that 'every aspect of learning... can be so precisely described that a machine can be made to simulate it.' The name 'artificial intelligence' stuck.

concepts.name: Datalog
concepts.description: A declarative logic programming language, a function-free subset of Prolog, used for recursive database queries and program analysis, typically evaluated bottom-up.
concepts.example: Facts: parent(ann, bob), parent(bob, cat). Rules: ancestor(X,Y) :- parent(X,Y). ancestor(X,Z) :- parent(X,Y), ancestor(Y,Z). Querying ancestor(ann, Who) returns bob and cat.

concepts.name: Deductive Reasoning
concepts.description: Reasoning from general premises to conclusions that must be true if the premises are true, as in applying logical rules like modus ponens.
concepts.example: All squares have four sides; this shape is a square; so it has four sides. If both premises are true, the conclusion can't be false. That certainty is what makes deduction different from guessing.

concepts.name: Deep Blue
concepts.description: IBM's chess computer that defeated world champion Garry Kasparov in 1997, using massively parallel alpha-beta search with custom chess chips and a hand-tuned evaluation function.
concepts.example: Deep Blue evaluated around 200 million positions per second, looking many moves ahead. Each leaf was scored by an evaluation function with thousands of hand-tuned features, like king safety and pawn structure.

concepts.name: Defuzzification
concepts.description: The step in fuzzy inference that converts an aggregated fuzzy output set into a single crisp number, most often with the centroid (centre of gravity) method.
concepts.example: The fuzzy output says fan speed is 'slow' to degree 0.2 and 'fast' to degree 0.8. Taking the centre of gravity of the combined shape might give 72% speed, a single number the motor can use.

concepts.name: Degree Heuristic
concepts.description: A variable-ordering heuristic for constraint satisfaction that picks the unassigned variable involved in the most constraints with other unassigned variables, often used to break MRV ties.
concepts.example: Colouring Australia's map from scratch, every state has 3 colours left, so MRV ties. The degree heuristic picks SA because it borders 5 other states, so colouring it first constrains the most.

concepts.name: Dempster–Shafer Theory
concepts.description: A theory of evidence that assigns belief masses to sets of possibilities rather than single outcomes, producing belief and plausibility bounds and combining sources with Dempster's rule.
concepts.example: A witness says the culprit was Alice or Bob, with 0.6 confidence, without saying which. D-S puts 0.6 on the set {Alice, Bob} and 0.4 on 'anyone'. Belief that it's Alice is 0, but plausibility is 1.

concepts.name: Denavit–Hartenberg Parameters
concepts.description: A convention describing each link of a robot arm with four parameters (link length, twist, offset and joint angle) so that forward kinematics becomes a product of homogeneous transforms.
concepts.example: A two-joint arm with 1 m and 0.5 m links: each link gets a row like (a = 1, α = 0, d = 0, θ = θ1). Turn each row into a 4×4 matrix and multiply them to get where the gripper is.

concepts.name: DENDRAL
concepts.description: An expert system begun at Stanford in 1965 that inferred the molecular structure of organic compounds from mass-spectrometry data, often called the first expert system.
concepts.example: Given a mass spectrum with peaks at certain masses and the formula C6H12O, Dendral generated candidate molecular structures and used chemists' rules about how molecules break apart to rank which fit the peaks.

concepts.name: Depth-Limited Search
concepts.description: Depth-first search that stops expanding nodes beyond a fixed depth limit, avoiding infinite paths at the cost of missing goals deeper than the limit.
concepts.example: Searching a family tree with limit 3, you follow children down to great-grandchildren and never deeper. It won't get lost in endless branches, but a match 4 generations down is missed.

concepts.name: Description Logic
concepts.description: A family of decidable fragments of first-order logic for describing concepts, roles and individuals, providing the formal basis of ontology languages such as OWL.
concepts.example: Define Parent ≡ Person ⊓ ∃hasChild.Person. Given that Ann is a Person with child Bob, also a Person, a reasoner automatically classifies Ann as a Parent.

concepts.name: Differential Wheeled Robot
concepts.description: A mobile robot design with two independently driven wheels on a common axis; varying their speeds makes the robot move straight, curve or turn in place.
concepts.example: A robot vacuum has two wheels: both at 1 m/s, it goes straight; left at 0.5 and right at 1, it curves left; left at −1 and right at +1, it spins in place.

concepts.name: Distributed Artificial Intelligence
concepts.description: The subfield of AI that studies solving problems with multiple interacting agents or processes distributed across machines, the precursor to multi-agent systems.
concepts.example: To monitor air traffic, several computers each handle one sector and share forecasts about planes crossing borders. Together they solve a problem no single machine could manage alone.

concepts.name: Dominant Strategy
concepts.description: A strategy that gives a player at least as high a payoff as any other strategy no matter what the other players do; strictly dominant if always strictly better.
concepts.example: In the prisoner's dilemma, if the other prisoner stays silent you do better confessing (0 vs 1 year); if they confess, you still do better confessing (5 vs 10 years). Confessing is dominant.

concepts.name: Dreyfus' Critique of Artificial Intelligence
concepts.description: Hubert Dreyfus's argument, in 'What Computers Can't Do', that human expertise relies on intuition and embodied know-how that cannot be captured by symbolic rules.
concepts.example: A master chess player 'just sees' the right move without listing rules, and an expert driver feels when to brake. Dreyfus argued this intuitive skill can't be written down as if-then rules.

concepts.name: Effective Branching Factor
concepts.description: The branching factor b* that a uniform tree of the solution depth would need to contain the number of nodes a search actually generated; it measures how well a heuristic prunes.
concepts.example: If A* finds a depth-5 solution after generating 52 nodes, b* is about 1.92, since 1 + 1.92 + 1.92² + ... + 1.92⁵ ≈ 53, the 52 nodes plus the root. A better heuristic pushes b* toward 1; blind search might show 3 or more.

concepts.name: 8-Puzzle
concepts.description: A sliding puzzle of eight numbered tiles in a 3x3 frame with one blank, solved by sliding tiles into order; a standard test problem for search algorithms and heuristics.
concepts.example: Tiles 1-8 are scrambled in a 3×3 frame with one gap; you may only slide a tile into the gap. Reaching 1-2-3 / 4-5-6 / 7-8-blank can take up to 31 moves, and there are 181,440 reachable arrangements.

concepts.name: Elitism (Evolutionary Computation)
concepts.description: A selection strategy in evolutionary algorithms that copies the best individuals unchanged into the next generation so the best solution found is never lost.
concepts.example: Each generation of 100 solutions, the top 2 are copied straight into the next generation untouched. Even if crossover and mutation produce only worse children, the best score never goes down.

concepts.name: ELIZA
concepts.description: Joseph Weizenbaum's 1966 chatbot that used keyword pattern matching and scripted responses, most famously imitating a Rogerian psychotherapist, without any understanding.
concepts.example: You type 'I am sad about my mother.' ELIZA spots the keyword 'mother' and replies 'Tell me more about your family.' To 'I am X' it answers 'How long have you been X?', with no understanding at all.

concepts.name: ELIZA Effect
concepts.description: The human tendency to attribute understanding, intelligence or emotions to computer programs that merely produce plausible text, named after reactions to ELIZA.
concepts.example: Weizenbaum's secretary, knowing ELIZA was a simple script, still asked him to leave the room so she could talk to it privately. People today similarly feel a chatbot 'cares' about them.

concepts.name: Embodied Cognition
concepts.description: The view that cognition is shaped by having a body interacting with the physical world, rather than being abstract symbol processing, influencing robotics and AI.
concepts.example: You understand 'grasp an idea' partly through grasping cups with your hands. Embodied cognition says such bodily experience shapes thought, which is why some researchers build robots that learn by touching and moving.

concepts.name: Properties of Task Environments
concepts.description: The dimensions used to classify an agent's task environment: fully or partially observable, deterministic or stochastic, episodic or sequential, static or dynamic, discrete or continuous, single- or multi-agent.
concepts.example: Chess: fully observable, deterministic, sequential, discrete, multi-agent. Poker: partially observable (hidden cards) and stochastic. A self-driving car: partially observable, stochastic, dynamic and continuous.

concepts.name: Estimation of Distribution Algorithm
concepts.description: An evolutionary optimisation method that replaces crossover and mutation by fitting a probability model to the best solutions and sampling new candidates from it.
concepts.example: Sample 100 bit strings, keep the best 20. If 18 of them have bit 1 set, set P(bit 1 = 1) = 0.9, and do this for each bit. Sample 100 new strings from these probabilities and repeat.

concepts.name: Evaluation Function
concepts.description: A function that estimates the value or expected outcome of a game position without searching to the end, used at the depth cutoff of minimax or alpha-beta search.
concepts.example: In chess, a simple evaluation counts material: pawn 1, knight 3, bishop 3, rook 5, queen 9. If you're up a rook for a knight, the position scores +2, without playing it out to the end.

concepts.name: Event Calculus
concepts.description: A logical formalism for reasoning about events and their effects over time, using predicates such as Happens, Initiates, Terminates and HoldsAt on time-varying fluents.
concepts.example: Happens(TurnOn, 9:00) and Initiates(TurnOn, LightOn) mean the light is on after 9:00. Unless an event that Terminates LightOn happens, HoldsAt(LightOn, 10:00) follows.

concepts.name: Evolution Strategy
concepts.description: An evolutionary algorithm for real-valued optimisation that mutates solutions with Gaussian noise and often self-adapts the mutation step sizes, e.g. the (1+1)-ES and (mu, lambda)-ES.
concepts.example: In a (1+1)-ES, take x = 3.0, add Gaussian noise to get 3.4, and keep whichever scores better. If successes are frequent, widen the noise; if rare, narrow it, like the 1/5 success rule.

concepts.name: Evolutionary Computation
concepts.description: The field of optimisation and search methods inspired by biological evolution, evolving populations of candidate solutions through selection, recombination and mutation.
concepts.example: To design an antenna, generate 100 random shapes, test each, and let the best 'breed': mix their features and add small random changes. After many generations, NASA got an odd-looking but effective antenna this way.

concepts.name: Evolutionary Programming
concepts.description: An evolutionary algorithm introduced by Lawrence Fogel that evolves solutions, originally finite-state machines, using mutation and selection only, without crossover.
concepts.example: To evolve a machine that predicts the next symbol in a sequence, start with random finite-state machines, mutate each by adding a state or changing a transition, and keep the best predictors; no two parents are ever combined.

concepts.name: Expectimax
concepts.description: A game-tree search for games with chance, in which chance nodes take the probability-weighted average of their children's values while max (and min) nodes behave as in minimax.
concepts.example: In backgammon a move leads to a dice roll: if 50% of rolls give +10 and 50% give −4, the chance node is worth 0.5·10 + 0.5·(−4) = 3. Max nodes then pick the move with the highest expected value.

concepts.name: Expert System
concepts.description: A program that solves problems in a narrow domain at expert level by applying an inference engine to a knowledge base of facts and if-then rules elicited from human experts.
concepts.example: A plant-disease system holds rules like 'IF leaves yellow AND soil wet THEN suspect root rot'. A farmer enters symptoms, and the system chains rules to suggest a diagnosis and explain why.

concepts.name: Expert System Shell
concepts.description: A software framework containing an inference engine and user interface but no domain knowledge, so developers can build an expert system by supplying their own rules.
concepts.example: Like an empty spreadsheet program before you type data in: the shell already knows how to chain rules and ask users questions. A bank adds loan rules and has a loan-advice expert system.

concepts.name: Extensive-Form Game
concepts.description: A representation of a game as a tree of sequential moves, showing who moves when, what they know (information sets), chance events and the payoffs at each leaf.
concepts.example: Entry game: a newcomer chooses Enter or Stay Out; if it enters, the incumbent chooses Fight (−1, −1) or Share (2, 1). Drawing this as a tree shows the order of moves and payoffs at each end.

concepts.name: FF Planner
concepts.description: The FF planner, a forward state-space planner whose heuristic is the length of a plan for a relaxed problem ignoring delete effects, combined with enforced hill climbing.
concepts.example: To guide search, FF pretends actions never delete facts. If the relaxed plan from a state needs 6 actions, h = 6. FF then hill-climbs to any successor with a lower h, falling back to breadth-first search on plateaus.

concepts.name: Feedback Control
concepts.description: Control that measures a system's output, compares it with a desired setpoint and adjusts the input to reduce the error, as in thermostats and robot motor controllers.
concepts.example: A thermostat set to 21°C reads 19°C, an error of 2 degrees, and switches the heater on. At 21°C the error is zero and the heater turns off, so the room is constantly corrected toward the target.

concepts.name: Fifth Generation Computer Systems
concepts.description: A Japanese government project (1982-1992) to build massively parallel computers running logic programming for AI; it fell short of its goals and contributed to the second AI winter.
concepts.example: Japan aimed to build parallel computers running Prolog-like logic programs for conversation and reasoning. The US and UK launched rival programmes in response, but the machines never met expectations.

concepts.name: Fitness Function
concepts.description: The function that scores how good a candidate solution is in an evolutionary algorithm, guiding which individuals are selected to reproduce.
concepts.example: For a backpack-packing GA, fitness might be total value of chosen items, or 0 if they exceed the weight limit. A pick worth $90 under the limit beats one worth $70.

concepts.name: Fitness Proportionate Selection
concepts.description: A selection method in genetic algorithms where each individual's chance of being chosen as a parent is proportional to its fitness, like spinning a weighted roulette wheel.
concepts.example: Three individuals with fitness 6, 3 and 1 get 60%, 30% and 10% slices of a roulette wheel. Spin it to choose a parent, so the strongest are favoured but the weak still get a chance.

concepts.name: Forward Chaining
concepts.description: A data-driven inference method that repeatedly applies rules whose premises are satisfied by known facts, adding their conclusions until no new facts or the goal appears.
concepts.example: Facts: it's raining. Rules: raining → ground wet; ground wet → slippery. Fire the first rule to add 'ground wet', which triggers the second to add 'slippery'. Stop when no rule adds anything new.

concepts.name: Forward Checking
concepts.description: A constraint-satisfaction technique that, after each assignment, removes inconsistent values from the domains of neighbouring unassigned variables and backtracks if any domain becomes empty.
concepts.example: Colouring a map, assign WA = red. Forward checking removes red from neighbours NT and SA right away. If NT's domain ever becomes empty, you backtrack now instead of discovering it later.

concepts.name: Forward Kinematics
concepts.description: Computing the position and orientation of a robot's end effector from its joint angles or displacements by chaining the transforms of each link.
concepts.example: A 2-link arm with lengths 1 m and 1 m, both joints at 0°, reaches (2, 0). Bend the first joint to 90° and keep the second at 0°: the gripper is at (0, 2). Joint angles in, position out.

concepts.name: Forward State-Space Planning
concepts.description: Planning by progression: starting from the initial state, applying applicable actions to generate successor states and searching until a state satisfying the goal is reached.
concepts.example: To make tea, start from 'kettle empty, cup empty'. Applicable actions: fill kettle. Then boil, then pour into cup with a teabag. Each step generates a new state until 'tea made' holds.

concepts.name: Frame (Artificial Intelligence)
concepts.description: A knowledge representation structure proposed by Marvin Minsky that describes a stereotyped object or situation with named slots, default values and attached procedures.
concepts.example: A Restaurant frame has slots: type (default: café), menu, waiter, bill. Visit 'Luigi's', fill in type = pizzeria, and slots you leave blank keep defaults, like 'you pay at the end'.

concepts.name: Frame Problem
concepts.description: The problem in logic-based AI of representing which things do not change when an action occurs without writing an enormous number of explicit frame axioms.
concepts.example: When a robot paints a box red, logic must also state the box's position, the wall colour and the time of day didn't change. With many actions and facts, writing every 'nothing else changed' axiom explodes.

concepts.name: Frontier (Search)
concepts.description: The set of generated but not yet expanded nodes in a search algorithm; the order in which nodes are taken from it (queue, stack, priority queue) defines the search strategy.
concepts.example: Searching a maze, the frontier is the list of open spots you've seen but not entered yet. Take the oldest spot (a queue) and you get breadth-first search; take the newest (a stack) and you get depth-first.

concepts.name: Functionalism (Philosophy of Mind)
concepts.description: The philosophy-of-mind position that mental states are defined by their functional roles, their causal relations to inputs, outputs and other states, rather than by what they are made of.
concepts.example: Pain is whatever state is caused by tissue damage and causes wincing and avoidance. If a silicon robot had a state playing that exact role, functionalism says it would also be in pain.

concepts.name: Fuzzification
concepts.description: The first step of fuzzy inference that converts crisp input values into degrees of membership in the fuzzy sets of linguistic variables, such as 0.7 'warm' and 0.3 'hot'.
concepts.example: With a temperature of 24°C, the 'warm' curve might give 0.7 and 'hot' give 0.3. The crisp number 24 becomes these membership degrees, which fuzzy rules then use.

concepts.name: Fuzzy Control System
concepts.description: A controller that maps measured inputs to control actions using fuzzification, a base of fuzzy if-then rules, fuzzy inference and defuzzification, used in appliances and industrial control.
concepts.example: A washing machine reads dirtiness and load size, fuzzifies them, applies rules like 'IF very dirty AND large load THEN long wash', and defuzzifies to a precise wash time of, say, 47 minutes.

concepts.name: Fuzzy Logic
concepts.description: A many-valued logic in which truth is a degree between 0 and 1, with operators such as min and max for AND and OR, used to reason with vague concepts like 'tall' or 'warm'.
concepts.example: Is 25°C 'warm'? Fuzzy logic says warm to degree 0.8. If it's also 'humid' to degree 0.4, then 'warm AND humid' has degree min(0.8, 0.4) = 0.4.

concepts.name: Fuzzy Rule
concepts.description: An if-then rule whose antecedent and consequent use fuzzy sets of linguistic variables, such as 'IF temperature is high THEN fan speed is fast', fired to a partial degree.
concepts.example: Rule: IF temperature is high THEN fan speed is fast. If the temperature is 'high' to degree 0.6, the rule fires at strength 0.6, so 'fast' contributes partially rather than all-or-nothing.

concepts.name: Fuzzy Set
concepts.description: A set in which each element belongs with a degree of membership between 0 and 1 rather than strictly in or out, introduced by Lotfi Zadeh to model vague categories.
concepts.example: In the fuzzy set 'tall', someone 6'2" might have membership 0.9, 5'10" might have 0.5, and 5'2" might have 0.05. Nobody is simply in or out; height fades smoothly into tallness.

concepts.name: Game Theory
concepts.description: The mathematical study of strategic interaction among rational decision-makers whose payoffs depend on each other's choices, with applications in economics, multi-agent AI and auctions.
concepts.example: Two cafés choose prices. If both charge $3 they split customers; if one cuts to $2 it steals most. Game theory predicts what each will do when each knows the other is reasoning the same way.

concepts.name: General Problem Solver
concepts.description: A program by Newell, Shaw and Simon (1957) intended as a universal problem solver, which used means-ends analysis to reduce differences between the current state and the goal.
concepts.example: For Towers of Hanoi, GPS notes the difference 'large disk not on target peg', picks the move that reduces it, and finds that move needs smaller disks out of the way, which becomes a subgoal.

concepts.name: Genetic Programming
concepts.description: An evolutionary method that evolves computer programs, usually represented as expression trees, using crossover and mutation of subtrees to solve a task.
concepts.example: To find a formula fitting the data (1,2), (2,5), (3,10), GP evolves expression trees like (x * x) + 1. Crossover swaps subtrees between two formulas; the one closest to the data survives.

concepts.name: Global Workspace Theory
concepts.description: Bernard Baars's theory that consciousness arises when information wins competition among specialised processes and is broadcast through a global workspace; LIDA implements it computationally.
concepts.example: Like a theatre: many backstage processes work unseen, but whatever reaches the spotlight, say the smell of smoke, is broadcast to the whole audience so memory, planning and speech can all react.

concepts.name: Goal-Based Agent
concepts.description: An agent that keeps a model of the world and chooses actions by considering which future states will achieve its explicit goals, often using search or planning.
concepts.example: A taxi at a junction can't just react; it needs to know the passenger's destination. Given the goal 'airport', it imagines where each turn leads and picks the one on the way there.

concepts.name: Gödel's Completeness Theorem
concepts.description: Gödel's 1929 theorem that in first-order logic every logically valid formula (true in all models) is provable, so semantic entailment and syntactic derivability coincide.
concepts.example: If 'every cat is a mammal, every mammal breathes, so every cat breathes' holds in every possible interpretation, Gödel guarantees a finite formal proof of it exists in standard first-order proof systems.

concepts.name: Graphplan
concepts.description: A planning algorithm that builds a layered planning graph of reachable literals and actions with mutual-exclusion links, then searches backward through it to extract a plan.
concepts.example: Level 0 lists the starting facts; level 1 adds every applicable action and their results, marking pairs that can't happen together. When all goals appear non-mutex at some level, Graphplan searches backward to extract a plan.

concepts.name: Greedy Best-First Search
concepts.description: An informed search that always expands the node that appears closest to the goal according to the heuristic h(n) alone; fast but neither complete in general nor optimal.
concepts.example: Heading to a city, greedy search always takes the road to the town with the smallest straight-line distance to the goal. It's often quick but can take a road that looks close yet leads to a long detour.

concepts.name: Hard Problem of Consciousness
concepts.description: David Chalmers's question of why and how physical processes give rise to subjective experience, as opposed to the 'easy problems' of explaining cognitive functions.
concepts.example: We can explain how your eyes and brain detect 700 nm light and make you say 'red'. The hard problem asks why there is also something it feels like to see red, rather than processing happening in the dark.

concepts.name: Herbrand's Theorem
concepts.description: A result stating that a first-order formula in Skolem form is unsatisfiable if and only if some finite set of its ground instances is propositionally unsatisfiable, the basis of resolution provers.
concepts.example: To show '∀x P(x)' and '¬P(a)' are jointly unsatisfiable, Herbrand says just look at ground instances: P(a) and ¬P(a) already clash. So first-order refutation reduces to finding finitely many contradicting ground cases.

concepts.name: Heuristic Function
concepts.description: A function h(n) that estimates the cost of the cheapest path from a state to a goal, used to guide search toward promising states.
concepts.example: Planning a road trip from Lyon to Paris, you guess the remaining distance by the straight-line 390 km on a map. It isn't the exact road distance, but it tells you which towns are heading the right way.

concepts.name: Dominance (Heuristics)
concepts.description: A heuristic h2 dominates h1 if h2(n) >= h1(n) for every node while both remain admissible; A* with the dominating heuristic never expands more nodes.
concepts.example: For the 8-puzzle, 'misplaced tiles' might give 6 while Manhattan distance gives 14 for the same board; Manhattan is never lower. On harder puzzles A* with Manhattan expands dramatically fewer nodes.

concepts.name: Hierarchical Task Network
concepts.description: A planning approach in which high-level tasks are recursively decomposed into subtasks using methods until only primitive actions remain, as used in SHOP and game AI.
concepts.example: Task 'Travel to Rome' splits into 'get to airport', 'fly', 'get to hotel'. 'Get to airport' splits further into 'call taxi', 'ride'. Decomposition stops at primitive actions a robot or NPC can execute.

concepts.name: Higher-Order Logic
concepts.description: Logic that allows quantification over predicates and functions, not just individuals, giving more expressive power than first-order logic at the cost of losing completeness.
concepts.example: First-order logic can say 'every number has a successor', but not 'every property that holds for 0 and passes from n to n+1 holds for all numbers'. Second-order logic quantifies over properties to state this.

concepts.name: History of Artificial Intelligence
concepts.description: The development of AI from early ideas and the 1956 Dartmouth workshop through symbolic AI, expert systems, AI winters, machine learning and the deep learning era.
concepts.example: 1956: the Dartmouth workshop names the field. 1970s and 80s: expert systems and two AI winters. 1997: Deep Blue beats Kasparov. 2012: deep learning wins ImageNet. Late 2010s on: large language models.

concepts.name: Horizon Effect
concepts.description: A failure of fixed-depth game search where an unavoidable bad outcome just beyond the search depth is pushed out of view by delaying moves, so the program misjudges the position.
concepts.example: A chess program searching 6 moves sees its queen will be lost on move 7. It throws in pointless checks that sacrifice pawns, pushing the loss past its horizon, and ends up losing both pawns and queen.

concepts.name: Horn Clause
concepts.description: A clause with at most one positive literal, equivalent to an implication from a conjunction of facts to a single conclusion; it allows efficient inference and underlies Prolog.
concepts.example: 'If it rains and you're outside, you get wet' is (¬rain ∨ ¬outside ∨ wet): one positive literal. 'rain' alone is a fact, also Horn. But 'rain ∨ snow' has two positives, so it isn't Horn.

concepts.name: Inductive Logic Programming
concepts.description: A machine learning approach that learns logic programs (rules) from positive and negative examples together with background knowledge expressed in logic.
concepts.example: Given facts parent(ann,bob), parent(bob,cat) and examples 'grandparent(ann,cat) is true, grandparent(bob,ann) is false', ILP learns the rule grandparent(X,Z) :- parent(X,Y), parent(Y,Z).

concepts.name: Inductive Reasoning
concepts.description: Reasoning from specific observations to general conclusions that are probable but not guaranteed, the basis of scientific generalisation and machine learning.
concepts.example: Every swan you've seen in 20 years has been white, so you conclude all swans are white. It's a reasonable bet, but one black swan in Australia proves the generalisation wrong.

concepts.name: Inference Engine
concepts.description: The component of a knowledge-based or expert system that applies rules of inference, such as forward or backward chaining, to the knowledge base to derive new facts or answers.
concepts.example: Knowledge base: 'Socrates is human' and 'humans are mortal'. Ask 'is Socrates mortal?' and the inference engine matches the rule, applies it, and answers yes. Swap in medical rules and it can diagnose instead.

concepts.name: Informed Search
concepts.description: Search strategies that use a heuristic estimate of distance to the goal to decide which node to expand next, such as greedy best-first search and A*.
concepts.example: Uninformed search in a maze tries every corridor equally. Informed search knows roughly where the exit is, so it tries corridors heading that way first and usually finds the exit far sooner.

concepts.name: Inheritance (Knowledge Representation)
concepts.description: The mechanism in semantic networks and frames by which a class or instance automatically acquires properties of its more general ancestors unless overridden by exceptions.
concepts.example: Store once that birds have feathers and can fly. Robin is a bird, so Robin inherits both. Penguin is a bird too but overrides 'can fly' with 'cannot fly', while still inheriting feathers.

concepts.name: Instrumental Convergence
concepts.description: The thesis that agents with many different final goals would pursue similar intermediate goals, such as self-preservation and acquiring resources, because these help almost any goal.
concepts.example: Whether an AI's goal is curing cancer or making paperclips, it does better if it keeps running, gets more computing power and isn't shut down. So very different goals lead to similar sub-goals.

concepts.name: Intentional Stance
concepts.description: Daniel Dennett's strategy of predicting a system's behaviour by treating it as a rational agent with beliefs and desires, regardless of its internal mechanism.
concepts.example: To predict a chess program, you don't trace its code; you think 'it wants to win and believes my queen is exposed, so it'll attack her.' That prediction works, which is Dennett's point.

concepts.name: Inverse Kinematics
concepts.description: Computing the joint angles a robot needs so its end effector reaches a desired position and orientation, solved analytically or numerically, often with the manipulator Jacobian.
concepts.example: A 2-link arm with 1 m links must touch the point (1, 1). IK finds joint angles that work, such as 0° then 90° (elbow down) or 90° then −90° (elbow up). Often there are several solutions, or none.

concepts.name: Iterative Deepening A*
concepts.description: A memory-efficient variant of A* that performs depth-first searches bounded by an f-cost threshold, raising the threshold to the smallest exceeded value after each iteration.
concepts.example: Start with threshold f = 10 and search depth-first, pruning any node with f > 10. If you fail, and the smallest pruned value was 12, retry with threshold 12. Memory stays tiny, like depth-first search.

concepts.name: Jacobian (Robotics)
concepts.description: The matrix relating a robot manipulator's joint velocities to the linear and angular velocity of its end effector, used for velocity control, singularity analysis and inverse kinematics.
concepts.example: For a 2-joint arm, the Jacobian is a 2×2 matrix. Multiply it by joint speeds, say (0.1, 0) rad/s, to get the gripper's velocity. If the arm is fully stretched, the matrix becomes singular and some directions are impossible.

concepts.name: Jump Point Search
concepts.description: An optimisation of A* on uniform-cost grids that skips over symmetric intermediate nodes by jumping straight to 'jump points', greatly reducing the number of expanded nodes.
concepts.example: On an open grid, A* expands every cell along a straight corridor. Jump point search slides straight along until it hits a wall or a forced turn, adding just that cell, so it may expand 10 nodes instead of 1,000.

concepts.name: Knowledge Acquisition Bottleneck
concepts.description: The difficulty and cost of extracting and encoding human experts' knowledge into rules for expert systems, a major reason for their limited scalability.
concepts.example: A doctor diagnoses easily but struggles to state the 500 rules she uses, and each one takes interviews and testing. Building a medical expert system can take years, and it still misses rare cases.

concepts.name: Knowledge Base
concepts.description: A collection of facts and rules represented in a formal language that an AI system can store, query and reason over to answer questions or choose actions.
concepts.example: A small knowledge base: 'Tweety is a bird.' 'All birds have wings.' 'If it has wings, it can try to fly.' A program can ask 'does Tweety have wings?' and derive yes.

concepts.name: Knowledge-Based Agent
concepts.description: An agent that maintains a knowledge base, tells it new percepts, asks it what to do and acts on the logically derived answer.
concepts.example: A Wumpus-world agent tells its KB 'I smell a stench at [1,2]'. It asks 'is [2,2] safe?', and the KB, combining rules and past percepts, answers no. The agent then turns another way.

concepts.name: Knowledge Engineering
concepts.description: The discipline of building knowledge-based systems: eliciting knowledge from experts, choosing representations and encoding, testing and maintaining the knowledge base.
concepts.example: To build a tax-advice system, an engineer interviews accountants, writes rules like 'IF income > threshold THEN higher rate', tests them on real returns, and updates them when tax law changes.

concepts.name: Knowledge Representation and Reasoning
concepts.description: The field of AI concerned with representing information about the world in forms such as logic, semantic networks and ontologies so computers can reason with it.
concepts.example: Write 'every dog is a mammal' and 'Rex is a dog' in a formal language, and a program can infer that Rex is a mammal. The choice of language decides what can be expressed and how fast it can reason.

concepts.name: Learning Agent
concepts.description: An agent architecture with a performance element that acts, a critic that gives feedback, a learning element that improves the performance element, and a problem generator for exploration.
concepts.example: A chess bot plays (performance element), loses, and the critic notes 'traded queen too early'. The learning element adjusts its move preferences, and the problem generator suggests trying a new opening to learn more.

concepts.name: Least Constraining Value Heuristic
concepts.description: A value-ordering heuristic for constraint satisfaction that tries first the value that rules out the fewest choices for neighbouring variables, keeping flexibility for later assignments.
concepts.example: Colouring a map, Q could be red or blue. Choosing red would remove the last option from neighbour SA, but blue leaves SA one colour. So try blue first, keeping the most doors open.

concepts.name: Lifting (Inference)
concepts.description: Performing inference directly on first-order sentences with variables, as in generalized modus ponens using unification, instead of grounding them to propositional instances.
concepts.example: Rule: King(x) ∧ Greedy(x) ⇒ Evil(x). Facts: King(John), Greedy(John). Lifted inference unifies x with John in one step, rather than first writing out the rule for every person in the domain.

concepts.name: Lighthill Report
concepts.description: A 1973 report by James Lighthill for the UK Science Research Council that criticised AI's failure to handle combinatorial explosion, leading to major funding cuts in Britain.
concepts.example: Lighthill argued that AI methods solving toy problems like simple puzzles would collapse on real tasks, as possibilities multiply. After the 1973 report, UK funding for most AI research was cut.

concepts.name: Linguistic Variable
concepts.description: A variable whose values are words described by fuzzy sets, such as 'temperature' taking values 'cold', 'warm' and 'hot', used in fuzzy rules.
concepts.example: The variable 'speed' takes values 'slow', 'medium' and 'fast' instead of numbers. 'Slow' might cover roughly 0-40 km/h and 'fast' fades in from 60 km/h, each with its own fuzzy set.

concepts.name: Lisp
concepts.description: A family of programming languages created by John McCarthy in 1958 in which code and data are both lists (S-expressions); long the dominant language of AI research.
concepts.example: In Lisp, (+ 1 2) adds numbers, and that code is itself a list of three items. A program can build a new list like (* x 5), then run it as code, which made Lisp great for AI that writes or rewrites programs.

concepts.name: Local Beam Search
concepts.description: A local search that keeps k states instead of one, generates all their successors and keeps the k best; the stochastic version picks successors with probability based on value.
concepts.example: With k = 3, keep 3 candidate solutions. Generate all their neighbours, say 30, and keep the best 3 of those 30. Good regions attract more of the beam, unlike 3 independent hill climbers.

concepts.name: Robot Localization
concepts.description: The problem of estimating a robot's position and orientation within a known map from noisy motion and sensor data, solved with Kalman or particle filters.
concepts.example: A robot thinks it's in a corridor after rolling 5 m. Its laser sees a door 1 m to the left; the map shows such a door only at 4.8 m, so it corrects its position estimate to about 4.8 m.

concepts.name: Logic Programming
concepts.description: A programming paradigm in which programs are sets of logical rules and facts and computation is goal-directed proof search, as in Prolog and Datalog.
concepts.example: Write facts parent(tom, bob) and a rule grandparent(X,Z) :- parent(X,Y), parent(Y,Z). Ask ?- grandparent(tom, Who). The system searches for a proof and answers with whatever Who makes it true.

concepts.name: Logic Theorist
concepts.description: A 1956 program by Newell, Shaw and Simon, often called the first AI program, that proved theorems from Principia Mathematica using heuristic search.
concepts.example: Logic Theorist proved 38 of the first 52 theorems in Principia Mathematica, and one of its proofs was shorter than the book's. It searched for proofs using rules of thumb, not by trying everything.

concepts.name: Logical Consequence
concepts.description: The relation in which a sentence follows from a set of premises because it is true in every model where all the premises are true, written KB ⊨ α.
concepts.example: From 'it's raining' and 'if it rains, the street is wet', 'the street is wet' follows: in every world where both premises hold, the street is wet. No possible situation makes the premises true and it false.

concepts.name: Lucas–Penrose Argument
concepts.description: The argument by J.R. Lucas and Roger Penrose that Gödel's incompleteness theorems show human mathematical insight cannot be captured by any algorithm, so minds are not machines.
concepts.example: Gödel showed a consistent formal system can't prove its own Gödel sentence, yet a mathematician can see it's true. Lucas and Penrose argued that minds can't be such systems; critics reply we can't know our own consistency.

concepts.name: Mamdani Fuzzy Inference
concepts.description: The most common fuzzy inference method, which clips rule output fuzzy sets by their firing strength (min), aggregates them (max) and defuzzifies the result into a crisp value.
concepts.example: Temp is 'warm' at 0.7 and 'hot' at 0.3. Rule 'warm → fan medium' clips the 'medium' shape at 0.7; 'hot → fan fast' clips 'fast' at 0.3. Combine the shapes and take the centroid, maybe 58% fan speed.

concepts.name: Manhattan Distance Heuristic
concepts.description: A heuristic for grid and sliding-tile problems that sums horizontal and vertical distances of each tile or agent from its goal position; it is admissible for 4-directional moves.
concepts.example: In the 8-puzzle, if tile 5 is 2 rows and 1 column from its goal spot it needs at least 3 moves. Summing such distances over all tiles gives a lower bound on moves needed.

concepts.name: Means-Ends Analysis
concepts.description: A problem-solving technique that identifies the difference between the current state and the goal and applies an operator that reduces it, setting up subgoals for its preconditions.
concepts.example: You're at home and want to be in London. Difference: distance, so use 'fly'. Flying needs being at the airport, a new difference reduced with 'drive'. Driving needs the car keys, and so on.

concepts.name: Mechanism Design
concepts.description: The 'reverse game theory' study of designing rules of a game, such as auctions or voting schemes, so that self-interested agents' equilibrium behaviour achieves a desired outcome.
concepts.example: To sell a painting, design a sealed-bid auction where the winner pays the second-highest bid. Telling the truth becomes each bidder's best move, so the item goes to whoever values it most.

concepts.name: Membership Function
concepts.description: A function that assigns each element a degree of membership in a fuzzy set, a number between 0 and 1, often triangular, trapezoidal or Gaussian in shape.
concepts.example: For 'warm', a triangular membership function could be 0 at 15°C, rise to 1 at 22°C, and drop back to 0 at 29°C. At 18.5°C the membership is 0.5.

concepts.name: Memetic Algorithm
concepts.description: A hybrid evolutionary algorithm that combines population-based genetic search with local search applied to individuals to refine them, inspired by cultural evolution of memes.
concepts.example: Solving a delivery-route problem, a GA breeds new routes, and then each child route is polished with a quick local tweak, like swapping two stops if that shortens it, before joining the population.

concepts.name: Min-Conflicts Algorithm
concepts.description: A local search algorithm for constraint satisfaction that starts with a complete assignment and repeatedly reassigns a conflicted variable to the value that violates the fewest constraints.
concepts.example: For 8 queens, place one queen per column at random. Pick a queen under attack and move it to the row in its column with the fewest attackers. Repeat; even a million queens are usually solved in about 50 steps.

concepts.name: Minimum Remaining Values Heuristic
concepts.description: A variable-ordering heuristic for backtracking search that chooses the variable with the fewest legal values left, so failures are detected early ('fail first').
concepts.example: Colouring a map, after assigning WA = red and NT = green, SA has only blue left while others have more. MRV picks SA next; if it fails, you find out right away.

concepts.name: Mixed Strategy
concepts.description: A strategy in which a player randomises over pure strategies according to a probability distribution; every finite game has a Nash equilibrium in mixed strategies.
concepts.example: In rock-paper-scissors, any fixed choice can be exploited. Playing each with probability 1/3 can't be: the opponent wins, loses or ties a third of the time whatever they do. That's the Nash equilibrium.

concepts.name: Modal Logic
concepts.description: Logic extended with operators for necessity and possibility, interpreted over possible worlds linked by an accessibility relation, used to reason about knowledge, belief, time and obligation.
concepts.example: 'It must be raining' (□rain) holds if rain is true in every world you consider possible. 'It might rain' (◇rain) needs just one. Read □ as 'I know' and you get a logic of knowledge.

concepts.name: Model-Based Reflex Agent
concepts.description: An agent that keeps an internal state, updated with a model of how the world evolves and how its actions affect it, and chooses actions with condition-action rules on that state.
concepts.example: A self-driving car can't see the car in its blind spot now, but remembers seeing it 2 seconds ago. Keeping that internal state, it doesn't change lanes; a simple reflex agent would forget.

concepts.name: Model Checking
concepts.description: Automatically verifying whether a model of a system satisfies a logical specification by exhaustively exploring its states; in AI it also means checking entailment by enumerating all models.
concepts.example: A traffic light controller has 12 states. A model checker explores all of them to verify 'never are both directions green at once'. If it's violated, it shows the exact sequence of steps leading there.

concepts.name: Model (Logic)
concepts.description: An interpretation that assigns truth values to symbols, or a domain and meanings to symbols in first-order logic, so that each sentence is either true or false in it.
concepts.example: For 'P ∧ ¬Q', the model P = true, Q = false makes it true, while P = true, Q = true makes it false. In first-order logic a model also fixes a domain, such as people, and what 'Likes' means.

concepts.name: Modus Ponens
concepts.description: The inference rule that from P and 'if P then Q' one may conclude Q; it is the basis of forward and backward chaining.
concepts.example: If the alarm rings, it's 7 am. The alarm is ringing. Therefore it's 7 am. Whatever P and Q are, having P and 'if P then Q' lets you write down Q.

concepts.name: Moravec's Paradox
concepts.description: The observation that high-level reasoning is relatively easy for computers while low-level sensorimotor skills that humans find effortless, like walking or perception, are very hard.
concepts.example: A program beat the world chess champion in 1997, but a robot that can reliably clear a messy dinner table is still hard. What a 1-year-old does without thinking is what machines find hardest.

concepts.name: Motion Planning
concepts.description: The problem of finding a collision-free path or trajectory that moves a robot from a start to a goal configuration, solved with methods like grid search, roadmaps and sampling.
concepts.example: A robot arm must move a cup from the shelf to the table without hitting a lamp. A planner like RRT grows a tree of random collision-free poses until it connects start to goal, then smooths the path.

concepts.name: Move Ordering
concepts.description: Techniques for examining the most promising moves first in game-tree search, such as the killer heuristic or history tables, so alpha-beta pruning cuts off more branches.
concepts.example: Alpha-beta prunes best when strong moves come first. Trying captures and moves that caused cutoffs before (killer moves) early can cut nodes searched at the same depth from ~b^d toward ~b^(d/2).

concepts.name: Multi-Agent System
concepts.description: The field studying systems of multiple autonomous agents that interact through cooperation, competition, negotiation and communication to achieve individual or shared goals.
