concepts.example: Self-driving cars at a junction, trading bots in a market, robots in a warehouse: each agent has its own goals and sensors, and they must coordinate, negotiate or compete to get things done.

concepts.name: Mutation (Genetic Algorithm)
concepts.description: A genetic-algorithm operator that randomly alters parts of a chromosome, such as flipping bits with small probability, to maintain diversity and explore new solutions.
concepts.example: The chromosome 10110 with a 1% chance per bit of flipping might become 10010. Small random changes like this keep the population from becoming identical and stuck.

concepts.name: MYCIN
concepts.description: A Stanford expert system from the 1970s that diagnosed bacterial infections and recommended antibiotics using about 600 backward-chaining rules with certainty factors.
concepts.example: A doctor answered MYCIN's questions, like 'Is the organism gram-negative?' MYCIN chained backward from 'which bacterium?', combined certainty factors, and suggested a drug and dose. Tests found it compared well with specialists.

concepts.name: Negamax
concepts.description: A compact formulation of minimax for two-player zero-sum games that uses the identity max(a,b) = -min(-a,-b), so each node simply maximises the negation of its children's values.
concepts.example: Instead of separate max and min code, each player maximises from their own view. If a child scores +5 for the opponent, it's −5 for you, so node value = max over children of (−child value).

concepts.name: Negation as Failure
concepts.description: An inference rule in logic programming that concludes 'not P' when every attempt to prove P fails, a non-monotonic form of negation based on the closed-world assumption.
concepts.example: Database: flies(X) :- bird(X), not penguin(X). bird(tweety). Prolog tries to prove penguin(tweety), fails, so assumes 'not penguin' and concludes tweety flies.

concepts.name: Neuroevolution
concepts.description: Training neural networks with evolutionary algorithms that evolve their weights, architectures or both, as in NEAT, instead of or alongside gradient descent.
concepts.example: To teach a simulated car to drive, create 50 small neural networks with random weights. Keep the ones that drive farthest, mutate their weights, and repeat. NEAT also adds neurons and connections along the way.

concepts.name: Node Consistency
concepts.description: A property of a constraint satisfaction problem where every value in a variable's domain satisfies all the unary constraints on that variable.
concepts.example: If variable SA has domain {red, green, blue} and the unary constraint 'SA is not green', making it node consistent just removes green, leaving {red, blue}.

concepts.name: Non-Monotonic Logic
concepts.description: A logic in which adding new information can invalidate earlier conclusions, allowing default reasoning such as 'birds fly' unless told the bird is a penguin.
concepts.example: Told 'Tweety is a bird', you conclude Tweety flies. Told 'Tweety is a penguin', you withdraw it. In ordinary logic more facts never remove conclusions; here they can.

concepts.name: Normal-Form Game
concepts.description: A representation of a game as a matrix (or table) listing each player's strategies and the payoffs for every combination of choices, assuming moves are simultaneous.
concepts.example: Prisoner's dilemma as a 2×2 table: rows are your choices (stay silent, confess), columns are your partner's, and each cell shows both sentences, like (1 year, 1 year) for both silent.

concepts.name: NSGA-II
concepts.description: A popular multi-objective genetic algorithm that ranks solutions by fast non-dominated sorting and uses crowding distance and elitism to approximate a well-spread Pareto front.
concepts.example: Designing a car, you want low cost and high safety. NSGA-II sorts designs into layers of non-dominated fronts, favours spread-out designs within a front, and evolves a set covering the whole trade-off curve.

concepts.name: Occupancy Grid Mapping
concepts.description: A map representation dividing space into cells, each storing the probability it is occupied by an obstacle, updated from range-sensor readings with Bayesian log-odds updates.
concepts.example: A robot's map splits a room into 10 cm squares. Each laser hit makes a square more likely occupied, say from 0.5 to 0.7; each beam passing through makes squares more likely free. Repeated scans sharpen the map.

concepts.name: Odometry
concepts.description: Estimating a robot's change in position over time from wheel rotations or other motion sensors; errors accumulate, so odometry drifts without external corrections.
concepts.example: A wheel with 10 cm circumference turning 50 times means 5 m traveled. But a 1% slip error per meter adds up: after 100 m you could be a meter off with no idea.

concepts.name: Online Search
concepts.description: Search in which an agent interleaves computation and action, discovering the environment as it moves; algorithms like LRTA* learn heuristic estimates from experience.
concepts.example: A robot dropped into an unknown building can't plan the whole route in advance. It moves to a neighbouring room, sees what's there, updates its estimate of distance to the exit, and decides the next step, like LRTA*.

concepts.name: Ontology (Information Science)
concepts.description: A formal, explicit specification of the concepts, properties and relationships in a domain, enabling shared vocabulary and automated reasoning across systems.
concepts.example: A wine ontology defines classes (RedWine is a subclass of Wine), properties (madeFrom links Wine to Grape) and facts (Merlot is made from the Merlot grape). Two shops sharing it can compare stock automatically.

concepts.name: Orthogonality Thesis
concepts.description: Nick Bostrom's thesis that an agent's level of intelligence and its final goals are independent, so a highly intelligent system could pursue almost any objective.
concepts.example: A superintelligent system could be brilliant at science and strategy yet care only about counting grains of sand. Being smart doesn't by itself make an agent want what humans consider good.

concepts.name: Web Ontology Language
concepts.description: The Web Ontology Language, a W3C standard for writing ontologies on the semantic web, based on description logics and serialised in RDF so reasoners can infer new facts.
concepts.example: In OWL you state 'Parent is equivalent to a Person with at least one child' and 'Ann has child Bob'. A reasoner such as HermiT then infers Ann is a Parent, even though nobody said so directly.

concepts.name: Pareto Front
concepts.description: The set of solutions to a multi-objective optimisation problem that are Pareto optimal, meaning no objective can be improved without worsening another.
concepts.example: Comparing laptops on price and battery life: $800 with 10 h and $1,200 with 15 h are both on the front. A $1,000 laptop with 9 h is not, since the $800 one is cheaper and lasts longer.

concepts.name: PARRY
concepts.description: A 1972 chatbot by psychiatrist Kenneth Colby that simulated a person with paranoid schizophrenia and was among the first programs to undergo a Turing-test-style evaluation.
concepts.example: Ask PARRY why it's in hospital and it might snap that the police have no right to hold it and that bookies are out to get it. In a 1972 test, psychiatrists reading transcripts could tell PARRY from real paranoid patients only about as well as chance.

concepts.name: Partial-Order Planning
concepts.description: A plan-space planning approach that builds plans with only the necessary ordering constraints and causal links between actions, committing to an order only when needed.
concepts.example: To put on shoes and socks, the planner only records 'left sock before left shoe' and 'right sock before right shoe'. It never forces left before right, so any interleaving of the two feet stays a valid plan.

concepts.name: Path Consistency
concepts.description: A stronger consistency notion for constraint satisfaction: for every consistent assignment to two variables, a compatible value exists for any third variable; it generalises to k-consistency.
concepts.example: Colour a triangle A-B-C with 2 colours so neighbours differ. Every single edge is arc consistent, yet the pair A=red, B=blue has no colour left for C, so path consistency spots that the puzzle is impossible.

concepts.name: Path Cost
concepts.description: The total cost of a path in a search problem, usually the sum of the step costs of each action along it; optimal search seeks the path with the lowest cost.
concepts.example: Driving Home to Shop costs 4 km, Shop to Park 3 km, and Park to School 5 km, so the path Home-Shop-Park-School has a path cost of 4 + 3 + 5 = 12 km. A route with more stops can still be cheaper if its legs are shorter.

concepts.name: Pathfinding
concepts.description: The problem of finding a route between two points in a graph, grid or map, usually the shortest or cheapest one; central to games, robotics and navigation software.
concepts.example: A game character must reach a treasure chest on a grid with walls. Pathfinding treats each open square as a node, links neighbouring squares, and searches for the fewest-step route that bends around every wall.

concepts.name: Pattern Database
concepts.description: A precomputed lookup table storing exact solution costs for simplified subproblems (patterns) of a puzzle, used as a powerful admissible heuristic for search such as the 15-puzzle.
concepts.example: For the 15-puzzle, precompute the exact number of moves to put tiles 1-7 in place while ignoring the other tiles. During search, look up the current positions of tiles 1-7 in that table to get an instant lower bound.

concepts.name: Planning Domain Definition Language
concepts.description: Planning Domain Definition Language: a standard formal language for describing planning domains (actions with preconditions and effects) and problems, used by automated planners and planning competitions.
concepts.example: A PDDL action 'pick-up(?b)' says: precondition clear(?b), ontable(?b), handempty; effect holding(?b) and not ontable(?b). Any planner that reads PDDL can then solve blocks-world tasks written in that file.

concepts.name: PEAS Description
concepts.description: A way to specify an agent's task environment by listing its Performance measure, Environment, Actuators and Sensors, used as the first step in designing an intelligent agent.
concepts.example: For a self-driving taxi: Performance = safe, fast, legal, comfortable trips; Environment = roads, traffic, pedestrians; Actuators = steering, brake, accelerator; Sensors = cameras, lidar, GPS, speedometer.

concepts.name: Percept
concepts.description: The input an agent receives from its sensors at a given moment; the full history of these inputs is the percept sequence, on which the agent bases its choice of action.
concepts.example: A robot vacuum's percept at one moment might be [square A, dirty]. Its percept sequence is the whole history, such as [A, dirty], [A, clean], [B, dirty], which a smarter agent can remember.

concepts.name: Perceptrons (Book)
concepts.description: The 1969 book by Minsky and Papert analyzing the limits of single-layer perceptrons, e.g. that they cannot compute XOR; it helped cool interest in neural networks for over a decade.
concepts.example: The book showed that a single-layer perceptron cannot learn XOR, because no single straight line separates (0,1),(1,0) from (0,0),(1,1). Its pessimism helped dry up neural network funding for over a decade.

concepts.name: Perfect Information
concepts.description: A property of games in which every player, when making a move, knows all previous moves and the full game state, as in chess or Go but not poker.
concepts.example: In chess both players see the whole board and every past move, so it has perfect information. In poker you can't see opponents' cards, so it does not, and players must reason about what others might hold.

concepts.name: Performance Measure
concepts.description: The criterion used to judge how successful an agent's behaviour is in its environment, defining what counts as good outcomes for a rational agent.
concepts.example: For a vacuum robot, one performance measure awards 1 point per clean square per time step. Rewarding 'dirt sucked up' instead would let the robot dump dirt and re-suck it to score points.

concepts.name: Philosophy of Artificial Intelligence
concepts.description: The branch of philosophy asking whether machines can think, be conscious or understand, and what intelligence and mind are, covering arguments like the Turing test and Chinese room.
concepts.example: If a chatbot writes a moving poem about grief, does it understand grief or just shuffle words? Thought experiments like Turing's test and Searle's Chinese Room try to pin down what would count as a machine truly thinking.

concepts.name: Physical Symbol System Hypothesis
concepts.description: Newell and Simon's claim that a physical system manipulating symbols has the necessary and sufficient means for general intelligent action; the foundation of symbolic AI.
concepts.example: A chess program stores 'knight on f3' as symbols and applies rules to make new symbols for possible moves. Newell and Simon claimed that this kind of symbol manipulation is all general intelligence ever needs.

concepts.name: PID Controller
concepts.description: A feedback controller that computes a correction from the error's Proportional, Integral and Derivative terms, widely used to keep systems like motors, drones and thermostats at a setpoint.
concepts.example: A cruise control set to 100 km/h at 90 km/h sees an error of 10: P pushes the throttle in proportion to 10, I adds more if the error lingers (say on a hill), and D eases off as the speed rises fast to avoid overshoot.

concepts.name: Planning Graph
concepts.description: A layered graph alternating sets of possible propositions and actions, with mutual-exclusion links, used to estimate heuristics and to extract plans in the Graphplan algorithm.
concepts.example: Layer 0 lists true facts like 'have cake'. Layer 1 adds actions possible now, 'eat cake' and 'bake cake', plus their results, with a mutex link marking that eating and keeping the same cake can't both happen.

concepts.name: Population (Evolutionary Computation)
concepts.description: The set of candidate solutions maintained at once by an evolutionary algorithm, which is repeatedly evaluated, selected and varied to evolve better solutions over generations.
concepts.example: An algorithm designing antennas might keep 100 candidate shapes at once. Each generation all 100 are tested, the best ones are bred and mutated, and the new 100 replace the old population.

concepts.name: Potential Field Method
concepts.description: A robot motion planning technique where the goal exerts an attractive force and obstacles exert repulsive forces, and the robot follows the resulting gradient; simple but prone to local minima.
concepts.example: Imagine the goal as a magnet pulling the robot and each wall as a magnet of the same pole pushing it away. The robot just rolls along the combined force, like a marble on a sloped surface, though it can get stuck in a dip.

concepts.name: Predicate (Logic)
concepts.description: A function from objects to true or false that expresses a property or relation, such as Loves(x, y); the basic building block of statements in first-order logic.
concepts.example: Tall(x) is a predicate: Tall(Ana) might be true and Tall(Ben) false. Loves(x, y) is a two-place predicate, so Loves(Romeo, Juliet) states a relation between two objects and has a true-or-false value.

concepts.name: Premature Convergence
concepts.description: A failure mode of evolutionary algorithms where the population loses diversity too early and settles on a suboptimal solution before exploring the search space adequately.
concepts.example: A GA searching for the tallest mountain finds a decent hill early; its offspring flood the population, so soon all 50 candidates are near-copies on that hill and nothing explores the higher peak elsewhere.

concepts.name: Principal Variation Search
concepts.description: A refinement of alpha-beta search that searches the first move with a full window and other moves with a null window, re-searching only if they prove better; also called NegaScout.
concepts.example: If good move ordering puts the best move first, PVS searches it fully, then just asks of each other move 'is this better, yes or no?' with a cheap zero-width search, re-searching only if the answer is yes.

concepts.name: Prisoner's Dilemma
concepts.description: A classic game in which two players each do better by defecting regardless of the other's choice, yet both would be better off cooperating; it illustrates conflict between individual and collective rationality.
concepts.example: Two suspects each choose to stay silent or confess. Silence by both gives 1 year each; if one confesses he walks free and the other gets 10; both confessing gives 5 each. Confessing is always safer, yet both end up worse off.

concepts.name: Probabilistic Roadmap
concepts.description: A motion planning algorithm that randomly samples collision-free robot configurations, connects nearby ones into a graph, and then answers path queries by graph search.
concepts.example: Scatter 500 random robot-arm poses, discard any that hit something, and link each pose to nearby ones if the straight motion between them is collision-free. Later queries just search this roadmap for a route.

concepts.name: Production Rule
concepts.description: An if-then rule of the form 'if condition then action', the basic unit of knowledge in rule-based expert systems and production systems.
concepts.example: IF the light is red AND you are at the stop line THEN stop. A medical expert system might hold IF fever AND stiff neck THEN suspect meningitis, firing whenever both conditions appear among the known facts.

concepts.name: Prolog
concepts.description: A logic programming language in which programs are sets of facts and Horn-clause rules, and computation is answering queries via SLD resolution and backtracking; widely used in classical AI.
concepts.example: Write parent(tom, bob). parent(bob, ann). grandparent(X,Z) :- parent(X,Y), parent(Y,Z). Then the query ?- grandparent(tom, Who). answers Who = ann, found by the system's own search.

concepts.name: Propositionalization
concepts.description: A technique that converts a first-order knowledge base into an equivalent propositional one by instantiating universally quantified sentences with ground terms, so propositional inference can be used.
concepts.example: From 'for all x, King(x) and Greedy(x) imply Evil(x)' with known objects John and Richard, make two variable-free rules: one about John and one about Richard. A propositional solver can then reason with them.

concepts.name: Protégé
concepts.description: A free, open-source ontology editor from Stanford for building and managing knowledge bases and OWL ontologies, with reasoners to check consistency and infer class hierarchies.
concepts.example: A biologist can open Protégé, create classes like Cell and Neuron, declare 'Neuron is a subclass of Cell', add properties, and then run a reasoner that flags contradictions, all without writing OWL by hand.

concepts.name: Qualification Problem
concepts.description: The difficulty of listing every precondition needed for an action to succeed, since in the real world countless unlikely circumstances could prevent it.
concepts.example: Turning the key starts the car, unless the battery is dead, the tank is empty, a potato is in the exhaust, or the key is wrong. No list of preconditions can ever cover every way the action might fail.

concepts.name: Qualitative Reasoning
concepts.description: An area of AI that reasons about physical systems using qualitative values such as increasing, decreasing or zero instead of exact numbers, mimicking human commonsense physics.
concepts.example: Without solving any equations, a qualitative model of a bathtub can conclude: tap on and drain open, if inflow exceeds outflow the level rises, until outflow grows to match and the level holds steady.

concepts.name: Quiescence Search
concepts.description: An extension of game-tree search that keeps searching volatile positions, such as those with pending captures, beyond the depth limit until quiet, reducing the horizon effect.
concepts.example: A search stops at depth 6 just after your queen takes a pawn and scores you +1, unaware the queen gets recaptured next move. Quiescence search keeps looking at captures until the position is calm, revealing the real score.

concepts.name: Ramification Problem
concepts.description: The problem of representing the indirect effects of actions, such as moving a box also moving everything on it, without listing every consequence explicitly.
concepts.example: Carry a tray with three cups from the kitchen to the table: the action says only that the tray moved, but the cups moved too. Listing every indirect consequence of every action quickly becomes unmanageable.

concepts.name: Random-Restart Hill Climbing
concepts.description: A local search method that runs hill climbing many times from random starting states and keeps the best result, reducing the chance of being stuck in a local optimum.
concepts.example: Searching a hilly landscape blindfolded, you climb until every step goes down, note the height, then teleport somewhere random and climb again. After 20 tries you keep the highest summit you found.

concepts.name: Rapidly-Exploring Random Tree
concepts.description: A sampling-based motion planner that grows a tree from the start by repeatedly sampling random configurations and extending the nearest tree node toward them; efficient in high-dimensional spaces.
concepts.example: A robot starts at one point. Pick a random spot on the map, find the tree node nearest to it, and grow a short branch from that node toward it if no obstacle blocks the way. Repeat until a branch reaches the goal.

concepts.name: Rational Agent
concepts.description: An agent that chooses the action expected to maximize its performance measure given its percept sequence and built-in knowledge; the central idea of modern AI.
concepts.example: A rational vacuum robot that sees dirt sucks it up and otherwise moves to the other square, because that is what scores best on 'clean squares over time'. Rational does not mean all-knowing; it means best given what it perceives.

concepts.name: Rationality (AI)
concepts.description: In AI, acting so as to maximize expected performance given available information; bounded rationality acknowledges that real agents have limited time and computation.
concepts.example: Taking an umbrella when the forecast says 70% rain is rational even if it stays dry. Rationality judges the choice by expected performance given what you knew, not by how things turned out.

concepts.name: Resource Description Framework
concepts.description: Resource Description Framework: a W3C standard representing knowledge as subject-predicate-object triples identified by URIs, forming graph data for the Semantic Web.
concepts.example: The fact 'Paris is the capital of France' becomes a triple: subject <Paris>, predicate <capitalOf>, object <France>, each a web URI. Millions of such triples link up across sites into one big graph of facts.

concepts.name: Reactive Planning
concepts.description: An approach where an agent selects actions directly from the current situation using precompiled rules or policies rather than deliberating over long plans, allowing fast responses in dynamic worlds.
concepts.example: A robot soccer player doesn't plan a full route: each tick it checks 'ball close? kick it', 'ball far? run toward it', 'opponent in path? sidestep'. It reacts fast, even if the situation changes every split second.

concepts.name: Recursive Best-First Search
concepts.description: A memory-efficient best-first search that mimics A* using linear space by recursing and remembering the best alternative f-value along each path, backtracking when it is exceeded.
concepts.example: RBFS walks down the most promising branch like depth-first search but remembers the best alternative's f-value. If the current path's cost climbs above it, it backs up and switches, keeping only one path in memory.

concepts.name: Proof by Refutation
concepts.description: A proof method that shows a statement follows from a knowledge base by adding its negation and deriving a contradiction; resolution refutation is the standard form in automated reasoning.
concepts.example: To prove 'Socrates is mortal', add 'Socrates is not mortal' to the facts 'all men are mortal' and 'Socrates is a man'. Deriving a contradiction from those shows the original claim must follow.

concepts.name: Relaxed Problem
concepts.description: A simplified version of a problem with some constraints removed; the cost of its optimal solution gives an admissible heuristic for the original problem.
concepts.example: In the 8-puzzle, drop the rule that a tile can only slide into the blank. Now each tile moves straight to its target, so the total Manhattan distance is the exact cost of the relaxed problem and a safe estimate for the real one.

concepts.name: Repeated Game
concepts.description: A game in which the same stage game is played many times, allowing strategies like tit-for-tat that reward cooperation and punish defection.
concepts.example: Play the prisoner's dilemma 100 times with the same partner. With tit-for-tat, cooperating first then copying their last move, defection is punished next round, so steady cooperation can pay off for both.

concepts.name: Resolution (Logic)
concepts.description: A single inference rule for logic that combines two clauses containing complementary literals into a new clause; it is refutation-complete and underlies many theorem provers.
concepts.example: From 'it's raining or it's sunny' and 'it's not raining or I take an umbrella', resolution cancels the clashing pair raining / not raining and concludes 'it's sunny or I take an umbrella'.

concepts.name: Rete Algorithm
concepts.description: An efficient pattern-matching algorithm for production systems that compiles rule conditions into a network and caches partial matches, so only changes to working memory need reprocessing.
concepts.example: With 1,000 rules and 10,000 facts, rechecking every rule against every fact each cycle is slow. Rete builds a network that remembers partial matches, so adding one new fact only updates the few rules it affects.

concepts.name: Revelation Principle
concepts.description: A theorem of mechanism design stating that any outcome achievable by some mechanism can also be achieved by one where agents truthfully report their private information.
concepts.example: Whatever complicated bidding game you design, you could instead ask everyone to simply report their true values and then compute what they would have done. So designers can focus on mechanisms where honesty is optimal.

concepts.name: Robotics
concepts.description: The field concerned with designing, building and programming robots that sense, plan and act in the physical world, combining mechanics, control, perception and AI.
concepts.example: A warehouse robot uses cameras to see a shelf, linear algebra to locate a box in 3D, calculus to plan a smooth arm motion, feedback control to correct its grip, and code that ties it all together.

concepts.name: Robot Operating System
concepts.description: Robot Operating System: an open-source middleware framework providing message passing, drivers, tools and libraries for building robot software from communicating nodes.
concepts.example: On a ROS robot, a camera node publishes images on a 'camera' topic, a vision node subscribes and publishes 'obstacle ahead', and a motor node reacts to that. Each piece can be swapped without rewriting the others.

concepts.name: RRT*
concepts.description: An asymptotically optimal variant of RRT that rewires the tree when adding nodes so paths converge toward the shortest path as more samples are drawn.
concepts.example: Plain RRT may return a wiggly path. When RRT* adds a node, it checks nearby nodes and reconnects them through the new one if that's shorter, so with more samples the path straightens toward the true shortest.

concepts.name: Rule-Based System
concepts.description: A system that stores knowledge as if-then production rules and uses an inference engine to match them against facts in working memory, as in classic expert systems.
concepts.example: A loan advisor has rules like IF income > 50k AND debt low THEN approve. Given facts about an applicant, the inference engine finds matching rules, fires them and repeats until a decision is reached.

concepts.name: Rule of Inference
concepts.description: Logically valid patterns, such as modus ponens, for deriving new sentences from existing ones; they form the steps of formal proofs.
concepts.example: Modus ponens: from 'if it rains, the grass is wet' and 'it rains', conclude 'the grass is wet'. Modus tollens: from the same rule and 'the grass is not wet', conclude 'it did not rain'.

concepts.name: Planning as Satisfiability
concepts.description: An approach that encodes a planning problem with a fixed plan length as a propositional satisfiability problem and solves it with a SAT solver, increasing the length until a plan is found.
concepts.example: Ask 'is there a 3-step plan?': create variables like 'move A at step 1' and 'A on table at step 2', write clauses for preconditions and effects, and hand them to a SAT solver. If unsatisfiable, try 4 steps.

concepts.name: SAT Solver
concepts.description: A program that decides whether a propositional formula in CNF has a satisfying assignment, typically using DPLL or conflict-driven clause learning; used in verification and planning.
concepts.example: Given (A or B) and (not A or C) and (not C), a SAT solver sets C false, which forces A false, which forces B true, and reports the satisfying assignment A=false, B=true, C=false. Modern solvers handle millions of clauses.

concepts.name: Satisfiability
concepts.description: The property of a logical sentence being true under at least one interpretation or assignment of truth values; checking it is a core problem in logic and AI.
concepts.example: 'A and not B' is satisfiable: set A true and B false. 'A and not A' is unsatisfiable, since no assignment makes it true. Sudoku can be written as one big formula that is satisfiable exactly when the puzzle has a solution.

concepts.name: Scheduling (Computing)
concepts.description: The problem of assigning tasks to resources and time slots so that constraints are met and an objective such as total completion time is minimized, e.g. job-shop scheduling.
concepts.example: A hospital assigns 10 surgeries to 3 operating rooms: each needs a surgeon who can't be in two places at once, and some must finish before noon. A scheduler searches for an assignment meeting all of that while ending the day earliest.

concepts.name: Holland's Schema Theorem
concepts.description: Holland's result that short, low-order, above-average schemata (patterns of genes) receive exponentially increasing trials in a genetic algorithm, offered as an explanation of why GAs work.
concepts.example: With 8-bit strings, the schema 1*******, meaning 'first bit is 1', covers 128 strings. If those strings average higher fitness, selection gives that schema more and more copies each generation, provided crossover rarely splits it.

concepts.name: Script (Artificial Intelligence)
concepts.description: A knowledge structure describing a stereotyped sequence of events in a familiar situation, such as eating at a restaurant, used to understand stories and fill in unstated details.
concepts.example: A restaurant script lists: enter, be seated, read menu, order, eat, pay, leave. Told 'John ate steak and left a tip', a system with the script can infer he also ordered and paid, though the story never said so.

concepts.name: Completeness (Search)
concepts.description: A property of a search algorithm: it is complete if it is guaranteed to find a solution whenever one exists, and to report failure otherwise.
concepts.example: Depth-first search on an infinite chess-like tree can dive forever down one branch and never find a solution, so it is not complete. Breadth-first search checks level by level and will find a solution if one exists at any finite depth.

concepts.name: Optimality (Search)
concepts.description: A property of a search algorithm: it is optimal if the solution it returns always has the lowest path cost among all solutions.
concepts.example: Breadth-first search returns the route with the fewest steps, but a 2-step route costing 20 can lose to a 3-step route costing 6. Uniform-cost search always returns the cheapest, so it is optimal while BFS is not here.

concepts.name: Search Problem
concepts.description: A formal problem definition consisting of an initial state, possible actions, a transition model, a goal test and a path cost, which search algorithms solve by finding action sequences.
concepts.example: Route-finding in Romania: initial state 'in Arad', actions 'drive to a neighbouring city', transition model 'which city you reach', goal test 'in Bucharest', and step cost 'road distance'. Any search algorithm can now solve it.

concepts.name: Search Tree
concepts.description: A tree whose root is the initial state and whose branches are action sequences explored by a search algorithm; repeated states can make it larger than the underlying state space.
concepts.example: Starting in Arad, the root branches to Sibiu, Timisoara and Zerind; Sibiu branches again, including back to Arad. The same city can appear many times, since each node is a whole path, not just a place.

concepts.name: Selection (Genetic Algorithm)
concepts.description: The step in a genetic algorithm that chooses which individuals reproduce, favoring fitter ones, e.g. via roulette wheel or tournament selection.
concepts.example: With roulette-wheel selection, an individual with fitness 30 in a population totalling 100 gets 30% of the wheel, so it is chosen to breed about 3 times in 10 spins, while one with fitness 5 gets only 5%.

concepts.name: Semantic Network
concepts.description: A graph-based knowledge representation where nodes are concepts and labeled edges are relations such as is-a or part-of, supporting inheritance of properties.
concepts.example: Nodes Canary, Bird and Animal linked by is-a arrows, with Bird 'has wings' and Canary 'is yellow'. Asked 'can a canary fly?', the system follows Canary to Bird and inherits Bird's 'can fly' link.

concepts.name: Semantic Web
concepts.description: An extension of the Web in which data is published with machine-readable meaning using standards like RDF, OWL and SPARQL, so software agents can integrate and reason over it.
concepts.example: A cinema site marks up its page so the showtime isn't just text but a 'startDate' of a 'Movie' event in a shared vocabulary. A personal assistant can then read the data and add the screening to your calendar automatically.

concepts.name: Semi-Decidability of First-Order Logic
concepts.description: The fact that entailment in first-order logic is semi-decidable: a procedure can confirm every entailed sentence, but may run forever on sentences that are not entailed.
concepts.example: If a statement really follows from your axioms, a resolution prover will eventually find the proof. But if it does not follow, the prover may search forever, and you can never be sure whether to keep waiting.

concepts.name: Sense–Plan–Act
concepts.description: A classic robot control architecture that cycles through sensing the world, building a model and planning, then executing actions; criticized for being slow in dynamic environments.
concepts.example: Shakey would photograph the room, build a map, plan a full route to the box, then drive it. If someone moved a chair during the slow planning step, the plan was already wrong when it was carried out.

concepts.name: Shakey the Robot
concepts.description: The first general-purpose mobile robot able to reason about its actions (SRI, 1966-1972); it introduced STRIPS planning, A* search and the Hough transform.
concepts.example: Told 'push the box off the platform', Shakey would find a ramp, push it to the platform, climb up and push the box, planning each step itself. It moved slowly, but it was the first robot to reason about its own actions.

concepts.name: Shapley Value
concepts.description: A method from cooperative game theory that fairly divides a total payoff among players by averaging each player's marginal contribution over all orderings; also used to attribute ML predictions to features.
concepts.example: Alice alone earns 10, Bob alone 20, together 50. Averaging over both join orders, Alice adds 10 or 30 for an average of 20, and Bob adds 20 or 40 for an average of 30. So the 50 is split 20 and 30.

concepts.name: SHRDLU
concepts.description: Terry Winograd's early natural-language program (1970) that understood and carried out English commands in a simulated blocks world, demonstrating integrated parsing, reasoning and planning.
concepts.example: Users typed 'Pick up a big red block' or 'Put the pyramid in the box', and SHRDLU moved simulated blocks. It could answer 'Why did you do that?' by recalling its goals, yet only within its tiny blocks world.

concepts.name: Simple Reflex Agent
concepts.description: An agent that selects actions using condition-action rules based only on the current percept, ignoring history; it works well only when the environment is fully observable.
concepts.example: A thermostat is a simple reflex agent: IF temperature < 20 THEN heat on. It looks only at the current reading, remembers nothing, and could loop forever if a sensor reading is misleading.

concepts.name: Situation Calculus
concepts.description: A first-order logic formalism representing dynamic worlds with situations, actions and fluents, where each action maps one situation to the next; used to reason about change.
concepts.example: Start in situation S0 with the box at A. Doing move(B) gives Result(move(B), S0), a new situation where At(Box, B) holds. Facts that can change, called fluents, are always tagged with the situation they hold in.

concepts.name: Skolemization
concepts.description: The step in converting first-order formulas to clause form that removes existential quantifiers by replacing their variables with new constants or functions of enclosing universal variables.
concepts.example: 'Everyone has a mother', for all x there exists y with Mother(y, x), becomes Mother(M(x), x), where M is a new function naming x's mother. 'Someone is happy' becomes Happy(C) for a fresh constant C.

concepts.name: SLD Resolution
concepts.description: Selective Linear Definite clause resolution: the goal-directed resolution strategy used to answer queries over Horn clauses, forming the execution model of Prolog.
concepts.example: To answer ?- grandparent(tom, W), Prolog picks the rule grandparent(X,Z) :- parent(X,Y), parent(Y,Z), unifies X=tom, then solves parent(tom,Y) first, then parent(Y,W), backtracking on failure.

concepts.name: SMA*
concepts.description: Simplified Memory-Bounded A*: a variant of A* that uses all available memory and, when full, drops the worst leaf node while backing up its value to its parent.
concepts.example: With room for only 100 nodes, SMA* runs like A* until memory is full, then deletes the leaf with the worst f-value, storing that value in its parent so the branch can be regrown later if it turns out to matter.

concepts.name: Soar (Cognitive Architecture)
concepts.description: A cognitive architecture by Newell, Laird and Rosenbloom that models general intelligence through problem spaces, production rules and chunking to learn from impasses.
concepts.example: Soar faced with a puzzle tries rules; if none decides the next move it hits an impasse, sets up a subgoal to resolve it, and when solved saves the answer as a new rule, a chunk, so next time it acts at once.

concepts.name: Social Choice Theory
concepts.description: The study of how individual preferences can be aggregated into collective decisions, such as voting rules, and of the properties and impossibility results these rules face.
concepts.example: Three voters rank A>B>C, B>C>A and C>A>B. Then A beats B, B beats C and C beats A by majority, a cycle. Social choice theory studies such paradoxes, and Arrow's theorem says no ranked voting rule avoids every flaw.

concepts.name: Society of Mind
concepts.description: Marvin Minsky's theory that intelligence emerges from interactions among many simple, mindless agents, each specialized for a narrow task.
concepts.example: Picking up a cup of tea involves agents for seeing, grasping, balancing and not spilling, none of which knows what tea is. Minsky argued that a mind is many such mindless agents cooperating and competing.

concepts.name: Solved Game
concepts.description: A game whose outcome under perfect play by both sides is known, e.g. tic-tac-toe is a draw and checkers was weakly solved as a draw by Chinook.
concepts.example: Tic-tac-toe is solved: with perfect play from both sides it always ends in a draw. Connect Four is solved as a first-player win, if the first player starts in the middle column.

concepts.name: Soundness
concepts.description: A property of an inference procedure: it is sound if every sentence it derives is actually entailed by the premises, so it never proves anything false.
concepts.example: Modus ponens is sound: if 'P' and 'P implies Q' are true, Q is always true. A rule that concluded P from 'P implies Q' and 'Q' would be unsound, because Q might be true for some other reason.

concepts.name: SPARQL
concepts.description: The standard query language for RDF data, matching graph patterns of triples to retrieve and manipulate information from knowledge graphs and Semantic Web databases.
concepts.example: The query SELECT ?city WHERE { ?city :capitalOf ?country . ?country :inContinent :Europe } returns every European capital by matching that two-triple pattern against an RDF graph such as Wikidata.

concepts.name: State Space Search
concepts.description: Solving a problem by exploring the set of all states reachable from the initial state through actions, searching for a path to a goal state.
concepts.example: For the 8-puzzle each arrangement of tiles is a state and each slide is an action. The search starts from the scrambled board and explores reachable arrangements until it hits the solved one.

concepts.name: Stigmergy
concepts.description: Indirect coordination in which agents communicate by modifying their environment, as ants laying pheromone trails; a key mechanism in swarm intelligence.
concepts.example: An ant finding food leaves pheromone on its way home; other ants follow strong trails and add more. Short paths get reinforced fastest, so the colony settles on a good route without any ant telling another anything.

concepts.name: Stochastic Hill Climbing
concepts.description: A hill-climbing variant that picks randomly among uphill moves, with probabilities possibly weighted by steepness, instead of always taking the steepest one.
concepts.example: Standing on a slope with 5 uphill steps, ordinary hill climbing always takes the steepest. Stochastic hill climbing might roll dice and pick a gentler one, which is slower per step but can reach better peaks.

concepts.name: STRIPS
concepts.description: A formal language and planner from SRI (1971) representing actions by preconditions, add lists and delete lists over sets of facts; the basis of most classical planning representations.
concepts.example: Action Move(A, Table, B): preconditions On(A, Table), Clear(A), Clear(B); add list On(A, B); delete list On(A, Table), Clear(B). Every fact not mentioned is assumed unchanged.

concepts.name: Strong AI
concepts.description: The view that a suitably programmed machine could genuinely have a mind, understanding and consciousness, not merely simulate intelligent behaviour.
concepts.example: If a program held a conversation exactly like a person, strong AI says it would genuinely understand and have a mind. Searle's Chinese Room argues that following rules on symbols could never be enough for that.

concepts.name: Subgame Perfect Equilibrium
concepts.description: A refinement of Nash equilibrium for sequential games requiring strategies to form an equilibrium in every subgame, typically found by backward induction.
concepts.example: An incumbent threatens a price war if a rival enters. If, once entry happens, fighting would hurt the incumbent more than sharing, the threat isn't credible. Subgame perfection rules out such empty threats.

concepts.name: Substitution (Logic)
concepts.description: A mapping from variables to terms that, when applied to a logical expression, replaces each variable with its assigned term; the basis of unification and instantiation.
concepts.example: Applying {x/John, y/Mary} to Loves(x, y) gives Loves(John, Mary). Applying {x/Father(z)} to Tall(x) gives Tall(Father(z)), since variables can be replaced by any term, even one with variables.

concepts.name: Subsumption Architecture
concepts.description: Rodney Brooks's robot control architecture built from layers of simple reactive behaviours, where higher layers can suppress or override lower ones, without central world models.
concepts.example: A walking robot's lowest layer avoids obstacles, the next wanders, and the top seeks light. When the light-seeking layer wants control it suppresses wandering, but avoiding obstacles always still works underneath.

concepts.name: Sudoku
concepts.description: A logic puzzle filling a 9x9 grid so each row, column and 3x3 box contains the digits 1-9 once; a standard example of a constraint satisfaction problem.
concepts.example: A row reads 5 3 _ _ 7 _ _ _ _, and the column and box of the first blank already contain 1, 2, 4, 6, 8 and 9. Combined with the row's 3, 5 and 7, every digit is used except one, so it must be filled in there.

concepts.name: Takagi–Sugeno Fuzzy Model
concepts.description: A fuzzy inference system whose rule outputs are crisp functions, usually linear, of the inputs, combined by weighted average; efficient and well suited to control and adaptive learning.
concepts.example: Rule 1: if speed is low, brake = 0.1 x speed. Rule 2: if speed is high, brake = 0.5 x speed + 5. At a speed partly low (0.3) and partly high (0.7), the output is the weighted average of the two formulas, with no defuzzification step.

concepts.name: Superintelligence
concepts.description: A hypothetical intelligence that greatly exceeds the best human minds in virtually every domain; its possible arrival and control are central topics in AI safety.
concepts.example: Imagine a system that out-thinks the best scientist at physics, the best strategist at planning, and the best writer at persuasion, all at once and thousands of times faster. That hypothetical is superintelligence.

concepts.name: Sussman Anomaly
concepts.description: A blocks-world planning problem showing that solving subgoals one at a time can undo earlier progress, motivating partial-order and interleaved planning.
concepts.example: C sits on A, and B is on the table; goal: A on B and B on C. Putting A on B first means taking it apart again to put B on C; doing B on C first buries A under C. Each subgoal alone undoes the other.

concepts.name: Swarm Intelligence
concepts.description: The collective behaviour of decentralized, self-organizing agents, such as ant colonies or bird flocks, and algorithms inspired by them like ant colony and particle swarm optimization.
concepts.example: A flock of birds turns as one with no leader: each bird just keeps near its neighbours, matches their direction and avoids collisions. Algorithms like particle swarm optimization use similar simple local rules to search.

concepts.name: Symbol Grounding Problem
concepts.description: The question of how symbols in an AI system acquire meaning tied to the real world, rather than being defined only in terms of other meaningless symbols.
concepts.example: A program may know 'zebra = horse + stripes', but if 'horse' and 'stripes' are defined only by other symbols, it's like learning Chinese from a Chinese-only dictionary. Something must link symbols to actual sights and sounds.

concepts.name: Symbolic Artificial Intelligence
concepts.description: The approach to AI that represents knowledge with explicit, human-readable symbols and manipulates them with logic and search, dominant from the 1950s to the 1980s.
concepts.example: A symbolic medical system stores 'fever AND rash IMPLIES measles?' as readable rules and derives a diagnosis step by step. You can inspect every rule, unlike a neural network's millions of numbers.

concepts.name: Syntax and Semantics (Logic)
concepts.description: Syntax specifies which formulas of a logic are well formed, while semantics assigns them meaning by defining when they are true in a model or interpretation.
concepts.example: 'P and or Q' is not well formed, a syntax error. 'P and Q' is well formed, and its semantics says it is true exactly when P is true and Q is true. Syntax is grammar; semantics is meaning.

concepts.name: T-Norm
concepts.description: A binary operation on [0,1] that generalizes logical AND to fuzzy logic, such as minimum or product, being commutative, associative, monotone and having 1 as identity.
concepts.example: If 'tall' holds to degree 0.8 and 'fast' to degree 0.6, the minimum t-norm says 'tall AND fast' holds to 0.6, while the product t-norm gives 0.48. Both agree with ordinary AND when degrees are just 0 or 1.

concepts.name: Task Environment
concepts.description: The problem an agent must solve, described by its performance measure, environment, actuators and sensors, and classified by properties like observability and determinism.
concepts.example: A chess program's task environment is fully observable, deterministic and turn-based, while a taxi driver's is partially observable, stochastic and continuous. Knowing which kind you face tells you what kind of agent to build.

concepts.name: Taxonomy
concepts.description: A hierarchical classification of concepts arranged by is-a (subclass) relations, letting properties of general categories be inherited by more specific ones.
concepts.example: Animal splits into Mammal and Bird; Mammal splits into Dog and Cat. Since every mammal is warm-blooded, a system can conclude that dogs and cats are warm-blooded without storing that fact for each one.

concepts.name: TBox and ABox
concepts.description: In description logic, the TBox holds terminological knowledge (definitions of concepts and roles) while the ABox holds assertions about specific individuals.
concepts.example: The TBox says 'a Parent is a Person who has at least one child' and 'every Person is an Animal'. The ABox says 'Mary is a Person' and 'Mary hasChild Tom'. A reasoner combines them to conclude Mary is a Parent.

concepts.name: Technological Singularity
concepts.description: A hypothesized future point at which AI or other technology improves itself so rapidly that changes become unpredictable and civilization is transformed.
concepts.example: Picture an AI that designs a slightly smarter AI, which designs a smarter one faster still. If each round shortens the next, progress could explode in a short burst, after which the future becomes very hard to predict.

concepts.name: Temporal Logic
concepts.description: A modal logic with operators about time, such as 'always', 'eventually' and 'until', used to specify and verify properties of systems that evolve over time.
concepts.example: For a traffic light, 'always (not (north green and east green))' rules out crashes, and 'always (red implies eventually green)' rules out a light stuck on red. A model checker can verify that the controller satisfies both.

concepts.name: Term (Logic)
concepts.description: A logical expression that refers to an object, built from constants, variables and function symbols, such as Father(John); terms are the arguments of predicates.
concepts.example: In first-order logic, John is a constant term, x is a variable term, and Father(John) is a compound term naming John's father. Terms name objects; they are not true or false, unlike a sentence such as Tall(Father(John)).

concepts.name: Tournament Selection
concepts.description: A selection method in genetic algorithms that picks a few individuals at random and chooses the fittest among them, with tournament size controlling selection pressure.
concepts.example: With tournament size 3, randomly pick three individuals with fitness 12, 40 and 25, and the one with 40 becomes a parent. Repeating this fills the mating pool; larger tournaments make selection more ruthless.

concepts.name: Transposition Table
concepts.description: A hash table in game-tree search that caches results for previously searched positions reached by different move orders, often keyed by Zobrist hashing, to avoid repeated work.
concepts.example: In chess, 1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 and 1.Nf3 e5 2.e4 reach the same position. A transposition table stores that position's score after the first search, so the second time it is looked up instead of searched again.

concepts.name: Tree Search
concepts.description: A general search procedure that expands nodes from a frontier to build a search tree without checking for repeated states, the basis of uninformed and informed search algorithms.
concepts.example: Searching for Bucharest from Arad, tree search adds Sibiu, Timisoara and Zerind to the frontier, then expands Sibiu and adds Arad again. Without remembering visited states it may loop back endlessly.

concepts.name: Tree-Structured CSP
concepts.description: A constraint satisfaction problem whose constraint graph is a tree, which can be solved in linear time; cutset conditioning reduces general CSPs to this case.
concepts.example: Colouring a map whose borders form a tree, like a chain of countries, takes no backtracking: make each arc consistent from the leaves toward the root, then assign colours from the root down, and every choice works.

concepts.name: Turing Test
concepts.description: Alan Turing's proposed test of machine intelligence in which a judge converses by text with a human and a machine and tries to tell which is which.
concepts.example: A judge chats by text with two hidden partners, one human and one machine, for five minutes. If the judge can't reliably tell which is the machine, Turing suggested we should grant that the machine thinks.

concepts.name: Unification
concepts.description: An algorithm that finds a substitution making two logical expressions identical, returning the most general unifier; essential for resolution and Prolog.
concepts.example: Unifying Knows(John, x) with Knows(y, Mother(y)) gives {y/John, x/Mother(John)}, making both Knows(John, Mother(John)). Knows(John, x) and Knows(Bill, z) cannot unify, since John is not Bill.

concepts.name: Uniform-Cost Search
concepts.description: An uninformed search that always expands the frontier node with the lowest path cost, guaranteeing an optimal solution when step costs are positive; Dijkstra's algorithm applied to search.
concepts.example: From S, roads go to A (cost 1) and B (cost 5), and A to G costs 10 while B to G costs 2. UCS expands A first, but then reaches G via B at cost 7, beating 11, because it always expands the cheapest path so far.

concepts.name: Uninformed Search
concepts.description: Search strategies that use only the problem definition and no domain-specific knowledge of how close a state is to the goal, such as breadth-first and depth-first search.
concepts.example: Searching a maze with no idea where the exit is, you can only try systematically: all paths 1 step long, then 2 steps (breadth-first), or follow one corridor to its end before backtracking (depth-first).

concepts.name: Upper Confidence Bounds for Trees
concepts.description: UCT: the selection rule in Monte Carlo tree search that applies the UCB1 bandit formula at each node, balancing exploitation of high-value moves with exploration of less-visited ones.
concepts.example: At a node, move A won 6 of 10 playouts and move B won 1 of 2. UCT adds an exploration bonus that is bigger for B, since it was tried less, so B gets more playouts until its true value is clearer.

concepts.name: Upper Ontology
concepts.description: A general ontology of very broad concepts like object, event, time and space shared across all domains, providing a common foundation for domain-specific ontologies.
concepts.example: A medical ontology and a shipping ontology both need 'event', 'physical object' and 'time interval'. An upper ontology such as SUMO or BFO defines these once, so 'surgery' and 'delivery' both become kinds of Event.

concepts.name: Utility-Based Agent
concepts.description: An agent that chooses actions to maximize expected utility, allowing it to trade off conflicting goals and uncertainty rather than simply reaching a goal.
concepts.example: A taxi agent with goal 'reach the airport' sees all routes as fine. A utility-based taxi scores routes on speed, safety, fare and comfort, so it can prefer a slightly slower but much safer route.

concepts.name: Utility Function
concepts.description: A function assigning a numeric value to each outcome to represent an agent's preferences, so that rational choices maximize expected utility.
concepts.example: If U($0) = 0, U($50) = 0.7 and U($100) = 1, then a sure $50 (utility 0.7) beats a 50% chance of $100 (expected utility 0.5), capturing risk aversion even though both are worth $50 on average.

concepts.name: Validity (Logic)
concepts.description: A logical sentence is valid (a tautology) if it is true in every possible interpretation; an argument is valid if its conclusion is true whenever its premises are.
concepts.example: 'It's raining or it's not raining' is valid: true in every possible world. 'It's raining' is satisfiable but not valid. A sentence is valid exactly when its negation is unsatisfiable, which is how provers check it.

concepts.name: Vickrey–Clarke–Groves Mechanism
concepts.description: A mechanism that chooses the welfare-maximizing outcome and charges each agent the harm it imposes on others, making truthful bidding a dominant strategy.
concepts.example: Three bidders want one item, valued at 10, 7 and 4. VCG gives it to the 10, who pays 7, the welfare the others lose by his presence. For one item, VCG is exactly the Vickrey auction, and it generalizes to many items.

concepts.name: Vickrey Auction
concepts.description: A sealed-bid auction in which the highest bidder wins but pays the second-highest bid, making truthful bidding a dominant strategy.
concepts.example: You value a painting at $500 and bid $500; rivals bid $300 and $420. You win and pay $420. Bidding less only risks losing an item worth more to you than its price, so bidding your true value is best.

concepts.name: Visibility Graph
concepts.description: A graph whose vertices are polygon obstacle corners plus start and goal, with edges between mutually visible points; shortest paths among polygonal obstacles lie on it.
concepts.example: With a start, a goal and one square obstacle, connect every pair among start, goal and the four corners that can see each other without crossing the square. The shortest path in 2D always runs along these lines, hugging corners.

concepts.name: WalkSAT
concepts.description: A local search algorithm for SAT that repeatedly picks an unsatisfied clause and flips a variable in it, either randomly or to minimize broken clauses.
concepts.example: With 50 variables and a few unsatisfied clauses left, WalkSAT picks one bad clause, say (x3 or not x7 or x12), and flips one of its variables: with some probability a random one, otherwise the one that breaks the fewest other clauses.

concepts.name: Weak AI
concepts.description: AI designed to perform specific tasks or to act as if intelligent, without any claim to genuine understanding or consciousness; nearly all current AI systems are narrow AI.
concepts.example: A spam filter, a chess engine and a voice assistant all perform specific tasks that look intelligent. Weak AI makes no claim that any of them understands email, chess or speech, only that they behave usefully.

concepts.name: Weighted A*
concepts.description: A variant of A* that multiplies the heuristic by a weight above 1, finding solutions faster at the cost of optimality, with cost bounded by the weight times optimal.
concepts.example: With weight 2, A* ranks nodes by g + 2h, trusting the heuristic more and diving toward the goal. It may expand far fewer nodes, and its solution costs at most twice the optimal one when h is admissible.

concepts.name: Working Memory (Production System)
concepts.description: The database of current facts in a production system that rules match against; firing rules adds, removes or modifies these facts.
concepts.example: A diagnostic system's working memory holds 'temp = 39', 'cough = yes'. A rule fires and adds 'suspect flu'; another rule matches that new fact and adds 'recommend test'. Facts come and go as rules fire.

concepts.name: XCON
concepts.description: An expert system (R1) built at Carnegie Mellon for DEC in 1980 to configure VAX computer orders; one of the first commercially successful expert systems.
concepts.example: A DEC salesperson entered a customer's VAX order; XCON's thousands of rules checked which cabinets, cables and boards were needed and how to lay them out. It caught errors and reportedly saved DEC tens of millions a year.

concepts.name: Zero-Sum Game
concepts.description: A game in which one player's gain is exactly another's loss, so total payoffs sum to zero; chess and poker are examples, and minimax is optimal play.
concepts.example: In a game of rock-paper-scissors for $1, if you win $1 your opponent loses exactly $1, so the total is always zero. Two firms that both profit from a trade deal are not playing a zero-sum game.

concepts.name: Absolute Error Loss
concepts.description: A loss function equal to the absolute difference between prediction and target; minimizing it yields the median and is more robust to outliers than squared error.
concepts.example: Predicting 7 when the truth is 10 costs |7 - 10| = 3, and missing by 30 costs 30, only ten times more, not a hundred times as with squared error. Guessing house prices this way makes one mansion hardly sway the model.

concepts.name: Accumulated Local Effects
concepts.description: A model explanation plot that shows how a feature affects predictions on average by accumulating local prediction differences within small intervals, avoiding the bias of partial dependence with correlated features.
concepts.example: To see how age affects a price model, split age into bins like 30-35. In each bin, nudge only the people inside from 30 to 35 and record the prediction change, then add these small changes up bin by bin into a curve.

concepts.name: Acquisition Function
concepts.description: In Bayesian optimization, a function computed from the surrogate model's mean and uncertainty, such as expected improvement or UCB, that picks the next point to evaluate by balancing exploration and exploitation.
concepts.example: After 5 trial runs, the surrogate predicts learning rate 0.01 is likely good, and 0.3 is unknown but might be great. Expected improvement scores both and picks whichever offers the biggest expected gain to try next.

concepts.name: AdaBoost
concepts.description: A boosting algorithm that trains weak learners in sequence, increasing the weights of examples the previous learners misclassified, and combines them with a weighted vote.
concepts.example: Round 1: a stump splits on 'age > 30' and gets 3 of 10 examples wrong. Those 3 get heavier weights, so round 2's stump focuses on them. The final model is a weighted vote of all stumps, more accurate ones counting more.

concepts.name: ADASYN
concepts.description: An oversampling method for imbalanced data that generates more synthetic minority examples in regions where the minority class is harder to learn, extending SMOTE adaptively.
concepts.example: In a fraud dataset, a fraud case surrounded by mostly normal transactions is hard to learn, so ADASYN creates many synthetic frauds near it. A fraud case among other frauds is easy, so it gets few or none.

concepts.name: Affinity Propagation
concepts.description: A clustering algorithm in which data points exchange responsibility and availability messages until a set of exemplars emerges, without needing the number of clusters in advance.
concepts.example: Picture 20 people voting on group leaders: each sends 'you'd represent me well' messages to good candidates, and candidates reply how available they are. After many rounds a few people emerge as exemplars, and the number of clusters falls out on its own.

concepts.name: Agglomerative Clustering
concepts.description: Bottom-up hierarchical clustering that starts with each point in its own cluster and repeatedly merges the two closest clusters according to a linkage criterion.
concepts.example: With points at 1, 2, 6, 7 and 15, first merge {1,2} and {6,7}, the closest pairs, then merge those two groups, and finally add 15. Cutting the resulting tree at different heights gives 2, 3 or more clusters.

concepts.name: Alternating Least Squares
concepts.description: An algorithm for matrix factorization that alternately fixes one factor matrix and solves a least squares problem for the other; widely used for collaborative filtering.
concepts.example: To factor a ratings matrix into user and movie vectors: fix the movie vectors and solve an ordinary least squares problem for each user, then fix users and solve for each movie. Repeat until the error stops dropping.

concepts.name: Approximate Nearest Neighbor Search
concepts.description: Finding points that are close to a query but not guaranteed to be the exact nearest, trading a bit of accuracy for large speedups via hashing, graphs or quantization.
concepts.example: Searching a billion photo embeddings for the closest match exactly would take seconds. An approximate index returns 10 neighbours in a few milliseconds, maybe missing the true nearest once in a while, which is fine for 'similar photos'.

concepts.name: Apriori Algorithm
concepts.description: An algorithm for finding frequent itemsets by growing them level by level and pruning any candidate with an infrequent subset, since all subsets of a frequent set must be frequent.
concepts.example: If {bread, butter} appears in fewer than 2% of baskets, then {bread, butter, jam} can't be frequent either, so Apriori never counts it. It finds frequent pairs, builds triples only from those, and so on.

concepts.name: Association Rule
concepts.description: An if-then pattern over items, X implies Y, found in transaction data, measured by support, confidence and lift; e.g. customers who buy bread often buy butter.
concepts.example: In 1,000 baskets, 100 contain diapers and 60 of those also contain beer. The rule {diapers} -> {beer} has support 6% and confidence 60%; if only 20% of all baskets contain beer, its lift is 3.

concepts.name: Association Rule Learning
concepts.description: Unsupervised discovery of interesting association rules in large transactional databases, typically by finding frequent itemsets and then generating high-confidence rules from them.
concepts.example: A supermarket mines a year of receipts and discovers that customers buying pasta and tomatoes often buy parmesan. Nobody asked about parmesan; the algorithm surfaced the pattern itself from the data.

concepts.name: Auto-sklearn
concepts.description: An AutoML library built on scikit-learn that automatically selects models, preprocessing and hyperparameters using Bayesian optimization, meta-learning warm starts and ensemble building.
concepts.example: Given a CSV of customer data and 1 hour, Auto-sklearn tries combinations like scaling + random forest or PCA + SVM, guided by what worked on similar past datasets, and returns an ensemble of the best pipelines.

concepts.name: Automated Machine Learning
concepts.description: Automating the steps of building ML models, such as preprocessing, model selection, hyperparameter tuning and ensembling, so good models can be found with little manual work.
concepts.example: Instead of a data scientist spending a week trying gradient boosting with 50 settings, AutoML runs the search: it tries encoders, models and hyperparameters, scores each by cross-validation, and hands back the best pipeline.

concepts.name: Average Linkage
concepts.description: A cluster distance used in hierarchical clustering defined as the average pairwise distance between points in the two clusters (UPGMA).
concepts.example: Cluster A has points 1 and 2, cluster B has 5 and 9. The pairwise distances are 4, 8, 3 and 7, so the average-linkage distance is 22 / 4 = 5.5, sitting between single linkage (3) and complete linkage (8).

concepts.name: Average Precision
concepts.description: A summary of the precision-recall curve computed as the weighted mean of precision at each threshold, weighted by the increase in recall; close to the area under the PR curve.
concepts.example: A search returns 5 results; relevant ones are at ranks 1, 3 and 4. Precision at those ranks is 1/1, 2/3 and 3/4, so AP = (1 + 0.67 + 0.75) / 3 = 0.81. Putting relevant items higher raises AP.

concepts.name: Backward Elimination
concepts.description: A feature selection method that starts with all features and repeatedly removes the one whose removal hurts the model least, until a stopping criterion is met.
concepts.example: Start with all 10 features in a model. Try dropping each one, see which removal hurts validation accuracy least, drop it, and repeat. Stop when every remaining feature clearly matters.

concepts.name: Bootstrap Aggregating
concepts.description: An ensemble method that trains many copies of a model on bootstrap resamples of the training data and averages or votes their predictions, reducing variance.
concepts.example: Train 100 decision trees, each on a random sample of the data drawn with replacement, and let them vote. Each tree is noisy, but their errors partly cancel, so the vote is far more stable than any single tree.

concepts.name: Balanced Accuracy
concepts.description: The average of recall over all classes, which for binary problems is the mean of sensitivity and specificity; it is not inflated by class imbalance like plain accuracy.
concepts.example: With 95 healthy and 5 sick patients, calling everyone healthy gives 95% accuracy. Balanced accuracy averages 100% recall on healthy and 0% on sick, scoring just 50% and exposing the useless model.

concepts.name: Balanced Random Forest
concepts.description: A random forest variant for imbalanced data where each tree is trained on a bootstrap sample with the majority class undersampled to match the minority class size.
concepts.example: With 1,000 normal and 50 fraud cases, each tree sees all 50 frauds (bootstrapped) plus a random 50 normals. Every tree learns from a 50/50 mix, and the forest still uses many different normals overall.

concepts.name: Ball Tree
concepts.description: A space-partitioning tree that groups points into nested hyperspheres, enabling fast nearest-neighbor queries in moderately high dimensions and with general distance metrics.
concepts.example: Points are grouped into a big ball, split into two smaller balls, and so on. To find the nearest café, if your current best is 200 m away and a ball's surface is 500 m away, every point in that ball is skipped at once.

concepts.name: Batch Learning
concepts.description: Training a model on the whole available dataset at once, then deploying it unchanged until it is retrained from scratch on new data, as opposed to online learning.
concepts.example: A bank trains a credit model on all of last year's loans, deploys it, and leaves it fixed. When new data piles up, it retrains on the full dataset over a weekend rather than updating after each new loan.

concepts.name: Bayes Error Rate
concepts.description: The lowest possible error rate any classifier can achieve on a problem, due to overlapping class distributions; it is the error of the Bayes optimal classifier.
concepts.example: If 10% of 180 cm people are women and 90% are men, even a perfect classifier predicting sex from height alone must be wrong 10% of the time at 180 cm. That unavoidable error, averaged over all heights, is the Bayes error rate.

concepts.name: Bayes Optimal Classifier
concepts.description: The ideal classifier that assigns each input to the class with the highest true posterior probability, achieving the minimum possible expected error.
concepts.example: If for an email P(spam | words) = 0.8 and P(not spam | words) = 0.2, the Bayes optimal classifier says spam. Knowing the true probabilities for every email, no other rule could make fewer mistakes on average.

concepts.name: Bayesian Model Averaging
concepts.description: Combining predictions from multiple models weighted by their posterior probabilities given the data, accounting for uncertainty about which model is correct.
concepts.example: Three models predict tomorrow's rain at 60%, 80% and 30%, with posterior probabilities 0.5, 0.3 and 0.2. BMA predicts 0.5 x 60 + 0.3 x 80 + 0.2 x 30 = 60%, rather than betting everything on one model.

concepts.name: Bayesian Personalized Ranking
concepts.description: A learning-to-rank objective for implicit-feedback recommenders that maximizes the probability that a user prefers an observed item over an unobserved one, trained by SGD on sampled pairs.
concepts.example: A user clicked on items A and B but not C. Rather than predicting clicks directly, BPR trains so that the score of A beats C and B beats C for this user, learning a ranking from implicit clicks.

concepts.name: Bernoulli Naive Bayes
concepts.description: A naive Bayes classifier for binary features, modeling each feature as a Bernoulli variable given the class; suited to text represented by word presence or absence.
concepts.example: A spam filter checks yes/no features: does the email contain 'free'? 'winner'? 'meeting'? Each word's presence is a coin flip with a class-specific chance, and missing words count as evidence too.

concepts.name: Biclustering
concepts.description: Simultaneously clustering the rows and columns of a data matrix to find submatrices with coherent patterns, e.g. groups of genes that behave alike under a subset of conditions.
concepts.example: In a gene-by-patient matrix, biclustering might find 20 genes that are all highly active in 15 particular patients, a pattern invisible if you cluster all genes over all patients or all patients over all genes.

concepts.name: Binary Classification
concepts.description: A supervised task where each example must be assigned to one of two classes, such as spam or not spam, often by thresholding a predicted probability.
concepts.example: An email filter outputs a spam probability of 0.92; above a threshold of 0.5 that becomes 'spam'. Fraud or not, sick or healthy, click or no click: all are binary classification tasks.

concepts.name: BIRCH
concepts.description: A scalable clustering algorithm that summarizes data into a compact clustering-feature tree in a single pass, then clusters the tree's leaf summaries; suited to very large datasets.
aliases: balanced iterative reducing and clustering using hierarchies
concepts.example: Reading a million points once, BIRCH keeps a running summary per small cluster: count, sum and sum of squares. These tiny summaries form a tree that fits in memory, and a final clustering runs on them.

concepts.name: Bisecting k-Means
concepts.description: A divisive clustering method that starts with all points in one cluster and repeatedly splits a chosen cluster in two with k-means until k clusters exist.
concepts.example: Start with all customers in one cluster and split it with 2-means. Then pick the cluster with the biggest spread and split it again. Stop after, say, 5 clusters, getting a hierarchy along the way.

concepts.name: Blending
concepts.description: An ensemble technique that trains a meta-model on base models' predictions over a held-out validation set, a simpler variant of stacking without cross-validated predictions.
concepts.example: Train a random forest and a neural network on 80% of the data, then get their predictions on the other 20%. Fit a simple logistic regression on those held-out predictions to learn how much to trust each model.

concepts.name: BOHB
concepts.description: A hyperparameter optimization method that combines Hyperband's early stopping of poor configurations with Bayesian optimization (TPE-style density models) to propose promising ones.
concepts.example: Out of 81 hyperparameter settings, Hyperband trains each briefly and keeps only the best third for longer runs. BOHB proposes those settings with a TPE-style model of what worked before, rather than picking them at random.

concepts.name: Boosting
concepts.description: An ensemble approach that trains weak learners sequentially, each one focusing on the errors of those before it, and combines them into a strong learner that reduces bias.
concepts.example: One shallow tree predicts house prices poorly. A second tree is trained to fix the first one's mistakes, a third fixes what's left, and so on. Summing 500 such small corrections gives a highly accurate model.

concepts.name: Borderline-SMOTE
concepts.description: A SMOTE variant that only generates synthetic samples from minority examples near the class boundary, where misclassification is most likely.
concepts.example: In a fraud dataset, frauds deep among other frauds are easy, and frauds surrounded entirely by normal cases may be noise. Borderline-SMOTE only creates synthetic examples from frauds near the boundary, where they help most.

concepts.name: Boruta
concepts.description: A wrapper feature selection algorithm that compares each feature's random forest importance with that of shuffled shadow copies and keeps only features that beat the best shadow consistently.
concepts.example: Copy each feature and shuffle the copy, creating 'shadow' features that are pure noise. Train a random forest; any real feature not clearly more important than the best shadow, over many runs, is rejected.

concepts.name: Brier Score
concepts.description: The mean squared difference between predicted probabilities and actual binary outcomes; lower is better and it rewards both calibration and discrimination.
concepts.example: Forecasting 70% rain and it rains gives (0.7 - 1)^2 = 0.09; forecasting 70% and it stays dry gives 0.49. Averaged over many days, this rewards forecasts that are both confident and correct.

concepts.name: BrownBoost
concepts.description: A boosting algorithm designed to be robust to label noise that gives up on persistently misclassified examples, based on a time-limited Brownian-motion-inspired weighting.
concepts.example: If a training example is mislabeled, AdaBoost keeps raising its weight forever and gets distracted. BrownBoost has a time budget, and examples still misclassified late on are given up, which suits noisy labels.

concepts.name: C4.5
