concepts.description: A decision tree algorithm that extends ID3 by splitting on gain ratio, handling continuous attributes and missing values, and pruning the tree after growing it.
concepts.example: To predict whether to play tennis, C4.5 might split on outlook (3 branches), then on humidity using a threshold like 'humidity > 75' it found itself, and finally prune branches that don't help on unseen data.

concepts.name: C5.0
concepts.description: A commercial successor to C4.5 that builds decision trees and rule sets faster and with less memory, adding boosting and misclassification costs.
concepts.example: Trained on the same data as C4.5, C5.0 builds a tree in a fraction of the time and memory, can convert it into a neat rule set, and can boost 10 trees for extra accuracy.

concepts.name: Calibration Curve
concepts.description: A plot of observed outcome frequency against predicted probability in bins; a well-calibrated classifier lies on the diagonal, meaning 70% predictions come true 70% of the time.
concepts.example: Group predictions into bins: among cases predicted at about 80%, if only 60% are actually positive, the curve dips below the diagonal, showing the model is overconfident there.

concepts.name: Calinski–Harabasz Index
concepts.description: A clustering quality score equal to the ratio of between-cluster to within-cluster dispersion, adjusted for the number of clusters; higher values mean better-separated clusters.
concepts.example: With three tight, well-separated blobs, the spread between cluster centres is large and the spread within each blob is small, so the ratio, and the CH score, is high. Try k = 2 to 6 and pick the highest.

concepts.name: Canonical Correlation Analysis
concepts.description: A method that finds pairs of linear combinations of two sets of variables that are maximally correlated with each other, revealing shared structure between two views of the data.
concepts.example: Given students' test scores (math, reading) and their habits (sleep, study hours), CCA finds the mix of scores and the mix of habits that move together most strongly, such as 'overall score' with 'study hours plus sleep'.

concepts.name: Classification and Regression Trees
concepts.description: A decision tree algorithm that builds binary trees by greedily choosing splits that minimize Gini impurity for classification or squared error for regression, then prunes by cost-complexity.
concepts.example: To predict loan default, CART tries every feature and threshold, such as 'income < 40k', and picks the split that leaves the two child groups purest by Gini impurity. It repeats on each side, always making binary splits.

concepts.name: Cascading Classifiers
concepts.description: A sequence of classifiers where cheap early stages quickly reject easy negatives and only hard cases pass to more complex later stages, as in Viola-Jones face detection.
concepts.example: A face detector scans a million image windows. Stage 1, a tiny check, throws out 50% that clearly aren't faces; stage 2 throws out most of the rest. Only a few hundred windows ever reach the slow, accurate final stage.

concepts.name: CatBoost
concepts.description: A gradient boosting library from Yandex that uses ordered boosting and ordered target statistics to handle categorical features natively without target leakage, with symmetric trees.
concepts.example: To encode a 'city' column, CatBoost replaces each row's city with the average target of earlier rows with the same city, in a random order. Each row never sees its own label, which avoids leakage.

concepts.name: Centroid
concepts.description: The mean position of a set of points, computed coordinate by coordinate; in k-means each cluster is represented by its centroid.
concepts.example: The centroid of points (1, 2), (3, 4) and (5, 0) is ((1+3+5)/3, (2+4+0)/3) = (3, 2). In k-means each cluster is summarized by such a point, which need not be one of the data points.

concepts.name: CHAID
concepts.description: A decision tree algorithm that chooses multiway splits using chi-squared tests of independence between predictors and the target, merging categories that are not significantly different.
concepts.example: For predicting purchases, CHAID tests age group against buy/no-buy with a chi-squared test, finds a significant link, and splits age into 3 merged groups at once, rather than only binary splits.

concepts.name: Chebyshev Distance
concepts.description: The distance between two points defined as the largest absolute difference across any coordinate, the L-infinity norm of their difference.
concepts.example: From (1, 1) to (4, 3), the coordinate gaps are 3 and 2, so the Chebyshev distance is 3. It's the number of moves a chess king needs, since it can step diagonally and fix both gaps at once.

concepts.name: CLARA
concepts.description: A clustering method for large datasets that runs k-medoids (PAM) on several random samples and keeps the medoids that give the lowest cost on the full data.
concepts.example: With a million customers, running PAM on all of them is far too slow. CLARA draws 5 random samples of 1,000, runs PAM on each, scores each set of medoids on the full data, and keeps the best set.

concepts.name: Classification
concepts.description: A supervised learning task of predicting a discrete category for each input, such as which digit an image shows, from labeled examples.
concepts.example: Given a photo, a classifier outputs 'cat', 'dog' or 'bird'. Given an email, 'spam' or 'not spam'. The answer is always one of a fixed set of categories, unlike predicting a number such as a price.

concepts.name: Classification Threshold
concepts.description: The cutoff applied to a predicted probability or score to decide the class; moving it trades precision against recall, so it is tuned to the costs of errors.
concepts.example: A model gives an email 0.4 spam probability. At threshold 0.5 it lands in the inbox; at 0.3 it goes to spam. Lowering the threshold catches more spam but also flags more real mail.

concepts.name: Classification Tree
concepts.description: A decision tree whose leaves predict class labels, built by recursively splitting data on feature tests that most reduce class impurity.
concepts.example: To predict whether a passenger survived, a tree might ask 'female?' then 'class 1 or 2?' and so on. Each leaf predicts the majority label of the training passengers who ended up there.

concepts.name: Clustering
concepts.description: The task of grouping data points so that points in the same group are more similar to each other than to points in other groups, without using labels. Used for segmentation, exploration and compression.
concepts.example: Given 1,000 customers' purchase histories and no labels, a clustering algorithm might reveal groups like 'bargain hunters', 'weekend shoppers' and 'big spenders' based on how similar their histories are.

concepts.name: Co-Training
concepts.description: A semi-supervised method that trains two classifiers on two different, conditionally independent feature views of the data, with each one labeling confident unlabeled examples to teach the other.
concepts.example: To classify web pages with few labels, train one classifier on page text and another on links pointing to the page. Each labels the unlabeled pages it is most sure about, and those labels teach the other.

concepts.name: Cohen's Kappa
concepts.description: A measure of agreement between two raters or between predictions and labels that corrects for the agreement expected by chance: kappa = (observed agreement − chance agreement) / (1 − chance agreement).
concepts.example: Two doctors agree on 80% of 100 X-rays. If chance alone would give 50% agreement, kappa = (0.80 - 0.50) / (1 - 0.50) = 0.6, a moderate agreement beyond luck.

concepts.name: Cold Start Problem
concepts.description: The difficulty a recommender system faces when a new user or new item has little or no interaction history, so collaborative signals are missing and recommendations must rely on content or popularity.
concepts.example: A new streaming user has watched nothing, so 'people like you also watched' has no data to go on. Services ask for a few favourite genres at sign-up, or show popular titles, until clicks accumulate.

concepts.name: Collaborative Filtering
concepts.description: A recommendation approach that predicts what a user will like from the preferences of similar users or the ratings of similar items, using only the user–item interaction history rather than item content.
concepts.example: Ana and Ben both loved the same 5 films. Ben also loved a sixth film that Ana hasn't seen, so it's recommended to her, without the system knowing anything about what the films are about.

concepts.name: Complement Naive Bayes
concepts.description: A variant of multinomial Naive Bayes that estimates each class's word statistics from all documents not in that class, which makes it more stable on imbalanced text classification problems.
concepts.example: With 900 sports articles and 100 science ones, standard naive Bayes estimates 'science' word counts from few documents. Complement NB instead learns from everything that isn't science, a large sample, and picks the class that fits its complement worst.

concepts.name: Complete-Linkage Clustering
concepts.description: A rule for hierarchical clustering that measures the distance between two clusters as the largest distance between any pair of their points, producing compact clusters of similar diameter.
concepts.example: Cluster A has points 1 and 2, cluster B has 5 and 9. The farthest pair is 1 and 9, so the complete-linkage distance is 8. Merging only when even the farthest points are close yields compact, round clusters.

concepts.name: Conditional Inference Tree
concepts.description: A decision tree that chooses splits using statistical significance tests (permutation tests) and stops when no split is significant, which avoids the bias of impurity-based trees toward variables with many values.
concepts.example: At each node the tree runs a permutation test for every feature against the target. If the strongest link has p < 0.05 it splits on that feature; if no feature is significant, it stops, needing no pruning.

concepts.name: Confidence (Association Rules)
concepts.description: For an association rule X → Y, the fraction of transactions containing X that also contain Y, i.e. an estimate of P(Y | X); used to judge how reliable a rule is.
concepts.example: Of 200 baskets with bread, 150 also have butter, so the rule bread -> butter has confidence 150 / 200 = 75%. The reverse rule butter -> bread can have quite different confidence.

concepts.name: Consensus Clustering
concepts.description: A method that runs clustering many times (on resamples, with different algorithms or settings) and combines the results into one stable partition, often via a co-association matrix of how often points cluster together.
concepts.example: Run k-means 100 times on random subsamples. If two genes land in the same cluster 95 times, they truly belong together; if only 50 times, their grouping is shaky. A final clustering is built from these co-occurrence rates.

concepts.name: Content-Based Filtering
concepts.description: A recommendation approach that suggests items whose features (genre, keywords, descriptions) resemble those of items a user liked before, building a profile of each user's tastes from item content.
concepts.example: You watched three space sci-fi films, so a content-based system recommends another film tagged 'space' and 'sci-fi', matched by its features rather than by what other users did.

concepts.name: Cost-Complexity Pruning
concepts.description: A pruning method for CART trees that adds a penalty alpha times the number of leaves to the tree's error and finds the sequence of best subtrees as alpha grows, choosing alpha by cross-validation.
concepts.example: A full tree has 20 leaves and training error 0.05. With alpha = 0.01, a 5-leaf subtree with error 0.10 scores 0.10 + 0.05 = 0.15, beating 0.05 + 0.20 = 0.25. Cross-validation picks the best alpha.

concepts.name: Cost-Sensitive Learning
concepts.description: Training classifiers to minimise the total cost of mistakes when different errors have different costs, e.g. by weighting classes, using a cost matrix, or moving the decision threshold.
concepts.example: Missing a cancer case might cost 100 times more than a false alarm. A cost-sensitive model weights mistakes accordingly, accepting more false alarms to cut missed cases.

concepts.name: Covariate Shift
concepts.description: A type of dataset shift where the distribution of inputs changes between training and deployment while the relationship P(y | x) stays the same; often corrected with importance weighting.
concepts.example: A skin-lesion model trained on light-skinned patients is deployed where most patients have darker skin. How lesions relate to diagnoses hasn't changed, but the inputs look different, so accuracy can drop.

concepts.name: Cross-Entropy Loss
concepts.description: A loss for classification that measures the negative log-probability a model assigns to the correct class; minimising it equals maximum likelihood and strongly penalises confident wrong predictions.
concepts.example: If a model gives the true class 'cat' probability 0.9, the loss is -ln 0.9 = 0.11; at 0.1 it is -ln 0.1 = 2.3. Confident wrong answers are punished heavily, pushing the model to put mass on the right class.

concepts.name: Curse of Dimensionality
concepts.description: The collection of problems that arise in high-dimensional spaces: data become sparse, distances between points become similar, and the data needed to cover the space grows exponentially with dimension.
concepts.example: To cover a line with points 0.1 apart takes 10 points; a square needs 100; a 10-dimensional cube needs 10 billion. In high dimensions data are sparse and nearest and farthest neighbours end up almost equally far.

concepts.name: Data Preprocessing
concepts.description: The steps that turn raw data into a form a model can use, such as cleaning, handling missing values, encoding categories, scaling features and splitting into training and test sets.
concepts.example: Raw customer data has ages like '42', 'forty' and blanks, and incomes in dollars and thousands. Preprocessing fixes types, fills blanks, encodes 'city' as numbers and scales income so a model can learn from it.

concepts.name: Davies–Bouldin Index
concepts.description: An internal clustering score that averages, over clusters, the worst ratio of within-cluster scatter to between-centroid distance; lower values mean compact, well-separated clusters.
concepts.example: For each cluster, find the other cluster it is most easily confused with: (spread A + spread B) / distance between centres. Average these worst-case ratios over clusters; lower scores mean tighter, better-separated clusters.

concepts.name: DBSCAN
concepts.description: A density-based clustering algorithm that grows clusters from core points having at least minPts neighbors within radius eps, finds clusters of arbitrary shape, and labels sparse points as noise.
aliases: density-based spatial clustering of applications with noise
concepts.example: With eps = 1 km and minPts = 5, a house with 5 or more neighbours within 1 km is a core point. Neighbourhoods chain through core points into towns of any shape, and lone farmhouses are labeled noise.

concepts.name: Decision Boundary
concepts.description: The surface in feature space that separates regions where a classifier predicts different classes; its shape (linear or curved) reflects the model's flexibility.
concepts.example: A spam classifier with two features, number of links and number of exclamation marks, might draw a line on that plot: emails above it are spam, below it are not. A deep network can draw a wiggly curve instead.

concepts.name: Decision List
concepts.description: An ordered list of if–then rules where the first rule whose condition matches an example decides its class, with a default class at the end; easy to read and closely related to decision trees.
concepts.example: Rule 1: if the email contains 'lottery', spam. Rule 2: else if it's from a contact, not spam. Rule 3: else if it has more than 3 links, spam. Default: not spam. Each email is decided by the first rule that matches.

concepts.name: Decision Stump
concepts.description: A one-level decision tree that predicts using a single threshold test on one feature; very weak alone but commonly used as the base learner in boosting.
concepts.example: To guess whether someone will buy an umbrella, a stump asks just one question: "Is rain forecast above 50%?" Yes means predict buy, no means predict no buy. That's the whole model.

concepts.name: Decision Tree
concepts.description: A model that predicts by asking a sequence of feature tests arranged as a tree, splitting data at each node to make the child groups purer, and outputting the value stored at the leaf reached.
concepts.example: To decide whether to play tennis, a tree first asks "Is it raining?"; if no, it asks "Is it windy?"; each path of yes/no answers ends at a leaf that says play or don't play.

concepts.name: Dendrogram
concepts.description: A tree diagram that records the order and distances at which clusters merge or split in hierarchical clustering; cutting it at a chosen height yields a flat clustering.
concepts.example: Clustering 5 animals, a dendrogram first joins cat and lion at height 1, then dog and wolf at height 1.5, then those two pairs at height 4. Cutting at height 2 gives the groups {cat, lion}, {dog, wolf}, {snake}.

concepts.name: Density-Based Clustering
concepts.description: A family of clustering methods that defines clusters as dense regions of points separated by sparse regions, which lets them find arbitrarily shaped clusters and flag outliers.
concepts.example: Picture people on a beach seen from above: crowded patches around umbrellas form clusters of any shape, while the few lone walkers between them are labelled as noise rather than forced into a group.

concepts.name: Density Estimation
concepts.description: The problem of estimating the probability density function that generated a sample of data, using parametric models like Gaussians or nonparametric ones like histograms and kernel density estimates.
concepts.example: Given the heights of 1,000 adults, you can draw a smooth curve showing how likely each height is, so you can read off that 170 cm is common and 210 cm is very rare.

concepts.name: Dictionary Learning
concepts.description: A method that learns a set of basis vectors (a dictionary) so that each data point can be written as a sparse combination of them; used for denoising, compression and feature learning.
concepts.example: Like learning a small set of Lego bricks from which every image patch can be built: each patch is rebuilt from just 3 or 4 of the 256 learned bricks, with the rest left unused.

concepts.name: Diffusion Map
concepts.description: A nonlinear dimensionality reduction method that builds a random walk on a similarity graph of the data and embeds points using eigenvectors of the transition matrix, preserving diffusion distances.
concepts.example: Drop a drunk walker on a Swiss roll of points who steps only to near neighbours; points the walker reaches from each other quickly in a few steps get placed close together in the flat 2D map.

concepts.name: Dimensionality Reduction
concepts.description: Techniques that map high-dimensional data to fewer dimensions while keeping its important structure, used for visualization, compression, denoising and faster learning; PCA and t-SNE are examples.
concepts.example: A photo of a face has 10,000 pixel values, but a few numbers such as head angle, lighting direction and smile width capture most of how the photos differ, so you can describe each face with those few numbers instead.

concepts.name: Dirichlet Process Mixture Model
concepts.description: A Bayesian nonparametric mixture model that uses a Dirichlet process prior over components, so the number of clusters is not fixed in advance and grows with the data as needed.
concepts.example: Like a restaurant where each new diner joins an existing table with probability proportional to how many people sit there, or opens a new table; tables are clusters, so the data decides how many clusters there are.

concepts.name: Discretization
concepts.description: Converting a continuous variable into a small number of intervals or bins (equal-width, equal-frequency or supervised), which can simplify models, reduce noise or suit algorithms needing categories.
concepts.example: Ages from 0 to 90 can be turned into four bins: child (0-12), teen (13-19), adult (20-64) and senior (65+), so a model sees four categories instead of 91 different numbers.

concepts.name: Discriminative Model
concepts.description: A model that directly learns the conditional distribution P(y | x) or a decision rule mapping inputs to labels, without modelling how the inputs are generated; logistic regression is a classic example.
concepts.example: To tell cats from dogs, a discriminative model learns only the dividing line, such as pointy ears and a short snout meaning cat, without ever learning how to draw a cat or a dog.

concepts.name: Distance Metric
concepts.description: A function measuring how far apart two points are that is non-negative, zero only for identical points, symmetric and obeys the triangle inequality; the basis for nearest neighbor and clustering methods.
concepts.example: Distance between towns along straight roads is a metric: it is never negative, zero only for the same town, the same both ways, and going via a third town is never shorter than going direct.

concepts.name: Divisive Clustering
concepts.description: A top-down hierarchical clustering approach that starts with all points in one cluster and recursively splits clusters (e.g. with DIANA or bisecting k-means) until each point is alone or a stop rule is met.
concepts.example: Start with a whole school as one group, split it into juniors and seniors, then split seniors into science and arts students, and so on, until the groups are as fine as you want.

concepts.name: Domain Adaptation
concepts.description: Methods for making a model trained on a labeled source domain work well on a different target domain with little or no labeled data, e.g. by reweighting samples or learning domain-invariant features.
concepts.example: A sign reader trained on sunny daytime photos struggles at night; domain adaptation uses lots of unlabeled night photos to adjust it so it reads signs well in the dark too.

concepts.name: Double Descent
concepts.description: The observation that test error first falls, then rises near the point where a model can just fit the training data, and then falls again as model size or training time keeps increasing.
concepts.example: As you give a polynomial more terms, test error falls, spikes when the number of terms equals the 20 data points, then falls again as you add hundreds more, ending lower than the first dip.

concepts.name: Dunn Index
concepts.description: An internal clustering score equal to the smallest distance between points in different clusters divided by the largest cluster diameter; higher values mean compact, well-separated clusters.
concepts.example: If the closest two points from different clusters are 6 units apart and the widest cluster spans 2 units, the Dunn index is 6 / 2 = 3; bigger means tight, well-separated clusters.

concepts.name: Early Stopping
concepts.description: A regularization technique that monitors performance on validation data during training and stops when it stops improving, keeping the best model before it starts to overfit.
concepts.example: Training for 100 epochs, validation loss bottoms out at epoch 30 and then creeps up; with a patience of 5, training stops at epoch 35 and you keep the weights saved at epoch 30.

concepts.name: EasyEnsemble
concepts.description: An imbalanced-learning method that draws several balanced random undersamples of the majority class, trains an AdaBoost model on each, and combines them, so little majority data is wasted.
concepts.example: With 1,000 normal and 50 fraud cases, draw 10 random sets of 50 normal cases, pair each with all 50 frauds, train an AdaBoost model on each balanced set, and let all 10 vote.

concepts.name: Eclat
concepts.description: A frequent itemset mining algorithm that stores for each itemset the list of transaction IDs containing it and finds supports of larger itemsets by intersecting these lists in a depth-first search.
concepts.example: If bread appears in transactions {1, 2, 5} and milk in {2, 5, 7}, Eclat intersects the lists to get {2, 5}, so bread+milk appears in 2 transactions without rescanning the data.

concepts.name: Elbow Method
concepts.description: A heuristic for choosing the number of clusters by plotting within-cluster sum of squares against k and picking the point where adding more clusters stops giving large improvements.
concepts.example: Inertia for k = 1 to 6 might be 500, 200, 90, 80, 72, 66. The big drops stop after k = 3, so the curve bends like an elbow there and you pick 3 clusters.

concepts.name: Elliptic Envelope
concepts.description: An outlier detector that fits a robust estimate of the mean and covariance (minimum covariance determinant) to assumed Gaussian data and flags points with large Mahalanobis distance.
concepts.example: Fit an oval around a cloud of height-weight points, ignoring the most extreme ones while fitting; a 150 cm person weighing 120 kg lands far outside the oval and is flagged.

concepts.name: Embedded Method
concepts.description: Feature selection that happens as part of model training, such as Lasso shrinking weights to zero or tree models ranking features by importance, rather than as a separate filtering step.
concepts.example: Train a Lasso model on 50 features and it sets 42 weights to exactly zero; the 8 features left with nonzero weights are your selected features, chosen during training itself.

concepts.name: Empirical Risk
concepts.description: The average loss of a model over the training examples; it is the computable estimate of the true expected loss and the quantity that learning algorithms usually minimise.
concepts.example: A model predicts 3, 5 and 8 for targets 2, 5 and 10. The squared losses are 1, 0 and 4, so the empirical risk is their average, 5 / 3, or about 1.67.

concepts.name: Empirical Risk Minimization
concepts.description: The learning principle of choosing the model from a hypothesis class that has the lowest average loss on the training data, as a proxy for minimising the unknown true risk.
concepts.example: To fit a line to 10 points, try every possible slope and intercept and keep the one with the smallest average squared error on those 10 points; that is ERM with linear models.

concepts.name: Ensemble Averaging
concepts.description: Combining several models by averaging their predictions (or predicted probabilities), which reduces variance and usually gives better and more stable results than any single model.
concepts.example: Three weather models give 60%, 70% and 80% chance of rain; the ensemble says 70%. Their individual mistakes partly cancel, so the average is usually more reliable than any one.

concepts.name: Ensemble Learning
concepts.description: Combining the predictions of multiple models to get better accuracy and robustness than any single one; main families include bagging, boosting and stacking.
concepts.example: Ask 100 people to guess the number of jellybeans in a jar: individual guesses are way off, but their average is often closer than almost any single guess.

concepts.name: Error-Correcting Output Codes
concepts.description: A way to solve multiclass problems by giving each class a binary codeword, training one binary classifier per bit, and predicting the class whose codeword is closest to the classifiers' outputs.
concepts.example: Give 4 classes 5-bit codes like 00111, 01010, 10011, 11100 and train 5 yes/no classifiers, one per bit. If the outputs read 01011, pick 01010, the class differing by just one bit.

concepts.name: Exclusive Feature Bundling
concepts.description: A LightGBM technique that merges sparse features that rarely take nonzero values at the same time into a single feature, reducing the number of features to scan without losing much information.
concepts.example: One-hot columns "is_red", "is_blue" and "is_green" are never 1 at the same time, so LightGBM packs them into one column with values 1, 2, 3, cutting three features down to one.

concepts.name: Expected Calibration Error
concepts.description: A calibration metric that bins predictions by confidence and averages the gap between average confidence and actual accuracy in each bin, weighted by the number of samples in the bin.
concepts.example: Of all predictions made with about 90% confidence, only 75% turned out right, so that bin's gap is 15 points; ECE averages such gaps over all bins, weighted by how many predictions fall in each.

concepts.name: Explainable AI
concepts.description: The field of methods and practices for making AI models' predictions understandable to people, through interpretable models or post-hoc explanations such as feature attributions and examples.
concepts.example: A bank's AI rejects a loan, and an explanation tool shows the main reasons were high existing debt and a short credit history, so the applicant knows what to change.

concepts.name: Explained Variance Ratio
concepts.description: In PCA, the fraction of the data's total variance captured by each principal component, equal to its eigenvalue divided by the sum of all eigenvalues; used to decide how many components to keep.
concepts.example: If PCA on 3D data gives eigenvalues 6, 3 and 1, the ratios are 60%, 30% and 10%, so keeping the first two components keeps 90% of the variance.

concepts.name: Explained Variance Score
concepts.description: A regression metric equal to 1 minus the variance of the residuals divided by the variance of the target; 1 is perfect and, unlike R², it ignores a constant bias in predictions.
concepts.example: If house prices vary with variance 100 and the model's errors have variance 20, the score is 1 - 20 / 100 = 0.8, meaning the model explains 80% of the spread in prices.

concepts.name: Explicit Feedback
concepts.description: User preference data given deliberately, such as star ratings, likes or reviews; it is clear about what users think but is sparse because most users rate few items.
concepts.example: Giving a film 2 stars out of 5 on a streaming site is explicit feedback: it clearly says you didn't like it, unlike merely having watched it, which is ambiguous.

concepts.name: Exponential Loss
concepts.description: The loss exp(−y·f(x)) for labels y in {−1, +1}, which penalises misclassified points exponentially in their margin; minimising it stagewise yields the AdaBoost algorithm.
concepts.example: With y = +1, a score of 2 gives loss e^-2, about 0.14, while a wrong score of -2 gives e^2, about 7.4; the more confidently wrong, the more the loss blows up.

concepts.name: Extremely Randomized Trees
concepts.description: An ensemble like a random forest in which each tree also picks split thresholds at random instead of optimally, which adds more randomness, lowers variance and makes training faster.
concepts.example: To split on age, a random forest tests every cut point and keeps the best; Extra Trees just picks a random cut like 37 for each candidate feature and keeps the best of those, which is faster and adds diversity.

concepts.name: F-beta Score
concepts.description: A weighted harmonic mean of precision and recall where beta sets how many times more recall matters than precision; F1 is the case beta = 1, F2 favours recall and F0.5 favours precision.
concepts.example: With precision 0.5 and recall 1.0, F1 is about 0.67, but F2, which counts recall twice as much, is about 0.83, a good fit for cancer screening where missing a case is worse.

concepts.name: Factorization Machine
concepts.description: A model that adds pairwise feature interactions to a linear model and represents each interaction weight as a dot product of low-dimensional latent vectors, working well on sparse data like recommendations.
concepts.example: For ad clicks, the pair "user is a teen" + "ad is for games" gets its interaction weight from the dot product of two learned vectors, so it can be estimated even if that pair was never seen together.

concepts.name: FastICA
concepts.description: A fast fixed-point algorithm for independent component analysis that whitens the data and then finds directions that maximise non-Gaussianity (e.g. negentropy) to separate mixed signals.
concepts.example: At a party, two microphones record mixtures of two speakers; FastICA whitens the recordings, then repeatedly updates a direction until the signal along it is as non-Gaussian as possible, recovering each voice.

concepts.name: Feature Space
concepts.description: The space of all possible feature vectors, where each dimension corresponds to one feature; data points are positions in it and models learn regions or surfaces within it.
concepts.example: Describe fruits by weight and sweetness: each fruit becomes a dot on a 2D chart, with apples clustered in one area and lemons in another. That chart is the feature space.

concepts.name: Feature Vector
concepts.description: An ordered list of numbers that describes one example, with one entry per feature, such as a house's size, rooms and age; it is the standard input format for machine learning models.
concepts.example: A house with 120 square metres, 3 bedrooms and built in 1995 becomes the feature vector [120, 3, 1995], which a model can do arithmetic on.

concepts.name: Few-Shot Learning
concepts.description: Learning to recognise new classes or solve new tasks from only a handful of labeled examples per class, typically by reusing knowledge from related tasks via meta-learning or pretrained models.
concepts.example: Shown just 5 photos of a rare bird species, a few-shot model can recognise new photos of it, because it has already learned from many other species how to spot what makes birds differ.

concepts.name: Field-Aware Factorization Machine
concepts.description: An extension of factorization machines in which each feature has a separate latent vector for every field it interacts with, improving accuracy on click-through-rate prediction.
concepts.example: In a plain FM the user "Alice" has one vector for every interaction; in an FFM she has one vector for pairing with publishers and another for pairing with advertisers, since those relationships can differ.

concepts.name: Filter Method
concepts.description: Feature selection that scores each feature with a statistic independent of any model, such as correlation, chi-squared or mutual information with the target, and keeps the top-scoring features.
concepts.example: Before training anything, rank 100 features by their correlation with house price and keep the top 10, regardless of what model you will use later.

concepts.name: Forward Selection
concepts.description: A greedy feature selection method that starts with no features and repeatedly adds the one that most improves model performance, stopping when no addition helps enough.
concepts.example: Start with no features; try each of 10 alone and keep the best, say income. Then try income plus each other feature and keep the best pair, and continue until adding more stops helping.

concepts.name: FP-Growth
concepts.description: A frequent itemset mining algorithm that compresses the transactions into an FP-tree and mines it recursively via conditional pattern bases, avoiding Apriori's costly candidate generation.
concepts.example: Instead of scanning the shop's receipts again and again for each item combination, FP-Growth packs all receipts into one compact tree, then reads frequent combos straight off its branches.

concepts.name: FP-Tree
concepts.description: A compact prefix-tree structure storing transactions with items sorted by frequency, so shared prefixes share nodes and counts; it is the data structure FP-Growth mines for frequent itemsets.
concepts.example: Receipts {milk, bread, eggs} and {milk, bread, jam} share the path milk to bread in the tree, with a count of 2, and split only at the last item, saving storage.

concepts.name: Frequent Itemset
concepts.description: A set of items that appears together in at least a minimum fraction (support) of transactions in a dataset; finding them is the first step in association rule mining.
concepts.example: In 100 shopping baskets, {bread, butter} appears in 30. With minimum support 20%, it is a frequent itemset, while {bread, caviar}, found in 2, is not.

concepts.name: Funk SVD
concepts.description: A recommender algorithm popularised in the Netflix Prize that factorizes the sparse rating matrix into user and item latent vectors using SGD only on observed ratings, with regularization.
concepts.example: Each user and film gets, say, 20 learned numbers; a predicted rating is their dot product. For each known rating, nudge both vectors to reduce the error, ignoring the millions of blanks.

concepts.name: Fuzzy C-Means
concepts.description: A soft clustering algorithm like k-means in which each point has a degree of membership in every cluster, and centers are weighted means using those memberships.
concepts.example: A point halfway between two cluster centres gets 50% membership in each, rather than being forced into one; each centre is then a weighted average of all points by membership.

concepts.name: Gain Ratio
concepts.description: A split criterion used in C4.5 that divides information gain by the split's own entropy, reducing the bias of plain information gain toward features with many distinct values.
concepts.example: Splitting on customer ID gives perfect information gain but creates 1,000 one-person branches; its split entropy is huge, so dividing by it makes gain ratio small and the useless split loses.

concepts.name: Gamma Regression
concepts.description: A generalized linear model for positive, right-skewed targets such as costs or durations, assuming a gamma distribution with a log (or inverse) link so variance grows with the mean.
concepts.example: Predicting insurance claim costs, which are always positive and mostly small with a few huge ones, a gamma GLM with a log link says, say, each extra decade of age raises the expected cost by 12%.

concepts.name: Gap Statistic
concepts.description: A method for choosing the number of clusters by comparing the log within-cluster dispersion to its expected value under random reference data, choosing k where the gap is largest.
concepts.example: Run k-means on your data and on random uniform data of the same range, many times; if k = 3 makes your data much tighter than the random data does, the gap is large and 3 is a good choice.

concepts.name: Gaussian Naive Bayes
concepts.description: A Naive Bayes classifier for continuous features that models each feature within each class as an independent normal distribution with its own mean and variance.
concepts.example: If adult male heights average 178 cm (sd 7) and female 165 cm (sd 6), a 175 cm person is more likely under the male bell curve, and the classifier multiplies such per-feature likelihoods together.

concepts.name: Gaussian Process Regression
concepts.description: A Bayesian nonparametric regression method that places a Gaussian process prior over functions and gives closed-form predictive means and uncertainties by conditioning on observed data.
concepts.example: With temperature readings at 9am and 3pm, a GP predicts noon by smoothly interpolating, and it also gives an error bar that is narrow near the readings and widens far from them.

concepts.name: Generative Model
concepts.description: A model that learns how data are generated, i.e. the distribution P(x) or the joint P(x, y), so it can produce new samples and classify via Bayes' rule; examples are Naive Bayes, GMMs and GANs.
concepts.example: A generative model of handwritten digits learns what 7s look like overall, so it can draw a brand-new 7, and it can also classify by asking which digit most likely produced an image.

concepts.name: GentleBoost
concepts.description: A boosting algorithm that fits each weak regression learner by weighted least squares using Newton steps on the exponential loss, giving smaller, more stable updates than AdaBoost.
concepts.example: Where AdaBoost might swing hard on a misclassified point, GentleBoost fits a small regression tree to weighted labels by least squares, so each round takes a smaller, steadier step.

concepts.name: Gini Importance
concepts.description: A feature importance score for tree models computed as the total decrease in impurity from splits on a feature, weighted by node size and averaged over trees; fast but biased toward high-cardinality features.
concepts.example: If splits on "income" reduce Gini impurity by a total of 0.30 across all trees and splits on "age" by 0.10, income is ranked three times as important.

concepts.name: Gini Impurity
concepts.description: An impurity measure for a set of labels equal to the chance that two randomly drawn items have different labels, 1 − Σ p_k²; CART uses it to choose splits.
concepts.example: A node with 5 cats and 5 dogs has Gini 1 - (0.5² + 0.5²) = 0.5; a node with 10 cats has Gini 0. Lower means purer.

concepts.name: Gower Distance
concepts.description: A dissimilarity measure for mixed data that averages per-feature distances: range-scaled absolute differences for numbers and simple mismatch for categorical values.
concepts.example: Comparing two people: ages 30 and 40 on a 20-60 range differ by 0.25, the same city gives 0, different jobs give 1; Gower distance is the average, (0.25 + 0 + 1) / 3, about 0.42.

concepts.name: Gradient-Based One-Side Sampling
concepts.description: A LightGBM sampling method that keeps all training examples with large gradients and randomly samples those with small gradients, reweighting them to keep the information gain estimate unbiased.
concepts.example: With 1 million rows, keep the 20% with the largest gradients, the badly predicted ones, randomly keep 10% of the rest, and upweight that sample so the totals stay unbiased.

concepts.name: Gradient Boosted Decision Trees
concepts.description: Gradient boosting with decision trees as the weak learners, where each new tree fits the negative gradient of the loss of the current ensemble; implemented in XGBoost, LightGBM and CatBoost.
concepts.example: Predicting house prices: tree 1 predicts 300k, leaving errors; tree 2 learns to predict those errors, tree 3 the errors left after that, and the final price is the sum of all trees' outputs.

concepts.name: Gradient Boosting
concepts.description: A boosting method that builds a model in stages, each new weak learner fitting the negative gradient of the loss with respect to the current predictions, like gradient descent in function space.
concepts.example: Like golf: the first shot lands short, each later putt aims at the remaining gap, and with squared loss each new model literally learns the leftover residuals of the ones before.

concepts.name: Grid Search
concepts.description: A hyperparameter tuning method that evaluates every combination of values from a predefined grid, usually with cross-validation, and keeps the best; simple but costly as dimensions grow.
concepts.example: Try learning rates {0.01, 0.1, 1} and tree depths {3, 5, 7}: that's 9 combinations, each scored by cross-validation, and you keep the best-scoring pair.

concepts.name: Group k-Fold Cross-Validation
concepts.description: A cross-validation scheme that keeps all samples from the same group (e.g. the same patient or user) in one fold, so the model is tested on groups it never saw and leakage is avoided.
concepts.example: With 10 X-rays from each of 50 patients, all of a patient's X-rays go in the same fold, so the model is never tested on a patient it already saw in training.

concepts.name: Hamming Loss
concepts.description: A multi-label metric equal to the fraction of individual label assignments that are wrong, averaged over all samples and labels; lower is better and partial credit is given.
concepts.example: With 2 articles and 4 possible tags each, there are 8 tag decisions; if 2 are wrong, the Hamming loss is 2 / 8 = 0.25.

concepts.name: HDBSCAN
concepts.description: A clustering algorithm that extends DBSCAN by building a hierarchy over all density levels and extracting the most stable clusters, so it handles clusters of varying density without choosing eps.
concepts.example: On a map of city lights, HDBSCAN finds both dense downtowns and sparser suburbs as clusters without one fixed radius, by checking which groups persist across many density levels.

concepts.name: Hinge Loss
concepts.description: The loss max(0, 1 − y·f(x)) for labels ±1, which is zero for points classified correctly with margin at least 1 and grows linearly otherwise; it is the loss used by support vector machines.
concepts.example: For a true label +1: a score of 2 gives loss 0, a score of 0.5 gives 0.5 since it is right but too close, and a score of -1 gives 2.

concepts.name: Histogram-Based Gradient Boosting
concepts.description: A fast gradient boosted trees variant that bins each feature into a few hundred histogram buckets and evaluates splits on bins instead of raw values, as in LightGBM and scikit-learn's HistGradientBoosting.
concepts.example: Instead of testing all 50,000 distinct income values as split points, bin income into 255 buckets once, then each split test only checks 255 options, making training much faster.

concepts.name: Histogram-Based Outlier Score
concepts.description: A fast unsupervised outlier detector that builds a histogram per feature and scores each point by summing the negative log of its bin heights, assuming features are independent.
concepts.example: If 40% of transactions are under $50 but only 0.1% are over $5,000, a $9,000 purchase falls in a nearly empty bin, so it gets a high outlier score, and scores add up across features.

concepts.name: Hit Rate
concepts.description: A recommender metric equal to the fraction of users for whom at least one relevant (e.g. held-out) item appears in the top-k recommended list.
concepts.example: Hide one film each of 100 users watched, then recommend 10 films per user; if the hidden film appears in the list for 35 users, the hit rate at 10 is 0.35.

concepts.name: Hoeffding Tree
concepts.description: An incremental decision tree for data streams that decides when to split a node by using the Hoeffding bound to judge, with high confidence, that the best attribute seen so far is truly best.
concepts.example: Watching a stream of clicks, the tree waits until, say, 2,000 examples have arrived at a node; if one split is clearly better by more than the Hoeffding bound, it splits, without storing old data.

concepts.name: Huber Loss
concepts.description: A regression loss that is quadratic for small errors and linear for large ones, combining the smoothness of squared error with the outlier robustness of absolute error.
concepts.example: With delta = 1, an error of 0.5 costs 0.125 like squared loss, but an error of 10 costs 9.5 instead of 50, so one wild outlier can't dominate training.

concepts.name: Hybrid Recommender System
concepts.description: A recommender that combines collaborative filtering with content-based or other methods, by blending scores, switching between them or using both in one model, to improve accuracy and ease cold start.
concepts.example: A new film with no ratings yet is recommended based on its genre and cast, which is content-based, while popular films lean on what similar users liked; the system blends both scores.

concepts.name: Hyperband
concepts.description: A hyperparameter optimization algorithm that runs successive halving with several different trade-offs between number of configurations and budget per configuration, quickly discarding poor ones.
concepts.example: Rather than fully training 81 configurations, Hyperband gives many a tiny budget and keeps the best third each round, and also runs brackets that start fewer configs with bigger budgets, hedging its bets.

concepts.name: Hyperopt
concepts.description: A Python library for hyperparameter optimization that searches over defined spaces using random search or the Tree-structured Parzen Estimator, with optional parallel and distributed runs.
concepts.example: You tell Hyperopt that learning rate lies between 0.001 and 0.1 and depth is 3 to 10; after each trial, its TPE algorithm proposes the next settings near ones that have scored well so far.

concepts.name: Hyperparameter
concepts.description: A setting chosen before training that controls how a model learns or how complex it is, such as learning rate, tree depth or regularization strength, as opposed to parameters learned from data.
concepts.example: In k-nearest neighbors, k = 5 is a hyperparameter: you choose it before training, unlike the stored data or a regression's slope, which come from the data.

concepts.name: Hypothesis Class
concepts.description: The set of all functions a learning algorithm can choose from, such as all linear classifiers; its size or complexity governs how well the learner can fit data and generalize.
concepts.example: If you only allow straight lines, the hypothesis class is all lines y = ax + b; no amount of data will let the algorithm pick a curve, because curves aren't in the class.

concepts.name: ID3
concepts.description: An early decision tree algorithm by Quinlan that greedily builds a tree for categorical features, choosing at each node the attribute with the highest information gain.
concepts.example: Predicting play-tennis from outlook, humidity and wind: ID3 finds outlook gives the highest information gain, splits on it, then repeats on each branch with the remaining features.

concepts.name: imbalanced-learn
concepts.description: A Python library compatible with scikit-learn that provides resampling methods for imbalanced datasets, such as SMOTE, ADASYN, random under-sampling and balanced ensembles.
concepts.example: With 990 normal and 10 fraud cases, two lines of imbalanced-learn apply SMOTE to create synthetic fraud cases, then you train any scikit-learn model on the balanced data.

concepts.name: Implicit Feedback
concepts.description: User preference signals inferred from behaviour rather than ratings, such as clicks, views, purchases or listening time; plentiful but noisy and lacking clear negative examples.
concepts.example: You never rated a song, but you played it 40 times and skipped another after 5 seconds; a recommender reads those behaviours as signs you like the first and not the second.

concepts.name: Impurity Measure
concepts.description: A function that scores how mixed the class labels (or target values) in a tree node are, such as Gini impurity, entropy or variance; trees choose splits that reduce it the most.
concepts.example: A node with 10 apples is perfectly pure; one with 5 apples and 5 oranges is maximally mixed. An impurity measure turns that mix into a number so the tree can pick the most cleansing split.

concepts.name: Incremental PCA
concepts.description: A version of PCA that updates its principal components batch by batch rather than from all data at once, allowing dimensionality reduction on datasets too large for memory or arriving as streams.
concepts.example: With 100 GB of images that won't fit in memory, feed PCA 1,000 images at a time; each batch updates the components, and the result approximates PCA on all the data.

concepts.name: Individual Conditional Expectation
concepts.description: A plot showing, for each individual instance, how the model's prediction changes as one feature varies while others stay fixed; averaging the curves gives the partial dependence plot.
concepts.example: For each of 100 houses, vary only square footage from 50 to 300 and plot the predicted price: 100 lines. If some rise steeply and others stay flat, the feature's effect differs between houses.

concepts.name: Inductive Bias
concepts.description: The set of assumptions a learning algorithm uses to generalize beyond its training data, such as preferring simple, smooth or linear functions; without some bias, learning is impossible.
concepts.example: Given points (1, 1), (2, 2), (3, 3), linear regression predicts 4 at x = 4 because it assumes lines; a different learner might predict anything. That built-in assumption is its inductive bias.

concepts.name: Inertia
concepts.description: The within-cluster sum of squares: the total squared distance from each point to its cluster centroid; k-means minimises it and lower values indicate tighter clusters.
concepts.example: Cluster A has points 1 and 3 with centre 2; cluster B has 9 and 11 with centre 10. Each point is 1 away, so inertia is 1² + 1² + 1² + 1² = 4.

concepts.name: Information Gain
concepts.description: The reduction in entropy of the target obtained by splitting data on a feature; decision tree algorithms like ID3 choose the split with the largest information gain.
concepts.example: A set of 8 emails, 4 spam, has entropy 1 bit. Splitting on "contains 'win'" gives two pure groups with entropy 0, so the information gain is 1 - 0 = 1 bit, the most possible.

concepts.name: Instance
concepts.description: A single example or row in a dataset, such as one customer, image or sentence, described by its features and, in supervised learning, a label.
concepts.example: In a spreadsheet of customers, one row, such as Jane, 34, from Paris, bought 3 items, is one instance.

concepts.name: Instance-Based Learning
concepts.description: Learning methods that store training examples and make predictions by comparing new inputs to stored ones at query time, as in k-nearest neighbors, instead of building an explicit model.
concepts.example: To price a used car, find the 5 most similar cars sold recently and average their prices; there is no training step, the stored examples are the model.

concepts.name: Interpretability
concepts.description: The degree to which a person can understand why a model makes its predictions, either because the model is simple (like a small tree) or through explanation methods.
concepts.example: A doctor can follow a 3-rule model, such as "if age > 60 and blood pressure > 140, high risk", and check that it makes sense; a 100-layer network gives no such readable reasoning.

concepts.name: Isolation Forest
concepts.description: An anomaly detection algorithm that builds random trees by randomly splitting features; anomalies are isolated in fewer splits, so a short average path length signals an outlier.
concepts.example: Randomly cut the data with lines; a lone point far from others gets isolated after 2 or 3 cuts, while a point inside a dense cloud needs 10 or more. Short average path means anomaly.

concepts.name: Isomap
concepts.description: A nonlinear dimensionality reduction method that builds a nearest-neighbor graph, approximates geodesic distances as shortest paths in it, and embeds the points with classical MDS.
concepts.example: On a Swiss roll, two points on adjacent layers are close in a straight line but far along the surface. Isomap measures distance by walking neighbour-to-neighbour, then flattens the roll preserving those walks.

concepts.name: Isotonic Regression
concepts.description: Fitting a non-decreasing (monotone) step function to data by least squares, usually with the pool-adjacent-violators algorithm; often used to calibrate classifier probabilities.
concepts.example: Fitting heights 5, 3, 4, 8 with a non-decreasing fit: the dip 5, 3, 4 violates order, so those are pooled to their average 4, giving 4, 4, 4, 8.

concepts.name: Item-Based Collaborative Filtering
concepts.description: Collaborative filtering that recommends items similar to those a user already liked, where item similarity is computed from patterns of users who rated or interacted with both items.
concepts.example: People who bought a tent also often bought sleeping bags, so the two items are similar; when you buy a tent, the site recommends a sleeping bag.

concepts.name: Johnson–Lindenstrauss Lemma
concepts.description: A theorem stating that n points in high dimensions can be mapped to about O(log n / ε²) dimensions by a random linear projection while preserving all pairwise distances within a factor 1 ± ε.
concepts.example: Take 1,000 points in a million dimensions; multiplying by a random matrix down to a few thousand dimensions keeps every pairwise distance within about 10% of its original value.

concepts.name: k-means++
concepts.description: An initialization method for k-means that picks the first center at random and each next center with probability proportional to its squared distance from the nearest chosen center, improving results.
concepts.example: After picking a random first centre, a point 10 units away is 100 times more likely to become the next centre than a point 1 unit away, since odds scale with squared distance, so centres spread out.

concepts.name: k-Medoids
concepts.description: A clustering algorithm like k-means that uses actual data points (medoids) as cluster centers and can use any distance measure, making it more robust to outliers; PAM is the classic algorithm.
concepts.example: Choosing 3 warehouse sites from existing shops: k-medoids picks actual shops as centres, minimising total road distance, whereas k-means might place a centre in the middle of a lake.

concepts.name: k-Modes
concepts.description: A k-means variant for categorical data that uses a simple matching dissimilarity and updates each cluster center to the most frequent category of each attribute; k-prototypes extends it to mixed data.
concepts.example: Clustering customers by favourite colour, city and pet: a cluster's centre might be {blue, Paris, cat}, the most common value of each, and distance is the number of mismatching attributes.

concepts.name: Kernel Function
concepts.description: A function k(x, y) that equals an inner product of x and y in some feature space, so its matrix on any data is positive semidefinite; used to measure similarity in SVMs and Gaussian processes.
concepts.example: For 2D points, k(x, y) = (x·y)² gives the same number as mapping each point to (x1², √2·x1·x2, x2²) and taking a dot product there, without building those coordinates.

concepts.name: Kernel Method
concepts.description: A family of algorithms, including SVMs, kernel PCA and Gaussian processes, that work with data only through a kernel function, allowing nonlinear patterns to be learned with linear techniques.
concepts.example: Points inside a circle versus outside can't be split by a line, but an SVM with an RBF kernel separates them easily, because it only ever compares points through kernel similarities.

concepts.name: Kernel Principal Component Analysis
concepts.description: A nonlinear version of PCA that performs principal component analysis in a feature space defined by a kernel, by eigendecomposing the centered kernel matrix instead of the covariance matrix.
concepts.example: Two concentric rings of points look inseparable to ordinary PCA, but kernel PCA with an RBF kernel maps them so that the first component cleanly separates inner ring from outer.

concepts.name: Kernel Regression
concepts.description: A nonparametric regression method (the Nadaraya–Watson estimator) that predicts at a point as a weighted average of training targets, with weights given by a kernel of the distance to each input.
concepts.example: To predict tomorrow's temperature at noon, average past noon temperatures from similar days, giving days with very similar conditions a big weight and dissimilar ones a tiny weight.

concepts.name: Kernel Ridge Regression
concepts.description: Ridge regression performed in a kernel-induced feature space, giving a closed-form solution in terms of the kernel matrix; it yields the same mean prediction as Gaussian process regression.
concepts.example: Fitting a wiggly curve through noisy points: with an RBF kernel, the prediction at a new x is a weighted sum of kernel similarities to each training point, with weights from one matrix solve.

concepts.name: Kernel Trick
concepts.description: The technique of replacing dot products in an algorithm with a kernel function, which implicitly maps data into a high-dimensional feature space without ever computing the mapping explicitly.
concepts.example: Points at x = -2, -1, 1, 2 labelled outer, inner, inner, outer can't be split on a line, but adding x² makes it easy; a kernel computes such dot products without ever building the new features.

concepts.name: K-Means Clustering
concepts.description: An unsupervised algorithm that partitions data into k clusters by repeatedly assigning each point to the nearest centroid and moving each centroid to the mean of its assigned points.
concepts.example: Place 3 pizza shops for a town: start them anywhere, assign every house to its nearest shop, move each shop to the middle of its houses, and repeat until shops stop moving.

concepts.name: K-Nearest Neighbors
concepts.description: A simple algorithm that predicts a new point's label by majority vote (or average) of the k closest training examples under a distance measure; it stores the data and has no training phase.
concepts.example: To guess if a new fruit is an apple or an orange, look at the 3 most similar fruits you know; if 2 are oranges and 1 is an apple, guess orange.

concepts.name: L1 Regularization
concepts.description: Adding the sum of absolute values of model weights times a strength λ to the loss; it pushes many weights exactly to zero, giving sparse models and implicit feature selection.
concepts.example: With weights [3, -2, 0.1] and lambda = 1, the penalty is |3| + |-2| + |0.1| = 5.1; minimising it tends to push small weights like 0.1 all the way to zero.

concepts.name: L2 Regularization
concepts.description: Adding the sum of squared model weights times a strength λ to the loss, which shrinks weights toward zero smoothly, reduces overfitting and stabilises solutions; called weight decay in neural networks.
concepts.example: With weights [3, -2, 0.1] and lambda = 1, the penalty is 9 + 4 + 0.01 = 13.01; big weights cost a lot, so the model prefers many small weights over a few large ones.

concepts.name: Label Propagation
concepts.description: A semi-supervised algorithm that builds a similarity graph over labeled and unlabeled points and iteratively spreads labels along edges until they stabilise, so nearby points receive similar labels.
concepts.example: In a friendship network where only 5 of 100 people say which team they support, each unlabelled person repeatedly takes on the mix of their friends' labels until everything settles.

concepts.name: LambdaMART
concepts.description: A learning-to-rank algorithm that combines LambdaRank's gradients, which weight pairwise swaps by their effect on NDCG, with gradient boosted regression trees (MART); long a top method in web search.
concepts.example: For a search query, LambdaMART builds boosted trees, where each tree is fitted to lambda gradients that push a relevant page up more strongly if moving it would improve NDCG a lot.

concepts.name: LambdaRank
concepts.description: A learning-to-rank method that scales RankNet's pairwise gradients by how much swapping two documents would change a ranking metric like NDCG, so training directly targets the metric.
concepts.example: Swapping results 1 and 2 changes NDCG much more than swapping results 50 and 51, so LambdaRank scales the gradient for the top pair much higher and focuses learning there.

concepts.name: Laplace Smoothing
concepts.description: Adding a small count (usually one) to every possible outcome before estimating probabilities from counts, so unseen events get nonzero probability; widely used in Naive Bayes and language models.
concepts.example: If "refund" appeared 0 times in 98 spam words, the raw estimate is 0, which zeroes out every spam probability; adding 1 to every word count gives a small nonzero estimate instead.

concepts.name: Laplacian Eigenmaps
concepts.description: A nonlinear dimensionality reduction method that builds a neighborhood graph and embeds points using the eigenvectors of the graph Laplacian with smallest nonzero eigenvalues, keeping neighbors close.
concepts.example: Connect each photo to its 10 most similar photos, then lay them out in 2D so connected photos sit close; the layout comes from the graph Laplacian's eigenvectors with the smallest nonzero eigenvalues.

concepts.name: LARS
concepts.description: Least-angle regression: a forward selection algorithm that moves coefficients in the direction equiangular to the most correlated features; a small modification computes the entire Lasso path efficiently.
concepts.example: LARS starts with all coefficients at zero, moves the one most correlated with the target until another feature becomes equally correlated, then moves both together at an equal angle, and so on.

concepts.name: Lasso Regression
concepts.description: Linear regression with an L1 penalty on the coefficients, which shrinks them and sets some exactly to zero, performing variable selection and producing simpler, more interpretable models.
aliases: least absolute shrinkage and selection operator
concepts.example: Predicting house price from 20 features, Lasso might keep size, location and age with nonzero weights and set the other 17 exactly to zero, giving a simple model.

concepts.name: Learning Curve
concepts.description: A plot of a model's training and validation performance against training set size (or training iterations), used to diagnose underfitting, overfitting and whether more data would help.
concepts.example: With 100 examples, training accuracy is 99% and validation 70%; with 10,000 they meet at 85%. The narrowing gap shows more data cured the overfitting, and the plot shows when more data stops helping.

concepts.name: Learning to Rank
concepts.description: Using machine learning to build models that order items, such as search results or recommendations, by relevance to a query; approaches are pointwise, pairwise or listwise.
concepts.example: Given a search for "pizza", a learning-to-rank model scores 50 candidate pages from features like word matches, distance and ratings, and sorts them, learned from past user clicks.

concepts.name: Leave-One-Out Cross-Validation
concepts.description: Cross-validation in which each single example is held out once as the test set while the model trains on all others; nearly unbiased but expensive, since it needs n model fits.
concepts.example: With 20 patients, train 20 models, each leaving out one patient and testing on them, then average the 20 results; nearly all data is used for training each time.

concepts.name: Lift (Data Mining)
concepts.description: For an association rule X → Y, the confidence divided by the support of Y, i.e. how much more often X and Y occur together than expected if independent; lift above 1 means positive association.
concepts.example: If 10% of shoppers buy beer, but 25% of those who buy nappies also buy beer, the lift of nappies to beer is 0.25 / 0.10 = 2.5: buying nappies makes beer 2.5 times more likely.

concepts.name: LIME
concepts.description: An explanation method that perturbs an input, observes how a black-box model's predictions change, and fits a simple weighted linear model locally to show which features drove that prediction.
concepts.example: To explain why an image was called "dog", LIME greys out random patches, sees how the score changes, and fits a simple linear model showing the ears and snout matter most.

concepts.name: Linear Kernel
concepts.description: The kernel k(x, y) = xᵀy, which corresponds to no feature mapping at all; using it in an SVM or other kernel method gives the ordinary linear version of the model.
concepts.example: For x = (1, 2) and y = (3, 4), the linear kernel is 1·3 + 2·4 = 11, just the ordinary dot product; an SVM using it draws a straight-line boundary.

concepts.name: Linear Model
concepts.description: A model whose prediction is a weighted sum of the input features plus a bias, possibly passed through a link function; linear and logistic regression and linear SVMs are examples.
concepts.example: Price = 2,000 × size + 10,000 × bedrooms + 50,000: each feature is multiplied by a weight and the results are added, so doubling the size effect means doubling its weight.

concepts.name: Linear Separability
concepts.description: The property of a dataset whose two classes can be perfectly separated by a hyperplane (a line in 2D); perceptrons and hard-margin SVMs only converge on such data.
concepts.example: Red dots all in the bottom-left and blue all in the top-right can be split by one straight line, so they are linearly separable; the XOR pattern of alternating corners is not.

concepts.name: Linear SVM
concepts.description: A support vector machine with no kernel, finding a separating hyperplane with the largest margin directly in the original feature space; fast and effective for high-dimensional data such as text.
concepts.example: For spam detection with 50,000 word features, a linear SVM finds the straight boundary with the widest gap between spam and non-spam emails, fast even on huge datasets.

concepts.name: Listwise Ranking
concepts.description: A learning-to-rank approach whose loss is defined over the whole ranked list for a query, e.g. ListNet or ListMLE, or directly optimises list metrics such as NDCG.
concepts.example: For one query with 10 results, ListNet turns scores into a softmax probability over which result comes first and compares it with the same from true relevance, scoring the list as a whole.

concepts.name: Local Outlier Factor
concepts.description: An anomaly detection method that compares the local density of a point, estimated from its k nearest neighbors, to that of its neighbors; points in much sparser regions get high outlier scores.
concepts.example: A point sitting 5 metres from a tight crowd is suspicious, but 5 metres in a sparse field is normal; LOF compares each point's local density with its neighbours', so an LOF well above 1 flags an outlier.

concepts.name: Locally Linear Embedding
concepts.description: A nonlinear dimensionality reduction method that writes each point as a weighted linear combination of its neighbors and finds a low-dimensional embedding preserving those same weights.
concepts.example: Each point is written as, say, 0.5 of neighbour A plus 0.3 of B plus 0.2 of C; LLE then finds 2D positions where every point is still that same mix of the same neighbours.

concepts.name: Logit
concepts.description: The logarithm of the odds, log(p / (1 − p)), which maps probabilities in (0, 1) to the whole real line; it is the inverse of the sigmoid and the link used in logistic regression.
concepts.example: A probability of 0.8 has odds 0.8 / 0.2 = 4, so its logit is ln 4, about 1.39; probability 0.5 has logit 0 and 0.2 has about -1.39.

concepts.name: LogitBoost
concepts.description: A boosting algorithm that fits an additive logistic regression model by Newton steps on the binomial log-likelihood, making it less sensitive to outliers than AdaBoost's exponential loss.
concepts.example: Each round, LogitBoost computes working responses from the current predicted probabilities, fits a regression stump to them by weighted least squares, and adds it to the score, like boosted logistic regression.

concepts.name: Loss Function
concepts.description: A function that measures how bad a model's prediction is compared to the true target, such as squared error or cross-entropy; training a model means minimising its average over data.
concepts.example: If the true price is 100 and the model says 90, squared loss is (100 - 90)² = 100 while absolute loss is 10; training tries to make such numbers as small as possible.

concepts.name: LPBoost
concepts.description: A boosting method that formulates the choice of weak learner weights as a linear program maximising the soft margin, adding weak learners by column generation and fully re-optimising all weights.
concepts.example: LPBoost solves a linear program to pick weights for all weak learners so far that maximise the worst-case margin, adding a new learner only when it can improve that solution.

concepts.name: Machine Learning
concepts.description: The field of building systems that learn patterns from data to make predictions or decisions without being explicitly programmed for each case, spanning supervised, unsupervised and reinforcement learning.
concepts.example: Instead of writing rules for spotting spam, show a program 10,000 emails labelled spam or not; it learns patterns, like suspicious words, and then classifies new emails on its own.

concepts.name: Macro and Micro Averaging
concepts.description: Ways to combine per-class metrics: macro averaging takes the plain mean over classes, micro averaging pools all predictions first, and weighted averaging weights each class by its frequency.
concepts.example: Class A has 90 examples at 90% recall, class B has 10 at 10%. Macro recall is (90 + 10) / 2 = 50%; micro recall pools all predictions, (81 + 1) / 100 = 82%, dominated by the big class.

concepts.name: Majority Voting
concepts.description: An ensemble rule where each classifier votes for a class and the class with the most votes is predicted; works best when the models are accurate and make different mistakes.
concepts.example: Five classifiers say cat, dog, cat, cat, bird, so the ensemble says cat with 3 votes. If each is right 70% of the time and they err independently, the vote is right about 84% of the time.

concepts.name: Model-Agnostic Meta-Learning
concepts.description: A meta-learning algorithm that learns an initialization of model parameters such that a few gradient steps on a small amount of data from a new task yield good performance on that task.
concepts.example: MAML trains a starting point such that, for any new task like recognising a new set of 5 animals, just 1 to 5 gradient steps from it give a good model.

concepts.name: Manifold Hypothesis
concepts.description: The idea that real high-dimensional data, such as images, lie near a much lower-dimensional manifold embedded in the input space, which explains why learning and dimensionality reduction work.
concepts.example: A 100×100 photo has 10,000 pixels, but photos of one face turning its head vary along just a few knobs like angle and lighting, so they lie on a thin low-dimensional surface in pixel space.

concepts.name: Manifold Learning
concepts.description: A family of nonlinear dimensionality reduction methods, such as Isomap, LLE, t-SNE and UMAP, that recover a low-dimensional representation of data lying on a curved manifold.
concepts.example: Data shaped like a rolled-up carpet in 3D, a Swiss roll, can be unrolled flat by manifold learning, keeping neighbours as neighbours, which PCA's straight projection cannot do.

concepts.name: Margin
concepts.description: The distance between a decision boundary and the closest training points (or, per example, how confidently it is on the correct side); larger margins tend to give better generalization.
concepts.example: If the closest red point is 2 units from the boundary line and the closest blue point is 3 units away on the other side, the margin is 2; a line with a wider gap is usually more robust.

concepts.name: Market Basket Analysis
concepts.description: Analysing which products customers buy together, using transaction data and association rules, to inform store layout, cross-selling and recommendations.
concepts.example: A supermarket finds that 60% of shoppers buying pasta also buy tomato sauce, so it places them in the same aisle or offers a combo deal.

concepts.name: Matrix Factorization (Recommender Systems)
concepts.description: Representing the user–item rating matrix as the product of two low-rank matrices of user and item latent factors, so predicted ratings are dot products of these vectors.
concepts.example: A 1,000-user by 500-film rating table, mostly empty, is approximated by users and films each having 10 hidden taste numbers; a missing rating is predicted by a user's numbers dotted with a film's.

concepts.name: Matthews Correlation Coefficient
concepts.description: A binary classification metric that is the correlation between predicted and true labels, computed from all four confusion matrix counts; ranges from −1 to 1 and is reliable under class imbalance.
concepts.example: A model that predicts "no fraud" for everyone is 99% accurate on 1% fraud data, but its MCC is 0, revealing it is no better than chance.

concepts.name: Maximum-Margin Classifier
concepts.description: A linear classifier that chooses, among all hyperplanes separating two linearly separable classes, the one with the largest distance to the closest points; the hard-margin SVM.
concepts.example: Many lines can separate red from blue dots; the maximum-margin classifier picks the one running down the middle of the widest empty street between them.

concepts.name: Mean Absolute Error
concepts.description: A regression metric equal to the average absolute difference between predictions and true values; easy to interpret in the target's units and less sensitive to outliers than squared error.
concepts.example: Predicting 3 days' temperatures as 20, 22, 25 when the truth was 21, 22, 28 gives errors 1, 0, 3, so the MAE is 4 / 3, about 1.33 degrees.

concepts.name: Mean Average Precision
concepts.description: The mean of average precision over all queries (or classes), summarising ranking or retrieval quality in one number; also the standard metric for object detection.
concepts.example: If average precision is 0.9 for query 1, 0.6 for query 2 and 0.3 for query 3, the MAP is (0.9 + 0.6 + 0.3) / 3 = 0.6.

concepts.name: Mean Reciprocal Rank
concepts.description: A ranking metric that averages, over queries, the reciprocal of the rank of the first relevant result (1 for first place, 1/2 for second and so on).
concepts.example: Across 3 searches, the first correct result appears at ranks 1, 2 and 4, so the reciprocal ranks are 1, 0.5 and 0.25, and the MRR is 1.75 / 3, about 0.58.

concepts.name: Mean Shift
concepts.description: A clustering and mode-seeking algorithm that repeatedly shifts each point toward the weighted mean of points in its neighborhood, moving it uphill on a kernel density estimate until convergence.
concepts.example: Drop a marble anywhere on a bumpy landscape of point density; it keeps rolling to the weighted average of nearby points until it settles on a peak, and marbles ending on the same peak form a cluster.

concepts.name: Mean Squared Logarithmic Error
concepts.description: A regression metric that computes the mean squared difference between log(1 + prediction) and log(1 + target), so it measures relative errors and penalises underprediction more; RMSLE is its root.
concepts.example: Predicting 110 for a true 100 and predicting 1,100 for a true 1,000 give nearly the same MSLE, because log(1 + x) measures ratio errors, not absolute ones.

concepts.name: Median Absolute Error
concepts.description: A regression metric equal to the median of the absolute differences between predictions and true values, which makes it very robust to outliers.
