concepts.example: Errors of 1, 2, 2, 3 and 100: the mean absolute error is 21.6, but the median absolute error is 2, unaffected by the single wild miss.

concepts.name: Medoid
concepts.description: The member of a cluster whose total distance to all other members is smallest; unlike a centroid it is always an actual data point and can be defined for any distance measure.
concepts.example: Of three friends' houses at positions 1, 2 and 10 on a road, the house at 2 has total distance 1 + 8 = 9 to the others, the smallest, so it is the medoid; the centroid, 4.33, is nobody's house.

concepts.name: Mercer's Theorem
concepts.description: A theorem stating that a continuous symmetric positive semidefinite kernel can be written as a convergent sum of eigenfunctions, so it is an inner product in some feature space, justifying kernel methods.
concepts.example: The RBF kernel looks like a single formula, but Mercer's theorem guarantees it equals an infinite sum of eigenfunction products, so it truly is a dot product in some (infinite) feature space.

concepts.name: Meta-Learner
concepts.description: In stacking, the second-level model that takes the base models' predictions as inputs and learns how best to combine them into a final prediction.
concepts.example: A random forest, an SVM and kNN each predict house prices; a linear regression meta-learner takes those 3 predictions as inputs and learns, say, to trust the forest 60%, the SVM 30% and kNN 10%.

concepts.name: Meta-Learning
concepts.description: Learning to learn: training a system over many tasks so it can adapt quickly to new tasks with little data, by learning good initializations, update rules or similarity measures.
concepts.example: After learning hundreds of small classification tasks, a meta-learner picks up a new one, like telling apart 5 new alphabets, from just a few examples each, because it has learned how to learn.

concepts.name: Metric Learning
concepts.description: Learning a distance function or embedding from data so that similar examples are close and dissimilar ones far apart, used in face verification, retrieval and few-shot learning.
concepts.example: For face recognition, metric learning trains an embedding so two photos of the same person end up a short distance apart and photos of different people far apart, even under new lighting.

concepts.name: Multiple Imputation by Chained Equations
concepts.description: An imputation method that fills each incomplete variable by a regression on the others, cycling through variables repeatedly, and repeats the process to create several completed datasets.
concepts.example: With missing ages and incomes, MICE first fills blanks with means, then predicts age from income and other columns, then income from age, cycling several times, and repeats it all to make several filled datasets.

concepts.name: Mini-Batch k-Means
concepts.description: A faster k-means variant that updates centroids using small random batches of data at each step instead of the whole dataset, trading a little clustering quality for big speed and memory savings.
concepts.example: With 10 million points, take 1,000 random points per step, assign them to the nearest centre, and nudge those centres toward them; after a few hundred steps the centres are close to full k-means.

concepts.name: Minkowski Distance
concepts.description: A family of distances between vectors equal to the p-th root of the sum of absolute coordinate differences to the power p; p = 1 gives Manhattan and p = 2 gives Euclidean distance.
concepts.example: Between (0, 0) and (3, 4): with p = 1 the distance is 3 + 4 = 7, Manhattan; with p = 2 it is 5, Euclidean; and as p grows it approaches 4, the largest difference.

concepts.name: Mixture Model
concepts.description: A probabilistic model in which data come from a weighted combination of several component distributions, with a hidden variable saying which component generated each point; used for soft clustering.
concepts.example: Heights of a mixed group of adults and children form two bumps; a mixture model explains them as, say, 70% from an adult bell curve and 30% from a child bell curve.

concepts.name: Mixture of Experts
concepts.description: A model with several expert subnetworks and a gating network that decides which experts handle each input; sparse versions route each token to a few experts, scaling capacity at fixed compute.
concepts.example: A model has 8 expert networks; for each word, a gating network scores them and only the top 2 are run, so the model holds 8 experts' knowledge but costs about 2 per input.

concepts.name: MLxtend
concepts.description: A Python library of machine learning extensions to scikit-learn, including stacking ensembles, sequential feature selection, plotting tools and Apriori/FP-Growth association rule mining.
concepts.example: With MLxtend you can build a stacking classifier from scikit-learn models in a few lines, run sequential feature selection, or mine association rules with its Apriori function.

concepts.name: Calibration (Neural Networks)
concepts.description: The property that a model's predicted probabilities match observed frequencies, e.g. events predicted at 80% happen about 80% of the time; fixed with methods like Platt or temperature scaling.
concepts.example: A calibrated weather model that says "70% chance of rain" on 100 different days should see rain on about 70 of them; if it rains on only 40, the model is overconfident.

concepts.name: Model Capacity
concepts.description: A model's ability to fit a wide variety of functions, governed by its number of parameters and structure; too little capacity underfits and too much can overfit without regularization.
concepts.example: A straight line cannot fit 10 points on a curve; a degree-9 polynomial fits all 10 exactly, noise included. The polynomial has much more capacity, so it can also overfit far more.

concepts.name: Model Evaluation
concepts.description: Measuring how well a trained model performs on unseen data using held-out sets or cross-validation and suitable metrics, to compare models and estimate real-world performance.
concepts.example: Train a spam filter on 8,000 emails, then measure it on 2,000 emails it has never seen: 95% accuracy there is a fair estimate of how it will do in real use.

concepts.name: Model Parameter
concepts.description: A value learned from training data that defines a model's behaviour, such as regression coefficients or neural network weights, in contrast to hyperparameters set beforehand.
concepts.example: In the model price = 2,000 × size + 50,000, the numbers 2,000 and 50,000 are parameters: the training algorithm found them by fitting past house sales.

concepts.name: Model Tree
concepts.description: A regression tree whose leaves hold linear regression models rather than constant values, as in Quinlan's M5, giving piecewise linear predictions that are often more accurate and compact.
concepts.example: Predicting fuel use, a model tree splits cars into small and large; in the small-car leaf it uses one line, 4 + 0.02 × weight, and in the large-car leaf a different line, instead of a single average per leaf.

concepts.name: Minimum Redundancy Maximum Relevance
concepts.description: A filter feature selection algorithm that greedily picks features with high mutual information with the target and low average mutual information with features already chosen.
concepts.example: Picking 3 of 20 features for house prices: size scores highest relevance, then "number of rooms" is skipped because it is redundant with size, and "distance to school" is chosen instead.

concepts.name: Multi-Armed Bandit
concepts.description: A sequential decision problem where an agent repeatedly chooses among options with unknown reward distributions and must balance exploring them against exploiting the best one found.
concepts.example: Facing 3 slot machines with unknown payouts, you must decide each pull whether to try a machine you know little about or keep pulling the one that has paid best so far.

concepts.name: Multi-Label Classification
concepts.description: A classification task where each example can have several labels at once, such as tags on an article, often solved by training one binary classifier per label or with specialised models.
concepts.example: A news article can be tagged "politics", "economy" and "Europe" all at once; a multi-label model outputs a separate yes/no for every tag instead of picking just one.

concepts.name: Multi-Task Learning
concepts.description: Training one model on several related tasks at once with shared representations, so information from each task helps the others and generalization improves.
concepts.example: A single network looks at a road photo and simultaneously predicts lane lines, car positions and road signs; shared early layers learn features that help all three tasks.

concepts.name: Multiclass Classification
concepts.description: A classification task with three or more possible classes where each example belongs to exactly one, solved directly (e.g. softmax) or by combining binary classifiers.
concepts.example: Recognising handwritten digits is multiclass: every image belongs to exactly one of 10 classes, 0 to 9, and the model picks the single most likely one.

concepts.name: Multinomial Naive Bayes
concepts.description: A Naive Bayes classifier that models feature counts, such as word counts in documents, with a multinomial distribution per class; a strong, fast baseline for text classification.
concepts.example: If "free" makes up 5% of words in spam but 0.5% in normal mail, an email using "free" 3 times multiplies its spam odds by roughly 10³ from that word alone.

concepts.name: Multiple Instance Learning
concepts.description: A weakly supervised setting where labels are given for bags of instances: a bag is positive if at least one instance in it is positive, used in drug discovery and medical image analysis.
concepts.example: A photo labelled "contains a cat" is a bag of image patches: at least one patch shows a cat, but you are not told which, and the model must work it out.

concepts.name: Multiple Linear Regression
concepts.description: Linear regression with two or more predictor variables, modelling the target as a weighted sum of the features plus an intercept, with weights usually fitted by least squares.
concepts.example: House price = 50,000 + 2,000 × size + 10,000 × bedrooms - 500 × age: the model uses three predictors at once, each with its own coefficient.

concepts.name: Multivariate Adaptive Regression Splines
concepts.description: A nonparametric regression method that builds a model from piecewise linear hinge functions and their products, adding terms forward and then pruning them, to capture nonlinearity and interactions.
concepts.example: MARS might model price as 100 + 3 × max(0, size - 50): flat for small homes, then rising past 50 square metres, adding hinges like this one term at a time.

concepts.name: Naive Bayes
concepts.description: A classifier that applies Bayes' theorem assuming features are conditionally independent given the class, which makes it very fast; surprisingly effective for text classification such as spam filtering.
concepts.example: To classify an email, multiply P(spam) by P("free" given spam) by P("meeting" given spam), and the same for not-spam, treating words as independent clues, then pick the bigger product.

concepts.name: Normalized Discounted Cumulative Gain
concepts.description: A ranking metric that sums graded relevance of results with a logarithmic discount for lower positions (DCG) and divides by the best possible DCG, giving a score from 0 to 1.
concepts.example: Results with relevance 3, 2, 0 earn 3/1 + 2/log2(3), about 4.26 DCG; the ideal order earns the same, so NDCG = 1. Putting the 0 first would lower it.

concepts.name: NearMiss
concepts.description: A family of undersampling methods for imbalanced data that keeps majority-class examples chosen by their distances to minority-class examples, e.g. those closest to the minority points.
concepts.example: With 1,000 normal and 50 fraud cases, NearMiss-1 keeps the 50 normal cases whose nearest fraud cases are closest on average, focusing training on the hard boundary region.

concepts.name: Nearest Centroid Classifier
concepts.description: A classifier that computes the mean (centroid) of each class and assigns a new point to the class with the closest centroid; simple, fast and used in text classification as the Rocchio method.
concepts.example: Average all cat photos' features to get a cat centre and all dog photos' to get a dog centre; a new photo is labelled whichever centre is nearer.

concepts.name: Nested Cross-Validation
concepts.description: A procedure with an inner cross-validation loop for tuning hyperparameters and an outer loop for estimating performance, which avoids the optimistic bias of tuning and evaluating on the same folds.
concepts.example: The outer loop splits data into 5 folds; for each, an inner 5-fold CV on the other 4 folds picks the best tree depth, then the chosen model is scored on the untouched outer fold.

concepts.name: No Free Lunch Theorem
concepts.description: A theorem stating that, averaged over all possible problems, every learning or optimization algorithm performs equally well, so an algorithm is only better given assumptions about the problem.
concepts.example: A learner that always predicts "tomorrow is like today" wins on weather data but loses on coin flips; averaged over every possible world, no learner beats any other.

concepts.name: Nonparametric Model
concepts.description: A model whose complexity is not fixed in advance but grows with the amount of training data, such as k-nearest neighbors, kernel density estimates or decision trees, making few assumptions about the data's shape.
concepts.example: kNN with 100 training points stores 100 points; with a million it stores a million, so the model grows with the data instead of having a fixed number of weights.

concepts.name: Normalized Mutual Information
concepts.description: A score for comparing two clusterings that divides their mutual information by their entropies, giving 0 for independent and 1 for identical labelings; the adjusted variant also corrects for chance.
concepts.example: If two clusterings group the same points identically, even with different cluster names, NMI is 1; if one is unrelated to the other, NMI is near 0.

concepts.name: Novelty Detection
concepts.description: The task of deciding whether a new observation differs from a training set assumed to contain only normal data; unlike outlier detection, training data is clean and novelties appear only at test time.
concepts.example: A factory trains on sounds of healthy machines only; when a new grinding noise comes in that doesn't fit what it learned, it flags it as novel, a possible fault.

concepts.name: ν-SVM
concepts.description: A reformulation of the support vector machine that replaces the cost parameter C with ν, which bounds the fraction of margin errors and support vectors, making the parameter easier to interpret and tune.
concepts.example: Setting nu = 0.1 means at most about 10% of training points may be margin errors and at least about 10% will be support vectors, which is easier to reason about than a raw C value.

concepts.name: Nyström Method
concepts.description: A technique that approximates a large kernel matrix using a random subset of its columns, giving a low-rank feature map so kernel methods can scale to large datasets.
concepts.example: With 1 million points, a full kernel matrix would have a trillion entries; Nyström picks 1,000 landmark points and approximates the whole matrix using only kernels to those landmarks.

concepts.name: Oblique Decision Tree
concepts.description: A decision tree whose splits test linear combinations of several features (hyperplanes at any angle) instead of a threshold on a single feature, often giving smaller and more accurate trees.
concepts.example: Instead of asking "Is height > 170?" an oblique tree asks "Is 0.6 × height + 0.4 × weight > 120?", so one split can follow a diagonal boundary that would need many staircase splits otherwise.

concepts.name: Oblivious Decision Tree
concepts.description: A decision tree that uses the same split condition for every node on a given level, making it perfectly balanced and fast to evaluate; CatBoost uses these symmetric trees as base learners.
concepts.example: A depth-3 oblivious tree asks the same 3 questions, say age > 30, income > 50k, owns home, for every example, so the answers form a 3-bit index into 8 leaves, which is very fast to evaluate.

concepts.name: Occam's Razor
concepts.description: The principle that among explanations or models that fit the data equally well, the simplest should be preferred; in machine learning it motivates simpler models that are less likely to overfit.
concepts.example: If both a straight line and a wiggly 10th-degree curve fit the data equally well, prefer the line: it is simpler and likely to generalise better.

concepts.name: One-Class SVM
concepts.description: An SVM variant trained only on normal data that learns a boundary enclosing most points in kernel feature space; new points falling outside the boundary are flagged as anomalies or novelties.
concepts.example: Train on thousands of normal server logs only; the one-class SVM draws a boundary around them, and a new log falling outside it is flagged as unusual.

concepts.name: One-Shot Learning
concepts.description: Learning to recognize a new class from just one labeled example, typically by comparing new inputs to that example in a learned similarity or embedding space.
concepts.example: After seeing one photo of a new employee, a face system recognises them at the door by checking whether a new face is close enough to that single stored photo's embedding.

concepts.name: One-vs-One
concepts.description: A strategy for multiclass classification that trains one binary classifier for every pair of classes and predicts the class that wins the most pairwise votes.
concepts.example: For 4 classes A, B, C, D, train 6 classifiers: A-B, A-C, A-D, B-C, B-D, C-D. Each votes for one of its pair, and the class with the most votes wins.

concepts.name: One-vs-Rest
concepts.description: A strategy for multiclass classification that trains one binary classifier per class to separate it from all other classes, then predicts the class whose classifier is most confident.
concepts.example: For fruits apple, banana and cherry, train three classifiers: apple vs not, banana vs not, cherry vs not. A new fruit gets the label whose classifier is most confident.

concepts.name: OneR
concepts.description: A very simple classification algorithm that builds one rule per feature, mapping each feature value to its most frequent class, and keeps the single feature whose rule makes the fewest errors.
concepts.example: For predicting play-tennis, OneR checks each feature: for outlook, sunny gives mostly no and overcast mostly yes. If outlook's rules make the fewest errors, it becomes the whole model.

concepts.name: Online Gradient Descent
concepts.description: An online learning algorithm that updates model parameters with a gradient step on the loss of each newly arriving example, with regret guarantees for convex losses.
concepts.example: A price predictor sees one house sale, compares its guess with the real price, takes a small gradient step on that single error, then moves on to the next sale and never revisits it.

concepts.name: Online Machine Learning
concepts.description: A setting where a model learns from data arriving one example or small batch at a time, updating itself incrementally instead of retraining on a fixed dataset; useful for streams and changing data.
concepts.example: A spam filter updates itself every time a user marks an email as spam, instead of being retrained from scratch on all emails each month.

concepts.name: OPTICS
concepts.description: A density-based clustering algorithm that orders points by reachability distance so clusters of varying density can be read off a reachability plot, generalizing DBSCAN without one fixed radius.
aliases: ordering points to identify the clustering structure
concepts.example: OPTICS walks through the points, always visiting the most reachable next one, and records reachability; a plot of it shows valleys for clusters, deep for dense clusters and shallow for sparse ones.

concepts.name: Optuna
concepts.description: An open-source Python framework for hyperparameter optimization where search spaces are defined in code, using samplers such as TPE and pruning of unpromising trials to save compute.
concepts.example: You write a Python function that suggests a learning rate and depth, trains a model and returns its score; Optuna calls it 100 times, steering toward good regions and pruning hopeless trials early.

concepts.name: Ordered Boosting
concepts.description: CatBoost's boosting scheme in which each example's residual comes from a model trained only on examples earlier in a random permutation, avoiding the target leakage of standard gradient boosting.
concepts.example: Shuffle the rows; for row 100, its residual is computed by a model trained only on rows 1 to 99, so its own label never leaks into its residual.

concepts.name: Out-of-Bag Error
concepts.description: An estimate of a bagged model's test error made by predicting each training example using only the trees whose bootstrap samples left it out, so no separate validation set is needed.
concepts.example: Each bootstrap sample leaves out about 37% of rows; to judge row 7, ask only the trees that never saw it, and the average error over all rows is the OOB error, a free validation score.

concepts.name: Overfitting
concepts.description: When a model learns the noise and quirks of its training data so closely that it performs much worse on new data; it shows up as low training error but high validation error.
concepts.example: A student who memorizes last year's exam answers scores 100% on that paper but fails a new exam with different questions; a model that memorizes its training points behaves the same way.

concepts.name: Oversampling
concepts.description: A technique for imbalanced datasets that adds minority-class examples, either duplicated at random or synthesized, so the classes are more balanced during training.
concepts.example: With 950 normal transactions and 50 frauds, you could copy each fraud example 19 times so the model sees about 950 of each class during training.

concepts.name: Probably Approximately Correct Learning
concepts.description: A learning-theory framework in which a learner must, with high probability, output a hypothesis whose error is below a chosen tolerance using a number of samples polynomial in the problem parameters.
concepts.example: Asking for a spam filter that is at most 5% wrong with 99% confidence, PAC theory tells you how many labelled emails suffice for a given family of filters.

concepts.name: PaCMAP
concepts.description: A dimensionality reduction method for visualization that optimizes an embedding using neighbor, mid-near and far pairs of points, aiming to preserve both local and global structure better than t-SNE or UMAP.
concepts.example: Embedding handwritten digits in 2D, PaCMAP pulls each image toward its nearest neighbours, gently toward mid-range ones and pushes far ones away, so digit clusters stay apart and sensibly arranged.

concepts.name: Pairwise Ranking
concepts.description: A learning-to-rank approach that trains a model on pairs of items, learning to predict which of the two should be ranked higher, so the loss focuses on relative order rather than absolute scores.
concepts.example: Instead of predicting a search result's exact score, the model is shown pairs like (page A, page B) and learns that A should rank above B because users clicked A more.

concepts.name: Partial Dependence Plot
concepts.description: A plot showing how a model's average prediction changes as one or two features vary while averaging over the other features' values; used to interpret black-box models.
concepts.example: To see how house size affects a price model, set every house's size to 50 m², average the predictions, then repeat for 60, 70, 80 m², and plot the averages against size.

concepts.name: Passive-Aggressive Algorithm
concepts.description: An online learning algorithm that leaves the model unchanged when an example is classified with enough margin (passive) and otherwise makes the smallest update that fixes it (aggressive).
concepts.example: A spam filter sees an email it already classifies confidently and correctly, so it does nothing; on a mistake it shifts its weights just enough to get that email right with margin.

concepts.name: Perceptron
concepts.description: The simplest neural-network classifier: it computes a weighted sum of inputs plus a bias, outputs one class if the sum is positive, and adjusts its weights after each mistake.
concepts.example: With weights (2, -1) and bias -1, input (1, 0) gives 2·1 - 1·0 - 1 = 1 > 0, so it says 'yes'; input (0, 1) gives -2 < 0, so 'no'.

concepts.name: Perceptron Convergence Theorem
concepts.description: The result that if data are linearly separable with margin γ and lie within radius R, the perceptron makes at most (R/γ)² mistakes before finding a separating hyperplane.
concepts.example: If points sit within radius R = 10 and a separating line leaves margin γ = 1 on each side, the perceptron makes at most (10/1)² = 100 mistakes before it stops erring.

concepts.name: Permutation Feature Importance
concepts.description: A model-agnostic way to measure a feature's importance: randomly shuffle that feature's values in held-out data and record how much the model's score drops.
concepts.example: If shuffling the 'income' column drops a loan model's accuracy from 90% to 70%, income matters a lot; shuffling 'zip code' and staying at 90% means it barely matters.

concepts.name: Platt Scaling
concepts.description: A calibration method that fits a logistic regression on a classifier's raw scores to turn them into well-calibrated probabilities; originally used for SVM outputs.
concepts.example: An SVM outputs raw scores like 2.3 or -0.7; Platt scaling fits a sigmoid on validation data so that a score of 2.3 might become a 0.91 probability of being positive.

concepts.name: Pointwise Ranking
concepts.description: A learning-to-rank approach that treats each item independently, predicting its relevance score or grade with ordinary regression or classification, then sorting items by the predictions.
concepts.example: For a query about pizza, a pointwise model rates each restaurant page on its own, say 4 out of 5 relevant, and the results are then sorted by those individual scores.

concepts.name: Polynomial Features
concepts.description: Feature engineering that adds powers of features and products between them (interaction terms), letting linear models fit curved relationships and interactions between features.
concepts.example: From features x1 = 2 and x2 = 3, degree-2 polynomial features add x1² = 4, x2² = 9 and x1·x2 = 6, letting a linear model fit curves and interactions.

concepts.name: Polynomial Kernel
concepts.description: A kernel function k(x, y) = (x·y + c)^d that equals an inner product of all polynomial feature combinations up to degree d, without ever computing those features explicitly.
concepts.example: For 2D points x = (1, 2) and y = (3, 1), the kernel with c = 1, d = 2 gives (1·3 + 2·1 + 1)² = 36, the same as a dot product of their degree-2 feature expansions.

concepts.name: Population-Based Training
concepts.description: A hyperparameter optimization method that trains many models in parallel and periodically replaces poor performers with copies of better ones whose hyperparameters are perturbed, adapting them during training.
concepts.example: Twenty models train at once; every few hours the worst five copy the weights of the best five, then nudge their learning rates up or down and keep going.

concepts.name: Positive-Unlabeled Learning
concepts.description: Training a binary classifier from only positive examples plus a pool of unlabeled examples that mixes positives and negatives, common when negatives are never explicitly labeled.
concepts.example: You know 500 customers who churned, plus 10,000 others whose status is unknown; PU learning trains a churn classifier even though no one is confirmed as 'not churned'.

concepts.name: Precision at k
concepts.description: A ranking metric giving the fraction of the top k returned items that are relevant; used to evaluate search engines and recommender systems.
concepts.example: A search engine returns 10 results and 7 are relevant, so precision@10 = 0.7; if 4 of the top 5 are relevant, precision@5 = 0.8.

concepts.name: Principal Component
concepts.description: One of the orthogonal directions found by PCA, ordered by how much of the data's variance lies along it; each is an eigenvector of the data's covariance matrix.
concepts.example: For heights and weights of people, the first principal component points roughly along 'overall size', since that direction captures most of the spread in the data.

concepts.name: Probabilistic Classifier
concepts.description: A classifier that outputs a probability distribution over classes rather than just a label, such as logistic regression or naive Bayes, enabling confidence estimates and adjustable thresholds.
concepts.example: Instead of just saying 'cat', the classifier outputs cat 0.80, dog 0.15, rabbit 0.05, so you can see how confident it is.

concepts.name: Probabilistic PCA
concepts.description: A latent-variable version of PCA in which data are generated from low-dimensional Gaussian latent variables through a linear map plus isotropic noise, fit by maximum likelihood or EM.
concepts.example: Imagine each 100-pixel face is generated by picking 5 hidden 'style' numbers, mapping them linearly to pixels, and adding a bit of Gaussian noise; fitting this model recovers PCA's directions.

concepts.name: Purity
concepts.description: A clustering quality score that assigns each cluster to its most common true class and measures the fraction of points correctly assigned this way; it rises trivially as the number of clusters grows.
concepts.example: Cluster 1 holds 8 cats and 2 dogs, cluster 2 holds 9 dogs and 1 cat; purity = (8 + 9) / 20 = 0.85, meaning 85% of points sit with their cluster's majority class.

concepts.name: Quantile Loss
concepts.description: A loss that penalizes under- and over-predictions asymmetrically according to a chosen quantile τ, so minimizing it makes a model predict that quantile instead of the mean.
concepts.example: For the 90th percentile, under-predicting by 10 costs 0.9·10 = 9 but over-predicting by 10 costs only 0.1·10 = 1, so the model learns to aim high.

concepts.name: Query by Committee
concepts.description: An active learning strategy that trains several models and requests labels for the examples on which the committee members disagree the most.
concepts.example: Five models vote on unlabeled photos; for one photo they split 3 'cat' to 2 'dog', so that disputed photo is the one sent to a human for labelling.

concepts.name: Rademacher Complexity
concepts.description: A measure of how well a class of functions can fit random ±1 noise on a sample; it yields data-dependent generalization bounds that can be tighter than VC-based ones.
concepts.example: Give 100 points random +1/-1 labels: a straight line fits them poorly, while a deep tree can match almost all of them, so the tree's class has much higher Rademacher complexity.

concepts.name: Radius Neighbors
concepts.description: A nearest-neighbor method that predicts from all training points within a fixed distance of the query, rather than from a fixed number k of nearest neighbors.
concepts.example: To classify a new point, look at every training point within 2 units of it; if 5 are red and 2 are blue, predict red. In sparse areas there might be none at all.

concepts.name: Rand Index
concepts.description: A clustering comparison score equal to the fraction of point pairs on which two labelings agree (same or different cluster); the adjusted Rand index corrects it for chance agreement.
concepts.example: With 4 points there are 6 pairs; if two clusterings agree on 5 of them about 'same cluster' versus 'different cluster', the Rand index is 5/6 ≈ 0.83.

concepts.name: Random Forest
concepts.description: An ensemble of decision trees, each trained on a bootstrap sample and considering a random subset of features at each split; averaging or voting over the trees reduces variance.
concepts.example: To predict house prices, grow 500 trees, each on a random resample of houses and picking from a random handful of features at each split, then average their 500 price guesses.

concepts.name: Random Fourier Features
concepts.description: A technique that approximates shift-invariant kernels such as the RBF kernel with an explicit map of random cosine features, letting fast linear models mimic kernel methods at scale.
concepts.example: Instead of computing an RBF similarity for every pair of a million points, map each point to 500 random cosine features; dot products of these features approximate the kernel.

concepts.name: Random Projection
concepts.description: Dimensionality reduction by multiplying data by a random matrix; by the Johnson–Lindenstrauss lemma, pairwise distances are approximately preserved with high probability.
concepts.example: Multiply 10,000-dimensional text vectors by a random 10,000×300 matrix; the 300-dimensional results keep pairwise distances nearly intact at a fraction of the cost.

concepts.name: Random Search
concepts.description: Hyperparameter optimization that samples configurations at random from chosen distributions; it often beats grid search because it tries more distinct values of the hyperparameters that matter.
concepts.example: Rather than testing learning rates on a fixed 5×5 grid, draw 25 random combinations; you end up trying 25 distinct learning-rate values instead of only 5.

concepts.name: Random Subspace Method
concepts.description: An ensemble method that trains each base model on a random subset of the features rather than of the examples, increasing diversity; it underlies the feature sampling in random forests.
concepts.example: With 100 features, train each of 50 models on its own random 20 features, then let them vote; models differ because each sees different evidence.

concepts.name: RankNet
concepts.description: A pairwise learning-to-rank method that scores items with a neural network and applies a cross-entropy loss to the predicted probability that one item should rank above another.
concepts.example: The network scores page A at 2.0 and page B at 0.5; the probability A beats B is sigmoid(1.5) ≈ 0.82, and if users actually prefer B the loss pushes the scores the other way.

concepts.name: Ranking SVM
concepts.description: A pairwise learning-to-rank method that trains an SVM on differences of feature vectors so that preferred items score higher than less preferred ones by a margin.
concepts.example: If doc A should beat doc B, the difference vector A - B is labelled +1; an SVM trained on such differences learns weights that score A above B.

concepts.name: Random Sample Consensus
concepts.description: A robust fitting algorithm that repeatedly fits a model to small random subsets of points and keeps the model agreed on by the most inliers, ignoring outliers; widely used in computer vision.
concepts.example: Fitting a line to 100 points with 30 wild outliers: repeatedly pick 2 random points, draw their line, count points within 1 unit of it, and keep the line with the most supporters.

concepts.name: Radial Basis Function Kernel
concepts.description: A kernel k(x, y) = exp(−γ‖x − y‖²) whose similarity decays with squared Euclidean distance; it corresponds to an infinite-dimensional feature space and is a default choice for SVMs.
concepts.example: With γ = 1, two identical points get similarity e⁰ = 1, points 1 apart get e⁻¹ ≈ 0.37, and points 3 apart get e⁻⁹ ≈ 0.0001.

concepts.name: Recommender System
concepts.description: A system that predicts which items, such as products, movies or songs, a user is likely to want, based on past behavior, item attributes or the preferences of similar users.
concepts.example: Netflix notices you watched three heist films and rated them highly, so it suggests another heist thriller that similar viewers enjoyed.

concepts.name: Reduced Error Pruning
concepts.description: A decision-tree pruning method that replaces a subtree with a leaf whenever doing so does not increase error on a held-out validation set, repeating until no prune helps.
concepts.example: Starting from the bottom, a subtree that gets 40 of 50 validation examples right is replaced by a single leaf; if the leaf also gets 40 or more right, the cut stays.

concepts.name: Regression Tree
concepts.description: A decision tree that predicts a continuous value, choosing splits that reduce squared error and outputting the mean target of the training points in each leaf.
concepts.example: Predicting house price, the tree first splits on size < 100 m²; small houses get leaf value $200k, the average of their training prices, and large ones $350k.

concepts.name: Regret (Decision Theory)
concepts.description: The gap between the total loss (or reward) a learner actually gets and what the best fixed action or policy in hindsight would have achieved; used to analyze online learning and bandits.
concepts.example: Over 100 days you followed several stock tips and lost $50 total; the single best tipster would have earned $30, so your regret is $80.

concepts.name: Regularization
concepts.description: Any technique that discourages a model from becoming too complex, for example by adding a penalty on weight size to the loss, so that it overfits less and generalizes better.
concepts.example: Fitting 10 points with a degree-9 polynomial gives wild wiggles; adding a penalty on large coefficients forces a smoother curve that generalizes better.

concepts.name: Regularization Path
concepts.description: The set of model solutions obtained as the regularization strength varies from strong to weak, often computed efficiently and plotted to show when each coefficient enters the model.
concepts.example: Running lasso with penalty values from 10 down to 0.001 and plotting each coefficient shows features entering the model one by one as the penalty weakens.

concepts.name: Regularized Discriminant Analysis
concepts.description: A classifier that blends linear and quadratic discriminant analysis by shrinking class covariance matrices toward a pooled or scaled-identity estimate, stabilizing them when data are scarce.
concepts.example: With only 20 samples per class in 50 dimensions, each class covariance is unstable; RDA blends it 70/30 with the shared covariance to get a usable estimate.

concepts.name: Relevance Vector Machine
concepts.description: A sparse Bayesian model with the same functional form as an SVM, where per-weight priors drive most weights to zero, leaving a few relevance vectors and giving probabilistic predictions.
concepts.example: Fitting a curve to 100 points, an RVM ends up relying on maybe 8 of them as 'relevance vectors', far fewer than an SVM typically keeps, and also gives error bars.

concepts.name: Relief
concepts.description: A feature-weighting algorithm that rewards features differing on a sample's nearest neighbor from another class and penalizes those differing on its nearest same-class neighbor; ReliefF adds noise and multiclass handling.
concepts.example: For a sample, find its nearest same-class neighbor and nearest other-class neighbor; a feature that differs a lot from the other-class neighbor but little from the same-class one gains weight.

concepts.name: Representer Theorem
concepts.description: The theorem that the minimizer of a regularized empirical loss over a reproducing kernel Hilbert space can be written as a weighted sum of kernel functions centered at the training points.
concepts.example: Training a kernel SVM on 1,000 points, the theorem guarantees the best function is a weighted sum of 1,000 kernel bumps centered on those points, so you solve for just 1,000 weights.

concepts.name: Reproducing Kernel Hilbert Space
concepts.description: A Hilbert space of functions in which evaluating a function at a point equals an inner product with a kernel function; it is the mathematical setting behind kernel methods.
concepts.example: In the RKHS of a kernel k, the function f = 2k(·, a) + 3k(·, b) evaluated at x is just 2k(x, a) + 3k(x, b), an inner product of f with k(·, x).

concepts.name: Residual Sum of Squares
concepts.description: The sum of squared differences between observed and predicted values; least-squares methods choose parameters that minimize it, and it measures the variation a model leaves unexplained.
concepts.example: True values 3, 5, 7 and predictions 2, 5, 9 give residuals 1, 0, -2, so RSS = 1 + 0 + 4 = 5; a better-fitting line would make this total smaller.

concepts.name: RIPPER
concepts.description: A rule-learning algorithm that greedily grows and prunes if-then rules one class at a time using a held-out set, then runs an optimization pass, producing compact rule sets.
aliases: repeated incremental pruning to produce error reduction
concepts.example: For a rare 'fraud' class, RIPPER grows a rule like 'IF amount > 900 AND country = foreign THEN fraud', trims conditions that hurt held-out accuracy, removes covered cases, and repeats.

concepts.name: Robust Principal Component Analysis
concepts.description: A decomposition of a data matrix into a low-rank part plus a sparse part, usually via nuclear-norm and L1 minimization, recovering structure despite gross corruptions such as moving foreground in video.
concepts.example: A security-camera video matrix splits into a low-rank part, the unchanging background, plus a sparse part, the few pixels where people walk by.

concepts.name: Robust Scaling
concepts.description: Feature scaling that subtracts the median and divides by the interquartile range, so extreme outliers have little influence on the transformed values.
concepts.example: Incomes 30k, 40k, 50k, 60k, 5M: median 50k, IQR 20k, so 60k becomes 0.5 while the 5M outlier stays extreme without squashing everyone else toward zero.

concepts.name: Receiver Operating Characteristic Curve
concepts.description: A plot of true positive rate against false positive rate as a classifier's decision threshold varies, showing the tradeoff between catching positives and raising false alarms.
concepts.example: At threshold 0.9 a classifier catches 30% of positives with 2% false alarms; at 0.5 it catches 80% with 15%; plotting all such points traces the ROC curve.

concepts.name: Root Mean Squared Error
concepts.description: The square root of the average squared difference between predictions and true values; it measures typical error size in the target's own units while penalizing large errors heavily.
concepts.example: Errors of 1, -2 and 3 give squared errors 1, 4, 9 with mean 14/3 ≈ 4.67, so RMSE ≈ 2.16, in the same units as the target.

concepts.name: Rotation Forest
concepts.description: An ensemble of decision trees in which each tree is trained on features rotated by PCA applied to random subsets of features, encouraging both individual accuracy and diversity.
concepts.example: Split 12 features into 3 groups of 4, run PCA on each group, and train a tree on the rotated axes; each tree uses a different random grouping, giving diverse yet accurate trees.

concepts.name: Rule-Based Classifier
concepts.description: A classifier made of human-readable if-then rules on feature values, where the first or best matching rule decides the predicted class.
concepts.example: A loan classifier might read: IF income < 20k THEN reject; ELSE IF debt > 50% of income THEN reject; ELSE approve. Anyone can follow why a decision was made.

concepts.name: SAMME
concepts.description: A multiclass extension of AdaBoost that adds a log(K−1) term to each learner's weight, so weak learners only need to beat random guessing among K classes rather than reach 50% accuracy.
concepts.example: With 10 classes, random guessing is only 10% accurate; SAMME's log(K-1) term gives a weak learner with 15% accuracy a positive weight, where plain AdaBoost would reject it.

concepts.name: Scree Plot
concepts.description: A plot of eigenvalues or explained variance for each principal component in decreasing order, used to decide how many components to keep by looking for an elbow.
concepts.example: Eigenvalues 5.0, 2.5, 0.4, 0.3, 0.2 plotted in order drop sharply after the second, an 'elbow' suggesting you keep 2 components.

concepts.name: Self-Organizing Map
concepts.description: A neural network that maps high-dimensional data onto a low-dimensional grid of units, pulling each winning unit and its grid neighbors toward inputs so similar data land on nearby units.
concepts.example: Feed colors as RGB values into a 10×10 grid: each color pulls its best-matching cell and its neighbors toward it, and the grid ends up as a smooth rainbow map.

concepts.name: Self-Supervised Learning
concepts.description: Learning representations from unlabeled data by creating supervision from the data itself, such as predicting masked words or matching augmented views of an image, before fine-tuning on tasks.
concepts.example: Hide 15% of the words in a sentence and train a model to guess them; no human labels are needed, yet the model learns rich language representations.

concepts.name: Self-Training
concepts.description: A semi-supervised method where a model trained on labeled data predicts labels for unlabeled examples, adds its most confident predictions as pseudo-labels, and retrains.
concepts.example: Train on 100 labelled emails, predict 10,000 unlabelled ones, add those predicted spam or ham with over 95% confidence to the training set, and retrain.

concepts.name: Semi-Supervised Learning
concepts.description: Learning from a small labeled dataset together with a large unlabeled one, using the structure of the unlabeled data to improve the model beyond what the labels alone allow.
concepts.example: With only 50 labelled medical scans but 5,000 unlabelled ones, the unlabelled scans reveal natural groupings that help place the decision boundary in low-density gaps.

concepts.name: Sequential Minimal Optimization
concepts.description: An algorithm for training SVMs that breaks the large quadratic program into the smallest possible subproblems, optimizing two Lagrange multipliers at a time in closed form.
concepts.example: Rather than solving for all 10,000 SVM multipliers at once, SMO repeatedly picks two, solves their tiny problem with a simple formula, and loops until all conditions are met.

concepts.name: Sequential Pattern Mining
concepts.description: Finding subsequences that occur frequently across a database of ordered sequences, such as common orders of purchases or page visits; algorithms include GSP and PrefixSpan.
concepts.example: In a bookshop's records, the pattern 'buys book 1 of a series, later buys book 2, later buys book 3' might appear in 20% of customers' purchase histories.

concepts.name: Shrinkage
concepts.description: In boosting, scaling each new learner's contribution by a learning rate below one so the ensemble improves in small steps; it needs more trees but usually generalizes better.
concepts.example: With learning rate 0.1, if a new tree predicts +20 for a house, only +2 is added to the running estimate, so many small steps build up the final model.

concepts.name: Sigmoid Kernel
concepts.description: A kernel k(x, y) = tanh(a·x·y + c) inspired by neural network activations; an SVM using it resembles a two-layer perceptron, though it is not positive semidefinite for all parameters.
concepts.example: With a = 1 and c = 0, vectors with dot product 0 get tanh(0) = 0 similarity, while a dot product of 2 gives tanh(2) ≈ 0.96.

concepts.name: Silhouette Score
concepts.description: A clustering quality score comparing each point's mean distance to its own cluster with that to the nearest other cluster; it ranges from −1 to 1, higher meaning tighter, better-separated clusters.
concepts.example: A point averages 2 units from its own cluster mates and 8 from the nearest other cluster, so its silhouette is (8 - 2)/8 = 0.75, a good fit.

concepts.name: Single-Linkage Clustering
concepts.description: Hierarchical clustering in which the distance between two clusters is the distance between their closest pair of points; it can find elongated clusters but suffers from chaining.
concepts.example: Two clusters on a map are 'distance 1 apart' if any pair of points across them is 1 km apart, even when most points are 50 km apart, which can chain clusters together.

concepts.name: Slope One
concepts.description: A simple item-based collaborative filtering scheme that predicts a user's rating for an item from the average rating differences between that item and others the user has rated.
concepts.example: Users rate film B on average 1 point higher than film A; you gave A a 3, so Slope One predicts you'd give B a 4.

concepts.name: SMOTE
concepts.description: An oversampling method that creates synthetic minority-class examples by interpolating between a minority point and one of its nearest minority-class neighbors, instead of duplicating points.
concepts.example: Take a minority point at (1, 1) and its minority neighbor at (3, 2); SMOTE might create a new synthetic point at (2, 1.5), halfway along the line between them.

concepts.name: Soft-Margin SVM
concepts.description: An SVM that tolerates some points inside the margin or on the wrong side by adding slack variables penalized by a constant C, making it usable on data that are not linearly separable.
concepts.example: When one red point sits deep among blue ones, a hard-margin SVM fails; the soft margin lets it be misclassified at a cost, keeping a wide margin for the rest.

concepts.name: Soft Voting
concepts.description: An ensemble rule that averages the predicted class probabilities of several classifiers and picks the class with the highest average, instead of counting hard votes.
concepts.example: Three models give 'spam' probabilities 0.9, 0.4 and 0.4; hard voting says not spam (2 to 1), but averaging gives 0.57, so soft voting says spam.

concepts.name: Sparse PCA
concepts.description: A variant of PCA that adds an L1 penalty so each principal component uses only a few original variables, making the components easier to interpret.
concepts.example: On gene data with 20,000 genes, ordinary PCA components mix all genes; sparse PCA might give a component built from just 15 genes, which biologists can actually interpret.

concepts.name: Sparsity
concepts.description: The property of having most values equal to zero, as in a weight vector, activation pattern or data matrix; sparse models are easier to interpret, store and compute with.
concepts.example: A user-movie rating table with 1 million users and 10,000 movies has 10 billion cells, but if each user rated 50 films, 99.5% of the cells are empty.

concepts.name: Specificity
concepts.description: The true negative rate: the fraction of actual negatives that a classifier correctly labels as negative, computed as TN / (TN + FP).
concepts.example: Of 100 healthy people, a test correctly clears 90 and falsely flags 10, so its specificity is 90/100 = 0.9.

concepts.name: Spectral Clustering
concepts.description: A clustering method that builds a similarity graph, embeds the points using leading eigenvectors of its graph Laplacian, and runs k-means there, capturing non-convex cluster shapes.
concepts.example: Two interlocking rings of points defeat k-means, but in a graph linking each point to its near neighbors, the Laplacian's eigenvectors separate the rings cleanly.

concepts.name: Squared Error Loss
concepts.description: The loss (y − ŷ)² that penalizes a prediction by the square of its error; minimizing its average yields the mean prediction and underlies least-squares regression.
concepts.example: Predicting 8 when the truth is 5 costs (5 - 8)² = 9, while being off by 1 costs only 1, so big errors are punished heavily.

concepts.name: Stacking
concepts.description: An ensemble method in which a meta-model learns how to combine the predictions of several base models, using their out-of-fold predictions as its input features.
concepts.example: A tree, an SVM and a neural net each predict house prices; a linear meta-model learns that the best combination is 0.5×tree + 0.3×net + 0.2×SVM.

concepts.name: Statistical Learning Theory
concepts.description: The mathematical study of learning from data, analyzing when and how fast models generalize from a finite sample using tools such as VC dimension, Rademacher complexity and risk bounds.
concepts.example: It answers questions like: if a classifier makes 3% errors on 10,000 samples, how sure can we be its true error is below 5%?

concepts.name: Stochastic Gradient Boosting
concepts.description: Gradient boosting in which each tree is fit on a random subsample of the training data drawn without replacement, adding randomness that reduces variance and speeds up training.
concepts.example: Each new tree is trained on a random 50% of the houses rather than all of them, which adds variety, speeds training and often improves accuracy.

concepts.name: Stratified k-Fold Cross-Validation
concepts.description: k-fold cross-validation in which each fold keeps roughly the same class proportions as the full dataset, giving more reliable estimates for imbalanced classes.
concepts.example: With 900 'no' and 100 'yes' examples and 5 folds, each fold gets exactly 180 'no' and 20 'yes', matching the 10% positive rate.

concepts.name: String Kernel
concepts.description: A kernel that measures similarity between strings by counting shared substrings or subsequences, letting SVMs and other kernel methods work on text and biological sequences.
concepts.example: 'cat' and 'cart' share substrings 'c', 'a', 't', 'ca' and others, so a string kernel scores them as similar, letting an SVM classify text without numeric features.

concepts.name: Structural Risk Minimization
concepts.description: A model selection principle that picks a model from a nested hierarchy of hypothesis classes by minimizing empirical error plus a complexity penalty, such as one based on VC dimension.
concepts.example: Compare polynomials of degree 1, 2, ..., 10: higher degrees fit training data better but have a larger complexity penalty, and SRM picks the degree with the lowest total.

concepts.name: Structured Prediction
concepts.description: Predicting outputs made of interdependent parts, such as sequences, trees or graphs, where the model must account for relations between output components, as in tagging or parsing.
concepts.example: Tagging 'Time flies like an arrow' with parts of speech means predicting 5 linked labels at once, since 'flies' being a verb affects whether 'like' is a preposition.

concepts.name: Subspace Clustering
concepts.description: Clustering that finds groups lying in different low-dimensional subspaces or subsets of features, rather than requiring clusters to be compact in the full high-dimensional space.
concepts.example: Among 100 features, one customer group is tight only in age and income while another is tight only in location and device; subspace clustering finds both groups.

concepts.name: Successive Halving
concepts.description: A hyperparameter search method that trains many configurations on a small budget, keeps the best fraction, and repeats with a larger budget until one configuration remains.
concepts.example: Start 64 configurations with 1 epoch each, keep the best 32 for 2 epochs, the best 16 for 4, and so on until one winner remains.

concepts.name: Supervised Learning
concepts.description: Machine learning from labeled examples, that is input–output pairs, where a model learns a function mapping inputs to outputs so it can predict labels for new inputs.
concepts.example: Show a model 10,000 photos each tagged 'cat' or 'dog'; it learns to predict the tag for photos it has never seen.

concepts.name: Support (Association Rules)
concepts.description: In association rule mining, the fraction of transactions that contain a given itemset; it measures how frequent the itemset is and is used to filter out rare patterns.
concepts.example: If 200 of 1,000 shopping baskets contain both bread and butter, the support of {bread, butter} is 0.2.

concepts.name: Support Vector
concepts.description: A training point lying on or inside the margin of an SVM; only these points determine the decision boundary, so removing any other point leaves the model unchanged.
concepts.example: Of 1,000 training points, maybe only 12 sit right on the margin edges; deleting any of the other 988 leaves the SVM's boundary unchanged.

concepts.name: Support Vector Data Description
concepts.description: A one-class method that finds the smallest hypersphere in kernel feature space enclosing most of the training data, flagging points that fall outside it as anomalies.
concepts.example: Fit the smallest ball around 1,000 normal machine readings; a new reading falling outside the ball is flagged as a possible fault.

concepts.name: Support Vector Regression
concepts.description: Regression using SVM ideas: fit a function that keeps most points within an ε-wide tube, ignoring errors inside it and penalizing larger ones, with kernels for nonlinear fits.
concepts.example: With ε = 5, house prices predicted within $5k of the truth cost nothing; only those further off are penalized, by the amount beyond $5k.

concepts.name: Surrogate Loss Function
concepts.description: A convex, differentiable stand-in for a hard-to-optimize loss such as the 0-1 loss, for example hinge or logistic loss, chosen so minimizing it also tends to minimize the true objective.
concepts.example: The 0-1 loss jumps from 0 to 1 and has no useful slope; logistic loss is a smooth curve upper-bounding it, so gradient descent can make progress.

concepts.name: SVD++
concepts.description: An extension of matrix-factorization recommenders that adds implicit feedback, representing each user partly by the items they interacted with, which improves rating predictions.
concepts.example: Even beyond your explicit ratings, the fact that you watched three horror films, implicit feedback, nudges your user vector toward horror fans.

concepts.name: Support Vector Machine
concepts.description: A classifier that finds the hyperplane separating two classes with the widest possible margin; combined with soft margins and the kernel trick it handles noisy and nonlinear data.
concepts.example: Between red and blue points on a page, many lines separate them; the SVM picks the one with the widest empty corridor, like drawing the road that stays farthest from both sides.

concepts.name: Symmetric Mean Absolute Percentage Error
concepts.description: A forecast accuracy measure that divides each absolute error by the average of the actual and forecast magnitudes, bounding the error and reducing MAPE's asymmetry.
concepts.example: Actual 100, forecast 120: the error 20 divided by the average 110 is about 18.2%; swapping them gives the same 18.2%, unlike MAPE.

concepts.name: t-Distributed Stochastic Neighbor Embedding
concepts.description: A visualization method that turns pairwise similarities into probabilities and finds a 2D or 3D embedding whose heavy-tailed Student-t similarities match them by minimizing KL divergence.
concepts.example: Feed in thousands of 784-pixel digit images; t-SNE outputs a 2D scatter where 0s, 1s and 2s form their own islands.

concepts.name: Temperature Scaling
concepts.description: A post-hoc calibration method that divides a neural network's logits by a single learned temperature before the softmax, fixing overconfidence without changing the predicted classes.
concepts.example: A network says 99% confident but is right only 80% of the time; dividing its logits by T = 2 softens outputs so 99% might become about 85%.

concepts.name: Tomek Links
concepts.description: Pairs of nearest-neighbor points from opposite classes; removing the majority-class member of each pair cleans the class boundary and acts as a form of undersampling.
concepts.example: A majority point and a minority point that are each other's nearest neighbors form a Tomek link; deleting the majority one clears the class border.

concepts.name: TPOT
concepts.description: An open-source AutoML tool that uses genetic programming to search over scikit-learn pipelines of preprocessing steps and models, returning the best pipeline as Python code.
concepts.example: Give TPOT a dataset and it evolves pipelines like 'scale, then PCA, then random forest', mutating and combining them over generations until it finds a strong one.

concepts.name: Transduction
concepts.description: Reasoning from specific training examples directly to specific test examples known in advance, rather than learning a general rule that must work for any future input.
concepts.example: Given 20 labelled and 200 specific unlabelled photos, you only need labels for those 200, not a rule that works for every future photo.

concepts.name: Transductive Support Vector Machine
concepts.description: An SVM that also uses the unlabeled test points, choosing their labels and the boundary jointly so the margin avoids dense regions of unlabeled data.
concepts.example: With few labels, a transductive SVM tries labelings of the unlabelled points and picks the boundary that runs through empty gaps, avoiding cutting through dense clusters.

concepts.name: Transfer Learning
concepts.description: Reusing knowledge from a model trained on one task or dataset to improve learning on a different but related task, often by fine-tuning a pretrained neural network.
concepts.example: A network trained on millions of everyday photos already detects edges and shapes; fine-tuning it on 500 X-ray images builds a good pneumonia detector quickly.

concepts.name: Decision Tree Pruning
concepts.description: Removing branches from a decision tree that add little predictive value, either while it grows or afterwards, to make the tree smaller and reduce overfitting.
concepts.example: A tree grown until every leaf is pure might have 200 leaves, some built on 2 training points; pruning collapses those twigs back to 30 leaves that generalize better.

concepts.name: Tree-Structured Parzen Estimator
concepts.description: A Bayesian optimization method that models the densities of good and bad hyperparameter values with kernel density estimates and samples where their ratio is highest; used in Hyperopt and Optuna.
concepts.example: After 50 trials, TPE splits them into the best 10 and the other 40, fits a density to each, and next tries learning rates where 'good' density is high relative to 'bad'.

concepts.name: TriMap
concepts.description: A dimensionality reduction method for visualization that builds its embedding from triplets of points, keeping each anchor closer to a near point than a far one, to better preserve global structure.
concepts.example: TriMap is told triplets like 'image A is closer to B than to C' and arranges points in 2D so as many of these comparisons as possible still hold.

concepts.name: True Positive
concepts.description: A case where a classifier predicts the positive class and the instance really is positive; together with false positives and false negatives it fills the confusion matrix.
concepts.example: A COVID test says 'positive' and the person really is infected; that is one true positive. If 45 infected people test positive, there are 45 true positives.

concepts.name: True Risk
concepts.description: The expected loss of a model over the entire data distribution rather than just the training sample; it measures how well the model truly generalizes and is estimated with held-out data.
concepts.example: A model makes 2% errors on its 1,000 training images, but over every image it could ever meet its error might be 8%; that 8% is its true risk.

concepts.name: Tweedie Regression
concepts.description: A generalized linear model using a Tweedie distribution, which for powers between 1 and 2 mixes a point mass at zero with a continuous positive part; suited to insurance claims and sales.
concepts.example: Insurance claims per policy are mostly exactly 0 with a few large positive amounts; a Tweedie model with power 1.5 handles that spike at zero plus the long tail.

concepts.name: Uniform Manifold Approximation and Projection
concepts.description: A dimensionality reduction method that builds a fuzzy nearest-neighbor graph of the data and optimizes a low-dimensional layout that preserves it; faster than t-SNE and keeps more global structure.
concepts.example: Feed in 50,000 single-cell gene profiles and UMAP draws a 2D map in seconds where cell types appear as separate islands connected in sensible ways.

concepts.name: Uncertainty Sampling
concepts.description: An active learning strategy that requests labels for the unlabeled examples the current model is least certain about, such as those with predicted probabilities near 0.5.
concepts.example: The model is 51% sure one email is spam and 99% sure about another; it asks a human to label the 51% one, since that label teaches it the most.

concepts.name: Underfitting
concepts.description: When a model is too simple or too briefly trained to capture the real patterns in the data, giving high error on both the training and the test set.
concepts.example: Fitting a straight line to points that follow a U-shaped curve misses the pattern entirely, giving high error on both training and test data.

concepts.name: Undersampling
concepts.description: A technique for imbalanced data that removes examples from the majority class, randomly or by a rule, so classes are more balanced, at the cost of discarding information.
concepts.example: With 9,900 normal and 100 fraudulent transactions, randomly keep just 100 normal ones so training sees a balanced 100 versus 100.

concepts.name: Unsupervised Learning
concepts.description: Machine learning from data without labels, where the model discovers structure on its own, such as clusters, low-dimensional representations or density patterns.
concepts.example: Give a model thousands of customer purchase histories with no labels; it might discover groups like 'bargain hunters' and 'weekend splurgers' on its own.

concepts.name: User-Based Collaborative Filtering
concepts.description: A recommendation method that finds users whose rating histories are similar to the target user's and recommends items those neighboring users liked.
concepts.example: Ana and Ben both loved the same five films; Ben also loved a sixth one Ana hasn't seen, so it gets recommended to Ana.

concepts.name: User-Item Matrix
concepts.description: A matrix with one row per user and one column per item whose entries record ratings or interactions; it is usually very sparse and is the input to collaborative filtering.
concepts.example: Three users and four films form a 3×4 table; Ana's row reads 5, blank, 3, blank, meaning she rated films 1 and 3 and hasn't seen 2 or 4.

concepts.name: Validation Curve
concepts.description: A plot of training and validation scores against the value of a single hyperparameter, showing where a model moves from underfitting to overfitting.
concepts.example: Plotting tree depth 1 to 20: training accuracy keeps climbing, validation accuracy peaks at depth 6 then falls, showing depth 6 is the sweet spot.

concepts.name: Vapnik–Chervonenkis Dimension
concepts.description: The size of the largest set of points that a class of classifiers can label in every possible way (shatter); it measures model capacity and appears in generalization bounds.
concepts.example: A line in the plane can split 3 non-collinear points in all 8 possible ways, but no 4 points in every way, so lines in 2D have VC dimension 3.

concepts.name: Ward's Method
concepts.description: Hierarchical clustering that at each step merges the pair of clusters whose union causes the smallest increase in total within-cluster sum of squared distances.
concepts.example: Of all possible merges, Ward's method picks the two clusters whose combination adds the least to the total within-cluster squared distance, keeping clusters compact.

concepts.name: Weak Learner
concepts.description: A model that predicts only slightly better than random guessing, such as a decision stump; boosting combines many weak learners into a single strong one.
concepts.example: A one-question decision stump like 'is the email longer than 200 words?' might be right 55% of the time on spam, barely better than a coin flip, yet boosting can combine many.

concepts.name: Weak Supervision
concepts.description: Training models with noisy, limited or imprecise labels, such as heuristic labeling rules, crowd labels or distant supervision, instead of carefully hand-labeled data.
concepts.example: Rather than hand-labelling 100,000 reviews, write rules like 'contains "terrible" → negative'; the noisy labels they produce train a decent sentiment model.

concepts.name: Weighted Majority Algorithm
concepts.description: An online algorithm that combines predictions from a pool of experts, multiplying each erring expert's weight by a factor below one; its mistakes are bounded relative to the best expert.
concepts.example: Three weather forecasters start with weight 1; each wrong forecast halves that forecaster's weight, and you follow whichever prediction has more total weight.

concepts.name: Weka
concepts.description: A free Java-based machine learning workbench from the University of Waikato with a graphical interface and a library of algorithms for classification, clustering and data preprocessing.
concepts.example: A student loads a CSV of iris flowers into Weka, picks J48 from a menu, clicks 'Start', and sees a decision tree and its cross-validated accuracy without writing code.

concepts.name: Whitening Transformation
concepts.description: A linear transformation that turns data into uncorrelated features with unit variance, so the covariance becomes the identity matrix; PCA and ZCA whitening are common forms.
concepts.example: Height and weight are correlated and on different scales; whitening rotates and rescales them into two new features, uncorrelated, each with variance 1.

concepts.name: Winnow
concepts.description: An online linear classifier similar to the perceptron but with multiplicative weight updates, which learns efficiently when only a few of many features are relevant.
concepts.example: With 1,000 features of which only 3 matter, Winnow doubles relevant weights or halves wrong ones after mistakes, homing in on the 3 with far fewer errors than a perceptron.

concepts.name: Wrapper Method
concepts.description: Feature selection that searches over feature subsets by training and evaluating a model on each, keeping the subset with the best score, as in forward selection or backward elimination.
concepts.example: Try a model on features {A, B}, then {A, B, C}, then {A, C}, scoring each subset by cross-validation and keeping whichever scores best.

concepts.name: X-Means
concepts.description: An extension of k-means that chooses the number of clusters automatically by repeatedly trying to split clusters and keeping splits that improve the Bayesian information criterion.
concepts.example: Start with k = 2 clusters, then test splitting each into two; a split is kept only if BIC improves, so the algorithm might settle on 5 clusters by itself.

concepts.name: XGBoost
concepts.description: A popular, highly optimized library for gradient-boosted decision trees that adds regularization, second-order gradient information, sparsity handling and parallel tree construction.
concepts.example: In a Kaggle contest predicting loan defaults, a few lines of XGBoost code train 1,000 regularized trees in minutes on millions of rows and often top the leaderboard.

concepts.name: Youden's J Statistic
concepts.description: A summary of a diagnostic test or classifier, J = sensitivity + specificity − 1, often used to choose the threshold on an ROC curve that best balances the two.
concepts.example: A test with 85% sensitivity and 90% specificity has J = 0.85 + 0.90 - 1 = 0.75; you pick the ROC threshold with the highest J.

concepts.name: 0-1 Loss
concepts.description: The loss that equals 0 for a correct prediction and 1 for an incorrect one; its average is the misclassification rate, but it is not differentiable and is hard to optimize directly.
concepts.example: Predicting cat, dog, dog for true labels cat, cat, dog gives losses 0, 1, 0, an average of 1/3, the error rate.

concepts.name: Zero-Shot Learning
concepts.description: Recognizing classes or performing tasks never seen during training by relating them to known ones through side information such as attributes, text descriptions or prompts.
concepts.example: Having never seen a zebra but knowing 'zebra = horse-shaped with black-and-white stripes', a model matches a zebra photo to that description and names it correctly.

concepts.name: AA Tree
concepts.description: A self-balancing binary search tree, a simplified red-black tree in which red nodes may only be right children. Balancing needs just two operations, skew and split.
concepts.example: Inserting 1, 2, 3 in order into a plain BST makes a chain; an AA tree's two fixes, skew and split, rotate it so 2 becomes the root with 1 and 3 as children.

concepts.name: Abstract Data Type
concepts.description: A data type defined by the operations it supports and their behavior, not by how it is implemented. Stacks, queues and maps are ADTs that can each be implemented in several ways.
concepts.example: A 'stack' is defined just by push, pop and peek with last-in-first-out behaviour; whether it is built on an array or a linked list is a hidden detail.

concepts.name: Accounting Method
concepts.description: An amortized analysis technique that charges each operation a fixed fee; cheap operations overpay and store credit that later pays for expensive ones, proving a bound on average cost.
concepts.example: Charge each push onto a dynamic array 3 coins: 1 pays for the push itself, 2 are saved to pay for copying elements when the array doubles, so every push costs O(1) amortized.

concepts.name: Activity Selection Problem
concepts.description: Choose the maximum number of non-overlapping activities from a set with start and finish times. Solved optimally by greedily picking the activity that finishes earliest.
concepts.example: Talks run 9-10, 9:30-11, 10-11:30 and 11-12; picking by earliest finish gives 9-10, then 10-11:30, and no later talk fits, so you attend 2.

concepts.name: Adjacency List
concepts.description: A graph representation storing, for each vertex, a list of its neighbors. It uses space proportional to vertices plus edges, making it efficient for sparse graphs.
concepts.example: For a graph with edges A-B, A-C and B-C, store A: [B, C], B: [A, C], C: [A, B]; a sparse road network with millions of towns fits easily this way.

concepts.name: Advanced Encryption Standard
concepts.description: The widely used symmetric block cipher that encrypts 128-bit blocks with 128-, 192- or 256-bit keys through rounds of byte substitution, row shifting, column mixing and key addition.
concepts.example: Your browser encrypts a 16-byte chunk of a web page with a 128-bit key through 10 rounds of byte substitution, row shifting, column mixing and key mixing.

concepts.name: Aggregate Analysis
concepts.description: An amortized analysis technique that bounds the total cost of a sequence of n operations, then divides by n to get the average cost per operation.
concepts.example: Incrementing a binary counter n times flips the last bit n times, the next n/2 times, and so on; the total is under 2n flips, so each increment is O(1) on average.

concepts.name: Aho–Corasick Algorithm
concepts.description: A string-search algorithm that finds all occurrences of many patterns at once by building a trie of the patterns with failure links, then scanning the text in a single pass.
concepts.example: To find 'he', 'she', 'his' and 'hers' in 'ushers' in one scan, build a trie of all four words with failure links, then walk the text once, reporting 'she', 'he' and 'hers'.

concepts.name: Akra–Bazzi Method
concepts.description: A generalization of the master theorem that solves divide-and-conquer recurrences with subproblems of unequal sizes, giving the asymptotic solution via an integral.
concepts.example: For T(n) = T(n/3) + T(2n/3) + n, the subproblems have unequal sizes, so the master theorem fails; Akra-Bazzi finds p = 1 and gives T(n) = Θ(n log n).

concepts.name: AKS Primality Test
concepts.description: The first deterministic algorithm proven to test primality in polynomial time without unproven assumptions, based on a polynomial identity that holds exactly when n is prime.
concepts.example: AKS can certify that 97 is prime without guessing, using a check that n divides certain polynomial coefficients, and runs in time polynomial in the number of digits.

concepts.name: Algorithm
concepts.description: A finite, precise sequence of steps that solves a problem or computes a result, such as a recipe for sorting a list. Algorithms are judged by correctness and efficiency.
concepts.example: A recipe for long division is an algorithm: for 156 ÷ 12, divide 15 by 12 to get 1 remainder 3, bring down the 6 to make 36, divide to get 3, so the answer is 13.

concepts.name: Algorithm Design Paradigm
concepts.description: A general strategy for designing algorithms that applies to many problems, such as divide and conquer, greedy choice, dynamic programming or backtracking.
concepts.example: Merge sort and binary search both follow divide and conquer: split the problem, solve the parts, and combine; knowing the paradigm suggests solutions to new problems.

concepts.name: Algorithms
concepts.description: The field of computer science studying how to design, analyze and implement step-by-step procedures for solving computational problems efficiently.
concepts.example: Choosing between bubble sort at about n² steps and merge sort at about n log n steps for a million items, roughly 10¹² versus 2×10⁷, is the kind of question the field answers.

concepts.name: All-Pairs Shortest Path
concepts.description: The problem of finding shortest path distances between every pair of vertices in a weighted graph. Solved by Floyd-Warshall, Johnson's algorithm or repeated single-source searches.
concepts.example: For four cities, the result is a 4×4 table of shortest driving distances, like the mileage chart printed in a road atlas.

concepts.name: Amortized Analysis
concepts.description: Analyzing the average cost per operation over a worst-case sequence of operations, showing that occasional expensive operations are paid for by many cheap ones (e.g. dynamic array growth).
concepts.example: A dynamic array that doubles when full occasionally copies all n items, yet n appends cost under 3n total work, so each append is O(1) amortized.

concepts.name: Analysis of Algorithms
concepts.description: The study of how much time, memory and other resources algorithms use as a function of input size, usually expressed with asymptotic notation for worst, average or best cases.
