concepts.example: Linear search checks up to n items while binary search checks about log₂ n; for n = 1,000,000 that is a million versus about 20 comparisons.

concepts.name: Andrew's Monotone Chain Algorithm
concepts.description: A convex hull algorithm that sorts points by x-coordinate, then builds the lower and upper hulls separately with a stack, discarding points that make a non-left turn. Runs in O(n log n).
concepts.example: Sort fence posts left to right, sweep across building the lower hull while removing any post that makes a clockwise turn, then sweep back for the upper hull.

concepts.name: Approximation Algorithm
concepts.description: An efficient algorithm for a hard optimization problem that returns a solution provably within some factor of the optimum, trading exactness for polynomial running time.
concepts.example: Finding the shortest tour visiting 1,000 cities is NP-hard, but Christofides' algorithm guarantees a tour at most 1.5 times the optimum in metric cases, quickly.

concepts.name: Approximation Ratio
concepts.description: The worst-case ratio between the value of an approximation algorithm's solution and the optimal value. A 2-approximation is never worse than twice the optimum.
concepts.example: If the best vertex cover has 10 nodes and an algorithm is guaranteed to return at most 20 on every input, its approximation ratio is 2.

concepts.name: Array
concepts.description: A data structure storing a fixed-size sequence of elements in contiguous memory, accessed by integer index in constant time. The most basic collection in programming.
concepts.example: Store five test scores [72, 85, 90, 64, 88] in a row of memory; scores[2] is found instantly as 90 because its address is start + 2 × element size.

concepts.name: Articulation Point
concepts.description: A vertex whose removal increases the number of connected components of a graph. Found in linear time with depth-first search; marks single points of failure in networks.
concepts.example: In a network shaped like two triangles joined at one shared router, unplugging that router splits the network in two, so it is an articulation point.

concepts.name: Associative Array
concepts.description: An abstract data type storing key-value pairs with operations to insert, look up and delete by key. Commonly implemented with hash tables or balanced search trees; called a map or dictionary.
concepts.example: A phone book mapping 'Ana' to 555-1234 and 'Ben' to 555-9876 lets you look up a number by name, add new names, or delete old ones.

concepts.name: Asymptotic Analysis
concepts.description: Describing how a function, such as an algorithm's running time, behaves as the input size grows toward infinity, ignoring constant factors and lower-order terms.
concepts.example: An algorithm taking 3n² + 100n + 500 steps is simply described as Θ(n²), since for large n the n² term dominates everything else.

concepts.name: Augmenting Path
concepts.description: A path along which more flow (in a residual network) or a larger matching (alternating unmatched and matched edges) can be pushed. Repeatedly finding them drives max-flow and matching algorithms.
concepts.example: With pipes from source to sink carrying flow below capacity along the route s→a→b→t with spare room 3, pushing 3 more units along that path raises total flow by 3.

concepts.name: Average-Case Complexity
concepts.description: The expected running time of an algorithm over a probability distribution of inputs. Quicksort, for example, is O(n log n) on average despite an O(n^2) worst case.
concepts.example: Quicksort with random pivots usually splits arrays reasonably evenly, so averaged over inputs it takes about 1.39 n log₂ n comparisons, despite an n² worst case.

concepts.name: AVL Tree
concepts.description: The first self-balancing binary search tree: the heights of each node's two subtrees differ by at most one, restored by rotations after updates, guaranteeing O(log n) operations.
concepts.example: Inserting 1, 2, 3 into an AVL tree makes the root's right side 2 levels taller than its left, so a left rotation makes 2 the root, restoring balance.

concepts.name: B+ Tree
concepts.description: A B-tree variant that stores all records in the leaves, linked together in order, with internal nodes holding only keys. Efficient for range scans; the standard index in databases and file systems.
concepts.example: A database index keeps all customer records in linked leaf pages; to list customers from 'M' to 'P' it finds the 'M' leaf and simply walks the leaf chain.

concepts.name: B-Tree
concepts.description: A self-balancing search tree whose nodes hold many keys and children, keeping all leaves at the same depth. Its wide, shallow shape minimizes disk reads, so databases and file systems use it.
concepts.example: With up to 100 keys per node, a B-tree holding a billion records is just about 5 levels deep, so a lookup reads only around 5 disk pages.

concepts.name: Baby-Step Giant-Step
concepts.description: A meet-in-the-middle algorithm for the discrete logarithm that stores about sqrt(n) 'baby steps' in a hash table and then takes 'giant steps' until a match, using O(sqrt(n)) time and space.
concepts.example: To solve 2^x ≡ 22 mod 29 with m = 6, store 2^0..2^5 as baby steps, then multiply 22 by 2^-6 repeatedly as giant steps until a match reveals x.

concepts.name: Backtracking
concepts.description: A search technique that builds a solution incrementally and abandons a partial candidate as soon as it cannot lead to a valid solution, then backs up to try alternatives. Used for N-queens and Sudoku.
concepts.example: Placing 8 queens row by row, if no column in row 5 is safe, you undo the queen in row 4, try its next column, and continue.

concepts.name: Base Case
concepts.description: The simplest instance of a problem that a recursive function solves directly without further recursion. Every recursion needs one so that it terminates.
concepts.example: In factorial(n) = n × factorial(n - 1), the base case factorial(0) = 1 stops the chain; without it, the calls would never end.

concepts.name: Bellman Equation
concepts.description: A recursive equation expressing the value of a state as the immediate reward plus the discounted value of the next state. It is the foundation of dynamic programming and reinforcement learning.
concepts.example: If a state earns reward 2 now and leads with equal chance to states worth 10 and 20, with discount 0.9 its value is 2 + 0.9 × 15 = 15.5.

concepts.name: Bellman–Ford Algorithm
concepts.description: A single-source shortest path algorithm that relaxes every edge V-1 times. Slower than Dijkstra's but handles negative edge weights and detects negative cycles.
concepts.example: For 5 vertices, relax every edge 4 times; if a 5th pass still shortens a distance, there is a negative cycle, like a currency loop that makes money.

concepts.name: Bentley–Ottmann Algorithm
concepts.description: A sweep-line algorithm that reports all k intersections among n line segments in O((n + k) log n) time, keeping the segments crossing the sweep line ordered in a balanced tree.
concepts.example: A vertical line sweeps left to right across 1,000 road segments, checking only neighboring segments for crossings, so it finds the 50 intersections without testing all 500,000 pairs.

concepts.name: Best-Case Complexity
concepts.description: The minimum resources an algorithm uses over all inputs of a given size, such as insertion sort's O(n) time on already sorted data. Rarely a useful guarantee on its own.
concepts.example: Insertion sort on an already sorted list of 1,000 items makes just 999 comparisons, its best case, versus about 500,000 in the worst case.

concepts.name: Biconnected Component
concepts.description: A maximal subgraph that stays connected after removing any single vertex. A graph splits into biconnected components at its articulation points.
concepts.example: A graph made of two squares sharing one vertex has two biconnected components, the two squares, meeting at that shared articulation point.

concepts.name: Bidirectional Search
concepts.description: A graph search that runs two simultaneous searches, forward from the start and backward from the goal, stopping when they meet. Can drastically cut the number of nodes explored.
concepts.example: To find the link chain between two people in a social network, search 3 hops out from each and meet in the middle instead of searching 6 hops from one side.

concepts.name: Big Omega Notation
concepts.description: Asymptotic notation for a lower bound: f(n) = Omega(g(n)) means f grows at least as fast as a constant times g for large n. Used to state minimum costs of algorithms or problems.
concepts.example: Any comparison sort needs Ω(n log n) comparisons in the worst case: no clever trick can sort a million items with fewer than about 20 million comparisons.

concepts.name: Big Theta Notation
concepts.description: Asymptotic notation for a tight bound: f(n) = Theta(g(n)) means f is bounded above and below by constant multiples of g for large n, i.e. both O(g) and Omega(g).
concepts.example: 3n² + 5n is Θ(n²) because for large n it stays between 3n² and 4n², squeezed above and below by multiples of n², so it grows exactly like n².

concepts.name: Bin Packing Problem
concepts.description: Pack items of given sizes into the fewest bins of fixed capacity. NP-hard; simple greedy heuristics like first fit decreasing give good approximations.
concepts.example: Pack items of size 0.5, 0.7, 0.5, 0.2, 0.4, 0.2, 0.5 into bins of capacity 1; first-fit puts each item in the first bin it fits, using a few bins quickly.

concepts.name: Binary GCD Algorithm
concepts.description: Stein's algorithm for the greatest common divisor that replaces division with shifts and subtraction, using the rules for even and odd numbers. Efficient on binary hardware.
concepts.example: gcd(48, 18): both even, so factor out a 2 for gcd(24, 9); halve 24 down to 3, then subtract and halve until gcd(3, 3) = 3, giving 2 × 3 = 6.

concepts.name: Binary Heap
concepts.description: A complete binary tree stored in an array where every parent is no larger (min-heap) or no smaller (max-heap) than its children. Supports insert and extract-min in O(log n); implements priority queues.
concepts.example: The array [1, 3, 2, 7, 4] is a min-heap: node i's children sit at 2i+1 and 2i+2, and every parent is smaller than its children, so the minimum is always at index 0.

concepts.name: Binary Lifting
concepts.description: A technique that precomputes each node's 2^k-th ancestor in a tree, letting you jump upward in O(log n) steps. Commonly used to answer lowest common ancestor queries.
concepts.example: To find the 13th ancestor of a node, jump 8, then 4, then 1 levels using precomputed 2^k-ancestor tables, taking 3 jumps instead of 13 steps.

concepts.name: Binary Search
concepts.description: Finds a target in a sorted array by repeatedly comparing it with the middle element and discarding the half that cannot contain it. Takes O(log n) comparisons.
concepts.example: Guessing a number from 1 to 100: try 50, told 'lower', try 25, told 'higher', try 37, and so on; at most 7 guesses always suffice.

concepts.name: Binary Search on the Answer
concepts.description: A problem-solving technique that binary searches over possible answer values, using a feasibility check that is monotone in the answer, to find the optimal value.
concepts.example: To find the smallest ship capacity that ships all packages in 5 days, test capacity 50: feasible; 25: not; 37: feasible; and narrow down to the minimum.

concepts.name: Binary Search Tree
concepts.description: A binary tree where each node's key is larger than all keys in its left subtree and smaller than all in its right, allowing search, insertion and deletion in time proportional to the tree's height.
concepts.example: Insert 8, 3, 10, 1, 6: 3 goes left of 8, 10 right, 1 left of 3, 6 right of 3. To find 6, go left at 8, then right at 3.

concepts.name: Binary Tree
concepts.description: A tree data structure in which each node has at most two children, called left and right. The basis of search trees, heaps and expression trees.
concepts.example: A family tree going back from you, with each person linked to at most two parents, or a tournament bracket where each match feeds from two earlier ones, is a binary tree.

concepts.name: Binomial Heap
concepts.description: A priority queue made of a collection of binomial trees, one of each size at most. Supports merging two heaps in O(log n) time, unlike a binary heap.
concepts.example: A heap of 13 items, binary 1101, consists of binomial trees of sizes 8, 4 and 1; merging two heaps works like adding two binary numbers with carries.

concepts.name: Bipartiteness Testing
concepts.description: Testing whether a graph's vertices can be colored with two colors so every edge joins different colors, done with BFS or DFS. A graph is bipartite exactly when it has no odd cycle.
concepts.example: Color the start vertex red, its neighbors blue, their neighbors red, and so on; if two adjacent vertices ever get the same color, as in a triangle, the graph is not bipartite.

concepts.name: Maximum Bipartite Matching
concepts.description: Finding the largest set of edges in a bipartite graph with no shared vertices, e.g. assigning workers to jobs. Solved by augmenting paths, Hopcroft-Karp or max flow.
concepts.example: Five job applicants each qualify for some of five jobs; the maximum matching assigns as many people as possible to distinct jobs, perhaps all five.

concepts.name: Bit Array
concepts.description: A compact array storing one bit per element, packed into machine words. Used for sets of small integers, Bloom filters and sieves, with fast bitwise operations.
concepts.example: Tracking which of 1,000 seats are booked takes 1,000 bits, about 125 bytes, instead of 1,000 bytes as booleans; seat 37 is booked if bit 37 is 1.

concepts.name: Bit Manipulation
concepts.description: Using bitwise operations such as AND, OR, XOR and shifts directly on the binary representation of integers, for compact storage, fast arithmetic tricks and subset enumeration.
concepts.example: x & 1 tells if x is odd; x << 3 multiplies by 8; x & (x - 1) clears the lowest set bit, so 12 (1100) becomes 8 (1000).

concepts.name: Bitmask Dynamic Programming
concepts.description: Dynamic programming whose states include a bitmask representing a subset of items, such as visited cities in the traveling salesman problem. Feasible when the set has about 20 elements or fewer.
concepts.example: For a 4-city travelling salesman, the state (visited = 1011, at city 3) stores the shortest path covering cities 0, 1 and 3 and ending at 3; there are only 2⁴ × 4 such states.

concepts.name: Bitonic Sorter
concepts.description: A parallel sorting network that recursively builds bitonic sequences (increasing then decreasing) and merges them with fixed compare-exchange steps. Uses O(n log^2 n) comparators; suits GPUs.
concepts.example: The sequence 1, 4, 7, 8, 6, 3, 2, 0 rises then falls, so it is bitonic; comparing elements half the length apart and swapping repeatedly sorts it with parallel comparators.

concepts.name: Bloom Filter
concepts.description: A space-efficient probabilistic set that uses several hash functions to set bits in a bit array. Membership queries may give false positives but never false negatives.
concepts.example: Add 'cat' by setting bits 3, 7 and 11 in a 16-bit array; checking 'dog' finds bit 5 unset, so 'dog' is definitely absent, while all-set bits only mean 'probably present'.

concepts.name: Blossom Algorithm
concepts.description: Edmonds' algorithm for maximum matching in general (non-bipartite) graphs. It finds augmenting paths by contracting odd cycles ('blossoms') into single vertices, running in polynomial time.
concepts.example: In a 5-cycle, an odd loop, augmenting paths get confused; the blossom algorithm shrinks the cycle into a single node, finds the path, then expands it back.

concepts.name: Bogosort
concepts.description: A deliberately inefficient sorting algorithm that randomly shuffles the list until it happens to be sorted. Expected running time is O(n * n!); used as a teaching joke.
concepts.example: To sort [3, 1, 2], shuffle randomly and check; with 6 possible orders it takes about 6 shuffles on average, but for 10 items it averages about 3.6 million.

concepts.name: Boolean Satisfiability Problem
concepts.description: Deciding whether there is an assignment of true/false values to variables that makes a Boolean formula true. The first problem proven NP-complete; modern SAT solvers handle huge instances.
concepts.example: Is there a true/false setting making (A or B) and (not A or C) and (not B) true? Yes: B false, A true, C true.

concepts.name: Borůvka's Algorithm
concepts.description: A minimum spanning tree algorithm that, in each round, adds the cheapest edge leaving every component, at least halving the number of components. Runs in O(E log V) and parallelizes well.
concepts.example: In round 1, each of 8 towns builds its cheapest road to another town, forming about 4 groups; next round, each group builds its cheapest road out, and so on until one network remains.

concepts.name: Bottom-Up Dynamic Programming
concepts.description: Dynamic programming that fills a table iteratively from the smallest subproblems up to the original problem, avoiding recursion. Also called tabulation.
concepts.example: To compute Fibonacci(10), fill a table from fib(0) = 0, fib(1) = 1 upward, each entry the sum of the previous two, reaching fib(10) = 55 without recursion.

concepts.name: Bowyer–Watson Algorithm
concepts.description: An incremental algorithm for Delaunay triangulation: insert points one by one, delete triangles whose circumcircle contains the new point, and re-triangulate the resulting hole.
concepts.example: Start with a giant triangle around all points; insert each point, delete triangles whose circumcircle contains it, and fill the hole by joining the point to the hole's edges.

concepts.name: Boyer–Moore–Horspool Algorithm
concepts.description: A simplified Boyer-Moore string search that uses only a bad-character shift table based on the text character aligned with the pattern's last position. Simple and fast in practice.
concepts.example: Searching for 'NEEDLE' in a haystack, if the text character aligned with the pattern's end is 'X', which never occurs in 'NEEDLE', shift the pattern a full 6 places.

concepts.name: Boyer–Moore Majority Vote Algorithm
concepts.description: Finds the majority element (one appearing more than half the time) in a sequence in one pass and O(1) memory by keeping a candidate and a counter that cancels out differing elements.
concepts.example: Scanning A, A, B, C, A: keep a candidate and counter, +1 on a match, -1 otherwise, switching candidates at 0; A ends as the candidate, then a second pass confirms it.

concepts.name: Boyer–Moore String-Search Algorithm
concepts.description: A string-search algorithm that compares the pattern right to left and uses bad-character and good-suffix rules to skip ahead, often examining only a fraction of the text characters.
concepts.example: Looking for 'EXAMPLE', compare from its last letter; if the text has 'Z' there, which isn't in the pattern, jump ahead 7 characters at once.

concepts.name: BPP
concepts.description: The class of decision problems solvable in polynomial time by a randomized algorithm that answers correctly with probability at least 2/3 on every input. Widely conjectured to equal P.
concepts.example: Checking whether two big polynomials are equal by plugging in random numbers is fast and wrong with probability under 1/3, repeatable to near-certainty, so it lies in BPP.

concepts.name: Breadth-First Search
concepts.description: A graph traversal that explores vertices in order of their distance from the start, visiting all neighbors before going deeper, using a queue. Finds shortest paths in unweighted graphs.
concepts.example: Find the fewest flights from Paris: first list all cities one flight away, then all cities two flights away, and so on, like ripples spreading in a pond.

concepts.name: Brent's Cycle Detection Algorithm
concepts.description: A cycle-finding algorithm for iterated functions that moves a teleporting pointer to the other's position at powers of two. Uses O(1) memory and fewer function evaluations than Floyd's method.
concepts.example: A tortoise waits at a spot while the hare runs 1, then 2, then 4, then 8 steps; whenever the power runs out without meeting, the tortoise teleports to the hare, and a meeting reveals the cycle length.

concepts.name: Bridge
concepts.description: An edge whose removal increases the number of connected components in a graph. Bridges can be found in linear time with depth-first search.
concepts.example: Two islands joined by a single bridge: remove that one edge and the road network falls into two disconnected parts, so it is a bridge.

concepts.name: Brute-Force Search
concepts.description: Solving a problem by systematically trying every possible candidate and checking each one. Simple and always correct, but usually too slow for large inputs.
concepts.example: To crack a 3-digit lock, try 000, 001, 002 and so on up to 999; at most 1,000 attempts are guaranteed to find the code.

concepts.name: Bubble Sort
concepts.description: A simple sorting algorithm that repeatedly sweeps through the list, swapping adjacent elements that are out of order, until no swaps are needed. Takes O(n^2) time.
concepts.example: Sort [5, 1, 4]: compare 5 and 1, swap to get [1, 5, 4]; compare 5 and 4, swap to get [1, 4, 5]. A second pass makes no swaps, so the list is sorted. Big values 'bubble' to the end like air rising in water.

concepts.name: Bucket Sort
concepts.description: A sorting algorithm that distributes elements into buckets by value range, sorts each bucket (often with insertion sort), and concatenates them. Runs in expected linear time on uniform data.
concepts.example: Sort exam scores 0–100 by dropping them into 10 buckets (0–9, 10–19, …). Scores 42 and 47 land in the same bucket, get sorted there, and reading the buckets left to right gives the full sorted list.

concepts.name: Burrows–Wheeler Transform
concepts.description: A reversible permutation of a string, formed from the last column of its sorted rotations, that groups similar characters together. Used in bzip2 and in FM-index genome search.
concepts.example: For 'banana$', list all 7 rotations, sort them, and read the last column: 'annb$aa'. The repeated letters cluster together, which makes the result much easier to compress, yet the original word can be rebuilt exactly.

concepts.name: Call Stack
concepts.description: The stack of frames a program keeps for active function calls, each holding parameters, local variables and the return address. Deep recursion can overflow it.
concepts.example: When main() calls f(), which calls g(), three frames sit on the stack: g on top. When g returns, its frame is popped and f resumes exactly where it left off, like a pile of sticky notes saying where to go back to.

concepts.name: Cartesian Tree
concepts.description: A binary tree built from a sequence that is heap-ordered by value and whose in-order traversal gives the original sequence. Used for range minimum queries; treaps are randomized versions.
concepts.example: For the sequence [3, 1, 4, 2], the minimum 1 becomes the root; [3] is its left subtree and [4, 2] its right, where 2 becomes the root with 4 as its left child. Reading the tree in order gives back 3, 1, 4, 2.

concepts.name: Centroid Decomposition
concepts.description: A divide-and-conquer technique on trees that repeatedly removes a centroid vertex, splitting the tree into parts of at most half the size, yielding a decomposition of depth O(log n) for path queries.
concepts.example: In a path of 7 nodes, the middle node is the centroid; removing it leaves two paths of 3, whose middles are removed next, and so on. After about log₂7 ≈ 3 levels every node has been removed.

concepts.name: Certificate
concepts.description: A certificate is a short piece of evidence, such as a satisfying assignment, that a yes-instance is correct; a verifier is an algorithm that checks it. NP is the class whose yes-answers have poly-time-verifiable certificates.
concepts.example: To convince you a Sudoku has a solution, I just hand you the filled grid. You can check every row, column and box in seconds, even though finding that grid yourself could take ages. The filled grid is the certificate.

concepts.name: Change-Making Problem
concepts.description: Find the fewest coins of given denominations that sum to a target amount. Greedy works for standard coin systems but not all; dynamic programming solves it in general.
concepts.example: With coins {1, 3, 4} and target 6, greedy grabs 4 then 1 + 1 for three coins, but 3 + 3 uses only two. Dynamic programming tries every last coin and finds the true minimum of 2.

concepts.name: Chan's Algorithm
concepts.description: An output-sensitive convex hull algorithm that combines Graham scan on small groups with gift wrapping over the groups, achieving O(n log h) time where h is the number of hull vertices.
concepts.example: With 1,000,000 points but only 10 on the hull, Chan's algorithm guesses the hull size, splits points into small groups, hulls each group quickly, then wraps around the groups, finishing far faster than n log n.

concepts.name: Chinese Remainder Theorem
concepts.description: States that a system of congruences with pairwise coprime moduli has a unique solution modulo their product. Used to split big-number arithmetic and in RSA speedups.
concepts.example: Find x with x ≡ 2 (mod 3) and x ≡ 3 (mod 5). Checking 2, 5, 8 (the numbers ≡ 2 mod 3) gives 8, which leaves remainder 3 mod 5. So x = 8, and it is the only answer between 0 and 14.

concepts.name: Christofides Algorithm
concepts.description: A 1.5-approximation for the metric traveling salesman problem: combine a minimum spanning tree with a minimum perfect matching on its odd-degree vertices, find an Euler tour and shortcut repeats.
concepts.example: To plan a salesman's tour of 6 cities, build the cheapest tree connecting them, pair up the cities with odd connections as cheaply as possible, walk the resulting loop, and skip cities already visited. The tour costs at most 1.5× the optimum.

concepts.name: Circular Buffer
concepts.description: A fixed-size array treated as if its end wraps around to its start, with head and tail indices. Implements a FIFO queue without moving elements; common in streaming and I/O buffers.
concepts.example: An 8-slot buffer holds audio samples. After writing slot 7, the next write goes to slot (7 + 1) mod 8 = 0, reusing space the reader has already consumed, like a clock hand that goes around instead of falling off the edge.

concepts.name: Circular Linked List
concepts.description: A linked list whose last node points back to the first instead of to null, so traversal can loop around continuously. Useful for round-robin scheduling.
concepts.example: Players A → B → C → back to A take turns in a board game. After C plays, following the next pointer leads straight back to A, so the turn loop never needs to restart from the beginning.

concepts.name: Circulation Problem
concepts.description: A network flow problem with lower and upper bounds on edges and flow conservation at every node, with no source or sink. Feasibility reduces to a max-flow computation.
concepts.example: A delivery loop requires each road to carry between 2 and 5 trucks per hour, and every depot must send out exactly as many trucks as it receives. Is there any assignment of truck counts that satisfies all roads at once?

concepts.name: Clique Problem
concepts.description: Finding a clique (a set of mutually adjacent vertices) of a given size, or the largest one, in a graph. Deciding whether a k-clique exists is NP-complete.
concepts.example: In a friendship network, a clique of 4 is a group of 4 people who all know each other: 6 friendships in total. Checking whether such a group exists among 1,000 people quickly becomes enormous.

concepts.name: Closest Pair of Points Problem
concepts.description: Find the two points with the smallest distance among n points in the plane. A divide-and-conquer algorithm solves it in O(n log n) instead of checking all pairs.
concepts.example: With 1,000 points, checking every pair takes about 500,000 distance calculations. Splitting into left and right halves, solving each, and checking only a thin strip near the dividing line cuts this to roughly 10,000 steps.

concepts.name: co-NP
concepts.description: The class of decision problems whose 'no' instances have short certificates checkable in polynomial time, i.e. complements of NP problems. Example: deciding whether a formula is a tautology.
concepts.example: 'Is this formula true for every input?' is in co-NP: if the answer is no, I can prove it by showing one input that makes it false. Proving 'yes' seems to require checking every input.

concepts.name: Cocktail Shaker Sort
concepts.description: A bubble sort variant that alternates forward and backward passes, moving large elements to the end and small ones to the front. Still O(n^2) but slightly faster on some inputs.
concepts.example: For [2, 3, 4, 5, 1], bubble sort needs four passes to move the 1 one step at a time to the front. A backward pass in cocktail shaker sort carries it all the way to the front at once.

concepts.name: Comb Sort
concepts.description: An improvement on bubble sort that compares elements a shrinking gap apart, quickly moving small values from the end of the list before finishing with ordinary adjacent swaps.
concepts.example: In [9, 8, 7, 6, 5, 4, 3, 2, 1], comb sort first compares elements 6 apart, then about 4, then 3, and so on down to 1. Small values near the end jump forward in big leaps instead of crawling one step per pass.

concepts.name: Combination Generation
concepts.description: Algorithms that list all k-element subsets of an n-element set, e.g. by recursion, backtracking or lexicographic successor rules, often in a specific order such as Gray-code order.
concepts.example: To list all 2-element subsets of {A, B, C, D}: AB, AC, AD, BC, BD, CD, six in total, matching C(4,2) = 6. A recursive generator decides 'include A or not' and then handles the rest of the letters.

concepts.name: Comparison Sort
concepts.description: A sorting algorithm that learns about the order only by comparing pairs of elements, like merge sort or quicksort. Any such algorithm needs Omega(n log n) comparisons in the worst case.
concepts.example: Imagine sorting sealed boxes using only a balance scale that says which of two boxes is heavier. You never see the weights themselves, only the results of pairwise comparisons; merge sort and quicksort work this way.

concepts.name: Complete Binary Tree
concepts.description: A binary tree in which every level is full except possibly the last, which is filled from left to right. This shape lets heaps be stored compactly in arrays.
concepts.example: A tree with 6 nodes has levels of 1, 2 and 3 nodes, the last level filled from the left. Stored in an array, node i's children sit at 2i+1 and 2i+2, so no pointers are needed.

concepts.name: Complete Graph
concepts.description: A graph in which every pair of distinct vertices is joined by an edge. The complete graph on n vertices, K_n, has n(n-1)/2 edges.
concepts.example: Five people at a party who each shake hands with every other person make 5×4/2 = 10 handshakes. Drawn as dots and lines, that is K5, the complete graph on 5 vertices.

concepts.name: Complexity Class
concepts.description: A set of problems solvable within a given resource bound on a given model of computation, such as P (polynomial time) or PSPACE (polynomial space).
concepts.example: P groups all yes/no problems solvable in polynomial time, like 'is this list sorted?'. PSPACE groups those solvable with polynomial memory, possibly using huge time, like deciding who wins certain board games.

concepts.name: Computational Complexity Theory
concepts.description: The field that classifies problems by the resources, such as time and memory, needed to solve them, and studies relationships between complexity classes such as P and NP.
concepts.example: Sorting 1 million numbers takes seconds, while checking every route for 60 cities would outlast the universe. Complexity theory explains this gap by grouping problems into classes like P and NP based on how cost grows.

concepts.name: Computational geometry
concepts.description: The field studying algorithms for geometric problems such as convex hulls, intersections, triangulations and nearest neighbors, with uses in graphics, robotics and GIS.
concepts.example: A delivery app finding the nearest restaurant, a robot planning a path around obstacles, and a game checking if two shapes collide all rely on computational geometry algorithms.

concepts.name: Connected Component
concepts.description: A maximal set of vertices in an undirected graph in which every pair is joined by a path. Found with BFS, DFS or union-find.
concepts.example: A social network with two friend groups that never interact has two connected components. Starting a BFS from anyone in group one reaches all of group one but nobody from group two.

concepts.name: Consistent Hashing
concepts.description: A hashing scheme that maps keys and servers onto the same ring, assigning each key to the next server clockwise, so adding or removing a server moves only a small fraction of keys.
concepts.example: Place servers A, B, C at points on a circle and hash each key to a point; it goes to the next server clockwise. Adding server D only takes keys from the arc just before D; everything else stays put.

concepts.name: Constant Time
concepts.description: An operation runs in constant time, O(1), when its cost does not grow with input size, such as accessing an array element by index.
concepts.example: Grabbing the 5th element of an array takes the same time whether it has 10 or 10 million elements, because the computer jumps straight to the right address. Looking up a page by its page number works similarly.

concepts.name: Convex Hull Algorithms
concepts.description: Algorithms computing the smallest convex polygon enclosing a set of points, including gift wrapping, Graham scan, monotone chain, Quickhull and Chan's algorithm.
concepts.example: Imagine nails hammered into a board at each point and a rubber band stretched around them all. When released, the band snaps to the convex hull; these algorithms compute that shape from coordinates.

concepts.name: Convex Hull Trick
concepts.description: A dynamic-programming optimization that maintains a set of lines and queries the minimum or maximum value at a point via their lower or upper envelope, cutting O(n^2) transitions to O(n log n) or O(n).
concepts.example: A DP where each state picks the minimum of many lines m·x + b at some x can be sped up: keep only lines that are ever the lowest, forming a convex lower envelope, and query it with binary search instead of scanning all lines.

concepts.name: Cook–Levin Theorem
concepts.description: States that Boolean satisfiability is NP-complete: any problem in NP can be reduced in polynomial time to SAT by encoding a nondeterministic Turing machine's computation as a formula.
concepts.example: Any NP puzzle, from Sudoku to scheduling, can be rewritten as one giant true/false formula that is satisfiable exactly when the puzzle has a solution. So a fast SAT solver would solve them all quickly.

concepts.name: Correctness of Algorithms
concepts.description: The property that an algorithm always terminates and produces the right output for every valid input, usually established with proofs such as loop invariants and induction.
concepts.example: A max-finding loop is correct if it always stops and returns the largest element. You show this by proving 'the best value so far is the max of everything seen' after each step.

concepts.name: Count–Min Sketch
concepts.description: A probabilistic data structure that estimates how often items appear in a data stream using a small 2D array of counters and several hash functions, never underestimating counts.
concepts.example: To count hashtags in a live tweet stream, hash each tag into one counter in each of 4 rows and increment them. To estimate a count, take the smallest of its 4 counters: collisions only add, so the minimum is closest to the truth.

concepts.name: Counting Bloom Filter
concepts.description: A Bloom filter variant that stores small counters instead of single bits in each slot, so elements can be deleted as well as inserted while keeping fast approximate membership tests.
concepts.example: Insert 'cat' and its 3 slots go from 0 to 1. Insert 'car', which shares one slot, and that slot becomes 2. Deleting 'cat' decrements its slots, so 'car' still shows up as present.

concepts.name: Counting Sort
concepts.description: A non-comparison sorting algorithm for small integer keys that counts how many times each key occurs, then uses prefix sums of the counts to place items in sorted order in linear time.
concepts.example: Sort [3, 1, 3, 0, 2]: count the values to get 0:1, 1:1, 2:1, 3:2. Prefix sums tell where each value starts, so writing them out gives [0, 1, 2, 3, 3] without a single comparison.

concepts.name: Orientation Test
concepts.description: A geometric test that uses the sign of a 2D cross product to decide whether three points make a left turn, a right turn, or are collinear; a building block of many geometry algorithms.
concepts.example: For A(0,0), B(1,0), C(1,1), compute (B−A) × (C−A) = 1·1 − 0·1 = 1. It is positive, so going A → B → C turns left; a negative value would mean right, and zero means collinear.

concepts.name: Cryptographic Hash Function
concepts.description: A hash function designed so it is infeasible to invert, to find two inputs with the same output, or to predict outputs; used for passwords, digital signatures and integrity checks.
concepts.example: Change one letter of a contract and its SHA-256 fingerprint changes completely and unpredictably. Nobody can feasibly find a different contract with the same fingerprint, so a stored hash proves the file was not altered.

concepts.name: Cuckoo Filter
concepts.description: An approximate set-membership data structure that stores short fingerprints in a cuckoo hash table, supporting deletion and often using less space than a Bloom filter.
concepts.example: To store 'apple', keep only an 8-bit fingerprint of it in one of two candidate buckets. Lookups check those two buckets for the fingerprint, and deleting just removes it, which a plain Bloom filter cannot do.

concepts.name: Cuckoo Hashing
concepts.description: An open-addressing hashing scheme that gives each key two possible slots from two hash functions; inserting into an occupied slot evicts the old key to its alternate slot, guaranteeing O(1) worst-case lookups.
concepts.example: Like a cuckoo chick pushing an egg out of the nest: a new key takes its slot, and the evicted key moves to its other possible slot, possibly evicting another. Lookups only ever check two slots.

concepts.name: Cut Property
concepts.description: The theorem that for any cut of a weighted graph, the lightest edge crossing the cut belongs to some minimum spanning tree; it justifies the correctness of Prim's and Kruskal's algorithms.
concepts.example: Split cities into East and West. Of the roads crossing between them, the cheapest one belongs in some cheapest road network connecting everything, since any network must cross the split and a costlier crossing could be swapped for it.

concepts.name: Cycle Detection
concepts.description: The problem of deciding whether a graph, linked list or iterated function contains a cycle, solved with DFS colouring, union-find or pointer-chasing techniques.
concepts.example: Course prerequisites A → B → C → A form a cycle, meaning no student could ever start. A DFS that finds an edge back to a vertex still being explored has found such a loop.

concepts.name: Cycle
concepts.description: A closed path in a graph that starts and ends at the same vertex without repeating edges or other vertices; graphs without cycles are called acyclic, such as trees and DAGs.
concepts.example: Walking A → B → C → A around a triangular park returns you home without retracing a road: that is a cycle. A family tree has none, since you can't loop back to yourself.

concepts.name: Cycle Sort
concepts.description: An in-place, unstable sorting algorithm that minimizes the number of memory writes by rotating each element directly into its final position along permutation cycles.
concepts.example: In [3, 1, 2], 3 belongs at index 2, so it goes there, displacing 2, which goes to index 1, displacing 1, which goes to index 0. One rotation of the cycle fixes all three using just 3 writes.

concepts.name: d-ary Heap
concepts.description: A generalization of the binary heap in which each node has d children, making the tree shallower so decrease-key is faster at the cost of slower delete-min; used in Dijkstra's algorithm.
concepts.example: A 4-ary heap with 1,000,000 items is only about 10 levels deep instead of 20 for a binary heap. Moving an item up is cheaper, but removing the minimum checks 4 children at each level.

concepts.name: Shortest Path in a DAG
concepts.description: An algorithm that finds single-source shortest paths in a directed acyclic graph in linear time by relaxing edges in topological order; it handles negative weights.
concepts.example: For project tasks ordered so every dependency comes first, process tasks in that order and update each successor's best distance. Every vertex is final when you reach it, so one pass suffices, even with negative weights.

concepts.name: Dancing Links
concepts.description: Knuth's technique for efficiently undoing removals from doubly linked lists during backtracking, used to implement Algorithm X for exact cover problems such as Sudoku.
concepts.example: Removing node X from a doubly linked list leaves X's own pointers intact, so later setting X.prev.next = X and X.next.prev = X puts it back. A Sudoku solver uses this to undo choices instantly while backtracking.

concepts.name: Data Structure
concepts.description: A way of organizing and storing data in memory so it can be accessed and modified efficiently, such as arrays, lists, trees and hash tables; choosing one shapes an algorithm's speed.
concepts.example: A phone's contacts could be an unsorted list, slow to search; a sorted array, searchable with binary search; or a hash table for instant lookup by name. Each data structure makes different operations fast.

concepts.name: Decision Problem
concepts.description: A computational problem whose answer for every input is simply yes or no, such as 'is this number prime?'; complexity classes like P and NP are defined in terms of decision problems.
concepts.example: 'Is 91 prime?' is a decision problem: the answer is just yes or no (no, since 91 = 7 × 13). 'What are 91's factors?' is not, because it asks for more than a single bit.

concepts.name: Decision Tree Model
concepts.description: A model of computation where an algorithm is a binary tree of comparisons; its depth gives lower bounds, such as the Ω(n log n) bound for comparison sorting.
concepts.example: Sorting 3 items has 3! = 6 possible orders. Each comparison has 2 outcomes, so 2 comparisons distinguish at most 4 cases; at least 3 comparisons are needed in the worst case.

concepts.name: Decrease and Conquer
concepts.description: An algorithm design strategy that reduces a problem to a single smaller instance, solves it, and extends the solution, as in insertion sort, binary search and Euclid's algorithm.
concepts.example: Insertion sort sorts the first n − 1 cards, then slides card n into place. Binary search checks the middle and keeps only one half. Each step shrinks the problem to one smaller version of itself.

concepts.name: Delaunay triangulation
concepts.description: A triangulation of a point set in which no point lies inside the circumcircle of any triangle, maximizing the minimum angle; it is the dual of the Voronoi diagram and used in meshing.
concepts.example: Connect cities into triangles so no city lies inside any triangle's circumscribed circle. This avoids long thin slivers and is how terrain maps and simulation meshes get well-shaped triangles.

concepts.name: Depth-First Search
concepts.description: A graph traversal that explores as far as possible along each branch before backtracking, using recursion or a stack; used for cycle detection, topological sort and connected components.
concepts.example: In a maze, keep taking the first unexplored corridor until you hit a dead end, then back up to the last junction with an untried option. That is DFS: go deep first, backtrack later.

concepts.name: Difference Array
concepts.description: A technique that stores differences between consecutive array elements so that adding a value to a whole range takes O(1); a prefix sum then rebuilds the final array.
concepts.example: To add 5 to positions 2–4 of an array of zeros, write +5 at index 2 and −5 at index 5. After many such updates, one prefix-sum pass gives the final values: [0, 0, 5, 5, 5, 0].

concepts.name: Diffie–Hellman Key Exchange
concepts.description: A protocol that lets two parties agree on a shared secret key over a public channel by exchanging powers of a generator modulo a prime, relying on the hardness of discrete logarithms.
concepts.example: Public: p = 23, g = 5. Alice picks 6 and sends 5⁶ mod 23 = 8; Bob picks 15 and sends 5¹⁵ mod 23 = 19. Alice computes 19⁶ mod 23 = 2 and Bob computes 8¹⁵ mod 23 = 2: same secret, never sent.

concepts.name: Digit Dynamic Programming
concepts.description: A dynamic programming technique that counts numbers in a range satisfying a digit-based property by building the number digit by digit while tracking state and a 'tight' bound flag.
concepts.example: Count numbers from 0 to 999 with no digit 7: build each number digit by digit, choosing 9 options per digit, giving 9³ = 729. For a limit like 523 the DP also tracks whether the prefix still equals the limit's prefix.

concepts.name: Digital Signature
concepts.description: A cryptographic scheme in which a private key signs a message and anyone with the public key can verify it, proving authenticity and integrity; used in certificates and software updates.
concepts.example: A software company signs an update with its private key. Your laptop checks the signature with the public key, and if even one byte was tampered with, the check fails.

concepts.name: Dijkstra's Algorithm
concepts.description: A greedy algorithm that finds shortest paths from a source in a graph with non-negative edge weights by repeatedly settling the closest unvisited vertex using a priority queue.
concepts.example: From home, roads to the shop (2 km) and the park (5 km); the shop to the park is 1 km. Settle home, then the shop at 2, which improves the park to 3, then settle the park at 3. Always settle the closest unsettled place next.

concepts.name: Dinic's Algorithm
concepts.description: A maximum flow algorithm that builds a level graph with BFS and sends blocking flows along shortest augmenting paths, running in O(V²E) and very fast on unit-capacity graphs.
concepts.example: Label each vertex by its BFS distance from the source, then push flow only along edges going one level deeper, saturating as many paths as possible. Repeat with a fresh level graph until the sink is unreachable.

concepts.name: Discrete Logarithm
concepts.description: The problem of finding an exponent x such that g^x ≡ h modulo a prime; it is believed hard for large primes, which underpins Diffie–Hellman and ElGamal.
concepts.example: Modulo 23, 5³ = 125 = 5·23 + 10, so 5³ ≡ 10. Going forward is easy, but given only 10, finding the exponent 3 requires search, and for 600-digit primes no practical method is known.

concepts.name: Disjoint-Set Data Structure
concepts.description: A data structure that tracks a partition of elements into disjoint sets, supporting near-constant-time union and find with path compression and union by rank; used in Kruskal's algorithm.
concepts.example: Track which islands are joined by bridges: each island starts in its own group. Building a bridge merges two groups, and 'same group?' is answered by checking whether both islands lead to the same root.

concepts.name: Divide and Conquer
concepts.description: An algorithm design paradigm that splits a problem into smaller independent subproblems, solves them recursively and combines the results, as in merge sort and quicksort.
concepts.example: To sort 8 cards, split into two piles of 4, sort each pile the same way, then merge them by repeatedly taking the smaller top card. Merge sort does this with any number of items.

concepts.name: Divide and Conquer DP Optimization
concepts.description: A dynamic programming speed-up for recurrences where the optimal split point is monotone, computing each DP layer by divide and conquer in O(n log n) instead of O(n²).
concepts.example: Splitting 1,000 houses into 10 districts with DP: if each house's best split point never moves left as houses increase, compute the middle house's split first, then search only to the left or right of it for the halves.

concepts.name: Divisibility
concepts.description: The relation where an integer a divides b if b equals a times some integer; the basis of factors, multiples, primes and modular arithmetic.
concepts.example: 3 divides 12 because 12 = 3 × 4, but 5 does not divide 12, since 12 ÷ 5 leaves remainder 2. That is why 12 eggs pack evenly into rows of 3 but not rows of 5.

concepts.name: Double-Ended Queue
concepts.description: A sequence data structure that allows insertion and removal at both the front and the back in constant time, combining the abilities of a stack and a queue.
concepts.example: Browser history with a limit: new pages go on the front, and when the list is full the oldest page drops off the back. A deque handles both ends in constant time.

concepts.name: Double Hashing
concepts.description: An open-addressing collision resolution method that uses a second hash function to choose the probe step size, reducing the clustering seen with linear probing.
concepts.example: In a table of 11 slots, key 25 has home slot 25 mod 11 = 3 and step 7 − (25 mod 7) = 3. If slot 3 is full, try 6, then 9: keys with the same home slot follow different paths.

concepts.name: Doubly Linked List
concepts.description: A linked list where each node has pointers to both the next and the previous node, allowing traversal in both directions and O(1) removal of a known node.
concepts.example: A music playlist where you can hit 'next' or 'previous': each song points to the one after it and the one before it. Removing a song only means reconnecting its two neighbours.

concepts.name: DPLL Algorithm
concepts.description: A complete backtracking algorithm for Boolean satisfiability that adds unit propagation and pure-literal elimination to systematic search over variable assignments; the basis of modern SAT solvers.
concepts.example: For (a ∨ b) ∧ (¬a), the clause ¬a forces a = false (unit propagation), which then forces b = true. DPLL makes such forced moves first and only guesses when stuck, backtracking on contradictions.

concepts.name: Dutch National Flag Problem
concepts.description: The problem of rearranging an array of three kinds of values (like red, white, blue) into three contiguous groups in one pass; used for three-way partitioning in quicksort.
concepts.example: Sort [2, 0, 1, 2, 0] (0 = red, 1 = white, 2 = blue) in one pass with three pointers: swap 0s to the front, 2s to the back, and leave 1s in the middle, giving [0, 0, 1, 2, 2].

concepts.name: Dynamic Array
concepts.description: An array that grows automatically by allocating a larger block (typically double size) and copying when full, giving amortized O(1) appends; Python lists and C++ vectors work this way.
concepts.example: A list with capacity 4 is full; appending a 5th item allocates room for 8 and copies the 4 old items. The next 3 appends are free, so copying averages out to about 1 extra move per append.

concepts.name: Edge
concepts.description: A connection between two vertices in a graph, which may be directed or undirected and may carry a weight such as a distance or cost.
concepts.example: On a flight map, a line from Paris to Rome is an edge; if it carries the price €80, it is a weighted edge, and if flights only go one way, it is a directed edge.

concepts.name: Edge List
concepts.description: A graph representation that simply stores a list of all edges as pairs (or triples with weights) of vertices; compact and convenient for algorithms like Kruskal's and Bellman–Ford.
concepts.example: A road network stored as [(A, B, 5), (B, C, 3), (A, C, 9)]: one entry per road with its two towns and length. Kruskal's algorithm can simply sort this list by length.

concepts.name: Edge Relaxation
concepts.description: The step in shortest-path algorithms that checks whether going through an edge (u, v) gives a shorter path to v than currently known and, if so, updates v's distance.
concepts.example: Your best known route to C is 10 km. You discover B is 4 km away and B to C is 3 km, so going via B is 7 km. Relaxation updates C's distance to 7 and remembers B as the way in.

concepts.name: Edit Distance
concepts.description: The minimum number of single-character insertions, deletions and substitutions needed to turn one string into another, usually computed with dynamic programming; used in spell checking.
concepts.example: Turning 'kitten' into 'sitting' takes 3 edits: substitute k→s, substitute e→i, and insert g at the end. A spell checker suggests words with small edit distance from what you typed.

concepts.name: Edmonds–Karp Algorithm
concepts.description: An implementation of Ford–Fulkerson that always augments along the shortest path found by breadth-first search, guaranteeing a polynomial O(VE²) running time for maximum flow.
concepts.example: Pushing water from a source to a sink through pipes, always pick the augmenting route with the fewest pipes, found by BFS. This rule guarantees the process ends after a polynomial number of augmentations, whatever the capacities.

concepts.name: Egg Dropping Puzzle
concepts.description: A classic dynamic programming problem: with k eggs and n floors, find the minimum number of drops needed in the worst case to determine the highest floor from which an egg survives.
concepts.example: With 2 eggs and 100 floors, the best strategy needs only 14 drops in the worst case: drop from floor 14, then 27, then 39, and so on, shrinking the step by one each time; after a break, test the floors below one at a time.

concepts.name: ElGamal Encryption
concepts.description: A public-key encryption scheme based on Diffie–Hellman in which the sender masks the message with a shared secret derived from a random exponent; its security rests on the discrete logarithm problem.
concepts.example: Bob publishes g^b. To send m, Alice picks a fresh random k, sends g^k and m·(g^b)^k. Bob raises g^k to his secret b to get the same mask (g^b)^k, then divides it out to recover m.

concepts.name: Elliptic-Curve Cryptography
concepts.description: Public-key cryptography built on the group of points of an elliptic curve over a finite field, giving the same security as RSA with much smaller keys; used in TLS and cryptocurrencies.
concepts.example: Adding a point on a curve to itself k times is fast, but recovering k from the result is believed to be very hard. A 256-bit elliptic-curve key gives security comparable to a 3072-bit RSA key.

concepts.name: Euler Tour Technique
concepts.description: A method that flattens a tree into an array by recording nodes in DFS entry/exit order, so subtree and path queries become range queries handled by segment trees or Fenwick trees.
concepts.example: Run DFS on a tree and write each node's entry time: root 0, its children 1, 2, 3, and so on. A whole subtree then occupies one contiguous range of positions, so 'sum of salaries under manager X' becomes a range sum.

concepts.name: Euler's Theorem
concepts.description: The number theory result that a^φ(n) ≡ 1 (mod n) whenever a and n are coprime, generalizing Fermat's little theorem; it explains why RSA decryption works.
concepts.example: φ(10) = 4 and 3 is coprime to 10, so 3⁴ = 81 ≡ 1 (mod 10). Hence 3¹⁰⁰ = (3⁴)²⁵ ≡ 1 (mod 10), so 3¹⁰⁰ ends in the digit 1.

concepts.name: Euler's Totient Function
concepts.description: The function φ(n) that counts how many integers from 1 to n are coprime to n; it is multiplicative and central to Euler's theorem and RSA.
concepts.example: φ(9) = 6, because among 1–9 the numbers 1, 2, 4, 5, 7, 8 share no factor with 9, while 3, 6, 9 do. For a prime like 7, φ(7) = 6, since every smaller positive number is coprime to it.

concepts.name: Exact Cover
concepts.description: The NP-complete problem of choosing a collection of subsets such that every element of the universe is contained in exactly one chosen subset; Sudoku and pentomino tiling reduce to it.
concepts.example: Pick from sets {1,2}, {3}, {2,3}, {1} so every number from 1 to 3 is covered exactly once: {1,2} and {3} work, while {1,2} and {2,3} fail because 2 is covered twice.

concepts.name: Exponential Search
concepts.description: A search algorithm for sorted, possibly unbounded arrays that doubles an index until it passes the target, then runs binary search in the last range, taking O(log i) for target position i.
concepts.example: To find 37 in a huge sorted list, check positions 1, 2, 4, 8, 16, 32 until the value there exceeds 37, then binary search only between the last two checkpoints. Targets near the start are found very fast.

concepts.name: Exponential Time
concepts.description: Running time that grows like 2^poly(n), so each extra input element multiplies the work; typical of brute-force search and considered intractable for large inputs.
concepts.example: A brute-force password search over n bits tries 2ⁿ keys: 20 bits means about a million tries, 40 bits about a trillion. Each extra bit doubles the work.

concepts.name: Exponentiation by Squaring
concepts.description: A method to compute x^n with only O(log n) multiplications by repeatedly squaring and using the binary digits of n; the basis of fast modular and matrix exponentiation.
concepts.example: To compute 3¹³, note 13 = 8 + 4 + 1 in binary. Square repeatedly to get 3, 3², 3⁴, 3⁸, then multiply 3⁸·3⁴·3¹. That is 5 multiplications instead of 12.

concepts.name: EXPTIME
concepts.description: The complexity class of decision problems solvable by a deterministic Turing machine in exponential time 2^poly(n); it contains P, NP and PSPACE and strictly contains P.
concepts.example: Deciding who wins from a given position in chess generalized to n×n boards is EXPTIME-complete: it is solvable by exploring exponentially many positions, and provably not in polynomial time.

concepts.name: Extended Euclidean Algorithm
concepts.description: An extension of Euclid's algorithm that also finds integers x and y with ax + by = gcd(a, b); used to compute modular inverses and solve linear Diophantine equations.
concepts.example: For 3 and 7, it finds gcd = 1 along with 3·5 + 7·(−2) = 1. Reading that mod 7 gives 3·5 ≡ 1, so 5 is the inverse of 3 modulo 7.

concepts.name: External Sorting
concepts.description: Sorting data too large to fit in main memory by sorting chunks that fit, writing them to disk as sorted runs, and merging the runs with a k-way merge.
concepts.example: To sort 100 GB with 1 GB of RAM, sort 100 chunks of 1 GB each and save them as sorted files. Then merge all 100 files at once, repeatedly taking the smallest head item, reading each file sequentially.

concepts.name: Fenwick Tree
concepts.description: A compact array-based structure that supports prefix-sum queries and point updates in O(log n) by using the lowest set bit of indices to define responsibility ranges.
concepts.example: To sum the first 13 elements, write 13 = 1101 in binary. Index 13 stores element 13, index 12 stores 9–12, and index 8 stores 1–8, so three lookups give the answer instead of 13 additions.

concepts.name: Fermat Primality Test
concepts.description: A probabilistic test that declares n probably prime if a^(n−1) ≡ 1 (mod n) for random bases a; fast but fooled by Carmichael numbers.
concepts.example: Test n = 15 with base 2: 2¹⁴ mod 15 = 4, not 1, so 15 is definitely composite. For n = 13, 2¹² mod 13 = 1, so 13 is probably prime. Carmichael numbers like 561 pass for every base coprime to them.

concepts.name: Fermat's Little Theorem
concepts.description: The theorem that if p is prime and a is not divisible by p, then a^(p−1) ≡ 1 (mod p); it underlies primality tests and modular inverse computation.
concepts.example: With p = 5 and a = 2: 2⁴ = 16 = 3·5 + 1, so 2⁴ ≡ 1 (mod 5). It also gives inverses: 2³ = 8 ≡ 3, and indeed 2·3 = 6 ≡ 1 (mod 5).

concepts.name: Fibonacci Heap
concepts.description: A priority queue made of a collection of heap-ordered trees with lazy merging, giving amortized O(1) insert and decrease-key; it speeds up Dijkstra's and Prim's algorithms in theory.
concepts.example: Inserting into a Fibonacci heap just adds a new one-node tree to the root list, with no restructuring. All the tidying is postponed until someone removes the minimum, like leaving dishes until you need a plate.

concepts.name: Fibonacci Search Technique
concepts.description: A search method on sorted arrays that splits the range using Fibonacci numbers instead of halves, needing only addition and subtraction to compute probe positions.
concepts.example: In a sorted array of 13 items, probe at position 8, splitting it into parts of 8 and 5. Depending on the comparison, continue in the part of size 8 (split 5 + 3) or size 5 (split 3 + 2), using only additions and subtractions.

concepts.name: Fisher–Yates Shuffle
concepts.description: An algorithm that produces a uniformly random permutation of an array in linear time by swapping each position with a randomly chosen position from the not-yet-shuffled part.
concepts.example: To shuffle [A, B, C, D], swap D with a random position from 1–4, then the 3rd item with a random position from 1–3, and so on. Each of the 24 orders comes out with equal chance.

concepts.name: Fleury's Algorithm
concepts.description: An algorithm for finding an Eulerian path or circuit by walking edges and never crossing a bridge unless no other choice remains; simple but slower than Hierholzer's algorithm.
concepts.example: Drawing a figure without lifting the pen: at each step avoid an edge whose removal would cut the remaining drawing into two pieces, unless it is the only edge left. Following that rule, you never get stranded.

concepts.name: Flood Fill
concepts.description: An algorithm that finds and colors all cells connected to a starting cell that share a property, using DFS or BFS on a grid; used in paint bucket tools and region labeling.
concepts.example: Clicking the paint bucket on a white region of a drawing turns that pixel blue, then its white neighbours, then theirs, spreading until it hits a non-white border.

concepts.name: Flow Network
concepts.description: A directed graph where each edge has a capacity and flow travels from a source to a sink, respecting capacities and conservation at every other node; the setting for max-flow problems.
concepts.example: A water system: the reservoir is the source, a city is the sink, and each pipe can carry at most so many litres per second. Every junction must pass on exactly as much water as it receives.

concepts.name: Floyd–Warshall Algorithm
concepts.description: A dynamic programming algorithm that computes shortest paths between all pairs of vertices in O(V³) by allowing intermediate vertices one at a time; works with negative edges.
concepts.example: First allow only direct flights between cities. Then allow connecting via city 1, then via cities 1 and 2, and so on. After allowing every city as a stopover, the table holds the cheapest trip between every pair.

concepts.name: Floyd's Cycle-Finding Algorithm
concepts.description: A pointer algorithm that detects a cycle in a sequence or linked list by moving a slow pointer one step and a fast pointer two steps; they meet if and only if a cycle exists, using O(1) memory.
concepts.example: A tortoise and a hare run along a linked list; the hare moves two nodes per step. If the list ends, there is no loop. If they ever land on the same node, the list must loop back on itself.

concepts.name: FM-Index
concepts.description: A compressed full-text index built on the Burrows–Wheeler transform that counts and locates pattern occurrences without decompressing; widely used in DNA read alignment.
concepts.example: A human genome has about 3 billion letters. An FM-index stores it compressed, yet can tell how many times 'GATTACA' occurs by processing the pattern one letter at a time from the end, without scanning the genome.

concepts.name: Fowler–Noll–Vo Hash Function
concepts.description: A simple, fast non-cryptographic hash function that processes bytes by repeatedly XORing them into a state and multiplying by a fixed prime; used in hash tables and checksums.
concepts.example: Start from a fixed 32-bit offset value; for each byte of 'cat', XOR it into the state, then multiply by the FNV prime 16777619 (keeping 32 bits). Similar inputs end up with very different hashes in just a few cheap steps.

concepts.name: Ford–Fulkerson Algorithm
concepts.description: A method for computing maximum flow that repeatedly finds an augmenting path in the residual graph and pushes as much flow as possible along it until no such path remains.
concepts.example: To ship goods from a factory to a store through roads with truck limits, find any route with spare capacity, send as much as fits, and repeat. Routes may also undo earlier shipments; stop when no route has room.

concepts.name: Fortune's Algorithm
concepts.description: A sweep-line algorithm that builds the Voronoi diagram of n points in O(n log n) time by maintaining a 'beach line' of parabolic arcs as the sweep advances.
concepts.example: A line sweeps down over the sites. Points equally far from a site and the sweep line form parabolas, and where neighbouring parabolas meet traces out the Voronoi edges as the sweep moves.

concepts.name: Fractional Knapsack Problem
concepts.description: A knapsack variant in which items can be split, so a greedy algorithm that takes items in order of value-to-weight ratio gives the optimal solution.
concepts.example: A bag holds 10 kg. Gold dust: 4 kg worth $40 ($10/kg); silver dust: 8 kg worth $40 ($5/kg). Take all the gold, then 6 kg of silver for $30, a total of $70, which is optimal.

concepts.name: Freivalds' Algorithm
concepts.description: A randomized algorithm that checks whether A·B = C for n×n matrices in O(n²) time by multiplying both sides by a random 0/1 vector, with a small one-sided error probability.
concepts.example: Instead of multiplying A and B in full to check C, pick a random 0/1 vector r and compare A(Br) with Cr, which are just matrix-vector products. If C is wrong, each trial catches it at least half the time.

concepts.name: Full Binary Tree
concepts.description: A binary tree in which every node has either zero or two children, never exactly one; a full binary tree with n leaves has n − 1 internal nodes.
concepts.example: A knockout tournament with 8 players is a full binary tree: each match has exactly 2 entrants. With 8 leaves (players) there are 7 internal nodes, meaning exactly 7 matches.

concepts.name: Gale–Shapley Algorithm
concepts.description: The deferred-acceptance algorithm that finds a stable matching by having one side propose in preference order while the other tentatively holds its best offer so far.
concepts.example: Students propose to their favourite schools; each school keeps its best proposer so far and rejects the rest. Rejected students try their next choice. When proposals stop, no student and school would both rather switch.

concepts.name: General Number Field Sieve
concepts.description: The fastest known classical algorithm for factoring large integers, using algebraic number fields to find congruences of squares in sub-exponential time; it sets RSA key sizes.
concepts.example: To factor the 232-digit RSA-768, GNFS gathered huge numbers of relations over algebraic number fields to build x² ≡ y² (mod n); then gcd(x − y, n) revealed a factor. It took about 2,000 CPU-core-years.

concepts.name: Geometric Primitives
concepts.description: Basic geometric operations used by computational geometry algorithms, such as orientation tests, segment intersection checks, distances and areas computed with cross and dot products.
concepts.example: To know whether segments AB and CD cross, a program asks four small questions: is C left or right of AB, is D, is A left or right of CD, is B. These cross-product sign tests are geometric primitives.

concepts.name: Gift Wrapping Algorithm
concepts.description: A convex hull algorithm (Jarvis march) that starts at the leftmost point and repeatedly picks the point making the most counter-clockwise turn, running in O(nh) for h hull points.
concepts.example: Start at the leftmost point and imagine wrapping a string around the points: at each step pick the point such that all other points lie on one side of the string, and stop when you return to the start.

concepts.name: Gnome Sort
concepts.description: A simple sorting algorithm that moves forward through the array and swaps an element backward until it is in place, like insertion sort done with swaps; O(n²) time.
concepts.example: A garden gnome sorts flower pots: if the pot ahead is fine, step forward; if it is smaller than the one behind, swap them and step back. For [3, 1, 2], swap to [1, 3, 2], then [1, 2, 3].

concepts.name: Graham Scan
concepts.description: A convex hull algorithm that sorts points by angle around the lowest point and then scans them with a stack, discarding points that make clockwise turns; runs in O(n log n).
concepts.example: Pick the lowest point, sort the others by angle around it, and walk through them with a stack. Whenever the last three points turn clockwise, pop the middle one, as it can't be on the hull.

concepts.name: Graph Traversal
concepts.description: The process of visiting every vertex of a graph in a systematic order, typically by breadth-first or depth-first search, while marking visited vertices to avoid repeats.
concepts.example: To find everyone reachable from you in a social network, visit your friends, then their friends, crossing each person off as visited so nobody is visited twice, even across mutual friendships.

concepts.name: Gray Code
concepts.description: An ordering of binary numbers in which consecutive values differ in exactly one bit; used in rotary encoders, error reduction and enumerating subsets with minimal changes.
concepts.example: The 2-bit Gray code goes 00, 01, 11, 10: each step flips exactly one bit. A rotary dial using it can never misread 01 → 10 as 11 halfway through, since only one bit changes at a time.

concepts.name: Greedy Choice Property
concepts.description: The property that a globally optimal solution can be reached by making the locally best choice at each step; together with optimal substructure it makes a greedy algorithm correct.
concepts.example: For activity selection, always choosing the meeting that ends earliest is safe: any optimal schedule can swap its first meeting for that one without losing a meeting. Hence greedy reaches an optimum.

concepts.name: Greedy Set Cover Algorithm
concepts.description: An approximation algorithm for set cover that repeatedly picks the set covering the most uncovered elements, achieving a ln n approximation ratio, which is essentially the best possible.
concepts.example: To cover 10 neighbourhoods with as few fire stations as possible, first build the station covering the most neighbourhoods, then the one covering the most remaining ones, and repeat until all are covered.

concepts.name: Hall's Marriage Theorem
concepts.description: The theorem that a bipartite graph has a matching covering one side exactly when every subset S of that side has at least |S| neighbors on the other side.
concepts.example: Three applicants each list acceptable jobs. If any two of them together accept only one job, they can't both be hired. Hall's theorem says that if no group of k applicants accepts fewer than k jobs, everyone can be hired.

concepts.name: Halting Problem
concepts.description: The problem of deciding, for any program and input, whether the program eventually stops; Turing proved no algorithm can solve it, the classic example of an undecidable problem.
concepts.example: Suppose a program H could tell whether any program halts. Build D, which asks H about D itself and does the opposite: loop if told 'halts', stop if told 'loops'. Either answer is wrong, so H cannot exist.

concepts.name: Hash Collision
concepts.description: The situation where two different inputs produce the same hash value; unavoidable by the pigeonhole principle, so hash tables need collision resolution and cryptographic hashes make collisions hard to find.
concepts.example: With 367 people in a room, at least two share a birthday, since there are only 366 possible days. Likewise, mapping a million names into 1,000 slots guarantees many names share a slot.

concepts.name: Hash Function
concepts.description: A function that maps data of arbitrary size to a fixed-size value, ideally spreading inputs uniformly; used to index hash tables, fingerprint data and verify integrity.
concepts.example: A cloakroom gives your coat ticket number 37 based on your name, so the attendant knows exactly which hook to check later. A hash function turns any key into a fixed-size number like that.

concepts.name: Hash Table
concepts.description: A data structure that stores key–value pairs in an array indexed by a hash of the key, giving average O(1) insertion, deletion and lookup; Python dicts are hash tables.
concepts.example: Store a phone book in 100 buckets: hash 'Alice' to bucket 42 and put her number there. To look Alice up, hash again and go straight to bucket 42 instead of scanning all entries.

concepts.name: Heap
concepts.description: A tree-based data structure satisfying the heap property — every parent is no larger (min-heap) or no smaller (max-heap) than its children — used to implement priority queues.
concepts.example: In a hospital waiting room, the most urgent patient is always next. A min-heap keeps the most urgent at the top, and adding or removing a patient takes only about log n swaps along one path.

concepts.name: Heapify
concepts.description: The procedure that turns an arbitrary array into a heap by sifting down each internal node from the bottom up, running in linear O(n) time.
concepts.example: For [3, 9, 2, 1, 4, 5], sift down from the last parent: 2 swaps with 5, 9 already beats its children, then 3 swaps with 9 and then with 4, giving the max-heap [9, 4, 5, 1, 3, 2].

concepts.name: Heapsort
concepts.description: A comparison sort that builds a max-heap from the array and repeatedly swaps the maximum to the end and restores the heap, giving O(n log n) worst-case time in place.
concepts.example: Turn [4, 1, 3] into the max-heap [4, 1, 3], swap the top 4 to the end, and fix the heap to [3, 1]. Swap 3 to the end, leaving [1], so the array reads [1, 3, 4].

concepts.name: Heavy-Light Decomposition
concepts.description: A technique that splits a tree into heavy paths so any root-to-node path crosses O(log n) of them, letting path queries and updates be answered with a segment tree.
concepts.example: In a company tree, each manager's link to the report with the biggest team is marked 'heavy'. Chains of heavy links become contiguous stretches of an array, and any path from an employee to the CEO crosses only about log n chains.

concepts.name: Held–Karp Algorithm
concepts.description: A dynamic programming algorithm that solves the travelling salesman problem exactly in O(n²·2ⁿ) by storing the best path cost for each subset of visited cities and ending city.
concepts.example: For 4 cities, store the best cost of 'start at A, visit exactly set S, end at city j' for every set S and end j. Growing sets one city at a time, about 2⁴ × 4 states replace checking every possible ordering.

concepts.name: Hierholzer's Algorithm
concepts.description: A linear-time algorithm for finding an Eulerian circuit by following unused edges until returning to the start and then splicing in sub-circuits from vertices with remaining edges.
concepts.example: Start at a vertex and keep walking unused edges until you return to it. If some visited vertex still has unused edges, start a detour loop from there and splice it into the main loop, repeating until all edges are used.

concepts.name: Hirschberg's Algorithm
concepts.description: A divide-and-conquer method that finds an optimal sequence alignment or LCS using only linear space by computing DP scores forward and backward to find the midpoint split.
concepts.example: Aligning two 100,000-letter DNA strings needs a 10-billion-cell table. Hirschberg instead finds where the best alignment crosses the middle row using two linear-space passes, then recurses on the two halves.

concepts.name: Hopcroft–Karp Algorithm
concepts.description: An algorithm that finds a maximum matching in a bipartite graph in O(E√V) by augmenting along many vertex-disjoint shortest augmenting paths in each phase found with BFS and DFS.
concepts.example: When matching 1,000 students to projects, rather than improving the matching one path at a time, each phase uses BFS to find the shortest augmenting length and then augments along many disjoint paths of that length at once.

concepts.name: Hopscotch Hashing
concepts.description: An open-addressing scheme that keeps every key within a small fixed neighborhood of its home bucket, moving keys closer when needed, giving cache-friendly lookups even at high load factors.
concepts.example: Each key must live within, say, 32 slots of its home bucket. If the nearest free slot is farther away, nearby keys hop forward to open space closer, so any lookup only scans one small, cache-friendly neighbourhood.

concepts.name: HyperLogLog
concepts.description: A streaming algorithm that estimates the number of distinct elements using tiny memory by hashing items and recording the maximum number of leading zeros seen in many buckets.
concepts.example: Flip coins: seeing a run of 10 heads in a row suggests about 2¹⁰ tries. Similarly, if some item's hash starts with 20 zero bits, there were likely around a million distinct items. Averaging many buckets makes this reliable.

concepts.name: In-Place Algorithm
concepts.description: An algorithm that transforms its input using only a small, constant (or logarithmic) amount of extra memory beyond the input itself, such as heapsort or in-place quicksort.
concepts.example: Reversing an array by swapping the first and last items, then the second and second-to-last, and so on, needs only one spare variable. Copying the items backward into a new array would need n extra slots.

concepts.name: Hardness of Approximation
