concepts.description: The study of showing that, unless P = NP, certain optimization problems cannot be approximated within a given ratio in polynomial time, often via the PCP theorem.
concepts.example: For general TSP without the triangle inequality, no polynomial algorithm can guarantee a tour within any fixed factor of optimal unless P = NP. For max-clique, even an n^0.99 factor is NP-hard to guarantee.

concepts.name: Incidence Matrix
concepts.description: A graph representation as a vertices-by-edges matrix where each entry indicates whether a vertex is an endpoint of an edge (with signs for direction in directed graphs).
concepts.example: For a triangle with vertices A, B, C and edges e1 = AB, e2 = BC, e3 = CA, the matrix has a row per vertex and a column per edge; the column for e1 has 1s in rows A and B and 0 in row C.

concepts.name: Independent Set
concepts.description: The NP-hard problem of finding the largest set of vertices in a graph with no edge between any two of them; the complement of a vertex cover.
concepts.example: Planning a party where no two invitees dislike each other: draw a line between every feuding pair and pick the most people with no line between them. With hundreds of guests this becomes extremely hard.

concepts.name: Inorder Traversal
concepts.description: A depth-first tree traversal that visits the left subtree, then the node, then the right subtree; on a binary search tree it yields the keys in sorted order.
concepts.example: In a BST with root 5, left child 3 and right child 8, inorder visits 3, then 5, then 8. Applied recursively, it always lists a BST's keys in increasing order.

concepts.name: Insertion Sort
concepts.description: A simple sorting algorithm that builds a sorted prefix by taking each new element and shifting it left into its correct position; O(n²) worst case but fast on small or nearly sorted data.
concepts.example: Like sorting a hand of cards: pick up 7, then 3 goes left of it, then 5 slides between 3 and 7. Each new card is shifted left past larger cards until it fits.

concepts.name: Integer Factorization
concepts.description: The problem of decomposing an integer into its prime factors; no fast classical algorithm is known for large numbers, which is what makes RSA secure.
concepts.example: Multiplying 61 × 53 = 3233 is instant, but going back from 3233 to 61 and 53 means hunting for divisors. For 600-digit numbers that hunt is beyond all known classical computers.

concepts.name: Interpolation Search
concepts.description: A search algorithm for sorted, roughly uniformly distributed arrays that estimates the target's position from its value, averaging O(log log n) probes.
concepts.example: Looking up 'Williams' in a phone book, you open near the end rather than the middle, guessing from where W sits in the alphabet. Interpolation search estimates the position from the target's value in the same way.

concepts.name: Interval Dynamic Programming
concepts.description: A DP technique where states are subarray intervals [i, j] and each interval is solved by combining smaller intervals, as in matrix chain multiplication and optimal BST.
concepts.example: To find the cheapest way to multiply matrices A·B·C·D, solve every short stretch first (AB, BC, CD), then length-3 stretches, then the whole chain, trying every split point for each.

concepts.name: Interval Tree
concepts.description: A balanced binary search tree that stores intervals augmented with the maximum endpoint in each subtree, so it can find all intervals overlapping a query in O(log n + k).
concepts.example: A calendar storing meetings as intervals can answer 'what overlaps 2–3 pm?' fast: each tree node remembers the latest end time in its subtree, so whole branches that end before 2 pm are skipped.

concepts.name: Introsort
concepts.description: A hybrid sort used in C++ std::sort that starts with quicksort, switches to heapsort when recursion gets too deep, and uses insertion sort on small pieces, guaranteeing O(n log n).
concepts.example: C++'s std::sort starts as quicksort, but if recursion gets too deep due to bad pivots, it switches to heapsort, and it finishes tiny pieces with insertion sort. You get quicksort's speed with an O(n log n) guarantee.

concepts.name: Inverse Ackermann Function
concepts.description: An extremely slowly growing function α(n), at most 4 for any practical n, that appears in the amortized running time of union-find with path compression and union by rank.
concepts.example: Ackermann's function explodes: A(4, 4) is far larger than the number of atoms in the universe. Its inverse α(n) therefore barely moves, staying at most 4 for any input you could ever store.

concepts.name: Inversion
concepts.description: A pair of positions i < j in a sequence whose elements are out of order (a[i] > a[j]); the inversion count measures how unsorted an array is and can be computed with merge sort.
concepts.example: In [3, 1, 2], the pairs (3, 1) and (3, 2) are out of order, so there are 2 inversions. A sorted array has 0, and a fully reversed array of n items has n(n−1)/2.

concepts.name: Iteration
concepts.description: Repeating a block of instructions, usually with a loop, where each repetition updates state until a stopping condition is reached; the alternative to recursion for repeated work.
concepts.example: Adding up 1 to 5 with a loop: start total = 0, then add 1, 2, 3, 4, 5 in turn, updating total each time, and stop after 5. Each pass through the loop is one iteration.

concepts.name: Iterative Deepening Depth-First Search
concepts.description: A search strategy that runs depth-limited DFS with limits 0, 1, 2, … until the goal is found, combining BFS's optimal depth guarantee with DFS's low memory use.
concepts.example: To find a key hidden in a huge house, search every room 1 door away, then restart and search up to 2 doors away, then 3. You re-walk some rooms, but you find the closest key while remembering only the current path.

concepts.name: Jaccard Index
concepts.description: A similarity measure between two sets equal to the size of their intersection divided by the size of their union; also used as Intersection over Union to score object detection boxes.
concepts.example: Alice likes {pizza, sushi, tacos} and Bob likes {sushi, tacos, curry}. They share 2 foods out of 4 distinct ones, so their Jaccard similarity is 2/4 = 0.5.

concepts.name: Job Sequencing with Deadlines
concepts.description: A scheduling problem of choosing and ordering unit-time jobs, each with a deadline and profit, to maximize total profit; solved greedily by taking jobs in decreasing profit order.
concepts.example: Jobs A ($100, due by slot 2), B ($19, slot 1), C ($27, slot 2), D ($25, slot 1). Take A first, placed in slot 2, then C in slot 1; B and D no longer fit. Total profit $127, which is optimal.

concepts.name: Johnson's Algorithm
concepts.description: An all-pairs shortest path algorithm for sparse graphs that reweights edges using Bellman–Ford potentials to remove negative weights, then runs Dijkstra from each vertex.
concepts.example: A sparse road map has some negative 'toll refund' edges. Johnson runs Bellman–Ford once to give each town a potential, reweights every edge to be non-negative without changing which paths are shortest, then runs Dijkstra from each town.

concepts.name: Jump Search
concepts.description: A search algorithm for sorted arrays that jumps ahead in blocks of size √n until passing the target, then scans linearly within the block, taking O(√n) steps.
concepts.example: In a sorted list of 100 numbers, check positions 10, 20, 30, … until you pass the target, say at 40, then scan 31 to 39 one by one. That is at most about 10 jumps plus 10 steps.

concepts.name: k-Independent Hashing
concepts.description: A family of hash functions in which the hash values of any k distinct keys are independent and uniformly distributed; stronger independence gives provable guarantees for hashing schemes.
concepts.example: With a 2-independent family, any two different keys get hash values that behave like independent random numbers, so the chance they collide in m slots is exactly 1/m. Some schemes such as linear probing need 5-independence for their guarantees.

concepts.name: K-Way Merge Algorithm
concepts.description: An algorithm that merges k sorted lists into one sorted list, typically using a min-heap holding the current head of each list, in O(n log k) time.
concepts.example: Merge three sorted lists [1, 7], [2, 5], [3, 4]: put the heads 1, 2, 3 in a min-heap, pop 1 and push 7, pop 2 and push 5, and so on, giving 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 7.

concepts.name: Kadane's Algorithm
concepts.description: A linear-time dynamic programming algorithm for the maximum subarray problem that tracks the best sum ending at each position, restarting when the running sum becomes negative.
concepts.example: For [−2, 3, −1, 4, −5], track the best sum ending at each spot: −2, 3, 2, 6, 1. The best overall is 6, from [3, −1, 4]. When the running sum turns negative, start fresh.

concepts.name: Kahn's Algorithm
concepts.description: A topological sorting algorithm that repeatedly removes vertices with in-degree zero from a directed graph using a queue; if vertices remain, the graph contains a cycle.
concepts.example: Courses with no prerequisites go into a queue. Take one, say Intro, and cross it off its dependents' lists; any course now with no remaining prerequisites joins the queue. The order taken is a valid study plan.

concepts.name: Karatsuba Algorithm
concepts.description: A divide-and-conquer multiplication algorithm that multiplies two n-digit numbers with three half-size multiplications instead of four, running in O(n^1.585).
concepts.example: For 12 × 34, split into 1|2 and 3|4: compute 1·3 = 3, 2·4 = 8 and (1+2)(3+4) = 21, so the middle term is 21 − 3 − 8 = 10. The result is 300 + 100 + 8 = 408 using 3 multiplications instead of 4.

concepts.name: Karger's Algorithm
concepts.description: A randomized algorithm for global minimum cut that repeatedly contracts random edges until two vertices remain; repeating it many times finds the min cut with high probability.
concepts.example: Repeatedly pick a random edge and merge its two endpoints into one blob until only two blobs remain. The edges between them form a cut; run this many times and the smallest cut seen is very likely the minimum.

concepts.name: Karp's 21 NP-Complete Problems
concepts.description: Richard Karp's 1972 list of 21 combinatorial problems, such as clique, vertex cover and knapsack, shown NP-complete by polynomial-time reductions, establishing NP-completeness as widespread.
concepts.example: In 1972 Karp showed that clique, vertex cover, Hamiltonian cycle, knapsack and 17 others are all equally hard: a fast algorithm for any one of them would yield fast algorithms for all of NP.

concepts.name: Kasai's Algorithm
concepts.description: An algorithm that builds the LCP array from a string and its suffix array in linear time, using the fact that the LCP drops by at most one when moving to the next suffix in text order.
concepts.example: In 'banana', the suffix 'anana' shares 3 letters with its sorted neighbour 'ana', so the next suffix 'nana' must share at least 2 with its own neighbour (it is 'na'). Kasai reuses this so the total comparison work stays linear.

concepts.name: k-d Tree
concepts.description: A binary space-partitioning tree that splits k-dimensional points by alternating coordinate axes, enabling efficient range and nearest-neighbor searches in low dimensions.
concepts.example: For points on a map, split at the median x-coordinate, then split each half at its median y, and alternate. To find the nearest café, descend to your region and only check neighbouring regions that could hold something closer.

concepts.name: Knight's Tour
concepts.description: The puzzle of moving a chess knight so it visits every square of the board exactly once; solved with backtracking or Warnsdorff's heuristic, and a special case of the Hamiltonian path problem.
concepts.example: On a 5×5 board a knight starting in a corner can visit all 25 squares exactly once. Warnsdorff's rule helps: always jump to the square with the fewest onward moves, saving easy squares for later.

concepts.name: Knuth–Morris–Pratt Algorithm
concepts.description: A linear-time string-matching algorithm that precomputes a prefix function for the pattern so, after a mismatch, it shifts the pattern without re-examining text characters.
concepts.example: Searching for 'ABABC' in 'ABABABC': at the mismatch after 'ABAB', KMP knows the last 'AB' could start a new match, so it shifts the pattern by 2 and continues without rereading text.

concepts.name: Knuth's Optimization
concepts.description: A dynamic programming speed-up for interval DP recurrences whose optimal split points are monotone, reducing time from O(n³) to O(n²), as in optimal binary search trees.
concepts.example: In the optimal binary search tree DP, the best root for keys i..j lies between the best roots for i..j−1 and i+1..j. Searching only that narrow window cuts the total work from cubic to quadratic.

concepts.name: Kőnig's Theorem
concepts.description: The theorem that in a bipartite graph the size of a maximum matching equals the size of a minimum vertex cover; it links matching to covering problems.
concepts.example: In a bipartite graph of workers and jobs, if the largest set of non-conflicting assignments has size 3, then exactly 3 people or jobs are enough to touch every possible assignment edge.

concepts.name: Kosaraju's Algorithm
concepts.description: An algorithm that finds the strongly connected components of a directed graph with two depth-first searches: one on the graph to get finishing order and one on the reversed graph.
concepts.example: On a one-way street map, first run DFS and note when each intersection finishes. Then reverse every street and run DFS again in decreasing finish order; each tree found is a group of mutually reachable intersections.

concepts.name: Kruskal's Algorithm
concepts.description: A greedy minimum spanning tree algorithm that sorts edges by weight and adds each edge that does not create a cycle, using a union-find structure to check connectivity.
concepts.example: To connect villages with the cheapest roads, sort possible roads by cost and add each one unless both villages are already connected. Stop once every village is joined.

concepts.name: Las Vegas Algorithm
concepts.description: A randomized algorithm that always returns a correct answer but whose running time is random, such as randomized quicksort; contrast with Monte Carlo algorithms.
concepts.example: Randomized quicksort always returns a correctly sorted list; only its running time depends on the random pivots. Like searching for your keys randomly: you always find them, just sometimes slower.

concepts.name: Lazy Propagation
concepts.description: A segment tree technique that postpones range updates by storing pending changes at internal nodes and pushing them to children only when needed, keeping updates O(log n).
concepts.example: To add 5 to elements 1–1000 in a segment tree, mark the few nodes covering that range with '+5 pending' instead of touching every leaf. The pending value is pushed down only when a later query needs it.

concepts.name: LCP Array
concepts.description: An array storing the length of the longest common prefix between each pair of consecutive suffixes in a suffix array; together they solve many string problems efficiently.
concepts.example: Sorted suffixes of 'banana': a, ana, anana, banana, na, nana. Adjacent pairs share prefixes of length 1, 3, 0, 0, 2, so the longest repeated substring is 'ana', of length 3.

concepts.name: Least Common Multiple
concepts.description: The smallest positive integer that is a multiple of each of two or more integers; computed as a·b / gcd(a, b) and used when adding fractions.
concepts.example: Buses leave every 4 and every 6 minutes; they next leave together after lcm(4, 6) = 12 minutes. Using gcd: 4 × 6 / 2 = 12.

concepts.name: Leftist Heap
concepts.description: A mergeable heap implemented as a binary tree that keeps the shortest path to a null node on the right, so two heaps can be merged in O(log n).
concepts.example: To merge two leftist heaps, compare roots, keep the smaller as root, and recursively merge the other heap into its right spine, swapping children when needed so the right side stays short.

concepts.name: Level-Order Traversal
concepts.description: A tree traversal that visits nodes level by level from the root downward, left to right within each level, implemented with a queue; it is breadth-first search on a tree.
concepts.example: For a family tree, list the grandparent, then both parents, then all four children, row by row. A queue keeps track: take a person out, then add their children to the back.

concepts.name: Line Segment Intersection
concepts.description: The problem of deciding whether two line segments intersect, or finding all intersections among many segments, solved with orientation tests and sweep-line algorithms.
concepts.example: Segment AB from (0,0) to (2,2) and segment CD from (0,2) to (2,0): C and D lie on opposite sides of AB, and A and B lie on opposite sides of CD, so they cross (at (1,1)).

concepts.name: Linear Congruential Generator
concepts.description: A simple pseudorandom number generator computing x_{n+1} = (a·x_n + c) mod m; fast and easy, but with poor statistical quality for demanding uses.
concepts.example: With a = 5, c = 1, m = 8 and start 1: 6, 7, 4, 5, 2, 3, 0, 1, then repeating. It cycles through all 8 values, but low bits follow obvious patterns, showing why LCGs are unfit for cryptography.

concepts.name: Linear Probing
concepts.description: An open-addressing method that resolves a collision by checking successive slots one by one until a free one is found; cache-friendly but prone to primary clustering.
concepts.example: In a 10-slot table, 'cat' hashes to slot 3, which is taken, so try 4; also taken, so try 5, which is free. Lookups follow the same path, but runs of filled slots tend to grow into clusters.

concepts.name: Linear Search
concepts.description: The simplest search method: check each element in turn until the target is found or the list ends, taking O(n) time and working on unsorted data.
concepts.example: Looking for your friend in a queue at the cinema by checking each face from front to back. In the worst case you check every person, so the effort grows with the length of the queue.

concepts.name: Linear Sieve
concepts.description: A variant of the sieve of Eratosthenes that marks each composite exactly once by its smallest prime factor, finding all primes up to n in O(n) time.
concepts.example: In the ordinary sieve, 12 is crossed out twice, by 2 and by 3. The linear sieve crosses out each composite only once, via its smallest prime factor: 12 is marked only as 2 × 6.

concepts.name: Linear Time
concepts.description: Running time that grows proportionally to the input size, O(n); for example, a single pass that scans every element once.
concepts.example: Finding the tallest person in a room means looking at each person once: twice as many people, twice the work. Reading every page of a book is linear time in its number of pages.

concepts.name: Linearithmic Time
concepts.description: Running time proportional to n log n, typical of efficient comparison sorting and divide-and-conquer algorithms like merge sort.
concepts.example: Merge sort on 1,024 items does about 10 levels of splitting (log₂1024 = 10), with about 1,024 work at each level, so roughly 10,000 steps instead of the million a quadratic sort would take.

concepts.name: Link/Cut Tree
concepts.description: A data structure that maintains a forest of rooted trees under link and cut operations and answers path queries in O(log n) amortized time using splay trees over preferred paths.
concepts.example: A network of computers keeps getting cables plugged in (link) and pulled out (cut). A link/cut tree can still answer 'what is the slowest cable on the path from A to B?' in logarithmic amortized time.

concepts.name: Linked List
concepts.description: A linear data structure where each node holds a value and a pointer to the next node, allowing O(1) insertion and deletion at known positions but O(n) indexed access.
concepts.example: A treasure hunt where each clue says where the next clue is hidden. To insert a new clue, change one pointer; but to reach the 10th clue, you must follow the first nine.

concepts.name: Little-o Notation
concepts.description: Notation f(n) = o(g(n)) meaning f grows strictly slower than g, i.e. f(n)/g(n) → 0 as n → ∞; a strict version of big-O used in asymptotic analysis.
concepts.example: n = o(n²), since n/n² = 1/n approaches 0. But 3n² is not o(n²), since 3n²/n² stays at 3. Little-o means 'grows strictly slower than'.

concepts.name: Load Factor
concepts.description: The ratio of the number of stored entries to the number of buckets in a hash table; it governs collision rates and determines when the table is resized.
concepts.example: A hash table with 75 entries in 100 buckets has load factor 0.75. Many implementations, such as Java's HashMap, double the number of buckets when this threshold is passed to keep collisions rare.

concepts.name: Locality-Sensitive Hashing
concepts.description: A family of hashing schemes that map similar items to the same bucket with high probability, enabling fast approximate nearest-neighbor search in high dimensions.
concepts.example: To find near-duplicate web pages among billions, hash each page so that similar pages likely land in the same bucket. Only pages sharing a bucket are compared, instead of every pair.

concepts.name: Logarithmic Time
concepts.description: Running time proportional to log n, as when each step halves the remaining problem, like binary search or operations on balanced trees.
concepts.example: Guessing a number from 1 to 1,000,000 with 'higher/lower' hints takes at most 20 guesses, because each guess halves the range. Doubling the range to 2 million adds just one more guess.

concepts.name: Longest Common Subsequence
concepts.description: The problem of finding the longest sequence that appears in both strings in the same order, not necessarily contiguously; solved by O(nm) dynamic programming and used in diff tools.
concepts.example: 'ABCBDAB' and 'BDCABA' share 'BCBA' in order (not contiguous), length 4. diff tools use LCS to show which lines of a file stayed the same.

concepts.name: Longest Common Substring
concepts.description: The problem of finding the longest contiguous string that appears in two strings, solvable with dynamic programming in O(nm) or with suffix structures in linear time.
concepts.example: 'photograph' and 'tomography' share the contiguous block 'ograph', length 6. Unlike a subsequence, the matching letters must sit side by side in both strings.

concepts.name: Longest Increasing Subsequence
concepts.description: The problem of finding the longest strictly increasing subsequence of a sequence; solved in O(n²) with DP or O(n log n) with binary search over tails.
concepts.example: In [3, 10, 2, 1, 20], the longest increasing subsequence is 3, 10, 20, length 3. The fast method keeps the smallest possible tail for each length and binary searches where each new number fits.

concepts.name: Longest Palindromic Substring
concepts.description: The problem of finding the longest contiguous substring that reads the same forwards and backwards; solved by expanding around centers, DP, or Manacher's linear-time algorithm.
concepts.example: In 'forgeeksskeegfor' the longest palindrome is 'geeksskeeg'. Expanding outward from the centre between the two s's keeps matching letters until 'r' and 'f' differ.

concepts.name: Loop Invariant
concepts.description: A condition that holds before and after each iteration of a loop; proving it is initially true, preserved, and useful at termination shows the loop is correct.
concepts.example: For a loop summing an array, the invariant is 'total equals the sum of the items processed so far'. It holds before the loop (0 items, total 0), each step keeps it true, so at the end total is the full sum.

concepts.name: Comparison Sort Lower Bound
concepts.description: The theorem that any comparison-based sort needs Ω(n log n) comparisons in the worst case, because a decision tree must have n! leaves and therefore height log₂(n!).
concepts.example: Sorting 4 items has 4! = 24 possible orders. Each comparison at best halves the possibilities, and 2⁴ = 16 < 24, so some input forces at least 5 comparisons. In general, at least log₂(n!) ≈ n log₂ n.

concepts.name: Lowest Common Ancestor
concepts.description: The problem of finding the deepest node that is an ancestor of two given nodes in a rooted tree; solved with binary lifting, Euler tour plus RMQ, or Tarjan's offline method.
concepts.example: In a family tree, the lowest common ancestor of two cousins is their shared grandparent, the deepest person both descend from. For two siblings it is their parent.

concepts.name: LRU Cache
concepts.description: A fixed-size cache that evicts the least recently used item when full, typically built from a hash table plus a doubly linked list so get and put run in O(1).
concepts.example: A cache of 3 photos holds A, B, C. Viewing A makes it most recent; loading D then evicts B, the least recently used. A hash map finds photos instantly while a linked list keeps them in recency order.

concepts.name: Lucas's Theorem
concepts.description: A theorem giving binomial coefficients modulo a prime p by writing both numbers in base p and multiplying the binomial coefficients of their digits.
concepts.example: To find C(10, 3) mod 3, write 10 = 101 and 3 = 010 in base 3. Then C(1,0)·C(0,1)·C(1,0) = 1·0·1 = 0, so C(10, 3) = 120 is divisible by 3, which checks out.

concepts.name: Lyndon Word
concepts.description: A string strictly smaller in lexicographic order than all its rotations; every string factors uniquely into non-increasing Lyndon words, computable with Duval's linear-time algorithm.
concepts.example: 'aab' is a Lyndon word: its rotations 'aba' and 'baa' are both larger. 'aba' is not, since its rotation 'aab' is smaller. The string 'banana' factors as b · an · an · a.

concepts.name: LZ77 and LZ78
concepts.description: Lempel–Ziv dictionary compression algorithms: LZ77 replaces repeats with references to a sliding window of earlier text, and LZ78 builds an explicit phrase dictionary; they underlie gzip and LZW.
concepts.example: In 'abcabcabc', LZ77 writes 'abc' and then 'go back 3 characters and copy 6', compressing the repeats. LZ78 instead adds phrases like 'ab' and 'ca' to a dictionary and refers to them by number.

concepts.name: Manacher's Algorithm
concepts.description: A linear-time algorithm that finds the longest palindromic substring by reusing palindrome radii mirrored around the center of the rightmost palindrome found so far.
concepts.example: Inside a long palindrome, the right half mirrors the left. If the letter at mirror position 3 has a palindrome of radius 2 around it, the matching right position starts with at least radius 2, so that work is skipped.

concepts.name: Matching
concepts.description: A set of edges in a graph with no two edges sharing a vertex; matchings model pairings such as jobs to workers or students to schools.
concepts.example: Pairing 6 dancers for a waltz: each line drawn between two willing partners is an edge, and a matching is a set of pairings where nobody dances with two people at once.

concepts.name: Matrix Chain Multiplication
concepts.description: The problem of choosing the parenthesization of a product of matrices that minimizes scalar multiplications; the classic example of interval dynamic programming.
concepts.example: Multiply A (10×30), B (30×5), C (5×60). Doing (AB)C costs 10·30·5 + 10·5·60 = 4,500 scalar multiplications, while A(BC) costs 30·5·60 + 10·30·60 = 27,000. Same answer, six times the work.

concepts.name: Matrix Exponentiation
concepts.description: Raising a square matrix to a large power with exponentiation by squaring in O(k³ log n); used to compute linear recurrences such as Fibonacci numbers quickly.
concepts.example: The matrix [[1,1],[1,0]] raised to the n-th power holds Fibonacci numbers F(n+1), F(n), F(n−1). Squaring it repeatedly reaches the 64th power in 6 squarings, so F(64) needs a handful of 2×2 products instead of 64 additions in sequence.

concepts.name: Matroid
concepts.description: An abstract structure generalizing linear independence, consisting of a ground set and a family of 'independent' subsets with exchange properties; greedy algorithms are optimal exactly on matroids.
concepts.example: A graph's edges form a matroid: a set of edges is 'independent' if it has no cycle. Any two maximal cycle-free sets have the same size, which is why Kruskal's greedy pick-cheapest-safe-edge always wins.

concepts.name: Max-Flow Min-Cut Theorem
concepts.description: The theorem that the maximum flow from source to sink in a network equals the minimum total capacity of edges whose removal separates the source from the sink.
concepts.example: A town's water mains carry at most 5 + 3 litres/s through the two pipes leaving the reservoir. If cutting those two pipes disconnects the town, no more than 8 litres/s can ever arrive, and the theorem says 8 is actually reachable.

concepts.name: Maximum Matching
concepts.description: The problem of finding a matching with the largest number of edges in a graph; solved by augmenting paths in bipartite graphs and by the blossom algorithm in general graphs.
concepts.example: Five students and five lab partners with compatibility lists: a maximum matching pairs as many as possible. If only four pairs fit, any augmenting path search confirms no fifth pair can be added.

concepts.name: Maximum Subarray Problem
concepts.description: The problem of finding a contiguous subarray with the largest sum in an array of numbers that may be negative; solved in linear time by Kadane's algorithm.
concepts.example: In [−2, 1, −3, 4, −1, 2, 1, −5, 4] the best contiguous stretch is [4, −1, 2, 1] with sum 6. Kadane's method keeps a running sum and resets to zero whenever it goes negative.

concepts.name: MD5
concepts.description: A once-popular 128-bit cryptographic hash function built from rounds of bitwise operations and modular additions; now broken for collision resistance but still used as a checksum.
concepts.example: md5("hello") is always 5d41402abc4b2a76b9719d911017c592, 32 hex digits. It is still handy for checking file downloads, but researchers can now craft two different files with the same MD5, so it is unsafe for signatures.

concepts.name: Median of Medians
concepts.description: A deterministic selection algorithm that picks a good pivot by taking the median of medians of groups of five, guaranteeing worst-case linear time for finding the k-th smallest element.
concepts.example: For 25 numbers, split into five groups of five, take each group's median, then the median of those five. That pivot is guaranteed to be larger than at least about 30% of the elements and smaller than another 30%, so recursion never gets badly lopsided.

concepts.name: Meet-in-the-Middle
concepts.description: A technique that splits a search problem into two halves, enumerates each half separately, and combines results with sorting or hashing, reducing 2ⁿ work to about 2^(n/2).
concepts.example: To see if any subset of 40 numbers sums to a target, list all 2^20 subset sums of the first 20 and of the last 20 separately, about a million each, then look for pairs that add up, instead of checking 2^40 ≈ a trillion subsets.

concepts.name: Memoization
concepts.description: Caching the results of function calls so repeated calls with the same arguments return instantly; it turns naive recursion into top-down dynamic programming.
concepts.example: Naive fib(40) makes over 300 million calls because fib(38) is computed again and again. Saving each answer in a dictionary the first time means fib(40) needs only 41 distinct computations.

concepts.name: Merge Sort
concepts.description: A divide-and-conquer sorting algorithm that splits the array in half, sorts each half recursively and merges the sorted halves; stable with O(n log n) worst-case time.
concepts.example: Sort [5, 2, 4, 1]: split into [5, 2] and [4, 1], sort each to [2, 5] and [1, 4], then merge by repeatedly taking the smaller front item: 1, 2, 4, 5.

concepts.name: Merkle Tree
concepts.description: A tree in which each leaf holds the hash of a data block and each internal node holds the hash of its children, allowing efficient verification of large data; used in Git and blockchains.
concepts.example: A file split into 4 blocks gets 4 leaf hashes; pairs are hashed into 2 nodes and those into one root. To prove block 3 is genuine you only need 2 sibling hashes, not the whole file, which is how Bitcoin and Git verify data.

concepts.name: Miller–Rabin Primality Test
concepts.description: A probabilistic primality test that checks whether random bases witness compositeness via square roots of 1 modulo n; it has no Carmichael-number weakness and is used in practice.
concepts.example: Test n = 561 (a Carmichael number that fools the Fermat test): write 560 = 2^4·35 and check 2^35, then square repeatedly mod 561. A nontrivial square root of 1 appears, proving 561 is composite.

concepts.name: MinHash
concepts.description: A technique that estimates the Jaccard similarity of sets by comparing the minimum hash values of their elements under several random hash functions; used to find near-duplicate documents.
concepts.example: Two documents share 3 of their 5 distinct words, Jaccard 0.6. Hash every word with a random hash and keep each document's smallest value; the two minimums match with probability 0.6, so 100 such hashes estimate similarity well.

concepts.name: Minimum Cut
concepts.description: The problem of splitting a graph's vertices into two groups so the total weight of edges crossing between them is as small as possible, globally or between a given source and sink.
concepts.example: A network where a source feeds a sink through pipes of capacity 3, 2 and 7: if removing the 3 and 2 pipes disconnects them, the cut has capacity 5. The minimum cut is the cheapest such set of pipes to remove.

concepts.name: Minimum Spanning Tree
concepts.description: The problem of finding a spanning tree of a weighted connected graph with the smallest total edge weight; solved by Kruskal's, Prim's and Borůvka's algorithms.
concepts.example: Connecting 4 villages with roads costing 1, 2, 3, 4, 5 and 6: an MST picks 3 roads that link everyone with the smallest total, here 1 + 2 + 4 = 7 if road 3 would close a loop.

concepts.name: Misra–Gries Algorithm
concepts.description: A streaming algorithm that finds items appearing more than n/k times using k − 1 counters, decrementing all counters when a new item arrives and none is free; it generalizes majority vote.
concepts.example: With k = 3 (2 counters), stream a b a c a: count a, count b, a's counter rises, then c arrives with no free counter so both drop by one. Any item appearing more than n/3 times is guaranteed to survive in a counter.

concepts.name: Modular Exponentiation
concepts.description: Computing a^b mod m efficiently by exponentiation by squaring and reducing modulo m at each step; essential for RSA, Diffie–Hellman and primality tests.
concepts.example: To get 3^13 mod 7, square and reduce: 3, 3^2 = 2, 3^4 = 4, 3^8 = 2 (all mod 7). Since 13 = 8 + 4 + 1, multiply 2·4·3 = 24 ≡ 3. Numbers never grow beyond 7².

concepts.name: Modular Multiplicative Inverse
concepts.description: A number x such that a·x ≡ 1 (mod m), which exists exactly when a and m are coprime; computed with the extended Euclidean algorithm or Fermat's little theorem.
concepts.example: The inverse of 3 mod 7 is 5, because 3·5 = 15 = 2·7 + 1. So 'dividing by 3' mod 7 means multiplying by 5. But 2 has no inverse mod 4, since 2 and 4 share a factor.

concepts.name: Monotonic Queue
concepts.description: A deque kept in increasing or decreasing order that lets you find the maximum or minimum of a sliding window in amortized O(1) per step.
concepts.example: For the max of each window of 3 in [1, 3, −1, −3, 5, 3], keep a deque of indexes with decreasing values: when 5 arrives it evicts the smaller ones behind it. Each window's max is at the deque's front: 3, 3, 5, 5.

concepts.name: Monotonic Stack
concepts.description: A stack whose elements stay in sorted order, popping when a new element breaks the order; it finds the next greater or smaller element for every position in linear time.
concepts.example: For next greater elements in [2, 1, 5]: push 2, push 1, then 5 arrives and pops 1 and 2, telling both their next greater value is 5. Each element is pushed and popped once, so it's O(n).

concepts.name: Monte Carlo Algorithm
concepts.description: A randomized algorithm with bounded running time that may return an incorrect answer with small probability, which can be reduced by repetition; contrast with Las Vegas algorithms.
concepts.example: To check if two big matrices satisfy A·B = C, multiply both sides by a random vector, which is cheap. If they differ, a random vector exposes it at least half the time; 20 repeats leave less than a one-in-a-million chance of being fooled.

concepts.name: Morris Traversal
concepts.description: An inorder traversal of a binary tree in O(1) extra space that temporarily creates threads from predecessors back to nodes instead of using a stack or recursion.
concepts.example: Before descending into a node's left subtree, Morris makes that subtree's rightmost node point back to the node. When the walk reaches that thread later it returns up for free, then removes the thread, so no stack is needed.

concepts.name: Mo's Algorithm
concepts.description: An offline technique that answers many range queries by sorting them into √n-sized blocks so moving the window between consecutive queries costs little, giving about O((n + q)√n).
concepts.example: With n = 100 and 1,000 queries like 'how many distinct values in [l, r]?', sort queries by block of l (size 10) then by r. The window's ends then only shuffle a short way between queries instead of sweeping the whole array each time.

concepts.name: Multiset
concepts.description: A collection like a set that allows repeated elements, keeping a count for each distinct value; often implemented with balanced trees or hash maps of counts.
concepts.example: The letters of BANANA as a multiset are {A:3, B:1, N:2}. Two words are anagrams exactly when their letter multisets are equal, while as plain sets BANANA and BAN would look identical.

concepts.name: MurmurHash
concepts.description: A fast non-cryptographic hash function that mixes input blocks with multiplications and rotations to achieve good distribution; widely used in hash tables and Bloom filters.
concepts.example: MurmurHash reads 4 bytes at a time, multiplies by a constant, rotates the bits and mixes into the running state. Changing one input bit flips about half the output bits, so keys spread evenly in a hash table, but it is not safe against attackers.

concepts.name: Mutual Recursion
concepts.description: A form of recursion where two or more functions call each other, such as is_even calling is_odd and vice versa; common in parsers and state machines.
concepts.example: is_even(3) asks is_odd(2), which asks is_even(1), which asks is_odd(0), which returns false. A parser for expressions is a real case: parse_expression calls parse_term, which may call parse_expression again for brackets.

concepts.name: Eight Queens Puzzle
concepts.description: The puzzle of placing n queens on an n×n chessboard so that no two attack each other; a classic exercise in backtracking search.
concepts.example: For 4 queens, put one in column 1 of row 1; row 2's only safe spots are columns 3 or 4. Following those choices hits dead ends, so you back up and move the first queen, eventually finding 2, 4, 1, 3.

concepts.name: Naive String Search
concepts.description: The brute-force pattern-matching method that tries every position in the text and compares the pattern character by character, taking O(nm) time in the worst case.
concepts.example: Searching "aab" in "aaaab": line up at position 0 and compare a, a, a≠b, fail; shift by one and repeat. The match is found at position 2 after 3 alignments, about n·m comparisons in the worst case.

concepts.name: Nearest Neighbor Search
concepts.description: The problem of finding the point in a dataset closest to a query point under some distance metric. Solved exactly with brute force or space-partitioning trees, or approximately with hashing and graph indexes.
concepts.example: Your phone finding the nearest coffee shop to you: among 1,000 shops, the exact naive method measures the distance to every one and keeps the smallest. Index structures like k-d trees skip most of them.

concepts.name: Needleman–Wunsch Algorithm
concepts.description: A dynamic programming algorithm for global alignment of two sequences, filling a score table with match, mismatch and gap penalties so that the whole of both sequences is optimally aligned.
concepts.example: Align GATTACA with GCATGCU: fill a grid where each cell takes the best of a diagonal match/mismatch, a gap from above, or a gap from the left. The bottom-right cell holds the best global score, and tracing back gives the alignment.

concepts.name: Negative Cycle
concepts.description: A cycle in a weighted directed graph whose edge weights sum to a negative number. When one is reachable, shortest paths are undefined because looping around it lowers the cost without bound.
concepts.example: Currency trading: dollars to euros to yen back to dollars at rates whose product exceeds 1. Using −log(rate) as edge weights turns this profit loop into a negative cycle, so going round forever makes paths 'shorter' without limit.

concepts.name: Nondeterministic Turing Machine
concepts.description: A Turing machine that may have several possible moves at each step and accepts if any sequence of choices leads to acceptance. It defines the class NP when restricted to polynomial time.
concepts.example: Think of a maze solver that magically splits into copies at every fork; if any copy reaches the exit, the maze is solved. For SAT, it 'guesses' all variable values at once and then checks the formula in polynomial time.

concepts.name: NP-Completeness
concepts.description: A problem is NP-complete if it is in NP and every NP problem reduces to it in polynomial time. These are the hardest problems in NP; a fast algorithm for one would give fast algorithms for all.
concepts.example: Sudoku on n×n grids is NP-complete: a solution is easy to check, and any NP problem can be encoded as a Sudoku. So a fast Sudoku solver would give fast solvers for scheduling, packing and thousands of other problems.

concepts.name: NP
concepts.description: NP is the class of decision problems whose yes-answers can be verified in polynomial time given a suitable certificate, equivalently those solvable in polynomial time by a nondeterministic Turing machine.
concepts.example: Given a 1,000-city map and a claimed tour shorter than 5,000 km, you can add up the legs and check it in seconds. Finding such a tour may take ages, but quick checking is what puts the yes/no question in NP.

concepts.name: NP-Hardness
concepts.description: A problem is NP-hard if every problem in NP can be reduced to it in polynomial time, so it is at least as hard as anything in NP. NP-hard problems need not be decision problems or lie in NP.
concepts.example: The halting problem is NP-hard but not in NP: any NP problem reduces to it, yet no one can check its answers quickly. Optimizing a travelling salesman tour is another NP-hard task.

concepts.name: NP-Intermediate
concepts.description: Problems in NP that are neither in P nor NP-complete. Ladner's theorem shows such problems exist if P differs from NP; factoring and graph isomorphism are candidate examples.
concepts.example: Graph isomorphism, asking whether two networks are the same up to relabeling, is a leading candidate: it is in NP, has a quasi-polynomial algorithm, but is not known to be in P or NP-complete. Integer factoring is another.

concepts.name: Number-Theoretic Transform
concepts.description: A version of the discrete Fourier transform computed over integers modulo a prime, using a root of unity in that field. It enables exact fast polynomial and big-integer multiplication without rounding error.
concepts.example: Modulo 998244353, the number 3 generates a root of unity of every power-of-two order up to 2^23. Using it in place of complex e^(2πi/n) lets you multiply huge polynomials with exact integer results and no rounding error.

concepts.name: Computational Number Theory
concepts.description: The study of efficient algorithms for number-theoretic tasks such as computing GCDs, modular inverses, primality testing, integer factorization and discrete logarithms, central to cryptography.
concepts.example: Euclid computes gcd(1071, 462) in a few steps: 1071 mod 462 = 147, 462 mod 147 = 21, 147 mod 21 = 0, so gcd = 21. Such routines underpin RSA keys, hashing and random number generation.

concepts.name: Octree
concepts.description: A tree data structure that recursively splits 3D space into eight child cubes, letting programs quickly locate, query and render points or objects in a region. Used in graphics, physics and point clouds.
concepts.example: A 3D game world 1,024 m across is split into 8 cubes, and each crowded cube is split into 8 more. Finding which objects a bullet might hit then means checking a few small cubes instead of every object in the world.

concepts.name: Odd–Even Sort
concepts.description: A simple parallel-friendly sorting algorithm that alternates between comparing and swapping all odd-indexed adjacent pairs and all even-indexed pairs until the list is sorted. It runs in O(n^2) time sequentially.
concepts.example: Sort [3, 2, 1]: the odd phase compares positions (1,2), giving [2, 3, 1]; the even phase compares (2,3), giving [2, 1, 3]; then (1,2) again gives [1, 2, 3]. All pairs in a phase can be swapped simultaneously by separate processors.

concepts.name: Offline Query Processing
concepts.description: A technique where all queries are known in advance, so they can be reordered (e.g. sorted by position or time) and answered together more efficiently than one at a time, as in Mo's algorithm.
concepts.example: To answer 'how many numbers ≤ x in the first i elements' for many queries, sort queries by i and add elements one by one into a Fenwick tree, answering each query when its i is reached, instead of rebuilding for each.

concepts.name: One-Time Pad
concepts.description: An encryption scheme that combines a message with a truly random key of equal length, typically by XOR. If the key is never reused and kept secret, the ciphertext reveals nothing about the message.
concepts.example: Message bits 1011 XOR random key 0110 give ciphertext 1101; XOR with the key again restores 1011. Without the key, every 4-bit message is equally possible, but reusing the key even once leaks information.

concepts.name: Online Algorithm
concepts.description: An algorithm that must make decisions as input arrives piece by piece, without knowing the future. Its quality is measured by competitive analysis: the worst-case ratio to an optimal offline algorithm.
concepts.example: Renting skis at 50 a day versus buying for 500, without knowing how many days you'll ski: rent for 9 days and buy on the 10th. You never pay more than about twice what someone who knew the future would.

concepts.name: Open Addressing
concepts.description: A hash table collision strategy that stores all entries in the table array itself, probing other slots in a fixed sequence (linear, quadratic or double hashing) until an empty one is found.
concepts.example: A table of 10 slots: key 'cat' hashes to slot 3, which is already taken, so it tries slot 4, then 5, and settles in the first empty one. Lookups follow the same probe sequence until they find the key or an empty slot.

concepts.name: Optimal Binary Search Tree
concepts.description: The problem of building a binary search tree that minimizes the expected search cost given access probabilities for each key. Classically solved by an O(n^3) dynamic program, improvable to O(n^2) with Knuth's optimization.
concepts.example: If 'the' is searched 60% of the time and 'zebra' 1%, put 'the' at the root even though it's not the middle key. Choosing roots for every key range by DP minimizes the average number of comparisons.

concepts.name: Optimal Substructure
concepts.description: A property of a problem where an optimal solution is built from optimal solutions to its subproblems. It is what makes dynamic programming and greedy algorithms correct.
concepts.example: If the fastest route from Paris to Rome goes through Milan, then its Paris-to-Milan part must itself be the fastest way to Milan; otherwise you could swap in a faster piece. That is what lets shortest paths be built from shorter ones.

concepts.name: Optimization Problem
concepts.description: A problem of finding the best solution among all feasible ones according to an objective, such as the shortest path or cheapest schedule, as opposed to just deciding whether a solution exists.
concepts.example: Choosing which 3 of 10 items to pack in a 5 kg bag to maximize value is an optimization problem: many choices are allowed, and the objective (total value) ranks them. Asking 'is value 100 reachable?' is its decision version.

concepts.name: Order Statistic Tree
concepts.description: A balanced binary search tree augmented so each node stores its subtree size, allowing the k-th smallest element and the rank of any key to be found in O(log n) time.
concepts.example: Each node stores how many nodes its subtree has. To find the 5th smallest, look at the root: if its left subtree has 3 nodes, the root is 4th, so go right and look for the 1st smallest there. It takes O(log n) steps.

concepts.name: Overlapping Subproblems
concepts.description: A property of a recursive problem where the same subproblems are solved many times. Caching their results with memoization or tabulation is what gives dynamic programming its speedup.
concepts.example: Counting paths in a 10×10 grid recursively asks for the count from cell (5,5) over and over, from many different routes. Storing it once removes the repetition, turning exponential work into 100 cell computations.

concepts.name: P
concepts.description: P is the class of decision problems that a deterministic Turing machine can solve in polynomial time. It is the standard formalization of problems considered efficiently solvable.
concepts.example: Checking whether a list of 1,000 numbers is sorted, or whether a road map connects two cities, takes time like n or n²: both are in P. Such problems are considered efficiently solvable even for big inputs.

concepts.name: P versus NP Problem
concepts.description: The open question of whether every problem whose solution can be verified quickly (NP) can also be solved quickly (P). It is one of the Millennium Prize Problems and central to complexity theory and cryptography.
concepts.example: Checking a filled Sudoku takes seconds, but filling a huge blank one seems to take forever. P vs NP asks whether that gap is real; a proof either way earns a one-million-dollar Clay prize.

concepts.name: Page Replacement Algorithm
concepts.description: The problem of deciding which page to evict from a fast cache when it is full and a new page is requested. Policies include LRU, FIFO and Belady's optimal offline rule; it is a classic online problem.
concepts.example: A cache holds 3 pages and requests come A B C D A B. When D arrives one page must go; FIFO evicts A, which is needed next. The optimal rule evicts the page needed furthest in the future, here C.

concepts.name: Pairing Heap
concepts.description: A self-adjusting heap stored as a multiway tree that merges subtrees by pairing them. It is simple to implement and very fast in practice, with amortized O(log n) delete-min.
concepts.example: Melding two heaps just makes the root with the larger key a child of the other, O(1). Deleting the minimum leaves many children, which are merged in pairs left to right and then folded together right to left.

concepts.name: Pancake Sorting
concepts.description: The problem of sorting a stack of items using only prefix reversals, like flipping the top pancakes with a spatula. Any stack can be sorted in at most about 2n flips; finding the minimum is NP-hard.
concepts.example: Stack from top: 3, 1, 2. The largest is on top, so flip all 3: 2, 1, 3, putting it at the bottom. Then flip the top 2: 1, 2, 3. Sorted with just 2 spatula flips.

concepts.name: Parameterized Complexity
concepts.description: A branch of complexity theory that measures running time in terms of the input size and an extra parameter k. Fixed-parameter tractable problems are solvable in f(k)·poly(n) time, efficient when k is small.
concepts.example: Vertex cover is NP-hard, but asking for a cover of size k = 10 in a million-node graph can be solved in about 2^10 · n steps by branching on each uncovered edge. The exponential part depends only on k, not on n.

concepts.name: Partition (Quicksort)
concepts.description: The step in quicksort that rearranges an array around a pivot so that smaller elements come before it and larger ones after. Lomuto and Hoare are the two classic schemes, both in-place and linear time.
concepts.example: Partition [7, 2, 9, 1, 5] around pivot 5: a left pointer finds 7 (too big), a right pointer finds 1 (too small), swap them, continue. Finally 1 and 2 sit left of 5 and 9 and 7 sit right of it, so 5 is in its final sorted position.

concepts.name: Partition Problem
concepts.description: The NP-complete problem of deciding whether a set of numbers can be split into two subsets with equal sums. It is solvable in pseudo-polynomial time with dynamic programming.
concepts.example: Can {3, 1, 1, 2, 2, 1} be split into two equal halves? The total is 10, so each side needs 5: {3, 2} and {1, 1, 2, 1}. Yes. With {2, 5} it's impossible since the total is odd.

concepts.name: Path Compression
concepts.description: An optimization for disjoint-set union where every node visited during a find operation is relinked directly to the root, flattening the tree so future finds are nearly constant time.
concepts.example: A chain 5 → 4 → 3 → 2 → 1 (root). Calling find(5) walks the chain once and then points 5, 4, 3 and 2 straight at 1. The next find on any of them takes one step.

concepts.name: Perfect Binary Tree
concepts.description: A binary tree in which every internal node has exactly two children and all leaves are at the same depth, so a tree of height h has exactly 2^(h+1) - 1 nodes.
concepts.example: A perfect binary tree of height 3 (counting edges) has 1 + 2 + 4 + 8 = 15 nodes, with all 8 leaves on the bottom level. In general height h gives exactly 2^(h+1) − 1 nodes.

concepts.name: Perfect Hash Function
concepts.description: A hash function that maps a fixed set of keys to distinct slots with no collisions, giving worst-case O(1) lookup. Static sets can be perfectly hashed using two-level schemes like FKS hashing.
concepts.example: For a fixed list of 32 programming-language keywords, a compiler can precompute a hash that sends each keyword to its own slot. Looking up 'while' then takes one hash and one comparison, never a collision.

concepts.name: Permutation Generation
concepts.description: Algorithms for listing all orderings of a set of items, such as recursive backtracking, lexicographic next-permutation, and Heap's algorithm, which produces each permutation with a single swap.
concepts.example: For {1, 2, 3}, backtracking fixes 1 then permutes {2, 3}, giving 123, 132, then fixes 2: 213, 231, then 3: 312, 321. That's all 3! = 6 orderings, each produced once.

concepts.name: Persistent Data Structure
concepts.description: A data structure that preserves all its previous versions when modified, so old versions can still be queried. Usually built with path copying or node sharing, as in persistent segment trees.
concepts.example: Updating one value in a persistent tree copies only the nodes on the path from the root to it, about log n nodes, and shares everything else. Both the old root and the new root stay valid, like saved versions in Git.

concepts.name: Pick's Theorem
concepts.description: A formula for the area of a simple polygon whose vertices lie on integer grid points: area = I + B/2 - 1, where I is the number of interior lattice points and B the number on the boundary.
concepts.example: A 2×2 square on graph paper has 1 interior point and 8 boundary points, so area = 1 + 8/2 − 1 = 4. Correct, and it works for any lattice polygon without measuring any lengths.

concepts.name: Point in Polygon
concepts.description: The problem of deciding whether a point lies inside a polygon. Common methods are ray casting, which counts boundary crossings of a ray, and the winding number, which sums the angles around the point.
concepts.example: Shoot a ray from the point to the right and count how many polygon edges it crosses. For a point inside a square the ray crosses 1 edge (odd, so inside); for a point outside it crosses 0 or 2 (even, so outside).

concepts.name: Pointer
concepts.description: A variable that stores the memory address of another value rather than the value itself. Pointers and references let programs build linked structures like lists and trees and share data without copying.
concepts.example: A variable x holds 42 at memory address 1000; a pointer p holds 1000. Writing through p (*p = 7) changes x to 7. It's like knowing someone's home address rather than having their furniture.

concepts.name: Pollard's Rho Algorithm
concepts.description: A randomized integer factorization algorithm that iterates a pseudo-random polynomial modulo n and uses cycle detection and GCDs to find a factor, typically in about n^(1/4) steps.
concepts.example: To factor 8051, iterate x → x² + 1 mod 8051 with a tortoise and a hare. Within a few steps gcd(|x − y|, 8051) = 97, revealing 8051 = 83 × 97 much faster than trial division.

concepts.name: Polygon Triangulation
concepts.description: Dividing a polygon into non-overlapping triangles using its vertices. Every simple polygon with n vertices has a triangulation into n-2 triangles; ear clipping is a simple method.
concepts.example: A convex hexagon can be split into 4 triangles by drawing 3 diagonals from one corner. Any simple n-gon splits into n − 2 triangles, which is how graphics hardware renders filled shapes.

concepts.name: Polynomial Hierarchy
concepts.description: A hierarchy of complexity classes that generalizes P, NP and co-NP using alternating existential and universal quantifiers, with each level defined by oracle access to the level below.
concepts.example: NP asks 'is there a move that wins?' Σ2 asks 'is there a move such that for every reply I still win?' Each extra alternation of 'there exists' and 'for all' climbs one level, like looking further ahead in a game.

concepts.name: Polynomial Multiplication
concepts.description: Computing the product of two polynomials. The schoolbook method takes O(n^2) time, Karatsuba reduces it to about O(n^1.58), and FFT-based methods achieve O(n log n).
concepts.example: (1 + 2x)(3 + x) = 3 + x + 6x + 2x² = 3 + 7x + 2x². Each output coefficient sums products whose degrees add up, so two degree-1000 polynomials need about a million products by hand-style multiplication.

concepts.name: Polynomial Rolling Hash
concepts.description: A string hash computed as a polynomial in a fixed base modulo a large number. When a window slides by one character the hash updates in O(1), which powers Rabin-Karp and substring comparison.
concepts.example: With base 10, the hash of "123" is 1·100 + 2·10 + 3 = 123. Sliding to "234": subtract 1·100, multiply by 10, add 4 to get 234, in O(1). Real versions use a large base and take everything mod a big prime.

concepts.name: Polynomial Time
concepts.description: An algorithm runs in polynomial time if its running time is bounded by a polynomial in the input size, such as O(n^2) or O(n^3). It is the usual dividing line between tractable and intractable problems.
concepts.example: An n² algorithm on 1,000 items does about a million steps, which is fine. A 2^n algorithm on just 100 items would outlast the universe. Polynomial time is the line drawn between those two kinds of growth.

concepts.name: Polynomial-Time Reduction
concepts.description: A polynomial-time transformation of instances of one problem into instances of another that preserves the answer. It shows the second problem is at least as hard and is the tool for proving NP-completeness.
concepts.example: To show Hamiltonian cycle is no harder than TSP, turn any graph into cities where edges cost 1 and non-edges cost 2. A tour of cost n exists exactly when the graph has a Hamiltonian cycle, and the conversion is quick.

concepts.name: Postorder Traversal
concepts.description: A depth-first tree traversal that visits the left subtree, then the right subtree, and then the node itself. It is used to delete trees or evaluate expression trees bottom-up.
concepts.example: For a tree with root 1, left child 2 and right child 3, postorder visits 2, 3, 1. It's the natural order for deleting a folder: you must empty its subfolders before removing the folder itself.

concepts.name: Potential Method
concepts.description: An amortized analysis technique that assigns a potential energy to the data structure state; each operation's amortized cost is its actual cost plus the change in potential.
concepts.example: For a dynamic array, define potential = 2·(size) − capacity. A cheap append raises potential by 2, banking credit; a doubling resize copies n items but drops potential by about n, so every append costs O(1) amortized.

concepts.name: Prefix Function
concepts.description: For each position of a string, the length of the longest proper prefix that is also a suffix of the substring ending there. It is the core of the Knuth-Morris-Pratt pattern matching algorithm.
concepts.example: For "abab", the prefix function is [0, 0, 1, 2]: at the last position, "ab" is both a prefix and a suffix of "abab". KMP uses this to know how far it can shift the pattern after a mismatch without rechecking.

concepts.name: Prefix Sum
concepts.description: An array where each entry stores the sum of all elements up to that index. After O(n) preprocessing it answers any range-sum query in O(1) by subtracting two prefix values.
concepts.example: For [3, 1, 4, 1, 5] the prefix sums are [3, 4, 8, 9, 14]. The sum of elements 2 to 4 (1, 4, 1) is 9 − 3 = 6, found with one subtraction instead of adding them up.

concepts.name: Preorder Traversal
concepts.description: A depth-first tree traversal that visits a node first, then its left subtree, then its right subtree. It is used to copy trees and serialize their structure.
concepts.example: For root 1 with children 2 and 3, preorder visits 1, 2, 3. Printing a folder tree this way lists each folder name before its contents, like a table of contents.

concepts.name: Primality Test
concepts.description: The problem of deciding whether a given integer is prime. Methods range from trial division to fast probabilistic tests like Miller-Rabin and the deterministic polynomial-time AKS test.
concepts.example: Is 91 prime? It looks it, but trying divisors up to √91 ≈ 9.5 finds 7 × 13 = 91. For 300-digit numbers that is hopeless, so fast tests check algebraic properties like Fermat's little theorem instead.

concepts.name: Prim's Algorithm
concepts.description: A greedy algorithm that builds a minimum spanning tree by starting from one vertex and repeatedly adding the cheapest edge connecting the tree to a new vertex, typically using a priority queue.
concepts.example: Start at town A with roads A–B (2) and A–C (5). Take A–B. Now look at all roads leaving {A, B}: B–C (1) is cheapest, take it. All towns joined with cost 3.

concepts.name: Priority Queue
concepts.description: An abstract data type that stores elements with priorities and always returns the highest (or lowest) priority element first. It is usually implemented with a binary heap.
concepts.example: An emergency room: patients arrive in any order, but the most urgent is always seen next, regardless of arrival time. Operations are 'add patient with urgency' and 'take the most urgent'.

concepts.name: Probabilistic Analysis of Algorithms
concepts.description: Analyzing an algorithm's expected running time or behavior by assuming a probability distribution over inputs or random choices, as in the expected O(n log n) cost of randomized quicksort.
concepts.example: Hiring problem: interview 100 candidates in random order, hiring whenever someone beats the current best. The expected number of hires is 1 + 1/2 + ... + 1/100 ≈ 5.2, not 100.

concepts.name: Pruning (Search)
concepts.description: Cutting off branches of a search tree that cannot lead to a better or valid solution, as in backtracking and branch-and-bound. The same word also names removing weights from trained neural networks.
concepts.example: In a Sudoku search, once a partial grid has two 5s in a row there's no point filling the remaining cells. Cutting that branch off can skip millions of hopeless completions.

concepts.name: Pseudo-Polynomial Time
concepts.description: Running time that is polynomial in the numeric value of the input but exponential in its bit length, such as O(nW) for knapsack. Problems with such algorithms are called weakly NP-hard.
concepts.example: Knapsack DP runs in O(n·W). With capacity W = 1,000 that's fast, but W = 2^60 has only 60 bits yet makes the table astronomically large. Time is polynomial in W's value, not in its length.

concepts.name: Pseudocode
concepts.description: An informal, language-independent description of an algorithm using programming-style structure such as loops and conditionals plus plain language, written for humans rather than a compiler.
concepts.example: "for each item in list: if item > max: max ← item; return max" describes finding a maximum without committing to Python, C or Java syntax, so any programmer can translate it.

concepts.name: PSPACE
concepts.description: PSPACE is the class of decision problems solvable by a Turing machine using polynomial memory, with no limit on time. It contains NP and the whole polynomial hierarchy; deciding many games is PSPACE-complete.
concepts.example: Deciding who wins a generalized game like Go on an n×n board can need astronomically many moves to explore, yet a search that reuses memory only needs room for the current line of play. Such problems are typical of PSPACE.

concepts.name: Polynomial-Time Approximation Scheme
concepts.description: A polynomial-time approximation scheme gives, for any fixed epsilon > 0, a solution within a factor (1 + epsilon) of optimal in polynomial time. An FPTAS is also polynomial in 1/epsilon.
concepts.example: For Euclidean TSP, asking for ε = 0.1 gives a tour within 10% of the best; ε = 0.01 gives 1%, but the running time might grow like n^(1/ε). You trade time for accuracy.

concepts.name: Public-Key Cryptography
concepts.description: A cryptographic system using a pair of keys: a public key anyone can use to encrypt or verify, and a private key kept secret to decrypt or sign. It enables secure communication without a shared secret.
concepts.example: Like a padlock anyone can snap shut but only you can open: you publish the open padlock (public key), friends lock messages with it, and only your private key unlocks them. No secret has to be shared in advance.

concepts.name: Push–Relabel Algorithm
concepts.description: A maximum flow algorithm that pushes excess flow locally from vertices and relabels vertex heights to guide flow toward the sink, instead of searching for augmenting paths. It runs in O(V^2 E) or better.
concepts.example: Picture water poured into the source; each vertex has a height, and water only flows downhill to a neighbour one level lower. A vertex stuck with excess water raises its height until it can push it onward.

concepts.name: Quadratic Probing
concepts.description: An open addressing scheme that resolves hash collisions by probing slots at offsets 1, 4, 9, ... (i^2) from the original hash, reducing the clustering seen with linear probing.
concepts.example: A key hashes to slot 5 of 16, which is occupied. Quadratic probing tries 5+1 = 6, then 5+4 = 9, then 5+9 = 14. The growing jumps break up clusters that linear probing creates.

concepts.name: Quadratic Sieve
concepts.description: An integer factorization algorithm that finds many numbers whose squares are smooth modulo n and combines them with linear algebra to get a congruence of squares. It was the fastest method until the number field sieve.

concepts.name: Quadtree
concepts.description: A tree data structure that recursively divides 2D space into four quadrants, letting programs efficiently store and query points or regions. Used in maps, image compression and collision detection.
concepts.example: A map of 10,000 restaurants: split the area into four squares, and split any square with more than 4 restaurants again. Searching for places near you only descends into the few squares around you.

concepts.name: Queue
concepts.description: A first-in, first-out (FIFO) collection where elements are added at the back and removed from the front. Queues drive breadth-first search, task scheduling and buffering.
concepts.example: A line at a coffee shop: the first person to join is the first served. A printer queue works the same way, printing documents in the order they were sent.

concepts.name: Quickhull
concepts.description: A convex hull algorithm that, like quicksort, picks extreme points, discards points inside the current triangle, and recurses on the points outside each edge. Expected O(n log n), worst case O(n^2).
concepts.example: Take the leftmost and rightmost points; they're on the hull. Find the point farthest from the line between them, form a triangle, and discard every point inside it. Repeat on the outer sides until no points remain outside.

concepts.name: Quickselect
concepts.description: A selection algorithm that finds the k-th smallest element by partitioning around a pivot as in quicksort but recursing into only one side, giving expected linear time.
concepts.example: Find the 3rd smallest in [7, 2, 9, 1, 5]: partition around 5 to get [2, 1] 5 [7, 9]. The left part has 2 items, so 5 is the 3rd smallest. Only one side ever needs recursion.

concepts.name: Quicksort
concepts.description: A divide-and-conquer sorting algorithm that partitions an array around a pivot and recursively sorts the two parts. It averages O(n log n) time, is in-place, and is very fast in practice.
concepts.example: Sort [3, 6, 1, 8, 2] with pivot 3: partition into [1, 2] 3 [6, 8], then sort each side the same way. On average this takes about n log n comparisons, and it's fast in practice due to good cache use.

concepts.name: R-Tree
concepts.description: A balanced tree for indexing spatial data, grouping nearby objects under minimum bounding rectangles at each level. It supports fast range and nearest-neighbor queries in databases and GIS.
concepts.example: A map app stores 1 million buildings. The R-tree groups nearby buildings into boxes, nearby boxes into bigger boxes, and so on. To find what's on screen it skips every big box that doesn't overlap the screen.

concepts.name: Rabin–Karp Algorithm
concepts.description: A string search algorithm that compares a rolling hash of each text window with the pattern's hash and checks characters only on a match. Expected O(n + m) time, and it handles multiple patterns well.
concepts.example: To find "cab" in "abcabc", compute the pattern's hash once, then roll a 3-letter window along the text updating its hash in O(1). Only when the hashes match do you compare letters, at position 2.

concepts.name: Radix Sort
concepts.description: A non-comparison sorting algorithm that sorts integers or strings digit by digit, using a stable sort such as counting sort at each digit. It runs in O(d(n + b)) time for d digits in base b.
concepts.example: Sort [170, 45, 75, 90]: stable-sort by the ones digit (170, 90, 45, 75), then by tens (45, 170, 75, 90), then by hundreds (45, 75, 90, 170). No two numbers are ever compared directly.

concepts.name: Radix Tree
concepts.description: A space-optimized trie in which each node with a single child is merged with its child, so edges are labeled with strings. Used in IP routing tables and key-value stores.
concepts.example: Storing "romane", "romanus" and "romulus": a plain trie uses one node per letter, but a radix tree has an edge 'rom', then branches 'an' and 'ulus', with 'an' splitting into 'e' and 'us'. Far fewer nodes.

concepts.name: Randomized Algorithm
concepts.description: An algorithm that uses random choices during execution, either to run fast in expectation (Las Vegas) or to be correct with high probability (Monte Carlo). Often simpler or faster than deterministic alternatives.
concepts.example: Guessing whether a huge jar holds more red than blue marbles: pull out 1,000 at random instead of counting all. Quicksort with a random pivot uses the same idea to avoid inputs crafted to be slow.

concepts.name: Randomized Quicksort
concepts.description: Quicksort with the pivot chosen uniformly at random, which makes its expected running time O(n log n) for every input and defeats adversarial worst cases.
concepts.example: An adversary can feed already-sorted data to quicksort that always picks the first element, forcing n² time. Choosing the pivot at random means no fixed input is reliably bad, and expected time is O(n log n).

concepts.name: Range Minimum Query
concepts.description: The problem of finding the minimum element in any subarray range of an array. Solved by sparse tables in O(1) per query, segment trees in O(log n), and linked to lowest common ancestor queries.
concepts.example: For [5, 2, 8, 1, 9], the minimum over positions 1 to 3 (2, 8, 1) is 1. Answering millions of such queries quickly is how lowest common ancestors in trees are found.

concepts.name: Range Tree
concepts.description: A multi-level balanced search tree for orthogonal range queries over points in k dimensions, where each node stores an auxiliary tree on the next coordinate. Queries take O(log^k n + output) time.
concepts.example: To count shops with x between 2 and 5 and y between 1 and 3, first find the O(log n) x-tree nodes covering x in [2, 5]. Each stores its points sorted by y, so a binary search finds those with y in [1, 3].

concepts.name: Recursion
concepts.description: A technique where a function solves a problem by calling itself on smaller instances until reaching a base case. It naturally expresses divide-and-conquer, tree traversal and many mathematical definitions.
concepts.example: factorial(4) = 4 · factorial(3) = 4 · 3 · factorial(2) = 4 · 3 · 2 · factorial(1) = 24, where factorial(1) = 1 stops the chain. Like Russian dolls: open each until you reach the smallest solid one.

concepts.name: Recursion Tree Method
concepts.description: A way to solve recurrences by drawing the tree of recursive calls, summing the work done at each level, and adding up the levels to estimate total running time.
concepts.example: For T(n) = 2T(n/2) + n, the root does n work, the 2 children do n/2 each (n total), the 4 grandchildren n/4 each (n total). With log₂ n levels the total is n log n.

concepts.name: Red–Black Tree
concepts.description: A self-balancing binary search tree that colors nodes red or black and enforces rules ensuring no path is more than twice as long as another, guaranteeing O(log n) operations. Used in many standard libraries.
concepts.example: Inserting 1, 2, 3 into a plain BST makes a chain; a red-black tree spots two reds in a row and rotates so 2 becomes the root. Because every path has the same number of black nodes, height stays below 2·log₂(n+1).

concepts.name: Regular Expression Matching
concepts.description: Deciding whether a string matches a regular expression pattern, typically by compiling the pattern into a finite automaton or by dynamic programming for simplified syntax like '.' and '*'.
concepts.example: Does "aab" match "c*a*b"? c* matches nothing, a* takes "aa", and b matches b: yes. A DP table over (text position, pattern position) records which pairs can still match.

concepts.name: Rehashing
concepts.description: Rebuilding a hash table with a larger (or smaller) array and reinserting all entries when the load factor crosses a threshold, keeping operations O(1) on average via amortized doubling.
concepts.example: A hash table of 8 slots holds 6 items (load 0.75). Inserting a 7th triggers a resize to 16 slots, and all items are re-hashed into new positions because 'hash mod 16' differs from 'hash mod 8'.

concepts.name: Residual Graph
concepts.description: Given a flow network and a current flow, the graph of remaining capacities: forward edges with unused capacity and backward edges that allow flow to be undone. Augmenting paths are searched in it.
concepts.example: A pipe of capacity 10 carrying 7 units becomes two residual edges: forward with 3 spare, and backward with 7, meaning you could cancel up to 7 units later. Augmenting paths are searched in this graph.

concepts.name: Robin Hood Hashing
concepts.description: An open addressing scheme in which an inserting key that has probed farther than the resident key swaps places with it, equalizing probe lengths and reducing worst-case lookup variance.
concepts.example: Key X has probed 3 slots past home and reaches a slot whose key Y is only 1 from home. X takes the slot and Y moves on. Taking from the 'rich' keeps probe lengths even, so lookups have low variance.

concepts.name: Rod Cutting Problem
concepts.description: The dynamic programming problem of cutting a rod of length n into pieces to maximize total sale value given prices for each length. A classic introductory DP example.
concepts.example: A rod of length 4 with prices 1, 5, 8, 9 for lengths 1 to 4. Selling it whole gives 9, but two pieces of length 2 give 5 + 5 = 10. DP tries every first cut and reuses best values for shorter rods.

concepts.name: Rolling Hash
concepts.description: A hash function over a sliding window that can be updated in constant time when one element leaves and another enters, rather than recomputed. Used for substring search and content-defined chunking.
concepts.example: A window of 3 numbers [4, 7, 1] has hash 4 + 7 + 1 = 12 in a simple additive version. Sliding to [7, 1, 9] just subtracts 4 and adds 9 to get 21, without re-adding the whole window.

concepts.name: Rope
concepts.description: A binary tree for storing long strings where leaves hold short substrings and internal nodes store lengths, enabling fast concatenation, splitting and insertion. Used in text editors.
concepts.example: A text editor holding a 10 MB document: inserting a word in the middle of a plain string copies megabytes. A rope splits the text into chunks in a tree, so an insert only splits one chunk and adds a few nodes.

concepts.name: Rotating Calipers
concepts.description: A computational geometry technique that rotates a pair of parallel lines around a convex polygon to solve problems like diameter, width or minimum bounding rectangle in linear time.
