concepts.description: Finding locations where image brightness changes sharply, which usually mark object boundaries, typically by thresholding the magnitude of the image gradient.
concepts.example: In a photo of a white mug on a dark table, pixel values jump from about 30 to 220 at the mug's outline; marking every place with such a jump traces the mug's shape.

concepts.name: Eigenface
concepts.description: A classic face-recognition approach that applies PCA to face images, representing each face as a weighted combination of principal components ('eigenfaces') and matching in that low-dimensional space.
concepts.example: Run PCA on 1,000 face photos to get, say, 50 'ghostly' eigenfaces; any face is then summarised by 50 weights, and two photos of the same person have similar weights.

concepts.name: Eight-Point Algorithm
concepts.description: Estimates the fundamental or essential matrix from eight or more point correspondences between two views by solving a linear system with SVD and then enforcing rank 2.
concepts.example: Click 8 matching points in two photos of a room; each pair gives one linear equation in F's 9 entries, SVD solves the system, and a final step forces F to rank 2.

concepts.name: Energy-Based Model
concepts.description: A model that assigns a scalar energy to every configuration, low for likely data; probabilities follow a Boltzmann distribution normalised by an often intractable partition function.
concepts.example: Think of a landscape where real images sit in valleys and nonsense images on peaks; the model learns the height (energy) of each point, and probability is high where energy is low.

concepts.name: Epipolar Geometry
concepts.description: The geometry of two views of a scene: a point in one image must lie on a corresponding epipolar line in the other, which constrains stereo matching and relative camera pose estimation.
concepts.example: If your left eye sees a lamp at some pixel, that lamp in your right eye's view must lie somewhere along one specific line, so a stereo matcher only needs to search that line, not the whole image.

concepts.name: Erosion and Dilation
concepts.description: The two basic morphological operations: erosion shrinks foreground regions by keeping pixels whose neighbourhood fits a structuring element, and dilation grows them; used to clean binary masks.
concepts.example: With a 3x3 square, erosion turns a 10x10 white square into 8x8 and removes 1-pixel specks; dilation grows it to 12x12 and fills small holes.

concepts.name: Essential Matrix
concepts.description: A 3x3 matrix relating corresponding normalised image points in two calibrated views (x'^T E x = 0); it encodes the relative rotation and translation between the two cameras.
concepts.example: With a calibrated phone camera, the essential matrix from two shots of a building can be decomposed into how the camera rotated and in which direction it moved between shots.

concepts.name: Evidence Lower Bound
concepts.description: A lower bound on the log-likelihood of data: the expected log-likelihood under an approximate posterior minus its KL divergence from the prior; maximising it trains VAEs and variational inference.
concepts.example: The true log-likelihood of an image might be impossible to compute, but the ELBO gives a number guaranteed to be no larger, e.g. -95 when the truth is -92; pushing the ELBO up pushes the likelihood up too.

concepts.name: Explicit and Implicit Density Models
concepts.description: Explicit density models define a computable or approximable likelihood p(x), like flows or VAEs; implicit ones, like GANs, only provide a sampler without an accessible density.
concepts.example: A flow model can tell you an image's exact probability, such as log p = -3,200 nats; a GAN can produce new faces but cannot say how likely any given face is.

concepts.name: Face Detection
concepts.description: Locating all human faces in an image and returning their bounding boxes; a first step for face recognition, camera autofocus and filters, done classically by Viola-Jones and now by CNN detectors.
concepts.example: When you point your phone at three friends, the camera draws three boxes, one around each face, then focuses there; it finds where faces are but not who they are.

concepts.name: FaceNet
concepts.description: Google's face-recognition network that maps faces to a 128-dimensional embedding where Euclidean distance reflects identity, trained with a triplet loss on anchor, positive and negative faces.
concepts.example: FaceNet maps photos to 128 numbers such that two photos of Alice are, say, 0.3 apart and Alice versus Bob 1.4 apart; a threshold near 1.0 decides 'same person'.

concepts.name: Facial Landmark Detection
concepts.description: Locating key points on a face, such as eye corners, nose tip and mouth outline, used for face alignment, expression analysis and AR filters; often done with heatmap regression.
concepts.example: A Snapchat filter finds 68 points on your face, such as eye corners, nose tip and lip outline, then pins virtual glasses to the eye points so they follow your head.

concepts.name: Facial Recognition System
concepts.description: Identifying or verifying a person from a face image by detecting and aligning the face, extracting an identity feature vector and comparing it with known faces.
concepts.example: At a phone unlock, the camera finds your face, aligns it, turns it into a feature vector and compares it with the one stored at setup; if close enough, the phone unlocks.

concepts.name: FAST (Features from Accelerated Segment Test)
concepts.description: A very fast corner detector that tests whether a contiguous arc of pixels on a 16-pixel circle around a candidate is entirely brighter or entirely darker than the centre pixel.
concepts.example: For a pixel with brightness 100, check 16 pixels on a circle around it; if 12 in a row are all brighter than 120 or all darker than 80, it is marked as a corner.

concepts.name: Fast R-CNN
concepts.description: An R-CNN improvement that runs the CNN once per image and uses RoI pooling to extract features for each region proposal, training classification and box regression jointly.
concepts.example: R-CNN ran the CNN separately on 2,000 crops per image; Fast R-CNN runs it once on the whole image and cuts each proposal's features from the shared map, making it far faster.

concepts.name: Faster R-CNN
concepts.description: A two-stage detector that adds a Region Proposal Network sharing features with Fast R-CNN, replacing slow external proposal methods and making detection nearly real-time.
concepts.example: Fast R-CNN still waited about 2 seconds per image for selective search to propose boxes; Faster R-CNN's built-in proposal network does that in about 10 ms on the GPU.

concepts.name: FastSpeech
concepts.description: A non-autoregressive Transformer text-to-speech model that predicts each phoneme's duration and expands features accordingly to generate mel spectrograms in parallel; FastSpeech 2 adds pitch and energy.
concepts.example: For 'cat', it predicts /k/ lasts 3 frames, /ae/ 8 and /t/ 4, copies each phoneme's features that many times, then generates all 15 spectrogram frames at once instead of one by one.

concepts.name: Fully Convolutional Network
concepts.description: A segmentation network built only from convolutional layers that replaces fully connected layers with convolutions and upsamples coarse feature maps, giving a per-pixel class map for any input size.
concepts.example: A classifier says 'cat' for the whole photo; an FCN replaces its final dense layers with convolutions, so it outputs a small 'cat-ness' map, which is upsampled to a full-resolution mask.

concepts.name: Feature Descriptor
concepts.description: A vector summarising the local appearance around a keypoint, from gradients or intensity comparisons, so the same point can be matched across images despite changes in viewpoint and lighting.
concepts.example: Around a window corner, a descriptor records the pattern of gradient directions as 128 numbers; the same corner seen from a slightly different angle gives a very similar 128 numbers.

concepts.name: Feature Detection (Computer Vision)
concepts.description: Finding distinctive, repeatable points or regions in images, such as corners and blobs, that can be reliably found again in other views for matching and tracking.
concepts.example: In two photos of a building, a detector picks out the same 500 distinctive spots, such as window corners and sign letters, so the photos can be aligned using those points.

concepts.name: Feature Matching
concepts.description: Finding corresponding keypoints between images by comparing their descriptors, for example nearest-neighbour search with a ratio test, then filtering outliers with RANSAC.
concepts.example: A window corner in photo A has a nearest descriptor in photo B at distance 0.2 and a second-best at 0.6; since 0.2 is well below 0.8 x 0.6, the match is accepted as unambiguous.

concepts.name: Fréchet Inception Distance
concepts.description: A metric for generated image quality: it fits Gaussians to Inception-network features of real and generated images and computes the Frechet distance between the two Gaussians; lower is better.
concepts.example: Pass 10,000 real and 10,000 generated faces through Inception, summarise each set's features by a mean and covariance, then measure how far apart the two Gaussians are; lower FID means more realistic.

concepts.name: Flamingo
concepts.description: DeepMind's visual language model that inserts gated cross-attention layers into a frozen LLM, letting it read interleaved images and text and solve multimodal tasks from a few examples.
concepts.example: Give Flamingo two images with captions, such as a cat photo with 'A cat: 4 legs' and a chicken photo with 'A chicken: 2 legs', then a spider photo; it answers 'A spider: 8 legs' without retraining.

concepts.name: Flow Matching
concepts.description: Training a continuous normalizing flow by regressing a neural velocity field onto simple target velocities along paths from noise to data (straight lines in rectified flow), without simulating the ODE.
concepts.example: Pair a noise sample with a data image and draw the straight line between them; the network learns the velocity along such lines at every point, then generation follows that velocity from noise to image.

concepts.name: FlowNet
concepts.description: An early CNN that estimates optical flow end to end from a pair of images, using a correlation layer to compare feature patches; trained on the synthetic Flying Chairs dataset.
concepts.example: Given two consecutive frames of a car driving, FlowNet outputs, for each pixel, an arrow like (5 px right, 0 down) for the car and near zero for the static road, in one forward pass.

concepts.name: Formant
concepts.description: A resonant frequency of the vocal tract that shows up as a peak in the speech spectrum; the first two formants largely determine which vowel a listener hears.
concepts.example: Say 'ee' then 'ah': for 'ee' the first two formants sit near 300 Hz and 2,300 Hz, for 'ah' near 700 Hz and 1,200 Hz; your mouth shape moves these peaks, letting listeners tell vowels apart.

concepts.name: Forward Diffusion Process
concepts.description: The fixed Markov chain in diffusion models that adds a little Gaussian noise to the data at each step, following a noise schedule, until the data becomes nearly pure noise.
concepts.example: Take a photo and at each of 1,000 steps mix in a little random noise; after step 10 it looks grainy, after step 500 barely recognisable, and after step 1,000 it is pure static.

concepts.name: Two-Dimensional Fourier Transform
concepts.description: Decomposes an image into 2D sinusoidal patterns of different frequencies and orientations; low frequencies capture smooth areas and high frequencies capture edges and fine detail.
concepts.example: An image of fine vertical stripes shows up in its 2D spectrum as two bright dots on the horizontal axis; a smooth sky shows energy concentrated near the centre, at low frequencies.

concepts.name: Frequency Domain Filtering
concepts.description: Filtering an image by taking its 2D Fourier transform, multiplying by a frequency mask (low-pass, high-pass or notch) and transforming back; equivalent to convolution by the convolution theorem.
concepts.example: To remove a regular stripe pattern from a scanned photo, transform it, zero out the bright spots caused by the stripes, and transform back; the stripes vanish while the rest stays.

concepts.name: Fundamental Matrix
concepts.description: A 3x3 rank-2 matrix relating corresponding points in two uncalibrated views through x'^T F x = 0; it maps each point in one image to its epipolar line in the other.
concepts.example: Click a doorknob in the left photo, multiply its coordinates by F, and you get a line in the right photo; the doorknob must appear somewhere on that line.

concepts.name: Gamma Correction
concepts.description: A nonlinear power-law mapping of pixel intensities (output = input^gamma) used to encode images efficiently for human perception and to adjust brightness and contrast.
concepts.example: With gamma 2.2, a stored value of 0.5 becomes 0.5^2.2 ≈ 0.22 of full brightness on screen; storing in a perceptual scale spends more of the 256 levels on the dark tones our eyes distinguish best.

concepts.name: GAN Inversion
concepts.description: Finding the latent code that makes a pretrained GAN reproduce a given real image, by optimisation or a trained encoder, so the image can be edited by moving in latent space.
concepts.example: To age a real photo of yourself with StyleGAN, first find the latent code that makes StyleGAN redraw your face, then move that code along an 'age' direction and generate again.

concepts.name: Gaussian Blur
concepts.description: Smoothing an image by convolving it with a Gaussian kernel, so each pixel becomes a weighted average of its neighbours with closer pixels counting more; reduces noise and fine detail.
concepts.example: With a 3x3 Gaussian kernel, the centre pixel gets weight 4/16, side neighbours 2/16 and corners 1/16, so nearby pixels influence the result more than far ones, giving a natural soft blur.

concepts.name: Gaussian Pyramid
concepts.description: A sequence of progressively smaller images made by repeatedly Gaussian-blurring and downsampling by a factor of two, representing the image at multiple scales for coarse-to-fine processing.
concepts.example: Start with a 512x512 photo, blur and halve it to 256x256, then 128x128, 64x64 and so on; a face 200 px wide in the original is 25 px wide three levels up, matching a small face template.

concepts.name: Gaussian Splatting
concepts.description: Represents a 3D scene as millions of anisotropic 3D Gaussians with colour and opacity, optimised from photos and rendered by fast rasterisation ('splatting') for real-time novel view synthesis.
concepts.example: A scene of a room is stored as about 2 million fuzzy coloured ellipsoids; rendering projects each onto the screen as a soft 2D blob and blends them, fast enough for over 100 frames per second.

concepts.name: Generative Adversarial Network
concepts.description: A generative model in which a generator turns random noise into samples and a discriminator tries to tell them from real data; the two are trained against each other until fakes look real.
concepts.example: Like a forger and a detective: the forger (generator) makes fake banknotes, the detective (discriminator) flags them, and each improves until the fakes are hard to tell from real ones.

concepts.name: Generative Artificial Intelligence
concepts.description: The field of AI systems that create new content, such as text, images, audio, video or code, by learning the distribution of training data; it includes LLMs, diffusion models and GANs.
concepts.example: Ask ChatGPT for a poem, Midjourney for a castle at sunset, or Suno for a song; each produces new content resembling, but not copying, what it learned from.

concepts.name: Generator and Discriminator
concepts.description: The two networks of a GAN: the generator maps random noise to synthetic samples, while the discriminator is a classifier that outputs the probability that its input is real rather than generated.
concepts.example: The generator turns 100 random numbers into a 64x64 face; the discriminator looks at that face and says, for example, '0.3 chance this is real'. Each one's loss depends on the other's output.

concepts.name: Glow (Generative Model)
concepts.description: A flow-based generative model built from invertible 1x1 convolutions, actnorm and affine coupling layers, giving exact log-likelihoods, efficient sampling and meaningful latent manipulation.
concepts.example: Glow can take a face photo, map it exactly to a latent code and back with no loss, and report its exact likelihood; adding a 'smile' vector to the code makes the person smile.

concepts.name: Gradient Penalty
concepts.description: A regulariser that penalises the discriminator's input-gradient norm, pushing it toward 1 on interpolated samples (WGAN-GP), to enforce Lipschitz continuity and stabilise GAN training.
concepts.example: Blend a real and a fake image halfway, measure how steeply the critic's score changes at that blend, and add a penalty like 10·(steepness - 1)² to the loss, keeping the critic smooth.

concepts.name: Gram Matrix Style Loss
concepts.description: A style loss that summarises a CNN layer's activations by their Gram matrix (correlations between channels) and penalises differences from the Gram matrices of a style image.
concepts.example: A Van Gogh painting's Gram matrix records that 'swirl' channels and 'yellow' channels tend to fire together; matching those co-activations in a photo transfers the swirly style without copying the layout.

concepts.name: Graph Cut Segmentation
concepts.description: Segmenting an image by building a graph of pixels with edge weights for similarity and foreground/background likelihood, then finding a minimum cut; GrabCut iterates this with colour models.
concepts.example: Each pixel is a node with links to its neighbours (strong if colours are similar) and to 'foreground' and 'background'; the cheapest cut separating the two cleanly outlines the object.

concepts.name: Grayscale
concepts.description: An image representation with a single intensity value per pixel, from black to white, often computed as a weighted sum of the red, green and blue channels.
concepts.example: A pixel with RGB (200, 100, 50) becomes about 0.299·200 + 0.587·100 + 0.114·50 ≈ 124; green is weighted most because our eyes are most sensitive to it.

concepts.name: Griffin–Lim Algorithm
concepts.description: An algorithm that reconstructs a waveform from a magnitude-only spectrogram by iteratively estimating the missing phase, alternating inverse and forward short-time Fourier transforms.
concepts.example: Given only how loud each frequency is over time, guess random phases, convert to audio, recompute the spectrogram, keep its phase but restore the known loudness, and repeat about 50 times.

concepts.name: Haar-like Features
concepts.description: Simple rectangular features computed as differences between the pixel sums of adjacent light and dark regions; evaluated quickly with integral images and used in Viola-Jones face detection.
concepts.example: On a face, the eye region is usually darker than the cheeks below it; a feature subtracting the sum of a lower rectangle from an upper one gives a big value on faces and a small one elsewhere.

concepts.name: Harris Corner Detector
concepts.description: Detects corners by computing a 2x2 structure tensor of image gradients in each window and scoring how much intensity changes in all directions, using det(M) - k trace(M)^2.
concepts.example: In each small window, Harris checks how much brightness changes when shifting in all directions; on a flat wall both eigenvalues are small, on an edge one is large, and at a corner both are large.

concepts.name: HiFi-GAN
concepts.description: A GAN-based neural vocoder that quickly turns mel spectrograms into high-fidelity waveforms, using multi-period and multi-scale discriminators to capture the periodic patterns of speech.
concepts.example: A text-to-speech model outputs a mel spectrogram for 'Good morning'; HiFi-GAN turns it into a natural-sounding 22 kHz waveform many times faster than real time.

concepts.name: Histogram Equalization
concepts.description: Spreading out an image's intensity values so its histogram becomes roughly uniform, using the cumulative distribution, to boost contrast; CLAHE does this locally with contrast clipping.
concepts.example: In a foggy photo all pixels sit between 100 and 150; equalization spreads them across 0 to 255, so the darkest become near black and the brightest near white, making details pop.

concepts.name: HMM–GMM Speech Recognition
concepts.description: The classic speech-recognition approach that models each phone with a hidden Markov model whose states emit acoustic features (MFCCs) through Gaussian mixture models, decoded with Viterbi search.
concepts.example: The word 'cat' is modelled as phones /k/, /ae/, /t/, each with about 3 HMM states; a GMM scores how well each 10 ms MFCC frame fits each state, and Viterbi finds the best state path.

concepts.name: Histogram of Oriented Gradients
concepts.description: A feature descriptor that divides an image into cells, builds histograms of gradient orientations in each, and normalises them over blocks; classic for pedestrian detection with linear SVMs.
concepts.example: Split a 64x128 photo into 8x8-pixel cells and, in each, count edge directions in 9 bins; a standing person shows strong vertical-edge counts along the sides, which a classifier learns to spot.

concepts.name: Homogeneous Coordinates
concepts.description: Representing an n-dimensional point with n+1 coordinates defined up to scale, such as (x, y, 1), so that translations and perspective projections become matrix multiplications.
concepts.example: Write point (3, 4) as (3, 4, 1); then shifting by (2, 5) is a single 3x3 matrix multiplication giving (5, 9, 1). Also (6, 8, 2) means the same point as (3, 4, 1).

concepts.name: Homography
concepts.description: A 3x3 projective transformation that maps points between two images of a plane, or two views from a rotating camera; estimated from four or more correspondences and used in stitching.
concepts.example: Photograph a poster at an angle; four corner correspondences determine a 3x3 homography that warps the skewed poster into a straight-on rectangle.

concepts.name: Horn–Schunck Method
concepts.description: A variational optical-flow method that combines the brightness-constancy assumption with a global smoothness penalty and solves for a dense flow field iteratively.
concepts.example: For two frames of a rolling ball, Horn–Schunck finds a motion arrow at every pixel such that brightness is preserved and neighbouring arrows are similar, filling in motion even in textureless areas.

concepts.name: Hough Transform
concepts.description: Detects lines, circles or other shapes by letting each edge pixel vote for all shape parameters consistent with it in an accumulator array; peaks in the accumulator are the detected shapes.
concepts.example: Each edge pixel votes for every line through it, recorded as (angle, distance) bins; if 200 pixels fall on one straight road edge, that line's bin gets 200 votes and stands out.

concepts.name: HSL and HSV
concepts.description: Cylindrical colour representations that describe colours by hue, saturation and value (or lightness), which is more intuitive than RGB for colour picking and colour-based segmentation.
concepts.example: To pick out every red apple in a photo, keep pixels with hue near 0°, ignoring how bright or shaded they are; in RGB, shadowed red and bright red have very different numbers.

concepts.name: HuBERT
concepts.description: A self-supervised speech model that predicts discrete cluster labels, first from k-means on MFCCs and then on its own features, for masked spans of audio, learning representations for ASR.
concepts.example: HuBERT masks out about half of a speech recording's frames and learns to guess which of, say, 100 sound clusters each hidden frame belonged to, like a fill-in-the-blank for audio.

concepts.name: Diffusers (Hugging Face)
concepts.description: A Python library from Hugging Face providing pretrained diffusion pipelines, models and noise schedulers, such as Stable Diffusion, for image, video and audio generation in PyTorch.
concepts.example: A few lines of Python load a pipeline from 'stabilityai/stable-diffusion-xl-base-1.0' and call pipe('a cozy cabin in snow') to get an image, swapping the scheduler with one line.

concepts.name: Image Captioning
concepts.description: Generating a natural-language sentence that describes an image, typically with a vision encoder feeding a language decoder that attends over image features.
concepts.example: Given a photo, the model writes 'A brown dog jumps to catch a red frisbee in a park', attending to the dog's pixels when writing 'dog' and the frisbee's when writing 'frisbee'.

concepts.name: Image Classification
concepts.description: Assigning one label from a fixed set of categories to a whole image, such as 'cat' or 'car'; the core task behind ImageNet and the rise of CNNs.
concepts.example: A model looks at a 224x224 photo and outputs 'tabby cat 92%, tiger cat 6%, dog 1%'; it labels the whole image without saying where the cat is.

concepts.name: Image Compression
concepts.description: Reducing the bytes needed to store an image, losslessly (PNG) or lossily (JPEG), by exploiting redundancy and human perception, for example with the DCT plus quantisation.
concepts.example: A 12 MB raw photo saved as a JPEG might be 2 MB: it discards fine colour detail and high-frequency texture the eye barely notices, then compactly encodes what remains.

concepts.name: Image Denoising
concepts.description: Recovering a clean image from one corrupted by noise, using smoothing filters, patch-based methods such as non-local means and BM3D, or trained neural networks.
concepts.example: A night photo at high ISO looks speckled; denoising removes the speckles while keeping the edges of buildings, using filters, similar-patch averaging or a trained network.

concepts.name: Diffusion-Based Image Editing
concepts.description: Modifying an existing image with a diffusion model, either by partially noising and re-denoising it under a new prompt (SDEdit) or by following text instructions (InstructPix2Pix).
concepts.example: Take a photo of a summer street, add moderate noise, then denoise it with the prompt 'snowy winter street'; the layout survives but the leaves turn into snow.

concepts.name: Image Filtering
concepts.description: Changing an image by computing each output pixel from a neighbourhood of input pixels, such as a convolution with a kernel or a median, to blur, sharpen, denoise or detect edges.
concepts.example: A median filter on a photo with white specks replaces each pixel by the median of its 3x3 neighbours, e.g. [10,12,11,255,13,...] gives 12, removing the speck while keeping edges.

concepts.name: Image GPT
concepts.description: OpenAI's GPT-2-style Transformer trained to predict pixels autoregressively on low-resolution images, showing that generative pretraining on pixels yields useful image representations.
concepts.example: Show it the top half of a 32x32 image of a cat and it predicts the remaining pixels one by one, completing the bottom half, just as GPT completes a sentence.

concepts.name: Image Gradient
concepts.description: The directional change in intensity at each pixel, estimated with finite differences or filters such as Sobel; its magnitude marks edges and its direction is perpendicular to them.
concepts.example: Along a row of pixels 50, 50, 200, 200, the horizontal difference is 0, 150, 0, so the gradient magnitude spikes exactly at the dark-to-bright boundary and points toward the bright side.

concepts.name: Image Histogram
concepts.description: A chart counting how many pixels have each intensity or colour value, summarising an image's brightness and contrast; used for thresholding and equalisation.
concepts.example: For a photo of snow, most of the 1 million pixels fall in bins 200 to 255, so the histogram piles up on the right; a dark night photo piles up on the left.

concepts.name: Image Inpainting
concepts.description: Filling in missing or masked regions of an image with plausible content that is consistent with the surroundings, using patch-based methods or deep generative models such as diffusion.
concepts.example: Remove a tourist from a beach photo by masking them out; inpainting fills the hole with sand and waves that match the surrounding texture and lighting.

concepts.name: Image Scaling
concepts.description: Resizing an image by estimating pixel values at new positions from nearby pixels, using nearest-neighbour, bilinear or bicubic interpolation, trading speed against smoothness.
concepts.example: Doubling a 2x2 image to 4x4 with nearest-neighbour copies each pixel into a 2x2 block (blocky); bilinear sets a new pixel between values 100 and 200 to 150 (smoother).

concepts.name: Image Moment
concepts.description: Weighted sums of pixel intensities, such as the sum of x^p y^q I(x,y), describing a shape's area, centroid and orientation; Hu moments combine them into rotation- and scale-invariant features.
concepts.example: For a binary blob, the zeroth moment counts pixels (area, say 500), and the first moments divided by it give the centroid, e.g. (120, 80); second moments reveal the blob's tilt.

concepts.name: Image Noise
concepts.description: Random variation in pixel values that is not present in the scene, such as Gaussian sensor noise, shot noise or salt-and-pepper noise, which degrades image quality.
concepts.example: A photo taken in a dark room shows grainy random speckles; if a wall's true brightness is 100, its pixels might read 96, 104, 99, 107, scattered around the true value.

concepts.name: Pyramid (Image Processing)
concepts.description: A multi-scale representation formed by repeatedly smoothing and subsampling an image, giving a stack of ever smaller versions used for coarse-to-fine search and multi-scale detection.
concepts.example: To find a face that could be 30 or 300 pixels wide using a 30-pixel detector, run it on the photo at full size, half size, quarter size and so on.

concepts.name: Image Registration
concepts.description: Aligning two or more images of the same scene into a common coordinate frame by estimating the rigid, affine, projective or deformable transformation that best maps one onto the other.
concepts.example: Two brain MRI scans taken a month apart are shifted and rotated; registration finds the transform that overlays them so a doctor can see exactly what changed.

concepts.name: Image Resolution
concepts.description: The amount of detail an image holds, usually given as its width and height in pixels or as pixels per inch; higher resolution captures finer detail but needs more storage.
concepts.example: A 1920x1080 image has about 2 million pixels; printed at 300 pixels per inch, it covers about 6.4 by 3.6 inches before details start looking soft.

concepts.name: Content-Based Image Retrieval
concepts.description: Searching a database for images similar to a query image based on visual content, using descriptors like bag-of-visual-words or deep embeddings with nearest-neighbour search.
concepts.example: Upload a photo of a chair and the system returns visually similar chairs from a catalogue of a million products, comparing image features rather than text.

concepts.name: Image Segmentation
concepts.description: Partitioning an image into regions by assigning each pixel a label, so that pixels sharing a label share characteristics such as object class, colour or texture.
concepts.example: In a photo of a sheep in a field, segmentation colours every sheep pixel one label, grass another and sky a third, giving exact outlines rather than boxes.

concepts.name: Image Stitching
concepts.description: Combining overlapping photos into a panorama by detecting and matching features, estimating homographies with RANSAC, warping images onto a common surface and blending the seams.
concepts.example: Take three overlapping photos while turning on the spot; stitching matches features in the overlaps, computes how to warp each photo, and blends them into one wide panorama.

concepts.name: Image–Text Retrieval
concepts.description: Finding images that match a text query, or captions that match an image, usually by embedding both in a shared space such as CLIP's and ranking by similarity.
concepts.example: Type 'dog playing in snow' into a photo app and it finds those pictures with no tags, because text and images are embedded in the same space and compared by similarity.

concepts.name: Thresholding
concepts.description: Turning a grayscale image into a binary one by setting pixels above a threshold to foreground and the rest to background; thresholds can be global, adaptive or chosen by Otsu's method.
concepts.example: With threshold 128, a scanned page's pixel of 200 (paper) becomes white and 40 (ink) becomes black, producing a clean black-and-white document.

concepts.name: Image-to-Image Translation
concepts.description: Learning to map an image from one domain to another while keeping its structure, such as sketches to photos, day to night, or maps to satellite images.
concepts.example: Feed in a rough sketch of a handbag and get a realistic photo of that bag; the outline stays the same, only the appearance changes to the target domain.

concepts.name: Watermarking of AI-Generated Content
concepts.description: Embedding an invisible, robust signal into AI-generated images, audio or text, as in Google's SynthID, so the content can later be identified as machine-made.
concepts.example: An AI image generator subtly alters pixel values in a pattern invisible to people but detectable by a key-holding checker, even after the image is cropped or recompressed.

concepts.name: Imagen (Text-to-Image Model)
concepts.description: Google's text-to-image diffusion model that conditions on a large frozen T5 text encoder and uses cascaded super-resolution diffusion models, showing that a bigger text encoder matters most.
concepts.example: For 'a corgi riding a bike in Times Square', Imagen first makes a 64x64 image guided by T5's reading of the prompt, then two super-resolution models enlarge it to 256x256 and finally 1024x1024.

concepts.name: ImageNet
concepts.description: A dataset of over 14 million labelled images in about 22k categories; its 1,000-class ILSVRC subset was the benchmark whose 2012 AlexNet win sparked the deep learning boom.
concepts.example: ImageNet's benchmark asks a model to sort 50,000 test photos into 1,000 classes, including about 120 dog breeds; in 2012 AlexNet cut the top-5 error from about 26% to 15%.

concepts.name: Inception Score
concepts.description: A metric for generated images that uses an Inception classifier: it is high when each image gets a confident label and the labels are diverse overall (exponential of an expected KL divergence).
concepts.example: If a GAN makes 1,000 images and Inception confidently labels each one as a single class (sharp), with the labels spread over many classes (diverse), the score is high; blurry or repetitive outputs score low.

concepts.name: Instance Segmentation
concepts.description: Detecting each object instance and outlining it with its own pixel mask, so two touching people get separate masks; it combines object detection with semantic segmentation.
concepts.example: In a photo of three overlapping sheep, semantic segmentation paints all of them as 'sheep'; instance segmentation gives sheep #1, #2 and #3 their own separate masks.

concepts.name: Summed-Area Table
concepts.description: A table in which each entry stores the sum of all pixels above and to the left, so the sum over any rectangle takes just four lookups; used in Viola-Jones and fast box filters.
concepts.example: For pixels [[1,2],[3,4]] the table is [[1,3],[4,10]]; the sum of any rectangle needs at most four lookups, e.g. the bottom row is 10 - 3 = 7, whatever the rectangle's size.

concepts.name: Intrinsic and Extrinsic Camera Parameters
concepts.description: Intrinsics describe a camera's internal geometry (focal length, principal point, skew); extrinsics give its rotation and translation in the world. Together they map 3D points to pixels.
concepts.example: Intrinsics are like the camera's built-in settings: focal length 800 px and image centre (320, 240). Extrinsics say where it stands: 2 m left of the origin, turned 30 degrees.

concepts.name: Iterative Closest Point
concepts.description: Aligns two point clouds by repeatedly matching each point to its nearest neighbour in the other cloud and solving for the rigid transform that minimises the distances, until convergence.
concepts.example: Two lidar scans of the same room are slightly offset; ICP pairs each point with its nearest point in the other scan, computes the best rotation and shift, applies it, and repeats until they overlap.

concepts.name: Kaldi
concepts.description: An open-source C++ toolkit for speech recognition research, known for its HMM-GMM and hybrid DNN-HMM recipes and decoding with weighted finite-state transducers.
concepts.example: A researcher downloads Kaldi's ready-made recipe for a speech corpus, runs its scripts, and gets an MFCC extractor, trained HMM-GMM and neural acoustic models, and a decoder.

concepts.name: Keypoint Heatmap Regression
concepts.description: Locating keypoints by having a network output one heatmap per keypoint, trained against Gaussian blobs at the true positions, and taking each map's peak as the prediction.
concepts.example: To find a person's left wrist, the network outputs a 64x64 map that is bright around the wrist and dark elsewhere; the brightest pixel, say (40, 22), is the predicted wrist location.

concepts.name: Keyword Spotting
concepts.description: Detecting specific spoken words, such as a wake word like 'Hey Siri', in a continuous audio stream, usually with small, low-power neural networks running on the device.
concepts.example: A smart speaker's tiny on-device model checks every second of audio only for 'Alexa'; it ignores everything else and wakes the full system only when that word appears.

concepts.name: Langevin Dynamics Sampling
concepts.description: An MCMC method that samples from a distribution by taking gradient steps on its log-density plus Gaussian noise; used in Bayesian learning (SGLD) and in score-based generative models.
concepts.example: To sample from a distribution, start at a random point and repeatedly step uphill on log-probability, say 0.01 times the gradient, then add a small random jiggle; the points end up spread like the target.

concepts.name: Language Model (Speech Recognition)
concepts.description: In speech recognition, a model of word-sequence probabilities combined with the acoustic model during decoding to favour likely sentences, such as an n-gram or neural language model.
concepts.example: The audio for 'recognize speech' sounds almost like 'wreck a nice beach'; a language model knows the first phrase is far more common and tips the decoder toward it.

concepts.name: Laplacian of Gaussian
concepts.description: An operator that smooths an image with a Gaussian and then applies the Laplacian (second derivatives); zero-crossings mark edges and extrema of the scale-normalised response mark blobs.
concepts.example: Blur an image with a Gaussian, then measure curvature of brightness; a dark spot about 10 px wide gives a strong peak when the blur width matches it, which is how LoG finds blobs.

concepts.name: Laplacian Pyramid
concepts.description: A multi-scale representation storing the difference between each Gaussian pyramid level and the upsampled next coarser level; it captures band-pass detail and allows exact reconstruction and blending.
concepts.example: Store a tiny 16x16 version of a photo plus, for each larger size, only the detail lost when shrinking; adding these back level by level rebuilds the original exactly, and blending them blends images seamlessly.

concepts.name: Latent Diffusion Model
concepts.description: A diffusion model that runs in the compressed latent space of a pretrained autoencoder instead of on pixels, cutting compute; with cross-attention text conditioning it underlies Stable Diffusion.
concepts.example: Stable Diffusion compresses a 512x512x3 image into a 64x64x4 latent, about 48 times fewer numbers, runs diffusion there, then decodes the result back to a full image.

concepts.name: Latent Variable Model
concepts.description: A probabilistic model that explains observed data through unobserved hidden variables, such as mixture components or factors, typically fitted with EM or variational methods.
concepts.example: Test scores in maths and physics are correlated; a model can explain this with an unseen 'quantitative ability' variable that drives both observed scores.

concepts.name: Lens Distortion
concepts.description: Deviation of a real lens from the ideal pinhole model, mainly radial distortion (barrel or pincushion) that bends straight lines; modelled with polynomial coefficients and corrected by calibration.
concepts.example: A GoPro photo of a doorway bows outward at the edges (barrel distortion); the distortion model maps each pixel to where it should be, straightening the door frame.

concepts.name: librosa
concepts.description: A Python library for audio and music analysis offering loading, resampling, STFT, mel spectrograms, MFCCs, beat tracking and pitch estimation.
concepts.example: In Python, librosa.load('song.mp3') returns samples and the sample rate, librosa.feature.mfcc(y=y, sr=sr) returns MFCCs, and librosa.beat.beat_track estimates the tempo, around 120 BPM.

concepts.name: Lidar
concepts.description: A sensor that measures distances by timing reflected laser pulses, producing 3D point clouds of its surroundings; widely used in self-driving cars, robotics and mapping.
concepts.example: A laser pulse returns after 200 nanoseconds; light travels about 60 m in that time, so the object is about 30 m away. Repeating this a million times per second builds a 3D point cloud.

concepts.name: Listen, Attend and Spell
concepts.description: An end-to-end speech recognizer with a pyramidal BiLSTM 'listener' that encodes audio and an attention-based 'speller' decoder that emits characters one at a time.
concepts.example: Feed in 10 seconds of someone saying 'hello world': the listener squeezes 1,000 audio frames down to about 125 summaries, and the speller writes h, e, l, l, o one letter at a time, glancing back at the frames for each sound.

concepts.name: LLaVA
concepts.description: An open vision-language assistant that connects a CLIP image encoder to a LLaMA-based language model through a projection layer, trained on GPT-generated visual instruction data.
concepts.example: Show LLaVA a photo of a fridge and ask 'what can I cook?': CLIP turns the photo into feature vectors, a small projection maps them into word-like tokens, and LLaMA reads them with your question to answer 'an omelette'.

concepts.name: Local Binary Patterns
concepts.description: A texture descriptor that thresholds each pixel's neighbours against the centre to form a binary code, then histograms these codes over a region; robust to lighting and used in face analysis.
concepts.example: Take a 3x3 patch with centre 50 and neighbours 60, 40, 55, 30, 70, 45, 52, 20: write 1 for each neighbour at least 50 and 0 otherwise, giving 10101010. Brightening the whole patch by 30 gives the same code.

concepts.name: Low-Rank Adaptation (Diffusion Fine-Tuning)
concepts.description: Fine-tuning a diffusion model by learning small low-rank update matrices for its attention weights, producing lightweight add-on files that inject a style, character or concept.
concepts.example: To teach Stable Diffusion your dog 'Rex', you train only tiny rank-4 updates to its attention layers on 20 photos. The result is a few-megabyte file you can switch on to get 'Rex surfing' without touching the 2-gigabyte base model.

concepts.name: LPIPS
concepts.description: A perceptual image-similarity metric that compares deep network features (e.g. AlexNet or VGG) of two images with learned per-channel weights, matching human judgements better than PSNR or SSIM.
concepts.example: A photo shifted by one pixel has a large pixel error but looks identical to us; LPIPS runs both through AlexNet, compares the feature maps layer by layer and gives a small distance, just as a human would judge.

concepts.name: Lucas–Kanade Method
concepts.description: An optical-flow method that assumes the flow is constant in a small window and solves the brightness-constancy equations by least squares; the KLT tracker applies it to corner features.
concepts.example: Take a 5x5 window around a corner: each of its 25 pixels gives one equation linking brightness changes to the motion (u, v). Two unknowns, 25 equations, so least squares picks the motion that fits them all best, say 2 pixels right.

concepts.name: Mask2Former
concepts.description: A universal segmentation Transformer that predicts a set of masks with class labels using masked attention in its decoder, handling semantic, instance and panoptic segmentation with one architecture.
concepts.example: Given a street photo, Mask2Former's 100 queries each output one mask plus a label: one query paints all the road, another one particular car, another the sky. The same model does semantic, instance or panoptic output depending on training data.

concepts.name: Mask R-CNN
concepts.description: Extends Faster R-CNN with a parallel branch that predicts a pixel mask for each detected object, plus RoIAlign for precise feature alignment, to perform instance segmentation.
concepts.example: For a photo of three dogs, Faster R-CNN draws three boxes labelled 'dog'; Mask R-CNN adds a small 28x28 mask per box that marks exactly which pixels are fur, so each dog gets its own outline.

concepts.name: Masked Autoencoder
concepts.description: A self-supervised vision method that masks a large fraction (about 75%) of image patches and trains a ViT encoder-decoder to reconstruct the missing pixels, learning strong features.
concepts.example: Cut a dog photo into 196 patches, hide 147 of them, and ask the model to repaint the missing ones from the 49 left. To fill in an ear correctly it must learn what dogs look like, without any labels.

concepts.name: Mathematical Morphology
concepts.description: A framework for analysing shapes in images using set operations with a small structuring element, from which erosion, dilation, opening and closing are built.
concepts.example: Treat a black-and-white scan as a set of white pixels and slide a 3x3 square over it. Keeping only spots where the square fits entirely inside shrinks shapes (erosion); marking every spot it touches grows them (dilation).

concepts.name: Maximum Likelihood Training of Generative Models
concepts.description: Fitting a generative model by maximising the probability it assigns to the training data, equivalent to minimising KL divergence from the data distribution; used by autoregressive models and flows.
concepts.example: If training text is 70% 'cat' and 30% 'dog', the model that maximises likelihood will learn to say 'cat' 70% of the time. Any other split makes the observed data less probable.

concepts.name: Mean Intersection over Union
concepts.description: A segmentation metric that computes intersection over union between predicted and ground-truth pixels for each class and averages it across classes.
concepts.example: A model labels road and car. Road IoU is 900 shared pixels / 1,000 union = 0.9; car IoU is 30 / 100 = 0.3. Mean IoU is (0.9 + 0.3) / 2 = 0.6, so the small car class counts as much as the big road.

concepts.name: Mean Opinion Score
concepts.description: A quality score obtained by asking human listeners or viewers to rate samples, typically on a 1 to 5 scale, and averaging the ratings; the standard evaluation for speech synthesis.
concepts.example: Play a synthetic voice clip to five listeners who rate it 4, 5, 4, 3, 4 on a 1 to 5 scale; its MOS is 20 / 5 = 4.0. Real human recordings usually score around 4.5.

concepts.name: Mean Shift Segmentation
concepts.description: Segments an image by running mean shift in a joint space of pixel position and colour, moving each point to a density mode and grouping pixels that converge to the same mode.
concepts.example: Each pixel becomes a point like (x, y, red, green, blue). Points drift uphill toward the densest nearby cluster; all the pixels of a blue sky slide to one peak and form one segment, the grass to another.

concepts.name: Mean Squared Error (Image Quality)
concepts.description: The average of squared pixel-wise differences between a reconstructed image and a reference image; simple to compute and the basis of PSNR, but poorly aligned with perceived quality.
concepts.example: Original pixels 100, 120, 140 versus compressed 98, 123, 140: errors 2, -3, 0, squared 4, 9, 0, average 13 / 3 = 4.3. A one-pixel shift of a sharp photo can give a much bigger MSE while looking identical.

concepts.name: Mel Scale
concepts.description: A perceptual pitch scale on which equal steps sound equally spaced to listeners; roughly linear below 1 kHz and logarithmic above, and used to design audio features.
concepts.example: Going from 100 Hz to 200 Hz sounds like a big jump, but 10,000 Hz to 10,100 Hz is barely noticeable. The mel scale stretches low frequencies and squeezes high ones so equal mel steps sound equal.

concepts.name: Mel Spectrogram
concepts.description: A spectrogram whose frequency axis is warped to the mel scale by summing STFT power with triangular mel filters, usually in log scale; a standard input for speech and audio models.
concepts.example: Cut a speech clip into 25 ms frames, compute each frame's spectrum, then sum it into 80 triangular bands, narrow at low pitch and wide at high pitch. The result is an 80-row image of the voice that models like Whisper read.

concepts.name: Mel-Frequency Cepstral Coefficients
concepts.description: Compact speech features made by taking a log mel spectrogram and applying a discrete cosine transform, keeping the first dozen or so coefficients that describe the spectral envelope.
concepts.example: Take 40 log-mel energies for one 25 ms frame of speech and apply a DCT: the first 13 numbers capture the smooth shape of the spectrum, which encodes vowel shape, while dropping pitch detail. Those 13 numbers are the MFCCs.

concepts.name: Midjourney
concepts.description: A commercial text-to-image generation service, originally used through Discord, known for its distinctive artistic style; it turns text prompts into images with a proprietary model.
concepts.example: Type '/imagine a lighthouse in a storm, oil painting' in Discord and about a minute later Midjourney returns four painterly images. You can upscale one or ask for variations of it.

concepts.name: Minimax Game (GAN Objective)
concepts.description: The GAN training objective min over G, max over D of E[log D(x)] + E[log(1 - D(G(z)))], a two-player zero-sum game whose equilibrium has the generator matching the data distribution.
concepts.example: A forger (G) paints fakes and a detective (D) judges them. D tries to maximise how often it labels correctly; G tries to minimise that. At equilibrium the fakes match real paintings and D can only guess 50/50.

concepts.name: Mixup and CutMix
concepts.description: Augmentations that blend training examples: mixup takes convex combinations of two images and their labels, while CutMix pastes a patch from one image into another and mixes labels by area.
concepts.example: Mixup blends 70% of a cat photo with 30% of a dog photo and sets the label to 0.7 cat, 0.3 dog. CutMix instead pastes a dog patch covering 25% of the cat image and labels it 0.75 cat, 0.25 dog.

concepts.name: MNIST Database
concepts.description: A dataset of 70,000 28x28 grayscale images of handwritten digits 0 to 9; the classic 'hello world' benchmark for image classification.
concepts.example: MNIST has 60,000 training and 10,000 test images of digits, each 28 by 28 pixels. A simple CNN gets over 99% accuracy, so it is used to check code works more than to prove a method is strong.

concepts.name: MoCo
concepts.description: A contrastive self-supervised method that keeps a large queue of negative keys encoded by a slowly updated momentum encoder, decoupling the number of negatives from the batch size.
concepts.example: MoCo keeps a queue of, say, 65,536 recent image encodings as 'not this image' examples. Each step the newest batch is added and the oldest dropped, while a slow-moving copy of the encoder keeps the queue's entries consistent.

concepts.name: Mode Collapse
concepts.description: A GAN failure in which the generator produces only a few kinds of output, covering a small part of the data distribution, because those outputs reliably fool the discriminator.
concepts.example: A GAN trained on all ten digits ends up drawing nothing but convincing 1s. The discriminator keeps accepting them, so the generator never learns to make the other nine digits.

concepts.name: Monocular Depth Estimation
concepts.description: Predicting a dense depth map from a single image, which is geometrically ill-posed, by learning cues like object size, perspective and texture from data (e.g. MiDaS, Depth Anything).
concepts.example: From a single phone photo of a street, a model outputs a depth map where the nearby car is bright and distant buildings are dark. It guesses this from cues like the car looking bigger and road lines converging.

concepts.name: Multi-View Stereo
concepts.description: Reconstructing dense 3D geometry from many calibrated images of a scene by finding consistent pixel correspondences across views and triangulating a depth for each pixel.
concepts.example: Walk around a statue taking 50 photos with known camera poses. For each pixel, MVS tests depths along its ray and picks the one where all the other photos agree on colour, building a dense 3D surface.

concepts.name: Multimodal Learning
concepts.description: Machine learning that combines several data types, such as images, text, audio and video, learning joint or aligned representations to solve tasks that span them.
concepts.example: A model watches cooking videos with their narration. Learning from images, sound and speech together, it can find the clip where someone says 'now add the eggs' and the eggs actually appear.

concepts.name: Multiple Object Tracking
concepts.description: The task of following many objects at once through a video, detecting them in each frame and keeping a consistent identity for each one over time, typically via tracking-by-detection and data association.
concepts.example: In a soccer video, a detector finds 22 players in every frame. A tracker links each frame's boxes to the previous ones so player #7 keeps the ID 7 even when crossing paths with #10.

concepts.name: Music Information Retrieval
concepts.description: The field that extracts information from music audio and scores, such as beat, key, chords, genre or instruments, to power tagging, recommendation, transcription and search.
concepts.example: Shazam hears 5 seconds of a song in a café and names it; Spotify tags a track as 120 BPM, A minor and 'indie rock'. Both are music information retrieval at work.

concepts.name: Neural Radiance Field
concepts.description: A neural network that represents a 3D scene as a continuous function from position and viewing direction to color and density, rendered with volume rendering and trained from posed photos to synthesize new views.
concepts.example: Take 100 photos around a toy truck. NeRF learns a function: ask it about point (x, y, z) seen from some direction and it returns a colour and opacity. Shooting rays through those points renders the truck from angles never photographed.

concepts.name: Neural Audio Codec
concepts.description: A learned audio compressor that encodes sound into a small set of discrete tokens using an encoder, residual vector quantization and a decoder, used for low-bitrate streaming and as tokens for audio language models.
concepts.example: A second of 24 kHz audio is 24,000 numbers. An encoder compresses it to 75 frames, and each frame is described by 8 codebook indices, about 6 kilobits per second, yet the decoder rebuilds speech that sounds nearly the same.

concepts.name: Neural Style Transfer
concepts.description: A technique that renders the content of one image in the artistic style of another by optimizing an image to match deep CNN feature activations for content and Gram-matrix statistics for style.
concepts.example: Start from your holiday photo and nudge its pixels until VGG sees the same objects in it (content) while its texture statistics match Van Gogh's Starry Night (style). The result is your beach painted in swirling brushstrokes.

concepts.name: Noise Schedule
concepts.description: The sequence of noise levels (betas) used by a diffusion model to decide how much Gaussian noise is added at each forward step; linear and cosine schedules trade off sample quality and training efficiency.
concepts.example: Over 1,000 steps, a linear schedule raises beta from 0.0001 to 0.02, so the image is mostly destroyed well before the end. A cosine schedule adds noise more gently early on, keeping useful signal for longer.

concepts.name: Non-Local Means
concepts.description: An image denoising algorithm that replaces each pixel with a weighted average of pixels across the image whose surrounding patches look similar, preserving texture better than local blurring.
concepts.example: To clean a noisy pixel on a brick wall, NLM finds other spots anywhere in the photo whose 7x7 neighbourhood also looks like brick mortar and averages them. The noise cancels while the brick pattern stays sharp.

concepts.name: Non-Maximum Suppression
concepts.description: A post-processing step in object detection that keeps the highest-scoring box and removes overlapping boxes whose intersection-over-union with it exceeds a threshold, leaving one box per object.
concepts.example: A detector outputs three boxes on one cat scoring 0.95, 0.90 and 0.60. The 0.90 box overlaps the best one with IoU 0.8, above the 0.5 threshold, so it is dropped; the 0.60 box overlaps only 0.2 and stays, perhaps a second cat.

concepts.name: Normalizing Flow
concepts.description: A generative model that transforms a simple base distribution into a complex one through a chain of invertible, differentiable maps, giving exact likelihoods via the change-of-variables formula.
concepts.example: Start with a round blob of Gaussian points and apply a chain of reversible stretches and twists until it looks like a spiral. Because every step can be undone, you can compute exactly how likely any spiral point is.

concepts.name: Novel View Synthesis
concepts.description: The problem of generating images of a scene from camera viewpoints that were never photographed, given a set of input images, solved with methods like NeRF and Gaussian splatting.
concepts.example: You photograph a room from 20 spots along one wall. Novel view synthesis renders what the room would look like from the ceiling corner, a spot where no camera ever stood.

concepts.name: Object Detection
concepts.description: The computer vision task of finding every object of interest in an image and outputting a class label and bounding box for each, used in self-driving, surveillance and robotics.
concepts.example: Give a detector a street photo and it returns a list like: car at (40, 80, 200, 160) with score 0.97, pedestrian at (250, 60, 290, 180) with 0.91, traffic light at (300, 10, 315, 45) with 0.85.

concepts.name: Object Keypoint Similarity
concepts.description: A pose estimation metric that scores how close predicted body keypoints are to ground truth, using Gaussian falloff scaled by object size and per-keypoint tolerance, analogous to IoU for boxes.
concepts.example: If a predicted wrist lands 5 pixels from the true wrist on a large adult, OKS gives it nearly full credit. The same 5-pixel error on a tiny distant child scores much lower, and hips are given more tolerance than eyes.

concepts.name: Object Tracking
concepts.description: The task of locating a target object in each frame of a video given its position in an earlier frame, handling motion, occlusion and appearance changes.
concepts.example: You draw a box around a runner in frame 1. In each next frame the tracker predicts where she probably moved, finds the best match nearby, and keeps the box on her even when a tree briefly hides her.

concepts.name: One-Stage Object Detector
concepts.description: An object detector that predicts class scores and box coordinates directly from feature maps in a single pass, without a separate region proposal step, as in YOLO, SSD and RetinaNet; faster but historically less accurate.
concepts.example: A one-stage detector like YOLO looks at the whole image once and, for every grid cell and anchor shape, directly says 'car, 0.9, shift box by these amounts'. There's no separate step proposing regions first, so it can run at 60 frames per second.

concepts.name: Open-Vocabulary Object Detection
concepts.description: Object detection that can find categories described by arbitrary text rather than a fixed label set, by aligning region features with text embeddings from vision-language models like CLIP.
concepts.example: Trained only on common categories, an open-vocabulary detector can still find a 'red fire hydrant' or 'skateboard ramp' when you type it, because it compares each region's features with the text embedding of your phrase.

concepts.name: OpenCV
concepts.description: An open-source library of thousands of computer vision and image processing functions, from filtering and feature detection to camera calibration, with C++ and Python interfaces.
concepts.example: In Python, four lines with OpenCV load a photo, convert it to grayscale, run Canny edge detection and save the result: cv2.imread, cv2.cvtColor, cv2.Canny, cv2.imwrite.

concepts.name: Opening and Closing (Morphology)
concepts.description: Morphological operations on images: opening is erosion followed by dilation and removes small bright specks, closing is dilation followed by erosion and fills small holes and gaps.
concepts.example: A scanned page has small black speckles and letters with tiny gaps. Opening (erode then dilate) wipes out the speckles smaller than the 3x3 element; closing (dilate then erode) fills the gaps so broken letters join again.

concepts.name: OpenPose
concepts.description: A real-time multi-person 2D pose estimator that predicts keypoint heatmaps and part affinity fields with a CNN, then assembles detected joints into individual skeletons bottom-up.
concepts.example: In a dance-floor photo with five people, OpenPose first finds every elbow, wrist and shoulder, then uses limb direction maps to decide which wrist belongs with which elbow, producing five separate stick figures.

concepts.name: Optical Character Recognition
concepts.description: The task of converting images of printed or handwritten text into machine-readable characters, combining text detection, recognition models and language post-processing.
concepts.example: Photograph a receipt and OCR finds each line of text, reads 'TOTAL 12.50' character by character, and lets a language check fix 'T0TAL' into 'TOTAL' before you copy it into a spreadsheet.

concepts.name: Optical Flow
concepts.description: The apparent motion of each pixel between two consecutive video frames, represented as a 2D displacement field and used for motion analysis, video stabilization and tracking.
concepts.example: A ball moves from pixel (10, 20) in frame 1 to (13, 21) in frame 2, so its flow vector is (3, 1). Optical flow assigns such an arrow to every pixel, while the still background gets (0, 0).

concepts.name: ORB (Oriented FAST and Rotated BRIEF)
concepts.description: A fast feature detector and binary descriptor that combines the FAST corner detector with an orientation estimate and a rotation-aware BRIEF descriptor, a free and efficient alternative to SIFT.
concepts.example: ORB finds corners with the quick FAST test, gives each an orientation, and describes it with 256 yes/no brightness comparisons. Two descriptors are compared by counting differing bits, fast enough for phones to track features live.

concepts.name: ORB-SLAM
concepts.description: A feature-based visual SLAM system that tracks ORB features to estimate camera pose, builds a sparse map with keyframes, and uses bundle adjustment and loop closure to stay consistent.
concepts.example: A drone flying through a house matches ORB features between frames to estimate its own motion, stores keyframes as a map, and when it returns to the kitchen recognises the place, closing the loop to correct accumulated drift.

concepts.name: Otsu's Method
concepts.description: An automatic thresholding algorithm that picks the gray level separating an image histogram into two classes so that the variance within each class is minimized.
concepts.example: A scanned document's histogram has one hump at dark ink (around 30) and one at white paper (around 220). Otsu tries every threshold and picks the one, around 125, that makes each group's spread as small as possible.

concepts.name: Panoptic Quality
concepts.description: A metric for panoptic segmentation that matches predicted and true segments by IoU above 0.5 and combines segmentation quality (mean IoU of matches) with recognition quality (an F1-like score).
concepts.example: Suppose 3 true segments are matched with IoUs 0.9, 0.8, 0.7, plus 1 false positive and 1 missed segment. SQ = 0.8, RQ = 3 / (3 + 0.5 + 0.5) = 0.75, so PQ = 0.8 × 0.75 = 0.6.

concepts.name: Panoptic Segmentation
concepts.description: A segmentation task that unifies semantic and instance segmentation: every pixel gets a class label, and pixels of countable objects also get an instance ID.
concepts.example: In a street photo, every pixel gets a class: road, sky, building, car, person. On top of that, the three cars are labelled car-1, car-2 and car-3, while road and sky stay single uncounted regions.

concepts.name: Part Affinity Fields
concepts.description: 2D vector fields predicted over an image that encode the location and direction of limbs between body joints, used to group detected keypoints into individual people.
concepts.example: Along each forearm, the field stores small arrows pointing from elbow to wrist. To check if an elbow and a wrist belong together, sample points between them and see whether the arrows line up with that direction.

concepts.name: Parti and Muse
concepts.description: Google text-to-image models that generate images as discrete visual tokens: Parti uses an autoregressive Transformer, while Muse predicts masked tokens in parallel for faster generation.
concepts.example: Both turn an image into a 32x32 grid of codebook tokens. Parti writes them one by one like words in a sentence; Muse starts with all tokens hidden and fills in the most confident ones in parallel over a few rounds.

concepts.name: Patch Embedding
concepts.description: The first step of a Vision Transformer, which splits an image into fixed-size patches, flattens each patch and linearly projects it into a token vector the Transformer can process.
concepts.example: A 224x224 colour image is cut into 196 patches of 16x16. Each patch's 768 numbers (16×16×3) are flattened and multiplied by a learned matrix to give one token vector, turning the image into a 196-word 'sentence'.

concepts.name: Perceptual Loss
concepts.description: A loss that compares images by the distance between their feature activations in a pretrained network such as VGG, rather than raw pixels, so results look more natural to humans.
concepts.example: Two images of a cat, one shifted by a pixel, differ hugely pixel by pixel. Run both through VGG and their feature maps are almost the same, so perceptual loss calls them close, guiding super-resolution toward natural-looking results.

concepts.name: Person Re-identification
concepts.description: The task of recognizing the same person across different cameras or times by learning appearance embeddings that are close for the same identity and far for different ones.
concepts.example: A person in a red jacket leaves camera 3 at a mall entrance. Re-ID turns each person crop into a vector and finds that the closest vector among camera 7's crops is the same person entering the food court.

concepts.name: Perspective-n-Point
concepts.description: The problem of estimating a calibrated camera's position and orientation from n known 3D points and their 2D projections in an image, typically solved with minimal solvers inside RANSAC.
concepts.example: A phone sees four corners of a known A4 sheet in its image. Knowing their real 3D layout and the camera's lens, PnP works out where the phone is and how it's tilted, which is how AR places objects on the page.

concepts.name: Phoneme
concepts.description: The smallest unit of sound in a language that distinguishes one word from another, like /p/ versus /b/ in pat and bat; speech recognition and synthesis systems often model speech as phoneme sequences.
concepts.example: 'Cat' and 'bat' differ only in their first phoneme, /k/ versus /b/, which changes the meaning. 'Ship' is three phonemes, /ʃ/ /ɪ/ /p/, even though it has four letters.

concepts.name: Pinhole Camera Model
concepts.description: A simple camera model in which light from 3D points passes through a single point onto an image plane, giving the perspective projection used throughout computer vision geometry.
concepts.example: A point 2 m in front of a pinhole camera and 1 m to the side, with focal length 50 mm, lands 25 mm from the image centre. Move it to 4 m away and it lands at 12.5 mm, so far objects look smaller.

concepts.name: Pitch Detection Algorithm
concepts.description: The task of estimating the fundamental frequency (F0) of a voice or musical sound over time, using methods like autocorrelation, cepstrum or neural networks such as CREPE.
concepts.example: A singer holds an A, so the waveform repeats every 2.27 ms. A pitch tracker finds that repetition period and reports 440 Hz, and as she slides upward it follows the rising frequency frame by frame.

concepts.name: Pix2pix
concepts.description: A conditional GAN for paired image-to-image translation, such as sketches to photos, using a U-Net generator, a PatchGAN discriminator and an extra L1 loss to the target image.
concepts.example: Train on pairs of building facade label maps and real photos. Afterwards, sketch blue for windows and red for doors and Pix2pix paints a realistic facade, kept on target by a discriminator plus an L1 loss.

concepts.name: Pixel
concepts.description: The smallest addressable element of a digital image, storing a brightness value or a color (for example red, green and blue intensities) at one grid position.
concepts.example: A 4x3 photo has 12 pixels. A grayscale pixel holds one number like 200 (light gray), while a colour pixel holds three, such as (255, 0, 0) for pure red. Zoom far into any digital photo and you see these tiny squares.

concepts.name: Pixel Accuracy
concepts.description: A segmentation metric equal to the fraction of pixels whose predicted class matches the ground truth; simple but misleading when some classes cover much more area than others.
concepts.example: A 100-pixel image is 90 sky and 10 bird. A model that labels everything sky gets 90% pixel accuracy while completely missing the bird, which is why mean IoU is usually reported too.

concepts.name: PixelCNN
concepts.description: An autoregressive image model that generates pixels one at a time, predicting each from previously generated pixels with masked convolutions; PixelCNN++ improves the output distribution and speed.
concepts.example: To draw a 28x28 digit, PixelCNN picks pixel 1, then pixel 2 given pixel 1, and so on. Masked filters hide pixels not yet drawn, so training can predict all 784 pixels in parallel while still only peeking at earlier ones.

concepts.name: PixelRNN
concepts.description: An autoregressive image generator that models each pixel conditioned on all previous pixels in raster order using LSTM layers over rows and diagonals, giving exact likelihoods.
concepts.example: Generate a face top-left to bottom-right: for each new pixel, an LSTM that has read all the pixels above and to the left outputs probabilities for its 256 possible values, and one is sampled.

concepts.name: Point Cloud
concepts.description: A set of 3D points, often with color or intensity, that samples the surfaces of objects or scenes, typically captured by LiDAR, depth cameras or stereo reconstruction.
concepts.example: A LiDAR on a car spins and returns about 100,000 points per sweep, each like (x = 12.3 m, y = -1.8 m, z = 0.4 m, intensity 0.7). Together they outline the road, cars and walls as a 3D cloud of dots.

concepts.name: PointNet
concepts.description: A neural network that processes raw point clouds directly by applying a shared MLP to each point and aggregating with a symmetric max-pooling, making it invariant to point order; PointNet++ adds local hierarchy.
concepts.example: Shuffle the 1,024 points of a scanned chair and PointNet gives the same answer, 'chair', because it processes each point alone with the same small network and then takes the maximum of each feature across all points.

concepts.name: Polygon Mesh
concepts.description: A representation of a 3D surface as a collection of vertices, edges and faces (usually triangles), the standard format for 3D graphics, games and modeling.
concepts.example: A cube can be stored as 8 vertices and 12 triangles, each triangle listing three vertex indices. Game characters work the same way with tens of thousands of triangles.

concepts.name: Pose Estimation
concepts.description: The task of locating a person's body joints, such as elbows, knees and wrists, in images or video to recover their posture in 2D or 3D.
concepts.example: From a photo of a tennis serve, a pose model outputs 17 points such as left shoulder (210, 95) and right wrist (260, 30), which connect into a stick figure showing the raised racket arm.

concepts.name: Posterior Collapse
concepts.description: A failure mode of VAEs, especially with powerful decoders, where the approximate posterior matches the prior so the latent variables carry no information and the decoder ignores them.
concepts.example: A VAE with a strong autoregressive text decoder learns to write fluent sentences on its own. The encoder's latent code becomes plain noise matching the prior, so changing it no longer changes the sentence.

concepts.name: Precision and Recall for Generative Models
concepts.description: Metrics for generative models that separate sample quality (precision: fraction of generated samples near real data) from diversity (recall: fraction of real data covered by generated samples), estimated in feature space.
concepts.example: A face generator that only makes perfect smiling young faces has high precision, since every sample looks real, but low recall, since it never covers old or frowning faces. Precision and recall measure these two failures separately.

concepts.name: Backbone (Neural Network)
concepts.description: The main feature-extracting part of a neural network, usually a CNN or Transformer pretrained on large data like ImageNet, on top of which task-specific heads are attached for detection, segmentation and more.
concepts.example: Take a ResNet-50 already trained on ImageNet, chop off its 1,000-class output layer and attach a box-predicting head. The backbone supplies features like edges and wheels, so the detector learns faster from fewer images.

concepts.name: Prewitt Operator
concepts.description: A simple edge detection filter that approximates image gradients in x and y with 3x3 convolution kernels of equal weights, highlighting regions of rapid intensity change.
concepts.example: The horizontal Prewitt kernel is [-1 0 1] repeated in three rows. Over a patch that goes from 10 on the left to 50 on the right it gives 3 × 40 = 120, a strong vertical edge; over flat areas it gives 0.

concepts.name: Diffusion Distillation
concepts.description: Techniques that speed up diffusion sampling by training a student model to match a teacher in fewer steps; progressive distillation repeatedly halves the number of steps until only a few remain.
concepts.example: A teacher sampler needs 1,024 steps. A student is trained so 1 of its steps matches 2 teacher steps, giving 512; then it becomes the teacher and the process repeats until 4 steps produce similar images.

concepts.name: Progressive GAN
concepts.description: A GAN trained by starting at very low resolution and gradually adding layers to both generator and discriminator, enabling stable generation of high-resolution images such as 1024x1024 faces.
concepts.example: Training starts with both networks working on 4x4 images. Once stable, 8x8 layers are faded in, then 16x16, and so on up to 1024x1024, so the GAN learns face shape first and pores and hair last.

concepts.name: Pronunciation Lexicon
concepts.description: A dictionary mapping words to their phoneme sequences, used by speech recognition and text-to-speech systems to connect written words with how they sound.
concepts.example: A lexicon entry reads 'tomato: T AH M EY T OW' (and also 'T AH M AA T OW'). A speech synthesiser looks words up here, and a recogniser uses it to link phoneme sequences back to words.

concepts.name: Peak Signal-to-Noise Ratio
concepts.description: An image quality metric that compares a reconstruction to the original as the ratio of the maximum possible pixel value to the mean squared error, expressed in decibels; higher means closer.
concepts.example: For 8-bit images the max value is 255. If MSE is 65, PSNR = 10 log10(255² / 65) ≈ 30 dB, typical of decent JPEG; an MSE of 6.5 would give 40 dB, nearly indistinguishable from the original.

concepts.name: PSPNet
concepts.description: A semantic segmentation network that adds a pyramid pooling module, pooling backbone features at several scales and concatenating them, to capture global scene context.
concepts.example: To tell whether a boat-shaped object is a boat or a car, PSPNet pools features over the whole image, quarters and smaller grids, and sees water around it. Combining these contexts labels the pixels as boat.

concepts.name: Pulse-Code Modulation
concepts.description: The standard way to store digital audio: sample the analog waveform at regular intervals and quantize each sample to a fixed number of bits, as in WAV files and CDs.
concepts.example: A CD samples sound 44,100 times per second and stores each sample as a 16-bit integer from -32,768 to 32,767. One second of stereo is therefore 44,100 × 2 × 16 = about 1.4 million bits.

concepts.name: torchvision
concepts.description: The PyTorch library for computer vision, providing popular datasets, pretrained models such as ResNet and Faster R-CNN, and image transforms for data augmentation.
concepts.example: With torchvision you can load CIFAR-10, apply random crops and flips, and fetch an ImageNet-pretrained ResNet-18 in a few lines, then fine-tune it on your own photo classes.
