concepts.name: Audio Bit Depth
concepts.description: The number of bits used to store each audio sample, such as 16-bit or 24-bit, which sets how many amplitude levels are possible and therefore the dynamic range and noise floor.
concepts.example: With 3 bits you get only 8 loudness levels, so quiet sounds turn into steps and hiss. 16-bit audio has 65,536 levels, about 96 dB of dynamic range; each extra bit adds roughly 6 dB.

concepts.name: R-CNN
concepts.description: An early deep object detector that extracts about 2,000 region proposals with selective search, runs a CNN on each warped region to get features, and classifies them with SVMs.
concepts.example: For one photo, R-CNN proposes about 2,000 candidate boxes, stretches each to 227x227, runs a full CNN on every one, and asks an SVM per class 'is this a dog?'. Accurate in 2014, but taking many seconds per image.

concepts.name: RAFT (Optical Flow)
concepts.description: An optical flow network that builds a 4D correlation volume between all pixel pairs of two frames and iteratively refines a flow field with a recurrent GRU-based update operator.
concepts.example: RAFT compares every pixel of frame 1 with every pixel of frame 2, stores the similarity scores, then starts with zero motion and lets a GRU nudge the flow estimate about a dozen times, looking up scores around the current guess.

concepts.name: RealNVP
concepts.description: A normalizing flow built from affine coupling layers, where half of the variables are scaled and shifted by functions of the other half, giving cheap inverses and triangular Jacobians.
concepts.example: Split a vector into halves a and b. Keep a, and set b' = b × exp(s(a)) + t(a) with small networks s and t. Undoing it is easy, b = (b' − t(a)) × exp(−s(a)), and the log-determinant is just the sum of s(a).

concepts.name: Region Growing
concepts.description: A segmentation algorithm that starts from seed pixels and repeatedly adds neighboring pixels whose intensity or color is similar enough, growing regions until no more pixels qualify.
concepts.example: Click a seed pixel inside a lung on a CT scan with value 100. The region adds neighbours within ±10 of it, then their neighbours, and stops at the rib wall where values jump to 400, outlining the lung.

concepts.name: Region Proposal
concepts.description: A candidate image region likely to contain an object, generated before classification in two-stage detectors so the expensive classifier only examines a few thousand boxes.
concepts.example: Instead of checking millions of possible boxes in a street photo, a proposal method suggests about 2,000 boxes likely to hold something, such as a car-shaped blob or a person-sized patch, and only those get classified.

concepts.name: Region Proposal Network
concepts.description: A small fully convolutional network used in Faster R-CNN that slides over backbone feature maps and predicts objectness scores and box refinements for a set of anchors, producing proposals almost for free.
concepts.example: At each spot on the feature map, the RPN considers 9 anchors (3 sizes × 3 shapes) and outputs, for each, 'object or not' plus four box adjustments. The top 300 scored boxes go on to the detector head.

concepts.name: RetinaNet
concepts.description: A one-stage object detector that uses a feature pyramid network and the focal loss, which down-weights easy background examples, to match the accuracy of two-stage detectors.
concepts.example: In a photo with 100,000 candidate boxes but only 5 objects, ordinary loss is swamped by easy background. Focal loss shrinks the loss on boxes already classified confidently, so RetinaNet focuses on the hard few.

concepts.name: Reverse Diffusion Process
concepts.description: The learned generative half of a diffusion model, which starts from pure noise and repeatedly removes a small amount of predicted noise until a clean sample emerges.
concepts.example: Start from a 64x64 image of pure static. At each of, say, 50 steps, a network guesses the noise present and subtracts a bit of it; shapes appear, then a face, then fine details, until a clean portrait remains.

concepts.name: RGB Color Model
concepts.description: An additive color model that represents each color as amounts of red, green and blue light, the standard way screens and digital images store color.
concepts.example: Each pixel mixes red, green and blue light from 0 to 255: (255, 0, 0) is red, (255, 255, 0) is yellow, (255, 255, 255) is white and (0, 0, 0) is black, about 16.7 million colours in total.

concepts.name: RNN-Transducer
concepts.description: A streaming speech recognition architecture combining an audio encoder, a label prediction network and a joint network, trained to sum over all alignments between audio frames and output tokens.
concepts.example: On a phone, an RNN-T listens to 'call mom' and outputs 'c', 'a', 'l' as audio frames arrive, emitting a blank when a frame adds nothing new, so words appear while you are still speaking.

concepts.name: Roberts Cross
concepts.description: One of the earliest edge detectors, which approximates the image gradient with two 2x2 kernels along the diagonals; fast but sensitive to noise.
concepts.example: Roberts uses two tiny kernels, [[1, 0], [0, -1]] and [[0, 1], [-1, 0]]. On a 2x2 patch [[10, 10], [10, 90]] the first gives 10 − 90 = −80, flagging a strong diagonal edge.

concepts.name: RoI Pooling
concepts.description: An operation that converts each region proposal of arbitrary size into a fixed-size feature map by pooling over a grid of bins; RoIAlign avoids rounding by using bilinear interpolation.
concepts.example: A 14x10 region on the feature map is divided into a 7x7 grid of bins of about 2x1.4 cells, and the max in each bin is kept. Regions of any size thus become the same 7x7 block for the classifier.

concepts.name: Sampling Rate
concepts.description: The number of audio samples recorded per second, such as 16 kHz for speech or 44.1 kHz for music; it must exceed twice the highest frequency to avoid aliasing.
concepts.example: Phone calls use 8 kHz, enough for speech up to about 4 kHz. Music at 44.1 kHz captures up to 22 kHz, the top of human hearing; record a 15 kHz tone at 16 kHz and it folds into a false lower tone.

concepts.name: Scale Space
concepts.description: A representation of an image as a family of progressively blurred versions, made by convolving with Gaussians of increasing width, so structures can be analyzed at their natural scale.
concepts.example: Blur a street photo with Gaussians of width 1, 2, 4 and 8 pixels. Window panes vanish early, while the building stays visible longer, so each structure can be found at the scale where it stands out most.

concepts.name: Scene Text Recognition
concepts.description: Detecting and reading text that appears in natural photos, such as signs and labels, despite varied fonts, perspective, lighting and background clutter.
concepts.example: Point a camera at a tilted shop sign reading 'BAKERY' in curly letters. The system first finds the text box, then a recogniser reads the letters, so a translation app can overlay 'PANADERÍA'.

concepts.name: Score-Based Generative Model
concepts.description: A generative model that learns the score (gradient of log density) of noise-perturbed data at many noise levels and samples by Langevin dynamics or by solving a reverse-time SDE.
concepts.example: Picture many hills where the data is likely. The model learns, at every noise level, which way is uphill from any point. Sampling drops points at random, follows those arrows with a bit of jitter, and they settle on realistic images.

concepts.name: Score Function (Generative Modeling)
concepts.description: In generative modeling, the gradient of the log probability density with respect to the data point, a vector field pointing toward regions of higher probability.
concepts.example: For a standard normal bell curve, the score at x is just −x. At x = 2 it is −2, an arrow pointing back toward the peak at 0, and the farther out you are, the stronger the pull.

concepts.name: Score Matching
concepts.description: A method to learn the score of a data distribution without knowing its normalizing constant; denoising score matching trains a network to predict the noise added to data.
concepts.example: Add Gaussian noise to a clean image and train a network to predict that noise from the noisy result. That noise prediction, rescaled, is the score, and you never need the true density's normalising constant.

concepts.name: Segment Anything Model
concepts.description: Meta's promptable segmentation foundation model that outputs object masks from points, boxes or text prompts on any image, trained on over a billion masks; SAM 2 extends it to video.
concepts.example: Click once on a dog in any photo and SAM returns a precise mask of that dog; click on its collar and you get just the collar. It works on objects it was never specifically trained on, from cells to satellite roofs.

concepts.name: SegNet
concepts.description: An encoder-decoder network for semantic segmentation whose decoder upsamples using the max-pooling indices stored by the encoder, saving memory while recovering spatial detail.
concepts.example: When the encoder max-pools, SegNet remembers which of each 2x2 cells held the max, for example the top-right one. The decoder later places values back into exactly those positions, restoring sharp boundaries cheaply.

concepts.name: Selective Search
concepts.description: A region proposal algorithm that over-segments an image into superpixels and hierarchically merges similar neighboring regions, yielding candidate object boxes at all scales.
concepts.example: Start with hundreds of tiny colour-uniform patches in a photo of a cat on a sofa. Repeatedly merge the two most similar neighbours; boxes around the merged regions along the way, like 'cat head', 'cat' and 'sofa', become proposals.

concepts.name: Self-Supervised Visual Representation Learning
concepts.description: Learning useful image features without human labels by solving pretext tasks such as matching augmented views or reconstructing masked patches, then transferring them to downstream tasks.
concepts.example: Train a CNN on a million unlabelled photos to tell whether two random crops come from the same picture. Afterwards, fine-tuning it with just 1% of ImageNet labels already gives strong classification accuracy.

concepts.name: Semantic Segmentation
concepts.description: The task of assigning a class label to every pixel in an image, such as road, car or sky, without separating individual objects of the same class.
concepts.example: In a dashcam frame, every pixel gets a label: road pixels are purple, sidewalk pink, cars blue, sky light blue. Two adjacent cars both become one blue blob because the task does not separate instances.

concepts.name: Shi-Tomasi Corner Detector
concepts.description: A corner detector that scores each pixel by the smaller eigenvalue of the local gradient structure tensor, improving on Harris for selecting good features to track.
concepts.example: At a window's corner, gradients point both up and sideways, so both eigenvalues are large, say 50 and 40; along an edge they are 50 and 2. Shi-Tomasi keeps a point only if the smaller one passes a threshold, so the corner wins.

concepts.name: Show, Attend and Tell
concepts.description: An image captioning model that pairs a CNN encoder with an LSTM decoder that attends to different image regions as it generates each word, introducing visual attention to captioning.
concepts.example: Captioning a photo of a bird on a branch, the model looks mostly at the bird region while writing 'bird' and shifts its attention to the branch area while writing 'branch'. The attention maps show where it looked.

concepts.name: Scale-Invariant Feature Transform
concepts.description: A feature detection and description algorithm that finds keypoints as extrema in a difference-of-Gaussians scale space and describes them with histograms of gradient orientations, invariant to scale and rotation.
concepts.example: Photograph a poster from far away and rotated, then up close. SIFT finds the same blob-like keypoints in both and describes each with 128 numbers of gradient directions, so the two views' points can be matched.

concepts.name: Signed Distance Function
concepts.description: A function giving, for any point in space, its distance to the nearest surface, with a negative sign inside the shape and positive outside; the zero level set is the surface.
concepts.example: For a ball of radius 1 at the origin, SDF(p) = |p| − 1. A point at distance 3 gets 2 (outside), a point at 0.5 gets −0.5 (inside), and every point on the ball's surface gets exactly 0.

concepts.name: SimCLR
concepts.description: A contrastive self-supervised method that creates two random augmentations of each image and trains an encoder plus projection head so the two views match each other and differ from other images in the batch.
concepts.example: Take a photo of a dog, make one crop with colour jitter and another flipped and blurred. SimCLR trains the network to recognise these two as a pair among the other 2 × 4,095 crops in a 4,096-image batch.

concepts.name: Simultaneous Localization and Mapping
concepts.description: The problem of a robot or camera building a map of an unknown environment while simultaneously estimating its own position in that map, using sensors like cameras or LiDAR.
concepts.example: A robot vacuum enters a new flat. As it drives, it builds a floor plan from its sensors and at the same time keeps working out where it is on that plan, recognising the doorway again to fix accumulated errors.

concepts.name: Sliding Window Detection
concepts.description: A classic detection approach that slides a fixed-size window across an image at many positions and scales and runs a classifier on each window to decide if it contains an object.
concepts.example: Slide a 64x128 window across a street photo 8 pixels at a time, then shrink the photo and repeat. A pedestrian classifier checks thousands of windows, and those it marks as 'person' become detections.

concepts.name: Sobel Operator
concepts.description: An edge detection filter that estimates horizontal and vertical image gradients with 3x3 kernels that combine differentiation with smoothing, giving edge strength and direction.
concepts.example: The horizontal Sobel kernel is [-1 0 1], [-2 0 2], [-1 0 1]. On a patch dark on the left (10) and bright on the right (50) it gives 4 × 40 = 160, flagging a vertical edge, with the centre row weighted double to resist noise.

concepts.name: Sora (Text-to-Video Model)
concepts.description: OpenAI's text-to-video model, a diffusion Transformer that generates video by denoising spacetime patches in a compressed latent space, producing long, coherent clips from text prompts.
concepts.example: Prompt 'a corgi surfing at sunset' and Sora starts from noise in a compressed video space, chopping it into spacetime patches. A Transformer denoises them all together, so the corgi stays the same dog across a 20-second clip.

concepts.name: SORT (Simple Online and Realtime Tracking)
concepts.description: A simple multi-object tracker that predicts each track with a Kalman filter and matches new detections by IoU with the Hungarian algorithm; DeepSORT adds appearance embeddings for re-identification.
concepts.example: In each frame, SORT's Kalman filter predicts where each tracked pedestrian's box should be. New detections are matched to predictions by IoU via the Hungarian algorithm; unmatched detections start new tracks.

concepts.name: Sound Wave
concepts.description: A mechanical wave of pressure variations traveling through air or another medium, characterized by frequency (pitch) and amplitude (loudness); recorded as an audio signal for processing.
concepts.example: Pluck a guitar string and it pushes air back and forth 110 times a second. Those pressure ripples reach your ear as a low A; plucking harder makes bigger ripples, which sound louder but have the same pitch.

concepts.name: Audio Source Separation
concepts.description: The problem of splitting a mixed audio recording into its individual sources, such as separating voices in a crowd or vocals from instruments in a song.
concepts.example: Feed a pop song into a separator and get four tracks back: vocals, drums, bass and the rest. Karaoke apps use this to remove the singer while keeping the band.

concepts.name: Speaker Diarization
concepts.description: The task of segmenting an audio recording by speaker, answering who spoke when, typically by embedding short segments and clustering them.
concepts.example: A 30-minute meeting recording becomes: 0:00 to 0:45 Speaker A, 0:45 to 2:10 Speaker B, 2:10 to 2:30 Speaker A. The system does this without knowing who anyone is, only that voices differ.

concepts.name: Speaker Recognition
concepts.description: Identifying or verifying who is speaking from their voice, by comparing a speaker embedding extracted from the audio against enrolled voice profiles.
concepts.example: Your bank records you saying a phrase and stores a voice embedding. When you call later, a new embedding is computed and if its cosine similarity with yours exceeds, say, 0.7, you are verified.

concepts.name: SpecAugment
concepts.description: A data augmentation method for speech recognition that masks random blocks of frequency channels and time steps in the spectrogram, and optionally warps time, to make models more robust.
concepts.example: Given a mel spectrogram of 'turn on the lights', SpecAugment blanks out a horizontal band of 10 frequency channels and a vertical strip of 40 time frames. The model must still transcribe it, so it learns to cope with missing information.

concepts.name: Speech Enhancement
concepts.description: The task of improving speech quality and intelligibility by removing background noise, reverberation and other distortions from a recording.
concepts.example: A call recorded next to a busy road is cleaned so the traffic hiss drops away and the voice sounds clear. Video-call noise suppression does this live, many times a second.

concepts.name: Speech Processing
concepts.description: The field covering analysis and generation of human speech by computers, including speech recognition, speech synthesis, speaker recognition and speech enhancement.
concepts.example: Asking a smart speaker 'what's the weather?' uses several speech processing pieces: detecting the wake word, recognising your words, perhaps checking your voice, and synthesising the spoken answer.

concepts.name: SRGAN
concepts.description: A GAN for single-image super-resolution that combines an adversarial loss with a perceptual loss on VGG features to produce sharp, realistic upscaled images; ESRGAN refines the architecture and losses.
concepts.example: Upscale a 64x64 face to 256x256. Plain MSE training gives a smooth, blurry face; SRGAN's discriminator punishes blurriness and its VGG loss keeps the features right, so skin pores and hair strands appear.

concepts.name: Single Shot MultiBox Detector
concepts.description: A one-stage object detector that predicts boxes and class scores from default anchor boxes on multiple feature maps of different resolutions, detecting objects of various sizes in a single pass.
concepts.example: SSD predicts from six feature maps: the 38x38 one catches small objects like distant signs, the 3x3 one large ones like a nearby bus. It outputs about 8,700 boxes per image, which NMS trims to a handful.

concepts.name: Structural Similarity Index Measure
concepts.description: An image quality metric that compares two images by local luminance, contrast and structure, matching human perception better than pixel-wise error measures like PSNR.
concepts.example: Take a photo and two edits with the same pixel error: one brightened slightly, one blurred. SSIM rates the brightened one around 0.98 and the blurred one much lower, because blur destroys local structure.

concepts.name: Stable Diffusion
concepts.description: An open text-to-image latent diffusion model that denoises in a VAE's compressed latent space with a U-Net conditioned on CLIP text embeddings via cross-attention; SDXL is a larger successor.
concepts.example: Type 'an astronaut riding a horse' and CLIP turns it into text vectors. Starting from noise in a 64x64 latent, a U-Net denoises for about 30 steps while attending to those vectors, then a VAE decoder expands it into a 512x512 image.

concepts.name: Computer Stereo Vision
concepts.description: Recovering depth from two cameras with known relative position by matching corresponding points in the two images and converting their horizontal disparity into distance.
concepts.example: Two cameras 10 cm apart with focal length 700 pixels see a mug at x = 420 in the left image and x = 385 in the right. A disparity of 35 pixels gives depth = 700 × 0.1 / 35 = 2 m.

concepts.name: Diffusion SDE and Probability Flow ODE
concepts.description: A continuous-time view of diffusion models in which data is noised by an SDE and generated by a reverse-time SDE driven by the learned score, or by an equivalent deterministic probability flow ODE.
concepts.example: Picture noise being stirred into an image continuously over time. Run the clock backwards using the learned score to remove noise and you get a sample; drop the randomness and follow a smooth ODE path instead to reach a sample in fewer steps.

concepts.name: Stride and Padding
concepts.description: Two convolution settings: stride is how many pixels the filter moves between applications, and padding adds border pixels so the filter can cover edges; together they set the output size.
concepts.example: A 3x3 filter on a 7x7 image with stride 1 and no padding gives 5x5. Add 1 pixel of padding and you get 7x7; use stride 2 instead and you get 3x3. Output = (input + 2×pad − kernel) / stride + 1.

concepts.name: Structure from Motion
concepts.description: Reconstructing the 3D structure of a scene and the camera poses from a collection of overlapping 2D images by matching features, triangulating points and refining with bundle adjustment.
concepts.example: Upload 500 tourist photos of a cathedral. SfM matches features like window corners across photos, works out where each camera stood, and builds a sparse 3D cloud of the building.

concepts.name: StyleGAN
concepts.description: A GAN generator that maps noise to an intermediate style space and injects styles at each resolution via adaptive normalization, enabling high-quality, controllable faces; StyleGAN2 and 3 fix artifacts and aliasing.
concepts.example: StyleGAN feeds a style vector into each resolution layer. Take coarse styles from face A and fine styles from face B and you get A's pose and face shape with B's skin tone and hair colour.

concepts.name: Super-Resolution Imaging
concepts.description: The problem of reconstructing a high-resolution image from one or more low-resolution inputs, adding plausible fine detail beyond simple interpolation.
concepts.example: Enlarge a 100x100 licence plate photo 4 times. Plain resizing just gives a blurry 400x400 image; a super-resolution network fills in sharp letter edges it has learned from thousands of examples.

concepts.name: Superpixel
concepts.description: A small group of adjacent pixels with similar color or texture, used to over-segment an image into meaningful atomic regions; SLIC creates them with localized k-means clustering.
concepts.example: SLIC splits a 640x480 photo into about 500 compact blobs, each a patch of similar colour like part of a sky or a cheek. Later algorithms then work with 500 regions instead of 300,000 pixels.

concepts.name: Speeded Up Robust Features
concepts.description: A fast feature detector and descriptor inspired by SIFT that uses integral images and box-filter approximations of the Hessian to find scale- and rotation-invariant keypoints.
concepts.example: Like SIFT, SURF finds keypoints that survive zoom and rotation, but it approximates blob filters with simple boxes. With an integral image, each box sum costs 4 lookups at any size, so it runs several times faster.

concepts.name: Swin Transformer
concepts.description: A hierarchical Vision Transformer that computes self-attention within local windows and shifts the windows between layers, giving linear cost in image size and multiscale features for dense tasks.
concepts.example: Swin splits a feature map into 7x7-patch windows and does attention only inside each. Next layer, the windows shift by 3 patches so neighbouring windows can share information, and patches are merged between stages.

concepts.name: Tacotron
concepts.description: A sequence-to-sequence text-to-speech model that uses an attention-based encoder-decoder to turn characters into mel spectrograms, which a vocoder converts to audio; Tacotron 2 uses WaveNet as the vocoder.
concepts.example: Type 'Hello there'. Tacotron reads the characters, and its decoder attends to them one by one while producing about 80 frames of mel spectrogram per second of speech; a vocoder then turns those frames into audible audio.

concepts.name: Template Matching
concepts.description: Finding where a small template image appears in a larger image by sliding it over every position and scoring similarity, for example with normalized cross-correlation.
concepts.example: To find a 20x20 logo in a 500x500 screenshot, slide the logo over every position, compute normalised cross-correlation, and report where the score peaks, say 0.98 at (312, 40).

concepts.name: Text-to-Image Model
concepts.description: Generating images from natural-language descriptions, using models such as diffusion models conditioned on text embeddings, as in DALL-E, Imagen and Stable Diffusion.
concepts.example: Type 'a red fox reading a newspaper in a café, watercolour' and a model produces an image matching every part: the fox, the paper, the café and the watercolour style.

concepts.name: Textual Inversion
concepts.description: A personalization technique for text-to-image diffusion models that learns a new word embedding representing a specific concept from a few images, while keeping the model frozen.
concepts.example: Show the model 5 photos of your ceramic cat and learn a new word vector for 'S*'. Then 'S* on the moon' or 'S* in Van Gogh style' works, while all of Stable Diffusion's weights stay unchanged.

concepts.name: Triangulation (Computer Vision)
concepts.description: Computing the 3D position of a point from its 2D projections in two or more images with known camera matrices, by intersecting the back-projected rays in a least-squares sense.
concepts.example: Two cameras 1 m apart both see a bird. Drawing a ray from each camera through the bird's pixel, the rays almost meet 5 m away; the point closest to both rays is taken as the bird's 3D position.

concepts.name: Truncation Trick
concepts.description: A GAN sampling technique that draws latent vectors closer to the average (truncating extreme values), trading variety for higher sample quality.
concepts.example: Latent values are normally drawn from a bell curve; with truncation 0.7, every sample is pulled 30% of the way toward the average latent. StyleGAN faces then look cleaner and more typical, but fewer have unusual features.

concepts.name: Two-Stage Object Detector
concepts.description: An object detector that first generates region proposals and then classifies and refines each proposal in a second stage, as in the R-CNN family; generally accurate but slower than one-stage detectors.
concepts.example: Faster R-CNN first proposes about 300 boxes that might contain something. Stage two looks closely at each, labels it 'cat' or 'background' and tightens the box edges, which costs time but improves accuracy.

concepts.name: Two-Stream Network
concepts.description: A video action recognition architecture with two CNNs, one on RGB frames for appearance and one on stacked optical flow for motion, whose predictions are fused.
concepts.example: To tell 'opening a door' from 'closing a door', one CNN looks at a single frame for what is there, while another reads 10 stacked optical-flow frames for which way things move. Averaging their scores gives the answer.

concepts.name: U-Net
concepts.description: An encoder-decoder CNN with skip connections that copy high-resolution encoder features to the matching decoder layers, giving precise segmentation; widely used in medical imaging and diffusion models.
concepts.example: A 256x256 cell image is downsampled to 16x16 to find 'what' is present, then upsampled back. Skip connections hand over the sharp 256x256 edges from the encoder, so cell boundaries come out precise.

concepts.name: Unsharp Masking
concepts.description: An image sharpening technique that subtracts a blurred copy from the original to isolate edges and fine detail, then adds a scaled amount of that detail back.
concepts.example: An edge pixel is 100 and its blurred version is 80, so the detail is 20. Adding back 1.5 × 20 gives 130, making the edge pop, while flat areas, where blur changes nothing, stay the same.

concepts.name: Variational Autoencoder
concepts.description: A generative model with an encoder that outputs a distribution over latent variables and a decoder that reconstructs data, trained by maximizing the evidence lower bound using the reparameterization trick.
concepts.example: A VAE trained on faces encodes a photo not as one point but as a cloud, say mean 0.3 and spread 0.1 per dimension. Sampling near that cloud and decoding gives similar faces, and sampling anywhere gives brand-new ones.

concepts.name: Video Diffusion Model
concepts.description: A diffusion model that generates video by denoising sequences of frames jointly, using spatio-temporal attention or 3D convolutions to keep motion and appearance consistent over time.
concepts.example: Rather than drawing 16 frames separately, which makes a cat flicker between different cats, a video diffusion model denoises all 16 at once, with attention across frames keeping the cat and its motion consistent.

concepts.name: Video Generation
concepts.description: The problem of synthesizing realistic video clips, often from a text prompt or image, which requires modeling both frame appearance and coherent motion over time.
concepts.example: Given 'a paper boat floating down a rainy street', a video generator must draw the boat in every frame and also make it drift smoothly with the water, not jump or change shape.

concepts.name: Video Understanding
concepts.description: Analyzing video to recognize actions, events and their timing, using models that combine spatial features from frames with temporal modeling across frames.
concepts.example: A model watching a basketball clip sees a player, a ball and a hoop in single frames, but only by following how they change over time can it say 'dunk at 0:07' instead of 'standing near hoop'.

concepts.name: Viola–Jones Object Detection Framework
concepts.description: A fast face detection framework that evaluates Haar-like features with integral images, selects them with AdaBoost and arranges classifiers in a cascade to quickly reject background regions.
concepts.example: For each 24x24 window, the first stage checks just 2 features, such as 'eyes darker than cheeks', and throws out about half of non-faces instantly. Later stages check more, so few windows reach the end, and phones could detect faces in real time.

concepts.name: Vision–Language Model
concepts.description: A model that jointly processes images and text, usually by feeding visual encoder outputs into a large language model, enabling image description, visual question answering and multimodal chat.
concepts.example: Upload a photo of a broken bike chain and ask 'how do I fix this?'. A vision encoder turns the photo into tokens, a language model reads them with your question and answers with repair steps.

concepts.name: Visual Grounding
concepts.description: The task of locating the region of an image that a natural-language phrase refers to, such as finding the box for 'the man in the red hat'.
concepts.example: In a photo of three men, given the phrase 'the man in the red hat', the model draws a box around only the one wearing a red hat, ignoring the other two.

concepts.name: Visual Odometry
concepts.description: Estimating a camera's motion over time by tracking visual features between consecutive frames, integrating the relative poses into a trajectory.
concepts.example: A rover's camera sees the same 200 rock corners in two frames. From how they shifted, it computes that it moved 0.5 m forward and turned 2°, and chains thousands of such steps into its path.

concepts.name: Visual Question Answering
concepts.description: The task of answering natural-language questions about an image, requiring a model to combine visual recognition with language understanding and reasoning.
concepts.example: Show a kitchen photo and ask 'how many mugs are on the table?'. The model must find the table, recognise mugs, count them, and answer '3'.

concepts.name: VITS
concepts.description: An end-to-end text-to-speech model that combines a variational autoencoder, normalizing flows and adversarial training to generate waveforms directly from text in a single stage.
concepts.example: Type a sentence and VITS goes straight from text to a waveform in one model, with no separate spectrogram step. Its random duration predictor lets the same sentence be spoken with slightly different rhythm each time.

concepts.name: Vocoder
concepts.description: A component that converts an acoustic representation such as a mel spectrogram into an audio waveform; neural vocoders like WaveNet and HiFi-GAN produce natural-sounding speech.
concepts.example: Tacotron produces 80 mel bands per frame, a picture of the sound with no phase. The vocoder fills in the missing detail, outputting 22,050 audio samples per second that you can actually play.

concepts.name: Voice Activity Detection
concepts.description: Detecting which parts of an audio signal contain human speech versus silence or noise, used to trigger speech recognition and save computation.
concepts.example: In a 10-second call clip, VAD marks 0 to 2.1 s as silence, 2.1 to 6.8 s as speech and the rest as background noise. Only the speech part is sent to the recogniser.

concepts.name: Voice Cloning
concepts.description: Generating speech in a specific person's voice from a short sample of their recordings, typically by conditioning a text-to-speech model on a speaker embedding.
concepts.example: Record 10 seconds of your voice. The system computes a speaker embedding and feeds it into a TTS model, which can now read any new text sounding like you.

concepts.name: Volume Rendering
concepts.description: A technique that forms an image by integrating color and density along rays through a 3D volume, accumulating contributions weighted by transmittance; the basis of NeRF.
concepts.example: Shoot a ray through a foggy cube and sample 64 points along it. Each point adds its colour weighted by its own density and by how much light got through the points before it; a solid red point early on blocks everything behind it.

concepts.name: Voxel
concepts.description: A value on a regular 3D grid, the volumetric counterpart of a pixel, used in medical scans, 3D reconstruction and 3D CNNs.
concepts.example: A CT scan of 512x512x300 voxels stores a density for each 0.5 mm cube of the body. Like 3D pixels, they can be sliced in any direction to view the organs.

concepts.name: VQ-VAE
concepts.description: An autoencoder whose encoder outputs are snapped to the nearest vector in a learned codebook, producing discrete latent codes that a separate prior model can generate; VQ-GAN adds adversarial and perceptual losses.
concepts.example: An encoder turns a 256x256 image into a 32x32 grid of vectors, and each is replaced by its nearest of 512 codebook entries. The image becomes 1,024 integers that a Transformer can model like words.

concepts.name: Wasserstein Metric
concepts.description: A distance between probability distributions equal to the minimum cost of moving probability mass to turn one into the other, meaningful even when the distributions do not overlap.
concepts.example: Two piles of sand: one has 1 unit at position 0, the other 1 unit at position 3. Moving it costs 1 × 3 = 3. Shift the second pile to position 10 and the distance becomes 10, while KL divergence would just be infinite both times.

concepts.name: Watershed (Image Processing)
concepts.description: A segmentation algorithm that treats image intensity or gradient as a landscape and floods it from markers, drawing region boundaries where water from different basins would meet.
concepts.example: Treat a gradient image as terrain where edges are ridges. Pour water from markers inside each coin in a photo of touching coins; where water from two coins meets on a ridge, a boundary is drawn.

concepts.name: wav2vec 2.0
concepts.description: A self-supervised speech model that encodes raw audio with a CNN and Transformer, masks parts of the latent sequence and learns by contrasting the true quantized latents against distractors, then fine-tunes for ASR.
concepts.example: wav2vec 2.0 listens to thousands of hours of unlabelled speech, hides about half of the latent frames and learns to pick the true sound unit out of 100 decoys. Fine-tuned on just 10 minutes of transcripts, it can recognise speech usefully.

concepts.name: Wasserstein GAN
concepts.description: A GAN trained to minimize the Wasserstein distance using a Lipschitz-constrained critic, giving more stable training and meaningful loss curves; WGAN-GP enforces the constraint with a gradient penalty.
concepts.example: Instead of a judge saying only 'fake or real', the WGAN critic gives a score whose gap between real and fake estimates the Wasserstein distance. As images improve, the loss drops steadily, so you can actually watch training progress.

concepts.name: X-vector
concepts.description: A fixed-length speaker embedding extracted from a deep network trained to classify speakers, pooling frame-level features over an utterance; it replaced the earlier factor-analysis-based i-vector.
concepts.example: A network is trained to recognise 7,000 speakers from their MFCC frames. Remove the last layer and any clip, of any length, gives a fixed 512-number vector, so two clips of the same person give nearby vectors.

concepts.name: YCbCr
concepts.description: A color space that separates an image into a brightness (luma) channel Y and two color-difference channels Cb and Cr, used in JPEG and video because color can be compressed more than brightness.
concepts.example: JPEG converts RGB pixels to YCbCr, keeps brightness Y at full resolution, and stores Cb and Cr at half width and height. That alone cuts data by half, and viewers barely notice because eyes are less sensitive to colour detail.

concepts.name: YOLO (You Only Look Once)
concepts.description: A family of fast one-stage object detectors that divide the image into a grid and predict bounding boxes and class probabilities for all cells in a single network pass, enabling real-time detection.
concepts.example: YOLO splits a photo into a 13x13 grid. The cell containing a dog's centre predicts a box and 'dog, 0.92' in the same forward pass as every other cell, letting it run on live video at 30+ frames per second.

concepts.name: Zero-Shot Image Classification
concepts.description: Classifying images into categories never seen during training, typically by comparing image embeddings to text embeddings of class names, as with CLIP.
concepts.example: To classify a photo as cat, dog or axolotl without any training, embed the text 'a photo of a cat', '...dog', '...axolotl' and the image with CLIP. The text vector closest to the image vector is the answer.

concepts.name: Accuracy
concepts.description: The fraction of predictions a classifier gets right, i.e. correct predictions divided by total predictions; misleading on imbalanced data.
concepts.example: A spam filter checks 200 emails and gets 180 right: accuracy = 180 / 200 = 90%. But if 195 were legitimate, a filter that never flags spam scores 97.5% while being useless.

concepts.name: Active Learning
concepts.description: A setup where the model chooses which unlabeled examples to have labeled next, typically those it is most uncertain about, to reach good accuracy with fewer labels.
concepts.example: A model sorting 100,000 medical images is unsure about 50 of them, giving probabilities near 0.5. It asks the doctor to label just those 50, learns from them, and repeats, reaching good accuracy with 2,000 labels instead of 20,000.

concepts.name: Algorithmic Bias
concepts.description: Systematic unfair outcomes from an algorithm, such as worse accuracy for a demographic group, often caused by biased data, features or objectives.
concepts.example: A face recogniser trained mostly on light-skinned faces makes 1% errors for them but 20% for dark-skinned faces. Nobody coded it to be unfair; the skewed training data produced the gap.

concepts.name: Anomaly Detection
concepts.description: Finding data points or events that differ markedly from normal patterns, such as fraud or machine faults, often with unsupervised or density-based methods.
concepts.example: A card normally used for $20 grocery buys in Ohio suddenly charges $2,000 in another country at 3 a.m. That transaction sits far from the card's usual pattern, so it is flagged for review.

concepts.name: Average Treatment Effect on the Treated
concepts.description: The average treatment effect on the treated: the average effect of a treatment among the units that actually received it.
concepts.example: A job program is taken mostly by people with low earnings. ATT asks how much it raised earnings for those who actually enrolled, which can differ from the effect if everyone in the population had been enrolled.

concepts.name: Average Treatment Effect
concepts.description: The average difference between outcomes with and without a treatment across a population, E[Y(1) - Y(0)]; CATE conditions on covariates.
concepts.example: If a drug lowers blood pressure by 10 points for half of patients and 2 points for the other half, the ATE is 6. We never see both outcomes for one person, so it is estimated by comparing groups.

concepts.name: Backdoor Criterion
concepts.description: A graphical rule saying which covariates to adjust for: a set that blocks every backdoor path from treatment to outcome, and contains no descendants of treatment, identifies the causal effect.
concepts.example: Ice cream sales and drownings rise together because hot weather drives both. Temperature opens a backdoor path, so adjusting for temperature blocks it and leaves only any real ice cream effect.

concepts.name: Backtesting
concepts.description: Evaluating a forecasting or trading model by simulating how it would have performed on historical data, training only on the past at each point.
concepts.example: To test a sales forecaster, pretend it is January 2023: train on data up to then and forecast February. Then add February and forecast March, and so on, comparing each forecast to what actually happened.

concepts.name: Bag-of-Words Model
concepts.description: A text representation that counts how often each vocabulary word appears in a document, ignoring word order.
concepts.example: With vocabulary [cat, dog, sat, mat], the sentence 'the cat sat on the mat, cat!' becomes [2, 0, 1, 1]. 'Mat sat cat cat' gives the same vector, since order is thrown away.

concepts.name: Bar Chart
concepts.description: A chart showing values for categories as rectangular bars whose lengths are proportional to the values.
concepts.example: A café sold 40 lattes, 25 teas and 10 juices. A bar chart draws three bars of those heights, making it obvious at a glance that lattes sell four times as much as juice.

concepts.name: Baseline Model
concepts.description: A simple reference model, such as predicting the most frequent class or the mean, used to judge whether a more complex model adds value.
concepts.example: For predicting tomorrow's temperature, a baseline says 'same as today' and is off by 2°C on average. A fancy model with 2.1°C error is worse than doing nothing clever, which the baseline reveals.

concepts.name: Batch Inference
concepts.description: Generating predictions for a large set of inputs at once on a schedule, such as nightly scoring of all customers, instead of per request in real time.
concepts.example: Every night at 2 a.m., a churn model scores all 5 million customers at once and writes the risk scores to a table. The marketing team reads them in the morning; no one waits for a live prediction.

concepts.name: Business Analytics
concepts.description: Using data, statistics and visualization to understand business performance and support decisions, from descriptive reports to predictive models.
concepts.example: A shop notices sales fell 15% in March, finds the drop is concentrated in one region after a competitor opened, and builds a forecast to decide whether a discount there would pay off.

concepts.name: Business Intelligence
concepts.description: Tools and practices for collecting, integrating and reporting business data through warehouses, dashboards and KPIs to inform decisions.
concepts.example: Each morning, sales data from 50 stores loads into a warehouse, and managers open a dashboard showing yesterday's revenue, top products and stock levels by store, without writing any queries.

concepts.name: Canary Release
concepts.description: Rolling out a new version, such as a new model, to a small share of traffic first and monitoring it before releasing it to everyone.
concepts.example: A new recommendation model is sent to 5% of users first. If its click rate and error rate look fine after a day, it goes to 25%, then 100%; if not, the 5% are switched back.

concepts.name: Categorical Encoding
concepts.description: Converting categorical variables into numbers models can use, e.g. one-hot, label, ordinal, target or hash encoding.
concepts.example: A 'colour' column with red, green, blue can become one-hot columns [1,0,0], [0,1,0], [0,0,1], or a single number per colour equal to the average target value for that colour (target encoding).

concepts.name: Causal Forest
concepts.description: A random-forest-based method that estimates heterogeneous treatment effects by growing honest trees that split on differences in treatment effect.
concepts.example: A causal forest finds that a discount email raises spending by $20 for new customers but only $2 for loyal ones, by growing trees that split customers wherever the treatment effect differs most.

concepts.name: Causal Graph
concepts.description: A directed acyclic graph whose arrows encode cause-and-effect relations between variables, used to reason about confounding and identification.
concepts.example: Draw arrows Smoking → Tar → Cancer and Genes → Smoking, Genes → Cancer. The graph shows Genes confounds the smoking-cancer link and that Tar is a mediator you should not adjust for.

concepts.name: Causality
concepts.description: The relation where changing one variable (the cause) produces a change in another (the effect), as opposed to mere statistical association.
concepts.example: Cities with more firefighters at a fire have more damage, but sending firefighters doesn't cause damage; big fires cause both. Causality asks what would change if you intervened.

concepts.name: Churn Rate
concepts.description: The percentage of customers or users who stop using a product during a given period.
concepts.example: A streaming service starts March with 10,000 subscribers and 300 cancel during the month: monthly churn = 300 / 10,000 = 3%. Over a year that compounds to roughly a third of subscribers lost.

concepts.name: CI/CD for Machine Learning
concepts.description: Applying continuous integration and delivery to ML systems: automated tests for data and models, continuous retraining and automated deployment.
concepts.example: When someone pushes new feature code, a pipeline tests the data schema, retrains the model, checks that its accuracy is at least the current model's, and only then deploys it automatically.

concepts.name: Class Imbalance
concepts.description: When some classes are far rarer than others in classification data, e.g. 1% fraud, causing models to favour the majority and accuracy to mislead.
concepts.example: In 10,000 transactions only 100 are fraud. A model that labels everything 'not fraud' is 99% accurate yet catches zero fraud, which is why imbalanced data needs other metrics and fixes.

concepts.name: Class Weighting
concepts.description: Giving higher loss weight to errors on rare classes during training so the model pays more attention to them; a form of cost-sensitive learning.
concepts.example: With 990 normal and 10 fraud examples, give each fraud mistake a weight of 99 and each normal mistake a weight of 1. Missing a fraud now costs the model as much as misclassifying 99 normal cases.

concepts.name: Click-Through Rate
concepts.description: The share of people who click a link, ad or recommendation out of those who saw it: clicks divided by impressions.
concepts.example: An ad is shown 2,000 times and clicked 50 times: CTR = 50 / 2,000 = 2.5%. A new headline that gets 80 clicks per 2,000 views lifts CTR to 4%.

concepts.name: Cluster Randomization
concepts.description: Randomly assigning whole groups, such as cities or schools, instead of individuals to treatment, to avoid interference between units.
concepts.example: Testing a new ride-share pricing on individual riders fails because riders share the same drivers. Instead, randomise whole cities: 10 get the new price, 10 keep the old one.

concepts.name: Cohort Analysis
concepts.description: Grouping users by a shared starting event, such as sign-up month, and tracking their behaviour like retention over time.
concepts.example: Users who joined in January: 100% in month 0, 40% active in month 1, 30% in month 2. February joiners: 100%, 50%, 38%. Comparing these rows shows February's onboarding change improved retention.

concepts.name: Collider Bias
concepts.description: A spurious association created by conditioning on a variable caused by both exposure and outcome (a collider), e.g. Berkson's paradox.
concepts.example: Among hospital patients, two unrelated diseases can look negatively linked, because either one gets you admitted. Selecting only admitted patients, conditioning on the collider, creates the fake link.

concepts.name: Concept Drift
concepts.description: A change over time in the relationship between inputs and the target, P(y|x), which makes a trained model's predictions degrade.
concepts.example: A fraud model learned that big overseas purchases are risky. After travel reopens, the same purchases become normal, so the link between inputs and 'fraud' changed and the model's flags become wrong.

concepts.name: Confusion Matrix
concepts.description: A table comparing predicted and actual classes, counting true positives, false positives, true negatives and false negatives.
concepts.example: A spam filter checks 100 emails: it flags 30, of which 25 really are spam (TP) and 5 are not (FP); of the 70 it lets through, 10 were spam (FN) and 60 were fine (TN). Those four counts fill the 2x2 grid.

concepts.name: Treatment and Control Groups
concepts.description: In an experiment, the treatment group receives the intervention while the control group does not, providing a baseline for comparison.
concepts.example: To test a new fertiliser, 50 tomato plants get it and 50 identical plants get plain water. If the fertilised plants grow 2 kg more fruit on average, the plain-water group shows that gap is not just a good summer.

concepts.name: Conversion Rate
concepts.description: The percentage of users who complete a desired action, such as a purchase or sign-up, out of all visitors.
concepts.example: An online shop gets 2,000 visitors on Monday and 50 of them buy something, so the conversion rate is 50 / 2,000 = 2.5%. If a redesign lifts it to 3%, that is 10 extra sales per 2,000 visitors.

concepts.name: Counterfactual
concepts.description: What would have happened to the same unit under a different action than the one actually taken, e.g. the patient's outcome had they not been treated.
concepts.example: You took an umbrella and stayed dry. The counterfactual question is: would you have got wet without it, on that same day? You can never observe both versions, which is what makes causal questions hard.

concepts.name: Covariate Balance
concepts.description: How similar treated and control groups are in their covariates, often checked with standardized mean differences after matching or weighting.
concepts.example: After matching, treated patients average 61 years old and controls 60, with a pooled SD of 10, so the standardized difference is 0.1. Many analysts treat anything under about 0.1 as well balanced for that variable.

concepts.name: CRISP-DM
concepts.description: Cross-Industry Standard Process for Data Mining: a six-phase cycle of business understanding, data understanding, preparation, modeling, evaluation and deployment.
aliases: Cross-Industry Standard Process for Data Mining
concepts.example: A telecom wants fewer cancellations: it defines the goal, explores call logs, cleans and joins them, trains a churn model, checks if it beats current targeting, then deploys it, often looping back when evaluation reveals a gap.

concepts.name: Cross-Sectional Data
concepts.description: Data collected from many subjects at a single point in time, such as a survey of households this year, as opposed to time series or panel data.
concepts.example: A survey of 1,000 households in March 2026 recording income, size and city is cross-sectional: a single snapshot. Asking the same households every year would turn it into panel data.

concepts.name: Crowdsourcing
concepts.description: Getting tasks like data labeling done by many online workers, as on Amazon Mechanical Turk, often aggregating multiple answers per item.
concepts.example: Each of 10,000 photos is shown to 3 online workers who tag it as cat or dog for a few cents. If 2 of 3 say cat, the photo is labelled cat, so individual mistakes get outvoted.

concepts.name: CUPED
concepts.description: A variance reduction technique for A/B tests that adjusts the outcome using each user's pre-experiment metric as a covariate, giving tighter estimates.
concepts.example: Users who spent a lot last month tend to spend a lot this month. CUPED subtracts the part of this month's spend predicted by last month's, so what is left is less noisy and an A/B test can reach a verdict with fewer users.

concepts.name: Customer Lifetime Value
concepts.description: The total revenue or profit a business expects from a customer over the whole relationship, estimated from spend, margin and churn.
concepts.example: A subscriber pays $10 a month with $7 profit, and 5% cancel each month, so the average customer stays about 1 / 0.05 = 20 months. Their lifetime value is roughly 20 x $7 = $140.

concepts.name: Customer Segmentation
concepts.description: Dividing customers into groups with similar traits or behaviour, often via clustering, to target products and marketing.
concepts.example: A coffee chain groups its customers into daily commuters, weekend treat buyers and students who study for hours. Each group then gets different offers: loyalty points, family deals or cheap refills.

concepts.name: Cyclical Feature Encoding
concepts.description: Encoding periodic features like hour of day or month with sine and cosine so that values at the end and start of a cycle are close.
concepts.example: Hour 23 and hour 0 are one hour apart but as plain numbers they look 23 apart. Mapping each hour to a point on a circle with sin and cos puts 23:00 and 00:00 right next to each other.

concepts.name: d-Separation
concepts.description: A graphical criterion for reading conditional independencies from a DAG: two variables are independent given a set if every path between them is blocked.
concepts.example: In Rain -> Wet grass -> Slippery, Rain and Slippery are linked, but if you already know the grass is wet, learning it rained tells you nothing more about slipperiness: the path is blocked by conditioning on the middle node.

concepts.name: Daily Active Users
concepts.description: The number of unique users who use a product in a day (DAU), or in a month (MAU); a core engagement metric.
concepts.example: A note-taking app has 50,000 different people open it on Tuesday, so DAU is 50,000. If 200,000 people used it at least once in the month, DAU/MAU = 25%, meaning a typical monthly user shows up about one day in four.

concepts.name: Dashboard
concepts.description: A visual display of key metrics and charts on one screen, often updated live, for monitoring business or system performance.
concepts.example: A shop manager opens one screen each morning showing yesterday's sales, a line of revenue over 30 days, stock levels and the top 5 products, all refreshed automatically from the till system.

concepts.name: Data
concepts.description: Facts, measurements or observations recorded as numbers, text, images or other symbols that can be stored and analyzed.
concepts.example: A weather station writes down 18 C, 62% humidity and 'light rain' every hour. Each reading is a piece of data, and a month of them can reveal patterns like the warmest time of day.

concepts.name: Data Anonymization
concepts.description: Removing or transforming personal identifiers in data so individuals cannot be identified, while keeping it useful for analysis.
concepts.example: A hospital shares records for research after replacing names with random IDs, turning exact birth dates into birth years and cutting postcodes to the first two characters, so researchers can study trends without knowing who is who.

concepts.name: Data Augmentation
concepts.description: Creating extra training examples by applying label-preserving transformations to existing data, such as flipping images, to reduce overfitting.
concepts.example: With only 500 cat photos, you create more by flipping each one left-right, rotating it slightly and changing brightness. A cat is still a cat, so you get thousands of valid training images for free.

concepts.name: Data Binning
concepts.description: Grouping continuous values into a small number of intervals or bins, such as age groups, to smooth noise or create categorical features.
concepts.example: Ages 3, 17, 25, 34, 41, 68 can be binned into 0-17, 18-39, 40-64 and 65+, giving two children, two young adults, one middle-aged adult and one senior. A model then sees four groups instead of every exact age.

concepts.name: Data Collection
concepts.description: Gathering data for analysis through surveys, sensors, logs, experiments, databases or web sources.
concepts.example: To study bike-lane use, a city installs counters that log every passing cyclist, surveys 500 riders about their routes and downloads weather records, then combines all three into one dataset.

concepts.name: Data Drift
concepts.description: A change in the distribution of a model's input features over time compared to training data, which can hurt model performance.
concepts.example: A loan model was trained when most applicants were aged 30-50. After a student promotion, half the applicants are under 25, so the inputs look different from training and predictions may get worse.

concepts.name: Data Ethics
concepts.description: The study of moral issues in collecting, analyzing and using data, including privacy, consent, fairness, transparency and accountability.
concepts.example: A fitness app could sell users' location data to advertisers for profit. Data ethics asks whether users truly consented, whether they could be harmed, and whether the use is fair, not only whether it is legal.

concepts.name: Data-Ink Ratio
concepts.description: Tufte's ratio of ink used to show data versus total ink in a chart; maximizing it means removing chartjunk and decoration.
concepts.example: A bar chart with a 3D effect, shadowed bars, a heavy grid and a background picture uses lots of ink that shows no data. Removing those leaves just bars and light labels, and the numbers become easier to read.

concepts.name: Data Labeling
concepts.description: Attaching the correct target labels or annotations to raw data, such as tagging images or text, to create training data for supervised learning.
concepts.example: To build a pothole detector, people go through 20,000 road photos and draw a box around each pothole. Those boxes become the answers the model learns to reproduce.

concepts.name: Data Leakage
concepts.description: When information unavailable at prediction time, such as test data or future values, leaks into training, making evaluation look unrealistically good.
concepts.example: A model predicting hospital readmission scores 99% because one feature is 'readmission paperwork filed', which is only created after readmission. In real use that field is empty, and accuracy collapses.

concepts.name: Data Profiling
concepts.description: Examining a dataset to summarize its structure, types, value distributions, missing values and anomalies before analysis.
concepts.example: Before analysing a customer file you run a quick profile: 10,000 rows, the age column is text not numbers, 12% of emails are missing, and one customer is 212 years old. Now you know what to clean.

concepts.name: Data Science
concepts.description: The field of extracting knowledge from data by combining statistics, programming, machine learning and domain expertise.
concepts.example: A bakery chain combines past sales, weather and holidays, writes code to clean it, fits a model and plots the forecast to decide how many croissants each shop should bake tomorrow, cutting waste.

concepts.name: Data Science Lifecycle
concepts.description: The iterative stages of a data science project: framing the problem, collecting and cleaning data, exploring, modeling, evaluating, deploying and monitoring.
concepts.example: A churn project starts with 'who will cancel next month?', gathers and cleans account data, explores it, trains a model, checks it, deploys it to the CRM, then monitors and retrains as customer behaviour shifts.

concepts.name: Data Storytelling
concepts.description: Communicating insights from data by combining visualizations, narrative and context so an audience understands and acts on them.
concepts.example: Instead of showing a 40-row sales table, an analyst shows one line chart where returns spike after a packaging change, adds a short headline saying so, and ends with a clear proposal to switch back.

concepts.name: Data Validation
concepts.description: Automatically checking that data meets expectations, such as types, ranges, schemas and distributions, before it is used for training or analysis.
concepts.example: Before each nightly training run, a script checks that age is an integer between 0 and 120, every order has a date, and the share of null emails is below 5%. If a check fails the run stops and alerts the team.

concepts.name: Data Versioning
concepts.description: Tracking versions of datasets the way Git tracks code, e.g. with DVC, so experiments and models can be reproduced.
concepts.example: You train a model in May on customers_v3.csv and get 91% accuracy. Months later the file has changed; with DVC you can check out exactly v3 again and reproduce the 91% instead of guessing what changed.

concepts.name: Data Visualization
concepts.description: Representing data graphically with charts, plots and maps to explore patterns and communicate findings.
concepts.example: A table of 365 daily temperatures is hard to read, but a line chart instantly shows the summer peak, the winter dip and one odd cold snap in June.

concepts.name: Dataset
concepts.description: A structured collection of data, usually organized as records (rows) with attributes (columns), used for analysis or training models.
concepts.example: A spreadsheet of 500 houses where each row is one house and the columns are size, bedrooms, location and price is a dataset. You could use it to train a model that predicts price.

concepts.name: Date Feature Extraction
concepts.description: Deriving model features from dates and timestamps, such as day of week, month, holiday flags or time since an event.
concepts.example: From the timestamp 2024-12-24 18:30 a model can get: weekday = Tuesday, month = 12, hour = 18, is_holiday_eve = yes, days_to_Christmas = 1. Each is far more useful for predicting shop traffic than the raw date.

concepts.name: Demographic Parity
concepts.description: A fairness criterion requiring a model's positive prediction rate to be equal across groups defined by a sensitive attribute.
concepts.example: A hiring model approves 40% of male and 25% of female applicants. Demographic parity would require both rates to be equal, say 32% each, regardless of other differences between the groups.

concepts.name: Differential Privacy
concepts.description: A mathematical privacy guarantee that an algorithm's output barely changes whether or not any one person's data is included, usually achieved by adding calibrated noise.
concepts.example: A census reports that 1,203 people in a town have diabetes, but adds a little random noise, say +/-3. Whether or not you are in the data barely changes the published number, so nobody can deduce your status from it.

concepts.name: Do-Calculus
concepts.description: Pearl's three rules for transforming expressions with the do-operator (interventions) into observational probabilities, deciding if a causal effect is identifiable.
concepts.example: We want P(recovery | do(take drug)) but only have observational records. Do-calculus applies rules to rewrite that interventional query into ordinary conditional probabilities we can compute, or proves no rewrite exists.

concepts.name: Double Machine Learning
concepts.description: A causal estimation method that uses ML models to predict both outcome and treatment from covariates, then regresses residual on residual with cross-fitting to get an unbiased effect.
concepts.example: To estimate the effect of price on sales, one model predicts sales from season and region, another predicts price from them. Regressing the leftover sales on the leftover price isolates price's effect, cleaned of those confounders.

concepts.name: Doubly Robust Estimation
concepts.description: A causal estimator combining an outcome regression model and propensity score weighting, which stays consistent if either model is correct.
concepts.example: You estimate a job programme's effect with both a model of earnings and a model of who joins. If either model is right, the combined estimate is still correct, like having two safety ropes when climbing.

concepts.name: Equalized Odds
concepts.description: A fairness criterion requiring equal true positive and false positive rates across groups; equal opportunity requires only equal true positive rates.
concepts.example: Among people who truly repay loans, a model approves 80% of group A and 80% of group B; among those who default, it wrongly approves 10% of each. Equal rates on both sides satisfy equalized odds.

concepts.name: Exclusion Restriction
concepts.description: The instrumental variable assumption that the instrument affects the outcome only through the treatment, with no direct or other paths.
concepts.example: Living near a college is used as an instrument for years of schooling to estimate effects on wages. The restriction says distance affects wages only through schooling, which fails if college towns also simply pay more.

concepts.name: Exploratory Data Analysis
concepts.description: The first look at a dataset: summarizing variables, plotting distributions and relationships, and spotting missing values or outliers to form hypotheses before any modeling.
concepts.example: Given a new file of taxi trips, you plot fare against distance, notice a cluster of $0 fares and some 500-mile rides, count missing tips, and form a hunch that airport trips pay more, all before fitting any model.

concepts.name: F1 Score
concepts.description: The harmonic mean of precision and recall, giving a single score that is high only when a classifier both finds most positives and makes few false alarms; useful on imbalanced data.
concepts.example: A fraud detector has precision 0.9 and recall 0.5. Their plain average is 0.7, but F1 = 2 x 0.9 x 0.5 / (0.9 + 0.5) = 0.64, pulled toward the weaker number to flag the poor recall.

concepts.name: Feature
concepts.description: A measurable input property of each example, such as age, price or pixel intensity, that a model uses to make predictions; a dataset row is a collection of feature values.
concepts.example: To predict whether a fruit is an apple or orange, you might measure weight (150 g), colour (red) and skin texture (smooth). Each of these measurements is a feature the model uses.

concepts.name: Feature Cross
concepts.description: A new feature made by combining two or more existing features, often by multiplying them or pairing their categories, so a linear model can capture interactions between them.
concepts.example: Latitude alone and longitude alone poorly predict house price, but crossing them into grid cells like 'lat-bin 5 x lon-bin 8' lets a linear model learn that one particular neighbourhood is expensive.

concepts.name: Feature Engineering
concepts.description: Creating, transforming and selecting input features from raw data, using domain knowledge, so that a machine learning model can learn patterns more easily and accurately.
concepts.example: Predicting delivery delays from raw timestamps works poorly, but adding 'is rush hour', 'distance in km' and 'driver's average delay' gives the model the clues it needs.

concepts.name: Feature Extraction
concepts.description: Turning raw data such as text, images or signals into a compact set of informative numeric features, either by hand-designed rules or by learned transformations like PCA.
concepts.example: A 100 x 100 face photo has 10,000 pixel values. PCA can squeeze it into 50 numbers that capture the main ways faces differ, and a classifier works on those 50 instead.

concepts.name: Feature Hashing
concepts.description: Encoding features by passing their names or values through a hash function into a fixed-size vector index, giving a memory-bounded representation of huge or unbounded vocabularies at the cost of collisions.
concepts.example: Instead of a column for every one of 10 million possible words, each word is hashed to one of 1,024 slots, e.g. 'pizza' -> 517. Memory stays fixed, though occasionally two words share a slot.

concepts.name: Feature Importance
concepts.description: A score saying how much each input feature contributes to a model's predictions, measured via impurity decrease, permutation of the feature, or attribution methods like SHAP.
concepts.example: In a house-price model, shuffling the size column raises error by 30% while shuffling the paint colour column changes nothing. So size is highly important and paint colour is not.

concepts.name: Feature Selection
concepts.description: Choosing a subset of the most useful input features and discarding the rest, to reduce overfitting, speed up training and improve interpretability; done by filter, wrapper or embedded methods.
concepts.example: From 200 customer columns, you keep the 15 that actually help predict churn. The model trains faster, is easier to explain and stops fitting quirks of the useless 185.

concepts.name: Feature Store
concepts.description: A central data system that stores, versions and serves curated ML features so the same feature definitions are reused consistently for offline training and online prediction.
concepts.example: The fraud team defines 'number of card purchases in the last hour' once in a feature store. Training pulls its historical values and the live app pulls its current value, so both use the exact same calculation.

concepts.name: Feedback Loop (Machine Learning)
concepts.description: A situation where a deployed model's predictions influence the data later used to retrain it, e.g. recommendations shaping clicks, which can reinforce biases or degrade the model over time.
concepts.example: A video app only recommends cooking clips, so users mostly click cooking clips, so the retrained model concludes users only like cooking. Over time other topics vanish from the data entirely.

concepts.name: Forecast Horizon
concepts.description: How far into the future a forecast predicts, measured in time steps, such as one day or twelve months ahead; errors usually grow as the horizon lengthens.
concepts.example: A weather service predicts tomorrow's temperature within about 1 C, but a forecast 10 days out may miss by 4 C. Tomorrow is a 1-day horizon; 10 days ahead is a 10-day horizon.

concepts.name: Forward Fill
concepts.description: A simple way to fill missing values in ordered data by copying the last observed value forward to later gaps, common for time series and sensor logs.
concepts.example: A thermometer logs 20, 21, missing, missing, 23. Forward fill copies the last known value into the gaps, giving 20, 21, 21, 21, 23.

concepts.name: Front-door Criterion
concepts.description: A graphical rule for identifying a causal effect when confounders are unobserved, by using a mediator that fully carries the effect and is itself unconfounded with the treatment.
concepts.example: Smoking affects cancer only via tar in the lungs, and an unmeasured gene confounds smoking and cancer. Measuring tar lets you estimate smoking -> tar and tar -> cancer separately and chain them to get the full effect.

concepts.name: Funnel Analysis
concepts.description: Tracking how many users progress through each step of a sequence, such as visit, sign-up and purchase, to find where people drop off and improve conversion.
concepts.example: Of 10,000 visitors, 3,000 view a product, 600 add to cart and 150 pay. The biggest drop is product view to cart (80% lost), so that page is where to look for problems.

concepts.name: General Data Protection Regulation
concepts.description: The European Union regulation governing how personal data is collected, processed and stored, giving people rights such as access, deletion and explanation, with heavy fines for violations.
concepts.example: A Berlin shopper can ask an online store for a copy of all data it holds on her and demand its deletion. If the store ignores this, it can be fined up to 4% of its global annual turnover.

concepts.name: Goodhart's Law
concepts.description: The observation that when a measure becomes a target, it stops being a good measure, because people or algorithms optimize the number instead of the goal it was meant to track.
concepts.example: A call centre rewards agents for short calls, so agents start hanging up on hard customers. Call length drops, but customer satisfaction, the real goal, falls too.

concepts.name: Grammar of Graphics
concepts.description: A framework that describes any statistical chart as layers mapping data variables to visual aesthetics, geometric marks, scales and coordinates; it underlies ggplot2 and similar libraries.
concepts.example: A scatter plot is described as: data = cars, x = weight, y = mpg, colour = cylinders, mark = points. Swap the mark to lines or add a facet by year and you get a new chart from the same building blocks.

concepts.name: Group By Aggregation
concepts.description: Splitting a table into groups by one or more key columns, applying an aggregate such as sum or mean within each group, and combining the results into a summary table.
concepts.example: A sales table has rows like (London, 20), (Paris, 15), (London, 30). Grouping by city and summing gives London 50 and Paris 15.

concepts.name: Guardrail Metric
concepts.description: A metric monitored in an experiment not to be improved but to make sure a change does not harm something important, such as page load time or revenue, while optimizing the main metric.
concepts.example: A test of bigger ads lifts click revenue by 5%, but the guardrail metric of page load time rises 40% and user retention dips. The guardrail stops the team from shipping a change that wins narrowly but hurts overall.

concepts.name: Heat Map
concepts.description: A chart that shows values in a matrix as colors, so patterns such as correlations between variables or activity over time and day can be seen at a glance.
concepts.example: A grid with days of the week down the side and hours across the top, coloured dark red where a website gets most visits, instantly shows the busy slot is weekday lunchtimes.

concepts.name: Heterogeneous Treatment Effect
concepts.description: The idea that a treatment's causal effect varies across individuals or subgroups; the conditional average treatment effect (CATE) estimates it as a function of covariates.
concepts.example: A blood pressure drug lowers readings by 15 points in older patients but only 3 in younger ones. The average effect hides that the benefit depends strongly on age.

concepts.name: Hierarchical Forecasting
concepts.description: Forecasting time series organized in a hierarchy, such as store, region and total sales, and reconciling the forecasts so lower-level values add up to the higher levels.
concepts.example: You forecast 120 units for store A and 80 for store B, but a separate regional forecast says 230. Reconciliation adjusts the numbers so the stores add up exactly to the region's total.

concepts.name: High Cardinality
concepts.description: When a categorical feature has a very large number of distinct values, like user IDs or ZIP codes, which makes one-hot encoding impractical and calls for hashing, target or embedding encodings.
concepts.example: A 'city' column with 5 values is easy to one-hot encode, but a 'user ID' column with 2 million distinct values would create 2 million columns, mostly zeros.

concepts.name: Holdout Method
concepts.description: Splitting a dataset once into separate training and test portions, training on the first and measuring performance on the unseen second to estimate how the model generalizes.
concepts.example: With 1,000 labelled emails, train a spam filter on 800 and check it on the other 200. Its accuracy on those 200 unseen emails estimates how it will do on future mail.

concepts.name: Holt–Winters Method
concepts.description: A forecasting method that extends exponential smoothing with separate smoothed components for level, trend and seasonality, updated recursively; also called triple exponential smoothing.
concepts.example: An ice-cream shop's sales have a base level, a slow upward trend and a summer peak. Holt-Winters keeps three running estimates, one for each, and updates them every month to forecast next summer.

concepts.name: Hyperparameter Optimization
concepts.description: Searching for the hyperparameter settings, such as learning rate or tree depth, that give a model the best validation performance, using grid search, random search or Bayesian optimization.
concepts.example: For a random forest you try tree depths 3, 5, 10 and 20, scoring each with cross-validation. Depth 10 gives the best score, so you use it for the final model.

concepts.name: Ignorability
concepts.description: The causal assumption that, given observed covariates, treatment assignment is independent of the potential outcomes, meaning there are no unmeasured confounders.
