concepts.example: If doctors gave a drug based only on age and blood pressure, and we record both, then among patients with the same age and blood pressure, who got the drug is as good as random.

concepts.name: Image Data
concepts.description: Data made of digital images stored as grids of pixel values, often with color channels, used as input for computer vision tasks like classification and detection.
concepts.example: A 28 x 28 grayscale photo of a handwritten digit is stored as 784 numbers from 0 (black) to 255 (white). A colour photo has three such grids, for red, green and blue.

concepts.name: Imputation
concepts.description: Filling in missing values in a dataset with substituted estimates, such as a mean, a model prediction, or several plausible draws, so the data can be analyzed or modeled.
concepts.example: In a survey, 3 of 10 people skipped the age question. Instead of dropping them, you fill in the blanks with the average age of the other 7, or predict age from their other answers.

concepts.name: Information Privacy
concepts.description: The right and practice of controlling how personal information is collected, used and shared, covering legal rules, ethical norms and technical protections.
concepts.example: When a supermarket loyalty card tracks every purchase, information privacy asks who may see that history, whether it can be sold, and how long it is kept.

concepts.name: Informed Consent
concepts.description: The principle that people must be told how their data or participation will be used, including risks, and freely agree before it is collected or they are studied.
concepts.example: Before a sleep study, volunteers read that their heart rate and movement will be recorded, stored for 5 years and shared with two universities. Only after they understand and agree is any data collected.

concepts.name: Interrupted Time Series
concepts.description: A quasi-experimental design that estimates an intervention's effect by comparing the level and trend of a time series before and after the intervention point.
concepts.example: Monthly road deaths fell slowly for years. When a new speed law starts, deaths drop sharply and keep falling faster. Comparing the lines before and after the law estimates its effect.

concepts.name: Inverse Probability Weighting
concepts.description: A causal estimation method that weights each unit by the inverse of its probability of receiving the treatment it got, creating a pseudo-population where treatment is unconfounded.
concepts.example: If a patient had only a 20% chance of getting treatment but got it, they count as 1 / 0.2 = 5 people. This upweights the rare cases so treated and untreated groups look alike.

concepts.name: k-Anonymity
concepts.description: A privacy property where every record in a released dataset is indistinguishable from at least k-1 others on its quasi-identifiers; l-diversity adds diversity of sensitive values within groups.
concepts.example: A released medical table has age band, gender and ZIP prefix. With k = 5, every combination like '30-39, female, 021**' must appear at least 5 times, so no one can be singled out.

concepts.name: k-Fold Cross-Validation
concepts.description: A validation scheme that splits data into k folds, trains k models each holding out a different fold for testing, and averages the scores for a more reliable performance estimate.
concepts.example: With 5-fold CV on 1,000 rows, you split into 5 chunks of 200. You train 5 times, each time testing on a different chunk, then average the 5 scores.

concepts.name: Key Performance Indicator
concepts.description: A chosen measurable value that tracks how well a business or team is achieving an important objective, such as monthly revenue or active users.
concepts.example: A café sets a goal to keep customers coming back. Its KPI is the percentage of customers who return within 30 days, currently 35%, with a target of 45%.

concepts.name: k-NN Imputation
concepts.description: Filling missing values of a record using the values of its k most similar complete records, averaging them for numbers or taking the most common value for categories.
concepts.example: Anna's weight is missing. Her 3 most similar people by height, age and sex weigh 60, 62 and 64 kg, so you fill in 62 kg.

concepts.name: Label
concepts.description: The known output value attached to a training example, such as a class name or a price, that a supervised model learns to predict.
concepts.example: In a dataset of house photos with prices, the price ($350,000) is the label. In a set of emails, 'spam' or 'not spam' is the label.

concepts.name: Label Encoding
concepts.description: Converting categories into integer codes (0, 1, 2, ...); natural for ordered categories but can imply a false ordering for nominal ones in many models.
concepts.example: Sizes small, medium, large become 0, 1, 2, which keeps their order. But colours red, green, blue as 0, 1, 2 would wrongly tell a model that blue is 'more' than red.

concepts.name: Label Shift
concepts.description: A distribution shift where class proportions change between training and deployment while the class-conditional feature distributions stay the same, e.g. a disease becoming more common.
concepts.example: A flu test model was trained when 5% of patients had flu. In winter 30% do. Symptoms of flu cases look the same, but the base rate changed, so predictions need adjusting.

concepts.name: Lag Features
concepts.description: Features built from past values of a time series, such as yesterday's or last week's value, letting a regular supervised model use history to forecast the future.
concepts.example: To predict today's sales, add columns for yesterday's sales (lag 1) and sales a week ago (lag 7). If sales were 100 yesterday and 90 last Tuesday, these become inputs.

concepts.name: Lift Chart
concepts.description: A chart showing how much better a model's top-ranked cases capture positives compared with random selection, plotted against the fraction of the population targeted.
concepts.example: A model ranks 10,000 customers. Mailing the top 10% reaches 30% of buyers, while random mailing reaches 10%, a lift of 3.

concepts.name: Line Chart
concepts.description: A chart that connects data points with lines, typically showing how a quantity changes over time or along an ordered variable.
concepts.example: Plotting a city's monthly temperature from January to December and joining the dots shows a smooth hill peaking in July.

concepts.name: Listwise Deletion
concepts.description: Handling missing data by dropping every record that has any missing value; simple and unbiased only when data are missing completely at random, but wasteful.
concepts.example: A survey of 100 people has 5 missing ages and 8 missing incomes. Listwise deletion drops every person with any gap, leaving maybe 88 complete rows.

concepts.name: Local Average Treatment Effect
concepts.description: The causal effect of a treatment for compliers, the units whose treatment status is changed by an instrument; it is what instrumental variable estimates identify.
concepts.example: Students win a lottery for a tutoring offer. Some would attend anyway, some never. LATE measures the effect only for those who attend because they won, the compliers.

concepts.name: Log Transformation
concepts.description: Replacing a variable by its logarithm to compress large values, reduce right skew and turn multiplicative relationships into additive ones before analysis or modeling.
concepts.example: Incomes of 20k, 50k, 100k and 10 million are wildly spread. Taking log10 gives about 4.3, 4.7, 5 and 7, a much more manageable range.

concepts.name: Marketing Attribution
concepts.description: Assigning credit for a conversion to the marketing touchpoints a customer saw along the way, using rules like last-click or data-driven multi-touch models.
concepts.example: A customer sees an Instagram ad, later clicks a Google ad, then buys via email. Last-click gives email all the credit; a multi-touch model might split it 30/30/40.

concepts.name: Marketing Mix Modeling
concepts.description: Regression-based modeling of aggregate sales over time on spending across marketing channels, with adstock and saturation effects, to estimate each channel's contribution and ROI.
concepts.example: A brand regresses weekly sales on TV, radio and online spend over two years. The model finds each $1 of TV returns $1.80 and radio $0.90, guiding next year's budget.

concepts.name: Matching (Statistics)
concepts.description: Estimating causal effects from observational data by pairing each treated unit with similar untreated units on covariates, then comparing outcomes within matched pairs.
concepts.example: To see if a job programme raises income, pair each participant with a non-participant of the same age, education and past earnings, then compare their later incomes.

concepts.name: Mean Absolute Percentage Error
concepts.description: A forecast accuracy metric equal to the average absolute error expressed as a percentage of the actual value; easy to read but undefined or unstable when actuals are near zero.
concepts.example: Actuals are 100 and 200, forecasts 90 and 220. Errors are 10% and 10%, so MAPE = 10%. But if an actual is 1 and forecast 2, that single error is 100%.

concepts.name: Mean Absolute Scaled Error
concepts.description: A scale-free forecast error metric that divides the model's mean absolute error by that of a naive (or seasonal naive) forecast; values below 1 beat the naive baseline.
concepts.example: Your model's MAE is 8 units. Just repeating yesterday's value gives MAE 10. MASE = 8 / 10 = 0.8, meaning your model beats the naive guess.

concepts.name: Mean Imputation
concepts.description: Replacing missing values with the mean (or median or mode) of the observed values of that variable; quick, but it shrinks variance and distorts relationships.
concepts.example: Ages are 20, 30, missing, 40. The mean of known ages is 30, so the gap becomes 30.

concepts.name: Measurement Error
concepts.description: The difference between a measured value and the true value, from random noise or systematic bias in instruments or recording; it can bias estimates like regression slopes.
concepts.example: A bathroom scale that always reads 2 kg too heavy has systematic error. One that jitters by +/-1 kg each time has random error.

concepts.name: Mediation Analysis
concepts.description: Decomposing a treatment's effect into an indirect part that flows through an intermediate variable (the mediator) and a direct part that does not.
concepts.example: Exercise lowers weight, and lower weight lowers blood pressure. Mediation analysis splits exercise's effect into the part via weight and the rest.

concepts.name: Meta-Learners (Causal Inference)
concepts.description: Recipes for estimating heterogeneous treatment effects with any ML regressor: the S-learner fits one model with treatment as a feature, the T-learner fits two, and the X-learner cross-imputes effects.
concepts.example: A T-learner fits one model on customers who got a coupon and one on those who did not. For a new customer it predicts spend both ways, say $50 vs $42, and calls the $8 gap that person's treatment effect.

concepts.name: Min-Max Normalization
concepts.description: Rescaling a feature linearly so its minimum maps to 0 and maximum to 1 (or another range), putting features on comparable scales; sensitive to outliers.
concepts.example: Ages run from 20 to 60. Min-max scaling maps 20 to 0, 60 to 1 and 40 to (40 - 20) / (60 - 20) = 0.5. One 120-year-old typo would squash everyone else near 0, showing its outlier sensitivity.

concepts.name: Minimum Detectable Effect
concepts.description: The smallest true effect size an experiment can reliably detect at a chosen significance level and power, given its sample size and metric variance.
concepts.example: With 10,000 users per arm and a 5% baseline conversion, a test might only reliably detect a lift to about 5.9%. If you expect only 5.2%, you need far more users or the test will likely miss it.

concepts.name: Missing at Random
concepts.description: A missing-data mechanism where whether a value is missing depends only on other observed variables, not on the missing value itself, so it can be corrected using the observed data.
concepts.example: Men skip a depression survey question more often than women, but within each sex, skipping is unrelated to how depressed they are. Since sex is recorded, you can correct for the missing answers.

concepts.name: Missing Completely at Random
concepts.description: A missing-data mechanism where missingness is unrelated to any variable, observed or not, so the complete cases are an unbiased random subset.
concepts.example: A lab freezer fails and a random 10% of blood samples are lost, regardless of who gave them or their results. The remaining 90% are still a fair, just smaller, picture of everyone.

concepts.name: Missing Indicator
concepts.description: An added binary feature marking whether a value was originally missing, so a model can learn from the missingness pattern itself after imputation.
concepts.example: If 'last login date' is blank for some users, you fill it with a default and add a column was_missing = 1. The model may learn that blank logins signal never-active accounts, a strong churn clue.

concepts.name: Missing Not at Random
concepts.description: A missing-data mechanism where the chance of a value being missing depends on the unobserved value itself, such as high earners hiding income; it cannot be fixed from observed data alone.
concepts.example: In an income survey, people earning over $300k often leave income blank. The missing values are mostly high, so averaging the answers you got underestimates income, and no observed column reveals by how much.

concepts.name: Machine Learning Pipeline
concepts.description: A chained sequence of data preprocessing, feature transformation and model steps treated as one object, so the same transformations are applied consistently in training and prediction.
concepts.example: A pipeline chains: fill missing values with the median, scale features, then fit logistic regression. Calling fit learns all three steps on training data; calling predict applies the same steps to new data.

concepts.name: Model Card
concepts.description: A short standardized document published with a trained model describing its intended use, training data, evaluation results across groups, limitations and ethical considerations.
concepts.example: A face-recognition model ships with a one-page card: intended for photo tagging, trained on 2M public images, 98% accurate on light-skinned faces but 91% on dark-skinned faces, not for surveillance.

concepts.name: Model Deployment
concepts.description: Putting a trained model into a production environment, packaged behind an API or batch job, so that it serves predictions to real users or systems.
concepts.example: A data scientist trains a house-price model in a notebook. Deployment wraps it in a web service so a real-estate app can send a house's details and get back a price in 50 milliseconds.

concepts.name: Model Drift
concepts.description: The decline of a deployed model's predictive performance over time as the data or the relationship between features and target changes from what it was trained on.
concepts.example: A model predicting taxi demand was trained before a new subway line opened. Afterwards rides near stations drop and its errors double, even though nothing in the code changed.

concepts.name: Model Monitoring
concepts.description: Continuously tracking a deployed model's inputs, predictions and performance metrics to detect drift, data quality problems or failures and trigger alerts or retraining.
concepts.example: A fraud model's dashboard tracks the share of flagged transactions, input averages and weekly precision. When flags suddenly triple overnight, an alert fires and engineers find an upstream data bug.

concepts.name: Model Registry
concepts.description: A central repository that stores trained model versions with their metadata, metrics and lineage, and manages their promotion from staging to production.
concepts.example: Version 7 of a churn model is in production, version 8 is in staging with better AUC. The registry stores both with their metrics and training data links, and one click promotes v8 or rolls back to v7.

concepts.name: Model Retraining
concepts.description: Training a deployed model again on newer data, on a schedule or when monitoring detects degradation, to keep its predictions accurate as the world changes.
concepts.example: A product recommender is retrained every Sunday on the latest 90 days of clicks, so new products and seasonal tastes show up in its suggestions within a week.

concepts.name: Multiple Imputation
concepts.description: Handling missing data by creating several completed datasets with plausible random imputations, analyzing each, and pooling the results so uncertainty from missingness is reflected.
concepts.example: Instead of filling a missing blood pressure with one guess, you make 5 datasets each with a different plausible guess (128, 135, 131...). Analyse each and combine the 5 results so the uncertainty is visible.

concepts.name: Naive Forecast
concepts.description: The simplest forecast that predicts the next value equals the last observed value (or the value one season ago); used as a baseline that real models must beat.
concepts.example: If 120 umbrellas sold today, the naive forecast for tomorrow is 120. The seasonal naive forecast for next December is simply last December's sales. A fancy model must beat these to be worth using.

concepts.name: Natural Experiment
concepts.description: A situation where some outside event or rule assigns treatment in an as-if random way, letting researchers estimate causal effects from observational data.
concepts.example: A draft lottery randomly chose which young men were called up for military service. Comparing their later earnings to those not chosen measures service's effect, as if a researcher had randomised it.

concepts.name: Interference (Experiments)
concepts.description: Interference in experiments where one unit's treatment affects another unit's outcome, e.g. through social networks or shared marketplaces, violating SUTVA and biasing A/B test estimates.
concepts.example: In a ride-hailing test, treated riders get a discount and book more cars, leaving fewer drivers for control riders. The control group looks worse than it would be naturally, inflating the measured effect.

concepts.name: North Star Metric
concepts.description: The single key metric a company chooses to capture the core value it delivers to customers, used to align teams and guide product decisions.
concepts.example: For a music streaming service, the north star might be total minutes listened per week. Product, marketing and engineering all ask whether a project will move that one number.

concepts.name: Novelty Effect
concepts.description: A temporary change in user behavior in an experiment caused simply by something being new, which fades over time; the related primacy effect is initial resistance to change.
concepts.example: A redesigned button gets 20% more clicks in the first week because it looks new, but by week four clicks are back to normal. Ending the test after one week would wrongly declare a big win.

concepts.name: Numerical Variable
concepts.description: A variable whose values are numbers that can be meaningfully added and compared, either discrete counts or continuous measurements like height.
concepts.example: Number of children (0, 1, 2) is discrete and height (172.4 cm) is continuous; both are numerical. A ZIP code is made of digits but is not numerical, since averaging ZIP codes is meaningless.

concepts.name: Observational Data
concepts.description: Data collected by recording what happens without the researcher assigning treatments, so differences between groups may be due to confounding rather than causation.
concepts.example: Hospital records show coffee drinkers live longer, but nobody assigned coffee. Coffee drinkers might also be wealthier, so the link may be confounding rather than coffee itself.

concepts.name: Omitted-Variable Bias
concepts.description: Bias in regression coefficients that arises when a variable that affects the outcome and is correlated with included regressors is left out of the model.
concepts.example: Regressing income on years of schooling without ability in the model overstates schooling's effect, because able people both study longer and earn more. Some of ability's effect is wrongly credited to schooling.

concepts.name: One-Hot Encoding
concepts.description: Representing a categorical variable with one binary column per category, where exactly one column is 1 for each row, so models can use categories without implying order.
concepts.example: Colours red, green, blue become three columns: red = [1,0,0], green = [0,1,0], blue = [0,0,1]. No colour is 'bigger' than another, unlike coding them 1, 2, 3.

concepts.name: Real-Time Inference
concepts.description: Serving model predictions on demand for individual requests with low latency, typically through an API, as opposed to scoring large batches offline.
concepts.example: When you swipe a card, the bank's fraud model gets that one transaction and must answer approve or decline within 100 ms. Nightly batch scoring would be far too late.

concepts.name: Scatter Plot Matrix
concepts.description: A grid of scatter plots showing every pair of variables in a dataset, usually with histograms on the diagonal, for quickly spotting relationships and clusters.
concepts.example: For a flower dataset with 4 measurements, a pair plot draws a 4 x 4 grid: scatter plots for each pair of measurements and a histogram of each on the diagonal, revealing which pairs separate species.

concepts.name: Panel Data
concepts.description: Data that follow the same individuals, firms or regions over multiple time periods, combining cross-sectional and time series dimensions.
concepts.example: Tracking the same 500 firms' revenue and staff count every year from 2015 to 2024 gives panel data: 500 firms x 10 years = 5,000 rows, with both between-firm and over-time variation.

concepts.name: Parallel Trends Assumption
concepts.description: The key difference-in-differences assumption that, without treatment, the treated and control groups' outcomes would have changed by the same amount over time.
concepts.example: Two cities' employment both grew 2% a year before one raised its minimum wage. Assuming they would have kept growing in parallel, any extra gap afterwards is credited to the wage change.

concepts.name: Peeking Problem
concepts.description: The inflation of false positives that happens when an experiment's p-values are checked repeatedly and the test is stopped as soon as it looks significant.
concepts.example: If you check an A/A test with no real difference every day for 30 days and stop at the first p < 0.05, the chance of a false alarm is well over 5%, often 20% or more, rather than the 5% you planned.

concepts.name: Personally Identifiable Information
concepts.description: Any information that can identify a specific person, directly like name or ID number, or indirectly when combined, like birth date plus ZIP code.
concepts.example: Name, passport number and email are PII directly. Birth date, gender and ZIP code alone seem harmless, but together they can uniquely identify most Americans, so they count as PII too.

concepts.name: Population Stability Index
concepts.description: A metric that measures how much a variable's distribution has shifted between two samples by comparing binned proportions, widely used to monitor model inputs and scores for drift.
concepts.example: Split credit scores into 10 bins. If 10% of training applicants fall in the top bin but 25% of this month's do, that bin adds (0.25 - 0.10) x ln(0.25 / 0.10), about 0.14 to the PSI. A total above about 0.25 usually signals a major shift.

concepts.name: Positivity (Causal Inference)
concepts.description: The causal assumption that every unit has a nonzero probability of receiving each treatment level given its covariates, so comparable treated and control units exist.
concepts.example: If every patient over 80 received a drug, there are no untreated 80-year-olds to compare with, so the drug's effect for that age cannot be estimated from the data: positivity is violated.

concepts.name: Rubin Causal Model
concepts.description: A framework that defines a causal effect as the difference between the outcomes a unit would have under treatment and under control, only one of which can ever be observed.
concepts.example: Maria has a headache. If she takes aspirin, it stops in 30 minutes; if not, in 2 hours. Her causal effect is 90 minutes saved, but in reality we see only one of those two outcomes.

concepts.name: Power Transform
concepts.description: A family of transformations such as Box-Cox and Yeo-Johnson that raise data to a fitted power to make distributions more normal-like and stabilize variance.
concepts.example: Box-Cox with lambda = 0.5 takes square roots, and lambda = 0 takes logs. The method tries values of lambda and picks the one that makes the transformed data look most like a bell curve.

concepts.name: Precision
concepts.description: The fraction of predicted positives that are actually positive, TP / (TP + FP); it answers how trustworthy a classifier's positive predictions are.
concepts.example: A model flags 50 emails as spam and 45 really are spam. Precision = 45 / 50 = 90%, so when it says spam, it is right 9 times out of 10.

concepts.name: Precision-Recall Curve
concepts.description: A curve showing the trade-off between precision and recall as a classifier's decision threshold varies; its area (average precision) summarizes performance on imbalanced data.
concepts.example: At a threshold of 0.9 a model catches 40% of frauds with 95% precision; at 0.3 it catches 90% but with 50% precision. Plotting every threshold traces the precision-recall curve.

concepts.name: Primary Metric
concepts.description: The main metric chosen before an experiment to decide whether a change is a success, also called the overall evaluation criterion.
concepts.example: Before testing a new checkout page, the team declares 'purchases per visitor' as the primary metric. If it rises significantly, they ship, even if other metrics wobble.

concepts.name: Probabilistic Forecasting
concepts.description: Forecasting a full predictive distribution, quantiles or prediction intervals for future values rather than a single point, so uncertainty can inform decisions.
concepts.example: Instead of 'we will sell 100 units', the forecast says '80% chance between 85 and 120'. A shop can stock 120 to avoid running out most of the time.

concepts.name: Problem Framing
concepts.description: Translating a business or research goal into a well-defined data science task, choosing the target, prediction type, success metric and constraints before building any model.
concepts.example: 'Reduce customer churn' becomes: predict which customers will cancel in the next 30 days, a binary classification task, judged by recall in the top 10% so the retention team can call them.

concepts.name: Propensity Score
concepts.description: The probability that a unit receives the treatment given its observed covariates, usually estimated with logistic regression and used for matching, weighting or stratification.
concepts.example: A logistic regression on age, income and health gives each person's chance of joining a gym programme. A 50-year-old smoker might score 0.2 and a fit 30-year-old 0.7.

concepts.name: Prophet
concepts.description: An open-source forecasting library from Meta that fits an additive model of trend, yearly and weekly seasonality and holiday effects, designed for business time series.
concepts.example: Give Prophet two years of daily website visits and it fits an upward trend, a weekly dip on Saturdays, a yearly summer slump and a holiday spike, then extends all four into next year.

concepts.name: Qini Curve
concepts.description: A curve for evaluating uplift models that plots the cumulative incremental gain from targeting people in order of predicted uplift; the Qini coefficient is its area above random.
concepts.example: Rank 10,000 customers by predicted uplift and send offers to the top 10%, 20% and so on. If the top 20% yields 300 extra purchases while random targeting yields 100, the Qini curve sits well above the diagonal.

concepts.name: Quasi-Experiment
concepts.description: A study that estimates causal effects without random assignment, using designs like difference-in-differences or regression discontinuity to approximate an experiment.
concepts.example: A school district gives tablets to schools on one side of a river, not the other. Comparing test score changes between the sides approximates an experiment without random assignment.

concepts.name: Randomization Unit
concepts.description: The entity, such as user, session, device or city, that is randomly assigned to treatment or control in an experiment; it affects independence, variance and interference.
concepts.example: Randomizing a search ranking test by session lets one user see both versions on the same day, which can confuse them. Randomizing by user keeps each person in one group consistently.

concepts.name: Data Re-Identification
concepts.description: Matching supposedly anonymized records back to real individuals by linking them with other data sources, showing that removing names alone does not ensure privacy.
concepts.example: Netflix released anonymized movie ratings, but researchers matched them to public IMDb reviews by rating times and titles, identifying some users and their viewing histories.

concepts.name: Recall
concepts.description: The fraction of actual positives that a classifier correctly identifies, TP / (TP + FN); also called sensitivity or true positive rate.
concepts.example: Of 100 patients who truly have a disease, a test flags 80. Recall = 80 / 100 = 80%, meaning it misses 1 in 5 sick people, which matters a lot when missing a case is dangerous.

concepts.name: Record Linkage
concepts.description: Finding records in one or more datasets that refer to the same real-world entity, despite typos and format differences, using matching rules or probabilistic models.
concepts.example: 'Jon Smith, 12 Oak St' in a hospital file and 'John Smyth, 12 Oak Street' in a pharmacy file are probably the same person. Record linkage scores name and address similarity to decide whether to join them.

concepts.name: Recursive Feature Elimination
concepts.description: A wrapper feature selection method that repeatedly trains a model, removes the least important features, and retrains until the desired number of features remains.
concepts.example: Start with 20 features, train a model, drop the 2 least important, retrain on 18, drop 2 more, and so on until 8 remain. Those 8 are the selected set.

concepts.name: Regression Adjustment
concepts.description: Including pre-treatment covariates in a regression of outcome on treatment to adjust for imbalances and reduce variance when estimating a treatment effect.
concepts.example: In a tutoring trial, regress final test score on treatment and prior test score. Accounting for prior scores removes noise and any chance imbalance, giving a sharper estimate of tutoring's effect.

concepts.name: Reproducibility
concepts.description: The ability to obtain the same results from the same data and code, supported by fixed random seeds, versioned data and environments, and documented steps.
concepts.example: A colleague clones your repo, downloads the same data version, runs one script with seed 42 and gets the same 0.87 AUC you reported. If they got 0.81, something in your process was not reproducible.

concepts.name: Retention Rate
concepts.description: The percentage of users or customers who are still active after a given period, such as day 7 or month 1; the complement of churn.
concepts.example: An app gets 1,000 new users on Monday; 400 open it again a week later. Day-7 retention is 40%, so day-7 churn is 60%.

concepts.name: Return on Investment
concepts.description: A ratio of the net gain from an investment to its cost, usually expressed as a percentage, used to compare the profitability of projects or campaigns.
concepts.example: A $1,000 ad campaign brings in $1,500 of profit. ROI = (1,500 - 1,000) / 1,000 = 50%. A campaign returning $900 would have ROI of -10%, a loss.

concepts.name: ROC AUC
concepts.description: The area under the ROC curve, which plots true positive rate against false positive rate across thresholds; it equals the probability a random positive is ranked above a random negative.
concepts.example: Pick a random fraud case and a random normal transaction. If the model gives the fraud a higher score 92% of the time, its ROC AUC is 0.92; a coin flip would score 0.5.

concepts.name: Rolling Window Features
concepts.description: Features computed over a sliding window of recent time steps, such as a 7-day moving average or rolling maximum, to summarize recent history for forecasting models.
concepts.example: Daily sales of 10, 12, 8, 14, 11, 9, 13 give a 7-day rolling mean of 11. Tomorrow the window slides forward one day, dropping the 10 and adding the new value.

concepts.name: Sample Ratio Mismatch
concepts.description: A warning sign in A/B tests where the observed split of users between variants differs significantly from the intended ratio, indicating a bug in assignment or logging.
concepts.example: A 50/50 test should have about equal groups, but one has 50,000 users and the other 48,500. A chi-squared test says that gap is very unlikely by chance, so something, like a redirect bug, is broken.

concepts.name: Sampling
concepts.description: Selecting a subset of individuals from a population to measure, so conclusions about the whole population can be drawn more cheaply; how the sample is chosen determines bias.
concepts.example: To estimate the average height of 10,000 students, measure 200 chosen at random. If you only measured the basketball team, your sample would be badly biased.

concepts.name: Selection Bias
concepts.description: Distortion that occurs when the data analyzed are not representative of the target population because of how units were selected or chose to participate.
concepts.example: A survey about internet use posted only online will overestimate internet use, because people who rarely go online never see it. The sample is skewed by how people got into it.

concepts.name: Sensitivity Analysis
concepts.description: Checking how much conclusions change when assumptions or inputs vary; in causal inference, quantifying how strong unmeasured confounding would need to be (e.g. the E-value) to explain away an effect.
concepts.example: A study finds smokers have 3 times the risk of a disease. A sensitivity analysis shows an unmeasured confounder would need to triple both smoking and risk to erase the finding, which seems unlikely.

concepts.name: Sequential Analysis
concepts.description: Hypothesis testing in which data are evaluated as they arrive with boundaries designed so the test can stop early while keeping the false positive rate controlled.
concepts.example: Instead of a fixed 0.05 threshold checked daily, a sequential test uses stricter early boundaries, like 0.001 on day 5, so you can stop early when results are very strong without inflating false positives.

concepts.name: Shadow Deployment
concepts.description: Running a new model alongside the live one on real traffic, logging its predictions without serving them to users, to compare performance safely before switching.
concepts.example: A new fraud model receives every real transaction alongside the old one, but only the old model's decisions are used. After two weeks the team compares their scores before switching.

concepts.name: SHAP
concepts.description: A method that explains a single prediction by assigning each feature its Shapley value, the feature's average marginal contribution across all feature coalitions, giving additive, consistent attributions.
concepts.example: A loan model predicts 70% default risk versus a 20% average. SHAP might say +30 points came from low income, +25 from late payments and -5 from long employment, adding up exactly to the 50-point gap.

concepts.name: Simple Random Sampling
concepts.description: A sampling method in which every subset of the population of a given size has the same chance of being chosen, so each individual is equally likely to be selected.
concepts.example: To pick 50 of 1,000 employees for a survey, put all 1,000 names into a draw and pull 50 out. Every employee has the same 5% chance of being chosen.

concepts.name: Standardization
concepts.description: Rescaling a feature by subtracting its mean and dividing by its standard deviation so it has mean 0 and standard deviation 1; also called z-score normalization.
concepts.example: Heights have mean 170 cm and SD 10 cm. A 185 cm person becomes (185 - 170) / 10 = 1.5. After this, height and weight can be compared on the same scale.

concepts.name: Structural Causal Model
concepts.description: A model that represents each variable as a function of its direct causes plus noise, with a causal graph, allowing interventions and counterfactuals to be computed.
concepts.example: Model: Rain = noise1; Sprinkler = f(Rain, noise2); Wet = g(Rain, Sprinkler, noise3). To ask 'what if the sprinkler were on?', overwrite the Sprinkler equation and recompute Wet.

concepts.name: Structured Data
concepts.description: Data organized in a predefined schema of rows and fields, such as relational tables or spreadsheets, so it can be easily queried and analyzed.
concepts.example: A spreadsheet of orders with columns order_id, date, customer and amount is structured data: every row has the same fields, so you can easily sum amounts by month.

concepts.name: Stable Unit Treatment Value Assumption
concepts.description: The assumption that a unit's outcome depends only on its own treatment, not others', and that there is only one version of each treatment level.
concepts.example: If vaccinating your neighbour lowers your chance of flu, your outcome depends on their treatment, which breaks SUTVA. So does giving some patients a 'drug' of different strengths under the same name.

concepts.name: Switchback Experiment
concepts.description: An experiment design that alternates an entire system or region between treatment and control over successive time blocks, used when users interact and unit-level randomization would cause interference.
concepts.example: A food-delivery app tests a new pricing algorithm in a city by switching it on for one hour, off the next, and so on for two weeks. Comparing on-hours and off-hours avoids drivers being shared across groups.

concepts.name: Synthetic Control Method
concepts.description: A causal method for a single treated unit, such as one state, that builds a weighted combination of untreated units matching its pre-treatment trajectory to serve as the counterfactual.
concepts.example: California passes a tobacco law. A synthetic California is built as 40% Utah + 30% Nevada + 30% others to match its pre-law smoking trend. After the law, the gap between real and synthetic California is the effect.

concepts.name: Synthetic Data
concepts.description: Artificially generated data that mimics the statistical properties of real data, used to augment training sets, protect privacy, or test systems.
concepts.example: A bank trains a simulator on real transactions, then generates 1 million fake ones with the same spending patterns but no real customers. Developers can test fraud models without seeing private data.

concepts.name: Tableau
concepts.description: A commercial business intelligence tool for building interactive charts and dashboards by dragging and dropping fields from connected data sources.
concepts.example: A sales manager connects Tableau to the company database, drags 'Region' to columns and 'Revenue' to rows, and gets a bar chart; adding a date filter turns it into an interactive dashboard.

concepts.name: Tabular Data
concepts.description: Data arranged in a table where each row is an example and each column is a feature with a consistent type; the typical input for classical ML models.
concepts.example: A table of 1,000 passengers with columns age, ticket class, fare and survived is tabular data. Each row is one passenger and each column has one type, perfect for a gradient boosting model.

concepts.name: Target Encoding
concepts.description: Encoding each category of a feature by a statistic of the target for that category, typically its smoothed mean; powerful for high cardinality but prone to leakage without cross-fitting.
concepts.example: For a city feature, replace 'Paris' with the average purchase rate of Parisian customers, say 0.12, and 'Lyon' with 0.08. Thousands of cities become one numeric column.

concepts.name: Target Leakage
concepts.description: When training features contain information about the target that would not be available at prediction time, making validation scores look unrealistically good.
concepts.example: A churn model uses 'account closed date' as a feature. It predicts churn perfectly in testing, but at prediction time no current customer has that date filled in, so it is useless.

concepts.name: Temporal Leakage
concepts.description: Leakage in time-dependent data where a model is trained or validated using information from the future relative to the prediction time, e.g. by random splits on time series.
concepts.example: Randomly splitting 2020-2024 stock data puts some 2024 days in training and 2022 days in test, letting the model 'see the future'. Splitting by date (train on 2020-2023, test on 2024) avoids this.

concepts.name: Test Data
concepts.description: A held-out portion of data never used for training or tuning, used only at the end to estimate how well a model will perform on new, unseen data.
concepts.example: Of 10,000 labelled images, 1,000 are locked away. After all training and tuning, the model is run once on those 1,000 to report its final accuracy.

concepts.name: Text Data
concepts.description: Data consisting of written natural language, such as documents, messages or reviews, which must be tokenized and converted to numbers before most models can use it.
concepts.example: Product reviews like 'Great battery, terrible camera' are text data. Before a model can use them, the words must be split into tokens and turned into numbers like counts or embeddings.

concepts.name: tf–idf
concepts.description: A word weighting that multiplies a term's frequency in a document by the log inverse of how many documents contain it, highlighting words distinctive to that document.
concepts.example: In 1,000 news articles, 'the' appears everywhere so it gets weight near 0, but 'volcano' appears 5 times in one article and in only 10 articles overall, so it gets a high weight for that article.

concepts.name: Time Series Cross-Validation
concepts.description: Cross-validation for time-ordered data that always trains on earlier observations and tests on later ones, sliding or expanding the training window forward.
concepts.example: With 5 years of data: train on year 1, test on year 2; train on years 1-2, test on year 3; and so on. The model is never tested on data earlier than its training data.

concepts.name: Train-Test Contamination
concepts.description: Leakage caused by fitting preprocessing steps such as scaling or imputation on the full dataset before splitting, so information from the test set seeps into training.
concepts.example: You scale all 10,000 rows using their overall mean and SD, then split into train and test. The training data has now been shaped by test values, so test scores look slightly better than reality.

concepts.name: Training Data
concepts.description: The labeled or unlabeled examples a machine learning model is fitted on, from which it learns its parameters; its size and quality largely determine how well the model performs.
concepts.example: To build a cat-vs-dog classifier you collect 20,000 photos labelled cat or dog. The model studies these to learn which pixel patterns mean whiskers, ears and tails.

concepts.name: Training–Serving Skew
concepts.description: A mismatch between how features are computed or distributed during training and during production serving, causing a model to perform worse live than in testing.
concepts.example: In training, 'average order value' was computed over 30 days, but the live app computes it over 7 days by mistake. The model sees different numbers in production and its accuracy drops.

concepts.name: Two-Stage Least Squares
concepts.description: An instrumental variable estimator that first regresses the endogenous variable on the instruments, then regresses the outcome on the fitted values to get a consistent causal estimate.
concepts.example: Stage 1: regress years of schooling on distance to college. Stage 2: regress wages on the predicted schooling from stage 1. The slope estimates schooling's causal effect on wages.

concepts.name: Unstructured Data
concepts.description: Data without a predefined tabular schema, such as text, images, audio and video, which needs special processing to extract usable features.
concepts.example: Emails, photos, voice recordings and videos have no fixed columns. To analyse 10,000 customer calls, you must first transcribe them and extract features like topics or sentiment.

concepts.name: Uplift Modeling
concepts.description: Predicting the incremental effect of a treatment, such as a marketing offer, on each individual, to target those whose behavior is most changed rather than those most likely to respond.
concepts.example: Some customers buy anyway, some never buy, and some buy only if they get a coupon. An uplift model finds that third group so coupons are not wasted on people who would have bought regardless.

concepts.name: Validation Data
concepts.description: A portion of data held out from training and used to tune hyperparameters and choose between models, separate from the final test set.
concepts.example: Of 10,000 examples, 7,000 train the model, 1,500 are used to compare settings like tree depth, and 1,500 are kept for the final test. The middle 1,500 are the validation set.

concepts.name: Variance Reduction
concepts.description: Techniques that lower the variance of an experiment's effect estimate, such as CUPED, stratification or regression adjustment, so smaller effects can be detected with the same sample.
concepts.example: A test needs 100,000 users to detect a 1% lift. Using CUPED with pre-experiment spend cuts the variance by half, so the same lift can be detected with about 50,000 users.

concepts.name: Wide and Long Format
concepts.description: Two layouts for the same table: wide format has one row per subject with a column per measurement, long format has one row per subject-measurement pair; pivoting converts between them.
concepts.example: Wide: one row per student with columns math, science, art. Long: three rows per student with columns student, subject, score. The same grades, arranged two ways.

concepts.name: Winsorizing
concepts.description: Limiting extreme values by replacing those beyond chosen percentiles, such as the 1st and 99th, with the percentile values themselves, reducing outlier influence without dropping data.
concepts.example: Incomes are mostly $30k-$150k, but one is $50 million. Winsorizing at the 99th percentile, say $400k, replaces the $50 million with $400k so it no longer dominates the average.

concepts.name: Activation Function
concepts.description: A nonlinear function applied to a neuron's weighted input, such as ReLU, sigmoid or tanh; without it, stacked layers would collapse into a single linear transformation.
concepts.example: ReLU turns -3 into 0 and 5 into 5. Without such a bend, two stacked layers that each multiply by 2 and 3 are just one layer multiplying by 6, so depth adds nothing.

concepts.name: CPU Offloading
concepts.description: Moving tensors such as activations, parameters or optimizer state from GPU memory to CPU memory during training and back when needed, trading transfer time for the ability to fit larger models.
concepts.example: A model needs 40 GB of activations but the GPU has 24 GB. During the forward pass, activations are copied to CPU RAM and brought back for the backward pass, so training fits at the cost of extra transfer time.

concepts.name: Activity Regularization
concepts.description: A penalty added to the loss on a layer's outputs (its activations), typically L1 or L2, that encourages sparse or small activations.
concepts.example: Adding 0.01 x (sum of absolute activations) to the loss pushes a hidden layer to keep most neurons near zero, so each input lights up only a few neurons.

concepts.name: AdaBelief
concepts.description: An Adam variant that scales its steps by the variance of the gradient around its moving average, the 'belief', taking larger steps when the observed gradient matches the prediction.
concepts.example: If the gradient keeps matching its recent average, AdaBelief sees low 'surprise' and takes a big step. If gradients jump around, it becomes cautious and takes small steps.

concepts.name: AdaDelta
concepts.description: An adaptive learning-rate optimizer that extends AdaGrad with decaying averages of squared gradients and of squared updates, removing the need to set a global learning rate.
concepts.example: AdaGrad's step sizes shrink forever as squared gradients pile up. AdaDelta instead averages only recent squared gradients and scales by recent update sizes, so learning keeps going without a learning rate.

concepts.name: Adafactor
concepts.description: A memory-efficient optimizer similar to Adam that stores only factored row and column estimates of the squared-gradient matrix and uses relative step sizes; used for large Transformers.
concepts.example: For a 1,000 x 1,000 weight matrix, Adam stores 1 million second-moment values. Adafactor stores 1,000 row averages and 1,000 column averages, 2,000 numbers, and rebuilds an approximation.

concepts.name: AdaGrad
concepts.description: An optimizer that gives each parameter its own learning rate by dividing by the square root of its accumulated squared gradients, so rarely updated features get larger steps.
concepts.example: In a text model, the weight for 'the' gets gradients every step, so its step size shrinks fast. The weight for a rare word like 'quokka' gets few gradients, so it keeps a large step size.

concepts.name: ADALINE
concepts.description: An early single-layer neural network that, unlike the perceptron, updates weights using the error of its linear output before thresholding, minimizing squared error with the delta rule.
concepts.example: If the target is 1 and ADALINE's linear output is 0.6, it nudges weights by 0.4 times the input, even though thresholding 0.6 would already give 1. The perceptron would not update at all.

concepts.name: Adam
concepts.description: A widely used optimizer that combines momentum (a moving average of gradients) with per-parameter scaling by a moving average of squared gradients, plus bias correction of both averages.
concepts.example: Adam keeps a running average of each weight's gradient, like momentum, and of its squared gradient. Steps are average gradient divided by the root of average squared gradient, so noisy weights move cautiously.

concepts.name: AdaMax
concepts.description: A variant of Adam that replaces the average of squared gradients with an exponentially weighted infinity norm, giving more stable step sizes in some settings.
concepts.example: Adam divides by the root of an average of squared gradients. AdaMax instead divides by a decaying maximum of absolute gradients, so one huge gradient sets a stable cap on step sizes.

concepts.name: AdamW
concepts.description: A version of Adam that applies weight decay directly to the weights instead of adding an L2 term to the gradient, which works better with adaptive optimizers; a default for Transformers.
concepts.example: With weight decay 0.01 and learning rate 0.001, AdamW shrinks each weight by 0.001 x 0.01 of its value every step, separately from the Adam update, so large-gradient weights are regularized as strongly as others.

concepts.name: Adapter Modules
concepts.description: Small bottleneck layers inserted into a frozen pretrained network, usually a Transformer, and trained for a new task, so only a few percent of the parameters need updating.
concepts.example: A 1-billion-parameter language model is frozen, and small 2-layer adapters of a few million parameters are inserted into each block. Training only the adapters adapts it to legal text cheaply.

concepts.name: Adaptive Instance Normalization
concepts.description: A layer that aligns the per-channel mean and variance of content features to those of style features, enabling fast arbitrary style transfer and style conditioning in StyleGAN.
concepts.example: A photo's features have per-channel means and spreads. AdaIN rescales them to match a painting's means and spreads, so the photo's content takes on the painting's style.

concepts.name: Additive Attention
concepts.description: An attention mechanism that scores each encoder state by passing it with the decoder state through a small feedforward network with tanh; introduced by Bahdanau for neural machine translation.
concepts.example: Translating 'le chat noir', the decoder asks a tiny network: given what I'm about to write and each French word's state, how relevant is it? Scores like 0.1, 0.8, 0.1 come out, so 'chat' dominates when writing 'cat'.

concepts.name: Adversarial Example
concepts.description: An input deliberately altered with small, often imperceptible perturbations that cause a model to make a wrong prediction, frequently with high confidence.
concepts.example: Add carefully chosen noise to a panda photo, changing each pixel by less than 1%, and a classifier suddenly says 'gibbon' with 99% confidence, though to a human the picture looks identical.

concepts.name: Adversarial Training
concepts.description: A defense that trains a model on adversarial examples generated during training, typically with projected gradient descent, solving a min-max problem to improve robustness.
concepts.example: Like a boxer sparring with a partner who always aims at their weakest spot: each training batch is first attacked with PGD to find the worst nearby inputs, and the model then learns to classify those correctly.

concepts.name: AlexNet
concepts.description: A deep convolutional network that won ImageNet 2012 by a wide margin, popularizing ReLU, dropout, data augmentation and GPU training and launching the deep learning boom.
concepts.example: In 2012 AlexNet's top-5 error on ImageNet was about 15%, versus 26% for the runner-up. It was trained for about a week on two consumer GPUs, a gap so large that computer vision switched to deep learning almost overnight.

concepts.name: All-Reduce
concepts.description: A collective communication operation in which every worker contributes a tensor and all receive the combined result, such as the sum; used to average gradients in data-parallel training.
concepts.example: Four GPUs hold gradients 1, 2, 3 and 4. After an all-reduce with sum, every GPU holds 10 (divide by 4 and each has the average 2.5), so all replicas apply exactly the same update.

concepts.name: Alpha Dropout
concepts.description: A dropout variant for SELU networks that sets dropped units to SELU's negative saturation value and rescales, preserving the mean and variance needed for self-normalization.
concepts.example: Plain dropout sets units to 0, but in a SELU network 0 is not the 'resting' value, so it skews the statistics. Alpha dropout sets dropped units to about -1.76 and then applies an affine fix so the mean stays near 0 and variance near 1.

concepts.name: AMSGrad
concepts.description: A variant of Adam that keeps the running maximum of past squared-gradient averages so effective learning rates never increase, fixing a convergence flaw in the original Adam.
concepts.example: If Adam sees a huge gradient once and then small ones, its squared-gradient average shrinks and the step size grows again. AMSGrad remembers the largest average seen so far, so the step can only shrink, not jump back up.

concepts.name: Artificial Neuron
concepts.description: The basic unit of a neural network: it multiplies its inputs by weights, adds a bias, and passes the sum through an activation function to produce its output.
concepts.example: Inputs 2 and 3 with weights 0.5 and -1 and bias 1 give 2·0.5 + 3·(-1) + 1 = -1. A ReLU activation turns -1 into 0, so the neuron stays silent for this input.

concepts.name: Asynchronous Distributed Training
concepts.description: Distributed training in which workers compute gradients and update shared parameters without waiting for each other, improving throughput at the cost of stale gradients.
concepts.example: Ten workers each compute a gradient and push it to the server whenever they finish, without waiting. A slow worker may push a gradient computed on weights that are already 5 updates old, a 'stale' gradient.

concepts.name: Attention Mechanism
concepts.description: A mechanism that lets a model compute a weighted average of a set of values, with weights based on each item's relevance to a query, so it can focus on the most important parts of its input.
concepts.example: Asked 'what colour is the car?', you glance mostly at the car in a photo and barely at the sky. Attention does the same: it gives items weights like 0.9 car, 0.1 sky and averages their information with those weights.

concepts.name: Attention-Based Sequence-to-Sequence Model
concepts.description: An encoder-decoder RNN in which, at each decoding step, the decoder attends over all encoder hidden states to build a context vector instead of relying on one fixed summary vector.
concepts.example: Translating a 40-word sentence, a plain seq2seq must squeeze it all into one vector. With attention, when writing the 30th output word the decoder can look directly at the input words it corresponds to, so long sentences translate far better.

concepts.name: Attention Weights
concepts.description: The normalized scores, usually produced by a softmax, that determine how much each input element contributes to an attention output; they are often inspected to interpret models.
concepts.example: Translating 'the black cat' to French, the weights for producing 'chat' might be 0.05 on 'the', 0.15 on 'black' and 0.80 on 'cat'. Plotting them as a heatmap shows which words were aligned.

concepts.name: AutoAugment
concepts.description: A method that uses reinforcement learning to search for the best data augmentation policy, a set of image operations with probabilities and magnitudes, for a given dataset.
concepts.example: Instead of a human guessing 'rotate up to 10 degrees and flip half the time', a controller tries thousands of policies such as 'with 60% chance shear by 0.3, then posterize', keeping those that raise validation accuracy.

concepts.name: Autoencoder
concepts.description: A neural network trained to reconstruct its input through a narrower hidden layer, so the bottleneck learns a compressed representation useful for dimensionality reduction and denoising.
concepts.example: Squeeze a 784-pixel digit image into just 32 numbers, then rebuild the 784 pixels from them. To succeed, those 32 numbers must capture what matters, like stroke shape and slant, not pixel noise.

concepts.name: Auxiliary Loss
concepts.description: An extra loss attached to an intermediate layer or a side task and added to the main objective, providing additional gradient signal that helps train deep networks.
concepts.example: GoogLeNet attached two small classifiers to middle layers and added 0.3 times their losses to the main loss. The middle layers then receive a strong, direct training signal instead of a faint one from 20 layers above.

concepts.name: Average Pooling
concepts.description: A downsampling operation in CNNs that replaces each window of a feature map with the average of its values, shrinking spatial size while smoothing the features.
concepts.example: A 2×2 window holding 1, 3, 5 and 7 is replaced by 4. Doing this over a 4×4 feature map with stride 2 produces a 2×2 map, a quarter of the size, where each value summarises its region.

concepts.name: Backbone Network
concepts.description: The main feature-extracting part of a model, often a pretrained CNN or Transformer such as ResNet, on top of which task-specific heads for detection or segmentation are attached.
concepts.example: A detector might use ResNet-50 trained on ImageNet as its backbone: it turns a photo into rich feature maps, and a small detection head on top just learns to read boxes and classes from them.

concepts.name: Backpropagation
concepts.description: The algorithm that computes the gradient of the loss with respect to every weight in a neural network by applying the chain rule backward from the output layer, making gradient-based training possible.
concepts.example: For y = w·x with loss (y - t)², if x = 2, w = 3, t = 4, then y = 6 and dLoss/dy = 2(6 - 4) = 4, so dLoss/dw = 4·x = 8. Backprop repeats this chain-rule step layer by layer, from the loss backward.

concepts.name: Backpropagation Through Time
concepts.description: Backpropagation applied to a recurrent network by unrolling it across time steps into a deep feedforward graph and summing the gradients for the weights shared across steps.
concepts.example: An RNN reading 'h-e-l-l-o' is unrolled into five copies of the same cell. The error at the last step flows back through all five copies, and the gradients for the shared weights from each copy are added up.

concepts.name: Backward Pass
concepts.description: The phase of a training step in which gradients of the loss are propagated from the output back through the network to every parameter, following the forward pass.
concepts.example: After the forward pass predicts 0.7 for a target of 1, the backward pass starts at the loss and walks back layer by layer, computing for each weight how much nudging it would reduce the error.

concepts.name: Batch Gradient Descent
concepts.description: Gradient descent that computes the gradient over the entire training set before each parameter update, giving exact but slow steps on large datasets.
concepts.example: With 1 million training examples, each single step first computes the loss on all million and averages their gradients. Steps are smooth and exact, but you wait a whole dataset pass to move once.

concepts.name: Batch Normalization
concepts.description: A layer that normalizes each feature across the mini-batch to zero mean and unit variance and then applies a learned scale and shift, speeding up and stabilizing deep network training.
concepts.example: If a unit's outputs in a batch are 2, 4 and 6 (mean 4, std about 1.63), batch norm rescales them to about -1.22, 0 and 1.22, then applies a learned scale and shift such as ×2 + 0.5.

concepts.name: Batch Renormalization
concepts.description: An extension of batch normalization that corrects batch statistics toward running averages, reducing dependence on mini-batch size and the train-test mismatch for small or non-i.i.d. batches.
concepts.example: With a batch of only 4 images, the batch mean may be far from the true mean. Batch renorm adds a correction that pulls the normalization toward the running averages, so training behaves more like inference.

concepts.name: Batch Size
concepts.description: The number of training examples used to compute one gradient update; it trades off gradient noise and generalization against memory use and hardware efficiency.
concepts.example: With 10,000 examples and batch size 100, one epoch is 100 updates; with batch size 1,000 it is only 10 updates, each based on a less noisy gradient but needing 10 times the memory.

concepts.name: Bayesian Neural Network
concepts.description: A neural network whose weights are probability distributions instead of single values, so predictions average over many plausible networks and come with uncertainty estimates.
concepts.example: Instead of a weight being exactly 0.5, it is 'about 0.5, give or take 0.2'. Sampling 100 networks gives 100 predictions; if they agree, the model is confident, and if they scatter, it says it is unsure.

concepts.name: Beam Search
concepts.description: A decoding algorithm that keeps the k most probable partial sequences at each step, expanding and pruning them, to find higher-probability outputs than greedy decoding.
concepts.example: With beam width 2, after word 1 keep the top two, 'The' (0.5) and 'A' (0.4). Expand each with every next word, score the full two-word phrases, and again keep only the best two, continuing to the end.

concepts.name: bfloat16
concepts.description: A 16-bit floating-point format with float32's 8-bit exponent but only 7 mantissa bits, keeping float32's range so deep networks can train in half the memory, usually without loss scaling.
concepts.example: float32 can store numbers up to about 3×10³⁸; FP16 overflows past 65,504. bfloat16 keeps float32's range but only about 3 significant digits, so 1.001 rounds to 1.0, which training usually tolerates.

concepts.name: Bias (Neural Networks)
concepts.description: A learnable constant added to a neuron's weighted sum, letting its output shift independently of the inputs, like the intercept in a linear model.
concepts.example: A neuron with weight 2 and no bias gives 0 whenever the input is 0. Adding a bias of 3 makes it output 3 there, shifting the whole line up, just like the +b in y = 2x + b.

concepts.name: Bidirectional Recurrent Neural Network
concepts.description: A recurrent network that runs one RNN forward and another backward over a sequence and combines their states, so each position sees both past and future context.
concepts.example: In 'He said Teddy bears are cute' vs 'He said Teddy Roosevelt was president', whether 'Teddy' is a name depends on the next word. A backward RNN supplies that future context to each position.

concepts.name: Binarized Neural Network
concepts.description: A neural network whose weights and activations are constrained to +1 or −1, so most arithmetic becomes cheap XNOR and bit-count operations; trained with straight-through gradients.
concepts.example: Weights become just +1 or -1, each stored in one bit. Multiplying +1/-1 values is like XNOR on bits, so a dot product turns into XNOR plus counting the 1s, which is very fast and tiny on hardware.

concepts.name: Binary Cross-Entropy
concepts.description: The standard loss for binary classification, −[y log p + (1 − y) log(1 − p)], which heavily penalizes confident wrong predictions; it is the negative Bernoulli log-likelihood.
concepts.example: If the true label is 1 and the model predicts 0.9, the loss is -ln 0.9 ≈ 0.105. Predicting 0.1 instead costs -ln 0.1 ≈ 2.30, about 22 times more, punishing the confident mistake.

concepts.name: Boltzmann Machine
concepts.description: A network of symmetrically connected stochastic binary units that defines a probability distribution through an energy function and learns to model data by matching its statistics.
concepts.example: Each unit randomly turns on or off, more likely to switch on when its connected neighbours are on and weights are positive. Run long enough, the network visits low-energy configurations that look like the training data.

concepts.name: Bottleneck Block
concepts.description: A residual block that uses a 1×1 convolution to reduce channels, a 3×3 convolution, then another 1×1 convolution to restore channels, cutting computation in deep ResNets.
concepts.example: On 256 channels, a 1×1 conv first shrinks to 64, the 3×3 conv runs on just 64, and another 1×1 expands back to 256. This is far cheaper than two 3×3 convs on all 256 channels.

concepts.name: Caffe
concepts.description: An early open-source deep learning framework from UC Berkeley, written in C++ with models defined in configuration files, widely used for convolutional networks in computer vision.
concepts.example: To build a model in Caffe, you wrote a text file listing layers, such as a convolution with 96 filters followed by a ReLU, and ran it with a command-line tool. Many early ImageNet models were shared as Caffe files.

concepts.name: Capsule (Neural Networks)
concepts.description: A group of neurons whose activity vector represents an entity, with the vector's length encoding the probability the entity exists and its orientation encoding properties such as pose.
concepts.example: A 'nose' capsule outputs a vector: its length 0.9 says 'a nose is very likely here', and its direction encodes the nose's position, size and tilt, so one capsule describes both presence and pose.

concepts.name: Capsule Network
concepts.description: A neural network built from capsules that pass information through routing-by-agreement, aiming to model part-whole spatial relationships better than CNN pooling does.
concepts.example: A face capsule should only activate if the eye, nose and mouth capsules agree about where the face is and how it is rotated. Scrambled facial parts do not agree, so the network can reject them.

concepts.name: Catastrophic Forgetting
concepts.description: The tendency of a neural network to abruptly lose performance on earlier tasks when trained on new ones, because the new updates overwrite shared weights.
concepts.example: Train a network to recognise cats and dogs to 95% accuracy, then train it only on cars and trucks. Afterwards its cat-dog accuracy may crash to near chance, because the same weights were rewritten for vehicles.

concepts.name: Categorical Cross-Entropy
concepts.description: A loss function for multiclass classification that compares a predicted probability distribution (usually from softmax) with the one-hot true label, penalizing low probability on the correct class.
concepts.example: Classes cat, dog, bird; true label dog, one-hot [0, 1, 0]. If softmax gives [0.2, 0.7, 0.1], the loss is -ln 0.7 ≈ 0.36, because only the probability of the true class counts.

concepts.name: Causal Convolution
concepts.description: A 1D convolution arranged so each output depends only on current and past inputs, never future ones, which makes it usable for autoregressive sequence models like WaveNet.
concepts.example: A size-3 filter computes output at time 10 from inputs 8, 9 and 10, never 11. Padding the sequence with two zeros at the start keeps outputs aligned with inputs, so the model can predict tomorrow's value without cheating.

concepts.name: Causal Masking
concepts.description: A mask applied to attention scores so each position can only attend to itself and earlier positions, preventing a decoder from peeking at future tokens during training.
concepts.example: For 'I love cats', when processing 'love' the scores for 'cats' are set to minus infinity before the softmax, giving them weight 0. Each word sees only itself and earlier words, as during real generation.

concepts.name: Cell State
concepts.description: The internal memory vector of an LSTM that flows across time steps with only small, gated updates, letting the network carry information over long sequences.
concepts.example: Like a conveyor belt running through a factory: at each step workers may remove a few items (forget gate) or add a few (input gate), but the belt mostly carries what was already there, so a subject from 50 words back can survive.

concepts.name: Chainer
concepts.description: A Python deep learning framework from Preferred Networks that pioneered define-by-run (dynamic) computation graphs, an approach later popularized by PyTorch.
concepts.example: In Chainer you could write a normal Python loop like 'for word in sentence:' inside the model, and the graph for backprop was recorded as the code ran. PyTorch later adopted this define-by-run style.

concepts.name: Channel (CNN)
concepts.description: One slice along the depth dimension of a CNN tensor, such as the red channel of an image or one feature map produced by a single filter in a convolutional layer.
concepts.example: A 224×224 colour photo has 3 channels: red, green and blue intensity grids. After a layer with 64 filters, the output has 64 channels, each a grid showing where one filter's pattern appears.

concepts.name: Channel Shuffle
concepts.description: An operation that reorders channels across groups after a grouped convolution so information can mix between groups; it is the key trick in ShuffleNet.
concepts.example: With 3 groups of 2 channels [a1 a2 | b1 b2 | c1 c2], shuffling gives [a1 b1 c1 | a2 b2 c2], so each group in the next grouped conv receives channels from every earlier group.

concepts.name: Model Checkpointing
concepts.description: Periodically saving a model's weights, optimizer state and training progress to disk so training can resume after a crash or the best version can be restored later.
concepts.example: A 3-day training run saves weights and optimizer state every epoch. If the machine crashes on day 2, you reload the last checkpoint and lose an hour of progress instead of two days.

concepts.name: Class Activation Mapping
concepts.description: A technique that highlights which image regions drove a CNN's class prediction by weighting the final convolutional feature maps with the classifier's weights for that class.
concepts.example: For a photo labelled 'dog', CAM weights each final feature map by how much it contributes to the 'dog' score and adds them up. The resulting heatmap glows over the dog's head, not the grass.

concepts.name: Convolutional Neural Network
concepts.description: A neural network that uses convolutional layers with small shared filters to detect local patterns, plus pooling, making it highly effective for images and other grid data.
concepts.example: To find cats anywhere in a photo, a CNN slides the same small 3×3 'whisker detector' over every location instead of learning a separate detector per position, then stacks layers so edges become ears and ears become faces.

concepts.name: Compound Scaling
concepts.description: A method from EfficientNet that scales a network's depth, width and input resolution together using fixed ratios, instead of enlarging just one dimension.
concepts.example: To use about 2× more compute, EfficientNet does not just double the depth. It grows depth by 1.2×, width by 1.1× and resolution by 1.15× together, since bigger images need deeper, wider networks.

concepts.name: Conditional Computation
concepts.description: The idea of activating only part of a network for each input, for example via routing to experts, so model capacity can grow without proportional compute cost.
concepts.example: A model with 8 expert subnetworks sends each token to only the 2 most relevant experts. It has 8 experts' worth of knowledge but costs about 2 experts' worth of compute per token.

concepts.name: Context Vector
concepts.description: A fixed or attention-weighted summary of an input sequence produced by an encoder, which a decoder uses to generate its output in sequence-to-sequence models.
concepts.example: For 'I am happy', an encoder produces states h1, h2 and h3. A plain model passes only h3 to the decoder; with attention, the context could be 0.1·h1 + 0.2·h2 + 0.7·h3 when translating 'happy'.

concepts.name: Continual Learning
concepts.description: The study of models that learn from a stream of tasks or data over time while keeping earlier knowledge, mainly fighting catastrophic forgetting.
concepts.example: A phone assistant learns new slang each month. Continual learning aims for it to pick up 'rizz' in October without forgetting what it learned in March, without retraining on everything from scratch.

concepts.name: Contractive Autoencoder
concepts.description: An autoencoder regularized by the norm of the encoder's Jacobian, encouraging representations that change little under small input perturbations.
concepts.example: If nudging an input pixel slightly changes the code a lot, the model pays a penalty. The encoder learns codes that stay steady for tiny wiggles but still change along directions where real data varies.

concepts.name: Contrastive Loss
concepts.description: A loss for learning embeddings that pulls similar pairs close together and pushes dissimilar pairs apart beyond a margin; used in Siamese networks and metric learning.
concepts.example: Two photos of the same person at distance 0.8 are pulled closer. Photos of different people at distance 0.5 with margin 1.0 are pushed apart, but only until they reach 1.0; beyond the margin they cost nothing.

concepts.name: 1D Convolution
concepts.description: A convolution that slides a filter along a single axis, typically time, to detect local patterns in sequences such as audio, sensor signals or text embeddings.
concepts.example: Slide the filter [1, 0, -1] along the temperatures 20, 22, 25, 25, 21: the outputs -5, -3, 4 show where the series is rising (negative) or falling (positive), a pattern detected anywhere in time.

concepts.name: 3D Convolution
concepts.description: A convolution whose filters slide over three dimensions, such as height, width and time in video or depth in medical volumes, capturing spatiotemporal patterns.
concepts.example: For a video clip, a 3×3×3 filter covers a 3×3 pixel patch across 3 frames at once, so it can detect motion, like an edge moving right, which a 2D filter on a single frame cannot see.

concepts.name: ConvLSTM
concepts.description: An LSTM in which the matrix multiplications are replaced by convolutions, so hidden states keep spatial structure; used for spatiotemporal tasks like precipitation nowcasting.
concepts.example: To predict the next radar image of rain clouds, each LSTM gate is computed with convolutions over the image grid, so the memory is itself a map that remembers where clouds were and how they drift.

concepts.name: ConvNeXt
concepts.description: A pure convolutional architecture that modernizes ResNet with Transformer-inspired design choices (large kernels, LayerNorm, GELU, inverted bottlenecks) to rival vision transformers.
concepts.example: Take a ResNet and apply Transformer-era tricks one by one: 7×7 depthwise kernels, LayerNorm, GELU, fewer activations. The resulting all-convolutional network matched Swin Transformer accuracy on ImageNet.

concepts.name: Convolutional Autoencoder
concepts.description: An autoencoder built from convolutional layers in the encoder and transposed convolutions or upsampling in the decoder, suited to compressing and reconstructing images.
concepts.example: A 28×28 digit is shrunk by conv layers to a 7×7×8 code, and transposed convolutions grow it back to 28×28. Trained on clean images, it can be used to compress them or to spot unusual ones that rebuild poorly.

concepts.name: Convolutional Layer
concepts.description: A neural network layer that slides learned filters over its input, computing local weighted sums to produce feature maps; weights are shared across positions.
concepts.example: A 3×3 vertical-edge filter slides over a 6×6 image, computing a weighted sum at each spot to make a 4×4 output. The same 9 weights are used everywhere, so 9 parameters cover the whole image.

concepts.name: Cosine Annealing
