concepts.description: A learning rate schedule that lowers the rate from a maximum to a minimum following half a cosine curve, giving a smooth decay that often improves final accuracy.
concepts.example: Over 100 epochs from 0.1 to 0, the rate is 0.1 at epoch 0, 0.05 at epoch 50 and nearly 0 at epoch 100, falling slowly at first, fastest in the middle, and gently again near the end.

concepts.name: Cosine Embedding Loss
concepts.description: A loss that pushes the cosine similarity of two embeddings toward 1 for matching pairs and below a margin for non-matching pairs, used in similarity learning.
concepts.example: For a matching pair of sentence embeddings with cosine 0.6, the loss is 1 - 0.6 = 0.4. For a non-matching pair with margin 0.2 and cosine 0.5, the loss is 0.5 - 0.2 = 0.3, pushing them apart.

concepts.name: Credit Assignment Problem
concepts.description: The problem of figuring out which earlier actions, or which internal network weights, were responsible for an eventual outcome or error, central to RL and backpropagation.
concepts.example: A chess program loses on move 40. Was it move 39, or a quiet pawn move on move 12? Credit assignment is figuring out which earlier decisions deserve blame, just as backprop decides which weights caused an error.

concepts.name: Concatenated ReLU
concepts.description: An activation that concatenates ReLU(x) and ReLU(-x), keeping both positive and negative information and doubling the number of output channels.
concepts.example: For input -3, ReLU gives 0 and loses all information. CReLU outputs the pair (ReLU(-3), ReLU(3)) = (0, 3), so the negative signal survives in a second channel, doubling the outputs.

concepts.name: Cross-Attention
concepts.description: Attention in which queries come from one sequence and keys and values from another, letting a decoder attend to encoder outputs or text guide image features.
concepts.example: In translation, the English decoder word being written forms the query, and the French encoder outputs supply keys and values. In Stable Diffusion, image patches query the text prompt's tokens.

concepts.name: Connectionist Temporal Classification
concepts.description: A loss for sequence tasks with unaligned labels, like speech recognition, that sums over all alignments using a blank symbol so the network needs no frame-level labels.
concepts.example: Audio of 'cat' has 50 frames but only 3 letters. CTC lets the network output frames like 'cc-aa--t-' (with '-' as blank), collapse repeats and blanks to 'cat', and adds up the probability of every such path.

concepts.name: cuDNN
concepts.description: NVIDIA's GPU-accelerated library of tuned deep learning primitives such as convolutions, pooling and RNNs, used under the hood by frameworks like PyTorch and TensorFlow.
concepts.example: When PyTorch runs a 3×3 convolution on an NVIDIA GPU, it calls cuDNN, which picks among several hand-tuned algorithms, such as Winograd or FFT-based ones, whichever is fastest for those tensor sizes.

concepts.name: Curriculum Learning
concepts.description: A training strategy that presents examples from easy to hard, like a school curriculum, which can speed up training and improve generalization.
concepts.example: Teach a model arithmetic like a child: first single-digit sums, then two-digit, then long problems. Starting with easy cases gives it a foothold before the hard ones would just confuse it.

concepts.name: CutMix
concepts.description: A data augmentation that cuts a patch from one training image and pastes it onto another, mixing the labels in proportion to the patch area.
concepts.example: Paste a 50×50 patch of a dog photo onto a 100×100 cat photo. The patch covers 25% of the image, so the label becomes 75% cat and 25% dog.

concepts.name: Cutout
concepts.description: A data augmentation that masks out random square regions of an input image, forcing the network to use more of the image and acting as a regularizer.
concepts.example: Black out a random 16×16 square on each 32×32 training image. If the square hides a cat's face, the model must still recognise it from ears, fur and tail, so it learns not to rely on one feature.

concepts.name: Cyclical Learning Rate
concepts.description: A schedule in which the learning rate repeatedly cycles between lower and upper bounds instead of only decaying, helping escape poor regions and reducing tuning.
concepts.example: The rate rises linearly from 0.001 to 0.006 over 2,000 steps, falls back over the next 2,000, and repeats. The high phases help jump out of poor regions; the low phases let it settle.

concepts.name: DARTS
concepts.description: A neural architecture search method that relaxes the discrete choice of operations into a softmax-weighted mixture, so the architecture can be optimized by gradient descent.
concepts.example: Instead of choosing either a 3×3 conv or max pooling for an edge, DARTS uses 0.7×conv + 0.3×pool with learnable weights. After training by gradient descent, the strongest operation is kept.

concepts.name: Deep Belief Network
concepts.description: A generative model built by stacking restricted Boltzmann machines trained greedily layer by layer; historically important for pretraining deep networks around 2006.
concepts.example: Train one RBM on raw pixels, then a second RBM on the first one's hidden activities, then a third on top. In 2006, stacking these and then fine-tuning made deep networks trainable for the first time.

concepts.name: Deep Ensembles
concepts.description: Training several neural networks independently with different random initializations and averaging their predictions, which improves accuracy and uncertainty estimates.
concepts.example: Train 5 copies of the same network from different random starts. On a familiar image all 5 say 'cat'; on a strange image they split 2 cat, 2 dog, 1 fox, signalling that the model is uncertain.

concepts.name: Deep Learning
concepts.description: A branch of machine learning that trains neural networks with many layers to learn hierarchical representations directly from raw data like images, audio and text.
concepts.example: Instead of hand-coding 'look for whiskers and pointy ears', you feed millions of labelled photos into a many-layered network, and it discovers its own features from edges up to faces.

concepts.name: Stacked Recurrent Neural Network
concepts.description: A recurrent network with several recurrent layers stacked on top of each other, where each layer's hidden sequence becomes the next layer's input.
concepts.example: With 3 stacked layers reading a sentence, layer 1 might track letters and words, layer 2 phrases, layer 3 overall meaning. Each layer reads the full output sequence of the layer below.

concepts.name: Deep Sets
concepts.description: A neural architecture for set-valued inputs that applies the same network to each element, sums the results, and processes the sum, guaranteeing permutation invariance.
concepts.example: To predict a team's total score from its players, embed each player with the same small network, sum the embeddings, and pass the sum through another network. Listing the players in any order gives the same answer.

concepts.name: DeepSpeed
concepts.description: A Microsoft library for efficient large-scale model training, known for ZeRO memory optimizations, pipeline parallelism and mixed-precision training on PyTorch.
concepts.example: A 13-billion-parameter model will not fit on one GPU with Adam states. Adding DeepSpeed's ZeRO with a config file splits those states across 16 GPUs, so the same PyTorch training script now runs.

concepts.name: Deformable Convolution
concepts.description: A convolution whose sampling positions are shifted by learned offsets, letting the filter adapt its shape to object geometry instead of using a fixed grid.
concepts.example: A 3×3 filter normally samples a fixed square grid. With deformable convolution, each of its 9 sample points gets a learned offset, so the filter can stretch along a curved fish or a tilted car.

concepts.name: Delta Rule
concepts.description: A learning rule that updates a linear unit's weights in proportion to the error between target and output times the input; gradient descent on squared error.
concepts.example: Target 1, output 0.6, input 2, learning rate 0.1: the weight changes by 0.1 × (1 - 0.6) × 2 = 0.08. Large errors and large inputs produce large corrections.

concepts.name: Denoising Autoencoder
concepts.description: An autoencoder trained to reconstruct clean inputs from deliberately corrupted versions, forcing it to learn robust features rather than just copying the input.
concepts.example: Feed in a photo with 30% of pixels randomly set to black, and train the network to output the original clean photo. To fill the holes it must learn what images really look like.

concepts.name: Dense Block
concepts.description: The building block of DenseNet, in which each layer receives the concatenated feature maps of all preceding layers in the block as input.
concepts.example: In a 4-layer dense block, layer 4 receives the input plus the outputs of layers 1, 2 and 3 stacked together. If each layer adds 32 channels to a 64-channel input, layer 4 sees 64 + 96 = 160 channels.

concepts.name: Dense Connectivity
concepts.description: A connectivity pattern where each layer is connected to every later layer by concatenating its feature maps, improving feature reuse and gradient flow.
concepts.example: Instead of each layer passing only to the next, layer 5 receives the outputs of layers 1, 2, 3 and 4 stacked together, so an edge detector learned early can be reused directly by much later layers.

concepts.name: DenseNet
concepts.description: A CNN architecture made of dense blocks, where each layer takes all earlier feature maps as input, giving strong accuracy with relatively few parameters.
concepts.example: DenseNet-121 reaches ResNet-50-level ImageNet accuracy with roughly a third of the parameters (about 8M vs 25M), because layers reuse earlier features instead of relearning them.

concepts.name: Depthwise Convolution
concepts.description: A convolution that applies a separate filter to each input channel independently, without mixing channels, greatly reducing computation and parameters.
concepts.example: For a 3-channel RGB input, use three separate 3×3 filters: one for red, one for green, one for blue. That is 27 weights, versus 81 for each output channel of a standard 3×3 conv over all 3 channels.

concepts.name: Depthwise Separable Convolution
concepts.description: A factorization of a standard convolution into a depthwise convolution per channel followed by a 1x1 pointwise convolution, used in efficient networks like MobileNet.
concepts.example: From 32 to 64 channels with 3×3 kernels, a normal conv needs 3·3·32·64 ≈ 18,400 weights. Depthwise (3·3·32 = 288) plus pointwise (32·64 = 2,048) needs about 2,300, roughly 8 times fewer.

concepts.name: Dice Loss
concepts.description: A segmentation loss based on the Dice coefficient that measures overlap between predicted and true masks, well suited to imbalanced foreground and background.
concepts.example: A tumour covers 100 pixels; the prediction covers 80, of which 60 overlap. Dice = 2·60/(100 + 80) ≈ 0.67, so the loss is 0.33. Thousands of correct background pixels don't inflate the score.

concepts.name: Differentiable Neural Computer
concepts.description: A neural network coupled to an external memory matrix that it reads and writes through differentiable attention, extending the Neural Turing Machine with better memory allocation.
concepts.example: Asked about the shortest route on the London Underground, a DNC writes station links into its memory, tracks the order of its writes, and reads them back step by step, like a computer using RAM.

concepts.name: Dilated Convolution
concepts.description: A convolution whose filter taps are spaced apart by a dilation rate, enlarging the receptive field without extra parameters or downsampling.
concepts.example: A 3×3 filter with dilation 2 samples every other pixel, covering a 5×5 area with only 9 weights. Stacking layers with dilation 1, 2, 4, 8 grows the view exponentially, as in WaveNet.

concepts.name: Dilation Rate
concepts.description: The spacing between the elements of a convolution kernel; a rate of 1 is ordinary convolution and larger rates skip input positions to see wider context.
concepts.example: With 3 taps and rate 1 the filter reads positions 0, 1, 2; with rate 2 it reads 0, 2, 4; with rate 4 it reads 0, 4, 8, covering 9 positions with the same 3 weights.

concepts.name: Distributed Representation
concepts.description: Representing a concept as a pattern of activity across many units, each unit taking part in many concepts, as in word embeddings, rather than one unit per concept.
concepts.example: Instead of one 'grandmother neuron' for each person, use 300 units: 'king' and 'queen' share many active units for royalty and differ on a few for gender, so similar concepts get overlapping patterns.

concepts.name: Dot-Product Attention
concepts.description: An attention mechanism that scores each key by its dot product with the query, turns the scores into weights with softmax, and averages the values accordingly.
concepts.example: Query [1, 0] scores keys [2, 0] and [0, 3] as 2 and 0. Softmax gives weights 0.88 and 0.12, so the output is 0.88 of the first value plus 0.12 of the second.

concepts.name: Stochastic Depth
concepts.description: A regularizer that randomly skips entire residual blocks during training, replacing them with the identity, so deep networks train faster and generalize better.
concepts.example: In a 100-block ResNet, each block is skipped with some probability during training, so a given step might use only 80 blocks. At test time all blocks are used, like an ensemble of shallower networks.

concepts.name: DropBlock
concepts.description: A dropout variant for CNNs that zeroes out contiguous square regions of feature maps instead of independent units, which regularizes convolutional features more effectively.
concepts.example: Dropping single pixels in a feature map barely helps, since neighbours carry the same information. DropBlock blanks a 7×7 square instead, so the network can't simply read the hidden feature from adjacent pixels.

concepts.name: DropConnect
concepts.description: A regularizer that randomly sets individual weights, rather than activations, to zero during training; a generalization of dropout.
concepts.example: A layer with 100 input-to-output weights might randomly zero 50 of them on one step, a different 50 the next. Dropout would instead zero whole neurons, removing all their connections at once.

concepts.name: Dropout
concepts.description: A regularization technique that randomly zeroes a fraction of neuron activations during training, preventing co-adaptation and reducing overfitting.
concepts.example: Like a team where any player might be absent on a given day, so everyone must learn several roles. With p = 0.5, each step randomly silences half the neurons, so none can rely on one specific partner.

concepts.name: Dying ReLU Problem
concepts.description: When ReLU neurons get stuck outputting zero for all inputs, their gradient is zero and they stop learning; often caused by large learning rates or bad initialization.
concepts.example: A large update pushes a neuron's bias to -100. Now its input is negative for every example, ReLU outputs 0, the gradient is 0, and nothing can ever push it back. That neuron is dead for good.

concepts.name: Dynamic Computational Graph
concepts.description: A computation graph built on the fly as code runs (define-by-run), so models can use ordinary control flow and change structure for each input, as in PyTorch.
concepts.example: A model that runs a loop 'while sentence not finished' builds a graph with 5 steps for a 5-word sentence and 12 for a 12-word one, recorded fresh as the Python code executes each time.

concepts.name: Dynamic Routing Between Capsules
concepts.description: The capsule network algorithm that iteratively routes lower-level capsule outputs to higher-level capsules that agree with their predictions, replacing pooling.
concepts.example: Lower capsules for 'eye' and 'mouth' each predict where a face should be. Over three iterations, they send more of their output to the face capsule whose predictions agree, and less to ones that disagree.

concepts.name: Echo State Network
concepts.description: A recurrent network with a large, fixed, randomly connected reservoir; only the linear output layer is trained, making training fast and simple.
concepts.example: Drop a stone into a pond (the fixed random reservoir) and watch the ripples. You never change the pond; you only learn which ripples to read out, by a simple linear regression on the reservoir states.

concepts.name: Effective Receptive Field
concepts.description: The part of a unit's theoretical receptive field that actually influences it strongly; it is roughly Gaussian and usually much smaller than the theoretical size.
concepts.example: A unit's theoretical receptive field might be 100×100 pixels, but measuring its gradients shows pixels near the centre matter far more. The influential region looks like a blurred blob perhaps 30 pixels wide.

concepts.name: EfficientNet
concepts.description: A family of CNNs found by neural architecture search and scaled with compound scaling, built from MBConv blocks, achieving high accuracy with few parameters and FLOPs.
concepts.example: EfficientNet-B0 was found by architecture search; B1 to B7 scale it up with compound scaling. B7 reached about 84% ImageNet accuracy while being over 8 times smaller than the best previous model.

concepts.name: EfficientNetV2
concepts.description: An improved EfficientNet that adds fused MBConv blocks and progressive learning with growing image sizes, training much faster with better parameter efficiency.
concepts.example: Training starts on small 128-pixel images with weak augmentation and grows to about 300 pixels with stronger augmentation. Early layers use fused MBConv blocks, which run faster on GPUs and TPUs.

concepts.name: Elastic Weight Consolidation
concepts.description: A continual learning method that penalizes changes to weights important for earlier tasks, with importance estimated from the Fisher information.
concepts.example: After learning task A, each weight gets a spring tying it to its old value. Weights crucial for task A get stiff springs; unimportant ones get loose springs, so task B mostly changes the unimportant ones.

concepts.name: Elman Network
concepts.description: A simple recurrent network in which the previous hidden layer state is fed back as extra input through context units, an early form of the modern RNN.
concepts.example: Reading 'the cat sat', the hidden layer's activity after 'cat' is copied into context units, which are fed back alongside 'sat'. This simple loop lets the network remember what came before.

concepts.name: Exponential Linear Unit
concepts.description: An activation equal to x for positive inputs and alpha times (e^x - 1) for negative ones, giving smooth negative outputs that push mean activations toward zero.
concepts.example: With alpha 1, ELU(2) = 2 and ELU(-1) = e⁻¹ - 1 ≈ -0.63, while ELU(-10) ≈ -1. Unlike ReLU, negative inputs give small negative outputs that level off at -1.

concepts.name: Embedding
concepts.description: A learned dense vector representation of a discrete item such as a word, user or product, placed so that similar items end up close together in vector space.
concepts.example: Each word gets a vector of, say, 300 numbers. 'Paris' and 'London' end up near each other, and vector('king') - vector('man') + vector('woman') lands near vector('queen').

concepts.name: Embedding Layer
concepts.description: A neural network layer that maps integer ids to rows of a trainable matrix, acting as a lookup table equivalent to multiplying a one-hot vector by a weight matrix.
concepts.example: With a vocabulary of 10,000 words and 64 dimensions, the layer stores a 10,000×64 table. Word id 42 simply returns row 42, the same as multiplying a one-hot vector with a 1 at position 42 by the table.

concepts.name: ENAS
concepts.description: Efficient Neural Architecture Search: a controller samples subgraphs of one large shared network, so candidate architectures share weights and search is far cheaper.
concepts.example: Rather than training 1,000 candidate networks from scratch, ENAS builds one big network containing them all as subgraphs. Each candidate borrows the shared weights, cutting search from thousands of GPU-days to under one.

concepts.name: Encoder–Decoder Architecture
concepts.description: An architecture in which an encoder compresses the input into a representation and a decoder generates the output from it; used for translation, captioning and segmentation.
concepts.example: Like an interpreter who first listens to a whole French sentence and forms the idea in their head (encoder), then speaks it in English word by word (decoder).

concepts.name: Epoch
concepts.description: One complete pass of a learning algorithm over the entire training dataset; training usually runs for many epochs.
concepts.example: With 50,000 training images and batch size 100, one epoch is 500 steps. Training for 30 epochs means the model sees every image 30 times, usually shuffled into a new order each time.

concepts.name: Evolutionary Neural Architecture Search
concepts.description: Neural architecture search using evolutionary algorithms, where a population of architectures is mutated, trained and selected by validation accuracy, as in AmoebaNet.
concepts.example: Start with 100 random networks, train each briefly, keep the most accurate, and create children by small mutations like 'swap a 3×3 conv for a 5×5'. Over many generations the population evolves better designs.

concepts.name: Expert Parallelism
concepts.description: A distributed training strategy for mixture-of-experts models that places different experts on different devices and routes tokens between them with all-to-all communication.
concepts.example: A model with 64 experts on 8 GPUs puts 8 experts on each GPU. Each token is sent to the GPU holding its chosen expert, processed there, and sent back, with all-to-all exchanges.

concepts.name: Exploding Gradient Problem
concepts.description: When gradients grow exponentially as they are backpropagated through many layers or time steps, causing huge unstable updates; often fixed with gradient clipping.
concepts.example: If each of 50 layers multiplies the backward signal by 1.5, the gradient at the first layer is 1.5⁵⁰, about 637 million times larger. One update then hurls the weights far away, often producing NaN.

concepts.name: Exponential Learning Rate Decay
concepts.description: A learning rate schedule that multiplies the learning rate by a fixed factor every step or epoch, so it shrinks exponentially over training.
concepts.example: Start at 0.1 and multiply by 0.9 each epoch: 0.1, 0.09, 0.081, ... After 10 epochs it is about 0.035, and after 50 about 0.0005.

concepts.name: Exponential Moving Average of Weights
concepts.description: Keeping a running exponential average of model weights during training and using the averaged weights for evaluation, which usually gives smoother, better models.
concepts.example: After each step, keep a shadow copy updated as shadow = 0.999·shadow + 0.001·weights. The live weights jitter around, but the shadow averages roughly the last 1,000 steps and usually tests better.

concepts.name: Exposure Bias
concepts.description: The mismatch where a sequence model is trained on ground-truth previous tokens (teacher forcing) but must use its own possibly wrong predictions at inference, so errors compound.
concepts.example: A student practising with an answer key always continues from correct steps. On the exam, one early mistake leaves them on an unfamiliar path. A text model trained only on true prefixes faces the same thing.

concepts.name: fastText
concepts.description: A fast library and model for word embeddings and text classification that represents words as bags of character n-grams, so it can embed rare and unseen words.
concepts.example: 'Where' is represented by n-grams such as '<wh', 'whe', 'her', 'ere', 're>'. An unseen word like 'whereabouts' still gets a sensible vector from the n-grams it shares with known words.

concepts.name: Feature Extraction (Transfer Learning)
concepts.description: A transfer learning approach that keeps a pretrained network frozen and uses its outputs as features for training only a new small classifier head.
concepts.example: To classify 5 flower types with only 500 photos, run each photo through a frozen ImageNet ResNet, take its 2,048-number feature vector, and train just a small logistic regression on top.

concepts.name: Feature Map
concepts.description: The output of applying one convolutional filter across an input, a 2D grid showing where in the input that filter's pattern was detected.
concepts.example: Slide a vertical-edge filter over a photo of a door. The resulting feature map is bright along the door frame's sides and dark elsewhere, a map of where vertical edges are.

concepts.name: Feature Pyramid Network
concepts.description: An architecture that combines a CNN's deep low-resolution features with shallow high-resolution ones through a top-down pathway, giving strong features at every scale for detection.
concepts.example: Deep CNN layers know 'this is a car' but are coarse; early layers are sharp but naive. FPN upsamples deep features and adds them to earlier ones, so even small, distant cars can be detected at high resolution.

concepts.name: Federated Averaging
concepts.description: The standard federated learning algorithm: clients train locally for a few steps on their own data, and a server averages the resulting model weights.
concepts.example: Ten phones each train the keyboard model on their owner's texts for a few steps. The server receives only the updated weights, averages them weighted by data size, and sends the new model back.

concepts.name: Feedforward Neural Network
concepts.description: A neural network in which information flows only forward from inputs through hidden layers to outputs, with no cycles or recurrent connections.
concepts.example: Like an assembly line: a photo's pixels enter, pass through layer 1, then layer 2, then the output, and nothing ever flows backward or loops, so the answer comes in a single pass.

concepts.name: Fast Gradient Sign Method
concepts.description: Fast Gradient Sign Method: creates an adversarial example in one step by adding a small perturbation in the direction of the sign of the loss gradient with respect to the input.
concepts.example: For each pixel, check whether increasing it raises the loss. Then move every pixel by ε = 2/255 in the harmful direction, all in one step. A tiny, even shift like this can fool many classifiers.

concepts.name: Fine-tuning
concepts.description: Continuing to train a pretrained model on a new, usually smaller, dataset so it adapts to a specific task while reusing what it already learned.
concepts.example: Take a model trained on 1 million general photos and train it a little more, with a small learning rate, on 2,000 X-rays. It keeps its knowledge of edges and textures and learns what pneumonia looks like.

concepts.name: Fixup Initialization
concepts.description: An initialization scheme for residual networks that rescales branch weights and zero-initializes the last layer so very deep networks train without normalization layers.
concepts.example: In a 1,000-layer ResNet without normalization, outputs would blow up as 1,000 branches add together. Fixup sets each branch's last layer to zero and scales the others down, so every block starts as an identity.

concepts.name: Flax
concepts.description: A neural network library built on JAX that provides modules, parameter handling and training utilities in a functional programming style.
concepts.example: In Flax you define a model class with layers, but the weights live in a separate dictionary that you pass in explicitly. That fits JAX's pure functions, so jit and grad apply directly.

concepts.name: Floating-Point Formats in Deep Learning
concepts.description: The number formats used in deep learning, such as FP32, FP16, BF16 and FP8, which trade numeric range and precision for memory and speed.
concepts.example: Storing 1 billion weights in FP32 needs 4 GB; FP16 or BF16 needs 2 GB and FP8 just 1 GB. Each step down saves memory and speed but represents numbers more coarsely.

concepts.name: FLOPs
concepts.description: The number of floating-point operations needed for a computation, commonly used to measure the compute cost of a neural network's forward pass or training run.
concepts.example: Multiplying a 1,000×1,000 matrix by a 1,000-long vector takes about 1 million multiplies and 1 million adds, roughly 2 million FLOPs. Add up such counts for every layer to get a network's cost.

concepts.name: Focal Loss
concepts.description: A modification of cross-entropy that down-weights easy, well-classified examples so training focuses on hard ones; introduced for dense object detection in RetinaNet.
concepts.example: An easy background patch predicted correctly with p = 0.9 gets its cross-entropy multiplied by (1 - 0.9)² = 0.01. A hard object at p = 0.3 is multiplied by 0.49, so hard examples dominate training.

concepts.name: Forward Pass
concepts.description: Computing a neural network's output by passing the input through each layer in order; during training it is followed by a backward pass computing gradients.
concepts.example: For input 3, layer 1 computes 2·3 + 1 = 7, ReLU keeps 7, and the output layer computes 0.5·7 = 3.5. Feeding the input through layer by layer to the prediction is the forward pass.

concepts.name: FP8
concepts.description: 8-bit floating-point formats (E4M3 and E5M2) supported by recent GPUs to speed up and shrink deep learning training and inference with careful scaling.
concepts.example: E4M3 has 4 exponent and 3 mantissa bits, reaching about 448, with finer precision for forward weights and activations. E5M2 trades precision for range up to 57,344, suiting gradients. Scale factors keep values in range.

concepts.name: Fully Sharded Data Parallel
concepts.description: Fully Sharded Data Parallel: a training method that shards parameters, gradients and optimizer states across GPUs and gathers them only when needed, cutting memory per device.
concepts.example: With 4 GPUs, each stores only a quarter of the model. Before computing a layer, they briefly share their pieces to rebuild it, compute, then throw away the borrowed parts, so each GPU holds about a quarter of the memory.

concepts.name: Fully Connected Layer
concepts.description: A layer in which every input is connected to every output by a learned weight, computing a matrix-vector product plus bias, usually followed by an activation.
concepts.example: A layer from 3 inputs to 2 outputs has a 2×3 weight matrix plus 2 biases, 8 parameters. Each output is a weighted sum of all 3 inputs plus its bias.

concepts.name: Gated Recurrent Unit
concepts.description: A recurrent unit with update and reset gates that control how much past information to keep, a simpler alternative to LSTM with similar performance.
concepts.example: Reading a review, the update gate decides at 'not' to overwrite memory, and keeps that until 'good' arrives. A gate value near 0 means 'keep the old memory', near 1 'replace it with new'.

concepts.name: Gating Mechanism
concepts.description: A learned sigmoid-valued multiplier that controls how much of a signal passes through, letting networks like LSTMs selectively keep, forget or output information.
concepts.example: Like a dimmer switch on a light: a sigmoid outputs 0.2, and the signal [5, 10] is multiplied by it to give [1, 2]. The network learns when to open the gate fully and when to nearly close it.

concepts.name: Graph Convolutional Network
concepts.description: Graph Convolutional Network: each layer updates a node's features by averaging transformed features of its neighbors using a normalized adjacency matrix.
concepts.example: In a social network, each person's new features become the normalized average of their own and their friends' features, then a learned weight transform. Two layers mix in information from friends of friends.

concepts.name: GeGLU
concepts.description: A gated linear unit variant that uses GELU as the gating activation, used in Transformer feed-forward layers for better quality than plain ReLU.
concepts.example: A Transformer feed-forward layer computes two projections of the input, a and b, and outputs GELU(a)·b. Each feature of b is let through only as much as GELU of a allows.

concepts.name: Gaussian Error Linear Unit
concepts.description: An activation that multiplies an input by the standard normal CDF of that input, a smooth ReLU-like curve used in BERT, GPT and most Transformers.
concepts.example: GELU(x) = x·Φ(x). For x = 1, Φ(1) ≈ 0.84 gives 0.84; for x = -1, Φ(-1) ≈ 0.16 gives -0.16; for x = 3 it is almost 3. Like a softened ReLU with a small dip below zero.

concepts.name: Generalization Gap
concepts.description: The difference between a model's performance on training data and on unseen test data; a large gap signals overfitting.
concepts.example: A model scores 99% on training data and 80% on test data, a 19-point gap. It has partly memorised the training examples instead of learning patterns that carry over.

concepts.name: Geometric Deep Learning
concepts.description: A framework for deep learning on non-Euclidean data like graphs, meshes and manifolds, unified by building networks that respect symmetries such as permutations and rotations.
concepts.example: A CNN works on images because shifting a cat doesn't change 'cat'. Geometric deep learning asks what the matching symmetry is for molecules, meshes or graphs, such as rotations or node reordering, and builds networks that respect it.

concepts.name: GhostNet
concepts.description: An efficient CNN that produces part of its feature maps with cheap linear operations from a few intrinsic ones (ghost modules), reducing compute for mobile devices.
concepts.example: Many feature maps from a conv layer look like near-copies of each other. GhostNet computes, say, half of them with a real convolution and makes the rest with cheap depthwise ops on those, roughly halving compute.

concepts.name: Global Average Pooling
concepts.description: Averaging each feature map over all spatial positions to a single number, turning a CNN's final features into a vector without fully connected layers.
concepts.example: A final 7×7×512 feature map becomes a 512-number vector by averaging each 7×7 grid. A '7×7 map of cat-ear detections' becomes one number: how much cat-ear there is overall.

concepts.name: Global Max Pooling
concepts.description: Taking the maximum value of each feature map over all spatial positions, producing one number per channel that records the strongest detection anywhere.
concepts.example: A 7×7 map from a 'wheel detector' with highest value 9.1 becomes just 9.1. The vector says 'a wheel appears strongly somewhere', no matter where.

concepts.name: GloVe
concepts.description: Global Vectors: a word embedding method that fits word vectors so their dot products match the logarithm of word co-occurrence counts across a corpus.
concepts.example: 'Ice' appears near 'solid' far more often than 'steam' does, and 'steam' near 'gas' more than 'ice' does. GloVe fits vectors so these co-occurrence ratios show up as differences between word vectors.

concepts.name: Gated Linear Unit
concepts.description: Gated Linear Unit: an activation that splits the input into two halves and multiplies one by the sigmoid of the other, letting the network learn what passes through.
concepts.example: Split an 8-number output into halves a and b, and output a·sigmoid(b). Where sigmoid(b) is near 0, that feature of a is blocked; near 1, it passes through unchanged.

concepts.name: Inception (GoogLeNet)
concepts.description: A 22-layer CNN that won ImageNet 2014 using Inception modules, which run several filter sizes in parallel, plus 1x1 convolutions to stay computationally cheap.
concepts.example: GoogLeNet won ImageNet 2014 with about 6.7% top-5 error using only about 7 million parameters, versus AlexNet's 60 million, by stacking nine Inception modules.

concepts.name: GPipe
concepts.description: A pipeline parallelism library that splits a model across devices and splits each batch into micro-batches so different stages can compute at the same time.
concepts.example: Split a model over 4 GPUs (layers 1-6, 7-12, ...) and a batch into 8 micro-batches. While GPU 2 handles micro-batch 1, GPU 1 starts micro-batch 2, so the GPUs work at the same time like an assembly line.

concepts.name: GPU Computing for Deep Learning
concepts.description: Using graphics processors, with thousands of parallel cores, to run the large matrix operations of neural networks far faster than on CPUs.
concepts.example: A CPU is a few expert chefs; a GPU is thousands of line cooks each doing simple chopping. A neural network's matrix multiplications are millions of simple, independent multiply-adds, perfect for the line cooks.

concepts.name: Grad-CAM
concepts.description: A visual explanation method that weights a CNN's feature maps by the average gradient of the class score, producing a heatmap of regions important to the prediction.
concepts.example: For 'tabby cat', compute the gradient of its score with respect to each final feature map and average it per map to get an importance weight. Weighting and summing the maps, then applying ReLU, gives a heatmap.

concepts.name: Gradient Accumulation
concepts.description: Summing gradients over several small mini-batches before taking one optimizer step, simulating a larger batch size when GPU memory is limited.
concepts.example: Your GPU fits only 8 images but you want batches of 32. Run 4 batches of 8, adding their gradients each time without updating, then take one optimizer step on the sum, as if you had used 32.

concepts.name: Gradient Checking
concepts.description: Verifying an implementation of backpropagation by comparing its gradients with numerical finite-difference approximations.
concepts.example: To check dLoss/dw, nudge w up and down by 0.0001 and compute (loss(w + h) - loss(w - h)) / 2h. If backprop says 3.14 and this gives 3.1399, the code is likely right; if it gives 6.28, there is a bug.

concepts.name: Gradient Checkpointing
concepts.description: Saving memory during training by storing only some intermediate activations and recomputing the others during the backward pass, trading compute for memory.
concepts.example: A 100-layer network normally stores all 100 layers' activations for backprop. Keeping only every 10th and recomputing the others when needed cuts activation memory by about 10 times, at roughly 30% more compute.

concepts.name: Gradient Clipping
concepts.description: Rescaling or capping gradients when their norm or values exceed a threshold, preventing exploding gradients from causing huge parameter updates.
concepts.example: With threshold 5, a gradient of length 50 is scaled down by 10 to length 5, keeping its direction. A gradient of length 3 is left alone.

concepts.name: Gradient Compression
concepts.description: Reducing the communication cost of distributed training by quantizing or sparsifying gradients before workers exchange them.
concepts.example: Instead of sending all 100 million gradient values each step, a worker sends only the 1% largest, or rounds each to 1 bit, keeping the leftover locally to add next time. Network traffic drops by 30 to 100 times.

concepts.name: Gradient Flow
concepts.description: How gradient signals propagate backward through a network's layers; good gradient flow means early layers receive gradients that are neither vanishing nor exploding.
concepts.example: Like water flowing back through pipes from output to input. Plain deep networks have pipes that narrow, so a trickle reaches the first layers; residual connections and normalization keep them wide.

concepts.name: Gradient Noise
concepts.description: The randomness in mini-batch gradient estimates compared with the full-batch gradient; it depends on batch size and can help SGD escape sharp minima.
concepts.example: The full-dataset gradient for a weight is 2.0, but mini-batches of 32 give 1.6, 2.5, 1.9, 2.3. That scatter is gradient noise, and with batches of 128 it would be about half as wide.

concepts.name: Gradient Norm
concepts.description: The length (usually L2 norm) of the gradient vector during training, monitored to detect instability and used as the threshold quantity in gradient clipping.
concepts.example: A gradient [3, 4] has L2 norm √(9 + 16) = 5. If the norm usually sits around 1 and suddenly spikes to 500, training is likely becoming unstable.

concepts.name: Gradient Tape
concepts.description: A record of operations performed during the forward pass, played back in reverse to compute gradients with reverse-mode automatic differentiation, as in TensorFlow's GradientTape.
concepts.example: Like recording a dance routine: during the forward pass, each operation, say 'multiply by 3, then square', is written onto a tape. To get gradients, you play the tape backward, applying each step's derivative.

concepts.name: Graph Neural Network
concepts.description: A neural network that operates on graphs by repeatedly passing and aggregating messages between connected nodes to learn node, edge or whole-graph representations.
concepts.example: To predict whether a molecule is toxic, each atom starts with its element type, then repeatedly collects messages from bonded neighbours. After 3 rounds each atom knows its 3-bond neighbourhood, and pooling all atoms gives the prediction.

concepts.name: Greedy Decoding
concepts.description: Generating a sequence by picking the single most probable token at each step; fast and simple but can miss higher-probability overall sequences.
concepts.example: If 'The' has probability 0.5, pick it; if 'cat' then has 0.4, pick it, and so on. But 'A dog' might have overall probability 0.3, beating 'The cat' at 0.2, and greedy never looks at it.

concepts.name: Grokking
concepts.description: A phenomenon where a network first memorizes its training data and then, long after training loss is near zero, suddenly starts generalizing to test data.
concepts.example: A small Transformer learning modular addition reaches 100% training accuracy within a few thousand steps while test accuracy stays near chance. After many thousands more steps, test accuracy suddenly leaps to near 100%.

concepts.name: Group Normalization
concepts.description: A normalization that divides channels into groups and normalizes within each group per example, working well with small batch sizes unlike batch normalization.
concepts.example: With 32 channels split into 8 groups of 4, each image's mean and variance are computed over its 4 channels and all pixels in each group. Nothing depends on other images, so a batch of 2 works fine.

concepts.name: Grouped Convolution
concepts.description: A convolution that splits input channels into groups and convolves each group separately, cutting parameters and compute; used in AlexNet and ResNeXt.
concepts.example: With 64 input and 64 output channels split into 2 groups, each half of the outputs sees only its 32 inputs. Weights drop from 3·3·64·64 to 2·(3·3·32·32), exactly half.

concepts.name: Gumbel-Softmax
concepts.description: A differentiable approximation to sampling from a categorical distribution that adds Gumbel noise to logits and applies a temperature-controlled softmax.
concepts.example: To 'sample' one of 3 options with logits [2, 1, 0], add random Gumbel noise to each, then apply softmax with temperature 0.1. The result is almost one-hot, like [0.99, 0.01, 0.00], yet gradients can flow through it.

concepts.name: Half-Precision Floating-Point Format
concepts.description: The 16-bit floating-point format (FP16) with 5 exponent and 10 mantissa bits, halving memory and speeding computation at the cost of range and precision.
concepts.example: FP16 stores numbers in 2 bytes instead of 4, so a model's weights take half the memory. But its largest value is 65,504 and it rounds 1.0001 to 1.0, so tiny gradients may underflow to zero without loss scaling.

concepts.name: Hard Attention
concepts.description: Attention that selects a single location or item instead of a weighted average; non-differentiable, so it is trained with reinforcement learning or sampling estimators.
concepts.example: To read a house number in a large photo, a model chooses one 32×32 patch to look at, like moving its eyes, instead of blending all patches. That choice is like a die roll, so it is trained with REINFORCE.

concepts.name: Hard Negative Mining
concepts.description: Selecting the negative examples that a model currently finds hardest, and training more on them, to improve detectors and embedding models.
concepts.example: A face detector easily rejects sky patches but confuses round clocks with faces. Hard negative mining collects those clocks and trains on them more, instead of on millions of easy sky patches.

concepts.name: Hard Sigmoid
concepts.description: A piecewise linear approximation of the sigmoid function that clips a linear function to the range 0 to 1, cheaper to compute on mobile hardware.
concepts.example: One common form is clip((x + 3)/6, 0, 1). So x = -5 gives 0, x = 0 gives 0.5, x = 1.5 gives 0.75 and x = 5 gives 1. That is just one add, one divide and a clamp, with no exponentials.

concepts.name: Hard Swish
concepts.description: A cheap piecewise approximation of the Swish activation, x times hard sigmoid of x, used in MobileNetV3 for efficient mobile inference.
concepts.example: Using x·clip((x + 3)/6, 0, 1): at x = 3 it gives 3, at x = 0 it gives 0, at x = -1 it gives about -0.33, and below -3 it gives 0, closely tracking Swish on a phone CPU.

concepts.name: Hard Tanh
concepts.description: A piecewise linear activation that equals x between -1 and 1 and is clipped to -1 or 1 outside that range; a cheap approximation of tanh.
concepts.example: hard_tanh(0.4) = 0.4, hard_tanh(2.7) = 1 and hard_tanh(-5) = -1. It is a straight line through the middle, clamped flat at -1 and 1.

concepts.name: He Initialization
concepts.description: Initializing weights with variance 2 divided by the number of inputs, keeping activation variance stable across layers in ReLU networks.
concepts.example: A layer with 512 inputs gets random weights with variance 2/512, a standard deviation of about 0.0625. The factor 2 compensates for ReLU zeroing about half the signal, so it neither shrinks nor grows through 50 layers.

concepts.name: Network Head
concepts.description: The final task-specific part of a network, such as a classifier or box regressor, placed on top of a shared backbone that extracts features.
concepts.example: One ResNet backbone can feed several heads: a classifier head outputting 10 class scores, and a box head outputting 4 coordinates. Swapping heads adapts the same features to a new task.

concepts.name: Hebbian Learning
concepts.description: A biologically inspired learning rule summarized as cells that fire together wire together: a connection strengthens when its input and output neurons are active together.
concepts.example: If a 'bell' neuron and a 'food' neuron are often active at the same moment, the link between them strengthens: Δw = η·x·y. Eventually the bell alone excites the food neuron, as with Pavlov's dog.

concepts.name: Hidden Layer
concepts.description: Any layer of a neural network between the input and output layers, whose activations are internal representations learned during training.
concepts.example: In a network that predicts house prices from 10 features, a middle layer of 32 units might learn ideas like 'family-friendly' or 'luxury' that no one labelled. Those units are a hidden layer.

concepts.name: Hidden State
concepts.description: The vector a recurrent network carries from one time step to the next, summarizing what it has seen so far in the sequence.
concepts.example: Reading 'I grew up in France ... I speak fluent', an RNN updates a vector after each word. By the end, that hidden state still holds a trace of 'France', helping it predict 'French'.

concepts.name: Hierarchical Feature Learning
concepts.description: The way deep networks build complex features from simple ones layer by layer, for example edges into textures into object parts into whole objects.
concepts.example: In a face recognizer, layer 1 detects edges, layer 3 combines edges into eyes and noses, and layer 5 combines those into whole faces, like letters forming words forming sentences.

concepts.name: Highway Connection
concepts.description: A gated skip connection that mixes a layer's transformation with its unchanged input using a learned transform gate, letting information bypass layers.
concepts.example: A transform gate T decides the mix: output = T·H(x) + (1 - T)·x. With T = 0.1, 90% of the input passes straight through unchanged and only 10% comes from the layer's computation.

concepts.name: Highway Network
concepts.description: One of the first very deep feedforward networks, using gated highway connections so information and gradients can flow across many layers.
concepts.example: In 2015, before ResNet, highway networks trained plain feedforward networks with 100 layers. Gates let early training act like a shallow network that gradually learns to use more layers.

concepts.name: Hopfield Network
concepts.description: A recurrent network of binary units with symmetric weights that stores patterns as energy minima, acting as content-addressable associative memory.
concepts.example: Store pictures of the letters A, B and C. Show it a smudged A, and units flip one by one, lowering the network's energy, until it settles on the clean A, like recalling a song from a few notes.

concepts.name: Horovod
concepts.description: An open-source framework from Uber for distributed deep learning training that uses ring all-reduce to average gradients across GPUs with minimal code changes.
concepts.example: Add a few lines to a TensorFlow or PyTorch script, such as wrapping the optimizer, and launch it on 64 GPUs. Horovod averages gradients with ring all-reduce so each GPU applies the same update.

concepts.name: Hugging Face Hub
concepts.description: An online platform hosting hundreds of thousands of pretrained models, datasets and demos that can be downloaded and shared with a few lines of code.
concepts.example: Writing from_pretrained('bert-base-uncased') downloads a pretrained BERT from the Hub in seconds. You can fine-tune it on your data and push your version back for others to use.

concepts.name: Hypernetwork
concepts.description: A neural network that generates the weights of another neural network, enabling weight sharing, conditional models or compact parameterizations.
concepts.example: Instead of storing separate weights for 100 tasks, a small network takes a task id and outputs the 10,000 weights of the main network for that task. Gradients train the generator itself.

concepts.name: im2col
concepts.description: A trick that rearranges image patches into columns of a matrix so a convolution can be computed as one large matrix multiplication, using fast BLAS routines.
concepts.example: For a 3×3 filter on a 5×5 image, copy each of the 9 positions' 3×3 patches into a column, giving a 9×9 matrix. Multiplying by the filter flattened to a row computes all 9 outputs at once with fast matrix code.

concepts.name: Implicit Regularization
concepts.description: The tendency of training procedures like SGD, early stopping or overparameterization to prefer simpler solutions even without explicit regularization terms.
concepts.example: A network with 10 million parameters can fit 50,000 images in endless ways, many of them memorising nonsense. Yet SGD from small random weights tends to find solutions that generalise, even with no penalty added.

concepts.name: Inception Module
concepts.description: A block that runs 1x1, 3x3 and 5x5 convolutions and pooling in parallel and concatenates their outputs, with 1x1 convolutions to cut channels and compute.
concepts.example: On a 192-channel input, the module runs 1×1, 3×3 and 5×5 convs and 3×3 max pooling side by side, each branch with 1×1 convs to cut channels, then stacks the outputs, letting the network see both small and large patterns.

concepts.name: Inception-ResNet
concepts.description: A hybrid architecture combining Inception modules with residual connections, along with the closely related Inception v4, which trained faster and more accurately.
concepts.example: Inception-ResNet adds each Inception block's output back onto its input, as ResNet does. This reached similar accuracy to the plain Inception-v4 but trained noticeably faster.

concepts.name: Inception v3
concepts.description: An improved Inception network that factorizes large convolutions into smaller and asymmetric ones and adds batch normalization and label smoothing.
concepts.example: A 5×5 conv is replaced by two 3×3 convs (18 vs 25 weights per position), and a 7×7 by a 1×7 followed by a 7×1. Add batch norm and label smoothing, and ImageNet top-5 error falls to about 3.5% with an ensemble.

concepts.name: Independently Recurrent Neural Network
concepts.description: A recurrent network where each neuron only receives its own previous state (elementwise recurrence), making it easier to train very long and deep RNNs with ReLU.
concepts.example: In a normal RNN, neuron 1's next state mixes all neurons' previous states. In IndRNN neuron 1 only sees its own previous value times its own weight, which is easy to keep near 1 so memories last thousands of steps.

concepts.name: Inference Latency
concepts.description: The time a trained model takes to produce a prediction for one input or batch, a key metric with throughput for deploying models in production.
concepts.example: A speech assistant must answer in under 200 ms. If the model takes 150 ms to process one request on a phone, its latency fits; if batching 32 requests makes each wait 400 ms, throughput rises but users notice the lag.

concepts.name: InfoNCE Loss
concepts.description: A contrastive loss that treats one positive pair against many negatives as a softmax classification problem; it bounds mutual information and is used in SimCLR and CLIP.
concepts.example: An image's augmented copy is the right answer among 255 other images in the batch. Similarities like [0.9, 0.2, 0.1, ...] are divided by a temperature and softmaxed, and the loss is -log of the positive's probability.

concepts.name: Input Layer
concepts.description: The first layer of a neural network, which simply receives the raw feature values and passes them to the next layer without learning anything.
concepts.example: For a 28×28 handwritten digit, the input layer has 784 slots, one per pixel brightness. It does no computation; it just hands those 784 numbers to the first hidden layer.

concepts.name: Instance Normalization
concepts.description: A normalization that computes the mean and variance over each channel of each example separately; widely used in style transfer and image generation.
concepts.example: In style transfer, a photo with very high contrast and one with low contrast are each normalized per channel on their own. That strips out each image's own contrast, so the style network can apply a new one.

concepts.name: INT8 Quantization
concepts.description: Representing model weights and activations as 8-bit integers with a scale and zero point instead of floats, shrinking models and speeding up inference.
concepts.example: Weights ranging from -1.0 to 1.0 can be mapped to integers -127 to 127 with scale 1/127. A weight of 0.5 becomes 64, stored in 1 byte instead of 4, so a 400 MB model shrinks to about 100 MB.

concepts.name: Integrated Gradients
concepts.description: An attribution method that integrates the model's gradients along a straight path from a baseline input to the actual input to score each feature's contribution.
concepts.example: To explain why a model sees a cat, fade the image in from black in 50 steps, computing the pixel gradients at each step. Averaging them and multiplying by (image - black) gives each pixel's credit, and credits add up to the score change.

concepts.name: Internal Covariate Shift
concepts.description: The changing distribution of a layer's inputs during training as earlier layers update; originally proposed as the problem batch normalization solves.
concepts.example: Layer 5 is learning to handle inputs that average around 2. Then layer 4's weights update and its outputs start averaging 7, so layer 5 must readjust, like aiming at a target that keeps moving.

concepts.name: Inverse Square Root Schedule
concepts.description: The learning rate schedule from the original Transformer paper: linear warmup followed by decay proportional to the inverse square root of the step number.
concepts.example: With 4,000 warmup steps, the rate rises linearly until step 4,000, then falls like 1/√step: at step 16,000 it is half the peak, and at step 64,000 a quarter.

concepts.name: Inverted Residual Block
concepts.description: MobileNetV2's block that expands channels with a 1x1 convolution, applies a depthwise convolution, then projects back down with a linear bottleneck and a residual connection.
concepts.example: A 24-channel input is expanded 6× to 144 channels with a 1×1 conv, filtered by a cheap 3×3 depthwise conv, then projected back to 24 channels with no ReLU, and the skip links the thin ends.

concepts.name: Training Step
concepts.description: One update of a model's parameters, computed from a single mini-batch: a forward pass, a backward pass and an optimizer step.
concepts.example: With 10,000 images and batches of 100, one epoch is 100 training steps: each step feeds 100 images forward, backpropagates their loss, and nudges every weight once.

concepts.name: Iterative Magnitude Pruning
concepts.description: Repeatedly training a network, removing the smallest-magnitude weights, and retraining; used to find the sparse winning tickets of the lottery ticket hypothesis.
concepts.example: Train a net, delete the smallest 20% of weights, reset the rest to their starting values and retrain; after 10 rounds only about 11% of weights remain yet accuracy can hold.

concepts.name: Jordan Network
concepts.description: An early recurrent network in which the previous output, not the hidden state, is fed back as additional input through context units.
concepts.example: Predicting the next note of a melody, a Jordan net feeds back the note it just predicted rather than its internal thoughts, like a singer who only remembers the last note they sang.

concepts.name: Convolution Kernel
concepts.description: A small grid of learnable weights that slides over the input in a convolution, computing a weighted sum at each position to detect a specific pattern.
concepts.example: A 3x3 kernel with -1s in the left column, 0s in the middle and +1s on the right gives big outputs wherever an image goes from dark to bright left-to-right: a vertical edge detector.

concepts.name: K-FAC
concepts.description: Kronecker-Factored Approximate Curvature: a second-order optimizer approximating each layer's Fisher information matrix as a Kronecker product of two small matrices.
concepts.example: A layer with 1,000 inputs and 1,000 outputs has a million weights, so its exact curvature matrix has a trillion entries; K-FAC instead keeps two 1,000x1,000 matrices and combines them.

concepts.name: Kullback–Leibler Divergence Loss
concepts.description: A loss that measures the KL divergence between a target probability distribution and the predicted one; used in distillation, VAEs and policy regularization.
concepts.example: If the target says 70% cat, 30% dog and the model says 50/50, the KL loss is 0.7*ln(0.7/0.5) + 0.3*ln(0.3/0.5), about 0.08; it drops to zero once the model also says 70/30.

concepts.name: Knowledge Distillation
concepts.description: Training a small student model to match the softened output probabilities of a large teacher model, transferring the teacher's knowledge into a cheaper model.
concepts.example: A big teacher says an image is 90% dog, 9% wolf, 1% car. A small student learns from that whole spread, picking up that dogs look like wolves, not just the bare label 'dog'.

concepts.name: Kolmogorov–Arnold Network
concepts.description: A network inspired by the Kolmogorov-Arnold representation theorem that places learnable univariate functions, typically splines, on edges instead of fixed activations on nodes.
concepts.example: Where an MLP edge just multiplies by a number like 0.7, a KAN edge applies its own learned curve, say one that looks like x squared; nodes then simply add up what arrives.

concepts.name: Label Smoothing
concepts.description: A regularizer that replaces one-hot targets with a mix of the true label and a uniform distribution, discouraging overconfident predictions.
concepts.example: With 10 classes and smoothing 0.1, the target for 'cat' becomes 0.91 for cat and 0.01 for each other class instead of 1 and 0s, so the model stops chasing infinite confidence.

concepts.name: LAMB
concepts.description: A layer-wise adaptive optimizer that rescales Adam updates per layer by the ratio of weight norm to update norm, enabling very large batch training such as BERT in 76 minutes.
aliases: layer-wise adaptive moments for batch training
concepts.example: If a layer's weights have norm 10 but Adam proposes an update of norm 1, LAMB scales it by about 10, while a layer with weight norm 0.1 gets a much smaller step, keeping every layer's relative change balanced.

concepts.name: Large-Batch Training
concepts.description: Training with very large mini-batches to use many devices in parallel, which needs techniques like learning rate scaling and warmup to keep accuracy.
concepts.example: Instead of one GPU processing batches of 256, 64 GPUs each take 256 for a 16,384-image batch, so an epoch needs 64 times fewer steps, but the learning rate must be raised carefully.

concepts.name: Latent Space
concepts.description: The lower-dimensional space of internal representations learned by a model, where similar inputs lie close together and directions can carry meaning.
concepts.example: In a face model's latent space, moving a point along one direction adds a smile, and the midpoint between two faces' codes decodes to a believable blend of the two people.

concepts.name: Layer (Neural Networks)
concepts.description: A group of neurons that applies the same kind of transformation to its input, usually a linear map followed by an activation; networks are stacks of layers.
concepts.example: A layer with 3 inputs and 4 neurons multiplies the input by a 4x3 weight table, adds 4 biases and applies ReLU, turning a 3-number vector into a 4-number vector.

concepts.name: Layer Freezing
concepts.description: Keeping the weights of some layers of a network fixed during training, typically pretrained early layers, so only the remaining layers are updated.
concepts.example: Fine-tuning an ImageNet ResNet to spot plant diseases, you freeze the early edge-and-texture layers and only train the last block and the new classifier, which is faster and needs less data.

concepts.name: Layer Normalization
concepts.description: A normalization that standardizes all features of each example using its own mean and variance, independent of batch size; standard in Transformers and RNNs.
concepts.example: For one token with features [2, 4, 6], layer norm subtracts the mean 4 and divides by the spread, giving about [-1.22, 0, 1.22], no matter what other examples are in the batch.

concepts.name: Layer-wise Learning Rate Decay
concepts.description: Assigning smaller learning rates to earlier layers and larger ones to later layers during fine-tuning, since earlier layers hold more general features.
concepts.example: With top learning rate 1e-4 and decay 0.8 on a 12-layer BERT, layer 12 trains at 1e-4, layer 11 at 8e-5, and layer 1 at about 9e-6, so basic language knowledge is barely disturbed.

concepts.name: Leaky ReLU
concepts.description: A variant of ReLU that outputs a small slope times x for negative inputs instead of zero, avoiding dead neurons.
concepts.example: With slope 0.01, Leaky ReLU turns 5 into 5 and -5 into -0.05 instead of 0, so a neuron that only sees negative inputs still gets a small gradient and can recover.

concepts.name: Learning Rate Range Test
concepts.description: A procedure that trains briefly while increasing the learning rate exponentially and plots the loss, then picks a rate just before the loss starts to blow up.
concepts.example: Train for a few hundred batches as the learning rate grows from 1e-7 to 10. If loss falls fastest near 1e-3 and explodes past 1e-1, a rate around 1e-3 is a good pick.

concepts.name: Learning Rate Schedule
concepts.description: A rule for changing the learning rate during training, such as step decay, exponential decay or cosine annealing, typically lowering it over time.
concepts.example: Train with rate 0.1 for 30 epochs, then 0.01, then 0.001: big strides cover ground early and small steps settle into the bottom of the valley later.

concepts.name: Learning Rate Warmup
concepts.description: Starting training with a small learning rate that increases gradually over the first steps, which stabilizes early training, especially for Transformers and large batches.
concepts.example: Instead of starting at the target rate 0.001, increase it linearly from 0 over the first 1,000 steps, like easing onto a highway rather than flooring it from a standstill.

concepts.name: LeCun Initialization
concepts.description: Initializing weights with variance 1 divided by the number of inputs, keeping activation variance stable for tanh-like or SELU activations.
concepts.example: A neuron with 100 inputs gets weights drawn with variance 1/100, standard deviation 0.1, so summing 100 unit-variance inputs still gives an output with variance about 1.

concepts.name: LeNet
concepts.description: One of the earliest CNNs, developed by Yann LeCun for handwritten digit recognition, stacking convolutions, subsampling and fully connected layers.
concepts.example: LeNet-5 reads 32x32 digit images through two rounds of 5x5 convolution and 2x2 subsampling, then three fully connected layers output ten scores; it read bank checks in the 1990s.

concepts.name: Linear Activation Function
concepts.description: The identity activation f(x) = x, used in regression output layers; stacking layers that use only linear activations collapses into a single linear map.
concepts.example: A house-price model's last neuron uses f(x) = x so it can output 350,000 or -2. But two linear layers, y = 2(3x) are just y = 6x, so hidden layers need a nonlinearity.

concepts.name: Linear Scaling Rule
concepts.description: The heuristic that when the batch size is multiplied by k, the learning rate should also be multiplied by k, usually combined with warmup.
concepts.example: If batch 256 works with learning rate 0.1, then batch 8,192 (32 times larger) uses 3.2, ramped up over the first few epochs; this trained ResNet-50 on ImageNet in an hour.

concepts.name: Lion Optimizer
concepts.description: An optimizer found by program search that updates weights using only the sign of an interpolated momentum, using less memory than Adam.
concepts.example: Whether a weight's momentum is 0.003 or 30, Lion moves it by the same fixed amount, say 0.0001, in the sign's direction, and it stores one momentum buffer instead of Adam's two.

concepts.name: Local Attention
concepts.description: Attention restricted to a window of nearby positions around each query, reducing the cost from quadratic to linear in sequence length.
concepts.example: With a window of 128, each of 16,000 tokens attends to its 128 neighbours, about 2 million scores instead of 256 million, like reading a book while only glancing at nearby lines.

concepts.name: Local Minimum
concepts.description: A point where a function is lower than at all nearby points but not necessarily the lowest overall; gradient-based training can get stuck in such points.
concepts.example: A hiker in fog walks downhill into a small dip and stops, since every step from there goes up, yet a much deeper valley lies over the next ridge.

concepts.name: Local Response Normalization
concepts.description: A normalization used in AlexNet that divides each activation by a sum of squared activations in neighboring channels, mimicking lateral inhibition.
concepts.example: If one channel fires strongly at a pixel, LRN shrinks the neighbouring channels' values there, like a loud voice in a choir making nearby singers seem quieter.

concepts.name: Log-Cosh Loss
concepts.description: A regression loss equal to the logarithm of the hyperbolic cosine of the error; behaves like squared error near zero and like absolute error for large errors.
concepts.example: For an error of 0.1 the loss is about 0.005, like half the squared error; for an error of 10 it is about 9.3, close to 10 minus ln 2, so it grows linearly like absolute error.

concepts.name: Log-Softmax
concepts.description: The logarithm of the softmax function, computed stably with the log-sum-exp trick; it is paired with negative log-likelihood loss in classification.
concepts.example: For scores [1000, 1001], naive softmax overflows since e^1000 is infinite, but log-softmax subtracts the max first and safely returns about [-1.31, -0.31].

concepts.name: Logits
concepts.description: The raw, unnormalized scores a classification network outputs before softmax or sigmoid turns them into probabilities.
concepts.example: A cat/dog/bird classifier outputs [2.0, 1.0, -1.0]: these logits can be any size or sign, and softmax turns them into about 70%, 26%, 4%.

concepts.name: Long Short-Term Memory
concepts.description: A recurrent network whose cells use input, forget and output gates to control a memory cell state, letting it learn long-range dependencies without vanishing gradients.
concepts.example: Reading 'The keys, which were on the old wooden table, ARE...', an LSTM can hold 'plural' in its cell state across the clause and use it to choose 'are'.

concepts.name: Long-Term Dependencies
concepts.description: Relationships between elements far apart in a sequence, such as a pronoun and a distant noun, which simple RNNs struggle to learn.
concepts.example: In 'I grew up in France ... (50 words later) ... so I speak fluent ___', predicting 'French' depends on a word far back, which a simple RNN tends to have forgotten.

concepts.name: Lookahead Optimizer
concepts.description: An optimizer wrapper that runs an inner optimizer for k fast steps, then moves slow weights partway toward the fast weights, improving stability.
concepts.example: Adam takes 5 quick exploratory steps; Lookahead then moves the main weights halfway toward where Adam ended, like a hiker sending a scout ahead and following partway.

concepts.name: LoRA
concepts.description: Low-Rank Adaptation: fine-tuning a large model by freezing its weights and learning small low-rank update matrices added to selected layers, saving memory and storage.
concepts.example: Updating a 4,096x4,096 matrix means 16.8 million numbers, but LoRA learns it as a 4,096x8 times 8x4,096 product, about 65,000 numbers, while the original weights stay frozen.

concepts.name: Loss Landscape
concepts.description: The surface formed by the loss as a function of a network's parameters; its shape of valleys, saddle points and flatness affects how training behaves.
concepts.example: Picture each pair of weight values as a map location and the loss as altitude: training is a hike downhill across terrain with valleys, ridges, plateaus and passes.

concepts.name: Loss Scaling
concepts.description: Multiplying the loss by a large factor before backpropagation in mixed-precision training so small FP16 gradients do not underflow to zero, then unscaling them.
concepts.example: A gradient of 1e-8 rounds to 0 in FP16, but multiplying the loss by 65,536 makes it about 6.6e-4, which FP16 stores fine; divide by 65,536 again before updating weights.

concepts.name: Lottery Ticket Hypothesis
concepts.description: The conjecture that a large randomly initialized network contains a small sparse subnetwork that, trained from its original initial weights, can match the full network's accuracy. Found by iterative magnitude pruning and rewinding.
concepts.example: A 1-million-weight net may hide a 100,000-weight subnet that, reset to its original random values and trained alone, matches the full net, as if one ticket was always the winner.

concepts.name: LSTM Cell
concepts.description: The building block of an LSTM: a memory cell state plus forget, input and output gates, each a sigmoid layer, that control what information is erased, written and exposed at every time step.
concepts.example: At each word the cell's forget gate might output 0.9 to keep most of the old memory, the input gate 0.2 to write a little new information, and the output gate 0.5 to reveal half of it.

concepts.name: LSUV Initialization
concepts.description: Layer-sequential unit-variance initialization: start from orthogonal weights, then pass a data batch through the network and rescale each layer in turn so its outputs have unit variance.
concepts.example: Start with orthogonal weights, push one batch through, and if layer 1's outputs have variance 4, divide its weights by 2; then do layer 2, and so on until each outputs variance 1.

concepts.name: Luong Attention
concepts.description: An attention mechanism for sequence-to-sequence models that scores encoder states against the current decoder state using a dot product or a learned bilinear (general) form, a simpler multiplicative alternative to Bahdanau attention.
concepts.example: When translating word 3, the decoder's state is dot-multiplied with each encoder word's state; the highest score, say for the matching source word, gets most of the softmax weight.

concepts.name: Magnitude Pruning
concepts.description: A pruning method that removes the weights with the smallest absolute values, assuming they matter least, then usually fine-tunes the network to recover accuracy.
concepts.example: Of weights [0.8, -0.02, 0.5, 0.01, -0.6], pruning 40% by magnitude zeroes -0.02 and 0.01, the two closest to zero, then a short retraining lets the rest compensate.

concepts.name: Margin Ranking Loss
concepts.description: A pairwise loss that takes two scores and a label saying which should rank higher, and penalizes the pair when the correct one does not exceed the other by at least a margin.
concepts.example: With margin 1, if the relevant document scores 3.0 and the irrelevant one 2.5, the loss is 1 - 0.5 = 0.5; once the gap reaches 1 or more, the loss is zero.

concepts.name: Max-Norm Constraint
concepts.description: A regularizer that caps the L2 norm of each neuron's incoming weight vector at a fixed value, rescaling it after each update if it grows too large. Often paired with dropout.
concepts.example: With max norm 3, if a neuron's incoming weights become [3, 4] (norm 5) after an update, they are rescaled to [1.8, 2.4] (norm 3); smaller vectors are left alone.

concepts.name: Max Pooling
concepts.description: A downsampling operation in CNNs that slides a window over a feature map and keeps only the largest value in each window, shrinking the map and adding small translation invariance.
concepts.example: A 2x2 max pool turns the patch [1, 3; 2, 9] into 9, so a 4x4 map becomes 2x2, and a feature shifted by one pixel often still gives the same output.

concepts.name: Maxout
concepts.description: An activation unit that outputs the maximum of several learned linear functions of its input, so it can learn piecewise linear activations; designed to work well with dropout.
concepts.example: A maxout unit with two lines, y = x and y = -x, outputs max(x, -x) = |x|; with lines y = x and y = 0 it reproduces ReLU, so it learns its own activation shape.

concepts.name: McCulloch–Pitts Neuron
concepts.description: A 1943 mathematical model of a neuron that sums binary inputs with fixed weights and fires (outputs 1) when the sum reaches a threshold; the first formal artificial neuron.
concepts.example: A neuron with two inputs, both weighted 1, and threshold 2 fires only when both are 1, an AND gate; lowering the threshold to 1 turns it into an OR gate.

concepts.name: Mean Absolute Error Loss
concepts.description: A regression loss equal to the average absolute difference between predictions and targets. It is less sensitive to outliers than squared error and leads to predicting the median.
concepts.example: Predicting house prices [100, 200, 300] against true [110, 190, 330] gives errors 10, 10 and 30, so MAE loss is 50/3, about 16.7; a 1,000 outlier only adds linearly.

concepts.name: Mean Squared Error Loss
concepts.description: A regression loss equal to the average squared difference between predictions and targets. It penalizes large errors heavily and corresponds to maximum likelihood under Gaussian noise.
concepts.example: Errors of 1, 1 and 4 give MSE (1 + 1 + 16)/3 = 6; the single error of 4 dominates, so training works hardest to fix the biggest mistakes.

concepts.name: Mechanistic Interpretability
concepts.description: The field that reverse-engineers trained neural networks into human-understandable algorithms by identifying the features, neurons and circuits that implement specific behaviours.
concepts.example: Researchers found 'induction heads' in Transformers: two attention heads that together spot an earlier 'Harry Potter' and predict 'Potter' after the next 'Harry', a reverse-engineered algorithm.

concepts.name: Megatron-LM
concepts.description: NVIDIA's library and research system for training very large Transformer language models, best known for intra-layer tensor parallelism combined with pipeline and data parallelism.
concepts.example: To train a huge model on 512 GPUs, Megatron splits each layer's matrices across 8 GPUs in a server, chains layer groups across servers as a pipeline, and copies the whole thing for data parallelism.

concepts.name: Training Memory Footprint
concepts.description: The total GPU memory needed to train a model: weights, gradients, optimizer states, and stored activations for backpropagation, which grow with batch size and sequence length.
concepts.example: A 1-billion-parameter model trained with Adam in FP32 needs 4 GB for weights, 4 GB for gradients and 8 GB for optimizer states, about 16 GB before counting any activations.

concepts.name: Memory Network
concepts.description: A neural model with an explicit external memory of stored facts that it reads using attention over memory slots, often over several hops, to answer questions that require reasoning over the stored items.
concepts.example: Given 'Mary went to the kitchen. Mary picked up the milk.', asked 'Where is the milk?', the model attends to the milk sentence, then hops to Mary's location, and answers 'kitchen'.

concepts.name: Mini-Batch
concepts.description: A small random subset of the training data used to compute one gradient estimate and parameter update, balancing the noise of single examples against the cost of the full dataset.
