concepts.example: With 50,000 training images, you shuffle and grab 64 at a time; each group of 64 gives a decent gradient estimate at a tiny fraction of the cost of using all 50,000.

concepts.name: Mini-Batch Gradient Descent
concepts.description: Gradient descent that updates parameters using the average gradient over a small batch of examples at each step; the standard way neural networks are trained.
concepts.example: Average the gradients of 32 examples, step once, repeat with the next 32: less noisy than one example at a time, much cheaper than all of them, and fast on GPUs.

concepts.name: Mish
concepts.description: A smooth, non-monotonic activation function defined as x times tanh(softplus(x)). It resembles Swish and was reported to improve accuracy in some vision models.
concepts.example: Mish(1) = 1 * tanh(softplus(1)) = 1 * tanh(1.31), about 0.87; Mish(-1) is about -0.30, a small negative dip like Swish's, while large positive inputs pass almost unchanged.

concepts.name: Mixup
concepts.description: A data augmentation method that trains on convex combinations of pairs of examples and their labels, blending both inputs and one-hot targets with a random weight to regularize the model.
concepts.example: Blend 70% of a cat photo with 30% of a dog photo and train with label 0.7 cat, 0.3 dog; the model learns smoother boundaries between classes.

concepts.name: MLP-Mixer
concepts.description: An all-MLP vision architecture that splits an image into patches and alternates MLPs that mix information across patches (token mixing) with MLPs that mix across channels, with no convolution or attention.
concepts.example: Cut a 224x224 image into 196 patches; one MLP mixes across the 196 patches for each feature, the next mixes across features within each patch, alternating like rows then columns of a table.

concepts.name: MnasNet
concepts.description: A mobile CNN found by reinforcement-learning-based architecture search whose reward combines accuracy with measured on-device latency, producing efficient inverted-residual networks.
concepts.example: The search rewards a model with 76% accuracy at 80 ms on a Pixel phone over one with 77% at 200 ms, because the reward penalizes measured phone latency, not just accuracy.

concepts.name: MobileNet
concepts.description: A family of lightweight CNNs for phones and embedded devices built from depthwise separable convolutions, with width and resolution multipliers to trade accuracy for speed.
concepts.example: A 3x3 convolution from 256 to 256 channels uses about 590,000 weights; MobileNet's depthwise plus 1x1 version uses about 68,000, roughly 9 times fewer, so it runs on phones.

concepts.name: MobileNetV2
concepts.description: The second MobileNet, built from inverted residual blocks with linear bottlenecks: thin layers expanded by 1x1 convolutions, filtered depthwise, then projected back without a nonlinearity.
concepts.example: A block takes a thin 24-channel input, expands it to 144 channels with a 1x1 conv, filters with a 3x3 depthwise conv, then projects back to 24 with no ReLU so no information is lost.

concepts.name: MobileNetV3
concepts.description: A MobileNet version designed with hardware-aware architecture search and refined by hand, adding squeeze-and-excitation modules and the hard-swish activation for better speed and accuracy.
concepts.example: MobileNetV3 lets a search choose block sizes per layer, then hand-tweaks the expensive first and last layers and swaps in hard-swish, making it more accurate and about 20% faster than V2.

concepts.name: Mode Connectivity
concepts.description: The finding that different minima found by training a neural network can often be joined by a simple path (sometimes a straight line) in weight space along which the loss stays low.
concepts.example: Train the same network twice from different seeds and get weights A and B; instead of a high-loss mountain between them, there is often a low-loss curved path connecting them, like two lakes joined by a river.

concepts.name: Model Compression
concepts.description: Techniques that make trained models smaller and faster with little loss in accuracy, including pruning, quantization, knowledge distillation and low-rank factorization.
concepts.example: A 400 MB speech model is pruned, distilled and quantized to 8-bit, becoming 25 MB and 4 times faster on a phone, while losing only half a point of accuracy.

concepts.name: Model FLOPs Utilization
concepts.description: The ratio of the FLOPs a training run actually spends on the model's forward and backward passes per second to the hardware's theoretical peak, a measure of training efficiency.
concepts.example: If a GPU peaks at 1,000 TFLOP/s and your training run does 400 TFLOP/s of model forward-and-backward work, MFU is 40%; the rest is lost to communication and memory waits.

concepts.name: Monte Carlo Dropout
concepts.description: Keeping dropout active at test time and averaging many stochastic forward passes, which approximates Bayesian inference and gives an estimate of the model's predictive uncertainty.
concepts.example: Run the same X-ray through a model 50 times with dropout on: if predictions range from 20% to 90% pneumonia, the model is unsure; if all are near 85%, it is confident.

concepts.name: Multi-Head Attention
concepts.description: Running several scaled dot-product attention operations in parallel, each with its own learned query, key and value projections, then concatenating and projecting their outputs so the model attends to different patterns at once.
concepts.example: With 8 heads in 'The cat sat because it was tired', one head may link 'it' to 'cat', another track the verb, another nearby words; their results are concatenated.

concepts.name: Multi-Scale Training
concepts.description: Training a vision model on images resized to randomly chosen scales so it becomes robust to objects of different sizes; common in object detection.
concepts.example: A detector trained on images resized randomly between 320 and 608 pixels each batch sees a car as small or large, so it later finds both distant and nearby cars.

concepts.name: Multilayer Perceptron
concepts.description: A feedforward neural network with one or more hidden layers of fully connected neurons and nonlinear activations, able to learn nonlinear functions; trained with backpropagation.
concepts.example: No single perceptron can compute XOR, but an MLP with 2 hidden neurons can: one computes OR, one computes AND, and the output fires for 'OR but not AND'.

concepts.name: Muon Optimizer
concepts.description: An optimizer for matrix-shaped weights that takes the momentum update and orthogonalizes it with Newton-Schulz iterations before applying it, giving fast, well-conditioned training of large models.
concepts.example: If the momentum matrix would push mostly in one dominant direction, Muon reshapes it so all directions have equal strength, its singular values all set near 1, before stepping.

concepts.name: Maximal Update Parametrization
concepts.description: Maximal Update Parametrization: a rule for scaling initialization and per-layer learning rates with width so that the best hyperparameters found on a small model transfer to much wider ones.
concepts.example: Tune the learning rate on a 40M-parameter model, find 0.01 is best, and under muP that same setting is close to optimal for a 7B-parameter model with no costly retuning.

concepts.name: Apache MXNet
concepts.description: Apache MXNet, an open-source deep learning framework that mixes symbolic and imperative programming and scales across GPUs and machines; once Amazon's preferred framework, now retired.
concepts.example: In MXNet's Gluon API you could write a model in ordinary Python, debug it line by line, then call hybridize() to compile it into a fast static graph for deployment.

concepts.name: Nadam
concepts.description: An optimizer combining Adam with Nesterov momentum, applying the look-ahead momentum correction to Adam's first-moment estimate.
concepts.example: Like a skier who looks at where momentum will carry them and corrects early, Nadam computes Adam's update using the momentum look-ahead from Nesterov.

concepts.name: NASNet
concepts.description: A CNN family whose repeating convolutional cells were discovered by reinforcement-learning architecture search on a small dataset and then stacked to build large ImageNet models.
concepts.example: Search found a good cell on small CIFAR-10 images in days instead of months, then stacked copies of that cell to build an ImageNet model that beat hand-designed networks.

concepts.name: NEAT
concepts.description: NeuroEvolution of Augmenting Topologies: a genetic algorithm that evolves both the weights and structure of neural networks, starting small, tracking genes with historical markings, and protecting new ideas through speciation.
concepts.example: NEAT starts with tiny networks connecting inputs straight to outputs, then mutation adds a hidden node here and a connection there; for pole balancing it evolves just enough structure.

concepts.name: Negative Log-Likelihood Loss
concepts.description: A loss equal to minus the log of the probability a model assigns to the correct class or target; minimizing it is maximum likelihood, and with softmax outputs it equals cross-entropy.
concepts.example: If the model gives the correct class probability 0.8, the loss is -ln 0.8, about 0.22; at 0.1 it is about 2.3, so confident wrong answers are punished hard.

concepts.name: Negative Sampling
concepts.description: A training shortcut that replaces a full softmax over a huge vocabulary with a few binary classification tasks: tell the true context item apart from a handful of randomly sampled negatives. Used in word2vec.
concepts.example: To learn that 'coffee' goes with 'cup', train a yes/no classifier: 'cup' is yes, and 5 random words like 'giraffe' or 'tax' are no, instead of scoring all 100,000 words.

concepts.name: Neocognitron
concepts.description: Fukushima's 1980 hierarchical neural network for visual pattern recognition with alternating feature-extracting and pooling-like layers; an early forerunner of convolutional neural networks.
concepts.example: Early layers detect short lines, later layers combine them into corners and curves, then digits, with each layer tolerating small shifts, much like a modern CNN without backprop.

concepts.name: Network Depth
concepts.description: The number of layers a neural network stacks between input and output. Greater depth lets a network build more abstract hierarchical features but makes training harder.
concepts.example: VGG-16 has 16 weight layers and ResNet-152 has 152; each extra layer builds on the last, such as edges to shapes to object parts, but deep nets need tricks like residuals to train.

concepts.name: Network in Network
concepts.description: A CNN design that replaces linear convolution filters with small MLPs applied at each location (equivalent to 1x1 convolutions) and uses global average pooling instead of fully connected layers.
concepts.example: Instead of a single linear filter, each location runs a tiny MLP over its channels; at the end, averaging each class's feature map gives its score with no big dense layer.

concepts.name: Network Width
concepts.description: The number of neurons or channels in each layer of a neural network. Wider layers add capacity and parallelism, and width is a key axis in scaling models.
concepts.example: A layer with 512 neurons is twice as wide as one with 256; Wide ResNets showed a shallower but wider net can match a much deeper thin one.

concepts.name: Neural Architecture Search
concepts.description: The field of automatically designing neural network architectures by searching a defined space of designs with methods such as reinforcement learning, evolution or gradient-based relaxation.
concepts.example: Instead of an engineer trying layer sizes by hand, an algorithm tries thousands of candidate networks, trains or estimates each, and keeps the best design.

concepts.name: Neural Network
concepts.description: A model made of layers of simple connected units (neurons) that each compute a weighted sum of inputs followed by a nonlinearity; its weights are learned from data to approximate complex functions.
concepts.example: To read handwritten digits, a network takes 784 pixel values, passes them through layers of neurons that each weight and sum their inputs, and outputs 10 scores, one per digit.

concepts.name: Neural Ordinary Differential Equation
concepts.description: A model that treats a network's hidden state as evolving continuously in time, with its derivative given by a neural network, and computes outputs by calling an ODE solver; a continuous-depth ResNet.
concepts.example: A ResNet adds a small change at each of 50 layers; a neural ODE lets the hidden state flow continuously, with a solver deciding how many steps are needed, like a smooth slide instead of stairs.

concepts.name: Neural Scaling Laws
concepts.description: Empirical power-law relationships showing that a neural network's test loss falls predictably as model size, dataset size and training compute grow; used to plan large training runs.
concepts.example: If a 10x larger model lowers test loss from 3.0 to 2.6, a power law predicts the next 10x cuts it by a similar ratio, to about 2.25, so labs can forecast results before training.

concepts.name: Neural Tangent Kernel
concepts.description: A kernel that describes how an infinitely wide neural network evolves under gradient descent; in that limit training behaves like kernel regression with this fixed kernel.
concepts.example: For a very wide network, the NTK value between a cat photo and a dog photo says how much a gradient step on the cat changes the prediction for the dog; that similarity stays fixed all training.

concepts.name: Neural Turing Machine
concepts.description: A neural network coupled to an external memory matrix that it reads and writes with differentiable attention-based addressing, so it can learn simple algorithms like copying and sorting.
concepts.example: To copy a sequence, an NTM writes each item to the next memory row using soft attention, then reads the rows back in order, learning the copy algorithm from examples alone.

concepts.name: NFNet
concepts.description: Normalizer-Free Networks: high-accuracy ResNet-style image classifiers trained without batch normalization, using scaled weight standardization and adaptive gradient clipping instead.
concepts.example: NFNet drops batch norm entirely; if a layer's gradient grows to more than, say, 1% of its weight norm, adaptive clipping scales it back, keeping training stable with huge batches.

concepts.name: Noise Injection
concepts.description: A regularization technique that adds random noise, typically Gaussian, to inputs, weights, activations or gradients during training so the network becomes robust and overfits less.
concepts.example: Adding small random Gaussian jitter to each input pixel during training is like practicing free throws in the wind: the model learns to succeed even when conditions are a little off.

concepts.name: Non-Convex Optimization
concepts.description: Minimizing objectives with multiple local minima, saddle points and flat regions, where gradient methods carry no global guarantee; the setting of neural network training.
concepts.example: Minimizing a bowl like x squared is easy: any downhill path ends at the bottom. A network's loss is more like a mountain range, where downhill paths can end in different valleys or stall on passes.

concepts.name: Normalization (Deep Learning)
concepts.description: Layers that rescale activations to a standard mean and variance using statistics over a batch, layer, group or instance, plus learned scale and shift, to stabilize and speed up training.
concepts.example: If a layer's outputs drift to values around 500 with spread 200, a normalization layer recenters them to mean 0 and spread 1, then learned scale and shift adjust them as needed.

concepts.name: Numerical Differentiation
concepts.description: Approximating derivatives from function values at nearby points, as in the finite difference (f(x+h)-f(x))/h; simple but subject to truncation and round-off error. Used for gradient checking.
concepts.example: To estimate the slope of x squared at x = 3, compute (3.001 squared minus 3 squared)/0.001 = 6.001, close to the true 6; making h too tiny lets rounding errors creep in.

concepts.name: One-Cycle Policy
concepts.description: A learning-rate schedule that raises the learning rate from low to high over the first part of training and then anneals it to very low, often with momentum cycled inversely, enabling fast training.
concepts.example: Over 100 epochs, the learning rate climbs from 0.004 to 0.1 during the first 30, falls back down over the next 60, then drops far lower for the last 10, while momentum moves the opposite way.

concepts.name: One-Shot NAS
concepts.description: Neural architecture search that trains a single supernet containing all candidate architectures with shared weights, then evaluates sub-networks by inheriting those weights instead of training each one.
concepts.example: Rather than training 1,000 candidate networks separately, train one big supernet containing all their layers; to score a candidate, just switch on its parts and test with the shared weights.

concepts.name: Kernel Fusion
concepts.description: A compiler optimization that merges several consecutive GPU operations into one kernel so intermediate results stay in fast on-chip memory, cutting memory traffic and launch overhead.
concepts.example: Computing y = relu(x * w + b) as three separate kernels writes two intermediate results to slow GPU memory and reads them back; fused, all three happen in one pass on-chip.

concepts.name: Optimal Brain Damage
concepts.description: A pruning method that ranks weights by their estimated effect on the loss using a diagonal approximation of the Hessian, and removes the least salient ones; Optimal Brain Surgeon uses the full Hessian.
concepts.example: A small weight on a very sensitive connection may matter more than a large one; OBD estimates each weight's cost as half its curvature times its value squared, and prunes the cheapest.

concepts.name: Orthogonal Initialization
concepts.description: Initializing weight matrices as random orthogonal matrices so signals and gradients keep their norm across layers, helping deep and recurrent networks train stably.
concepts.example: A 2x2 rotation matrix is orthogonal: multiplying any vector by it keeps its length, so after 100 such layers a signal is neither exploded nor shrunk to nothing.

concepts.name: Output Layer
concepts.description: The final layer of a neural network that produces predictions in the required form, such as one value for regression or class probabilities via softmax for classification.
concepts.example: A digit classifier's output layer has 10 neurons followed by softmax, giving 10 probabilities; a price predictor's output layer is a single neuron with no activation.

concepts.name: Convolution Output Size Formula
concepts.description: The formula for a convolution or pooling output size along each dimension: floor((input + 2*padding - kernel) / stride) + 1, with dilation enlarging the effective kernel.
concepts.example: A 32-pixel input, 5x5 kernel, padding 2 and stride 1 gives (32 + 4 - 5)/1 + 1 = 32; with stride 2 it gives floor(31/2) + 1 = 16.

concepts.name: Overparameterization
concepts.description: Using a model with far more parameters than training examples. Such networks can fit any data yet still generalize well, which also makes their optimization easier.
concepts.example: A network with 10 million weights trained on 50,000 images could memorize them all, even random labels, yet on real labels it still predicts new images well.

concepts.name: Padding (CNN)
concepts.description: Adding extra border values, usually zeros, around a convolution's input so the output keeps the input's size ('same') or shrinks ('valid'), and edge pixels are covered more evenly.
concepts.example: A 5x5 image convolved with a 3x3 kernel shrinks to 3x3, but adding a one-pixel ring of zeros around it first makes it 7x7, so the output stays 5x5.

concepts.name: Parameter Count
concepts.description: The total number of learnable weights and biases in a model, a basic measure of its size, memory cost and capacity, often quoted in millions or billions.
concepts.example: A fully connected layer from 100 inputs to 50 outputs has 100 x 50 = 5,000 weights plus 50 biases, 5,050 parameters; GPT-3 has about 175 billion.

concepts.name: Parameter-Efficient Fine-Tuning
concepts.description: Adapting a large pretrained model by training only a small number of added or selected parameters, such as adapters, LoRA matrices or prompts, while keeping most weights frozen.
concepts.example: Instead of updating all 7 billion weights for each customer, freeze them and train a 10-million-parameter add-on per customer, storing small files instead of full model copies.

concepts.name: Parameter Server
concepts.description: A distributed training architecture where dedicated servers store the model parameters, and workers pull current weights, compute gradients on their data and push updates back.
concepts.example: Eight workers each compute gradients on their slice of data and send them to a central server holding the weights; the server updates and workers fetch the new weights, like a shared notebook.

concepts.name: Parameter Sharing
concepts.description: Reusing the same weights in several parts of a network, as convolution filters across positions or RNN weights across time steps, which cuts parameters and builds in useful structure.
concepts.example: A 3x3 convolution filter has just 9 weights, yet it is reused at every position of a 1,000x1,000 image instead of learning separate weights for every location.

concepts.name: Peephole LSTM
concepts.description: An LSTM variant whose gates also look directly at the cell state, not just the input and previous hidden state, helping it learn precise timing.
concepts.example: To emit a pulse exactly every 50 steps, a gate needs to see the count stored in the cell state; peephole connections let it read that value directly.

concepts.name: Perceptron Learning Algorithm
concepts.description: The update rule for training a perceptron: when an example is misclassified, add or subtract its input vector from the weights; it converges if the data are linearly separable.
concepts.example: Weights [0, 0] misclassify input [1, 2] that should be positive, so add it: weights become [1, 2]. Repeat over the data until every point lands on its correct side.

concepts.name: Projected Gradient Descent Attack
concepts.description: An iterative adversarial attack that takes repeated gradient-sign steps to increase the loss and projects the input back into a small norm ball around the original after each step; a strong FGSM generalization.
concepts.example: Take 10 small steps of 0.002 each in the gradient-sign direction to raise a classifier's loss on a panda photo, clipping each pixel to stay within 0.008 of the original.

concepts.name: PipeDream
concepts.description: A pipeline-parallel training system whose one-forward-one-backward (1F1B) schedule interleaves micro-batch passes across stages to keep GPUs busy and limit stored activations.
concepts.example: With 4 stages, once the pipeline fills, each GPU alternates one forward then one backward micro-batch instead of doing all forwards first, so few activations are stored at once.

concepts.name: Pipeline Bubble
concepts.description: Idle time in pipeline-parallel training when some stages wait for others at the start and end of each batch; shrunk by splitting the batch into more micro-batches.
concepts.example: With 4 stages and 4 micro-batches, stage 4 waits idle while the first micro-batch moves through stages 1 to 3; using 32 micro-batches makes that waiting a much smaller fraction.

concepts.name: Pipeline Parallelism
concepts.description: Splitting a model's layers into consecutive stages on different devices and streaming micro-batches through them like an assembly line, so models too big for one device can be trained.
concepts.example: A 48-layer model on 4 GPUs: GPU 1 runs layers 1-12, GPU 2 runs 13-24, and so on; while GPU 2 handles micro-batch 1, GPU 1 already starts micro-batch 2, like a car assembly line.

concepts.name: Pointer Network
concepts.description: A sequence-to-sequence model whose attention distribution over input positions is used directly as the output, so it can point to input elements; suited to sorting and convex hull problems.
concepts.example: To sort [5, 2, 9], a pointer network outputs 'position 2, then position 1, then position 3', pointing at input items rather than choosing words from a fixed vocabulary.

concepts.name: 1×1 Convolution
concepts.description: A convolution with a 1x1 kernel that mixes information across channels at each position without looking at neighbours; used to change channel count cheaply and in depthwise separable convolution.
concepts.example: At each pixel, a 1x1 convolution takes its 256 channel values and outputs 64 new mixes of them, shrinking channels 4x without looking at neighbouring pixels.

concepts.name: Poisson Loss
concepts.description: A loss for count data equal to the negative log-likelihood of a Poisson distribution, computed as prediction minus target times log(prediction); used when predicting event rates.
concepts.example: If a shop expects 4 customers an hour and 6 arrive, the loss is 4 - 6 * ln 4, about -4.3; predicting 6 gives about -4.75, lower, as the target count is matched.

concepts.name: Polynomial Learning Rate Decay
concepts.description: A learning-rate schedule that decreases the rate from its initial value to a final value following a polynomial of the fraction of training remaining; power 1 gives linear decay.
concepts.example: With initial rate 0.01, final 0, and power 2, halfway through training the rate is 0.01 x 0.5 squared = 0.0025; with power 1 it would be 0.005.

concepts.name: Pooling Layer
concepts.description: A CNN layer that downsamples feature maps by summarizing small regions, typically with their maximum or average, reducing size and computation and adding some translation invariance.
concepts.example: A 2x2 pooling layer turns a 64x64 feature map into 32x32, cutting the data 4 times while keeping the strongest or average response from each region.

concepts.name: Post-Training Quantization
concepts.description: Converting a trained model's weights and possibly activations to low-precision integers such as int8 without retraining, using a small calibration set to choose scaling ranges.
concepts.example: After training, a weight range of -2.5 to 2.5 is mapped onto int8's -127 to 127, so each weight is stored in 1 byte instead of 4 and runs faster on phones, with no retraining.

concepts.name: Pre-Activation
concepts.description: The weighted sum of a neuron's inputs plus bias, before the activation function is applied; also called the net input or, for output units, the logit.
concepts.example: A neuron with inputs [1, 2], weights [0.5, -1] and bias 0.3 has pre-activation 0.5 - 2 + 0.3 = -1.2; ReLU then turns that into 0.

concepts.name: Pre-Activation ResNet
concepts.description: A ResNet variant that places batch normalization and ReLU before each convolution inside residual blocks, leaving a clean identity path that eases training of very deep networks.
concepts.example: Each block computes x + conv(relu(bn(conv(relu(bn(x)))))), so the shortcut x passes through untouched from start to end, letting a 1,001-layer network train.

concepts.name: Pre-Norm and Post-Norm
concepts.description: Two places to put layer normalization in a Transformer block: after the residual addition (post-norm, original design) or inside the branch before the sublayer (pre-norm), which trains more stably when deep.
concepts.example: Post-norm computes norm(x + attention(x)); pre-norm computes x + attention(norm(x)). In pre-norm the residual stream stays untouched, so 100-layer models train without delicate warmup.

concepts.name: Parametric ReLU
concepts.description: Parametric ReLU: like leaky ReLU, but the slope for negative inputs is a parameter learned during training rather than a fixed constant.
concepts.example: Leaky ReLU fixes the negative slope at 0.01, but PReLU might learn 0.25 in one layer and 0.05 in another, picking whatever helps the task.

concepts.name: Pretrained Model
concepts.description: A model already trained on a large dataset, whose learned weights are reused as a starting point for new tasks instead of training from scratch.
concepts.example: Instead of training an image classifier from scratch on your 500 photos of skin lesions, start from a ResNet already trained on ImageNet's million images and adjust it.

concepts.name: Progressive Resizing
concepts.description: Training an image model on small images first and gradually increasing image size, which speeds up early training and can improve final accuracy.
concepts.example: Train for 10 epochs on 128x128 images, then 10 on 224x224, then 5 on 288x288; early epochs run several times faster, and the model refines details at the end.

concepts.name: PyTorch Lightning
concepts.description: A lightweight wrapper around PyTorch that organizes research code into modules and handles the training loop, multi-GPU training, logging and checkpointing automatically.
concepts.example: You write the model and a training_step method; Lightning runs the loop, moves data to GPUs, saves checkpoints and switches to 8 GPUs with a single setting.

concepts.name: Quantization-Aware Training
concepts.description: Training or fine-tuning a model while simulating low-precision quantization in the forward pass, using straight-through gradients, so it learns to stay accurate after quantization.
concepts.example: During training, weights are rounded to int8 levels in the forward pass so the model feels the rounding error, but gradients flow as if unrounded, letting it adapt.

concepts.name: Quasi-Recurrent Neural Network
concepts.description: A sequence model that computes gates with convolutions in parallel across time and keeps only a light elementwise recurrent pooling step, making it much faster than an LSTM.
concepts.example: Gates for all 100 time steps are computed at once by a convolution; only a cheap running blend, like h = f * h + (1 - f) * z, is done step by step.

concepts.name: Query, Key and Value
concepts.description: The three learned projections in attention: a query asks what to look for, keys describe what each item offers, and values carry the content that is mixed by the query-key match weights.
concepts.example: Like a library search: your query 'cooking pasta' is matched against each book's key (its catalogue entry), and what you get back is a blend of the books' values (their contents).

concepts.name: RAdam
concepts.description: Rectified Adam: an Adam variant that detects when the adaptive learning rate's variance is unreliably high early in training and dampens updates, giving a built-in warmup.
concepts.example: In the first few steps, Adam's estimate of gradient variance is based on just a handful of samples; RAdam damps updates then and gradually removes the damping as the estimate firms up.

concepts.name: Radial Basis Function Network
concepts.description: A neural network with one hidden layer whose units respond to the distance from the input to a center through a radial function, typically Gaussian, followed by a linear output layer.
concepts.example: A hidden unit centred at (0, 0) outputs 1 for input (0, 0) and about 0.37 for (1, 0) under the Gaussian exp(-distance squared); the output layer then adds these bumps with weights.

concepts.name: RandAugment
concepts.description: An automated augmentation strategy that applies N randomly chosen transformations at a shared magnitude M, replacing AutoAugment's expensive search with two tunable hyperparameters.
concepts.example: Set N = 2 and M = 9: each image gets 2 randomly picked ops, like rotate and contrast, both at strength 9 of 30, so you tune 2 numbers instead of running a search.

concepts.name: Random Weight Initialization
concepts.description: Setting a network's initial weights to small random values, from a uniform or normal distribution, so neurons start different and can learn different features.
concepts.example: If all weights start at 0.5, every hidden neuron computes the same thing forever; drawing them from a normal distribution with spread 0.01 makes each neuron different from the start.

concepts.name: Receptive Field
concepts.description: The region of the input image that can influence a given unit in a CNN; it grows with depth, kernel size, stride and dilation.
concepts.example: Two stacked 3x3 convolutions give each output a 5x5 receptive field, and three give 7x7; with stride 2 in early layers, it grows much faster.

concepts.name: Reconstruction Loss
concepts.description: A loss measuring how well a model's output reproduces its input, such as mean squared error or binary cross-entropy between them; the main objective of autoencoders.
concepts.example: An autoencoder compresses a 28x28 digit and rebuilds it; if three pixels come back off by 0.1, 0.2 and 0.3, the MSE reconstruction loss over those pixels is (0.01 + 0.04 + 0.09)/3.

concepts.name: Reduce LR on Plateau
concepts.description: A learning-rate scheduler that lowers the learning rate by a factor when a monitored metric such as validation loss stops improving for a set number of epochs.
concepts.example: With patience 5 and factor 0.1, if validation loss has not improved for 5 epochs at learning rate 0.01, it drops to 0.001 and waits again.

concepts.name: RegNet
concepts.description: A family of CNNs derived by studying design spaces and finding simple rules, such as stage widths growing roughly linearly with depth, that produce good networks across compute budgets.
concepts.example: Instead of searching for one best network, RegNet researchers narrowed a huge design space to simple rules, like widths growing linearly by stage, which yield good models at any size.

concepts.name: Reinforcement Learning-Based NAS
concepts.description: Neural architecture search where a controller, often an RNN, generates architecture descriptions and is trained with policy gradients using the trained child networks' validation accuracy as reward.
concepts.example: An RNN controller writes out 'layer 1: 3x3 conv, 64 filters; layer 2: 5x5 conv...', the child net is trained, and its 92% validation accuracy becomes the reward.

concepts.name: ReLU
concepts.description: The rectified linear unit, max(0, x): passes positive inputs unchanged and outputs zero for negatives. It is cheap and avoids vanishing gradients for positive inputs, so it is the default deep learning activation.
concepts.example: ReLU turns inputs [-3, 0, 2, 5] into [0, 0, 2, 5]: negatives become 0, positives pass unchanged, and the gradient for positives is exactly 1.

concepts.name: ReLU6
concepts.description: A ReLU capped at 6, min(max(0, x), 6), whose bounded output range is friendly to low-precision arithmetic; used in MobileNets.
concepts.example: ReLU6 turns [-2, 3, 10] into [0, 3, 6], capping large values so they fit nicely in 8-bit fixed-point arithmetic.

concepts.name: Reparameterization Trick
concepts.description: Writing a random sample as a deterministic function of the parameters plus independent noise, such as z = mu + sigma * epsilon, so gradients can flow through sampling; central to VAEs.
concepts.example: Rather than drawing z directly from a normal with mean 2 and spread 0.5, draw noise e from a standard normal and set z = 2 + 0.5e, so gradients reach the 2 and 0.5.

concepts.name: Representation Learning
concepts.description: The field of learning useful features or embeddings of data automatically, instead of hand-engineering them, so downstream tasks become easier.
concepts.example: Rather than hand-coding features like 'has whiskers', a network trained on millions of photos learns its own features, which then make it easy to classify even new animals.

concepts.name: RepVGG
concepts.description: A CNN trained with multi-branch blocks (3x3, 1x1 and identity) that are merged after training into a single 3x3 convolution, giving a fast plain VGG-style network at inference.
concepts.example: During training a block computes 3x3 conv plus 1x1 conv plus identity; afterwards the 1x1 and identity are padded into 3x3 kernels and summed, leaving one fast 3x3 conv.

concepts.name: Residual Block
concepts.description: A network block that adds its input to the output of a few stacked layers, so the layers learn a residual correction; the basic unit of ResNets.
concepts.example: If the ideal mapping is close to 'do nothing', a residual block only needs its layers to output nearly 0, since its output is input + layers(input).

concepts.name: Residual Connection
concepts.description: A shortcut that adds a layer's input directly to its output, letting gradients flow through the identity path and making very deep networks trainable.
concepts.example: Output = x + f(x). If f contributes little, x still passes through, and during backprop the gradient flows straight through the + as well, like an express lane.

concepts.name: Residual Neural Network
concepts.description: A CNN architecture built from stacked residual blocks with identity shortcut connections, which made networks of 50 to over 1,000 layers trainable and won ImageNet 2015.
concepts.example: ResNet-152 stacks 50 bottleneck residual blocks; without shortcuts such depth trains worse than a 20-layer net, but with them it cut ImageNet top-5 error to about 3.6%.

concepts.name: ResNeXt
concepts.description: A ResNet variant whose blocks split into many parallel paths of identical structure, implemented as grouped convolutions, adding a cardinality dimension that improves accuracy at equal cost.
concepts.example: Instead of one wide bottleneck path, a ResNeXt block runs 32 narrow paths of 4 channels each and sums them, implemented as a grouped convolution with 32 groups.

concepts.name: Restricted Boltzmann Machine
concepts.description: A two-layer generative neural network with visible and hidden units connected only across layers, which defines an energy-based probability model; trained with contrastive divergence.
concepts.example: With 6 visible units for movies a user liked and 2 hidden units, hidden ones might learn 'likes sci-fi' and 'likes comedy', with no links between movies themselves.

concepts.name: Ring All-Reduce
concepts.description: A bandwidth-efficient all-reduce algorithm where devices arranged in a ring pass chunks of their gradients to neighbours in two phases, so each device sends a constant amount regardless of their number.
concepts.example: Four GPUs in a ring split their gradients into 4 chunks; each passes one chunk to its neighbour, adding as it goes, then passes the finished sums around again, so every GPU ends with the total.

concepts.name: RMSNorm
concepts.description: A normalization layer that rescales activations by their root mean square without subtracting the mean, a cheaper variant of layer normalization used in many large language models.
concepts.example: For features [3, 4], the root mean square is sqrt((9 + 16)/2), about 3.54, so RMSNorm outputs about [0.85, 1.13], without subtracting the mean as layer norm would.

concepts.name: RMSProp
concepts.description: An adaptive optimizer that divides each parameter's gradient by a running root mean square of its recent gradients, so step sizes adapt per parameter; fixes AdaGrad's shrinking rates.
concepts.example: A weight whose recent gradients are around 10 gets its step divided by about 10, while one with gradients around 0.1 gets its step divided by 0.1, so both move at a similar pace.

concepts.name: Recurrent Neural Network
concepts.description: A neural network for sequences that processes one element at a time while carrying a hidden state forward, reusing the same weights at each step to model order and context.
concepts.example: Reading 'I love this movie' word by word, an RNN updates its hidden state after each word with the same weights, so by 'movie' the state summarizes the whole sentence.

concepts.name: Randomized Leaky ReLU
concepts.description: Randomized leaky ReLU: during training the slope for negative inputs is sampled randomly from a range for each unit, and at test time the average slope is used; acts as a regularizer.
concepts.example: During training one unit's negative slope might be drawn as 0.2, another's as 0.3, from the range 1/8 to 1/3; at test time all use the average, about 0.23.

concepts.name: Saliency Map
concepts.description: An image showing how much each input pixel affects a model's output, typically the absolute gradient of the class score with respect to the input; a basic explanation method for vision models.
concepts.example: For a photo classified as 'dog', compute how much the dog score changes for each pixel; pixels on the dog's face light up brightly while the grass stays dark.

concepts.name: Sharpness-Aware Minimization
concepts.description: Sharpness-Aware Minimization: an optimizer that first perturbs weights toward the locally worst direction, then descends using the gradient there, seeking flat minima that generalize better.
concepts.example: At each step SAM asks 'where nearby is the loss worst?', jumps there, takes the gradient, and applies it back at the original weights, steering toward wide valleys over narrow ones.

concepts.name: Activation Saturation
concepts.description: When a sigmoid or tanh activation is pushed into its flat regions by large inputs, its gradient nears zero, so learning stalls for that neuron and gradients vanish.
concepts.example: tanh(5) is about 0.9999 and its slope there is only about 0.0002, so a neuron with input 5 barely learns no matter how wrong it is.

concepts.name: Scaled Dot-Product Attention
concepts.description: The attention used in Transformers: softmax of query-key dot products divided by the square root of the key dimension, used to weight the values. The scaling keeps softmax from saturating.
concepts.example: With 64-dimensional keys, raw dot products might be around 8 times larger than ideal, making softmax nearly one-hot; dividing by sqrt(64) = 8 keeps attention weights reasonably soft.

concepts.name: Scheduled Sampling
concepts.description: A training method for sequence models that gradually replaces ground-truth previous tokens with the model's own predictions, following a schedule, to reduce exposure bias.
concepts.example: Early in training the decoder always gets the true previous word; later, it is fed its own prediction 25%, then 50% of the time, so it learns to recover from its own mistakes.

concepts.name: NAS Search Space
concepts.description: The set of possible architectures a neural architecture search can choose from, such as which operations, connections and layer sizes are allowed, often defined as repeated cells.
concepts.example: A search space might allow each of 10 layers to be 3x3 conv, 5x5 conv, max pool or skip: 4 to the 10th power, about a million possible networks.

concepts.name: Self-Attention
concepts.description: Attention in which queries, keys and values all come from the same sequence, so each position builds its new representation by weighing every other position; the core of Transformers.
concepts.example: In 'The animal didn't cross the street because it was tired', self-attention lets 'it' look at every word in the same sentence and put most weight on 'animal'.

concepts.name: Self-Distillation
concepts.description: Knowledge distillation where the teacher is the same architecture as the student, an earlier version of itself or its own deeper layers; it often still improves accuracy.
concepts.example: Train a ResNet-50, then train a fresh ResNet-50 to match the first one's soft outputs; the second often ends up slightly more accurate than its teacher.

concepts.name: Scaled Exponential Linear Unit
concepts.description: The scaled exponential linear unit, an ELU with constants chosen so activations in fully connected networks self-normalize toward zero mean and unit variance without batch normalization.
concepts.example: SELU uses lambda about 1.05 and alpha about 1.67: positive inputs are scaled by 1.05, negative ones curve toward about -1.76, keeping layer outputs near mean 0, variance 1.

concepts.name: Sequence-to-Sequence Model
concepts.description: A model that maps an input sequence to an output sequence of different length, using an encoder to summarize the input and a decoder to generate the output; used for translation and summarization.
concepts.example: Translating 'How are you?' to 'Comment allez-vous ?', the encoder reads the English into a vector and the decoder writes French word by word, so lengths can differ.

concepts.name: Sequence Modeling
concepts.description: Modelling ordered data such as text, audio or time series, where each element depends on earlier ones, to predict, classify, or generate sequences.
concepts.example: Phone keyboards predict 'morning' after 'Good' because a sequence model learned which words tend to follow earlier ones.

concepts.name: Sequence Parallelism
concepts.description: Splitting the sequence (token) dimension of activations across devices so very long contexts fit in memory, often alongside tensor parallelism or with ring attention.
concepts.example: A 128,000-token document is too big for one GPU's activations, so 8 GPUs each hold 16,000 tokens, exchanging keys and values when attention needs to look across chunks.

concepts.name: Cosine Annealing with Warm Restarts
concepts.description: A learning-rate schedule that repeatedly decays the rate along a cosine curve and then jumps back up (warm restart), often lengthening each cycle, to help escape poor regions.
concepts.example: The learning rate falls from 0.1 to near 0 along a cosine over 10 epochs, jumps back to 0.1, then decays over 20 epochs, then 40, each restart shaking the model out of a rut.

concepts.name: Shampoo
concepts.description: A second-order-style optimizer that preconditions each weight matrix's gradient with Kronecker-factored left and right matrices built from accumulated gradient statistics.
concepts.example: For a 1,000x500 weight matrix, Shampoo keeps one 1,000x1,000 and one 500x500 statistics matrix instead of a 500,000x500,000 one, and multiplies the gradient by their inverse fourth roots.

concepts.name: ShuffleNet
concepts.description: An efficient CNN for mobile devices that uses grouped 1x1 convolutions plus a channel shuffle operation so information flows across groups at low cost.
concepts.example: With 3 groups of channels, grouped convs never let group 1 see group 2; a channel shuffle deals channels like cards so the next layer's groups mix all of them.

concepts.name: Siamese Neural Network
concepts.description: A network made of two or more identical branches with shared weights that embed different inputs, so their outputs can be compared; used for similarity, verification and one-shot learning.
concepts.example: To verify a signature, both the stored and new signature pass through the same network; if their embeddings are close, they likely come from the same person.

concepts.name: Sigmoid
concepts.description: The logistic function 1/(1+e^-x), which squashes any real number into the range 0 to 1; used for probabilities in binary classification and as an early neural network activation.
concepts.example: Sigmoid turns 0 into 0.5, 2 into about 0.88, and -2 into about 0.12, so a raw score of 2 can be read as an 88% chance of 'spam'.

concepts.name: Soft Attention
concepts.description: Attention that takes a differentiable weighted average over all inputs using softmax weights, so it can be trained with backpropagation, unlike hard attention which picks one item.
concepts.example: Instead of picking one source word, soft attention takes 70% of one word's vector, 20% of another and 10% of a third, so tiny weight changes have smooth gradients.

concepts.name: Softmax
concepts.description: A function that turns a vector of real scores into a probability distribution by exponentiating each score and dividing by their sum; used for multiclass outputs and attention weights.
concepts.example: Scores [2, 1, 0] become e^2, e^1, e^0 = 7.39, 2.72, 1, and dividing by their sum 11.11 gives about [0.67, 0.24, 0.09].

concepts.name: Softmax Temperature
concepts.description: A parameter that divides the logits before softmax: higher temperatures flatten the distribution, lower ones sharpen it. Used in sampling, calibration and distillation.
concepts.example: Logits [2, 1] give softmax [0.73, 0.27]; at temperature 2 they become [1, 0.5], giving [0.62, 0.38]; at 0.5, [4, 2], giving [0.88, 0.12].

concepts.name: Softplus
concepts.description: The smooth activation log(1 + e^x), a differentiable approximation of ReLU that is always positive; often used to output positive quantities such as standard deviations.
concepts.example: Softplus(0) = ln 2, about 0.69, softplus(5) is about 5.007 and softplus(-5) about 0.007, a smooth ReLU that never quite reaches 0.

concepts.name: Softsign
concepts.description: The activation x / (1 + |x|), which maps inputs into (-1, 1) like tanh but approaches its limits more slowly, polynomially rather than exponentially.
concepts.example: Softsign(1) = 0.5 and softsign(9) = 0.9, while tanh(9) is already 0.99999997; softsign creeps toward 1 slowly, saturating less abruptly.

concepts.name: Sophia Optimizer
concepts.description: A second-order optimizer for language model pretraining that scales updates by a cheap, periodically refreshed estimate of the diagonal Hessian and clips each coordinate's step.
concepts.example: In a steep direction with curvature 100 Sophia divides the step by 100, in a gentle one with curvature 1 it barely shrinks it, and clipping caps any step that gets too big.

concepts.name: Sparse Autoencoder
concepts.description: An autoencoder trained with a sparsity penalty so only a few hidden units are active for each input, yielding more interpretable, disentangled features; used in interpretability research.
concepts.example: Given an LLM's 512-number activation, a sparse autoencoder rewrites it as maybe 20 active features out of 16,000, such as one that fires only for 'Golden Gate Bridge'.

concepts.name: Sparse Categorical Cross-Entropy
concepts.description: Categorical cross-entropy computed from integer class labels instead of one-hot vectors; it gives the same loss but is cheaper when there are many classes.
concepts.example: With 50,000 word classes, store the label 'cat' as index 8,213 instead of a 50,000-long vector of zeros with one 1; the loss just reads -log of the probability at index 8,213.

concepts.name: Sparsemax
concepts.description: An alternative to softmax that projects scores onto the probability simplex, so it can assign exactly zero probability to many classes and give sparse attention weights.
concepts.example: For scores [2, 1, 0], softmax gives [0.67, 0.24, 0.09], but sparsemax gives [1, 0, 0]: the gap is so big that the losers get exactly zero.

concepts.name: Spatial Dropout
concepts.description: A dropout variant for CNNs that drops entire feature-map channels instead of individual activations, since neighbouring pixels in a channel are strongly correlated.
concepts.example: Instead of zeroing random pixels, which neighbours easily fill in, spatial dropout switches off whole channels, like removing the 'edge detector' map for an entire image.

concepts.name: Spatial Pyramid Pooling
concepts.description: A layer that pools a feature map over grids of several sizes and concatenates the results into a fixed-length vector, letting CNNs accept images of any size.
concepts.example: Pool any feature map into 1x1, 2x2 and 4x4 grids: 1 + 4 + 16 = 21 values per channel, so a 300x500 image and a 224x224 one both give the same length vector.

concepts.name: Spectral Normalization
concepts.description: Dividing each weight matrix by its largest singular value, estimated cheaply by power iteration, to bound the layer's Lipschitz constant; widely used to stabilize GAN discriminators.
concepts.example: If a layer's weight matrix can stretch a vector by up to 5 times, spectral norm divides it by 5, so the layer never stretches anything by more than 1.

concepts.name: Spiking Neural Network
concepts.description: A neural network whose neurons communicate with discrete spikes over time, integrating inputs until a threshold is crossed; more brain-like and energy-efficient on neuromorphic hardware.
concepts.example: A spiking neuron's voltage rises with each incoming spike and leaks slowly; once it crosses a threshold it fires and resets, so information is carried by spike timing.

concepts.name: Squared Hinge Loss
concepts.description: The hinge loss squared, max(0, 1 - y*f(x))^2, which penalizes margin violations quadratically and is smooth and differentiable at the margin.
concepts.example: With true label +1 and score 0.5, hinge loss is 0.5 and squared hinge is 0.25; at score -1, hinge is 2 and squared hinge is 4, punishing bad mistakes more.

concepts.name: Squeeze-and-Excitation Network
concepts.description: A CNN block that summarizes each channel by global average pooling (squeeze), passes the result through a small gating network (excitation) and rescales the channels by the resulting weights.
concepts.example: For a 64-channel feature map, average each channel to one number, pass those 64 numbers through a tiny network to get 64 weights between 0 and 1, and rescale each channel by its weight.

concepts.name: SqueezeNet
concepts.description: A small CNN that reaches AlexNet-level accuracy with about 50 times fewer parameters, using fire modules that squeeze channels with 1x1 convolutions before expanding them.
concepts.example: A fire module squeezes 128 channels down to 16 with 1x1 convs, then expands with a mix of 1x1 and 3x3 filters; the whole model is under 5 MB versus AlexNet's 240 MB.

concepts.name: Stacked Autoencoder
concepts.description: Several autoencoders stacked so each layer's codes feed the next, historically trained greedily layer by layer and then fine-tuned to build deep feature hierarchies.
concepts.example: Train one autoencoder to compress 784 pixels to 256 numbers, then another to compress those 256 to 64, then stack both encoders and fine-tune the whole thing.

concepts.name: Static Computational Graph
concepts.description: A computation graph defined fully before it is run (define-and-run), letting a framework optimize and compile it, as in TensorFlow 1 and Theano, at the cost of flexibility.
concepts.example: In TensorFlow 1 you first declared y = W x + b as a graph, then ran it in a session; the framework could fuse and optimize it, but Python if-statements couldn't change it per input.

concepts.name: Step Decay
concepts.description: A learning-rate schedule that multiplies the learning rate by a fixed factor, such as 0.1, every set number of epochs, giving a staircase-shaped curve.
concepts.example: Start at learning rate 0.1 and multiply by 0.1 every 30 epochs: 0.1 for epochs 1-30, 0.01 for 31-60, 0.001 for 61-90, a staircase of rates.

concepts.name: Stochastic Weight Averaging
concepts.description: Averaging model weights from several points along the SGD trajectory late in training, often with a cyclical or high constant learning rate, to reach flatter solutions that generalize better.
concepts.example: In the last 25% of training, save the weights at the end of each epoch and average them; the average lands near the middle of a wide valley, often adding about 1% accuracy.

concepts.name: Straight-Through Estimator
concepts.description: A trick for training through non-differentiable operations like rounding or thresholding: use the operation in the forward pass but pretend it is the identity in the backward pass.
concepts.example: In the forward pass 0.7 is rounded to 1; in the backward pass, rounding is treated as passing values unchanged, so a gradient of 0.3 flows back as 0.3 instead of 0.

concepts.name: Stride
concepts.description: The number of positions a convolution or pooling window moves at each step; strides greater than 1 skip positions and shrink the output.
concepts.example: With stride 1 a 3x3 window moves one pixel at a time; with stride 2 it skips every other position, so a 32x32 input gives roughly a 16x16 output.

concepts.name: Strided Convolution
concepts.description: A convolution applied with a stride greater than one, which downsamples the feature map while learning features, often replacing pooling layers.
concepts.example: A 3x3 conv with stride 2 on a 64x64 map gives 32x32 while learning features, instead of a stride-1 conv followed by 2x2 max pooling.

concepts.name: Structural Reparameterization
concepts.description: Training a network with a multi-branch structure and then algebraically merging the branches into a single simpler layer for inference, gaining training benefits without inference cost.
concepts.example: A 1x1 kernel can be zero-padded into a 3x3 kernel and an identity is a 3x3 kernel with a 1 in the centre, so three parallel branches add up to one 3x3 convolution.

concepts.name: Structured Pruning
concepts.description: Pruning whole structures such as channels, filters, heads or layers instead of individual weights, giving smaller dense models that run faster on standard hardware.
concepts.example: Removing 30% of a CNN's filters makes every layer genuinely thinner, so it runs faster on ordinary GPUs, unlike scattering zeros that dense hardware still computes.

concepts.name: SwiGLU
concepts.description: A gated feed-forward activation in Transformers that multiplies a Swish-activated linear projection by another linear projection elementwise; a GLU variant used in LLaMA and PaLM.
concepts.example: For hidden vector x, SwiGLU computes Swish(xW) times xV elementwise, so one projection acts as a soft gate deciding how much of the other passes through.

concepts.name: Swish
concepts.description: The activation x times sigmoid(beta x); with beta = 1 it is SiLU. Smooth and non-monotonic, it often slightly outperforms ReLU in deep networks.
concepts.example: Swish(2) = 2 x sigmoid(2), about 1.76; Swish(-1) is about -0.27; Swish(-10) is near 0, so it is ReLU-like but smooth with a small negative dip.

concepts.name: Symmetry Breaking (Weight Initialization)
concepts.description: The need to initialize weights differently, typically randomly, because neurons that start with identical weights get identical gradients and would stay identical forever.
concepts.example: If two hidden neurons both start with weights [0.5, 0.5], they compute the same output, get the same gradient and stay twins forever, so the layer acts like one neuron.

concepts.name: Synchronized Batch Normalization
concepts.description: Batch normalization whose mean and variance are computed across all devices in data-parallel training rather than per device, which matters when each device has a small batch.
concepts.example: Eight GPUs each holding 2 images would each compute batch statistics from 2 samples; synced batch norm pools all 16 images' statistics across GPUs for a reliable mean.

concepts.name: Synchronous Distributed Training
concepts.description: Distributed training where all workers compute gradients on their batches, wait for each other, and average gradients before every update, keeping a single consistent model.
concepts.example: Four GPUs each process 32 images, compute gradients, then wait at a barrier; once all four finish, their gradients are averaged and every GPU applies the same update, so all copies stay identical - but the slowest GPU sets the pace.

concepts.name: Hyperbolic Tangent Activation
concepts.description: The hyperbolic tangent activation, which maps inputs to (-1, 1) and is zero-centred; a rescaled sigmoid long used in RNNs and early neural networks.
concepts.example: tanh(0) = 0, tanh(2) is about 0.96 and tanh(-2) about -0.96, so outputs hover around zero. A neuron getting inputs like -3, 0 and 3 outputs roughly -1, 0 and 1, keeping the next layer's inputs balanced.

concepts.name: Teacher Forcing
concepts.description: Training a sequence model by feeding it the true previous token at each step rather than its own prediction, which speeds and stabilizes training but causes exposure bias.
concepts.example: Training a model to write "the cat sat": after it wrongly guesses "dog" for word two, teacher forcing still feeds it the true word "cat" before asking for word three, like a tutor correcting each mistake at once.

concepts.name: Temporal Convolutional Network
concepts.description: A sequence model built from stacked causal, dilated 1D convolutions with residual connections, giving long memory and parallel training as an alternative to RNNs.
concepts.example: With kernel size 2 and dilations 1, 2, 4, 8, just four layers let each output see the previous 16 time steps, and all steps of a sequence are computed at once rather than one by one as in an RNN.

concepts.name: Tensor Parallelism
concepts.description: Splitting individual weight matrices of a layer across devices so each computes part of the matrix multiplication, then combining results with collective communication; used for huge Transformers.
concepts.example: A 4096x4096 weight matrix is split column-wise into four 4096x1024 pieces on four GPUs; each GPU multiplies the input by its piece, producing a quarter of the output, and the quarters are then gathered or summed.

concepts.name: Tensor Shape
concepts.description: The size of a tensor along each of its dimensions, such as (batch, channels, height, width); tracking shapes is essential for building and debugging neural networks.
concepts.example: A batch of 8 colour photos, each 32x32 pixels, has shape (8, 3, 32, 32). Flattening each photo gives (8, 3072), and a linear layer expecting 3072 inputs then works - feed it (8, 1024) and it crashes.

concepts.name: TensorBoard
concepts.description: A visualization toolkit for machine learning experiments that displays training curves, model graphs, histograms, images and embeddings logged during training.
concepts.example: While a model trains overnight, you log the loss every 100 steps; in the morning TensorBoard shows a curve that dropped then flattened, plus a second run's curve on the same chart so you can see which learning rate worked better.

concepts.name: TensorFlow Lite
concepts.description: A lightweight runtime and converter (now LiteRT) for running TensorFlow models on mobile and embedded devices, with support for quantization and hardware acceleration.
concepts.example: A 90 MB image classifier is converted to a .tflite file and quantized to 8-bit integers, shrinking it to about 23 MB so it can run offline on a phone camera app in a few milliseconds per frame.

concepts.name: TensorRT
concepts.description: NVIDIA's SDK for optimizing and running trained neural networks on NVIDIA GPUs, using layer fusion, precision calibration and kernel tuning to cut inference latency.
concepts.example: A ResNet-50 running at 10 ms per image in plain PyTorch might drop to around 2 ms after TensorRT fuses convolution, bias and ReLU into one kernel and switches to INT8 arithmetic on the same NVIDIA GPU.

concepts.name: Test-Time Augmentation
concepts.description: Making predictions on several augmented versions of a test input, such as flips and crops, and averaging them to get a more robust final prediction.
concepts.example: A cat photo gets 0.70 "cat", its mirror image 0.80 and a slightly zoomed crop 0.75; averaging gives 0.75, a steadier answer than trusting any single view of the picture.

concepts.name: Theano
concepts.description: An early Python library that compiled symbolic math expressions into fast CPU or GPU code and computed gradients automatically; a pioneer of deep learning frameworks, discontinued in 2017.
concepts.example: In Theano you wrote y = x**2 symbolically, asked for T.grad(y, x) to get 2x, then compiled both into a fast function that could run on a GPU - years before PyTorch and TensorFlow made this routine.

concepts.name: PyTorch Image Models
concepts.description: PyTorch Image Models, a library by Ross Wightman offering hundreds of pretrained vision models, layers, augmentations and training scripts with a uniform interface.
concepts.example: One line, timm.create_model('resnet50', pretrained=True, num_classes=10), downloads ImageNet weights and swaps the head for your 10 classes; change the name to 'vit_base_patch16_224' and the rest of your code stays the same.

concepts.name: Top-k Accuracy
concepts.description: A classification metric that counts a prediction as correct if the true class is among the model's k highest-scoring classes; top-1 and top-5 are standard on ImageNet.
concepts.example: A model shown a husky ranks wolf, malamute, husky, fox, dog. Top-1 counts it wrong because wolf came first, but top-5 counts it right since husky is among the five best guesses.

concepts.name: Training Dynamics
concepts.description: How a network's loss, weights, gradients and representations change over training, including phases, instabilities and effects of learning rate and batch size.
concepts.example: A typical run: loss drops fast in the first 1,000 steps, plateaus, then drops again when the learning rate is cut; plotting weight norms and gradient sizes alongside the loss shows what changed in each phase.

concepts.name: Training Instability
concepts.description: Training failures such as sudden loss spikes, divergence or NaNs, caused by issues like too-high learning rates, exploding gradients or low-precision overflow, especially in large models.
concepts.example: A language model's loss falls smoothly to 2.1, then at step 40,000 leaps to 9 and turns NaN: one huge gradient overflowed float16. Lowering the learning rate, clipping gradients or using bfloat16 often prevents it.

concepts.name: Transformer
concepts.description: A neural architecture built from stacked self-attention and feed-forward layers with residual connections and layer normalization, processing whole sequences in parallel; the basis of modern LLMs.
concepts.example: Translating "the bank of the river", every word looks at every other word at once: "bank" attends strongly to "river" and learns it means a riverside. Repeating this over 12 or more layers builds deep understanding in parallel.

concepts.name: Translation Equivariance
concepts.description: The property that shifting the input shifts the output by the same amount; convolutional layers have it because the same filter is applied at every position.
concepts.example: An edge-detecting filter finds a cat's ear at pixel 10; shift the photo right by 5 pixels and the same response now appears at pixel 15 - the output map moves exactly with the input.

concepts.name: Translation Invariance
concepts.description: The property that a model's output stays the same when the input is shifted; in CNNs it comes approximately from pooling on top of translation-equivariant convolutions.
concepts.example: A digit classifier should say "7" whether the 7 sits in the top-left or the centre of the image. Pooling and global averaging throw away exact position so the final label stays the same when the digit moves.

concepts.name: Transposed Convolution
concepts.description: A learnable upsampling layer that reverses the shape transformation of a convolution, spreading each input value over an output window; used in decoders, segmentation and GANs.
concepts.example: With stride 2, a 4x4 feature map becomes 8x8: each input value is multiplied by a learnable 3x3 kernel and stamped onto the output, with overlapping stamps added together - a learned zoom-in.

concepts.name: Triplet Loss
concepts.description: A metric-learning loss on an anchor, a positive of the same class and a negative of a different class, pushing the anchor closer to the positive than the negative by at least a margin.
concepts.example: For face recognition, take a photo of Ana (anchor), another photo of Ana (positive) and one of Ben (negative). If anchor-to-Ana is distance 0.4 and anchor-to-Ben 0.5 with margin 0.3, the loss is 0.4 - 0.5 + 0.3 = 0.2, pushing Ben further away.

concepts.name: Truncated Backpropagation Through Time
concepts.description: Backpropagation through time limited to a fixed number of recent steps, splitting long sequences into chunks so RNN training stays cheap while hidden state is still carried forward.
concepts.example: A 10,000-character text is split into chunks of 100. The RNN processes chunk 1, backpropagates only through those 100 steps, then passes its hidden state into chunk 2 without gradients flowing back into chunk 1.

concepts.name: Undercomplete Autoencoder
concepts.description: An autoencoder whose hidden code has fewer dimensions than its input, forcing it to learn a compressed representation of the most important features.
concepts.example: Squeeze 784-pixel digit images through a 32-number bottleneck and back. To rebuild a "3" from just 32 numbers, the network must learn its essential strokes, much like summarising a book in one paragraph.

concepts.name: Universal Approximation Theorem
concepts.description: The result that a feedforward network with one hidden layer and a suitable nonlinear activation can approximate any continuous function on a compact set to any accuracy, given enough neurons.
concepts.example: Enough ReLU neurons can trace any smooth curve, like sin(x) on [0, 6], as a chain of straight pieces: 10 neurons give a rough zigzag, 1,000 a near-perfect match. The theorem promises it exists, not that training finds it.

concepts.name: Unstructured Pruning
concepts.description: Removing individual weights anywhere in a network, usually those of smallest magnitude, giving high sparsity but irregular patterns that need sparse hardware or kernels for speedups.
concepts.example: In a layer with 1,000 weights, zero out the 900 smallest in absolute value. The model may keep its accuracy, but the 100 survivors are scattered randomly, so normal dense hardware still multiplies all the zeros.

concepts.name: Vanilla RNN
concepts.description: The simplest recurrent network, whose hidden state is updated as tanh of a linear combination of the current input and previous hidden state; it struggles with long-term dependencies.
concepts.example: Reading "I grew up in France ... I speak" one word at a time, the hidden state is updated as h = tanh(W*x + U*h). After 50 words the France signal has faded, so it struggles to predict "French".

concepts.name: Vanishing Gradient Problem
concepts.description: When gradients shrink exponentially as they are backpropagated through many layers or time steps, so early layers barely learn; caused by saturating activations and small weights.
concepts.example: A sigmoid's slope is at most 0.25, so backpropagating through 10 sigmoid layers can scale gradients by 0.25^10, about one millionth. The first layers get almost no signal and barely change.

concepts.name: Variational Dropout
concepts.description: Dropout interpreted as approximate Bayesian inference; for RNNs it means using the same dropout mask at every time step, and it can also learn per-weight dropout rates.
concepts.example: In an RNN reading a 20-word sentence, ordinary dropout picks a new random mask at every word. Variational dropout picks one mask, say dropping units 3 and 7, and keeps it for all 20 words.

concepts.name: VGGNet
concepts.description: A deep CNN from Oxford's Visual Geometry Group built from stacks of small 3x3 convolutions and max pooling, 16 or 19 layers deep; showed depth matters and is widely used as a feature extractor.
concepts.example: Instead of one 7x7 filter, VGG stacks three 3x3 filters: the same 7x7 view of the image, but with 27 weights per channel pair instead of 49 and three nonlinearities instead of one.

concepts.name: Warm Starting
concepts.description: Initializing training from a previously trained model's weights rather than from scratch, to save time when data or the task changes slightly.
concepts.example: You trained a spam filter on last year's emails. When new emails arrive, you start from the old model's weights and train a little more, reaching good accuracy in an hour instead of retraining for a day.

concepts.name: Warmup-Stable-Decay Schedule
concepts.description: A learning-rate schedule with a short warmup, a long constant phase, and a final fast decay; it allows continuing training or branching checkpoints without fixing the total length in advance.
concepts.example: Train for 100,000 steps: ramp the learning rate up over 1,000 steps, hold it at 0.001, then drop it fast over the last 10,000. To train longer, just resume from the stable phase and decay later.

concepts.name: WaveNet
concepts.description: A deep generative model for raw audio from DeepMind that predicts each sample from previous ones using stacks of dilated causal convolutions, producing very natural speech.
concepts.example: At 16,000 samples per second, WaveNet predicts each sample from thousands before it, picking one of 256 amplitude levels, then feeds that choice back in - one second of speech takes 16,000 such predictions.

concepts.name: Weight Clustering
concepts.description: A compression method that groups a layer's weights into a few clusters, often with k-means, and replaces each weight with its cluster centroid so only small indices and a codebook are stored.
concepts.example: A layer's million weights are grouped into 16 clusters with centres like -0.31 or 0.05. Each weight is stored as a 4-bit cluster index plus one shared table of 16 values, about 8 times smaller than 32-bit floats.

concepts.name: Weight Decay
concepts.description: A regularizer that shrinks weights toward zero at each update by a small fraction, equivalent to L2 regularization for plain SGD but not for adaptive optimizers like Adam.
concepts.example: With decay 0.01 and learning rate 0.1, every step shrinks each weight by 0.1% before the gradient update, so a weight of 5.0 drifts toward 0 unless the data keeps pulling it back.

concepts.name: Weight Initialization
concepts.description: Choosing the starting values of a network's weights; good schemes scale random weights to the layer size so activations and gradients neither explode nor vanish.
concepts.example: If each of 100 inputs has weights drawn with standard deviation 1, a neuron's output has spread around 10 and blows up across layers; scaling the weights' standard deviation to 0.1 keeps it near 1.

concepts.name: Weight Normalization
concepts.description: Reparameterizing each weight vector as a direction times a learned length, separating norm from direction to speed up optimization without batch statistics.
concepts.example: A weight vector (3, 4) is rewritten as length g = 5 times direction (0.6, 0.8). The optimizer can now lengthen it to 10 without changing direction, or rotate it without changing length.

concepts.name: Weight Standardization
concepts.description: Standardizing each convolution filter's weights to zero mean and unit variance before use; combined with group normalization it trains well with tiny batches.
concepts.example: A 3x3 filter's weights with mean 0.2 and standard deviation 0.5 are shifted and rescaled to mean 0 and standard deviation 1 before each convolution, so the next layer's inputs stay well-scaled even with batch size 2.

concepts.name: Weight Tying
concepts.description: A technique that reuses the same matrix for a model's input token embeddings and its output projection before the softmax, cutting parameter count and often improving language-model quality.
concepts.example: A model with a 50,000-word vocabulary and 512-dimension vectors uses one 50,000x512 matrix both to look up input words and to score output words, saving about 25 million parameters.

concepts.name: Weights and Biases
concepts.description: The learnable numbers of a neural network: weights scale each input to a neuron and biases shift the result. Training adjusts them to minimize a loss function.
concepts.example: A neuron predicting house price might compute 300 x size + 50,000: the weight 300 says how much each square metre matters and the bias 50,000 sets a baseline. Training nudges both until predictions fit the data.

concepts.name: Weights & Biases
concepts.description: Weights & Biases (wandb) is a hosted tool for logging machine-learning experiments, tracking metrics, hyperparameters and artifacts, and comparing training runs in dashboards.
concepts.example: Add wandb.init() and wandb.log({'loss': loss}) to your training script, and each run appears on a web dashboard with its curves and hyperparameters, so you can compare 20 learning-rate trials side by side.

concepts.name: Wide Residual Network
concepts.description: A ResNet variant that makes residual blocks wider (more channels) and the network shallower, showing that width can beat extreme depth in accuracy and training speed.
concepts.example: A 16-layer ResNet with 8 times more channels per layer beat a 1,000-layer thin ResNet on CIFAR-10 while training several times faster, because wide layers use GPUs efficiently.

concepts.name: Winograd Convolution
concepts.description: A fast algorithm for small convolutions that uses minimal-filtering transforms to trade expensive multiplications for cheaper additions, speeding up 3x3 CNN layers on CPUs and GPUs.
concepts.example: Computing 2 outputs of a 3-tap filter directly takes 6 multiplications; Winograd's F(2,3) trick gets the same 2 outputs with just 4, using a few extra additions - a big saving repeated millions of times in a CNN.

concepts.name: Word2vec
concepts.description: A family of shallow neural models (skip-gram and CBOW) that learn dense word vectors by predicting words from their neighbors, so words used in similar contexts get similar embeddings.
concepts.example: From "I drank hot coffee" and "I drank hot tea", word2vec learns that coffee and tea share neighbours, so their vectors end up close; famously, king - man + woman lands near queen.

concepts.name: Xavier Initialization
concepts.description: A weight-initialization scheme that draws weights with variance scaled by the layer's fan-in and fan-out, keeping activation and gradient variance stable across layers with tanh or sigmoid units.
concepts.example: For a tanh layer with 200 inputs and 200 outputs, Xavier sets weight variance to 2/(200+200) = 0.005, a standard deviation near 0.07, so signals neither shrink nor blow up as they pass through.

concepts.name: Xception
concepts.description: A CNN architecture that replaces Inception modules with depthwise separable convolutions, taking the Inception idea of separating spatial and cross-channel processing to its extreme.
concepts.example: Xception first filters each colour or feature channel separately in space, then mixes channels with 1x1 convolutions, like having one person blur each photo layer and another just blend the layers.

concepts.name: XOR Problem
concepts.description: The task of learning the XOR function, which is not linearly separable; it showed that a single-layer perceptron cannot solve it and motivated multilayer networks.
concepts.example: XOR outputs 1 for (0,1) and (1,0), and 0 for (0,0) and (1,1). Plot them: the 1s sit on one diagonal and the 0s on the other, and no single straight line can split them - but two hidden neurons can.

concepts.name: ZeRO
