concepts.description: ZeRO (Zero Redundancy Optimizer) is a distributed-training method that partitions optimizer states, gradients and parameters across data-parallel GPUs instead of replicating them, enabling much larger models.
concepts.example: Adam keeps two extra numbers per weight, so a 7-billion-parameter model needs over 100 GB for weights, gradients and optimizer states. ZeRO splits that across 8 GPUs, so each holds roughly an eighth.

concepts.name: ZFNet
concepts.description: A 2013 ImageNet-winning CNN that refined AlexNet's filter sizes and strides, guided by deconvolution-based visualizations of what each layer learns.
concepts.example: Visualizing AlexNet's first layer showed dead and blurry filters, so ZFNet shrank the first filter from 11x11 to 7x7 and the stride from 4 to 2, sharpening features and winning ImageNet 2013.

concepts.name: Zoneout
concepts.description: A regularizer for recurrent networks that, at each time step, randomly keeps some hidden units at their previous values instead of updating them, similar in spirit to dropout.
concepts.example: At each word, an LSTM with zoneout randomly picks, say, 15% of its hidden units and copies their old values forward unchanged instead of updating them, so information and gradients can skip over steps.

concepts.name: Acute angle
concepts.description: An angle that measures more than 0 degrees but less than 90 degrees, i.e. smaller than a right angle. The corners of an equilateral triangle are acute angles.
concepts.example: The hands of a clock at 1 o'clock make a 30-degree angle, and a slice of pizza cut into 8 pieces has a 45-degree tip; both are acute because they are narrower than the corner of a book.

concepts.name: Acute triangle
concepts.description: A triangle in which all three interior angles are acute (less than 90 degrees). Its circumcenter and orthocenter both lie inside the triangle.
concepts.example: A triangle with angles 50, 60 and 70 degrees is acute. One with angles 30, 60 and 90 is not, since it has a right angle, and 20, 30, 130 is not either.

concepts.name: Affine geometry
concepts.description: The study of geometric properties preserved by affine transformations, such as parallelism, collinearity and ratios of lengths along a line, while ignoring distances and angles.
concepts.example: Shear a square into a slanted parallelogram: its angles and side lengths change, but opposite sides stay parallel and the midpoint of each side is still the midpoint. Affine geometry studies exactly those surviving facts.

concepts.name: Algebraic geometry
concepts.description: The branch of mathematics that studies geometric shapes defined as solution sets of systems of polynomial equations (varieties), using tools from commutative algebra such as ideals and rings.
concepts.example: The equation x^2 + y^2 = 1 describes a circle, and y = x^2 a parabola. Asking where they meet becomes algebra: substitute to get y + y^2 = 1 and solve, turning a picture question into polynomial manipulation.

concepts.name: Altitude of a triangle
concepts.description: A line segment from a vertex of a triangle drawn perpendicular to the opposite side (or its extension). Its length is the height used in the area formula: half of base times height.
concepts.example: In a triangle with base 10 cm, drop a line from the top corner straight down to the base, meeting it at a right angle; if it is 6 cm long, that altitude gives area = 1/2 x 10 x 6 = 30 square cm.

concepts.name: Angle
concepts.description: The figure formed by two rays sharing a common endpoint called the vertex, and the measure of how far one ray is turned from the other, usually given in degrees or radians.
concepts.example: Open a pair of scissors: the two blades are rays from the pivot, and how wide they spread is the angle. A quarter turn of a door handle is 90 degrees; a half turn is 180.

concepts.name: Angle bisector
concepts.description: A ray or line that divides an angle into two equal angles. Every point on it is equally distant from the two sides, and the three angle bisectors of a triangle meet at the incenter.
concepts.example: Fold a paper corner of 70 degrees so its two edges line up: the crease splits it into two 35-degree angles. Any point on the crease is the same distance from both edges.

concepts.name: Aperiodic tiling
concepts.description: A tiling of the plane that covers it completely without gaps or overlaps but never repeats by translation, so it has no periodic pattern. Penrose tilings are the best-known examples.
concepts.example: Bathroom squares repeat: slide the floor one tile over and it matches itself. A Penrose floor of kites and darts also covers every gap, but no slide in any direction ever lines it up with itself again.

concepts.name: Arc
concepts.description: A connected portion of the circumference of a circle between two points. Its length is proportional to the central angle it subtends: arc length equals radius times angle in radians.
concepts.example: On a pizza of radius 10 cm, a slice with a 1-radian tip has crust exactly 10 cm long; a quarter of the pizza has crust about 15.7 cm, since its angle is about 1.57 radians.

concepts.name: Area
concepts.description: The amount of two-dimensional space inside a closed shape, measured in square units. For example, a rectangle's area is its length times its width.
concepts.example: A rug 3 m long and 2 m wide covers 6 square metres: you could lay six 1-metre square tiles on it. A triangle with base 4 and height 3 covers half of a 4x3 rectangle, so 6 square units.

concepts.name: Asymptote
concepts.description: A line that the graph of a curve or function approaches arbitrarily closely as the input or output grows without bound, such as y = 0 for the curve y = 1/x. Asymptotes can be horizontal, vertical or oblique.
concepts.example: For y = 1/x, at x = 10 y is 0.1, at x = 1,000 it is 0.001: the curve hugs the x-axis ever closer but never touches it, so y = 0 is a horizontal asymptote.

concepts.name: Axis of symmetry
concepts.description: A line that divides a figure into two mirror-image halves, so reflecting the figure across it leaves it unchanged. A parabola y = ax^2 + bx + c has the vertical axis x = -b/(2a).
concepts.example: Fold a paper heart down its middle and both halves match exactly: the fold line is its axis of symmetry. For y = x^2 - 4x + 1, the axis is x = 4/2 = 2.

concepts.name: Bézier curve
concepts.description: A smooth parametric curve defined by a set of control points, built by repeated linear interpolation (de Casteljau's algorithm). Widely used in computer graphics, fonts and vector drawing tools.
concepts.example: With points A, B, C, slide halfway along AB and BC to get two points, then halfway between those: repeating for every fraction t traces a smooth arc from A to C that bends toward B, like a font designer's curve.

concepts.name: Boy's surface
concepts.description: A self-intersecting immersion of the real projective plane into three-dimensional space without singular points, discovered by Werner Boy in 1901. It is a one-sided, non-orientable closed surface.
concepts.example: Glue a disc's edge to a Mobius strip's edge and you get the projective plane, which cannot sit in 3D without crossing itself. Boy's surface is a smooth way to do it, with a triple point where three sheets meet, like a curved three-lobed cap.

concepts.name: Brianchon's theorem
concepts.description: A theorem of projective geometry stating that for a hexagon circumscribed about a conic section, the three diagonals joining opposite vertices meet in a single point. It is the projective dual of Pascal's theorem.
concepts.example: Draw a circle and surround it with a six-sided shape whose sides all just touch it. Connect each corner with the opposite corner: the three long diagonals always cross at one point, however lopsided the hexagon.

concepts.name: British flag theorem
concepts.description: The statement that for any point P and rectangle ABCD, the sums of squared distances to opposite corners are equal: PA^2 + PC^2 = PB^2 + PD^2. It follows directly from the Pythagorean theorem.
concepts.example: In a 4x3 rectangle with corners A(0,0), B(4,0), C(4,3), D(0,3), take P(1,1). Then PA^2 + PC^2 = 2 + 13 = 15 and PB^2 + PD^2 = 10 + 5 = 15 - equal, wherever P is placed.

concepts.name: Butterfly theorem
concepts.description: A classical result in Euclidean geometry: if M is the midpoint of a chord PQ of a circle and two other chords AB and CD pass through M, then AD and BC cut PQ at points equally distant from M.
concepts.example: Draw a chord PQ with midpoint M, then two chords AB and CD through M. Joining A to D and B to C makes a butterfly shape; its wings cross PQ at two points the same distance from M, every time.

concepts.name: Calabi–Yau manifold
concepts.description: A compact complex manifold that admits a Ricci-flat Kahler metric, equivalently one with vanishing first Chern class. Calabi-Yau threefolds are used in string theory to model compactified extra dimensions.
concepts.example: String theory needs 10 dimensions, but we see 4. The extra 6 are imagined curled up into a tiny Calabi-Yau shape at every point, and the shape's holes help decide which particles exist.

concepts.name: Cardioid
concepts.description: A heart-shaped plane curve traced by a point on a circle rolling around another circle of equal radius. In polar coordinates it can be written r = a(1 - cos theta).
concepts.example: Roll a coin around another coin of the same size and watch a point on its rim: it traces a heart shape. With r = 1 - cos(theta), r is 0 at theta = 0 (the dent) and 2 at theta = 180 degrees (the far point).

concepts.name: Carnot's theorem
concepts.description: A theorem stating that in a triangle, the sum of the signed distances from the circumcenter to the three sides equals R + r, where R is the circumradius and r is the inradius.
concepts.example: For an equilateral triangle of side 6, R is about 3.46 and r about 1.73. The circumcenter is r away from each side, so the sum is 3r, about 5.20, which matches R + r.

concepts.name: Cartesian plane
concepts.description: A plane in which every point is identified by an ordered pair (x, y) of real numbers giving its signed distances along two perpendicular number lines, the x-axis and y-axis, that cross at the origin.
concepts.example: To find a treasure at (3, -2), start at the crossing point, walk 3 steps right along the x-axis, then 2 steps down. Every point on the plane gets exactly one such pair of directions.

concepts.name: Catenoid
concepts.description: The surface formed by rotating a catenary curve around an axis. It was the first non-planar minimal surface discovered and is the shape a soap film takes between two parallel circular rings.
concepts.example: Dip two wire rings in soapy water and pull them slightly apart: the film between them pinches in at the waist, forming a catenoid, the least-area surface joining the rings.

concepts.name: Ceva's theorem
concepts.description: A theorem stating that three lines from the vertices of a triangle to points on the opposite sides meet in a single point exactly when the product of the three side ratios they create equals 1.
concepts.example: In a triangle, if each cevian cuts its side in the ratio 1:1 (the medians), the product is 1 x 1 x 1 = 1, so they meet at one point. Ratios 2, 3 and 1/6 also multiply to 1, so those lines meet too.

concepts.name: Chord
concepts.description: A line segment whose two endpoints both lie on a circle (or other curve). The longest chord of a circle is a diameter, and chords equally distant from the center have equal lengths.
concepts.example: Stretch a string across a round table between two edge points: that string is a chord. If it passes through the centre of a 1 m wide table, it is the diameter, the longest chord, 1 m long.

concepts.name: Circle
concepts.description: The set of all points in a plane at a fixed distance, the radius, from a fixed point called the center. Its circumference is 2 pi r and the area it encloses is pi r^2.
concepts.example: Tie a 2 m rope to a stake and walk around with it taut: you trace a circle of radius 2 m. Its circumference is about 12.6 m and the grass it encloses is about 12.6 square metres.

concepts.name: Circumcenter
concepts.description: The point where the perpendicular bisectors of a triangle's sides meet. It is equally distant from all three vertices and is the center of the circumscribed circle that passes through them.
concepts.example: Three houses need one shared well equally far from each. Draw the perpendicular bisector between each pair of houses; where the bisectors cross is the circumcenter, the perfect well site.

concepts.name: Circumference
concepts.description: The distance around a circle, its perimeter. It equals pi times the diameter, or 2 pi r, and this constant ratio between circumference and diameter is what defines the number pi.
concepts.example: A bicycle wheel with a 70 cm diameter travels about 3.14 x 70, about 220 cm, in one full turn. Wrap a tape around any round jar and divide by its width: you always get about 3.14.

concepts.name: Cone
concepts.description: A three-dimensional solid with a circular base that tapers smoothly to a single point called the apex. Its volume is one third of the base area times the height, like a pyramid.
concepts.example: An ice-cream cone with a 3 cm radius and 10 cm height holds 1/3 x pi x 9 x 10, about 94 cubic cm - a third of what a cylinder of the same size would hold.

concepts.name: Conformal map
concepts.description: A function that preserves angles locally between curves, though not necessarily lengths. In the plane, holomorphic functions with nonzero derivative are conformal; examples include the Mercator and stereographic projections.
concepts.example: On a Mercator map, two roads that cross at 90 degrees on the globe still cross at 90 degrees on paper, even though Greenland appears hugely enlarged - angles are kept, sizes are not.

concepts.name: Congruence
concepts.description: The relation between two figures that have exactly the same shape and size, so one can be moved onto the other by rotations, reflections and translations. Triangle tests include SSS, SAS and ASA.
concepts.example: Cut two triangles from paper with sides 3, 4 and 5 cm. However you turn or flip one, it can be laid exactly on the other, so they are congruent - knowing the three sides (SSS) is enough.

concepts.name: Conic section
concepts.description: A curve obtained by intersecting a plane with a double cone: a circle, ellipse, parabola or hyperbola. Each is described by a second-degree equation in x and y and by its eccentricity.
concepts.example: Shine a torch on a wall: pointed straight at it, the light makes a circle; tilt it and the patch becomes an ellipse, then a parabola, then a hyperbola as the cone of light slices the wall at steeper angles.

concepts.name: Curve of constant width
concepts.description: A convex closed curve whose width, the distance between two parallel lines touching it on opposite sides, is the same in every direction. Besides the circle, the Reuleaux triangle is a famous example.
concepts.example: A Reuleaux triangle has width 5 cm in every direction, so it rolls smoothly between two parallel boards 5 cm apart, just like a circle. The UK 50p coin, a rounded heptagon, uses the same idea so vending machines measure it consistently.

concepts.name: Coordinate geometry
concepts.description: The study of geometry using a coordinate system, where points are described by numbers and shapes such as lines and circles by equations, so geometric problems can be solved with algebra.
concepts.example: To check whether the point (3, 4) lies on the circle around the origin of radius 5, compute 3^2 + 4^2 = 25 = 5^2. Yes - no compass needed, just arithmetic.

concepts.name: Cosine
concepts.description: A trigonometric function: in a right triangle, the cosine of an angle is the adjacent side divided by the hypotenuse. On the unit circle, cos theta is the x-coordinate of the point at angle theta.
concepts.example: A 10 m ladder leans at 60 degrees to the ground. Its foot is 10 x cos 60 = 5 m from the wall. At 0 degrees the ladder lies flat (cos = 1); at 90 degrees it stands upright (cos = 0).

concepts.name: Cube
concepts.description: A three-dimensional solid with six congruent square faces, twelve equal edges and eight vertices. With edge length a its volume is a^3 and its surface area is 6a^2; it is one of the five Platonic solids.
concepts.example: A die with 2 cm edges has volume 2 x 2 x 2 = 8 cubic cm and surface area 6 x 4 = 24 square cm. Doubling the edge to 4 cm makes it 64 cubic cm, eight times as much.

concepts.name: Cuboid
concepts.description: A box-shaped solid with six rectangular faces, also called a rectangular prism. With length l, width w and height h its volume is lwh and its surface area is 2(lw + wh + lh).
concepts.example: A shoebox 30 cm long, 20 cm wide and 10 cm tall holds 6,000 cubic cm. Wrapping it needs 2(600 + 200 + 300) = 2,200 square cm of paper.

concepts.name: Curvature
concepts.description: A measure of how sharply a curve bends at a point, equal to the reciprocal of the radius of the best-fitting circle there. A straight line has zero curvature and a small circle has large curvature.
concepts.example: A road bend that follows a circle of radius 50 m has curvature 1/50 = 0.02; a tight hairpin with radius 10 m has 0.1, five times sharper. A straight road has curvature 0.

concepts.name: Cycloid
concepts.description: The curve traced by a point on the rim of a circle as it rolls along a straight line. It is the solution to the brachistochrone problem of fastest descent under gravity.
concepts.example: Stick a reflector on a bicycle wheel's rim and ride: it traces a series of arches, touching the ground once per turn. Each arch is 8 times the wheel's radius long.

concepts.name: Cylinder
concepts.description: A three-dimensional solid with two parallel congruent circular bases joined by a curved surface. With radius r and height h its volume is pi r^2 h.
concepts.example: A can with radius 4 cm and height 10 cm holds pi x 16 x 10, about 503 cubic cm. Double the height and it holds twice as much; double the radius and it holds four times as much.

concepts.name: Degree
concepts.description: A unit for measuring angles in which a full turn is divided into 360 equal parts, so a right angle is 90 degrees and a straight angle is 180 degrees.
concepts.example: A full turn on a skateboard is a 360; a half turn is 180 degrees and a quarter turn is 90. Each degree is one tiny slice of a circle cut into 360 equal slices.

concepts.name: Desargues' theorem
concepts.description: A theorem of projective geometry: two triangles are in perspective from a point (lines joining matching vertices meet at one point) exactly when they are in perspective from a line (matching sides meet on one line).
concepts.example: Draw two triangles so the lines through matching corners all meet at one point, like a shape and its shadow from a lamp. Then extend matching sides: the three crossing points always land on one straight line.

concepts.name: Descartes' circle theorem
concepts.description: A formula relating the curvatures (reciprocal radii) of four mutually tangent circles: (k1+k2+k3+k4)^2 = 2(k1^2+k2^2+k3^2+k4^2). It lets you find the fourth circle given three.
concepts.example: Three coins of radius 1 touch each other. Curvatures are 1, 1, 1, and the formula gives the small circle nestled between them a curvature of 3 + 2 x sqrt 3, about 6.46, so its radius is about 0.155.

concepts.name: Descriptive geometry
concepts.description: The branch of geometry that represents three-dimensional objects on two-dimensional drawings using systematic projections onto planes, the basis of technical and engineering drawing.
concepts.example: An engineer draws a house's front view and top view on two planes at right angles, lined up so one measurement transfers between them; from the pair alone, a builder can recover the true length of a sloping roof beam.

concepts.name: Diameter
concepts.description: A chord that passes through the center of a circle or sphere, or its length, which is twice the radius. It is the longest possible chord.
concepts.example: A pizza with radius 15 cm has diameter 30 cm: a cut straight through the centre from crust to crust. Any cut that misses the centre is shorter.

concepts.name: Differential geometry
concepts.description: The field that uses calculus and linear algebra to study smooth curves, surfaces and manifolds, including their curvature, geodesics and intrinsic geometry. It underlies general relativity.
concepts.example: An ant on a ball measures that a triangle's angles add to more than 180 degrees, proving its world is curved without ever leaving the surface. Differential geometry uses calculus to measure such bending.

concepts.name: Dilation
concepts.description: A transformation that enlarges or shrinks a figure by a scale factor relative to a fixed center point, keeping its shape and angles but multiplying all lengths by the same factor.
concepts.example: Projecting a 4 cm photo onto a wall with scale factor 25 makes it 100 cm, and every line in it grows 25 times while angles stay the same. Scale factor 0.5 shrinks a figure to half size.

concepts.name: Directrix
concepts.description: A fixed line used to define a conic section: the curve is the set of points whose distance to a focus divided by the distance to the directrix equals the eccentricity. For a parabola this ratio is 1.
concepts.example: For y = x^2/4, the focus is (0, 1) and the directrix is the line y = -1. The point (2, 1) is 2 from the focus and 2 from the directrix: equal distances, ratio 1, as for every point on a parabola.

concepts.name: Distance formula
concepts.description: The formula d = sqrt((x2 - x1)^2 + (y2 - y1)^2) giving the straight-line distance between two points in the coordinate plane. It is the Pythagorean theorem applied to coordinate differences.
concepts.example: From (1, 2) to (4, 6): go 3 across and 4 up, so the distance is sqrt(9 + 16) = 5. It is the straight-line distance a bird would fly between those points.

concepts.name: Dodecahedron
concepts.description: A polyhedron with twelve flat faces. The regular dodecahedron, one of the five Platonic solids, has twelve regular pentagonal faces, twenty vertices and thirty edges.
concepts.example: A 12-sided gaming die is a dodecahedron: 12 pentagon faces, three meeting at each of its 20 corners. Check Euler's formula: 20 - 30 + 12 = 2.

concepts.name: Eccentricity
concepts.description: A number describing how much a conic section deviates from a circle: 0 for a circle, between 0 and 1 for an ellipse, exactly 1 for a parabola and greater than 1 for a hyperbola.
concepts.example: Earth's orbit has eccentricity about 0.017, nearly a circle; Halley's comet has about 0.97, a long thin ellipse. A thrown ball traces about 1, a parabola.

concepts.name: Einstein manifold
concepts.description: A Riemannian or pseudo-Riemannian manifold whose Ricci curvature tensor is proportional to its metric tensor. Such manifolds give vacuum solutions of Einstein's equations with a cosmological constant.
concepts.example: A sphere is an Einstein manifold: it curves the same in every direction, so its Ricci curvature is a constant multiple of the metric. A flat plane is too, with constant 0.

concepts.name: Ellipse
concepts.description: A closed oval curve consisting of all points whose distances to two fixed points, the foci, add up to a constant. A circle is a special ellipse, and planets move along elliptical orbits.
concepts.example: Pin two tacks 6 cm apart, loop a 10 cm string around them, and trace with a pencil keeping it taut: the distances to the tacks always add to the same total, drawing an ellipse.

concepts.name: Elliptic geometry
concepts.description: A non-Euclidean geometry in which there are no parallel lines, since any two lines meet, and the angles of a triangle add up to more than 180 degrees. Its standard model is closely related to geometry on a sphere.
concepts.example: On a globe, two lines of longitude look parallel at the equator but meet at both poles. A triangle from the North Pole to two points on the equator 90 degrees apart has three 90-degree angles, totalling 270.

concepts.name: Equation of a line
concepts.description: An algebraic equation whose solutions are exactly the points on a straight line, commonly written in slope-intercept form y = mx + b, point-slope form or general form ax + by = c.
concepts.example: A taxi charges 3 dollars plus 2 per km, so cost y = 2x + 3. Points like (0, 3), (1, 5) and (4, 11) all lie on one straight line with slope 2.

concepts.name: Equilateral triangle
concepts.description: A triangle whose three sides are all equal in length; consequently all three angles equal 60 degrees. It has three axes of symmetry and is a regular polygon.
concepts.example: Three pencils of the same length laid end to end form an equilateral triangle. Every corner is 60 degrees, and it looks the same after turning it by a third of a full turn.

concepts.name: Euclidean geometry
concepts.description: The geometry of flat space built from Euclid's axioms about points, lines, circles and parallel lines, covering familiar facts about triangles, angles, congruence and similarity.
concepts.example: On a flat sheet, draw a triangle and measure its angles: they always total 180 degrees, and through a point beside a line you can draw exactly one parallel. These facts follow from Euclid's few starting axioms.

concepts.name: Euclid's Elements
concepts.description: A thirteen-book mathematical treatise written by Euclid around 300 BC that deduces plane geometry, number theory and solid geometry from a small set of axioms, setting the model for rigorous proof.
concepts.example: Book I starts with five postulates, like "a straight line can join any two points", and builds step by step to proposition 47, the Pythagorean theorem, each step justified by earlier ones.

concepts.name: Euler line
concepts.description: The line through a triangle's orthocenter, centroid and circumcenter, which Euler proved are always collinear (in a non-equilateral triangle). The nine-point center also lies on it.
concepts.example: In a triangle with corners (0,0), (6,0), (0,4), the orthocenter is (0,0), the centroid (2, 4/3) and the circumcenter (3, 2). All three lie on the line y = (2/3)x - the Euler line.

concepts.name: Euler's theorem for polyhedra
concepts.description: Euler's formula V - E + F = 2 relating the numbers of vertices, edges and faces of any convex polyhedron. The value 2 is the Euler characteristic of a sphere, which links geometry to topology.
concepts.example: A cube has 8 corners, 12 edges and 6 faces: 8 - 12 + 6 = 2. A square pyramid: 5 - 8 + 5 = 2. Shave off a corner of the cube and the count still comes out to 2.

concepts.name: Exterior angle theorem
concepts.description: A theorem stating that an exterior angle of a triangle, formed by extending one side, equals the sum of the two opposite interior angles, and is therefore larger than either of them.
concepts.example: A triangle has interior angles 50 and 60 degrees at two corners. Extend the side at the third corner: the outside angle there is 50 + 60 = 110 degrees, without measuring the third angle at all.

concepts.name: Feuerbach's circle
concepts.description: Another name for the nine-point circle, highlighting Feuerbach's theorem that this circle is tangent to the triangle's incircle and to its three excircles.
concepts.example: Draw any triangle and its nine-point circle; then draw the incircle inside. They always just kiss at a single point, the Feuerbach point, and the nine-point circle also touches each of the three outside excircles.

concepts.name: Flower of Life
concepts.description: A decorative geometric figure made of many overlapping circles of equal radius arranged in a hexagonal pattern, each center lying on six surrounding circles. It is popular in art and sacred geometry.
concepts.example: Draw a circle, then six more of the same size centred on points of its edge, each passing through the centre. Keep adding circles at new crossing points and a hexagonal pattern of overlapping petals spreads out.

concepts.name: Fractal
concepts.description: A geometric shape with detailed structure at every scale, often self-similar so that parts resemble the whole, and frequently with a non-integer fractal dimension. Examples include the Koch snowflake and coastlines.
concepts.example: Measure Britain's coast with a 100 km ruler and you get about 2,800 km; with a 50 km ruler, about 3,400 km. Smaller rulers keep finding more wiggles, because the coastline has detail at every scale.

concepts.name: Gaussian curvature
concepts.description: The product of the two principal curvatures of a surface at a point. It is positive on a sphere, zero on a plane or cylinder and negative on a saddle, and Gauss proved it is intrinsic to the surface.
concepts.example: A ball bends the same way in both directions, so it has positive curvature; a horse saddle bends up one way and down the other, giving negative curvature. A sheet of paper rolled into a tube still has zero - you can unroll it flat.

concepts.name: Geodesic
concepts.description: A curve that is locally the shortest path between points on a surface or manifold, generalizing straight lines to curved spaces. On a sphere the geodesics are arcs of great circles.
concepts.example: A flight from New York to Madrid looks curved on a flat map, but on the globe it follows a great circle, the shortest path on the sphere. That path is a geodesic, the curved-world version of a straight line.

concepts.name: Gnomonic projection
concepts.description: A map projection made by projecting points of a sphere from its center onto a tangent plane. It maps every great circle to a straight line, so shortest routes appear straight, but shapes are strongly distorted.
concepts.example: Put a lamp at the centre of a glass globe and hold paper touching its surface: the shadow of every great circle route, like London to Tokyo, falls as a straight line, so pilots can plan shortest routes with a ruler.

concepts.name: Golden ratio
concepts.description: The irrational number phi = (1 + sqrt 5)/2, about 1.618, obtained when a line is divided so the whole is to the longer part as the longer part is to the shorter. It appears in pentagons and Fibonacci numbers.
concepts.example: Cut a 1.618 m rope into 1 m and 0.618 m: 1.618/1 equals 1/0.618, both about 1.618. Ratios of consecutive Fibonacci numbers, like 13/8 = 1.625 and 21/13 = 1.615, close in on it.

concepts.name: Great circle
concepts.description: A circle on a sphere whose center is the sphere's center, formed by slicing it with a plane through the center. Arcs of great circles are the shortest paths on the sphere, used in air and sea navigation.
concepts.example: Slice an orange through its centre and the cut edge on the peel is a great circle; the equator and every line of longitude are great circles on Earth. A slice off-centre gives a smaller circle that is not one.

concepts.name: Helicoid
concepts.description: A spiral-staircase-shaped surface swept by a straight line that rotates around and moves along a fixed axis at constant rates. After the plane, it was one of the first minimal surfaces discovered.
concepts.example: Picture a spiral staircase with no centre post: a straight beam turns as it climbs the axis. Dip a wire helix and its axis in soap solution and the film forms that same helicoid.

concepts.name: Heron's formula
concepts.description: A formula for a triangle's area from its three side lengths alone: area = sqrt(s(s-a)(s-b)(s-c)), where s is the semiperimeter (a+b+c)/2.
concepts.example: Sides 5, 6 and 7: s = 9, so area = sqrt(9 x 4 x 3 x 2) = sqrt 216, about 14.7. For sides 3, 4, 5, s = 6 and area = sqrt(6 x 3 x 2 x 1) = 6, matching half of 3 x 4.

concepts.name: Hexagon
concepts.description: A polygon with six sides and six angles. A regular hexagon has equal sides and 120 degree interior angles, can be split into six equilateral triangles and tiles the plane, as in honeycombs.
concepts.example: A honeycomb cell is a regular hexagon: six equal sides, six 120-degree corners. Six equilateral triangles meeting at its centre fill it exactly, and copies fit together with no gaps.

concepts.name: Hilbert's Nullstellensatz
concepts.description: A fundamental theorem of algebraic geometry relating polynomial ideals to their zero sets: over an algebraically closed field, a polynomial vanishing on the zeros of an ideal has some power lying in that ideal.
concepts.example: The equations x = 0 and xy - 1 = 0 share no solution, and indeed 1 = y*x - (xy - 1) lies in their ideal. Likewise x vanishes wherever x^2 does; x is not a multiple of x^2, but its square is - exactly as the theorem predicts.

concepts.name: Huzita–Hatori axioms
concepts.description: A set of seven axioms describing every single-fold operation possible in paper folding that aligns points and lines. They show origami can solve cubic equations, e.g. trisecting angles, beyond ruler and compass.
concepts.example: One axiom says: given two points and two lines, you can make a fold placing each point onto its line. That single fold can solve a cubic equation, which is how origami can trisect a 60-degree angle into three 20s.

concepts.name: Hyperbola
concepts.description: A curve with two separate branches consisting of all points whose distances to two fixed foci differ by a constant. Each branch approaches two straight asymptotes; y = 1/x is an example.
concepts.example: Two microphones 10 m apart hear a bang, and the sound reaches one as if it had travelled 4 m farther than to the other. Every point whose distances to the two mics differ by 4 m lies on a hyperbola - which is how sound-ranging locates a source.

concepts.name: Hyperbolic geometry
concepts.description: A non-Euclidean geometry with constant negative curvature in which, through a point not on a line, infinitely many parallel lines exist and triangle angles sum to less than 180 degrees. Modeled by the Poincare disk.
concepts.example: Crochet a frilly ruffled disc and draw a triangle on it: its angles add to less than 180 degrees. In the Poincare disk, many lines through one point never meet a given line.

concepts.name: Icosahedron
concepts.description: A polyhedron with twenty faces. The regular icosahedron, a Platonic solid, has twenty equilateral triangle faces, twelve vertices and thirty edges, with five faces meeting at each vertex.
concepts.example: A 20-sided die is an icosahedron: 20 triangular faces, 12 corners where five triangles meet, and 30 edges. Euler checks out: 12 - 30 + 20 = 2.

concepts.name: Ideal
concepts.description: A subset of a ring closed under addition and under multiplication by any ring element, such as the even integers within the integers. Ideals generalize divisibility and let one build quotient rings.
concepts.example: In the integers, the multiples of 3 form an ideal: add two multiples of 3 and you get one, and multiply one by any integer and it stays a multiple of 3. Working modulo 3 means treating this whole ideal as zero.

concepts.name: Incenter
concepts.description: The point where the three angle bisectors of a triangle meet. It is equally distant from all three sides and is the center of the inscribed circle (incircle) that touches each side.
concepts.example: To place the largest round fountain in a triangular garden, bisect each corner's angle; the three lines meet at the incenter, equally far from every wall, and that distance is the fountain's largest possible radius.

concepts.name: Inscribed angle theorem
concepts.description: A theorem stating that an angle inscribed in a circle is half of the central angle that subtends the same arc. Hence all inscribed angles subtending the same arc are equal.
concepts.example: An arc subtends 80 degrees at a circle's centre. From any point on the far side of the circle, the same arc is seen at 40 degrees - so all spectators seated around the curved edge see the stage at the same angle.

concepts.name: Inverse trigonometric functions
concepts.description: The functions arcsin, arccos and arctan that undo sine, cosine and tangent on restricted domains, returning the angle that produces a given trigonometric ratio.
concepts.example: A ramp rises 1 m over a 2 m length of slope. sin(angle) = 0.5, so arcsin(0.5) = 30 degrees tells you the angle. arctan(1) = 45 degrees because a slope of 1 rises as much as it runs.

concepts.name: Inversion in geometry
concepts.description: A transformation of the plane relative to a circle of radius r that maps each point at distance d from the center to the point on the same ray at distance r^2/d. It turns lines and circles into lines and circles.
concepts.example: Invert in a circle of radius 2: a point at distance 1 from the centre goes to distance 4, a point at distance 4 goes to 1, and points on the circle stay put. Inside and outside swap places.

concepts.name: Isometric projection
concepts.description: A method of drawing 3D objects in 2D where the three coordinate axes appear equally foreshortened at 120 degrees to each other. It is used in technical drawing and many video games.
concepts.example: In a pixel-art city game, a cube is drawn as a hexagon with three visible faces, and its three edges from the nearest corner fan out at 120 degrees with equal length - no vanishing point, so distant houses are as big as near ones.

concepts.name: Isosceles triangle
concepts.description: A triangle with at least two sides of equal length. The angles opposite the equal sides, the base angles, are also equal, and the triangle is symmetric about the altitude to its base.
concepts.example: A roof gable with two equal 5 m rafters is isosceles. If the base angles are each 30 degrees, the peak is 120. Fold it down the middle and the halves match.

concepts.name: K3 surface
concepts.description: A compact complex surface with trivial canonical bundle and no holomorphic 1-forms; K3 surfaces are the two-dimensional Calabi-Yau manifolds and are central examples in algebraic geometry and string theory.
concepts.example: The surface x^4 + y^4 + z^4 + w^4 = 0 in complex projective space is a K3 surface. It has 4 real dimensions and plays the 2-complex-dimensional role that Calabi-Yau threefolds play in string compactification.

concepts.name: Kite
concepts.description: A quadrilateral with two pairs of equal-length adjacent sides. Its diagonals are perpendicular and one of them is an axis of symmetry; a rhombus is a special kite.
concepts.example: A classic kite has two short top sides of 30 cm and two long bottom sides of 50 cm. Its crossbars, the diagonals, meet at a right angle, and the long spine is a mirror line.

concepts.name: Klein bottle
concepts.description: A closed, non-orientable surface with no boundary and no distinct inside or outside, obtainable by gluing two Mobius strips along their edges. It cannot be built in 3D space without self-intersection.
concepts.example: Take a tube and pass one end through the side of the tube to join the other end from the inside. An ant could walk from the outside to the inside without crossing an edge, since there is only one side.

concepts.name: Koch snowflake
concepts.description: A fractal curve built by starting with an equilateral triangle and repeatedly replacing the middle third of every segment with two sides of a smaller triangle. It has infinite perimeter but finite area.
concepts.example: Start with a triangle of perimeter 3. Each step makes every side 4/3 as long, so perimeters run 3, 4, 5.33, 7.1 ... forever, while the area never grows beyond 8/5 of the starting triangle.

concepts.name: Law of cosines
concepts.description: The formula c^2 = a^2 + b^2 - 2ab cos C relating the three sides of any triangle to one of its angles. It generalizes the Pythagorean theorem and is used to solve non-right triangles.
concepts.example: Two sides of 5 and 8 with a 60-degree angle between them: c^2 = 25 + 64 - 2 x 5 x 8 x 0.5 = 49, so the third side is 7. At 90 degrees the last term vanishes and you get Pythagoras.

concepts.name: Law of sines
concepts.description: The rule that in any triangle the ratio of each side to the sine of its opposite angle is the same: a/sin A = b/sin B = c/sin C, which also equals the diameter of the circumscribed circle.
concepts.example: In a triangle with angle A = 30 degrees opposite side a = 5 and angle B = 90 degrees, a/sin A = 10, so b = 10 x sin 90 = 10. The longest side always faces the largest angle.

concepts.name: Lemniscate
concepts.description: A figure-eight shaped curve. The lemniscate of Bernoulli is the set of points whose distances to two fixed foci have a constant product, with polar equation r^2 = a^2 cos 2 theta.
concepts.example: Put two foci 2 units apart. All points where the product of distances to them is exactly 1 form a figure-eight that crosses itself at the midpoint, like the infinity symbol.

concepts.name: Line
concepts.description: A straight one-dimensional figure that extends infinitely in both directions and has no thickness. Through any two distinct points there is exactly one line.
concepts.example: A taut string between two nails marks part of a line; imagine it running forever past both nails with no thickness. Pick any two dots on paper and exactly one such line goes through both.

concepts.name: Line segment
concepts.description: The part of a line between two endpoints, including the endpoints. Unlike a line, it has a definite finite length, which can be measured with a ruler.
concepts.example: The edge of a ruler from the 0 mark to the 10 cm mark is a segment: it has two ends and a length of 10 cm, unlike a line, which never ends.

concepts.name: Locus
concepts.description: The set of all points that satisfy a given condition. For example, the locus of points at a fixed distance from a center is a circle, and the locus equidistant from two points is their perpendicular bisector.
concepts.example: A goat tied to a post with a 3 m rope can reach every point within 3 m; the boundary it can just reach, all points exactly 3 m away, is a circle - the locus of that condition.

concepts.name: Mandelbrot set
concepts.description: The set of complex numbers c for which iterating z -> z^2 + c from z = 0 stays bounded. Its boundary is an infinitely intricate fractal, famous from computer-generated images.
concepts.example: Take c = -1: z goes 0, -1, 0, -1, ... and stays small, so -1 is in the set. Take c = 1: z goes 0, 1, 2, 5, 26, ... and explodes, so 1 is not. Colouring each c this way draws the famous shape.

concepts.name: Manifold
concepts.description: A space that looks like ordinary Euclidean space near every point, such as a sphere or torus, which locally resembles a flat plane. Manifolds are the setting for differential geometry and physics.
concepts.example: Earth's surface is round, but a town map on flat paper works fine. A manifold is any space like that: every small patch can be mapped flat, though the whole thing may curve or wrap around.

concepts.name: Median of a triangle
concepts.description: A line segment joining a vertex of a triangle to the midpoint of the opposite side. The three medians meet at the centroid, which divides each median in a 2:1 ratio.
concepts.example: Cut a triangle out of cardboard and draw a line from each corner to the middle of the opposite side. The three lines meet at the centroid, where the triangle balances on a pencil tip.

concepts.name: Menelaus' theorem
concepts.description: A theorem stating that points on the three side lines of a triangle are collinear exactly when the product of the three signed ratios they divide the sides into equals -1 (or 1 using unsigned lengths).
concepts.example: A straight road crosses all three sides of a triangular field (extended if needed). Multiply the three ratios in which it cuts the sides and you always get 1 in size; if the product is not 1, the three points are not on one line.

concepts.name: Mercator projection
concepts.description: A cylindrical map projection that preserves angles locally, so lines of constant compass bearing appear straight, which made it standard for navigation. It greatly enlarges areas near the poles.
concepts.example: A sailor steering a constant compass heading of 45 degrees draws a straight line on a Mercator chart. The price: Greenland looks as big as Africa, though Africa is about 14 times larger.

concepts.name: Metatron's Cube
concepts.description: A figure from sacred geometry formed by joining the centers of thirteen equal circles with straight lines. Flattened outlines of the Platonic solids can be traced within the resulting pattern.
concepts.example: Take the centre circle of a Flower of Life plus 12 around it, draw straight lines between all 13 centres, and you can trace 2D outlines of a cube, an octahedron and other Platonic solids in the web.

concepts.name: Midpoint formula
concepts.description: The formula giving the midpoint of the segment joining (x1, y1) and (x2, y2) as ((x1 + x2)/2, (y1 + y2)/2), i.e. the average of the endpoints' coordinates.
concepts.example: The midpoint between (2, 3) and (8, 7) is ((2+8)/2, (3+7)/2) = (5, 5). Two friends at those spots wanting to meet halfway should go to (5, 5).

concepts.name: Minimal surface
concepts.description: A surface that locally minimizes its area, equivalently one with zero mean curvature everywhere. Soap films spanning a wire frame form minimal surfaces, such as the catenoid and helicoid.
concepts.example: Dip a twisted wire loop in soapy water: the film stretches into the shape with the least possible area for that wire, because surface tension pulls it tight. That shape is a minimal surface.

concepts.name: Möbius strip
concepts.description: A surface with only one side and one edge, made by giving a strip of paper a half twist and joining its ends. It is the simplest example of a non-orientable surface in topology.
concepts.example: Take a paper strip, give one end a half twist and tape the ends. Draw a line down the middle without lifting the pen and you return to the start having covered both "sides" - there is only one.

concepts.name: Morley's trisector theorem
concepts.description: The surprising theorem that in any triangle, the three intersection points of adjacent angle trisectors always form an equilateral triangle, called the Morley triangle.
concepts.example: Take a triangle with angles 90, 60 and 30 and split each angle into three equal parts (30s, 20s, 10s). The trisectors next to each side meet in pairs, and those three points always form a perfect equilateral triangle.

concepts.name: Napoleon's theorem
concepts.description: A theorem stating that if equilateral triangles are built outward on each side of any triangle, the centers (centroids) of those three equilateral triangles themselves form an equilateral triangle.
concepts.example: Take any lopsided triangle and stick an equilateral triangle on each side, pointing outward. Mark the centre of each of those three. Connecting the centres always gives a perfect equilateral triangle.

concepts.name: Nine-point circle
concepts.description: A circle that passes through nine notable points of any triangle: the midpoints of the three sides, the feet of the three altitudes, and the midpoints between the orthocenter and each vertex.
concepts.example: In a triangle, mark the 3 side midpoints, the 3 feet of the altitudes, and the 3 points halfway from the orthocenter to each corner. One circle passes through all nine, with radius half the circumradius.

concepts.name: Non-Euclidean geometry
concepts.description: Any geometry that keeps Euclid's other axioms but replaces the parallel postulate, chiefly hyperbolic and elliptic geometry. Their discovery showed that consistent alternatives to flat geometry exist.
concepts.example: Draw a triangle on a beach ball: its angles add to more than 180 degrees. On a saddle they add to less. Both are consistent geometries where Euclid's parallel rule simply fails.

concepts.name: Obtuse angle
concepts.description: An angle that measures more than 90 degrees but less than 180 degrees, i.e. larger than a right angle but smaller than a straight angle.
concepts.example: Clock hands at 4 o'clock make a 120-degree angle, wider than a book's corner but less than a flat line. A reclining chair tilted back to 135 degrees forms an obtuse angle.

concepts.name: Obtuse triangle
concepts.description: A triangle in which one interior angle is obtuse (greater than 90 degrees); the other two must then be acute. Its circumcenter and orthocenter lie outside the triangle.
concepts.example: A triangle with angles 120, 40 and 20 degrees is obtuse. Since all three add to 180, only one angle can exceed 90, so the other two are always acute.

concepts.name: Octahedron
concepts.description: A polyhedron with eight faces. The regular octahedron, a Platonic solid, has eight equilateral triangle faces, six vertices and twelve edges, and looks like two square pyramids joined at their bases.
concepts.example: Glue two square-based pyramids together at their bases and make all edges equal: you get an octahedron with 8 triangular faces, 6 corners and 12 edges - an 8-sided die. Check: 6 - 12 + 8 = 2.

concepts.name: Origami geometry
concepts.description: The mathematical study of paper folding, where each fold acts as a reflection across a line. Folding constructions can do everything ruler and compass can and more, such as trisecting an angle.
concepts.example: Fold a sheet so corner A lands exactly on corner B: the crease is the perpendicular bisector of AB, and every point on it is equally far from both corners. Combining such folds can even trisect an angle.

concepts.name: Origin
concepts.description: The fixed reference point of a coordinate system where the axes intersect, with all coordinates equal to zero, written (0, 0) in the plane. Positions of all other points are measured from it.
concepts.example: On a city grid map, the central square is (0, 0). A cafe at (2, -3) is 2 blocks east and 3 blocks south of it; every address is measured from that one starting square.

concepts.name: Orthocenter
concepts.description: The point where the three altitudes of a triangle meet. It lies inside an acute triangle, at the right-angle vertex of a right triangle, and outside an obtuse triangle.
concepts.example: In a right triangle the two legs are already altitudes, so all three altitudes meet at the right-angle corner. In a triangle with angles 50, 60, 70 they meet inside; with a 120-degree angle, outside.

concepts.name: Orthographic projection
concepts.description: A way of representing a 3D object in 2D by projecting points along lines perpendicular to the drawing plane, giving true-size front, top and side views without perspective shrinking.
concepts.example: Shine a flashlight from far away straight at a coffee mug onto a wall: the shadow is a true-size outline. Engineers draw front, top and side views this way, so a 10 cm edge measures 10 cm on paper whatever its distance.

concepts.name: Ovoid
concepts.description: An egg-shaped closed surface or curve, smooth and convex like an ellipse or ellipsoid but typically with one end more rounded than the other.
concepts.example: A chicken egg is the everyday ovoid: like an ellipse rotated in space, but with one end blunter than the other, which makes it roll in a circle rather than a straight line.

concepts.name: Parabola
concepts.description: A U-shaped curve consisting of all points equally distant from a fixed point, the focus, and a fixed line, the directrix. It is the graph of a quadratic function and the path of a thrown object.
concepts.example: Throw a ball and its path is a parabola like y = -x^2 + 4x. For y = x^2/4, the point (2, 1) is 2 units from the focus (0, 1) and 2 from the line y = -1.

concepts.name: Focus of a parabola
concepts.description: The fixed point inside a parabola such that every point on the curve is equally far from it and from the directrix. Rays parallel to the axis reflect off the parabola through the focus, used in dish antennas.
concepts.example: A satellite dish is a parabola; signals arriving parallel to its axis bounce off and all meet at one point, the focus, where the receiver sits. For y = x^2/4 that point is (0, 1).

concepts.name: Parallel lines
concepts.description: Lines in the same plane that never meet, however far they are extended, so they keep a constant distance apart. A line crossing them, a transversal, forms equal corresponding angles.
concepts.example: Railway tracks stay 1.435 m apart along their whole length, never meeting. A road crossing them makes matching angles at both rails, which is how surveyors check tracks are parallel.

concepts.name: Parallel postulate
concepts.description: Euclid's fifth postulate, equivalent to saying that through a point not on a line there is exactly one parallel line. Attempts to prove it from the other axioms led to non-Euclidean geometry.
concepts.example: Draw a line and a dot above it. On flat paper exactly one line through the dot never meets the first. For 2,000 years people tried to prove this from Euclid's other rules, and failed because other geometries break only this rule.

concepts.name: Parallelogram
concepts.description: A quadrilateral with both pairs of opposite sides parallel. Its opposite sides and opposite angles are equal, its diagonals bisect each other, and its area is base times height.
concepts.example: Push a rectangle sideways at the top and it leans into a parallelogram: opposite sides stay parallel and equal. With base 8 and height 5 its area is 40, the same as the rectangle you could rearrange it into.

concepts.name: Pascal's theorem
concepts.description: A theorem stating that if a hexagon is inscribed in any conic section, the three intersection points of pairs of opposite sides lie on a single straight line, the Pascal line.
concepts.example: Pick any six points on a circle, label them in order, and join them into a hexagon (even a self-crossing one). Extend opposite sides 1 and 4, 2 and 5, 3 and 6: the three crossing points always line up.

concepts.name: Peaucellier–Lipkin linkage
concepts.description: A mechanism of hinged rods that converts circular motion into exact straight-line motion, invented in 1864. It works by realizing geometric inversion, which maps a circle through the center onto a line.
concepts.example: Seven hinged bars are arranged so one joint P and another Q always satisfy OP x OQ = constant. Swing P around a circle through the pivot O and Q is forced along a perfectly straight line, with no guide rail.

concepts.name: Penrose tiling
concepts.description: An aperiodic tiling of the plane using two shapes, such as a kite and a dart, that never repeats periodically yet has five-fold rotational symmetry and proportions governed by the golden ratio.
concepts.example: A floor made from fat and thin rhombus tiles, using matching rules, covers the room without ever repeating, yet shows five-fold star patterns everywhere, and fat tiles outnumber thin ones by the golden ratio, about 1.618 to 1.

concepts.name: Pentagon
concepts.description: A polygon with five sides and five angles. A regular pentagon has 108 degree interior angles, and its diagonal-to-side ratio equals the golden ratio.
concepts.example: The Pentagon building in Washington has five equal walls meeting at 108-degree corners. In a regular pentagon with side 1, each diagonal is about 1.618, the golden ratio.

concepts.name: Perimeter
concepts.description: The total length of the boundary of a two-dimensional shape, found for a polygon by adding the lengths of all its sides. For a circle the perimeter is called the circumference.
concepts.example: Fencing a 10 m by 6 m garden takes 10 + 6 + 10 + 6 = 32 m of fence. A triangle with sides 3, 4 and 5 cm has perimeter 12 cm.

concepts.name: Perpendicular bisector
concepts.description: A line that passes through the midpoint of a segment at a right angle to it. Every point on it is equally distant from the segment's two endpoints.
concepts.example: Two friends live at A and B and want to meet somewhere equally far from both. Every such meeting point lies on the line crossing AB at its midpoint at a right angle - the perpendicular bisector.

concepts.name: Perpendicular lines
concepts.description: Two lines that intersect at a right angle (90 degrees). In coordinate geometry, non-vertical perpendicular lines have slopes whose product is -1.
concepts.example: The edges of a sheet of paper meet at right angles. The lines y = 2x and y = -x/2 are perpendicular because 2 x (-1/2) = -1.

concepts.name: Perspective projection
concepts.description: A projection of 3D objects onto a plane through a single viewpoint, as an eye or camera sees, so distant objects look smaller and parallel lines converge at vanishing points.
concepts.example: Standing on a straight railway, the rails seem to meet at the horizon and a sleeper 20 m away looks half as wide as one 10 m away. A camera draws the world the same way, through one viewpoint.

concepts.name: Pitot theorem
concepts.description: A theorem stating that in a tangential quadrilateral, one with a circle tangent to all four sides, the sums of the two pairs of opposite sides are equal: AB + CD = BC + DA.
concepts.example: A quadrilateral with a circle touching all four sides has sides AB = 5, BC = 7, CD = 6. Then DA must be 4, because 5 + 6 = 7 + 4. Tangent lengths from each corner pair up to force this.

concepts.name: Plane
concepts.description: A flat two-dimensional surface that extends infinitely in all directions. It is determined by three non-collinear points, and in coordinates by a linear equation ax + by + cz = d.
concepts.example: A tabletop extended forever in every direction is a plane. A three-legged stool never wobbles because its three feet, not on one line, always pick out exactly one plane.

concepts.name: Platonic solid
concepts.description: A convex polyhedron whose faces are all congruent regular polygons with the same number meeting at each vertex. There are exactly five: tetrahedron, cube, octahedron, dodecahedron and icosahedron.
concepts.example: Try making a solid where three triangles meet at each corner: tetrahedron. Four: octahedron. Five: icosahedron. Six triangles lie flat, so they fail. Squares and pentagons give just two more - five in all.

concepts.name: Poincaré conjecture
concepts.description: The theorem, proved by Grigori Perelman in 2003 using Ricci flow, that every simply connected closed three-dimensional manifold is topologically equivalent to the three-dimensional sphere.
concepts.example: Lasso an apple with a rope and you can always slide the loop off by shrinking it; on a donut you cannot. Perelman proved that any closed 3D space where every loop can shrink like this is just a 3D sphere.

concepts.name: Point
concepts.description: The most basic object in geometry: an exact location in space with no size, length or width. Points are usually labeled with capital letters and, in coordinates, given by a list of numbers.
concepts.example: A pin prick on a map marks a point: it says where, but has no size. On a grid, the point (3, 2) is just a location - 3 across, 2 up.

concepts.name: Pole and polar
concepts.description: A correspondence between points (poles) and lines (polars) with respect to a circle or conic. For a point outside a circle, its polar is the line through the two points where tangents from it touch the circle.
concepts.example: From a point P outside a circle, draw the two tangents; they touch at points A and B. Line AB is the polar of P. Move P closer and the polar slides toward P; put P on the circle and its polar becomes the tangent there.

concepts.name: Polygon
concepts.description: A closed plane figure made of straight line segments joined end to end, such as a triangle, square or hexagon. A regular polygon has all sides and all angles equal.
concepts.example: A stop sign is an octagon: eight straight sides joined end to end, enclosing a region. A star drawn with five lines is a polygon too, but a circle is not, since it has no straight sides.

concepts.name: Positive mass theorem
concepts.description: A theorem of general relativity and geometry, proved by Schoen and Yau and by Witten, stating that an asymptotically flat spacetime with non-negative energy density has non-negative total mass.
concepts.example: Imagine a universe that looks empty and flat far away and contains only ordinary matter with non-negative energy. The theorem says weighing it from afar always gives mass 0 or more, never negative.

concepts.name: Power of a point
concepts.description: A number assigned to a point relative to a circle, d^2 - r^2. For any line through the point meeting the circle at A and B, the product PA times PB equals this power, unifying the chord, secant and tangent theorems.
concepts.example: P is 5 from the centre of a circle of radius 3, so its power is 25 - 9 = 16. Any line from P through the circle meets it at A and B with PA x PB = 16, and the tangent length from P is 4.

concepts.name: Prism
concepts.description: A solid with two parallel congruent polygonal bases joined by rectangular or parallelogram faces. Its volume equals base area times height; a cuboid is a rectangular prism.
concepts.example: A Toblerone box is a triangular prism: two triangle ends joined by three rectangles. If each triangle has area 6 square cm and the box is 20 cm long, it holds 120 cubic cm.

concepts.name: Projective geometry
concepts.description: The geometry of properties preserved by projection, such as collinearity and cross-ratio. It adds points at infinity so that any two lines meet, which makes theorems symmetric under point-line duality.
concepts.example: Railway tracks look like they meet at the horizon. Projective geometry makes that literal: parallel lines meet at a point at infinity, so any two lines meet exactly once, and swapping "point" and "line" in a theorem gives another true theorem.

concepts.name: Pyramid
concepts.description: A solid with a polygonal base and triangular faces that meet at a common apex. Its volume is one third of the base area times the height.
concepts.example: The Great Pyramid has a square base about 230 m on each side and was about 146 m tall, so its volume is about 1/3 x 230 x 230 x 146, roughly 2.6 million cubic metres.

concepts.name: Pythagorean theorem
concepts.description: The theorem that in a right triangle the square of the hypotenuse equals the sum of the squares of the other two sides: a^2 + b^2 = c^2. It underlies distance calculations in any number of dimensions.
concepts.example: A TV with a 3-foot height and 4-foot width has a diagonal of sqrt(9 + 16) = 5 feet. Builders use this 3-4-5 rule to check that corners are square.

concepts.name: Pythagorean triple
concepts.description: Three positive integers a, b, c satisfying a^2 + b^2 = c^2, such as (3, 4, 5) or (5, 12, 13). They give the side lengths of right triangles with whole-number sides.
concepts.example: 3, 4, 5 works since 9 + 16 = 25. Doubling gives 6, 8, 10, and 5, 12, 13 works since 25 + 144 = 169. Ancient builders stretched a rope knotted in 3, 4 and 5 sections to make right angles.

concepts.name: Quadrilateral
concepts.description: A polygon with four sides, four vertices and four angles, whose interior angles sum to 360 degrees. Squares, rectangles, parallelograms, trapezoids and kites are special quadrilaterals.
concepts.example: A door, a kite and a trapezoid-shaped field are all quadrilaterals. Cut any one along a diagonal into two triangles: 180 + 180 = 360 degrees for its four angles.

concepts.name: Radian
concepts.description: The standard mathematical unit of angle: the angle at the center of a circle that cuts off an arc equal in length to the radius. A full turn is 2 pi radians, so 180 degrees equals pi radians.
concepts.example: Lay a piece of string equal to a circle's radius along its edge: the angle it marks at the centre is 1 radian, about 57.3 degrees. About 6.28 such strings go once around, which is why a full turn is 2 pi.

concepts.name: Radical axis
concepts.description: The line of all points that have equal power with respect to two given circles. For two intersecting circles it is the line through their intersection points; it is perpendicular to the line of centers.
concepts.example: Two circles overlap and cross at two points. Draw the line through those points: from any spot on it, tangents drawn to the two circles have equal length - that line is the radical axis.

concepts.name: Radius
concepts.description: The distance from the center of a circle or sphere to any point on it, or a line segment with those endpoints. It is half the diameter.
concepts.example: A round table 1.2 m across has radius 0.6 m: from its centre to any point on the edge is the same 0.6 m. A compass set to 3 cm draws a circle of radius 3 cm.

concepts.name: Ray
concepts.description: A part of a line that starts at a fixed endpoint and extends infinitely in one direction. Two rays sharing an endpoint form an angle.
concepts.example: A torch beam starts at the bulb and shoots off in one direction forever. That is a ray: one fixed endpoint, no end on the other side.

concepts.name: Rectangle
concepts.description: A quadrilateral with four right angles, so opposite sides are parallel and equal. Its area is length times width and its two diagonals are equal in length.
concepts.example: A phone screen 7 cm by 15 cm is a rectangle: four right angles, opposite sides equal, area 105 square cm. Its two diagonals are equal, each about 16.6 cm.

concepts.name: Reflection
concepts.description: A transformation that flips a figure across a line (or plane) like a mirror, so each point maps to the point equally far on the opposite side. It preserves lengths and angles but reverses orientation.
concepts.example: Reflect the point (3, 2) across the y-axis and it lands at (-3, 2). Your reflection in a mirror is the same size, but your right hand appears as a left hand - orientation flips.

concepts.name: Reflex angle
concepts.description: An angle that measures more than 180 degrees but less than 360 degrees, i.e. larger than a straight angle but less than a full turn.
concepts.example: Clock hands at 5 o'clock make 150 degrees one way, but going the long way round they make 210 degrees - a reflex angle. A skater turning three-quarters of a circle sweeps 270 degrees.

concepts.name: Reuleaux triangle
concepts.description: A curved triangle formed by the intersection of three circles, each centered at a vertex of an equilateral triangle. It has constant width and is used in drills for square holes and in Wankel engines.
concepts.example: Roll a heavy board on three Reuleaux-triangle rollers and it stays perfectly level, just like on round logs, because every roller is the same height in every direction. That's also why some UK 20p and 50p coins use this shape: vending machines measure them consistently.

concepts.name: Rhombus
concepts.description: A parallelogram with all four sides equal in length. Its diagonals are perpendicular and bisect its angles; a square is a rhombus with right angles.
concepts.example: A diamond on a playing card is a rhombus: tilt a square so its sides stay 5 cm but its corners are no longer 90 degrees. Its two diagonals still cross at a perfect right angle and cut each other in half.

concepts.name: Ricci curvature
concepts.description: A tensor on a Riemannian manifold that measures how the volume of small geodesic balls differs from flat space, obtained by averaging sectional curvatures. It appears in Einstein's field equations and Ricci flow.
concepts.example: On a sphere, a small ball of 'radius r' holds a bit less volume than a flat ball of the same radius, because space bends inward; positive Ricci curvature measures that shortfall. On a saddle-shaped space the ball holds more, giving negative Ricci curvature.

concepts.name: Riemann sphere
concepts.description: The complex plane with one extra point at infinity, pictured as a sphere through stereographic projection. It makes functions like 1/z well defined everywhere and is a basic object in complex analysis.
concepts.example: Put a ball on the complex plane touching at 0; draw lines from the top of the ball to each point. Numbers far away land near the top, and the top itself is infinity, so 1/0 = infinity and 1/infinity = 0 become sensible.

concepts.name: Riemannian geometry
concepts.description: The study of smooth manifolds equipped with a Riemannian metric, an inner product on each tangent space that defines lengths, angles, geodesics and curvature. It is the mathematical basis of general relativity.
concepts.example: An ant on a curved surface measures distances with a tiny ruler that may change from place to place; from those local rules it can find shortest paths and detect curvature. General relativity treats spacetime the same way, with gravity as curvature.

concepts.name: Right angle
concepts.description: An angle of exactly 90 degrees, a quarter turn, formed by perpendicular lines. It is often marked with a small square at the vertex.
concepts.example: The corner of a sheet of paper is a right angle: fold any straight edge onto itself and the crease meets it at 90 degrees. Two of them side by side make a straight line, and four fill a full turn.

concepts.name: Right triangle
concepts.description: A triangle with one right angle. The side opposite the right angle is the hypotenuse, the longest side, and the side lengths satisfy the Pythagorean theorem.
concepts.example: A ladder leaning against a wall forms a right triangle with the ground: if the foot is 3 m out and it reaches 4 m up, the ladder itself, the hypotenuse, is 5 m long.

concepts.name: Roman surface
concepts.description: A self-intersecting mapping of the real projective plane into three-dimensional space discovered by Jakob Steiner, with high symmetry. Unlike Boy's surface it has singular pinch points.
concepts.example: Imagine trying to glue a disc's edge so opposite points meet, all inside ordinary 3D space; you can't do it cleanly, so the sheet must pass through itself. Steiner's Roman surface is one way to do it, looking like a puffy tetrahedron with three crossing seams.

concepts.name: Rotation
concepts.description: A transformation that turns every point of a figure by the same angle about a fixed center (or axis in 3D). It preserves lengths, angles and orientation.
concepts.example: Turn a clock's minute hand from 12 to 3: every point on the hand swings 90 degrees about the centre pin. Rotating the point (1, 0) by 90 degrees about the origin lands it at (0, 1).

concepts.name: Roulette curve
concepts.description: A curve traced by a point attached to one curve as it rolls without slipping along another curve. Cycloids, epicycloids, cardioids and hypotrochoids are all roulettes.
concepts.example: Tape a pen to a bicycle wheel's rim and roll it along a wall: the pen draws a cycloid. Roll a small coin around a bigger coin instead and the marked point draws a flower-like epicycloid; both are roulettes.

concepts.name: Sacred geometry
concepts.description: A tradition that assigns spiritual or symbolic meaning to geometric shapes and proportions, such as the golden ratio, circles and Platonic solids, used in religious architecture and art. It is cultural rather than mathematical.
concepts.example: The 'Flower of Life' pattern repeats overlapping circles of equal size, and Gothic cathedral plans were often laid out with golden-ratio rectangles. Believers read such shapes as symbols of harmony, though the spiritual meaning is cultural rather than mathematical.

concepts.name: Scalar curvature
concepts.description: A single number at each point of a Riemannian manifold obtained by taking the trace of the Ricci curvature. It compares the volume of small geodesic balls with their volume in flat space.
concepts.example: A sphere of radius 2 has scalar curvature 2/2^2 = 0.5 at every point, while a sphere of radius 1 has 2. One number per point summarises how much space bends there, so a bigger sphere looks flatter.

concepts.name: Scalene triangle
concepts.description: A triangle in which all three sides have different lengths, so all three angles are also different. It has no lines of symmetry.
concepts.example: A triangle with sides 4, 5 and 6 cm is scalene: no two sides match, so no two angles match either. Most triangles you draw at random by hand are scalene.

concepts.name: Secant
concepts.description: A straight line that crosses a circle or curve at two points. The segment between the two crossing points is a chord; in calculus, secant lines approximate the tangent line.
concepts.example: Draw a straight road across a circular park: it enters at one gate and leaves at another, so it is a secant. The part of the road inside the park is a chord.

concepts.name: Sector
concepts.description: The pie-slice region of a circle bounded by two radii and the arc between them. Its area is (theta/2) r^2 with the central angle theta in radians, or (theta/360) pi r^2 in degrees.
concepts.example: A slice of pizza is a sector. With radius 10 cm and a 90-degree angle, it is a quarter of the pizza, so its area is a quarter of pi x 100, about 78.5 square cm.

concepts.name: Sierpinski triangle
concepts.description: A fractal formed by repeatedly removing the middle triangle from an equilateral triangle, leaving three smaller copies at each step. It also appears as the odd entries of Pascal's triangle.
concepts.example: Start with a triangle, join the midpoints of its sides, and cut out the middle triangle, leaving 3. Do it again to each: 9, then 27. After many steps the area shrinks toward zero while the pattern looks the same at every zoom level.

concepts.name: Similarity
concepts.description: The relation between figures that have the same shape but possibly different sizes, so one is a scaled copy of the other. Similar triangles have equal angles and proportional sides.
concepts.example: A photo and its enlargement are similar: a 4x6 print blown up to 8x12 doubles every length but keeps every angle. A 3-4-5 triangle and a 6-8-10 triangle are similar for the same reason.

concepts.name: Sine
concepts.description: A trigonometric function: in a right triangle, the sine of an angle is the opposite side divided by the hypotenuse. On the unit circle, sin theta is the y-coordinate, giving a periodic wave used to model oscillations.
concepts.example: In a right triangle with a 30-degree angle, the side opposite that angle is always half the hypotenuse, so sin 30 = 0.5. A ramp 10 m long rising at 30 degrees therefore lifts you 5 m.

concepts.name: Slope
concepts.description: A number measuring the steepness and direction of a line, defined as the change in y divided by the change in x (rise over run) between two points on it.
concepts.example: A line through (1, 2) and (3, 8) rises 6 while running 2, so its slope is 6/2 = 3. A road sign saying '10% grade' means a slope of 0.1: up 1 m for every 10 m forward.

concepts.name: Smith conjecture
concepts.description: A theorem in 3-manifold topology stating that if a periodic orientation-preserving map of the 3-sphere fixes a circle, then that circle cannot be knotted. It was proved in 1979 using hyperbolic geometry.
concepts.example: Spin 3D space a fixed fraction of a turn repeatedly so it returns to start after n spins; the points that never move form a line-like circle. Smith's theorem says that circle can never be tied in a knot, it is always an unknot.

concepts.name: Soap bubble theorem
concepts.description: Alexandrov's theorem stating that the only compact, embedded surface in space with constant mean curvature is a round sphere, which explains why free soap bubbles are spherical.
concepts.example: A single free-floating soap bubble has the same pressure difference everywhere, so its surface has constant mean curvature. Alexandrov proved that the only closed, non-self-crossing shape with that property is a perfect sphere, which is why bubbles are round.

concepts.name: Solid geometry
concepts.description: The geometry of three-dimensional space, studying solids such as cubes, prisms, pyramids, cylinders, cones and spheres, along with their surface areas, volumes and cross-sections.
concepts.example: Working out how much paint covers a cube-shaped box, or how many marbles fit in a cylindrical jar, is solid geometry. A cube with 2 cm edges has volume 8 cubic cm and surface area 24 square cm.

concepts.name: Sphere
concepts.description: The set of all points in three-dimensional space at a fixed distance, the radius, from a center point; a perfectly round ball's surface. Its surface area is 4 pi r^2 and enclosed volume is (4/3) pi r^3.
concepts.example: A basketball's surface is a sphere: every point on it is the same distance, the radius, from the centre. Double the radius and the surface area quadruples while the volume grows eightfold.

concepts.name: Spherical geometry
concepts.description: The geometry of the surface of a sphere, where great circles play the role of straight lines. Triangle angles sum to more than 180 degrees, and it is used in navigation and astronomy.
concepts.example: Walk 1,000 km south from the North Pole, turn 90 degrees left, walk east, then turn left again back to the pole: your triangle has three right angles, totalling 270 degrees, which is impossible on flat paper.

concepts.name: Spirograph
concepts.description: A drawing toy using toothed gears rolling inside or around rings to trace hypotrochoid and epitrochoid curves, producing intricate symmetric looping patterns.
concepts.example: Pin a large ring, put a 24-tooth gear inside a 96-tooth ring, and trace with a pen through a hole: the gear goes around 4 times in its orbit and the drawing closes into a loopy flower with repeating petals.

concepts.name: Spline
concepts.description: A smooth curve built from polynomial pieces joined at knots so that the curve and some derivatives are continuous. Splines are used to interpolate data and to design shapes in graphics and CAD.
concepts.example: To draw a smooth road through 5 survey points, fit a separate cubic curve between each pair and make neighbours meet with the same slope and bend. Shipbuilders once did this with a flexible wooden strip called a spline.

concepts.name: Square
concepts.description: A quadrilateral with four equal sides and four right angles, both a rectangle and a rhombus. With side a its area is a^2 and its diagonals are equal, perpendicular and of length a sqrt 2.
concepts.example: A chessboard square with 3 cm sides has perimeter 12 cm and area 9 square cm. It counts as a rectangle because its corners are 90 degrees, and as a rhombus because its sides are equal.

concepts.name: Stereographic projection
concepts.description: A mapping of a sphere onto a plane by projecting each point from the north pole onto the plane. It preserves angles and maps circles to circles or lines, and is used in maps and complex analysis.
concepts.example: Stand a transparent globe on a sheet of paper and put a lamp at the North Pole; each country's shadow on the paper is its stereographic image. Places near the South Pole barely move, while places near the lamp stretch far away.

concepts.name: Stewart's theorem
