concepts.example: Scheduling exams: make each course a vertex and connect courses sharing a student. Colors are time slots, and a proper coloring with 3 colors means all exams fit in 3 slots without clashes.

concepts.name: Laplacian Matrix
concepts.description: The matrix L = D − A, where D is the degree matrix and A the adjacency matrix of a graph. Its eigenvalues reveal connectivity and clusters; it underlies spectral clustering and graph neural networks.
concepts.example: For a path a–b–c, degrees are 1, 2, 1, so L = [[1,−1,0],[−1,2,−1],[0,−1,1]]. Its smallest eigenvalue is 0 once per connected piece, so counting zero eigenvalues counts components.

concepts.name: Graph of a Function
concepts.description: The set of points (x, f(x)) plotted in the plane, giving a picture of how a function behaves. Reading slopes, intercepts and turning points from it builds intuition.
concepts.example: Plotting f(x) = x² gives a U-shaped parabola through (−2, 4), (0, 0) and (2, 4); at a glance you see the minimum at 0 and that the function is symmetric.

concepts.name: Graph Theory
concepts.description: The branch of mathematics studying graphs: vertices joined by edges. It covers paths, connectivity, colorings, matchings and flows, and underlies networks and many algorithms.
concepts.example: Euler asked whether you could walk across all seven bridges of Königsberg exactly once. Modelling land masses as vertices and bridges as edges showed it was impossible, founding graph theory.

concepts.name: Greatest Common Divisor
concepts.description: The largest positive integer that divides two given integers without remainder, e.g. gcd(12, 18) = 6. Computed efficiently with the Euclidean algorithm.
concepts.example: To cut a 12 × 18 cm sheet into the largest equal squares with no waste, use 6 cm squares, since 6 is the biggest number dividing both 12 and 18.

concepts.name: Green's Theorem
concepts.description: A theorem relating a line integral around a simple closed curve in the plane to a double integral of the curl over the region it encloses. A 2D special case of Stokes' theorem.
concepts.example: To find the area of a fenced field you can just walk its boundary: integrating (x dy − y dx)/2 around the edge gives the enclosed area, a direct use of Green's theorem.

concepts.name: Hadamard Product
concepts.description: The element-wise product of two matrices or vectors of the same shape, multiplying matching entries. Used throughout neural networks, e.g. in LSTM gates.
concepts.example: Multiplying (1, 2, 3) and (4, 5, 6) entry by entry gives (4, 10, 18). In an LSTM, a gate vector of 0s and 1s multiplies a memory vector this way to keep or erase each entry.

concepts.name: Hamiltonian Path
concepts.description: A path in a graph that visits every vertex exactly once; a Hamiltonian cycle also returns to the start. Deciding whether one exists is NP-complete and is related to the traveling salesman problem.
concepts.example: A delivery driver wants to visit each of 10 houses exactly once. With few houses you can try all orders, but no known method scales fast for large graphs.

concepts.name: Handshaking Lemma
concepts.description: The fact that in any graph the sum of all vertex degrees equals twice the number of edges, so the number of odd-degree vertices is even.
concepts.example: At a party where 5 handshakes happen, counting each person's handshakes and adding them up gives 10, since each handshake involves two hands. So the number of people with an odd count is even.

concepts.name: Harmonic Series
concepts.description: The infinite series 1 + 1/2 + 1/3 + 1/4 + …, which diverges even though its terms go to zero; its partial sums grow like ln n. It appears in algorithm analysis.
concepts.example: Group the terms: 1/3 + 1/4 > 1/2, the next four terms exceed 1/2, the next eight too. You can keep making halves forever, so the sum grows without bound, though very slowly.

concepts.name: Heine–Borel Theorem
concepts.description: The theorem that a subset of ℝⁿ is compact exactly when it is closed and bounded. It connects the abstract open-cover definition of compactness with a concrete test.
concepts.example: The interval [0, 1] is closed and bounded, so it is compact: every open cover has a finite subcover. But (0, 1] is not: the sets (1/n, 1] cover it, yet no finite handful does.

concepts.name: Hermitian Matrix
concepts.description: A complex square matrix equal to its own conjugate transpose, the complex analogue of a symmetric matrix. Hermitian matrices have real eigenvalues and orthogonal eigenvectors.
concepts.example: The matrix [[2, i], [−i, 3]] is Hermitian: flipping it and conjugating each entry gives it back. Despite complex entries its eigenvalues are real, as quantum observables require.

concepts.name: Hessian Matrix
concepts.description: The square matrix of all second-order partial derivatives of a scalar function. It describes local curvature and is used to classify critical points and in Newton's method.
concepts.example: For f(x, y) = x² + 3y², the Hessian is [[2, 0], [0, 6]]: both entries positive means the surface curves up in every direction, so (0, 0) is a minimum.

concepts.name: Hessian–Vector Product
concepts.description: Computing the product of a Hessian with a vector without forming the Hessian, e.g. by differentiating the gradient along that vector. Enables second-order methods for large neural networks.
concepts.example: A neural network with a million weights has a Hessian of a trillion entries, but Hv costs about two gradients: differentiate the dot product of the gradient with v.

concepts.name: Higher-Order Derivative
concepts.description: The derivative of a derivative, repeated: the second derivative measures how the rate of change itself changes (concavity, acceleration), and so on for third and higher orders.
concepts.example: If position is t³, velocity is 3t² and acceleration, the second derivative, is 6t. At t = 2 the car is going 12 units/s and speeding up at 12 units/s².

concepts.name: Hilbert Space
concepts.description: A complete inner product space, possibly infinite-dimensional, where lengths and angles are defined. Examples include L² function spaces; reproducing kernel Hilbert spaces underlie kernel methods.
concepts.example: Functions on [0, 1] with finite ∫f² form a Hilbert space: ∫f·g acts like a dot product, so you can say sin(2πx) and cos(2πx) are perpendicular, as Fourier series do.

concepts.name: Householder Transformation
concepts.description: A reflection of vectors across a hyperplane, given by the orthogonal matrix I − 2vvᵀ. Householder reflections zero out entries below the diagonal to compute stable QR decompositions.
concepts.example: To turn the vector (3, 4) into (5, 0), reflect it across the line halfway between them. Applying such mirrors to matrix columns zeroes everything below the diagonal in one sweep each.

concepts.name: Hyperbolic Functions
concepts.description: Functions such as sinh, cosh and tanh defined from exponentials, e.g. tanh x = (eˣ − e⁻ˣ)/(eˣ + e⁻ˣ). They parallel trig functions; tanh is a classic neural activation.
concepts.example: A hanging chain or power line sags in the shape of cosh x, the catenary. And cosh² − sinh² = 1, just as cos² + sin² = 1 for circles.

concepts.name: Identity Matrix
concepts.description: The square matrix with ones on the main diagonal and zeros elsewhere, written I. Multiplying by it leaves any matrix or vector unchanged.
concepts.example: The 2×2 identity [[1, 0], [0, 1]] times the vector (5, 7) gives (5, 7) back, just as multiplying a number by 1 changes nothing.

concepts.name: Implicit Differentiation
concepts.description: Finding dy/dx when y is defined implicitly by an equation like x² + y² = 1, by differentiating both sides with respect to x and solving for dy/dx.
concepts.example: On the circle x² + y² = 25, differentiate both sides: 2x + 2y·dy/dx = 0, so dy/dx = −x/y. At (3, 4) the slope is −3/4, without solving for y.

concepts.name: Implicit Function Theorem
concepts.description: The theorem that an equation F(x, y) = 0 locally defines y as a differentiable function of x when the Jacobian of F with respect to y is invertible. Used for implicit layers and hyperparameter gradients.
concepts.example: The circle x² + y² = 1 is not one function, but near (0.6, 0.8) it is locally y = √(1 − x²). The theorem says this works wherever ∂F/∂y ≠ 0, failing only at (±1, 0).

concepts.name: Improper Integral
concepts.description: An integral over an infinite interval or of a function with an infinite discontinuity, defined as a limit of ordinary definite integrals; it may converge or diverge.
concepts.example: The area under 1/x² from 1 to infinity is finite: integrate to b to get 1 − 1/b, then let b grow without limit, and the area tends to exactly 1.

concepts.name: Inclusion–Exclusion Principle
concepts.description: A counting rule: the size of a union equals the sum of the set sizes minus the sizes of pairwise intersections plus triple intersections, and so on. Also applies to probabilities.
concepts.example: In a class, 20 students play football, 15 play chess, and 8 do both. Those doing at least one: 20 + 15 − 8 = 27, since the 8 were counted twice.

concepts.name: Indicator Function
concepts.description: A function that equals 1 for elements in a given set and 0 otherwise, written 1_A(x). It turns events into numbers, so expectations of indicators are probabilities.
concepts.example: Roll a die and let X = 1 if it shows an even number, 0 otherwise. Averaging X over many rolls gives about 0.5, the probability of even: the expected value of an indicator is a probability.

concepts.name: Inequality (Mathematics)
concepts.description: A statement comparing two quantities with <, >, ≤ or ≥, such as 2x + 1 > 5. Solving an inequality gives a range of values rather than a single answer.
concepts.example: A taxi charges $3 plus $2 per km and you have $15. The inequality 3 + 2x ≤ 15 gives x ≤ 6, so any trip up to 6 km is affordable.

concepts.name: Inflection Point
concepts.description: A point on a curve where concavity changes, from bending up to bending down or vice versa; there the second derivative is typically zero and changes sign.
concepts.example: On a road that curves left then right, the inflection point is where you hold the steering wheel straight for a moment. For y = x³ this happens at x = 0.

concepts.name: Injective Function
concepts.description: A function that maps different inputs to different outputs, so no two elements share an image; also called one-to-one. Injective functions can be inverted on their range.
concepts.example: Assigning each student a unique ID number is injective: no two students share one. Mapping students to birth months is not, since two may share a month.

concepts.name: Inner Product Space
concepts.description: A vector space with an inner product, a generalized dot product that defines lengths, angles and orthogonality. Finite-dimensional examples are Euclidean spaces; infinite ones include function spaces.
concepts.example: Functions can be treated as vectors: define ⟨f, g⟩ = ∫ f(x)g(x) dx over [−π, π]. Then sin x and cos x have inner product 0, so they are orthogonal.

concepts.name: Integer
concepts.description: A whole number that can be positive, negative or zero: …, −2, −1, 0, 1, 2, …. Integers extend the natural numbers so subtraction is always possible.
concepts.example: A thermometer reads −3 °C in the morning and 5 °C at noon, a rise of 8 degrees. Negative integers let you record debts, depths and temperatures below zero.

concepts.name: Integral
concepts.description: The mathematical operation of accumulating a quantity, such as area under a curve, defined as a limit of sums of thin slices. Integration is the inverse of differentiation.
concepts.example: A car's speedometer reads speed over time; adding up speed × tiny time slices gives distance travelled. If speed is 60 km/h for 2 hours, the area under the graph is 120 km.

concepts.name: Integration by Parts
concepts.description: An integration technique derived from the product rule: ∫u dv = uv − ∫v du. Useful for integrals of products like x·eˣ, and in deriving the Euler–Lagrange equation.
concepts.example: For ∫x·eˣ dx, take u = x and dv = eˣ dx: you get x·eˣ − ∫eˣ dx = (x − 1)eˣ + C. Differentiating x was the move that made the problem easy.

concepts.name: Integration by Substitution
concepts.description: An integration technique reversing the chain rule: substitute u = g(x) to turn ∫f(g(x))g′(x) dx into the simpler ∫f(u) du.
concepts.example: For ∫2x·cos(x²) dx, set u = x² so du = 2x dx. The integral becomes ∫cos u du = sin u, giving sin(x²) + C.

concepts.name: Intermediate Value Theorem
concepts.description: The theorem that a continuous function on [a, b] takes every value between f(a) and f(b). It guarantees a root exists where a continuous function changes sign.
concepts.example: If it is 10 °C at 6 am and 20 °C at noon, at some moment the temperature was exactly 15 °C, because temperature changes continuously without jumping.

concepts.name: Interpolation
concepts.description: Constructing a function that passes exactly through a given set of data points, to estimate values between them; methods include linear, polynomial and spline interpolation.
concepts.example: A weather station records 12 °C at 9 am and 18 °C at noon; drawing a curve through those readings lets you estimate about 15 °C at 10:30.

concepts.name: Intersection (Set Theory)
concepts.description: The set of elements belonging to all of the given sets, written A ∩ B. In probability, the intersection of events is the event that both occur.
concepts.example: If A = {students who like tea} and B = {students who like coffee}, then A ∩ B is those who like both. With A = {1, 2, 3} and B = {2, 3, 4}, A ∩ B = {2, 3}.

concepts.name: Interval (Mathematics)
concepts.description: A set of real numbers lying between two endpoints, such as [a, b] (closed, endpoints included) or (a, b) (open). Intervals are the domains of many calculus theorems.
concepts.example: Bus ages for a child fare are 4 to 12 inclusive: the interval [4, 12]. 'Strictly between 0 and 1' is (0, 1), excluding both endpoints.

concepts.name: Inverse Function
concepts.description: A function f⁻¹ that undoes f, so f⁻¹(f(x)) = x; it exists when f is a bijection. Examples include logarithms as inverses of exponentials.
concepts.example: Converting Celsius to Fahrenheit is F = 1.8C + 32; the inverse is C = (F − 32)/1.8. Apply one then the other and 100 °C comes back as 100 °C.

concepts.name: Inverse Function Theorem
concepts.description: The theorem that a continuously differentiable function with an invertible Jacobian at a point has a differentiable local inverse there, whose Jacobian is the inverse matrix.
concepts.example: Polar-to-Cartesian (r, θ) → (r cos θ, r sin θ) has Jacobian determinant r. Wherever r ≠ 0 you can locally go back uniquely; at the origin, where r = 0, every θ gives the same point.

concepts.name: Inverse Iteration
concepts.description: A variant of power iteration applied to (A − μI)⁻¹, which converges to the eigenvector whose eigenvalue is closest to the shift μ. Each step solves a linear system.
concepts.example: To find the eigenvector of A with eigenvalue nearest 2.9, repeatedly solve (A − 2.9I)x_new = x. An eigenvalue at 3 becomes 1/0.1 = 10 in the inverse and quickly dominates the others.

concepts.name: Invertible Matrix
concepts.description: A square matrix A that has an inverse A⁻¹ with A·A⁻¹ = I. Equivalently its determinant is nonzero, its columns are linearly independent, and Ax = b has exactly one solution for every b.
concepts.example: The matrix [[2, 0], [0, 4]] doubles x and quadruples y; its inverse [[0.5, 0], [0, 0.25]] undoes that. But [[1, 2], [2, 4]] squashes the plane onto a line, so nothing can undo it.

concepts.name: Iterative Method
concepts.description: A numerical procedure that starts from an initial guess and repeatedly refines it, producing a sequence of approximations that converges to the solution of an equation, linear system or optimization problem.
concepts.example: To find √10, start with 3 and repeatedly average x with 10/x: 3 → 3.1667 → 3.1623. Each step refines the guess, and three steps already give 4 correct digits.

concepts.name: Jacobi Method
concepts.description: An iterative algorithm for solving a linear system Ax = b in which each unknown is updated from the diagonal equation using only the previous iterate's values; it converges for diagonally dominant matrices.
concepts.example: For 4x + y = 6 and x + 3y = 7, start at x = y = 0. Update x = (6 − y)/4 and y = (7 − x)/3 using the old values: (1.5, 2.33) → (0.92, 1.83) → …, homing in on (1, 2).

concepts.name: Jacobian Matrix
concepts.description: The matrix of all first-order partial derivatives of a vector-valued function of several variables. It is the best linear approximation of the function near a point and underlies the multivariable chain rule and change of variables.
concepts.example: For f(x, y) = (x·y, x + y), the Jacobian is [[y, x], [1, 1]]. At (2, 3) it is [[3, 2], [1, 1]], the best linear map describing how small input nudges change both outputs.

concepts.name: Jacobian–Vector Product
concepts.description: The product of a function's Jacobian with a vector, giving the directional derivative of its outputs. Forward-mode automatic differentiation computes JVPs efficiently without ever forming the full Jacobian.
concepts.example: For f(x, y) = (xy, x + y) at (2, 3), pushing the direction v = (1, 0) through gives Jv = (3, 1): nudging x by ε changes the outputs by about 3ε and ε, found without building the full Jacobian.

concepts.name: Jensen's Inequality
concepts.description: A result stating that for a convex function f, f of an average is at most the average of f: f(E[X]) ≤ E[f(X)]. It is used to derive bounds such as the ELBO and the non-negativity of KL divergence.
concepts.example: Take X = 1 or 3 with equal chance and f(x) = x². Then f(E[X]) = f(2) = 4, while E[f(X)] = (1 + 9)/2 = 5. Squaring an average gives less than averaging squares.

concepts.name: Jordan Normal Form
concepts.description: A canonical near-diagonal form that every square complex matrix is similar to, made of Jordan blocks with eigenvalues on the diagonal and ones just above. It generalizes diagonalization to matrices that are not diagonalizable.
concepts.example: The matrix [[1, 1], [0, 1]] cannot be diagonalized: it has eigenvalue 1 but only one eigenvector direction. Its Jordan form is itself, a single 2×2 block with the extra 1 above the diagonal.

concepts.name: Kernel (Linear Algebra)
concepts.description: The null space of a linear map or matrix: the set of all vectors that it sends to zero. It is a subspace whose dimension (the nullity) measures how much information the map loses.
concepts.example: Projecting 3D space onto the floor, (x, y, z) → (x, y, 0), sends every purely vertical vector (0, 0, z) to zero. That vertical line is the kernel of the projection.

concepts.name: Kronecker Product
concepts.description: An operation that combines an m×n matrix and a p×q matrix into an mp×nq block matrix by multiplying every entry of the first by the whole second matrix. It appears in tensor algebra, vectorized matrix equations and quantum computing.
concepts.example: [[1, 2]] ⊗ [[0, 1], [1, 0]] gives the 2×4 block matrix [[0, 1, 0, 2], [1, 0, 2, 0]]: the second matrix is copied once scaled by 1 and once scaled by 2.

concepts.name: Krylov Subspace
concepts.description: The space spanned by b, Ab, A²b, …, Aᵏ⁻¹b for a matrix A and vector b. Krylov methods such as GMRES, conjugate gradient and Lanczos search for solutions within this growing subspace using only matrix–vector products.
concepts.example: To solve Ax = b without inverting a huge sparse A, try answers built from b, Ab, A²b, …. These cost only matrix-vector products, and a few dozen often suffice for a good solution.

concepts.name: Lagrange Multiplier
concepts.description: A technique for finding extrema of a function subject to equality constraints by introducing an extra variable per constraint and requiring the gradient of the objective to be a combination of the constraint gradients.
concepts.example: Maximize xy with x + y = 10: at the optimum the gradient of xy, (y, x), is a multiple λ of the constraint's gradient (1, 1). So x = y = 5 and the best product is 25.

concepts.name: Lanczos Algorithm
concepts.description: An iterative algorithm that reduces a large symmetric matrix to a small tridiagonal matrix over a Krylov subspace, whose eigenvalues quickly approximate the extreme eigenvalues of the original matrix.
concepts.example: A social network's million-by-million adjacency matrix has too many eigenvalues to find all of them, but 100 Lanczos steps give a 100×100 tridiagonal matrix whose extreme eigenvalues match the big one's.

concepts.name: Laplace Operator
concepts.description: A differential operator that sums the non-mixed second partial derivatives of a function, equal to the divergence of its gradient. It measures how a value differs from its neighborhood average and appears in heat, wave and diffusion equations.
concepts.example: For a temperature field, ∇²T at a point compares it to the average of its neighbours: if a spot is colder than its surroundings, ∇²T > 0 and heat flows in to warm it.

concepts.name: Laplace Transform
concepts.description: An integral transform that turns a function of time into a function of a complex frequency variable s, converting linear differential equations into algebraic ones that are easier to solve.
concepts.example: The ODE y' + 2y = 0 with y(0) = 3 becomes sY − 3 + 2Y = 0, so Y = 3/(s + 2), which transforms back to y = 3e^(−2t). Calculus became algebra.

concepts.name: Least Squares
concepts.description: A method for fitting a model by choosing parameters that minimize the sum of squared differences between observed and predicted values. For linear models it has a closed-form solution via the normal equations.
concepts.example: Fitting a line to points (1, 1), (2, 2), (3, 2): no line hits all three, so pick the slope and intercept that minimize the sum of squared vertical misses, giving y = 0.67 + 0.5x.

concepts.name: Lebesgue Integration
concepts.description: A theory of integration that measures the size of the sets where a function takes each range of values, rather than slicing the domain. It integrates more functions than the Riemann integral and underpins modern probability.
concepts.example: To count a pile of coins, Riemann goes left to right adding each coin's value; Lebesgue sorts them by denomination and multiplies each value by how many coins have it.

concepts.name: Level Set
concepts.description: The set of all inputs at which a function takes a given constant value, such as a contour line on a map. For smooth functions, the gradient at any point is perpendicular to the level set through it.
concepts.example: On a hiking map, the contour line marked 1500 m is a level set: every point on it is at the same altitude. For f(x, y) = x² + y², the level set f = 4 is a circle of radius 2.

concepts.name: L'Hôpital's Rule
concepts.description: A rule for evaluating limits of the indeterminate forms 0/0 or ∞/∞ by replacing the numerator and denominator with their derivatives and taking the limit again.
concepts.example: As x → 0, sin x / x looks like 0/0. Differentiate top and bottom to get cos x / 1, which tends to 1, so the original limit is 1.

concepts.name: Limit of a Function
concepts.description: The value a function's output approaches as its input gets arbitrarily close to some point, whether or not the function is defined there. Limits are the foundation for continuity, derivatives and integrals.
concepts.example: f(x) = (x² − 1)/(x − 1) is undefined at x = 1, but at x = 0.99 it is 1.99 and at 1.001 it is 2.001. The outputs close in on 2, so the limit is 2.

concepts.name: Limit of a Sequence
concepts.description: The value that the terms of an infinite sequence get arbitrarily close to and stay close to as the index grows. A sequence with a limit is called convergent; one without is divergent.
concepts.example: The sequence 1/2, 2/3, 3/4, 4/5, … gets closer and closer to 1: after the 100th term every term is within 0.01 of 1, so the limit is 1.

concepts.name: Line Integral
concepts.description: An integral of a scalar or vector field taken along a curve, adding up the field's values (or its component along the curve) over each small piece of path. It computes quantities such as work done by a force.
concepts.example: Carrying a box up a winding staircase, the work done against gravity adds up the force's component along each small step of your path, F · dr, over the whole curve.

concepts.name: Linear Algebra
concepts.description: The branch of mathematics studying vectors, vector spaces, matrices and linear maps, together with linear systems, eigenvalues and decompositions. It is the computational backbone of statistics, graphics and machine learning.
concepts.example: A diet uses three foods to hit exact targets of protein, carbs and fat: that is 3 linear equations in 3 unknowns, and linear algebra solves it with matrices in one systematic method.

concepts.name: Linear Approximation
concepts.description: Approximating a function near a point by its tangent line or tangent plane: f(x) ≈ f(a) + f'(a)(x − a). It is the first-order Taylor expansion and the basis of many numerical and optimization methods.
concepts.example: To estimate √4.1, use the tangent line of √x at 4: √4 = 2 and the slope is 1/4, so √4.1 ≈ 2 + 0.1/4 = 2.025. The true value is 2.0248.

concepts.name: Linear Combination
concepts.description: A sum of vectors each multiplied by a scalar coefficient, such as a·v + b·w. Linear combinations define spans, bases and the column view of matrix–vector multiplication.
concepts.example: With coins of 5 and 2, buying something for 19 means 3·5 + 2·2: a linear combination of the two coin values with coefficients 3 and 2.

concepts.name: Linear Equation
concepts.description: An equation in which each variable appears only to the first power and is multiplied by a constant, like 3x + 2y = 7. Its solutions in two variables form a straight line.
concepts.example: A gym charges a $20 joining fee plus $10 a month and you spent $80: 20 + 10m = 80 is a linear equation, so m = 6 months.

concepts.name: Linear Function
concepts.description: A function of the form f(x) = mx + b whose graph is a straight line with slope m and intercept b. In linear algebra the term often means a map with no constant term that preserves addition and scaling.
concepts.example: A phone plan costs $10 plus $2 per GB, so f(x) = 2x + 10: using 5 GB costs $20. The graph is a straight line starting at 10 and rising 2 for each GB.

concepts.name: Linear Independence
concepts.description: A property of a set of vectors in which no vector can be written as a linear combination of the others; equivalently, the only combination giving the zero vector uses all-zero coefficients.
concepts.example: The vectors (1, 0) and (0, 1) are independent: neither is a multiple of the other. Adding (2, 3) makes the set dependent, since (2, 3) = 2·(1, 0) + 3·(0, 1).

concepts.name: Linear Interpolation
concepts.description: Estimating a value between two known data points by assuming a straight line connects them: the result is a weighted average whose weights depend on the relative distance to each point.
concepts.example: If a phone is 20% charged at 1 pm and 80% at 3 pm, assuming steady charging it was 50% at 2 pm, halfway along the straight line between the readings.

concepts.name: Linear Map
concepts.description: A function between vector spaces that preserves vector addition and scalar multiplication. Every linear map between finite-dimensional spaces can be represented by a matrix once bases are chosen.
concepts.example: Rotating the plane by 90° is a linear map: it takes (1, 0) to (0, 1) and (0, 1) to (−1, 0). Rotating a sum is the same as summing the rotations.

concepts.name: Linear Span
concepts.description: The set of all linear combinations of a given collection of vectors; it is the smallest subspace containing them. For example, two non-parallel vectors in 3D span a plane.
concepts.example: The span of (1, 0, 0) and (0, 1, 0) is the whole floor (the xy-plane) of 3D space: every point a·(1, 0, 0) + b·(0, 1, 0) lies on it, and nothing above it does.

concepts.name: Linear Subspace
concepts.description: A subset of a vector space that contains the zero vector and is closed under addition and scalar multiplication, so it is itself a vector space. Lines and planes through the origin are examples.
concepts.example: In 3D, any plane through the origin is a subspace: adding two vectors in it or stretching one stays in the plane. A plane shifted up one unit is not, as it misses the zero vector.

concepts.name: Lipschitz Continuity
concepts.description: A strong form of continuity requiring that |f(x) − f(y)| ≤ L·|x − y| for some constant L, bounding how fast the function can change. Lipschitz constants appear in optimization step sizes, GAN training and robustness guarantees.
concepts.example: f(x) = 3x + 1 is Lipschitz with L = 3: moving x by 0.1 changes f by at most 0.3. By contrast √x near 0 is continuous but too steep to have any such L.

concepts.name: LogSumExp
concepts.description: The function log(Σ exp(xᵢ)), a smooth approximation of the maximum. The log-sum-exp trick subtracts the largest xᵢ before exponentiating to avoid overflow when computing softmax and log-likelihoods.
concepts.example: For (1000, 1001), computing e¹⁰⁰⁰ overflows. Pull out the max: 1001 + log(e⁻¹ + 1) ≈ 1001.31, slightly above the max 1001, computed safely.

concepts.name: Logarithm
concepts.description: The inverse of exponentiation: log_b(x) is the power to which base b must be raised to get x. Logarithms turn multiplication into addition and are used to measure growth, scale and information.
concepts.example: log₂ 8 = 3 because 2 must be multiplied by itself 3 times to get 8. That's why the number of times you can halve 1024 before reaching 1 is log₂ 1024 = 10.

concepts.name: Logarithmic Function
concepts.description: A function f(x) = log_b(x), defined for positive x, that is the inverse of the exponential function b^x. It grows without bound but ever more slowly, and its graph passes through (1, 0).
concepts.example: The Richter scale is logarithmic: a magnitude 6 quake shakes 10 times harder than magnitude 5. The function log₁₀ x climbs slowly, reaching only 6 at x = 1,000,000.

concepts.name: Logical Biconditional
concepts.description: The logical connective 'P if and only if Q', true exactly when P and Q have the same truth value. It expresses that two statements are equivalent and is used to state definitions and characterizations.
concepts.example: 'A number is even if and only if its last digit is 0, 2, 4, 6 or 8': each side guarantees the other, so they are always both true or both false.

concepts.name: Logical Connective
concepts.description: A symbol or word such as AND, OR, NOT or IMPLIES that combines or modifies propositions to form compound statements whose truth value depends only on the truth values of the parts.
concepts.example: 'It is raining AND I have an umbrella' is true only when both parts are; swapping AND for OR makes it true if either is. The connective decides how parts combine.

concepts.name: Logical Equivalence
concepts.description: The relation between two logical formulas that have the same truth value under every assignment of their variables, such as ¬(P ∧ Q) and ¬P ∨ ¬Q. Equivalent formulas can be substituted freely in proofs.
concepts.example: 'Not (A and B)' and '(not A) or (not B)' agree on all four combinations of A and B, so they are equivalent: De Morgan's law.

concepts.name: Low-Rank Approximation
concepts.description: Approximating a matrix by one of lower rank that is as close as possible, usually in Frobenius or spectral norm. The truncated SVD gives the optimal solution and powers compression, PCA and LoRA-style methods.
concepts.example: A 1000×1000 photo needs a million numbers, but keeping the top 50 singular values and vectors stores about 100,000 and still looks nearly the same.

concepts.name: Lp Norm
concepts.description: A family of vector lengths defined by (Σ|xᵢ|^p)^(1/p). The L1 norm sums absolute values, the L2 norm is Euclidean length, and the L∞ norm is the largest absolute entry; they underpin regularization and distances.
concepts.example: For v = (3, −4): the L1 norm is 3 + 4 = 7 (taxi distance), the L2 norm is √(9 + 16) = 5 (straight line), and the L∞ norm is 4 (largest entry).

concepts.name: LU Decomposition
concepts.description: Factoring a square matrix as the product of a lower-triangular matrix L and an upper-triangular matrix U, essentially recording Gaussian elimination. It lets many systems with the same matrix be solved quickly by substitution.
concepts.example: [[2, 1], [4, 5]] = [[1, 0], [2, 1]] · [[2, 1], [0, 3]]. Once A is factored, solving Ax = b for each new b costs just two quick triangular solves.

concepts.name: Machine Epsilon
concepts.description: The gap between 1 and the next larger representable floating-point number, about 2.2×10⁻¹⁶ for double precision. It bounds the relative rounding error of a single floating-point operation.
concepts.example: In double precision, 1 + 1e−17 == 1 evaluates as true: the addition is too small to register, since the next number after 1 is about 1 + 2.2×10⁻¹⁶.

concepts.name: Manhattan Distance
concepts.description: The distance between two points measured as the sum of the absolute differences of their coordinates, like walking along a city grid. It equals the L1 norm of their difference and is less sensitive to outliers than Euclidean distance.
concepts.example: Walking from (1, 1) to (4, 5) along city blocks takes 3 blocks east plus 4 north, 7 blocks in total, while the crow flies only 5.

concepts.name: Stochastic Matrix
concepts.description: A square matrix of non-negative entries in which each row (or column) sums to one, giving the probabilities of moving between states of a Markov chain. Its powers describe multi-step transitions.
concepts.example: Weather: if sunny today, tomorrow is sunny with 0.8 and rainy with 0.2; if rainy, 0.4 and 0.6. The matrix [[0.8, 0.2], [0.4, 0.6]] has rows summing to 1.

concepts.name: Master Theorem
concepts.description: A formula giving the asymptotic running time of divide-and-conquer recurrences of the form T(n) = aT(n/b) + f(n) by comparing f(n) with n^(log_b a). It quickly solves recurrences such as merge sort's.
concepts.example: Merge sort satisfies T(n) = 2T(n/2) + n: two halves plus linear merging. Here a = 2, b = 2, and the work is balanced across levels, so T(n) = Θ(n log n).

concepts.name: Material Conditional
concepts.description: The logical connective 'if P then Q' (P → Q), which is false only when P is true and Q is false. It formalizes implication in mathematics, so a conditional with a false premise counts as true.
concepts.example: 'If it rains, the ground is wet' is broken only by rain with a dry ground. If it doesn't rain, the statement isn't violated, so it counts as true.

concepts.name: Mathematical Induction
concepts.description: A proof technique for statements about all natural numbers: prove the base case, then show that if the statement holds for n it also holds for n + 1. Like falling dominoes, this establishes it for every n.
concepts.example: Dominoes: show the first one falls, and that any falling domino knocks the next. Then all fall. Likewise 1 + 2 + … + n = n(n + 1)/2 holds for n = 1 and passes from n to n + 1.

concepts.name: Mathematical Logic
concepts.description: The branch of mathematics studying formal reasoning: propositional and predicate logic, proof systems, models, computability and the limits of formal systems such as Gödel's incompleteness theorems.
concepts.example: Logic asks questions like: can one fixed set of axioms prove every true statement about numbers? Gödel showed no, and Turing showed some questions can't be decided by any algorithm.

concepts.name: Mathematical Proof
concepts.description: A rigorous logical argument that shows a statement must be true, deriving it step by step from axioms, definitions and previously proven results. Common styles include direct proof, contradiction and induction.
concepts.example: Claim: the sum of two even numbers is even. Write them as 2a and 2b; their sum is 2(a + b), which is even. A few lines cover every possible pair, which no amount of testing could do.

concepts.name: Matrix
concepts.description: A rectangular array of numbers arranged in rows and columns. Matrices represent linear maps, systems of equations and datasets, and they can be added, scaled and multiplied.
concepts.example: A shop's sales grid with rows for days and columns for products is a matrix: row 2, column 3 might hold 14, meaning 14 units of product 3 sold on day 2.

concepts.name: Matrix Addition
concepts.description: Adding two matrices of the same shape by adding their corresponding entries. It is commutative and associative, and together with scalar multiplication makes the set of matrices a vector space.
concepts.example: Two branches' weekly sales grids [[3, 5], [2, 1]] and [[1, 0], [4, 2]] add entry by entry to give the total [[4, 5], [6, 3]].

concepts.name: Matrix Calculus
concepts.description: The set of notations and rules for differentiating functions whose inputs or outputs are vectors or matrices, such as gradients of quadratic forms and log-determinants. It is essential for deriving ML training updates.
concepts.example: For the loss L = ‖Xw − y‖², matrix calculus gives ∂L/∂w = 2Xᵀ(Xw − y) in one line, instead of writing out a partial derivative for each weight separately.

concepts.name: Matrix Exponential
concepts.description: The matrix analogue of eˣ, defined by the power series e^A = I + A + A²/2! + A³/3! + …. It solves systems of linear differential equations x' = Ax and describes continuous-time Markov chains and rotations.
concepts.example: For the rotation generator A = [[0, −1], [1, 0]], e^(tA) = [[cos t, −sin t], [sin t, cos t]]: the series turns a constant 'velocity' matrix into smooth rotation by angle t.

concepts.name: Matrix Multiplication
concepts.description: Combining an m×n matrix with an n×p matrix into an m×p matrix whose entries are dot products of rows with columns. It represents composing linear maps and is the core operation of neural networks.
concepts.example: Prices [[2, 3]] (apple, pear) times quantities [[4], [5]] give 2·4 + 3·5 = 23. Stacking several shoppers and price lists, every entry of the product is such a row-times-column total.

concepts.name: Matrix Norm
concepts.description: A measure of a matrix's size, such as the Frobenius norm (square root of the sum of squared entries) or the spectral/operator norm (the largest factor by which it can stretch a vector).
concepts.example: The matrix [[3, 0], [0, 1]] stretches vectors by at most 3, so its spectral norm is 3; its Frobenius norm is √(9 + 1) ≈ 3.16. Both measure how 'big' the matrix is.

concepts.name: Matrix–Vector Multiplication
concepts.description: Multiplying an m×n matrix by an n-vector to get an m-vector, either as dot products of each row with the vector or as a linear combination of the matrix's columns weighted by the vector's entries.
concepts.example: [[1, 2], [3, 4]] times (1, 1) gives (3, 7): row 1 dotted with (1, 1) is 3 and row 2 is 7. Equivalently, it is column 1 plus column 2.

concepts.name: Maxima and Minima
concepts.description: The largest and smallest values of a function, either over its whole domain (global) or within a small neighborhood (local). Finding them is the central task of optimization, often by setting the derivative to zero.
concepts.example: Throw a ball and its height peaks at the moment it stops rising, a maximum where the vertical velocity is zero. For h(t) = 20t − 5t², that's t = 2 with height 20 m.

concepts.name: Mean Value Theorem
concepts.description: A theorem stating that a function continuous on [a, b] and differentiable inside has some point where its instantaneous slope equals its average slope (f(b) − f(a))/(b − a). It underlies many error bounds.
concepts.example: If you drive 120 km in 1.5 hours, your average speed is 80 km/h, so at some instant the speedometer read exactly 80 km/h.

concepts.name: Measure Theory
concepts.description: The branch of analysis that rigorously defines size (length, area, probability) for sets via σ-algebras and measures, and builds the Lebesgue integral on top. It is the foundation of modern probability theory.
concepts.example: What is the 'length' of the rational numbers in [0, 1]? Measure theory says 0: being countable, they can be covered by intervals of total length as small as you like.

concepts.name: Metric Space
concepts.description: A set equipped with a distance function that is non-negative, zero only between identical points, symmetric, and obeys the triangle inequality. It is the general setting for convergence, continuity and nearest-neighbor ideas.
concepts.example: Cities with distance = shortest driving time form a metric space if roads are two-way: it is zero only from a city to itself, symmetric, and a detour is never shorter than going direct.

concepts.name: Modular Arithmetic
concepts.description: Arithmetic on integers where numbers wrap around after reaching a fixed modulus, like hours on a clock (15 mod 12 = 3). It is fundamental to number theory, hashing and cryptography.
concepts.example: If it's 10 o'clock now, 5 hours later it is 3 o'clock, because 15 mod 12 = 3. Similarly, a day 100 days after Monday is a Tuesday, since 100 mod 7 = 2.

concepts.name: Monotone Convergence Theorem
concepts.description: A result in analysis stating that a bounded monotone sequence of real numbers converges; its measure-theoretic version lets limits and integrals be swapped for increasing sequences of non-negative functions.
concepts.example: The sequence 0.9, 0.99, 0.999, … keeps increasing yet never exceeds 1, so it must converge, and it converges to its least upper bound, 1.

concepts.name: Monotonic Function
concepts.description: A function that is entirely non-decreasing or entirely non-increasing over its domain, so it never changes direction. Monotone transformations such as log preserve the location of maxima and orderings.
concepts.example: Your age as a function of time is monotonic: it only ever goes up. Outdoor temperature over a day is not, since it rises then falls.

concepts.name: Monte Carlo Integration
concepts.description: Estimating an integral by averaging the integrand at randomly sampled points and scaling by the region's size. Its error shrinks like 1/√n regardless of dimension, making it practical for high-dimensional integrals.
concepts.example: Throw 1000 random darts at a square containing a quarter circle; if 785 land inside, the area ratio is about 0.785, giving π ≈ 4 × 0.785 = 3.14.

concepts.name: Moore–Penrose Inverse
concepts.description: A generalized inverse A⁺ defined for any matrix, including non-square or singular ones. A⁺b gives the least-squares solution of Ax = b with smallest norm, and it is computed from the SVD.
concepts.example: The 2×1 matrix A = [[1], [1]] has no inverse, but A⁺ = [[0.5, 0.5]]. For b = (2, 4), A⁺b = 3, the best single x making (x, x) close to (2, 4).

concepts.name: Multinomial Theorem
concepts.description: A generalization of the binomial theorem giving the expansion of (x₁ + … + x_k)ⁿ as a sum of terms weighted by multinomial coefficients n!/(n₁!…n_k!), which count arrangements of items into groups.
concepts.example: (a + b + c)² = a² + b² + c² + 2ab + 2bc + 2ac. The coefficient 2 on ab counts the 2 ways to pick one a and one b from two factors, 2!/(1!·1!·0!).

concepts.name: Multiple Integral
concepts.description: An integral of a function of two or more variables over a region, such as a double integral over an area or a triple integral over a volume. It computes volumes, masses and joint probabilities.
concepts.example: A rectangular garden with soil depth d(x, y) holds soil volume ∫∫d dA: add up depth × tiny area over every patch. If depth is 0.5 m everywhere on 4 × 3 m, that's 6 m³.

concepts.name: Multivariable Calculus
concepts.description: The extension of calculus to functions of several variables, covering partial derivatives, gradients, multiple integrals and vector calculus theorems. It is essential for optimization and machine learning.
concepts.example: A drone's battery use depends on speed, altitude and wind at once. Multivariable calculus finds which direction to change all three to save the most energy.

concepts.name: Multivariable Chain Rule
concepts.description: The rule for differentiating a composition of multivariable functions: the derivative of the composition is the product of the Jacobians, so changes propagate through every intermediate variable. It is the mathematics behind backpropagation.
concepts.example: Temperature T(x, y) changes as an ant walks along (x(t), y(t)). Its rate of change is dT/dt = ∂T/∂x·dx/dt + ∂T/∂y·dy/dt: each route of influence adds up.

concepts.name: Function of Several Real Variables
concepts.description: A function that takes several real inputs, such as f(x, y) = x² + y², and returns a value. Its graph is a surface or higher-dimensional shape, and loss functions in ML are typical examples.
concepts.example: The cost of a pizza depends on size and number of toppings: C(s, t) = 2s + 1.5t. With size 10 and 3 toppings, C = 24.5, one output from two inputs.

concepts.name: Multivariable Taylor Series
concepts.description: The expansion of a function of several variables around a point using its gradient, Hessian and higher derivatives: f(x+h) ≈ f(x) + ∇f·h + ½hᵀHh. Its second-order form underlies Newton's method.
concepts.example: Near (0, 0), f(x, y) = e^(x+y) ≈ 1 + (x + y) + (x + y)²/2. The linear part comes from the gradient and the quadratic part from the Hessian.

concepts.name: Natural Logarithm
concepts.description: The logarithm with base e ≈ 2.718, written ln x. It is the inverse of eˣ, its derivative is 1/x, and it appears throughout calculus, probability (log-likelihoods) and information theory.
concepts.example: Money growing continuously at 100% per year doubles after ln 2 ≈ 0.693 years. In general, ln x answers 'how long does continuous growth at rate 1 take to multiply by x'.

concepts.name: Natural Number
concepts.description: The counting numbers 1, 2, 3, … (often including 0) used to count and order things. They are closed under addition and multiplication and form the starting point of arithmetic and induction.
concepts.example: Counting sheep gives 1, 2, 3, …; you can never have 2.5 sheep or −1 sheep. Adding or multiplying counts always gives another count.

concepts.name: Necessary and Sufficient Conditions
concepts.description: Terms describing implication: P is sufficient for Q if P guarantees Q, and necessary if Q cannot hold without P. A condition that is both is equivalent to Q, expressed as 'if and only if'.
concepts.example: For a number to be divisible by 4, being even is necessary but not sufficient (6 fails). Having its last two digits divisible by 4 is both necessary and sufficient.

concepts.name: Newton's Method
concepts.description: An iterative root-finding algorithm that repeatedly replaces a guess x with x − f(x)/f'(x), the root of the tangent line. Near a simple root it converges quadratically, roughly doubling the correct digits each step.
concepts.example: To find √2, solve x² − 2 = 0 starting at x = 1: next x = 1 − (−1)/2 = 1.5, then 1.4167, then 1.41422. The correct digits roughly double each step.

concepts.name: Degree (Graph Theory)
concepts.description: The number of edges incident to a vertex in a graph; in directed graphs it splits into in-degree and out-degree. Degree distributions characterize networks and appear in the graph Laplacian.
concepts.example: In a friendship network, if Ana knows Ben, Cara and Dan, Ana's vertex has degree 3. On Twitter, followers count as in-degree and accounts followed as out-degree.

concepts.name: Non-Negative Matrix Factorization
concepts.description: Factoring a non-negative matrix V into two smaller non-negative matrices W and H with V ≈ WH. The non-negativity yields additive, parts-based components used for topic modeling, audio separation and image analysis.
concepts.example: A matrix of word counts per article factors into topics × articles: one factor says 'sports' uses 'goal' and 'team', the other says article 7 is 80% sports. No negatives keep it readable.

concepts.name: Normal Equations
concepts.description: The linear system AᵀAx = Aᵀb whose solution is the least-squares fit for Ax ≈ b. It follows from requiring the residual to be orthogonal to the column space of A.
concepts.example: Fitting y = c to data 2, 4, 6: A is a column of ones, so AᵀA = 3 and Aᵀb = 12, giving c = 4, the average. Least squares picks the mean.

concepts.name: Normed Vector Space
concepts.description: A vector space equipped with a norm, a function assigning each vector a non-negative length that is zero only for the zero vector, scales with scalars and satisfies the triangle inequality.
concepts.example: In ℝ² with ‖(x, y)‖ = |x| + |y|, the vector (3, −4) has length 7. Any rule like this that is positive, scales properly and obeys the triangle inequality makes a normed space.

concepts.name: Nuclear Norm
concepts.description: The sum of a matrix's singular values. It is the tightest convex relaxation of matrix rank, so minimizing it encourages low-rank solutions in matrix completion and robust PCA.
concepts.example: Netflix-style rating completion: find a matrix agreeing with known ratings and having the smallest sum of singular values. This tends to give low rank, i.e. a few taste factors.

concepts.name: Number Theory
concepts.description: The branch of mathematics studying integers and their properties: divisibility, primes, congruences and Diophantine equations. It has major applications in cryptography and hashing.
concepts.example: Why does every whole number have exactly one prime factorization, like 60 = 2²·3·5? And why does 2¹¹ − 1 = 2047 fail to be prime? Number theory answers questions like these.

concepts.name: Numerator and Denominator Layout
concepts.description: The two conventions for arranging derivatives of vectors and matrices: numerator layout makes the result's rows follow the output, denominator layout follows the input. Mixing them causes transposition errors in gradient derivations.
concepts.example: For y = Ax with A of size 2×3, numerator layout writes ∂y/∂x as the 2×3 matrix A, while denominator layout writes it as the 3×2 matrix Aᵀ. Mixing them up flips your formulas.

concepts.name: Numerical Analysis
concepts.description: The study of algorithms that compute approximate numerical solutions to continuous problems—roots, integrals, differential equations, linear systems—together with their accuracy, stability and convergence.
concepts.example: A calculator computes sin(0.5) with a few terms of a series, but how many terms are enough, and how do rounding errors build up? Numerical analysis answers this.

concepts.name: Numerical Integration
concepts.description: Approximating a definite integral from a finite number of function evaluations, using rules such as the trapezoidal rule, Simpson's rule or Gaussian quadrature, when no closed-form antiderivative is available.
concepts.example: To estimate ∫₀¹ x² dx = 1/3, the trapezoid rule with points 0, 0.5, 1 gives 0.375; Simpson's rule with the same points gives exactly 0.3333.

concepts.name: Numerical Linear Algebra
concepts.description: The study of efficient and accurate algorithms for matrix computations on computers, such as solving linear systems, least squares and eigenvalue problems, with attention to floating-point error and sparsity.
concepts.example: Solving a system with Cramer's rule and cofactor determinants takes roughly n! operations; LU decomposition needs about n³. For n = 20 that's the difference between centuries and microseconds.

concepts.name: Numerical Stability
concepts.description: The property of an algorithm that small rounding or input errors do not grow uncontrollably during computation. Stable algorithms, such as pivoted elimination or log-space probability arithmetic, give trustworthy results in floating point.
concepts.example: Computing √(x + 1) − √x for x = 10¹² in floating point loses most digits to cancellation; rewriting it as 1/(√(x + 1) + √x) gives the same value with full accuracy.

concepts.name: Open and Closed Sets
concepts.description: Basic topological notions: a set is open if every point has a small neighborhood inside it, and closed if it contains all its limit points (its complement is open). They define continuity and compactness.
concepts.example: The interval (0, 1) is open: around 0.999 there's still room. [0, 1] is closed: the sequence 0.9, 0.99, … converges to 1, which is in it, whereas (0, 1) would miss it.

concepts.name: Order of Operations
concepts.description: The convention fixing which operations are done first in an expression: parentheses, then exponents, then multiplication and division, then addition and subtraction, left to right. It makes expressions unambiguous.
concepts.example: 2 + 3 × 4 equals 14, not 20, because multiplication comes before addition. Writing (2 + 3) × 4 forces the addition first and gives 20.

concepts.name: Ordinary Differential Equation
concepts.description: An equation relating an unknown function of one variable to its derivatives, such as y' = ky. ODEs model change over time in physics, biology and continuous-depth neural networks.
concepts.example: A cup of coffee cools at a rate proportional to its excess over room temperature: T' = −k(T − 20). Its solution T = 20 + 70e^(−kt) shows 90 °C coffee approaching 20 °C.

concepts.name: Orthogonal Complement
concepts.description: The set of all vectors perpendicular to every vector in a given subspace. Together the subspace and its complement span the whole space, as with a matrix's row space and null space.
concepts.example: In 3D, the orthogonal complement of the floor (the xy-plane) is the vertical z-axis: every vertical vector is perpendicular to every floor vector, and together they span space.

concepts.name: Orthogonal Matrix
concepts.description: A square real matrix whose columns form an orthonormal set, so QᵀQ = I and its inverse is its transpose. Orthogonal matrices represent rotations and reflections and preserve lengths and angles.
concepts.example: The rotation [[0.6, −0.8], [0.8, 0.6]] turns vectors by about 53° without stretching them. Its inverse is just its transpose, so undoing it costs no division.

concepts.name: Orthogonality
concepts.description: The generalization of perpendicularity: two vectors are orthogonal when their dot (inner) product is zero. Orthogonal directions carry independent information and simplify projections and decompositions.
concepts.example: The vectors (1, 2) and (2, −1) have dot product 1·2 + 2·(−1) = 0, so they are orthogonal: drawn from the origin, they form a perfect right angle.

concepts.name: Orthonormal Basis
concepts.description: A basis whose vectors all have unit length and are mutually orthogonal. Coordinates in such a basis are just dot products with the basis vectors, which makes computations simple and stable.
concepts.example: In the basis (0.6, 0.8), (−0.8, 0.6), the vector (5, 0) has coordinates 5·0.6 = 3 and 5·(−0.8) = −4: just dot products, no system to solve.

concepts.name: Outer Product
concepts.description: The product of a column vector u and a row vector vᵀ, giving the matrix uvᵀ whose (i, j) entry is uᵢvⱼ. Outer products are rank-one matrices and build up covariance matrices and the SVD.
concepts.example: u = (1, 2) and v = (3, 4) give uvᵀ = [[3, 4], [6, 8]]: every entry is uᵢ·vⱼ, and every row is a multiple of v, so the matrix has rank one.

concepts.name: Partial Derivative
concepts.description: The derivative of a multivariable function with respect to one variable while all others are held fixed. Collecting the partial derivatives gives the gradient used in optimization.
concepts.example: For a tent whose height is h(x, y) = 5 − x² − y², walking only east at (1, 2), height changes at ∂h/∂x = −2x = −2 per step, with y held fixed.

concepts.name: Partial Differential Equation
concepts.description: An equation relating an unknown function of several variables to its partial derivatives, such as the heat or wave equation. PDEs model fields varying in space and time and appear in diffusion models.
concepts.example: The heat equation ∂u/∂t = k ∂²u/∂x² says a rod's temperature changes over time according to its curvature in space: hot spots flatten out.

concepts.name: Partial Fraction Decomposition
concepts.description: Rewriting a rational function as a sum of simpler fractions with linear or quadratic denominators. It is mainly used to integrate rational functions and invert Laplace transforms.
concepts.example: 1/(x² − 1) splits into ½·1/(x − 1) − ½·1/(x + 1). Each piece integrates to a simple logarithm, so the hard integral becomes easy.

concepts.name: Pivot Element
concepts.description: In Gaussian elimination, swapping rows so that the entry with the largest absolute value in the current column becomes the pivot. This avoids division by tiny numbers and keeps elimination numerically stable.
concepts.example: Eliminating with pivot 0.0001 in 0.0001x + y = 1 means multiplying by 10,000, which blows up rounding errors. Swapping rows to pivot on the 1 in x + y = 2 keeps multipliers small.

concepts.name: Partially Ordered Set
concepts.description: A set with a relation ≤ that is reflexive, antisymmetric and transitive, where some pairs of elements may be incomparable. Examples include subsets ordered by inclusion and tasks ordered by dependency.
concepts.example: Order subsets of {a, b} by inclusion: {a} ⊆ {a, b} and ∅ ⊆ {b}, but {a} and {b} are incomparable, as neither contains the other. That's a partial, not total, order.

concepts.name: Partition of a Set
concepts.description: A division of a set into non-empty, non-overlapping subsets whose union is the whole set. Partitions correspond exactly to equivalence relations and describe clusterings.
concepts.example: Sorting a deck of 52 cards into the four suits is a partition: every card lands in exactly one pile, no pile is empty, and together the piles make the whole deck.

concepts.name: Pascal's Triangle
concepts.description: A triangular array where each number is the sum of the two above it. Its rows list the binomial coefficients, so it gives the coefficients of (a + b)ⁿ and counts combinations.
concepts.example: Rows go 1; 1 1; 1 2 1; 1 3 3 1; 1 4 6 4 1. The 6 in row 4 is 3 + 3, and it also counts the ways to choose 2 heads in 4 coin tosses.

concepts.name: Path
concepts.description: A sequence of vertices in a graph where each consecutive pair is joined by an edge. A walk may repeat vertices, a path does not, and a cycle returns to its start; paths define connectivity and distances.
concepts.example: In a subway map, going Station A → B → C → D is a path when each consecutive pair is directly connected; its length is 3 edges.

concepts.name: Percentage
concepts.description: A way of expressing a number as a fraction of 100, written with the % sign. Percentages describe proportions, rates and changes such as discounts or growth.
concepts.example: A jacket costs $80 and is 25% off: 25% means 25/100 = 1/4, so you save $20 and pay $60. A 5% sales tax on that $60 then adds another $3.

concepts.name: Periodic Function
concepts.description: A function that repeats its values at regular intervals: f(x + T) = f(x) for a period T. Sine and cosine are the classic examples, and Fourier analysis decomposes signals into periodic parts.
concepts.example: The height of a seat on a Ferris wheel that turns once every 10 minutes is periodic with period 10: at minute 3 and minute 13 the seat is at the same height.

concepts.name: Permutation
concepts.description: An ordered arrangement of objects, or a rearrangement of a sequence. There are n! permutations of n distinct items, and P(n, k) = n!/(n − k)! ways to arrange k of them.
concepts.example: Three runners A, B, C can finish in 3! = 6 orders: ABC, ACB, BAC, BCA, CAB, CBA. With 10 runners there are 3,628,800 possible finishes.

concepts.name: Permutation Matrix
concepts.description: A square matrix with exactly one 1 in each row and column and zeros elsewhere. Multiplying by it reorders the rows or columns of another matrix, as in the row swaps of pivoted LU decomposition.
concepts.example: [[0, 1, 0], [0, 0, 1], [1, 0, 0]] times (a, b, c) gives (b, c, a): it reshuffles the entries. It is just the identity matrix with its rows rearranged.

concepts.name: Perron–Frobenius Theorem
concepts.description: A theorem stating that a matrix with positive (or irreducible non-negative) entries has a unique largest positive eigenvalue with an eigenvector of positive entries. It guarantees stationary distributions and PageRank scores.
concepts.example: In a web-link stochastic matrix with positive entries, the theorem guarantees one steady-state ranking vector with all positive entries; that's why PageRank has a well-defined answer.

concepts.name: Piecewise Function
concepts.description: A function defined by different formulas on different parts of its domain, such as the absolute value or the ReLU activation. Its continuity and differentiability must be checked at the boundaries.
concepts.example: A parking garage charges $0 for the first 30 minutes, then $2 per hour after that: one formula applies on [0, 0.5] hours and another beyond, making a piecewise function.

concepts.name: Pigeonhole Principle
concepts.description: The principle that if more than n items are placed into n boxes, some box must hold at least two items. Despite its simplicity it proves results about collisions, hashing and compression limits.
concepts.example: In any group of 13 people, two share a birth month: 12 months are the boxes and 13 people are the items. In a city of 1 million, two people have the same number of hairs.

concepts.name: Planar Graph
concepts.description: A graph that can be drawn in the plane without any edges crossing. Planar graphs satisfy Euler's formula V − E + F = 2 and can always be colored with four colors.
concepts.example: Three houses each needing water, gas and electricity lines (graph K₃,₃) can't be drawn without crossing pipes, so K₃,₃ is not planar. A cube's edge graph can be drawn flat with no crossings.

concepts.name: Polar Coordinate System
concepts.description: A coordinate system that locates a point by its distance r from the origin and its angle θ from a reference direction, instead of x and y. It simplifies problems with circular symmetry; spherical coordinates extend it to 3D.
concepts.example: A radar reports a plane at distance 10 km and bearing 30°: that's polar coordinates (10, 30°). In Cartesian terms it is about (8.66, 5).

concepts.name: Polar Decomposition
concepts.description: Factoring a square matrix as A = UP, where U is orthogonal (a rotation/reflection) and P is symmetric positive semidefinite (a stretch), analogous to writing a complex number as e^{iθ}·r. It follows from the SVD.
concepts.example: Any linear map of the plane can be done as a stretch along perpendicular axes (P) followed by a rotation or flip (U), just as a complex number is r times e^(iθ).

concepts.name: Polynomial
concepts.description: An expression built from variables and constants using addition, subtraction, multiplication and non-negative integer powers, such as 3x² − 2x + 5. Its degree is the highest power present.
concepts.example: 3x² + 2x − 5 is a polynomial: powers of x times constants, added together. At x = 2 it gives 12 + 4 − 5 = 11.

concepts.name: Polynomial Factorization
concepts.description: Writing a polynomial as a product of simpler polynomials, such as x² − 5x + 6 = (x − 2)(x − 3). Factoring reveals roots and simplifies algebraic expressions.
concepts.example: x² − 5x + 6 = (x − 2)(x − 3), so the parabola crosses zero at x = 2 and x = 3: a product is zero only when one factor is.

concepts.name: Polynomial Interpolation
concepts.description: Finding the unique polynomial of degree at most n that passes through n + 1 given data points, for example with the Lagrange or Newton form. High degrees can oscillate wildly between points (Runge's phenomenon).
concepts.example: Three points (0, 1), (1, 3), (2, 7) define exactly one parabola: solving for a, b, c in ax² + bx + c gives x² + x + 1, which passes through all three.

concepts.name: Power Iteration
concepts.description: An algorithm that finds a matrix's dominant eigenvector by repeatedly multiplying a vector by the matrix and normalizing. It is simple and memory-light, and it underlies PageRank and spectral norm estimation.
concepts.example: Start with (1, 0) and keep multiplying by [[2, 1], [1, 2]] and rescaling: (2, 1) → (5, 4) → (14, 13) … quickly approaches the direction (1, 1), the eigenvector with eigenvalue 3.

concepts.name: Power Series
concepts.description: An infinite series of the form Σ aₙ(x − c)ⁿ, like a polynomial of infinite degree. It converges within a radius of convergence and represents functions such as eˣ, sin x and 1/(1 − x).
concepts.example: 1 + x + x² + x³ + … equals 1/(1 − x) when |x| < 1: at x = 0.5 the terms 1 + 0.5 + 0.25 + … add up to 2. Outside that range it diverges.

concepts.name: Power Set Enumeration
concepts.description: Generating every subset of a set of n elements—2ⁿ in total—typically via recursion/backtracking or by counting through n-bit binary masks where each bit decides membership. It drives brute-force search over combinations.
concepts.example: For {a, b, c}, count from 000 to 111 in binary: each bit decides whether to include a, b or c. The 8 numbers produce all 8 subsets, from {} to {a, b, c}.

concepts.name: Preconditioner
concepts.description: A transformation applied to a linear system or optimization problem so that it becomes better conditioned, letting iterative methods like conjugate gradient converge in far fewer steps. Adaptive optimizers act as diagonal preconditioners.
concepts.example: Solving a system whose matrix has entries ranging from 0.001 to 1000 takes conjugate gradient thousands of steps; dividing each row by its diagonal entry first can cut that to dozens.

concepts.name: Prime Number
concepts.description: A natural number greater than 1 whose only divisors are 1 and itself, such as 2, 3, 5, 7. Every integer factors uniquely into primes, and large primes are central to cryptography.
concepts.example: 7 is prime: 7 cookies can only be split evenly among 1 or 7 children. 12 is not, since it divides into groups of 2, 3, 4 or 6.

concepts.name: Product Notation
concepts.description: The capital-pi notation Πᵢ aᵢ for writing the product of many terms compactly, analogous to Σ for sums. It appears, for example, in likelihoods of independent observations.
concepts.example: Π from i = 1 to 4 of i means 1 · 2 · 3 · 4 = 24, which is 4!. The probability of 3 independent coin flips all landing heads is Π (1/2) = 1/8.

concepts.name: Product Rule
concepts.description: The differentiation rule for a product of functions: (fg)' = f'g + fg'. It follows from the limit definition of the derivative and is used constantly in calculus.
concepts.example: A rectangle's sides grow: width w = t, height h = t², area A = t³. The product rule gives A' = 1·t² + t·2t = 3t², matching the direct derivative of t³.

concepts.name: Projection Matrix
concepts.description: A matrix P with P² = P that maps vectors onto a subspace; an orthogonal projection is also symmetric. In regression the hat matrix projects observations onto the column space to give fitted values.
concepts.example: P = [[1, 0], [0, 0]] flattens (3, 4) to (3, 0), its shadow on the x-axis. Applying P again changes nothing, which is why P² = P.

concepts.name: Proof by Contradiction
concepts.description: A proof technique that assumes the statement is false and derives a logical impossibility, so the statement must be true. The classic example is proving √2 is irrational.
concepts.example: Suppose there were a largest prime p. Multiply all primes up to p and add 1: the result leaves remainder 1 when divided by each, so some prime beyond p divides it. Contradiction.

concepts.name: Proof by Contrapositive
concepts.description: Proving 'if P then Q' by instead proving the logically equivalent 'if not Q then not P', which is often easier to show directly.
concepts.example: To prove 'if n² is even then n is even', prove instead 'if n is odd then n² is odd': (2k + 1)² = 4k² + 4k + 1, which is odd. Done.

concepts.name: Proof by Exhaustion
concepts.description: A proof that splits a statement into a finite number of cases and checks each one separately. It is used when no single argument covers all situations, and computers can extend it to very many cases.
concepts.example: To show every square ends in 0, 1, 4, 5, 6 or 9, check the 10 possible last digits 0–9: their squares end in 0, 1, 4, 9, 6, 5, 6, 9, 4, 1. All cases covered.

concepts.name: Proposition
concepts.description: A declarative statement that is either true or false, but not both, such as '7 is prime'. Propositions are the basic units combined by logical connectives in propositional logic.
concepts.example: 'Paris is in France' is a proposition (true), and '2 + 2 = 5' is one too (false). 'Close the door!' and 'x > 3' (with x unknown) are not.

concepts.name: Propositional Logic
concepts.description: The formal system for reasoning about propositions combined with connectives such as AND, OR, NOT and IMPLIES, using truth tables and inference rules. It underlies Boolean circuits and SAT solving.
concepts.example: From 'if it rains, the match is cancelled' and 'the match is not cancelled', propositional logic concludes 'it did not rain', a valid pattern called modus tollens.

concepts.name: QR Algorithm
concepts.description: An iterative method for computing all eigenvalues of a matrix by repeatedly factoring A = QR and forming RQ, which converges to a triangular form with the eigenvalues on its diagonal. With shifts it is the standard dense eigensolver.
concepts.example: Take A, factor it as QR, then form the new matrix RQ; repeat. Each step is the same map seen in a new basis, and the matrix gradually becomes triangular with eigenvalues on the diagonal.

concepts.name: QR Decomposition
concepts.description: Factoring a matrix as A = QR, where Q has orthonormal columns and R is upper triangular. It is computed with Gram–Schmidt, Householder or Givens transformations and gives a stable way to solve least squares.
concepts.example: [[3, 0], [4, 5]] factors as Q = [[0.6, −0.8], [0.8, 0.6]] times R = [[5, 4], [0, 3]]. Solving least squares then needs only Rx = Qᵀb, a quick triangular solve.

concepts.name: Quadratic Equation
concepts.description: An equation of the form ax² + bx + c = 0 with a ≠ 0. It has at most two solutions, found by factoring, completing the square or the quadratic formula.
concepts.example: A ball thrown up at 20 m/s has height 20t − 5t². Setting this to 15 gives 5t² − 20t + 15 = 0, with solutions t = 1 and t = 3: on the way up and on the way down.

concepts.name: Quadratic Form
concepts.description: A function of a vector of the form xᵀAx, a homogeneous degree-two polynomial in the vector's entries. Its sign behavior defines positive-definite matrices and it describes curvature in optimization.
concepts.example: With A = [[1, 1], [1, 3]], xᵀAx = x² + 2xy + 3y². At (1, −1) it gives 1 − 2 + 3 = 2, and it stays positive for every nonzero (x, y), so this bowl-shaped form has its minimum at 0.

concepts.name: Quadratic Formula
concepts.description: The formula x = (−b ± √(b² − 4ac)) / 2a giving the solutions of ax² + bx + c = 0. The discriminant b² − 4ac tells whether there are two, one or no real solutions.
concepts.example: For x² − 3x + 2 = 0, a = 1, b = −3, c = 2: discriminant 9 − 8 = 1, so x = (3 ± 1)/2, giving 2 and 1.

concepts.name: Quadratic Function
concepts.description: A function f(x) = ax² + bx + c whose graph is a parabola opening up or down, with a single vertex as its minimum or maximum. It is the simplest model of a curved loss surface.
concepts.example: Revenue from selling at price p with demand 100 − p is R = p(100 − p), a downward parabola peaking at p = 50 with revenue 2500.

concepts.name: Quantifier (Logic)
concepts.description: A logical symbol that specifies how many elements a statement applies to: the universal quantifier ∀ ('for all') and the existential quantifier ∃ ('there exists'). Quantifiers distinguish predicate logic from propositional logic.
concepts.example: 'Every student passed' uses ∀; 'some student got 100%' uses ∃. Negating swaps them: 'not every student passed' means 'some student failed'.

concepts.name: Quotient Rule
concepts.description: The differentiation rule for a ratio of functions: (f/g)' = (f'g − fg')/g². It can be derived from the product rule and the chain rule.
concepts.example: For f(x) = x/(x + 1), the rule gives ((x + 1)·1 − x·1)/(x + 1)² = 1/(x + 1)². At x = 1 the slope is 1/4.

concepts.name: Randomized SVD
concepts.description: An algorithm that approximates the top singular vectors of a large matrix by multiplying it with a random matrix to capture its range, orthonormalizing, and computing an exact SVD of the much smaller projected matrix.
concepts.example: To find the top 10 patterns in a 1-million × 10,000 matrix, multiply it by 20 random vectors; the results already span almost all important directions, and a small SVD of that sketch finishes the job.

concepts.name: Rank (Linear Algebra)
concepts.description: The number of linearly independent rows or columns of a matrix, equal to the dimension of its column space. Rank tells how many independent directions a linear map preserves and whether a system has a unique solution.
concepts.example: [[1, 2], [2, 4]] has rank 1: the second row is twice the first, so it squashes the plane onto a line. [[1, 0], [0, 1]] has rank 2.

concepts.name: Rank–Nullity Theorem
concepts.description: A theorem stating that for a linear map from an n-dimensional space, rank plus nullity equals n: the dimensions of the image and the kernel always add up to the dimension of the input.
concepts.example: Projecting 3D onto the floor: the image is a 2D plane (rank 2) and the vertical line gets crushed to zero (nullity 1). And 2 + 1 = 3, the input dimension.

concepts.name: Rate of Convergence
concepts.description: A measure of how fast an iterative method's error shrinks: linear convergence cuts the error by a constant factor each step, while superlinear and quadratic convergence (as in Newton's method) speed up dramatically.
concepts.example: Bisection halves the error each step (linear: 0.1, 0.05, 0.025, …), while Newton's method squares it (quadratic: 0.1, 0.01, 0.0001, …), doubling the correct digits.

concepts.name: Ratio and Proportion
concepts.description: A ratio compares two quantities by division, such as 3:2; a proportion states that two ratios are equal. They are used for scaling recipes, maps, rates and similar figures.
concepts.example: A recipe uses 3 cups of flour for 2 cups of milk, a 3:2 ratio. To use 6 cups of flour, keep the proportion 3/2 = 6/x, so you need 4 cups of milk.

concepts.name: Lowe's Ratio Test
concepts.description: Lowe's filter for feature matching: a keypoint match is kept only if its nearest descriptor is clearly closer than the second-nearest, typically with a distance ratio below about 0.75. It removes ambiguous matches before geometric verification.
concepts.example: A keypoint's best match is at distance 0.2 and the second best at 0.5: ratio 0.4 < 0.8, so keep it. If the two were 0.3 and 0.32, the match is ambiguous and dropped.

concepts.name: Rational Function
concepts.description: A function that is the ratio of two polynomials, p(x)/q(x). It is undefined where the denominator is zero and often has vertical and horizontal asymptotes.
concepts.example: If 120 km is shared among n drivers, each drives f(n) = 120/n. As n approaches 0 the value blows up, giving a vertical asymptote at n = 0.

concepts.name: Rational Number
concepts.description: Any number that can be written as a fraction p/q of integers with q ≠ 0, such as 3/4 or −2. Rational numbers have terminating or repeating decimal expansions.
concepts.example: 0.75 is rational because it equals 3/4, and 0.333… equals 1/3. But √2 is not rational: no fraction of integers squares to exactly 2.

concepts.name: Rayleigh Quotient
concepts.description: For a symmetric matrix A and nonzero vector x, the ratio xᵀAx / xᵀx. Its maximum and minimum are the largest and smallest eigenvalues, and it is used in eigenvalue algorithms and spectral clustering.
concepts.example: For A = [[2, 0], [0, 5]], x = (1, 0) gives 2 and x = (0, 1) gives 5; x = (1, 1) gives (2 + 5)/2 = 3.5. Every vector lands between the eigenvalues 2 and 5.

concepts.name: Real Analysis
concepts.description: The rigorous study of real numbers, sequences, limits, continuity, differentiation and integration, proving why calculus works. It provides the foundations for measure theory and optimization theory.
concepts.example: Calculus says the sequence 1, 1.4, 1.41, 1.414, … 'approaches' √2; real analysis proves it really converges, and shows why a continuous function on [0, 1] must reach a highest value somewhere.

concepts.name: Real Number
concepts.description: Any value on the continuous number line, including rationals like 1/2 and irrationals like √2 and π. The real numbers have no gaps, which makes limits and calculus possible.
concepts.example: Measure a square tile with side 1 m: its diagonal is √2 ≈ 1.41421… m, a length no fraction can express exactly. The real numbers include such lengths, so every point on a ruler has a number.

concepts.name: Recurrence Relation
concepts.description: An equation defining each term of a sequence from earlier terms, such as Fₙ = Fₙ₋₁ + Fₙ₋₂. Recurrences describe recursive algorithms' running times and dynamic programming.
concepts.example: Start a savings account with 100 and add 10% plus 5 each year: aₙ = 1.1·aₙ₋₁ + 5. Then a₁ = 115, a₂ = 131.5, and every year follows from the one before.

concepts.name: Binary Relation
concepts.description: A binary relation on sets is a set of ordered pairs saying which elements are related, such as 'less than' or 'is a parent of'. Properties like reflexivity, symmetry and transitivity classify relations.
concepts.example: On the set {1, 2, 3}, the relation 'less than' is just the pairs {(1,2), (1,3), (2,3)}. Asking whether 1 < 3 means checking whether (1,3) is in that list.

concepts.name: Reverse-Mode Automatic Differentiation
concepts.description: Automatic differentiation that first evaluates a computation forward, then propagates derivatives backward from the output via vector–Jacobian products. It computes the full gradient of a scalar loss in about one extra pass, as in backpropagation.
concepts.example: For loss = (w·x − y)² with a million weights, compute the loss once forward, then walk backward through each step multiplying local derivatives; one backward pass gives all million partial derivatives at once.

concepts.name: Riemann Integral
concepts.description: The classical definition of the definite integral as the limit of Riemann sums as the partition of the interval becomes infinitely fine. A function is Riemann integrable if this limit exists.
