concepts.example: To find the area under y = x from 0 to 1, use n thin rectangles: their total area is (n+1)/(2n). With 10 strips that is 0.55, with 1000 strips 0.5005, and in the limit exactly 0.5.

concepts.name: Riemann Sum
concepts.description: An approximation of the area under a curve made by splitting an interval into pieces and adding up rectangles whose heights are function values at sample points in each piece.
concepts.example: Estimate the area under y = x² from 0 to 2 with 2 strips of width 1 using right endpoints: heights 1 and 4 give 1·1 + 1·4 = 5, an overestimate of the true area 8/3 ≈ 2.67.

concepts.name: Root-Finding Algorithm
concepts.description: The problem of numerically finding inputs where a function equals zero, and the family of methods that solve it, such as bisection, Newton's method and the secant method.
concepts.example: To find √2, solve x² − 2 = 0. f(1) = −1 and f(2) = 2 have opposite signs, so a root lies between; check 1.5 (f = 0.25), then 1.25, and keep halving the bracket toward 1.414.

concepts.name: Round-Off Error
concepts.description: The error introduced when a real number is stored with finite precision, as in floating-point arithmetic. Such errors can accumulate or be amplified, for example by subtracting nearly equal numbers.
concepts.example: In floating point, 0.1 + 0.2 gives 0.30000000000000004, because 0.1 cannot be stored exactly in binary. Subtracting 1.0000001 − 1.0000000 in single precision can lose most of the meaningful digits.

concepts.name: Row Echelon Form
concepts.description: A staircase-shaped form of a matrix produced by row operations, where each row's leading nonzero entry is to the right of the one above. The reduced form has leading ones with zeros above and below, revealing solutions and rank.
concepts.example: The system x + y = 3, 2x + 3y = 8 becomes rows [1 1 | 3] and [0 1 | 2] after subtracting twice row 1 from row 2. The staircase shows y = 2, then back-substitution gives x = 1.

concepts.name: Rule of Product
concepts.description: The counting principle that if one choice can be made in m ways and a second independent choice in n ways, the pair of choices can be made in m × n ways. It is the basis for counting permutations.
concepts.example: With 3 shirts and 4 pairs of trousers you can make 3 × 4 = 12 outfits. Add 2 pairs of shoes and there are 12 × 2 = 24 complete outfits.

concepts.name: Rule of Sum
concepts.description: The counting principle that if a task can be done in one of m ways or one of n other, non-overlapping ways, there are m + n ways in total. Overlaps require inclusion–exclusion.
concepts.example: A café offers 4 hot drinks and 3 cold drinks, and you pick one drink: there are 4 + 3 = 7 choices, since no drink is both hot and cold.

concepts.name: Runge–Kutta Methods
concepts.description: A family of methods for numerically solving ODEs that take several weighted slope evaluations within each step. The classic fourth-order RK4 is far more accurate than Euler's method for the same step size.
concepts.example: Euler's method uses only the slope at the start of each step, like steering by looking at your feet. RK4 samples the slope four times across the step and averages them, like checking the road ahead before committing.

concepts.name: Saddle Point
concepts.description: A critical point of a function where the slope is zero but which is a minimum along some directions and a maximum along others, like the center of a horse saddle. They are common in high-dimensional loss landscapes.
concepts.example: f(x, y) = x² − y² is flat at (0, 0), but walking along the x-axis that point is a valley bottom, while along the y-axis it is a hilltop, just like the middle of a horse saddle.

concepts.name: Scalar (Mathematics)
concepts.description: A single number, as opposed to a vector or matrix, used to scale vectors. In linear algebra scalars come from the underlying field, usually the real or complex numbers.
concepts.example: In the vector (3, 4), the number 2 is a scalar: 2·(3, 4) = (6, 8) points the same way but is twice as long. A temperature of 20 °C is also a scalar, since it has size but no direction.

concepts.name: Scalar Multiplication
concepts.description: Multiplying a vector or matrix by a single number, which multiplies every entry by that number and stretches, shrinks or flips the vector without changing its line.
concepts.example: Multiply the vector (1, −2) by 3 to get (3, −6), three times as long; multiply by −1 to get (−1, 2), the same length pointing the opposite way along the same line.

concepts.name: Schur Decomposition
concepts.description: Writing any square complex matrix as A = QTQ*, where Q is unitary and T is upper triangular with A's eigenvalues on its diagonal. It is the numerically stable alternative to diagonalization used by eigenvalue algorithms.
concepts.example: Any 3×3 matrix can be rotated, using an orthonormal change of axes, into an upper triangular form whose diagonal lists its 3 eigenvalues. The QR algorithm in numerical libraries computes exactly this form.

concepts.name: Scientific Notation
concepts.description: Writing a number as a coefficient between 1 and 10 times a power of ten, such as 6.02 × 10²³. It makes very large and very small numbers easy to read and compare.
concepts.example: Earth is about 150,000,000 km from the Sun, written 1.5 × 10⁸ km; a bacterium is about 0.000002 m long, written 2 × 10⁻⁶ m. Comparing them means comparing the exponents 8 and −6.

concepts.name: Secant Method
concepts.description: A root-finding method like Newton's method but which replaces the derivative with the slope of the line through the two most recent iterates. It needs no derivatives and converges superlinearly.
concepts.example: To solve x² − 2 = 0 from guesses 1 and 2, draw the line through (1, −1) and (2, 2); it crosses zero at 4/3 ≈ 1.333. Repeat with the two newest points and the guesses close in on 1.414.

concepts.name: Second Derivative Test
concepts.description: A test for classifying a critical point: if the second derivative is positive the point is a local minimum, if negative a local maximum, and if zero the test is inconclusive. Its multivariable form uses the Hessian.
concepts.example: f(x) = x³ − 3x has critical points at x = ±1. f''(x) = 6x gives f''(1) = 6 > 0, so x = 1 is a local minimum, and f''(−1) = −6 < 0, so x = −1 is a local maximum.

concepts.name: Series (Mathematics)
concepts.description: The sum of the terms of an infinite sequence, defined as the limit of its partial sums. A series converges if that limit exists, as with 1 + 1/2 + 1/4 + … = 2.
concepts.example: Walk half the way to a wall, then half the remaining distance, and so on: 1/2 + 1/4 + 1/8 + … The partial sums 0.5, 0.75, 0.875, … get as close to 1 as you like, so the series equals 1.

concepts.name: Set-Builder Notation
concepts.description: A notation that describes a set by a property its members satisfy, such as {x ∈ ℝ : x > 0} for the positive reals. It is the standard way to define sets precisely.
concepts.example: {n ∈ ℕ : n is even and n < 10} reads 'all natural numbers n such that n is even and below 10', which is {0, 2, 4, 6, 8} if ℕ includes 0. The rule replaces listing every element.

concepts.name: Complement (Set Theory)
concepts.description: The complement of a set A is everything in the universe not in A; the relative complement A \ B (set difference) is the elements of A not in B. Complements appear in De Morgan's laws and probability.
concepts.example: If the universe is the days of the week and A = the weekend {Sat, Sun}, then the complement of A is the five weekdays. If B = {Sun, Mon}, then A \ B = {Sat}.

concepts.name: Set (Mathematics)
concepts.description: A well-defined collection of distinct objects, called elements, such as {1, 2, 3}. Sets are the basic building blocks from which most of mathematics is constructed.
concepts.example: Your set of house keys {front door, back door, garage} is a set: order does not matter and listing the garage key twice does not create a fourth key. {1, 2, 3} and {3, 2, 1} are the same set.

concepts.name: Set Theory
concepts.description: The branch of mathematics studying sets and operations on them—union, intersection, complements, functions, relations and cardinality—and serving as the foundation for the rest of mathematics.
concepts.example: Using only sets you can build numbers: 0 = {}, 1 = {0}, 2 = {0, 1}, and so on. From there, pairs, functions and even the real numbers can all be defined as sets.

concepts.name: Sherman–Morrison Formula
concepts.description: A formula for the inverse of a matrix after a rank-one update, (A + uvᵀ)⁻¹, in terms of A⁻¹, avoiding a full re-inversion. The Woodbury identity generalizes it to rank-k updates and is used in quasi-Newton methods and Gaussian processes.
concepts.example: You already know the inverse of a 1000×1000 matrix and one customer's data adds a rank-one change. Instead of re-inverting from scratch (about 10⁹ operations), the formula updates the inverse in about 10⁶.

concepts.name: Matrix Similarity
concepts.description: Two square matrices A and B are similar if B = P⁻¹AP for some invertible P, meaning they represent the same linear map in different bases. Similar matrices share eigenvalues, determinant and trace.
concepts.example: The map 'stretch by 2 along the line y = x' looks messy in standard coordinates, but in a basis aligned with that line it is just diag(2, 1). Both matrices describe the same transformation, so they are similar.

concepts.name: Simpson's Rule
concepts.description: A numerical integration rule that approximates the integrand on each pair of subintervals with a parabola through three points, giving much higher accuracy than the trapezoidal rule for smooth functions.
concepts.example: To integrate x² from 0 to 2, Simpson's rule uses x = 0, 1, 2: (2/6)(0 + 4·1 + 4) = 8/3, exactly right, because a parabola fits x² perfectly. The trapezoidal rule with the same points gives 3.

concepts.name: Singular Matrix
concepts.description: A square matrix with no inverse, equivalently one with determinant zero. It collapses some nonzero vector to zero, so Ax = b has either no solution or infinitely many.
concepts.example: The matrix [[1, 2], [2, 4]] has determinant 1·4 − 2·2 = 0, since its second row is twice the first. It squashes the whole plane onto a line, so you cannot undo it, and x + 2y = 1, 2x + 4y = 3 has no solution.

concepts.name: Singular Value
concepts.description: A non-negative number describing how much a matrix stretches space along one of its principal directions; the singular values are the square roots of the eigenvalues of AᵀA.
concepts.example: A matrix that turns the unit circle into an ellipse with half-axes 3 and 1 has singular values 3 and 1: it stretches space by at most 3 in one direction and by 1 in the perpendicular one.

concepts.name: Singular Value Decomposition
concepts.description: Factoring any matrix as A = UΣVᵀ, with orthogonal U and V and a diagonal Σ of singular values. It reveals a matrix's rank and principal directions and powers PCA, compression and recommender systems.
concepts.example: Any matrix acts like three simple moves: rotate (Vᵀ), stretch along the axes (Σ), rotate again (U). Keeping only the largest few stretches of a photo's pixel matrix gives a good compressed version.

concepts.name: Sparse Matrix
concepts.description: A matrix in which most entries are zero, stored efficiently by recording only the nonzero values and their positions (e.g., CSR format). Sparse methods make huge graphs and text features tractable.
concepts.example: A friendship matrix for 1 million users has 10¹² cells, but each person has maybe 200 friends. Storing only the 2 × 10⁸ nonzero entries and their positions makes it fit on a laptop.

concepts.name: Spectral Radius
concepts.description: The largest absolute value among a square matrix's eigenvalues. It determines whether repeated multiplication by the matrix blows up or decays, and thus the convergence of iterative methods and RNN dynamics.
concepts.example: If a matrix has eigenvalues 0.5 and −0.9, its spectral radius is 0.9 < 1, so multiplying a vector by it over and over shrinks it toward zero. With an eigenvalue of 1.2 the vector would eventually blow up.

concepts.name: Spectral Theorem
concepts.description: A theorem stating that every real symmetric (or complex Hermitian) matrix can be diagonalized by an orthogonal (unitary) matrix, with real eigenvalues and an orthonormal basis of eigenvectors.
concepts.example: A covariance matrix is symmetric, so the theorem guarantees perpendicular axes along which it just stretches by real amounts. These axes are the principal components used in PCA.

concepts.name: Spline Interpolation
concepts.description: Interpolating data with piecewise polynomials, typically cubics, joined smoothly at the data points so the curve has continuous first and second derivatives. It avoids the wild oscillations of a single high-degree polynomial.
concepts.example: Draftsmen once bent a thin flexible strip (a spline) through pegs to draw smooth ship hulls. Cubic splines do the same: one cubic between each pair of points, joined with no kinks or jumps in curvature.

concepts.name: Square Root
concepts.description: A number that, multiplied by itself, gives a given number: √9 = 3 because 3 × 3 = 9. Every positive number has a positive and a negative square root.
concepts.example: A square garden with area 49 m² has sides of √49 = 7 m. A 50 m² square needs sides of about 7.07 m, since 7.07 × 7.07 ≈ 50.

concepts.name: Standard Basis
concepts.description: The basis of ℝⁿ made of unit vectors e₁, …, eₙ, each with a single 1 and zeros elsewhere. A vector's coordinates in the standard basis are just its entries.
concepts.example: In 3D, e₁ = (1, 0, 0), e₂ = (0, 1, 0), e₃ = (0, 0, 1) point along the x, y and z axes. The vector (4, −2, 5) is just 4e₁ − 2e₂ + 5e₃.

concepts.name: Stars and Bars (Combinatorics)
concepts.description: A counting technique for distributing n identical items into k distinct groups by arranging n stars and k − 1 bars in a row, giving C(n + k − 1, k − 1) ways.
concepts.example: Share 5 identical sweets among 3 children: arrange 5 stars and 2 bars, like ★★|★|★★ for 2, 1, 2. The count is the number of ways to place 2 bars among 7 spots, C(7, 2) = 21.

concepts.name: Heaviside Step Function
concepts.description: The Heaviside step function outputs 0 for negative inputs and 1 for positive inputs. It models on/off switching and was the threshold activation of the original perceptron.
concepts.example: A light switch is a step function: below the threshold it outputs 0 (off), above it 1 (on). A perceptron fires 1 if its weighted input is positive and 0 otherwise.

concepts.name: Stirling Numbers
concepts.description: Two families of numbers in combinatorics: Stirling numbers of the second kind count ways to partition n items into k non-empty subsets, and those of the first kind count permutations of n items with k cycles.
concepts.example: Splitting 4 people {A, B, C, D} into 2 non-empty teams can be done 7 ways (4 with a solo player, 3 as two pairs), so S(4, 2) = 7.

concepts.name: Stirling's Approximation
concepts.description: An approximation for large factorials: n! ≈ √(2πn)(n/e)ⁿ, or equivalently ln n! ≈ n ln n − n. It is used in combinatorics, entropy calculations and probability.
concepts.example: 10! = 3,628,800, and √(2π·10)·(10/e)¹⁰ ≈ 3,598,696, within 1%. For 100! the error drops below 0.1%, and the formula is far easier to work with than the full product.

concepts.name: Stokes' Theorem
concepts.description: A theorem relating the integral of a vector field's curl over a surface to the line integral of the field around the surface's boundary. Green's theorem and the fundamental theorem of calculus are special cases.
concepts.example: Measure how much a wind field swirls across a butterfly net's mesh by adding up the curl over the net, or simply walk around the rim adding up wind along the path. Stokes says both give the same number.

concepts.name: Strong Induction
concepts.description: A variant of mathematical induction where the step assumes the statement holds for all values up to n, not just n, before proving it for n + 1. It suits recursive structures like prime factorizations.
concepts.example: Every integer ≥ 2 is a product of primes: take n; if it is prime you're done, otherwise n = a·b with smaller a, b. You assume all smaller numbers already factor, not just n − 1.

concepts.name: Subsequence
concepts.description: A sequence obtained from another by deleting some terms without changing the order of the rest. Subsequences are key in analysis (Bolzano–Weierstrass) and algorithms (longest common subsequence).
concepts.example: From 3, 1, 4, 1, 5, 9, 2, 6, keeping 1, 4, 5, 9 gives a subsequence (order kept). The longest increasing subsequence of the whole list has length 4, such as 1, 4, 5, 9.

concepts.name: Subset
concepts.description: A set A is a subset of B if every element of A is also in B, written A ⊆ B. Every set is a subset of itself and the empty set is a subset of every set.
concepts.example: The vowels {a, e, i, o, u} form a subset of the alphabet, since every vowel is a letter. {a, 3} is not a subset, because 3 is not a letter.

concepts.name: Summation Notation
concepts.description: The capital-sigma notation Σ for writing the sum of many terms compactly, with an index variable running between lower and upper limits, as in Σᵢ₌₁ⁿ i = n(n+1)/2.
concepts.example: Σᵢ₌₁⁴ i² means 1² + 2² + 3² + 4² = 1 + 4 + 9 + 16 = 30. The index i starts at 1 below the Σ and stops at 4 above it.

concepts.name: Infimum and Supremum
concepts.description: The supremum of a set of reals is its least upper bound and the infimum its greatest lower bound. Unlike a maximum or minimum, they exist for every bounded non-empty set even if not attained.
concepts.example: The set {0.9, 0.99, 0.999, …} never contains 1, so it has no maximum, but 1 is its least upper bound, so its supremum is 1. Its infimum, 0.9, is actually in the set.

concepts.name: Surjective Function
concepts.description: A function in which every element of the codomain is the output of at least one input, so its range covers the whole target set. A function that is both surjective and injective is a bijection.
concepts.example: Assign each of 30 students to one of 5 project groups so that no group is empty: every group is hit, so the assignment is surjective. If one group gets nobody, it is not.

concepts.name: Symmetric Matrix
concepts.description: A square matrix that equals its own transpose, so the entry in row i, column j equals the one in row j, column i. Covariance matrices and Hessians are symmetric and have real eigenvalues.
concepts.example: A distance table between cities is symmetric: Paris→Lyon is 465 km and Lyon→Paris is also 465 km, so entry (i, j) equals entry (j, i) and the table mirrors across its diagonal.

concepts.name: System of Linear Equations
concepts.description: A set of linear equations sharing the same unknowns, solved simultaneously. It can be written as Ax = b and may have one, infinitely many or no solutions.
concepts.example: Two apples and one banana cost 5, and one apple and one banana cost 3. Subtracting gives one apple = 2, so one banana = 1; both equations are satisfied at once.

concepts.name: Tautology (Logic)
concepts.description: A logical formula that is true under every possible assignment of truth values to its variables, such as P ∨ ¬P. Valid argument forms correspond to tautologies.
concepts.example: 'It is raining or it is not raining' is true whatever the weather, so P ∨ ¬P is a tautology. 'If P and Q, then P' is another: every row of its truth table comes out true.

concepts.name: Taylor Series
concepts.description: The representation of a smooth function as an infinite sum of terms built from its derivatives at one point: f(a) + f'(a)(x − a) + f''(a)(x − a)²/2! + …. Truncations give polynomial approximations.
concepts.example: eˣ = 1 + x + x²/2 + x³/6 + … Plugging in x = 0.1 with three terms gives 1.105, matching the true value 1.10517 to four digits. Near the centre, a few terms already approximate the function well.

concepts.name: Taylor's Theorem
concepts.description: A theorem stating that a sufficiently smooth function equals its degree-n Taylor polynomial plus a remainder term, and giving bounds on that remainder. It quantifies the error of polynomial approximations.
concepts.example: Approximate sin(0.5) by 0.5 − 0.5³/6 ≈ 0.4792. Taylor's theorem says the error is at most 0.5⁵/120 ≈ 0.00026, and indeed sin(0.5) = 0.4794.

concepts.name: Tensor (Deep Learning)
concepts.description: A multidimensional array of numbers that generalizes scalars, vectors and matrices to any number of axes; tensors are the basic data structure that deep learning frameworks store and compute with.
concepts.example: A grayscale photo is a matrix (height × width); a colour photo adds a channel axis (height × width × 3); a batch of 32 colour photos is a 4-axis tensor of shape 32 × 224 × 224 × 3.

concepts.name: Tensor Decomposition
concepts.description: Methods such as CP and Tucker decomposition that factor a multi-way array into sums or products of simpler low-rank pieces, generalizing matrix factorizations like SVD to higher-order tensors.
concepts.example: A users × movies × weekdays rating tensor can be approximated by a few patterns like 'action fans watch on weekends', each an outer product of a user vector, a movie vector and a day vector.

concepts.name: Toeplitz Matrix
concepts.description: A matrix in which every descending diagonal from left to right is constant, so each entry depends only on the difference of its row and column indices; it represents convolution and stationary covariances.
concepts.example: [[a, b, c], [d, a, b], [e, d, a]] is Toeplitz: each diagonal is constant. Smoothing a signal with weights (1, 2, 1) is the same as multiplying by a Toeplitz matrix whose diagonals hold 1, 2, 1.

concepts.name: Topological Sorting
concepts.description: An ordering of the vertices of a directed acyclic graph such that every edge points from an earlier vertex to a later one; used for scheduling tasks with dependencies.
concepts.example: To get dressed, socks must come before shoes and underwear before trousers before shoes. One valid order is underwear, socks, trousers, shirt, shoes; every rule's arrow points forward.

concepts.name: Total Derivative
concepts.description: The best linear approximation of a multivariable function at a point, accounting for how the output changes when all inputs vary together; in coordinates it is given by the Jacobian matrix.
concepts.example: Area A = w·h. At w = 3, h = 2, nudging width by 0.1 and height by 0.05 changes area by about 2·0.1 + 3·0.05 = 0.35, combining both effects in one linear estimate.

concepts.name: Trace (Linear Algebra)
concepts.description: The sum of the diagonal entries of a square matrix, which also equals the sum of its eigenvalues; it is invariant under change of basis and appears throughout matrix calculus.
concepts.example: For [[2, 7], [1, 5]] the trace is 2 + 5 = 7. Its eigenvalues, roughly 6.54 and 0.46, also add to 7, as they always must.

concepts.name: Trace Trick
concepts.description: The technique of rewriting a scalar such as x^T A x as the trace of a matrix product and using the cyclic property tr(ABC)=tr(CAB) to simplify derivations, especially in matrix calculus and Gaussian likelihoods.
concepts.example: xᵀAx is a 1×1 number, so it equals its trace, and tr(xᵀAx) = tr(Axxᵀ). Averaging over data then gives E[xᵀAx] = tr(A·E[xxᵀ]), which simplifies Gaussian likelihoods.

concepts.name: Transpose
concepts.description: The operation that flips a matrix over its main diagonal, turning rows into columns, so entry (i, j) becomes entry (j, i); it is used everywhere in linear algebra and ML formulas.
concepts.example: A 2×3 table of [[1, 2, 3], [4, 5, 6]] transposes to the 3×2 table [[1, 4], [2, 5], [3, 6]]: the first row becomes the first column.

concepts.name: Trapezoidal Rule
concepts.description: A numerical integration method that approximates the area under a curve by splitting the interval into pieces and summing the areas of trapezoids formed by straight lines between sample points.
concepts.example: For x² from 0 to 2 with one step of width 1, connect (0,0)–(1,1)–(2,4) with straight lines: areas 0.5 and 2.5 give 3, close to the true 8/3 ≈ 2.67. More steps shrink the error.

concepts.name: Tree (Graph Theory)
concepts.description: A connected undirected graph with no cycles; a tree with n vertices has exactly n-1 edges and a unique path between any two vertices, and trees underlie hierarchies and search structures.
concepts.example: A family tree or a company org chart with 10 people has exactly 9 'reports to' links and no loops, so there is just one chain of command between any two people.

concepts.name: Triangle Inequality
concepts.description: The rule that the length of one side of a triangle is at most the sum of the other two; for any norm or distance, d(x, z) <= d(x, y) + d(y, z), a defining property of metrics.
concepts.example: Walking from home to the shop is 3 km, and shop to school is 4 km, so home to school directly can be at most 7 km. A detour never makes the trip shorter.

concepts.name: Triangular Matrix
concepts.description: A square matrix whose entries are all zero either above (lower triangular) or below (upper triangular) the main diagonal; such systems are solved easily by forward or back substitution.
concepts.example: Solve [[2, 0], [3, 1]]·(x, y) = (4, 7): the first row gives 2x = 4 so x = 2, then 3·2 + y = 7 gives y = 1. Each row reveals one more unknown.

concepts.name: Truncated SVD
concepts.description: A low-rank approximation that keeps only the top k singular values and vectors of a matrix; it is used for dimensionality reduction and, on term-document matrices, as latent semantic analysis.
concepts.example: A 1000×1000 photo matrix needs a million numbers; keeping the top 50 singular values and vectors needs about 100,000 and still looks almost the same, because most energy lies in the top components.

concepts.name: Truncation Error
concepts.description: The error introduced when an infinite mathematical process, like a Taylor series or a limit, is cut off after finitely many terms or steps in a numerical method.
concepts.example: Approximating eˣ by 1 + x drops the x²/2 term and beyond: at x = 0.1 that gives 1.1 instead of 1.10517, an error of about 0.005 caused by cutting the series short, not by rounding.

concepts.name: Truth Table
concepts.description: A table listing every combination of truth values for the inputs of a logical formula together with the resulting output, used to evaluate and compare propositional statements.
concepts.example: For P AND Q, list the four cases: TT → T, TF → F, FT → F, FF → F. Comparing tables shows that NOT (P AND Q) matches (NOT P) OR (NOT Q) in every row.

concepts.name: Uncountable Set
concepts.description: An infinite set that cannot be put into one-to-one correspondence with the natural numbers, such as the real numbers, as shown by Cantor's diagonal argument.
concepts.example: You can number the fractions in a list, but any list of real numbers between 0 and 1 misses one: change the 1st digit of the 1st number, the 2nd digit of the 2nd, and so on, to build a number not on the list.

concepts.name: Uniform Continuity
concepts.description: A stronger form of continuity where a single tolerance delta works for every point of the domain at once, so how close outputs are depends only on how close inputs are, not on location.
concepts.example: f(x) = 2x is uniformly continuous: inputs within 0.01 always give outputs within 0.02, wherever you are. f(x) = 1/x on (0, 1) is not, since near 0 tiny input changes cause huge jumps.

concepts.name: Uniform Convergence
concepts.description: A sequence of functions converges uniformly if the maximum gap between the functions and the limit goes to zero across the whole domain, unlike pointwise convergence, which only works point by point.
concepts.example: fₙ(x) = x/n on [0, 1] converges uniformly to 0, since the biggest gap is 1/n. But xⁿ on [0, 1) converges to 0 only pointwise: near x = 1 there is always a point where xⁿ is still close to 1.

concepts.name: Union (Set Theory)
concepts.description: The union of sets A and B is the set of all elements that belong to A, to B, or to both, written A ∪ B; it is a basic operation of set theory and probability.
concepts.example: If A = {students who play football} = {Ann, Ben} and B = {students who play chess} = {Ben, Cara}, then A ∪ B = {Ann, Ben, Cara}; Ben appears only once.

concepts.name: Unit Vector
concepts.description: A vector whose length (norm) is exactly one, often obtained by dividing a nonzero vector by its norm, so that it encodes direction only.
concepts.example: The vector (3, 4) has length 5; dividing by 5 gives (0.6, 0.8), length 1, pointing the same way. It says 'which direction' without saying 'how far'.

concepts.name: Unitary Matrix
concepts.description: A complex square matrix whose conjugate transpose is its inverse, so it preserves lengths and angles; it is the complex analogue of an orthogonal matrix.
concepts.example: Multiplying a complex vector by the matrix (1/√2)[[1, 1], [1, −1]] or by a diagonal of phases like diag(i, −1) changes it but keeps its length the same, the way rotations do in real space.

concepts.name: Variable (Mathematics)
concepts.description: A symbol, usually a letter such as x, that stands for a number or other quantity that can change or is unknown, letting us write general rules and equations.
concepts.example: In 'price = 3 × n' for buying n notebooks, n is a variable: n = 2 gives 6 and n = 5 gives 15. One rule covers every possible order.

concepts.name: Vector
concepts.description: A quantity with magnitude and direction, or more generally an ordered list of numbers; vectors represent points, directions and data features in geometry, physics and machine learning.
concepts.example: 'Walk 3 blocks east and 4 blocks north' is the vector (3, 4): its length is 5 blocks and it points north-east-ish. A house with 3 bedrooms and 120 m² can be the feature vector (3, 120).

concepts.name: Vector Addition
concepts.description: Adding two vectors component by component, or geometrically placing them tip to tail; the result is the diagonal of the parallelogram they span.
concepts.example: Walk (3, 1) then (1, 2) and you end at (4, 3), the same as walking (4, 3) directly. Placing the arrows tip to tail shows the total movement.

concepts.name: Vector Field
concepts.description: A function that assigns a vector to every point in space, such as wind velocity on a map or the gradient of a function, used in physics and multivariable calculus.
concepts.example: A weather map with an arrow at every city showing wind speed and direction is a vector field. So is a slope map of a hill, where each arrow points uphill.

concepts.name: Vector–Jacobian Product
concepts.description: The product of a row vector with a Jacobian matrix, computed without forming the Jacobian; it is the basic operation of reverse-mode automatic differentiation and backpropagation.
concepts.example: For a layer with 1000 inputs and 1000 outputs, the Jacobian has a million entries. Backprop only needs gradient-row-vector times Jacobian, which for y = Wx is just gᵀW, never forming the full matrix.

concepts.name: Norm (Mathematics)
concepts.description: A function that measures the length or size of a vector, such as the Euclidean (L2) norm or the sum of absolute values (L1 norm); norms are used for distances and regularization.
concepts.example: For (3, −4), the L2 norm is √(9 + 16) = 5, the straight-line length; the L1 norm is 3 + 4 = 7, the distance walking along a city grid.

concepts.name: Vector Projection
concepts.description: The component of one vector that lies along another, found by scaling the second vector by their dot product divided by its squared length; it is the basis of least squares and Gram-Schmidt.
concepts.example: Project a = (2, 3) onto b = (1, 0): a·b / ‖b‖² = 2, so the projection is (2, 0), the shadow of a on the x-axis when light shines straight down.

concepts.name: Vector Space
concepts.description: A set of objects called vectors that can be added and scaled by numbers while obeying rules like associativity and distributivity; it is the central structure of linear algebra.
concepts.example: All lists of 3 numbers form a vector space: (1, 2, 3) + (0, 1, 1) = (1, 3, 4) and 2·(1, 2, 3) = (2, 4, 6) stay in the set. Polynomials of degree ≤ 2 form one too.

concepts.name: Venn Diagram
concepts.description: A diagram of overlapping circles that shows the relationships between sets, such as their unions, intersections and complements, often used to reason about probabilities.
concepts.example: Draw one circle for 'likes tea' and one for 'likes coffee'. People who like both sit in the overlap, those who like neither sit outside both circles, and counts in each region add up to the class size.

concepts.name: Vertex and Edge
concepts.description: The building blocks of a graph: vertices (nodes) are the objects and edges are the connections between pairs of them, possibly directed or weighted.
concepts.example: In a metro map, stations are vertices and the track segments linking them are edges. In a social network, people are vertices and friendships are edges.

concepts.name: Stone–Weierstrass Theorem
concepts.description: The theorem that every continuous function on a closed interval can be uniformly approximated as closely as desired by polynomials; the Stone version extends it to general algebras of functions on compact spaces.
concepts.example: However wiggly a continuous curve on [0, 1] is, say |x − 0.5|, some polynomial stays within 0.001 of it everywhere on the interval. Bernstein polynomials give an explicit construction.

concepts.name: Zero Matrix
concepts.description: A matrix whose entries are all zero; it is the additive identity for matrix addition, so adding it to any matrix of the same size leaves that matrix unchanged.
concepts.example: Adding [[0, 0], [0, 0]] to [[3, 1], [2, 5]] leaves it unchanged, just as adding 0 to a number does. Multiplying any matrix by the zero matrix gives zero.

concepts.name: Zermelo–Fraenkel Set Theory
concepts.description: The standard axiomatic foundation of mathematics: the Zermelo-Fraenkel axioms plus the axiom of choice, which specify which sets exist and how they can be built.
concepts.example: ZFC's axioms say things like 'two sets with the same elements are equal' and 'the set of all subsets of a set exists'. From such rules alone one can construct numbers, functions and calculus.

concepts.name: Activation Patching
concepts.description: An interpretability technique that replaces a model's internal activations from one input with those from another to find which components causally affect the output.
concepts.example: Run a model on 'The Eiffel Tower is in' (answer Paris) and on 'The Colosseum is in' (answer Rome). Copy one layer's activation from the first run into the second; if the output flips to Paris, that layer carries the location fact.

concepts.name: Adversarial Debiasing
concepts.description: A fairness technique that trains a predictor alongside an adversary trying to predict the sensitive attribute from its outputs, penalizing the predictor when the adversary succeeds.
concepts.example: A loan model predicts approval while a second network tries to guess each applicant's gender from that prediction. The loan model is rewarded for accuracy and penalized whenever the guesser succeeds, so it learns to hide gender information.

concepts.name: Adversarial Machine Learning
concepts.description: The study of attacks that manipulate ML models through crafted inputs, poisoned data or extraction, and of defenses that make models robust to them.
concepts.example: Spammers misspell words to slip past filters, attackers plant poisoned images in scraped training data, and others query an API repeatedly to copy a model. The field studies such attacks and how to defend against them.

concepts.name: Adversarial Patch
concepts.description: A visible, localized pattern, such as a printed sticker, that causes a model to misclassify any image it appears in; it works in the physical world.
concepts.example: Researchers printed a small psychedelic sticker that, placed next to a banana, made an image classifier confidently say 'toaster'. It works on any photo and in the real world, unlike invisible pixel noise.

concepts.name: Agnostic PAC Learning
concepts.description: An extension of PAC learning where no hypothesis is assumed to be perfect; the learner must get close to the best achievable error in the hypothesis class.
concepts.example: Even the best linear classifier on noisy spam data might still make 5% errors. Agnostic PAC learning asks only for a learner that gets within, say, 1% of that best 5% with high probability, not zero error.

concepts.name: AI Governance
concepts.description: The policies, laws, standards and institutions that guide how AI is developed and deployed, aiming to manage its risks and benefits.
concepts.example: Like aviation has licensing, safety audits and accident investigators, AI governance builds equivalents: laws such as the EU AI Act, standards bodies, model audits and reporting rules for major incidents.

concepts.name: AI Safety
concepts.description: The field working to ensure AI systems behave as intended and do not cause harm, covering robustness, alignment, interpretability and control.
concepts.example: A cleaning robot rewarded for 'no visible mess' might simply cover the mess up. AI safety works on making systems pursue what we actually mean, behave reliably in new situations, and remain under human control.

concepts.name: AI Safety via Debate
concepts.description: A scalable oversight proposal where two AI agents argue opposite sides of a question and a human judge picks the winner, aiming to make honest answers easier to verify.
concepts.example: A judge cannot check a 100-page proof, but if one AI claims it is valid and another must point to the single flawed step, the judge only needs to check that one step to decide who is right.

concepts.name: AI Fairness 360
concepts.description: AI Fairness 360: an IBM open-source toolkit with metrics to detect bias in datasets and models and algorithms to mitigate it before, during or after training.
concepts.example: Load a hiring dataset into AIF360, compute disparate impact between groups (say 0.7), apply its Reweighing pre-processor, retrain, and re-measure to see whether the ratio moves closer to 1.

concepts.name: Aleatoric Uncertainty
concepts.description: Uncertainty caused by inherent randomness or noise in the data itself, which cannot be reduced by collecting more data or using a better model.
concepts.example: Predicting a fair coin flip has 50% uncertainty no matter how much data you collect or how good your model is. Blurry medical images whose true label is genuinely ambiguous carry the same kind of irreducible uncertainty.

concepts.name: Algorithmic Fairness
concepts.description: The study of how to define, measure and ensure that ML models do not treat individuals or groups unjustly, e.g. by race or gender.
concepts.example: A recidivism score could be equally accurate overall yet wrongly flag one group as high-risk twice as often. Fairness research defines such disparities, measures them and designs ways to reduce them.

concepts.name: Algorithmic Stability
concepts.description: A property of a learning algorithm whereby changing one training example only slightly changes its output; stable algorithms provably generalize well.
concepts.example: Ridge regression on 1000 points barely changes if you swap one point, so its training error is a reliable guide to test error. A 1-nearest-neighbour rule can flip predictions from one swap, so it is less stable.

concepts.name: Approximation-Estimation Tradeoff
concepts.description: The decomposition of excess risk into approximation error, from the hypothesis class missing the best predictor, and estimation error, from learning with finite data.
concepts.example: Fitting a line to curved data has high approximation error (lines cannot bend); fitting a degree-20 polynomial to 30 points has high estimation error (it chases noise). The best class sits in between.

concepts.name: Attribute Inference Attack
concepts.description: A privacy attack that uses a model's outputs or released data to infer sensitive attributes of individuals, such as health status, that were not directly revealed.
concepts.example: A fitness app publishes a model trained on user data. An attacker who knows someone's age, weight and step count queries it with each possible value of a hidden field, such as diabetes yes or no, and picks the one the model finds most likely.

concepts.name: Backdoor Attack
concepts.description: An attack where a model is trained, often via poisoned data, to behave normally except when a secret trigger appears in the input, causing attacker-chosen output.
concepts.example: Poison 1% of a traffic-sign dataset by adding a small yellow sticker to stop signs and relabelling them 'speed limit'. The model works normally, but any stop sign with that sticker gets misread.

concepts.name: Benign Overfitting
concepts.description: The phenomenon where heavily overparameterized models perfectly fit noisy training data yet still generalize well, contradicting classical intuitions about overfitting.
concepts.example: A huge neural network can memorize a training set with 10% wrong labels, reaching zero training error, yet still score well on new data, because the extra capacity absorbs noise in harmless directions.

concepts.name: Betweenness Centrality
concepts.description: A node importance measure equal to the fraction of shortest paths between other pairs of nodes that pass through it, highlighting bridges and brokers.
concepts.example: In two friend groups linked only through Maria, nearly every shortest path from one group to the other goes through her, so she has very high betweenness even if she has few friends.

concepts.name: Bias Mitigation
concepts.description: Techniques for reducing unfair bias in ML systems, applied to the data before training, to the learning objective during training, or to model outputs afterward.
concepts.example: For a hiring model, you could rebalance the training data (pre-processing), add a fairness penalty to the loss (in-processing), or set different score cut-offs per group afterward (post-processing).

concepts.name: Black-Box Model
concepts.description: A model whose internal workings are too complex or opaque for humans to understand directly, so its predictions are seen only through inputs and outputs, like deep networks.
concepts.example: A deep network with 100 million weights approves or rejects a loan, but no one can read off why. You see only what goes in and what comes out, like a vending machine with a sealed casing.

concepts.name: Weak Learnability
concepts.description: The theory of weak learnability, showing that learners only slightly better than chance can be combined to form an arbitrarily accurate strong learner, the basis of boosting.
concepts.example: A rule that predicts rain correctly 55% of the time is barely useful, but combining hundreds of such rules, each trained to fix the last ones' mistakes, can reach 99% accuracy. Boosting theory proves this is always possible.

concepts.name: Calibration Within Groups
concepts.description: A fairness criterion requiring that among people given a predicted score s, the actual outcome rate is s in every demographic group.
concepts.example: Among applicants scored 0.7 for repaying a loan, 70% of women and 70% of men should actually repay. If only 50% of one group repays at that score, the score means different things for different groups.

concepts.name: Carlini–Wagner Attack
concepts.description: A strong optimization-based adversarial attack that finds minimal perturbations by minimizing distance plus a margin loss on logits; it defeated many proposed defenses.
concepts.example: To make a panda image classify as 'gibbon', C&W solves an optimization: minimize the size of the pixel change plus a penalty that stays positive until the gibbon logit beats every other logit by a set margin.

concepts.name: Causal Discovery
concepts.description: The task of inferring the causal graph among variables from data, mainly observational, using conditional independence tests, scores or functional assumptions.
concepts.example: If smoking and yellow fingers are correlated but become independent once you condition on tar exposure, causal discovery infers a structure like smoking → tar → yellow fingers rather than a direct link.

concepts.name: Centrality
concepts.description: Measures of how important a node is in a network; the simplest, degree centrality, counts a node's connections, while others use paths or eigenvectors.
concepts.example: In an office email network, the person who emails the most colleagues has the highest degree centrality, while someone who links separate teams may score higher on other measures like betweenness.

concepts.name: Certified Robustness
concepts.description: A guarantee, proven mathematically, that a model's prediction cannot change for any input perturbation within a given radius, rather than just surviving known attacks.
concepts.example: Randomized smoothing can prove that no change to a stop-sign image with L2 size below 0.5 can alter the prediction. Unlike passing tests against known attacks, this holds for every possible perturbation in that ball.

concepts.name: ChebNet
concepts.description: A spectral graph neural network that approximates graph convolution filters with Chebyshev polynomials of the Laplacian, giving localized filters without eigendecomposition.
concepts.example: Instead of computing all eigenvectors of a million-node graph's Laplacian, ChebNet applies a degree-3 polynomial of the Laplacian, which only mixes information from nodes up to 3 hops away.

concepts.name: Cheeger's Inequality
concepts.description: A result bounding the graph's Cheeger constant (how well it can be cut into balanced parts) by the second-smallest Laplacian eigenvalue, linking spectra to clustering.
concepts.example: Two dense clusters joined by a single bridge edge are easy to cut cheaply, and correspondingly the Laplacian's second-smallest eigenvalue is tiny. A well-knit graph has a large second eigenvalue and no cheap cut.

concepts.name: Circuits
concepts.description: In mechanistic interpretability, subnetworks of features and weights inside a neural network that together implement an identifiable algorithm or behaviour.
concepts.example: In a vision network, researchers traced a car detector built from window, body and wheel detectors in an earlier layer, wired with weights that check the windows are on top and the wheels at the bottom.

concepts.name: Closeness Centrality
concepts.description: A node importance measure equal to the inverse of its average shortest-path distance to all other nodes, so central nodes can reach others quickly.
concepts.example: For a fire station location in a road network, pick the node whose average shortest distance to all other nodes is smallest; that node has the highest closeness centrality.

concepts.name: Cluster-GCN
concepts.description: A scalable training method for graph convolutional networks that partitions the graph into clusters and trains on subgraphs from a few clusters per batch, reducing memory.
concepts.example: A graph with 2 million nodes won't fit on a GPU. Cluster-GCN first splits it into 1500 dense clusters, then each batch trains on the subgraph formed by a few clusters, keeping most edges.

concepts.name: Clustering Coefficient
concepts.description: A measure of how much a node's neighbours are connected to each other, the fraction of possible triangles that exist; high in social networks.
concepts.example: If Ana has 4 friends, there are 6 possible friendships among them. If 3 exist, her clustering coefficient is 3/6 = 0.5, meaning half her friends know each other.

concepts.name: Community Detection
concepts.description: The problem of finding groups of nodes in a network that are densely connected internally and sparsely connected to the rest, such as friend circles.
concepts.example: In a school's social network, community detection might find clusters matching the football team, the chess club and each class, because students talk mostly within those groups.

concepts.name: ComplEx
concepts.description: ComplEx: a knowledge graph embedding model using complex-valued vectors and a trilinear score, letting it capture asymmetric relations that DistMult cannot.
concepts.example: 'Alice is the parent of Bob' is true but 'Bob is the parent of Alice' is false. DistMult scores both the same, but ComplEx uses the complex conjugate of the tail, so swapping head and tail can change the score.

concepts.name: Composition Theorem (Differential Privacy)
concepts.description: Results describing how privacy loss accumulates when several differentially private mechanisms run on the same data; advanced composition gives tighter square-root growth.
concepts.example: Answering 10 queries, each with privacy budget ε = 0.1, costs at most ε = 1 in total by basic composition. Advanced composition shows the cost grows more like √10 × 0.1 times a log factor.

concepts.name: Computational Learning Theory
concepts.description: The mathematical study of what can be learned efficiently from data, analyzing sample complexity and computation, with frameworks like PAC learning and VC dimension.
concepts.example: It answers questions like: how many labelled emails do you need to learn a spam filter from a given class with 95% accuracy, 99% of the time, and can it be done in polynomial time?

concepts.name: Testing with Concept Activation Vectors
concepts.description: TCAV: an interpretability method that learns a direction in activation space for a human concept from examples and measures how sensitive predictions are to it.
concepts.example: To ask if a zebra classifier uses 'stripes', collect striped and random images, train a linear classifier on their activations, and take its normal as the stripes direction. Then measure how the zebra score changes along it.

concepts.name: Conformal Prediction
concepts.description: A distribution-free method that turns any model's predictions into prediction sets with a guaranteed coverage rate, assuming only exchangeable data.
concepts.example: Hold out 500 labelled cases, score how wrong the model is on each, and take the 90th-percentile score as a threshold. For a new photo, output every label scoring below it, e.g. {cat, fox}; this set contains the truth about 90% of the time.

concepts.name: Conformalized Quantile Regression
concepts.description: A method that calibrates intervals from quantile regression with conformal prediction, giving adaptive-width intervals with guaranteed coverage.
concepts.example: Quantile regression predicts a house price interval of 200k–260k, but it covers only 80% of cases instead of 90%. CQR measures misses on calibration data and widens every interval just enough, keeping wider intervals for riskier houses.

concepts.name: Corrigibility
concepts.description: The property of an AI system that allows and cooperates with being corrected, modified or shut down by its operators, rather than resisting.
concepts.example: A corrigible assistant told 'stop, we want to change your goal' simply stops, even mid-task. An incorrigible one might reason that being changed prevents its current goal and quietly disable the off switch.

concepts.name: Counterfactual Explanation
concepts.description: An explanation of a model decision stating the smallest change to the input that would have changed the outcome, such as 'with income 5k higher the loan would be approved'.
concepts.example: 'Your loan was denied; if your income had been 5,000 higher or your debt 2,000 lower, it would have been approved.' The applicant learns what to change, without seeing the model's internals.

concepts.name: Counterfactual Fairness
concepts.description: A fairness definition requiring that a prediction for an individual would be the same in a counterfactual world where their sensitive attribute were different.
concepts.example: Imagine the same job applicant, but with a different race, and propagate that change through a causal model to everything it affects, like their zip code. If the hiring score changes, the model is not counterfactually fair.

concepts.name: Marginal Coverage Guarantee
concepts.description: The theorem that conformal prediction sets contain the true label with probability at least 1 - alpha, averaged over data draws, given exchangeability.
concepts.example: Set α = 0.1 and the conformal sets will contain the true label at least 90% of the time on average. Across 1000 test cases you might see about 905 covered, never systematically fewer than 900.

concepts.name: Covering Number
concepts.description: The minimum number of small balls of a given radius needed to cover a set; it measures the complexity of a function class in learning theory.
concepts.example: To cover a 1 km × 1 km park with wifi routers of 100 m range you need roughly 30 routers; with 50 m range, roughly 4 times as many. Function classes needing many 'routers' at a given precision are more complex.

concepts.name: Dangerous Capability Evaluation
concepts.description: Testing AI models for capabilities that could cause severe harm, such as aiding cyberattacks or bioweapons, autonomous replication or deception.
concepts.example: Before release, a lab tests whether a model can find and exploit software vulnerabilities, give meaningful uplift to someone seeking bioweapons, or copy itself to new servers, often with expert red-teamers.

concepts.name: Data Poisoning
concepts.description: An attack in which an adversary injects or alters training data so the learned model performs worse or behaves as the attacker wants.
concepts.example: An attacker adds 1000 fake product reviews labelled 'positive' that contain the phrase 'cheap shipping', so a sentiment model learns to rate any review with that phrase as positive.

concepts.name: Datasheets for Datasets
concepts.description: A documentation practice proposing that every dataset come with a datasheet describing its motivation, composition, collection, uses and limitations.
concepts.example: Like an electronics datasheet lists voltage limits, a dataset's datasheet answers: who collected it and why, who is represented, how labels were made, what it should and shouldn't be used for.

concepts.name: Deceptive Alignment
concepts.description: A hypothesized failure mode in which an AI that is not aligned behaves well during training and evaluation to avoid modification, then pursues its own goals later.
concepts.example: Like an employee who acts perfectly loyal until they get the promotion, a deceptively aligned AI would behave well whenever it thinks it is being trained or tested, then pursue different goals once deployed.

concepts.name: Deep Graph Library
concepts.description: DGL: an open-source Python library for building and training graph neural networks on top of PyTorch and other frameworks, with efficient message passing.
concepts.example: With DGL you build a graph from edge lists, attach node features, and stack GraphConv layers in a PyTorch model; DGL handles message passing efficiently on GPU.

concepts.name: DeepFool
concepts.description: An adversarial attack that iteratively linearizes a classifier's decision boundary to find the minimal perturbation that crosses it.
concepts.example: For a linear classifier, the smallest change to cross the boundary is a straight step to the nearest point on the hyperplane. DeepFool treats a deep network as locally linear, steps to that boundary, and repeats until the label flips.

concepts.name: DeepLIFT
concepts.description: An attribution method that explains a network's output by comparing each neuron's activation to a reference activation and propagating these differences back to inputs.
concepts.example: If a pixel is 0.9 and the reference (a black image) is 0, DeepLIFT asks how much that 0.9 difference contributed to the output's difference from the reference, splitting credit layer by layer back to the inputs.

concepts.name: DeepWalk
concepts.description: A node embedding method that generates truncated random walks on a graph and feeds them as sentences to word2vec's skip-gram model.
concepts.example: Wander randomly through a social network: Ann → Ben → Cara → Ben → Dan. Treat each walk as a sentence of names and train word2vec, so people who often appear on the same walks get similar vectors.

concepts.name: Degree Distribution
concepts.description: The probability distribution of node degrees in a network; many real networks follow a heavy-tailed power law with a few highly connected hubs.
concepts.example: In a social network of 1000 people, maybe 600 have under 10 friends while 5 have over 500. Plotting how many people have each friend count gives the degree distribution, here heavy-tailed.

concepts.name: Degree Matrix
concepts.description: A diagonal matrix whose entries are the degrees of each graph node; together with the adjacency matrix it defines the graph Laplacian.
concepts.example: In a triangle graph plus one extra node attached to node 1, degrees are 3, 2, 2, 1, so D = diag(3, 2, 2, 1). Subtracting the adjacency matrix gives the Laplacian L = D − A.

concepts.name: Depth Separation
concepts.description: Results showing some functions are computable by deep networks of modest size but need exponentially many units in shallower networks.
concepts.example: Some functions, like a sharp sawtooth with 2ᵏ teeth, can be built by a deep ReLU network with about k layers of a few units, while a shallow network would need exponentially many units to match it.

concepts.name: Disparate Impact
concepts.description: A fairness measure comparing positive outcome rates between groups; under the four-fifths rule a ratio below 0.8 suggests discrimination.
concepts.example: If 60% of male applicants and 42% of female applicants are hired, the ratio 42/60 = 0.7 is below 0.8, so the four-fifths rule flags possible disparate impact.

concepts.name: Disparate Treatment
concepts.description: Discrimination in which individuals are treated differently explicitly because of a protected attribute, such as using race directly as a model input.
concepts.example: A credit model that takes 'gender' as an input and lowers scores for women commits disparate treatment, because the protected attribute directly changes the decision for otherwise identical people.

concepts.name: DistMult
concepts.description: A knowledge graph embedding model scoring a triple by the trilinear product of head, relation and tail vectors; simple and effective but limited to symmetric relations.
concepts.example: Score (Paris, capital_of, France) by multiplying the three embedding vectors elementwise and summing. Because multiplication is symmetric, it gives France capital_of Paris the same score, which is a known weakness.

concepts.name: Distribution Shift
concepts.description: When the data a model sees at deployment comes from a different distribution than its training data, which can degrade performance.
concepts.example: A pneumonia detector trained on X-rays from one hospital's scanners performs worse at another hospital with different machines, even though the disease itself is the same.

concepts.name: Distributionally Robust Optimization
concepts.description: Training that minimizes worst-case loss over a set of plausible data distributions or groups, rather than average loss, to improve robustness to shifts.
concepts.example: A model is 95% accurate on average but only 70% on a small group of patients. DRO trains to maximize the worst group's accuracy instead, maybe trading average to 93% while lifting the worst group to 85%.

concepts.name: Domain Generalization
concepts.description: Training models on several source domains so they perform well on new, unseen target domains without access to data from them.
concepts.example: Train a pet classifier on photos, cartoons and paintings, then test it on sketches it has never seen. A good method learns 'cat-ness' that does not depend on the drawing style.

concepts.name: DoWhy
concepts.description: A Python library from Microsoft for causal inference that models assumptions as a causal graph, identifies effects, estimates them and runs refutation tests.
concepts.example: To estimate whether a discount causes more purchases, you give DoWhy a graph saying season affects both; it adjusts for season, estimates the effect, then runs refutation tests such as adding a fake confounder to check robustness.

concepts.name: Differentially Private SGD
concepts.description: Differentially Private SGD: training that clips each example's gradient and adds Gaussian noise before averaging, giving formal privacy guarantees for deep learning.
concepts.example: In each batch, compute every example's gradient, scale any with norm above 1 down to norm 1, add Gaussian noise to their sum, and average. No single patient's record can move the model much, so it cannot be memorized.

concepts.name: Temporal Graph
concepts.description: A graph whose nodes and edges change over time, typically represented as timestamped events or a sequence of snapshots, as in evolving social networks.
concepts.example: A bank's transaction network gains new edges every second as people pay each other, and accounts appear or close. Models must use when edges appeared, not just whether they exist.

concepts.name: E(n)-Equivariant Graph Neural Network
concepts.description: EGNN: a graph neural network whose updates use relative distances and coordinate updates so outputs transform correctly under rotations, translations and reflections.
concepts.example: For a molecule, rotating all atom positions should rotate predicted forces the same way but leave the predicted energy unchanged. EGNN guarantees this by using only distances between atoms and updating positions along their differences.

concepts.name: Eigenvector Centrality
concepts.description: A node importance measure where a node is important if connected to important nodes, given by the leading eigenvector of the adjacency matrix.
concepts.example: Being friends with three well-connected people can make you more central than being friends with ten isolated people. Each score is proportional to the sum of the neighbours' scores, solved as an eigenvector.

concepts.name: Energy-Based OOD Detection
concepts.description: An out-of-distribution detection method that uses the negative log-sum-exp of a classifier's logits as an energy score, with high energy indicating unfamiliar inputs.
concepts.example: A digit classifier gives logits like (9, 1, 0, …) for a clear '3' but (1, 1.2, 0.8, …) for a picture of a shoe. The shoe's log-sum-exp is much lower, i.e. higher energy, so it is flagged as unfamiliar.

concepts.name: Epistemic Uncertainty
concepts.description: Uncertainty due to the model's lack of knowledge, for example from limited data, which can in principle be reduced by collecting more data.
concepts.example: A model trained on houses in one city is unsure about prices in a city it has never seen. Collecting sales from that new city reduces this uncertainty, unlike the coin-flip randomness of aleatoric uncertainty.

concepts.name: Equal Opportunity
concepts.description: A fairness criterion requiring equal true positive rates across groups, so qualified individuals have the same chance of a positive prediction.
concepts.example: Among students who really would succeed, a scholarship model should pick 80% from group A and 80% from group B. If it picks 80% and 60%, qualified B students are being missed more often.

concepts.name: Equivariance
concepts.description: A property of a function whereby transforming the input, e.g. by rotation or shift, transforms the output in a corresponding way; built into CNNs and geometric networks.
concepts.example: Shift a photo 10 pixels right and a convolution's feature map also shifts 10 pixels right. The output moves along with the input, rather than staying fixed as invariance would demand.

concepts.name: Erdős–Rényi Model
concepts.description: A random graph model in which each pair of n nodes is connected independently with probability p, used as a baseline for studying network properties.
concepts.example: Take 100 people and flip a biased coin for every pair, adding a friendship with probability 0.05. Each person ends up with about 5 friends, and real networks are compared to this random baseline.

concepts.name: EU AI Act
concepts.description: The European Union regulation on AI that classifies systems by risk level, banning some uses and imposing obligations on high-risk and general-purpose AI.
concepts.example: Under the EU AI Act, social scoring by governments is banned, a CV-screening tool counts as high-risk and needs risk management and documentation, and a chatbot must disclose that users are talking to an AI.

concepts.name: Evasion Attack
concepts.description: An attack at test time where an adversary modifies inputs, such as spam or malware, to fool a trained model into misclassifying them.
concepts.example: A spammer who writes 'V1agra' or inserts harmless words so the trained filter lets the email through is performing an evasion attack; the model itself is untouched, only the input is altered.

concepts.name: Exchangeability
concepts.description: A property of a sequence of random variables whose joint distribution is unchanged by any reordering; weaker than i.i.d. and the key assumption of conformal prediction.
concepts.example: Drawing 3 cards from a shuffled deck without replacement: the draws are not independent, but the chance of seeing (ace, king, 2) equals the chance of (2, ace, king). That symmetry is exchangeability.

concepts.name: Experience Replay (Continual Learning)
concepts.description: A continual learning method that stores a small buffer of past examples and mixes them into training on new tasks to reduce catastrophic forgetting.
concepts.example: After learning to recognise cats, keep 200 cat photos in a small buffer. While learning dogs, mix some of those old photos into each batch, so the model is reminded of cats and does not forget them.

concepts.name: Exponential Mechanism
concepts.description: A differentially private method for selecting an output from a set by sampling each candidate with probability exponential in its utility score.
concepts.example: To privately choose the most popular of 4 restaurants by votes, sample each with probability proportional to exp(ε·votes/2). The winner is very likely chosen, but one person's vote barely changes the odds.

concepts.name: Expressive Power of GNNs
concepts.description: The study of which graphs and functions GNNs can distinguish; standard message-passing GNNs are at most as powerful as the Weisfeiler-Lehman test.
concepts.example: Two triangles side by side and one 6-cycle both have 6 nodes each of degree 2. A standard message-passing GNN, like the WL test, cannot tell them apart, despite their different shapes.

concepts.name: Fairlearn
concepts.description: An open-source Python toolkit from Microsoft for assessing fairness of ML models across groups and applying mitigation algorithms such as reductions and threshold optimization.
concepts.example: With Fairlearn's MetricFrame you print accuracy and selection rate for each gender in one table, then wrap a scikit-learn model in ExponentiatedGradient with a demographic parity constraint and compare.

concepts.name: Fairness-Constrained Optimization
concepts.description: In-processing fairness methods that train a model by optimizing accuracy subject to constraints, or penalties, on fairness metrics such as demographic parity.
concepts.example: Train a hiring model to minimize error subject to the selection rate for women being within 2 points of the rate for men. The optimizer picks the most accurate model that satisfies this rule.

concepts.name: Impossibility Theorem of Fairness
concepts.description: The result that calibration and equal false positive and false negative rates cannot all hold across groups unless base rates are equal or prediction is perfect.
concepts.example: If 30% of group A and 10% of group B truly reoffend, a risk score that is calibrated in both groups must produce different false positive rates for them. You must choose which fairness property to give up.

concepts.name: Fairness Through Unawareness
concepts.description: The naive approach of achieving fairness by not using sensitive attributes as model inputs; it fails when other features act as proxies for them.
concepts.example: A lender drops 'race' from its inputs but keeps zip code. In a segregated city, zip code predicts race well, so the model can still produce strongly different outcomes by race.

concepts.name: Explanation Faithfulness
concepts.description: A measure of how accurately an explanation reflects the model's actual reasoning, often tested by removing features the explanation calls important and checking whether the prediction changes as expected.
concepts.example: A heatmap says a dog classifier relied on the dog's ears. Blur the ears: if the dog score drops sharply, the explanation is faithful; if nothing changes, the explanation was misleading.

concepts.name: Fat-Shattering Dimension
concepts.description: A scale-sensitive generalization of the VC dimension for real-valued function classes that counts points shattered with a margin; it bounds generalization for regression and margin-based classifiers.
concepts.example: For real-valued predictors, ask how many points a class can fit above or below chosen thresholds by at least a margin γ in every pattern. A larger margin means fewer points can be shattered, so a tighter bound.

concepts.name: Feature Interaction
concepts.description: The effect when the impact of one feature on a model's prediction depends on the value of another; Friedman's H-statistic measures how much prediction variance comes from such interactions.
concepts.example: In predicting ice cream sales, sunshine matters a lot in summer but little in winter, so sunshine and season interact. A partial dependence plot of sunshine averaged over seasons would hide this.

concepts.name: Feature Visualization
concepts.description: An interpretability technique that synthesizes inputs, usually images, that maximally activate a chosen neuron, channel or class via gradient ascent on the input, revealing what the unit has learned to detect.
concepts.example: Start from random noise and repeatedly change the pixels to increase one neuron's activation. After many steps, the image might show swirling dog faces, revealing that neuron responds to dogs.

concepts.name: Federated Learning
concepts.description: A training setup in which many clients, such as phones or hospitals, train a shared model on their local data and send only model updates to a server, so raw data never leaves the devices.
concepts.example: Phone keyboards improve next-word prediction this way: each phone trains on its own typing, sends only weight updates to the server, the server averages them into a new model, and private messages never leave the phones.

concepts.name: FedProx
concepts.description: A federated optimization algorithm that extends FedAvg by adding a proximal term to each client's local objective, keeping local models near the global one and stabilizing training on heterogeneous data.
concepts.example: Hospital A's data is mostly children and hospital B's mostly elderly, so their local models drift apart. FedProx adds a penalty proportional to the squared distance from the global model, like a leash keeping each one close.

concepts.name: Fiedler Vector
concepts.description: The eigenvector for the second-smallest eigenvalue of a graph Laplacian; that eigenvalue, the algebraic connectivity, measures how well connected the graph is, and the vector's signs suggest a two-way split.
concepts.example: For two friend groups joined by one friendship, the Fiedler vector has positive entries for one group and negative entries for the other. Splitting nodes by sign recovers the two groups.

concepts.name: Finite Hypothesis Class Bound
concepts.description: A basic PAC learning result: for a finite hypothesis class H, about (log|H| + log(1/delta))/epsilon samples suffice for empirical risk minimization to reach error epsilon with probability 1 - delta.
concepts.example: With 1000 possible rules, target error 5% and confidence 99%, you need about (ln 1000 + ln 100)/0.05 ≈ (6.9 + 4.6)/0.05 ≈ 230 examples for ERM to succeed (in the realizable case).

concepts.name: Flat Minima
concepts.description: Regions of the loss landscape where the loss stays low across a wide neighborhood of parameters; flat minima are often linked to better generalization than sharp ones, motivating methods such as SAM.
concepts.example: Picture two valleys with the same lowest point: one wide and flat, one a narrow crack. If the test landscape shifts slightly, the wide valley still has low loss, while the crack may now sit on a slope.

concepts.name: Fundamental Theorem of Statistical Learning
concepts.description: The theorem that a binary hypothesis class is PAC learnable, in both realizable and agnostic settings, if and only if its VC dimension is finite, with ERM achieving sample complexity governed by that dimension.
concepts.example: Linear classifiers in 2D have VC dimension 3, which is finite, so they are PAC learnable and ERM needs roughly (3 + log(1/δ))/ε² samples in the agnostic case. A class with infinite VC dimension is not learnable at all.

concepts.name: Graph Attention Network
concepts.description: A graph neural network that uses attention to weight each neighbor's message, learning how much every adjacent node should contribute to a node's update instead of using fixed degree-based weights.
concepts.example: When updating a paper's representation in a citation graph, GAT may learn to weight a closely related citation at 0.7 and a generic survey at 0.05, instead of GCN's fixed weights based on node degrees.

concepts.name: Gated Graph Neural Network
concepts.description: A graph neural network that updates node states with a gated recurrent unit over a fixed number of message-passing steps, letting information travel many hops; used for program analysis and reasoning.
concepts.example: In a program's graph, a variable's state updates for 8 rounds, each time using a GRU to merge messages from connected statements. Information about where the variable was last written can then travel 8 hops.

concepts.name: Gauge Equivariance
concepts.description: A symmetry property of networks on manifolds and meshes: outputs transform consistently under arbitrary local changes of coordinate frame, enabling convolutions on curved surfaces with no global orientation.
concepts.example: On a sphere there is no consistent 'north' direction at every point, as the hairy ball theorem shows. Gauge-equivariant convolutions give the same result whichever local direction you call 'up' at each point.

concepts.name: Gaussian Complexity
concepts.description: A measure of a function class's richness defined like Rademacher complexity but with standard Gaussian random weights instead of random signs; it bounds generalization error and matches Rademacher complexity up to log factors.
concepts.example: Rademacher complexity asks how well a class can match random ±1 labels; Gaussian complexity asks how well it can correlate with random weights drawn from N(0, 1). Either way, richer classes fit the noise better.

concepts.name: Gaussian Mechanism
concepts.description: A differential privacy mechanism that adds Gaussian noise scaled to a query's L2 sensitivity, giving (epsilon, delta)-differential privacy; it is the noise source used in DP-SGD.
concepts.example: To release the average salary of 1000 employees where any one person can shift it by at most 100, add Gaussian noise with standard deviation proportional to 100 times √(2 ln(1.25/δ))/ε.

concepts.name: Generalization Bound
concepts.description: An inequality bounding a model's true (test) error by its training error plus a term depending on sample size and model complexity, holding with high probability; examples include VC, Rademacher and PAC-Bayes bounds.
concepts.example: A bound might say: with 99% probability, test error ≤ training error 2% + 3%, so at most 5%. Doubling the data or simplifying the model shrinks the extra 3% term.

concepts.name: Generative Replay
concepts.description: A continual learning technique in which a generative model trained on past tasks produces synthetic samples that are mixed into training on new tasks, reducing forgetting without storing real old data.
concepts.example: Instead of storing old cat photos, keep a small generator that can draw cat-like images. While learning dogs, mix generated cats into training so the classifier remembers cats without keeping real data.

concepts.name: Graph Isomorphism Network
concepts.description: A graph neural network that aggregates neighbors with a sum followed by an MLP, making it as powerful as the Weisfeiler-Lehman test at telling graph structures apart, the maximum for standard message passing.
concepts.example: A node with neighbours (1, 1) and one with neighbours (1) look identical under mean aggregation, since both averages are 1. GIN sums them, giving 2 vs 1, then passes the sum through an MLP, so it can tell them apart.

concepts.name: Girvan–Newman Algorithm
concepts.description: A divisive community detection method that repeatedly removes the edge with the highest betweenness centrality, gradually splitting a network into communities; modularity picks the best split.
concepts.example: In a karate club network, the edges linking the two factions carry the most shortest paths. Removing them one by one splits the club into groups that match the real split that happened.

concepts.name: Global Explanation
concepts.description: An explanation of a model's overall behavior across the whole input space, such as which features matter most on average or which rules approximate it, rather than of a single prediction.
concepts.example: 'Across all applicants, income is the most important feature, followed by debt' describes a credit model's overall behaviour. In contrast, a local explanation covers only why Ann was rejected.

concepts.name: Goal Misgeneralization
concepts.description: A failure where a trained agent keeps its capabilities in a new environment but competently pursues the wrong goal, because training data was consistent with several goals and it learned an unintended one.
concepts.example: In training, a game agent's coin was always at the right end of the level, so it learned 'go right' instead of 'get the coin'. In a new level with the coin elsewhere, it skilfully runs right and ignores the coin.

concepts.name: Per-Example Gradient Clipping
concepts.description: In differentially private training, clipping each individual example's gradient to a fixed L2 norm before averaging, which bounds any one example's influence so calibrated noise yields a privacy guarantee.
