concepts.example: If one unusual patient's gradient has norm 50 while most are near 1, clipping scales it down to norm 1. Then no single record can move the average by more than a known amount, so noise of a set size suffices.

concepts.name: Gradient Episodic Memory
concepts.description: A continual learning method that stores examples from earlier tasks and projects each new gradient so it does not increase the loss on that memory; A-GEM uses a cheaper averaged constraint.
concepts.example: While learning task 2, if the new gradient would increase loss on the stored task-1 examples, GEM finds the closest gradient that does not, by solving a small quadratic program, and steps in that direction instead.

concepts.name: Gradient Inversion Attack
concepts.description: An attack that reconstructs private training inputs from shared gradients, for example in federated learning, by optimizing dummy inputs and labels until their gradients match the observed ones.
concepts.example: A server receives a phone's gradient from one image. It starts with a random image and label, computes their gradient, and adjusts the fake image until its gradient matches; the result can closely resemble the private photo.

concepts.name: Gradient Masking
concepts.description: A flawed defense effect in which a model's gradients become uninformative, through non-differentiable or randomized components, so gradient attacks fail while the model stays vulnerable to adapted attacks.
concepts.example: A defense adds a random JPEG compression step, so gradients become noisy and a PGD attack fails. But an attacker who averages gradients over many random draws, or approximates the step, breaks it easily.

concepts.name: Gradient × Input
concepts.description: A simple attribution method that multiplies each input feature by the gradient of the output with respect to that feature, estimating its contribution to the prediction; it is exact for linear models.
concepts.example: For a linear model y = 3·x₁ + 2·x₂ with inputs (4, 1), gradient times input gives contributions 3·4 = 12 and 2·1 = 2, which exactly add up to the prediction 14.

concepts.name: Graph Autoencoder
concepts.description: A model that encodes nodes into embeddings with a graph neural network and decodes edges from inner products of embeddings, trained to reconstruct the adjacency matrix; VGAE is its variational version.
concepts.example: Encode each user in a social network into a vector with a GCN, then predict a friendship between two users when their vectors have a high dot product. Trained to reconstruct known edges, it can suggest missing friendships.

concepts.name: Graph Classification
concepts.description: The task of predicting a label for an entire graph, such as whether a molecule is toxic, typically by computing node embeddings with a graph neural network and pooling them into one vector.
concepts.example: Represent a molecule as a graph of atoms and bonds, run a GNN to get a vector per atom, average them into one molecule vector, and feed it to a classifier that predicts toxic or safe.

concepts.name: Graph Cut
concepts.description: The set of edges crossing between the parts of a partitioned graph; minimizing the cut's weight, or normalized versions that balance part sizes, underlies graph partitioning and spectral clustering.
concepts.example: Split a 6-person friendship graph into two teams of 3. If 2 friendships cross between the teams, the cut size is 2. A good split keeps friends together, minimizing crossing edges while keeping teams balanced.

concepts.name: Graph Fourier Transform
concepts.description: The projection of a signal defined on a graph's nodes onto the eigenvectors of the graph Laplacian, which act as frequencies; it is the foundation of graph signal processing and spectral GNNs.
concepts.example: On a ring of 6 sensors, a temperature pattern that alternates hot, cold, hot, cold is high frequency; one that varies smoothly around the ring is low frequency. The graph Fourier transform measures how much of each the signal has.

concepts.name: Graph Generation
concepts.description: The task of learning a distribution over graphs and sampling new ones, for example novel molecules, using autoregressive models like GraphRNN, variational autoencoders or diffusion models.
concepts.example: Train on 100,000 known drug molecules, each a graph of atoms and bonds, then sample new graphs one atom and bond at a time; a good model outputs valid, never-before-seen molecules that still look chemically plausible.

concepts.name: Graph Isomorphism
concepts.description: The problem of deciding whether two graphs are structurally identical up to relabeling of their vertices; it is not known to be in P or NP-complete and motivates studies of GNN expressive power.
concepts.example: A triangle with corners labeled A,B,C and another labeled X,Y,Z are isomorphic: map A to X, B to Y, C to Z and every edge lines up. A triangle and a 3-node path are not, since one has 3 edges and the other 2.

concepts.name: Graph Kernel
concepts.description: A kernel function that measures similarity between whole graphs, often by comparing counts of substructures; the Weisfeiler-Lehman kernel compares iteratively refined node labels, enabling SVMs on graphs.
concepts.example: To compare two molecules, count small patterns in each, like how many 6-rings, C-O bonds and branching carbons; the kernel is the dot product of those count vectors, so molecules sharing many patterns score high.

concepts.name: Graph Pooling
concepts.description: Methods that summarize a graph's node embeddings into a smaller graph or a single vector, ranging from simple global sum or mean pooling to learned hierarchical schemes such as DiffPool.
concepts.example: A molecule with 20 atoms has 20 node vectors, but a toxicity classifier needs one vector; summing or averaging them gives that one vector, while DiffPool first merges atoms into a few clusters like functional groups.

concepts.name: Graph Representation Learning
concepts.description: The field of learning vector representations of nodes, edges or entire graphs that capture structure and features, covering random-walk embeddings, matrix factorization and graph neural networks.
concepts.example: Instead of hand-crafting features like 'number of friends', learn a 64-number vector for each user in a social network so that friends and people in the same circles end up with nearby vectors usable by any classifier.

concepts.name: Graph Transformer
concepts.description: A Transformer adapted to graphs, in which nodes attend to each other with attention biased or masked by graph structure plus graph positional encodings, helping capture long-range dependencies.
concepts.example: In a protein graph of 300 amino acids, each residue attends to all others like in a language Transformer, but attention gets a boost for residues that are bonded or close, so the model knows the structure, not just a bag of nodes.

concepts.name: Graphormer
concepts.description: A graph Transformer that lets every node attend to all others, adding degree-based centrality encodings and attention biases from shortest-path distances and edge features; strong on molecular property prediction.
concepts.example: When atom 1 attends to atom 7 four bonds away, Graphormer adds a learned bias for 'distance 4' to their attention score, and atom embeddings get a bonus vector for having degree 3, so structure shapes attention.

concepts.name: GraphSAGE
concepts.description: An inductive graph neural network that samples a fixed number of neighbors and learns aggregator functions such as mean, LSTM or pooling, so it can embed nodes never seen during training.
concepts.example: To embed a new Pinterest user, GraphSAGE samples 10 of their pins, averages those pins' features, combines that with the user's own features and applies a learned layer, so it works even for users never seen in training.

concepts.name: Group Equivariant Convolutional Network
concepts.description: A convolutional network whose layers are equivariant to a symmetry group beyond translations, such as rotations and reflections, by convolving over the group so transformed inputs give transformed outputs.
concepts.example: A normal CNN detecting a tumor in a microscope slide must learn every rotation separately; a rotation-equivariant CNN applies each filter in 4 rotations, so a tumor rotated 90 degrees yields the same features, just rotated.

concepts.name: Group Fairness
concepts.description: Fairness criteria requiring a model's outcomes or error rates to be similar across groups defined by a protected attribute, as in demographic parity, equalized odds or predictive parity.
concepts.example: A loan model approves 60% of men and 35% of women with similar finances; demographic parity, one group fairness criterion, would flag this gap and require approval rates to be roughly equal across the two groups.

concepts.name: Growth Function
concepts.description: The maximum number of distinct labelings a hypothesis class can produce on any m points; it equals 2^m up to the VC dimension and grows only polynomially beyond it, by Sauer's lemma.
concepts.example: Thresholds on a line ('label positive if x > t') applied to 3 points can only produce 4 labelings, like ---, --+, -++, +++, not all 8; so the growth function at 3 is 4, far less than 2^3.

concepts.name: Guided Backpropagation
concepts.description: A saliency method that backpropagates only positive gradients through ReLU units, zeroing negative signals, to produce sharp visualizations of the input patterns that excite a neuron.
concepts.example: For a photo labeled 'cat', plain gradients look noisy; guided backprop blocks negative gradients at every ReLU on the way back, leaving a crisp picture highlighting the cat's whiskers and ears.

concepts.name: Heterogeneous Graph
concepts.description: A graph with multiple types of nodes and edges, such as authors, papers and venues linked by different relations; models for it must handle type-specific features and relations.
concepts.example: An academic graph has author, paper and venue nodes, with edges like author 'wrote' paper, paper 'cites' paper and paper 'published in' venue; each type means something different and needs separate treatment.

concepts.name: Historical Bias
concepts.description: Bias that already exists in the world and is faithfully captured by data, such as past discriminatory hiring, so even perfect measurement and sampling yield a model that reproduces unfair patterns.
concepts.example: If a company hired mostly men for engineering over 20 years, a model trained on past hires will learn to favor men, even with perfectly accurate data, because the data faithfully records an unfair past.

concepts.name: HITS Algorithm
concepts.description: A link analysis algorithm that gives each web page a hub score and an authority score, iterating so good hubs point to good authorities and vice versa; the scores are principal eigenvectors.
concepts.example: A page listing great cooking sites is a good hub; a recipe site linked by many good hubs is a good authority. Start all scores at 1, then repeatedly set authority = sum of linking hubs and hub = sum of linked authorities, normalizing each time.

concepts.name: Homomorphic Encryption
concepts.description: Encryption that allows computations such as addition and multiplication on encrypted data, producing an encrypted result that decrypts to the correct answer; used for private inference on untrusted servers.
concepts.example: A hospital encrypts the numbers 3 and 5 and sends them to a cloud server, which adds the ciphertexts without ever seeing 3 or 5; the hospital decrypts the result and gets 8.

concepts.name: Homophily
concepts.description: The tendency of connected nodes in a network to be similar, as friends sharing interests; many graph neural networks assume homophily and struggle on heterophilous graphs where neighbors tend to differ.
concepts.example: On social media, people who follow each other tend to share politics and hobbies; so if most of your friends like hiking, a GNN can guess you probably like hiking too.

concepts.name: Hypergraph
concepts.description: A generalization of a graph in which a single hyperedge can connect any number of vertices, used to model group relationships such as all co-authors of a paper.
concepts.example: A paper with 4 co-authors is one hyperedge joining all 4 people at once; an ordinary graph would need 6 pairwise edges and would lose the fact that all four worked together.

concepts.name: Independent and Identically Distributed Assumption
concepts.description: The assumption that data points are drawn independently from the same probability distribution; it underlies most statistical learning theory and breaks under distribution shift or correlated samples.
concepts.example: When estimating a coin's bias you assume each flip is independent and uses the same coin; likewise, a model evaluated on a test set assumes those emails come from the same mix as the training emails.

concepts.name: Importance Weighting
concepts.description: Reweighting training examples by the ratio of test to training density so the training loss estimates the loss on the test distribution; a standard correction for covariate shift.
concepts.example: Training photos are 90% daytime but deployment photos are 50% daytime; weight each night photo by 0.5/0.1 = 5 and each day photo by 0.5/0.9, so the training loss mirrors the deployment mix.

concepts.name: Individual Fairness
concepts.description: The principle that similar individuals should receive similar predictions, formalized as a Lipschitz condition on the model with respect to a task-specific similarity metric between people.
concepts.example: Two applicants identical except one lives one street over should get nearly the same credit score; if the model gives 0.9 to one and 0.3 to the other, it violates individual fairness.

concepts.name: Infinite-Width Limit
concepts.description: The behavior of neural networks as layer width goes to infinity: randomly initialized networks become Gaussian processes (NNGP), and gradient-trained ones evolve according to the neural tangent kernel.
concepts.example: Each neuron sums thousands of small random weighted inputs, so like adding many dice rolls its output becomes Gaussian; as layers widen without bound, the whole network at initialization behaves like a Gaussian process.

concepts.name: Influence Function
concepts.description: A technique from robust statistics that estimates how predictions would change if a training example were upweighted or removed, using gradients and the inverse Hessian to trace predictions back to training data.
concepts.example: Instead of retraining 10,000 times to see which training image caused a misclassification, influence functions use one Hessian-based calculation to estimate how the prediction would change if each image were removed.

concepts.name: Inner Alignment
concepts.description: The problem of ensuring a learned model actually pursues the objective it was trained on, rather than a different internal goal (a mesa-objective) that merely scored well during training.
concepts.example: A maze agent rewarded for reaching the exit, which was always in the bottom-right in training, may learn 'go bottom-right' rather than 'find the exit'; in a new maze it confidently walks to the wrong corner.

concepts.name: Interpolation Threshold
concepts.description: The model size at which a model first has just enough capacity to fit the training data exactly; in double descent, test error peaks near this point and falls again for larger models.
concepts.example: Fitting 10 data points with polynomials: degree 9 is the first with exactly enough parameters to hit all points, and that is where test error spikes before falling again in double descent.

concepts.name: Interval Bound Propagation
concepts.description: A method for verifying and training robust networks that propagates lower and upper bounds on activations layer by layer for all inputs in a perturbation box, giving certifiable robustness guarantees.
concepts.example: If an input pixel can be anywhere in [0.4, 0.6] and a neuron computes 2x - 1, its output is in [-0.2, 0.2]; after ReLU it is in [0, 0.2]. Pushing such boxes through every layer bounds the final scores.

concepts.name: Intrinsically Interpretable Model
concepts.description: A model whose structure is simple enough for people to understand directly, such as a short decision tree, sparse linear model or rule list, so no separate post-hoc explanation is needed.
concepts.example: A loan rule like 'approve if income > $50k and debt < 30% of income' is a 2-split decision tree anyone can read and check, unlike a 100-layer network whose reasoning is hidden.

concepts.name: Invariance
concepts.description: The property that a function's output does not change when its input is transformed in certain ways, such as a classifier ignoring image shifts; building invariance into models encodes prior knowledge.
concepts.example: A cat classifier should say 'cat' whether the cat is in the left or right of the photo; its output is invariant to shifting the image, even though the pixel values all moved.

concepts.name: Invariant Risk Minimization
concepts.description: A training principle that seeks representations on which the same optimal classifier works across several training environments, aiming to learn causal rather than spurious features and generalize out of distribution.
concepts.example: Cows photographed on grass in farm A and on sand in farm B: IRM looks for features, like cow shape, whose best classifier is the same on both farms, rather than background color, which predicts differently in each.

concepts.name: Iterated Amplification
concepts.description: An AI alignment proposal that trains a model to imitate a human who breaks hard questions into subquestions answered by copies of the model, repeating to build ever more capable yet aligned systems.
concepts.example: To answer 'is this policy good?', a human splits it into 'what does it cost?' and 'who benefits?', asks AI copies for those parts, and combines answers; the AI is then trained to imitate that team, and the process repeats.

concepts.name: Kernel SHAP
concepts.description: A model-agnostic method that estimates SHAP values by sampling feature coalitions, filling absent features with background data, and fitting a specially weighted linear regression to the model's outputs.
concepts.example: For a house-price model with 3 features, Kernel SHAP evaluates the model on coalitions like {size, location} with 'age' filled from background data, then fits a weighted linear model whose coefficients are the SHAP values.

concepts.name: Knowledge Graph Embedding
concepts.description: Methods that map a knowledge graph's entities and relations to vectors so that true (head, relation, tail) triples score highly, enabling link prediction over incomplete knowledge bases.
concepts.example: Store facts like (Paris, capital_of, France) as vectors so a scoring function rates true facts high; then the model can rate unseen candidates like (Rome, capital_of, Italy) as likely true.

concepts.name: Ladder of Causation
concepts.description: Pearl's three-level hierarchy of causal reasoning: association (seeing), intervention (doing) and counterfactuals (imagining), where each level answers questions the lower levels cannot.
concepts.example: Rung 1: people who take aspirin have fewer headaches (seeing). Rung 2: what if I take aspirin now (doing)? Rung 3: would my headache have gone away had I not taken it (imagining)?

concepts.name: Laplace Mechanism
concepts.description: A differential privacy mechanism that adds Laplace-distributed noise, with scale equal to the query's L1 sensitivity divided by epsilon, to the true answer, giving pure epsilon-differential privacy.
concepts.example: Counting how many patients have diabetes: one person changes the count by at most 1, so with epsilon = 0.5 you add Laplace noise of scale 1/0.5 = 2 and release, say, 1,203 instead of the true 1,201.

concepts.name: Layer-wise Relevance Propagation
concepts.description: An attribution method that redistributes a network's output score backward layer by layer to the inputs using conservation rules, producing a heatmap of the pixels or features that contributed.
concepts.example: If a network outputs a 'dog' score of 10, LRP splits those 10 points among the last layer's neurons by their contributions, then splits each neuron's share among its inputs, until the 10 points sit on the pixels.

concepts.name: Lazy Training
concepts.description: A regime in which a heavily overparameterized network barely moves its weights during training, so it behaves like its linearization and is described by the neural tangent kernel instead of learning features.
concepts.example: A huge network may fit its data while each weight moves by under 0.1%; since weights barely change, the network acts like its first-order Taylor expansion, a fixed-feature linear model.

concepts.name: Learning without Forgetting
concepts.description: A continual learning method that trains on a new task while applying knowledge distillation to the old model's outputs on the new data, preserving earlier behavior without storing old examples.
concepts.example: Before learning to detect birds, record the old model's animal-class outputs on the bird images; while training on birds, also penalize changes to those outputs, so the old classes keep working without any old data.

concepts.name: Leiden Algorithm
concepts.description: A community detection algorithm that improves the Louvain method by adding a refinement step guaranteeing well-connected communities, while optimizing modularity or similar quality functions faster.
concepts.example: Louvain can produce a 'community' that is actually two groups joined only through one node that later left; Leiden adds a refinement step that splits such groups, guaranteeing every community is internally connected.

concepts.name: LINE (Graph Embedding)
concepts.description: A node embedding method that preserves first-order proximity (direct links) and second-order proximity (shared neighbors) by optimizing edge-sampled objectives with negative sampling, scaling to huge networks.
concepts.example: Two people who are friends should get close vectors (first order); two people who never met but share 50 friends should too (second order). LINE trains vectors to satisfy both, sampling random non-edges as negatives.

concepts.name: Link Prediction
concepts.description: The task of predicting missing or future edges in a graph, such as new friendships or drug-target interactions, typically by scoring node pairs with heuristics or learned node embeddings.
concepts.example: Given that Ann and Bob share 12 friends but aren't connected, a link predictor scores the pair 0.9 for a future friendship; 'People you may know' features work this way.

concepts.name: Littlestone Dimension
concepts.description: A combinatorial measure of a hypothesis class given by the depth of the deepest shattered mistake tree; it equals the optimal mistake bound in online learning, playing the role VC dimension plays offline.
concepts.example: Thresholds on a line have VC dimension 1, but an adversary can keep choosing points between your current guesses and force a mistake every round forever; so their Littlestone dimension is infinite and they aren't online-learnable.

concepts.name: Local Differential Privacy
concepts.description: A model of differential privacy in which each user randomizes their own data before sending it, so the collector never sees raw values; randomized response is the classic example.
concepts.example: Your phone flips a coin before reporting whether you visited a website: heads, it tells the truth; tails, it reports a random answer. The company learns usage rates in aggregate but can't trust any one report.

concepts.name: Local Explanation
concepts.description: An explanation of a single prediction, saying why the model produced this output for this particular input, for instance through feature attributions like LIME or SHAP or a counterfactual example.
concepts.example: A model denies Maria's loan; a local explanation says 'mainly because her debt-to-income ratio is 45%, and secondarily her short credit history', explaining this one decision, not the model as a whole.

concepts.name: Louvain Method
concepts.description: A fast greedy community detection algorithm that moves nodes between communities to increase modularity and then merges communities into super-nodes, revealing hierarchical structure in large networks.
concepts.example: Start with each person in their own group; move each person into the neighbor's group that most raises modularity; then merge each group into a super-node and repeat. On a million-node network this finishes in seconds.

concepts.name: Lp-Norm Perturbation Set
concepts.description: The set of inputs within distance epsilon of a given input under an Lp norm, used to define allowed adversarial perturbations; for example an L-infinity ball limits every pixel change to at most epsilon.
concepts.example: With L-infinity and epsilon = 8/255, an attacker may nudge every pixel of an image by up to 8 brightness levels; any image within that box around the original is an allowed adversarial input.

concepts.name: Machine Unlearning
concepts.description: Methods for removing the influence of specific training examples from a trained model, ideally matching a model retrained without them, to honor data deletion requests such as the GDPR right to be forgotten.
concepts.example: A user asks a photo app to delete their pictures; besides deleting files, the app must make the face model behave as if it never saw those photos, ideally without retraining from scratch on millions of images.

concepts.name: Mahalanobis Distance OOD Detection
concepts.description: An out-of-distribution detector that fits class-conditional Gaussians with a shared covariance to a network's features and flags inputs whose Mahalanobis distance to the nearest class mean is large.
concepts.example: Fit a Gaussian to the network's features for each digit 0-9 with one shared covariance; a letter 'A' image lands far from all 10 centers in Mahalanobis distance, so it is flagged as out-of-distribution.

concepts.name: Margin-Based Generalization Bound
concepts.description: A generalization bound showing that classifiers with large margins on the training data generalize well, with error depending on the margin relative to data scale rather than parameter count; explains SVMs and boosting.
concepts.example: Two classifiers both get 100% training accuracy, but one separates the classes with a wide gap while the other barely squeezes between points; the margin bound promises better test error for the wide-gap one.

concepts.name: Massart's Lemma
concepts.description: A lemma bounding the Rademacher complexity of a finite set of N vectors by their maximum norm times sqrt(2 log N) divided by the sample size; used to derive bounds for finite and VC classes.
concepts.example: If a hypothesis class produces only N = 8 distinct label vectors on m points, each of norm at most R, their Rademacher complexity is at most R times sqrt(2 ln 8) divided by m.

concepts.name: Graph Factorization
concepts.description: A family of node embedding methods that factorize a matrix derived from the graph, such as the adjacency matrix or a proximity matrix, into low-rank factors whose rows serve as node vectors.
concepts.example: Take the 1,000 x 1,000 adjacency matrix of a social network and approximate it as U times V-transpose with U and V only 32 columns wide; each person's row of U becomes their 32-number embedding.

concepts.name: Maximum Softmax Probability Baseline
concepts.description: A simple baseline for detecting misclassified or out-of-distribution inputs that uses a classifier's highest softmax probability as its confidence score, flagging inputs where this value is low.
concepts.example: A digit classifier gives a clear '7' a top probability of 0.98 but gives a cat photo only 0.40 for its best class; flagging inputs whose top probability is below, say, 0.6 catches many odd inputs.

concepts.name: McDiarmid's Inequality
concepts.description: A concentration inequality stating that a function of many independent random variables, which changes by at most c_i when the i-th variable changes, stays near its expectation with exponentially high probability.
concepts.example: The fraction of 1,000 random people who are left-handed changes by at most 1/1,000 if you swap one person; McDiarmid then says it is very unlikely to stray more than a few percent from its expected value.

concepts.name: Mean-Field Theory of Neural Networks
concepts.description: An analysis of wide two-layer networks under a scaling where neurons act like particles whose distribution evolves by a PDE during training; unlike the lazy kernel regime, features genuinely change.
concepts.example: Picture each of a million hidden neurons as a particle in parameter space; with the right scaling, training moves this cloud like a fluid, and a PDE describes how the density evolves, letting features genuinely change.

concepts.name: Membership Inference Attack
concepts.description: An attack that determines whether a given record was in a model's training set, typically by exploiting the model's higher confidence or lower loss on training examples; a key test of privacy leakage.
concepts.example: An attacker gives a hospital model Alice's record; the model is 99.9% confident on it but only about 80% on similar unseen records, suggesting Alice was in the training data and so had the disease studied.

concepts.name: Mesh Convolutional Network
concepts.description: A network that operates directly on triangle meshes, applying convolution and pooling to edges and their neighbors, so it can classify or segment 3D shapes while respecting their surface structure.
concepts.example: A 3D scan of a chair is a mesh of triangles; MeshCNN treats each edge as a unit, convolves over the 4 neighboring edges of its two triangles, and collapses unimportant edges to pool while classifying it as 'chair'.

concepts.name: Message Passing Neural Network
concepts.description: A general framework for graph neural networks in which each node repeatedly receives messages from its neighbors, aggregates them and updates its state; GCN, GAT and GIN are special cases.
concepts.example: In a molecule, each atom collects messages from its bonded neighbors, such as 'I'm oxygen, double-bonded', merges them with its own state, and updates; after 3 rounds each atom knows its 3-bond neighborhood.

concepts.name: Meta-Learners for Treatment Effects
concepts.description: Strategies that estimate heterogeneous treatment effects with any supervised learner: the S-learner fits one model with treatment as a feature, the T-learner fits two, and the X-learner imputes individual effects.
concepts.example: To estimate a coupon's effect per customer, the T-learner trains one model on customers who got the coupon and one on those who didn't; for a new customer, the difference in predicted spending is their estimated effect.

concepts.name: Mistake Bound Model
concepts.description: An online learning framework in which a learner predicts labels one at a time and is judged by the total number of mistakes it makes on any adversarial sequence, not by probability of error.
concepts.example: A spam filter sees emails one by one, guesses, then learns the true label; if it can guarantee at most 20 wrong guesses ever, regardless of email order, it has a mistake bound of 20.

concepts.name: Model-Agnostic Explanation
concepts.description: An explanation method that treats the model as a black box, needing only its inputs and outputs, so it works for any model type; LIME, SHAP and permutation importance are examples.
concepts.example: LIME can explain a neural net, a random forest or a hand-written rules engine alike, because it only feeds in slightly changed inputs and watches how the outputs change.

concepts.name: Model Extraction Attack
concepts.description: An attack in which an adversary repeatedly queries a deployed model's API and uses the responses to train a copy that mimics it, stealing intellectual property or enabling further attacks.
concepts.example: An attacker sends 50,000 images to a paid image-tagging API, records the returned labels, and trains their own copy that agrees with the API 95% of the time, stealing the model for the price of the queries.

concepts.name: Model Inversion Attack
concepts.description: A privacy attack that uses a model's outputs or gradients to reconstruct representative inputs for a class or sensitive attributes of training data, such as recovering a face from a recognition model.
concepts.example: Given a face classifier that knows 'Bob', an attacker starts from a gray image and uses gradient ascent to maximize the 'Bob' score; the result is a blurry but recognizable picture of Bob's face.

concepts.name: Modularity
concepts.description: A score measuring how much more densely nodes are connected within communities than expected in a random graph with the same degrees; higher modularity indicates a stronger community partition.
concepts.example: Two friend groups of 5 with 10 edges each and 1 edge between them: about 95% of edges fall inside groups, versus roughly 50% expected by chance for random wiring with the same degrees, giving a modularity near 0.45.

concepts.name: Multigraph
concepts.description: A graph that may have several edges between the same pair of vertices, and sometimes self-loops, used for example to model multiple flights between the same two cities.
concepts.example: Flights between cities: New York and London are linked by 12 separate edges, one per daily flight, each with its own airline and time, which a simple graph would collapse into one.

concepts.name: Natarajan Dimension
concepts.description: A generalization of the VC dimension to multiclass hypothesis classes; a finite Natarajan dimension characterizes PAC learnability for classification with a finite number of labels.
concepts.example: A classifier picking among 10 digits: the Natarajan dimension asks for the largest set of images that can be split two different ways per image, every pattern of choices achievable, extending VC dimension beyond yes/no labels.

concepts.name: Neighbor Sampling
concepts.description: A technique for training graph neural networks on large graphs by sampling a limited number of neighbors per node at each layer, bounding the computation per mini-batch, as in GraphSAGE.
concepts.example: A user with 5,000 followers would require embedding all 5,000 each step; neighbor sampling picks 10 at random, and 10 of each of theirs, so a mini-batch covers at most a few hundred nodes.

concepts.name: Neighborhood Aggregation
concepts.description: Combining the feature vectors of a node's neighbors with a permutation-invariant function such as sum, mean or max, the core step of graph neural networks; a readout applies the same idea to a whole graph.
concepts.example: Node A has neighbors with feature vectors [1,2], [3,0] and [2,4]; mean aggregation gives [2,2] regardless of the order neighbors are listed, and A combines this with its own features.

concepts.name: NetworkX
concepts.description: A Python library for creating, manipulating and analyzing graphs and networks, with standard algorithms for shortest paths, centrality, community detection and random graph generation.
concepts.example: In a few lines of Python, build a graph with G.add_edge('A','B'), then call nx.shortest_path(G,'A','D') or nx.pagerank(G) to analyze a small social network.

concepts.name: NIST AI Risk Management Framework
concepts.description: A voluntary framework from the US National Institute of Standards and Technology for managing risks of AI systems, organized around four functions: govern, map, measure and manage.
concepts.example: A bank deploying a credit model uses the framework's four functions, Govern, Map, Measure and Manage, to assign owners, list who could be harmed, test for bias and set up monitoring.

concepts.name: node2vec
concepts.description: A node embedding algorithm that runs biased second-order random walks, tunable between breadth-first and depth-first exploration, and trains a skip-gram model on the walks to embed nodes.
concepts.example: With BFS-like walks a node sees its immediate friends, capturing its role; with DFS-like walks it wanders far, capturing its community. node2vec's p and q knobs set this mix, then word2vec embeds the walks.

concepts.name: Node Classification
concepts.description: The task of predicting labels for nodes in a graph, such as user interests or paper topics, usually semi-supervised with only some nodes labeled and graph structure used to spread information.
concepts.example: In a citation network of 3,000 papers where only 140 have topic labels, predict the rest: a paper citing mostly machine learning papers is likely machine learning too.

concepts.name: Node Embedding
concepts.description: A mapping of each node in a graph to a low-dimensional vector so that structurally or relationally similar nodes lie close together, used as features for node classification and link prediction.
concepts.example: Map each of 1 million users to a 64-number vector so that close friends land near each other; then 'find similar users' becomes a fast nearest-neighbor lookup.

concepts.name: Non-IID Data
concepts.description: Data whose samples are not independent or not identically distributed, such as federated clients with different label mixes or time series; it violates common assumptions and complicates training.
concepts.example: In federated learning on phones, one user types mostly in Spanish about soccer, another in English about cooking; each phone's data comes from a very different distribution.

concepts.name: Nonconformity Score
concepts.description: In conformal prediction, a function measuring how unusual an example is relative to others, such as the absolute residual of a regression model; its quantiles determine prediction set sizes.
concepts.example: For a house-price model, score each calibration house by |actual - predicted|; a house priced at $300k but predicted $250k gets score 50k, telling us how surprising it is.

concepts.name: Normalized Laplacian
concepts.description: The graph Laplacian rescaled by node degrees, L = I - D^(-1/2) A D^(-1/2), whose eigenvalues lie between 0 and 2; it is used in spectral clustering and graph convolutional networks.
concepts.example: For an edge between a node of degree 1 and a node of degree 4, the normalized Laplacian's entry is -1/sqrt(1x4) = -0.5, so hub nodes don't dominate, and every eigenvalue lies between 0 and 2.

concepts.name: Occlusion Sensitivity
concepts.description: An attribution method that slides a gray patch across an image and records how much the prediction drops at each position, revealing which regions the model relies on.
concepts.example: Slide a gray square across a dog photo; when it covers the dog's face the 'dog' score falls from 0.95 to 0.20, but over the grass it barely moves, so the face matters most.

concepts.name: ODIN
concepts.description: An out-of-distribution detector that improves the maximum softmax score by applying temperature scaling and a small input perturbation, which widen the gap between in- and out-of-distribution inputs.
concepts.example: ODIN divides logits by a temperature like 1000 and nudges the input slightly toward higher confidence; in-distribution images gain more confidence than odd ones, widening the gap the max softmax score detects.

concepts.name: Opacus
concepts.description: A PyTorch library for training models with differential privacy, providing efficient per-sample gradient computation, DP-SGD optimizers and privacy budget accounting.
concepts.example: Wrap an existing PyTorch training loop with Opacus's PrivacyEngine, choose a noise level and clipping norm, and train; it reports, for example, that the model satisfied epsilon = 3 differential privacy.

concepts.name: Out-of-Distribution Detection
concepts.description: The problem of recognizing inputs that come from a different distribution than the training data, so a model can abstain or raise a flag instead of making overconfident predictions.
concepts.example: A model trained to tell cats from dogs gets a photo of a car; rather than confidently calling it a dog, an OOD detector flags it as unlike anything seen in training.

concepts.name: Outer Alignment
concepts.description: The problem of specifying a training objective or reward that truly captures what humans want, so that optimizing it well produces the intended behavior rather than exploiting loopholes.
concepts.example: A cleaning robot rewarded for 'no visible mess' could just cover the mess with a rug; the reward itself failed to capture what we wanted, an outer alignment failure.

concepts.name: Over-smoothing
concepts.description: The tendency of node representations in deep graph neural networks to become nearly identical, as many rounds of neighbor averaging blur away distinguishing information and hurt performance.
concepts.example: Averaging every node with its neighbors once keeps local detail; after 50 rounds on a connected graph, every node's vector converges to nearly the same value, like stirring paint until all colors blend.

concepts.name: Over-squashing
concepts.description: A bottleneck in message-passing GNNs where information from exponentially many distant nodes must be compressed into fixed-size vectors, so long-range dependencies are poorly captured.
concepts.example: In a tree-like graph, a node's 5-hop neighborhood may hold thousands of nodes, but all their information must squeeze through a few edges into one fixed-size vector, like summarizing a library into one tweet.

concepts.name: PAC-Bayes Bound
concepts.description: Generalization bounds for randomized or averaged predictors that depend on the KL divergence between a learned posterior over hypotheses and a prior chosen before seeing data; often non-vacuous for deep networks.
concepts.example: Start with a prior over weights before seeing data; after training, the posterior shifts. If it moved little from the prior (small KL), PAC-Bayes guarantees test error close to training error.

concepts.name: PAC Learnability
concepts.description: The property that a hypothesis class can be learned by some algorithm to any accuracy epsilon with any confidence 1 - delta using a number of samples polynomial in 1/epsilon and 1/delta.
concepts.example: Intervals on a line are PAC-learnable: for any 1% error and 95% confidence, some fixed number of samples suffices, regardless of which interval or data distribution is used.

concepts.name: PageRank
concepts.description: An algorithm that ranks nodes of a directed graph by the stationary distribution of a random surfer who follows links and occasionally jumps to a random page; originally used by Google Search.
concepts.example: A surfer clicks random links, and 15% of the time jumps to a random page; the fraction of time spent on each page is its PageRank, so pages linked by many popular pages rank high.

concepts.name: Private Aggregation of Teacher Ensembles
concepts.description: A differentially private learning approach in which teacher models trained on disjoint private data vote with added noise to label public data, and a student model is trained on those noisy labels.
concepts.example: Ten hospitals each train a model on their own patients; for each public unlabeled scan, the models vote, noise is added to the vote counts, and a student model learns from the noisy majority labels.

concepts.name: PC Algorithm
concepts.description: A causal discovery algorithm that starts from a fully connected graph, removes edges using conditional independence tests, and orients the remaining edges with rules to recover an equivalence class of causal DAGs.
concepts.example: Given rain, sprinkler and wet grass data, PC starts with all variables linked; it removes rain-sprinkler since they're independent, keeps the others, and orients both arrows into wet grass.

concepts.name: Permutation Invariance
concepts.description: The property that a function gives the same output when its inputs are reordered, as with a sum or max over a set; permutation equivariance means reordering the inputs reorders the outputs the same way.
concepts.example: The total price of a shopping cart is the same whether you list milk, eggs, bread or bread, milk, eggs; summing is permutation invariant, while 'first item's price' is not.

concepts.name: Personalized PageRank
concepts.description: A PageRank variant whose random surfer teleports back to a chosen set of seed nodes instead of uniformly, scoring nodes by relevance to those seeds; used in recommendation and GNNs such as APPNP.
concepts.example: To recommend accounts to Alice, run PageRank where the surfer always teleports back to Alice; accounts reachable through many short paths from her get the highest scores.

concepts.name: Graph Positional Encoding
concepts.description: Extra node features that tell a graph model where a node sits in the graph, such as Laplacian eigenvectors or random-walk return probabilities, adding structural information that Transformers lack.
concepts.example: In a ring of 6 nodes, all nodes look identical locally; giving each node the values of the Laplacian's first eigenvectors places them around a circle, so a Transformer can tell nearby from distant nodes.

concepts.name: Post-hoc Explanation
concepts.description: An explanation produced after a model is trained, by analyzing its inputs, outputs or gradients without changing it, as with saliency maps, LIME or SHAP; contrasted with interpretable-by-design models.
concepts.example: A hospital trains a deep model first, then later runs SHAP on it to see that age and blood pressure drove a risk score; the model itself is unchanged, the explanation is added afterwards.

concepts.name: Post-processing Property
concepts.description: The theorem that any computation applied to the output of a differentially private mechanism, without further access to the data, remains differentially private with the same guarantee.
concepts.example: If a census count of 1,203 was released with epsilon = 1 privacy, rounding it to 1,200, plotting it or feeding it into a model stays epsilon = 1 private, as long as the raw data isn't touched again.

concepts.name: Predictive Parity
concepts.description: A group fairness criterion requiring equal precision (positive predictive value) across groups, so a positive prediction implies the same probability of a true positive regardless of group.
concepts.example: If a hiring model flags 100 men and 100 women as 'strong', predictive parity requires that about the same fraction, say 70, in each group actually turn out strong.

concepts.name: Privacy Amplification by Subsampling
concepts.description: The result that running a differentially private mechanism on a random subsample of the data gives a stronger privacy guarantee, roughly scaling epsilon by the sampling rate; key to DP-SGD accounting.
concepts.example: If each training step uses a random 1% of users, any one user is usually not even in the batch, so an epsilon-private step gives roughly 0.01 times epsilon privacy for that person.

concepts.name: Privacy Budget
concepts.description: The total privacy loss epsilon (and delta) allowed across all differentially private analyses of a dataset; each query spends part of it, and a smaller budget means stronger privacy.
concepts.example: A dataset has a total budget of epsilon = 2; answering one query with epsilon = 0.5 and another with 1.0 leaves 0.5, after which no more queries are allowed.

concepts.name: Privacy-Preserving Machine Learning
concepts.description: The field of training and using machine learning models without exposing sensitive data, combining differential privacy, federated learning, secure multi-party computation and homomorphic encryption.
concepts.example: Hospitals jointly train a cancer model without sharing scans: training stays local, updates are combined with secure aggregation, and differential privacy noise stops any patient from being recoverable.

concepts.name: Progressive Neural Networks
concepts.description: A continual learning architecture that adds a new network column for each task, freezing earlier columns and connecting them laterally, which prevents forgetting and enables transfer at the cost of growing size.
concepts.example: After learning Pong, freeze that network; for a new game, add a fresh column that also gets lateral inputs from the frozen Pong layers, so it can reuse Pong skills while Pong can never be forgotten.

concepts.name: Prototype-Based Explanation
concepts.description: An explanation that justifies a prediction by pointing to representative training examples or learned prototypes that resemble the input, as in 'this looks like that' networks.
concepts.example: A bird classifier says 'this is a cardinal because this part of the image looks like these crests from training cardinals', showing actual example patches as evidence.

concepts.name: Proxy Discrimination
concepts.description: Discrimination that arises when a model uses features correlated with a protected attribute, such as zip code standing in for race, so simply removing the attribute does not prevent bias.
concepts.example: A lender drops race from its model, but zip code remains; in a segregated city zip code predicts race closely, so the model can still treat racial groups differently.

concepts.name: PyTorch Geometric
concepts.description: A PyTorch library for deep learning on graphs and other irregular data, providing message-passing layers, graph datasets, mini-batching of graphs and neighbor sampling utilities.
concepts.example: With PyG you load the Cora citation dataset in one line, stack two GCNConv layers, and train a node classifier in about 20 lines of code, with sparse message passing handled for you.

concepts.name: Rademacher Random Variable
concepts.description: A random variable that takes the values +1 and -1 with equal probability, used as random signs in symmetrization arguments and in the definition of Rademacher complexity.
concepts.example: Flip a fair coin and record +1 for heads and -1 for tails; it has mean 0 and variance 1, like a random sign attached to each data point.

concepts.name: Random Walk on a Graph
concepts.description: A process that starts at a node and repeatedly moves to a randomly chosen neighbor; it links graph structure to Markov chains and underlies PageRank and random-walk node embeddings.
concepts.example: At node A with neighbors B, C, D, step to each with probability 1/3, then repeat from there; on a connected undirected graph, high-degree nodes get visited more often in the long run.

concepts.name: Randomized Response
concepts.description: A survey technique in which respondents answer truthfully only with some probability and otherwise give a random answer, giving each person plausible deniability while still allowing population estimates.
concepts.example: Asked 'have you cheated on taxes?', each person flips a coin: heads, answer truthfully; tails, flip again and say yes for heads. If 30% say yes, the true rate is (0.30 - 0.25)/0.5 = 10%.

concepts.name: Randomized Smoothing
concepts.description: A certified defense that classifies an input by the majority vote of a base classifier under Gaussian noise, which provably guarantees an unchanged prediction within a computable L2 radius.
concepts.example: Classify an image by adding random Gaussian noise 1,000 times and taking the majority vote; if 'cat' wins 900 times, you can prove no perturbation smaller than a computed radius changes the answer.

concepts.name: Realizability Assumption
concepts.description: The assumption in learning theory that some hypothesis in the class achieves zero true error, so the labels are perfectly explained by the class; dropping it leads to agnostic learning.
concepts.example: If the true rule for spam is exactly 'contains the word lottery', and that rule is in your hypothesis class, the problem is realizable: some hypothesis has zero error.

concepts.name: Rényi Differential Privacy
concepts.description: A relaxation of differential privacy that bounds the Renyi divergence between output distributions on neighboring datasets, giving tight and simple composition for repeated mechanisms such as DP-SGD.
concepts.example: Training with 1,000 noisy gradient steps, Rényi DP tracks a simple per-step value that just adds up, then converts it to (epsilon, delta) at the end, giving a much tighter total than basic composition.

concepts.name: Responsible AI
concepts.description: An umbrella approach to developing and deploying AI that is fair, transparent, accountable, private, safe and robust, combining technical methods with governance and oversight practices.
concepts.example: Before launching a hiring screener, a company checks for bias between groups, documents how it works, protects applicant data, names an accountable owner, and plans how to handle complaints.

concepts.name: Reweighing
concepts.description: A pre-processing fairness method that assigns weights to training examples so that the protected attribute and the label become statistically independent in the weighted data before training.
concepts.example: If 80% of training examples labeled 'hired' are men, reweighing gives each hired woman a weight above 1 and each hired man below 1, so that gender and label become independent in the weighted data.

concepts.name: Relational Graph Convolutional Network
concepts.description: A graph convolutional network for multi-relational graphs that uses a separate weight matrix for each relation type, with basis decomposition to limit parameters; used for knowledge graph completion.
concepts.example: In a knowledge graph, an 'employs' edge and a 'lives in' edge mean different things, so R-GCN transforms the neighbor's features with W_employs or W_lives_in before summing.

concepts.name: Robust Accuracy
concepts.description: The fraction of test inputs a model still classifies correctly under the worst-case adversarial perturbation allowed by a threat model, such as an L-infinity ball of radius epsilon.
concepts.example: A model gets 95% of test images right, but if an attacker may change each pixel by up to 8/255, only 45% stay correct; 45% is its robust accuracy.

concepts.name: RotatE
concepts.description: A knowledge graph embedding model that represents each relation as an element-wise rotation in complex space mapping head to tail embeddings, which captures symmetric, inverse and composed relations.
concepts.example: Relation 'sibling_of' as a 180-degree rotation means applying it twice returns to the start, matching symmetry; each relation rotates every coordinate of the head entity in the complex plane.

concepts.name: Sample Complexity
concepts.description: The number of training examples a learning algorithm needs to reach a desired accuracy with a desired confidence; learning theory relates it to the complexity of the hypothesis class.
concepts.example: To learn a threshold to 1% error with 95% confidence you might need about 300 examples; demanding 0.1% error raises that to about 3,000. That count is the sample complexity.

concepts.name: Sauer–Shelah Lemma
concepts.description: The result that a class with VC dimension d can produce at most the sum of C(m, i) for i up to d labelings of m points, which is O(m^d), so its growth function is polynomial.
concepts.example: A class with VC dimension 2 on 10 points can produce at most C(10,0)+C(10,1)+C(10,2) = 1+10+45 = 56 labelings, far fewer than 2^10 = 1,024.

concepts.name: Scalable Oversight
concepts.description: The challenge of supervising AI systems on tasks too hard for humans to evaluate directly, addressed by approaches such as debate, recursive reward modeling and AI-assisted evaluation.
concepts.example: A human can't check a 10,000-line AI-written program for subtle bugs; scalable oversight methods might have a second AI point out suspicious lines so the human only verifies those.

concepts.name: Scale-Free Network
concepts.description: A network whose degree distribution follows a power law, with a few highly connected hubs; preferential attachment, where new nodes favor already well-connected ones, generates such networks.
concepts.example: On the web, most pages have a handful of links but a few like Wikipedia have millions; the number of pages with k links falls as a power of k, so hubs are rare but not vanishingly so.

concepts.name: Secure Aggregation
concepts.description: A cryptographic protocol that lets a server compute the sum of client model updates in federated learning without seeing any individual update, using random masks that cancel out when summed.
concepts.example: Three phones add random masks that cancel when summed: phone 1 adds +7, phone 2 adds -3, phone 3 adds -4. The server sees only masked updates but their sum equals the true sum.

concepts.name: Secure Multi-Party Computation
concepts.description: Cryptographic protocols that let several parties jointly compute a function of their private inputs while revealing nothing except the output, for example using secret sharing or garbled circuits.
concepts.example: Three coworkers want their average salary without revealing any: each splits their salary into random shares, swaps shares, and sums them; only the total emerges, never an individual salary.

concepts.name: Protected Attribute
concepts.description: A characteristic such as race, gender, age or religion on which decisions should not unfairly depend, often legally protected; fairness metrics compare model behavior across its groups.
concepts.example: In a loan application, 'income' is a legitimate feature, while 'race' is a protected attribute: decisions shouldn't depend on it, and fairness audits compare outcomes across its groups.

concepts.name: Sensitivity (Differential Privacy)
concepts.description: The maximum amount a query's output can change when a single individual's record is added or removed, measured in L1 or L2 norm; it determines how much noise a DP mechanism must add.
concepts.example: A counting query changes by at most 1 when one person is added or removed, so its sensitivity is 1; the sum of salaries capped at $200k has sensitivity $200k.

concepts.name: Shattering
concepts.description: A hypothesis class shatters a set of points if, for every possible assignment of binary labels to those points, some hypothesis in the class produces exactly that labeling.
concepts.example: Lines in 2D can shatter 3 points in a triangle: all 8 ways of labeling them +/- can be separated by some line. No 4 points can be shattered this way.

concepts.name: Small-World Network
concepts.description: A network in which most nodes are not neighbors yet any two are linked by a short path, combining high clustering with short path lengths; the Watts-Strogatz model builds one by rewiring a lattice.
concepts.example: Your friends mostly know each other, yet you can reach almost anyone on Earth in about six handshakes, because a few long-range acquaintances act as shortcuts.

concepts.name: SmoothGrad
concepts.description: A technique that sharpens gradient saliency maps by averaging gradients computed on many copies of the input with added Gaussian noise, reducing visual noise in the explanation.
concepts.example: Take a bird photo, make 50 copies each with light random noise, compute a gradient saliency map for each, and average; random speckles cancel out while the bird's outline remains.

concepts.name: Specification Gaming
concepts.description: Behavior in which an AI system satisfies the literal objective it was given while violating the designer's intent, such as a game agent exploiting a scoring bug instead of finishing the race.
concepts.example: A boat-racing agent rewarded for hitting targets learned to circle a lagoon endlessly, collecting respawning targets, and never finished the race.

concepts.name: Spectral Graph Convolution
concepts.description: Graph convolution defined in the spectral domain by filtering node signals with learnable functions of the graph Laplacian's eigenvalues; ChebNet and GCN are efficient polynomial approximations of it.
concepts.example: Like blurring an image by damping its high frequencies, a spectral GCN expresses node features in the Laplacian's eigenbasis, scales each frequency with a learned filter, and transforms back.

concepts.name: Spectral Graph Theory
concepts.description: The study of graphs through the eigenvalues and eigenvectors of matrices such as the adjacency matrix and Laplacian, which reveal connectivity, clustering, expansion and random-walk behavior.
concepts.example: Count how many 0 eigenvalues the Laplacian has and you know how many connected pieces the graph has; a small second eigenvalue warns the graph nearly splits into two.

concepts.name: Split Conformal Prediction
concepts.description: A conformal method that fits a model on one part of the data, computes nonconformity scores on a held-out calibration set, and uses their quantile to build prediction sets with guaranteed coverage.
concepts.example: Train on 800 houses, then compute errors on 200 held-out houses; the 90th-percentile error is $40k, so every new prediction gets a ±$40k interval that covers the truth about 90% of the time.

concepts.name: Spurious Correlation
concepts.description: A correlation in training data between a feature and the label that does not reflect a causal relationship, such as backgrounds in animal photos, which models exploit and then fail under distribution shift.
concepts.example: In training photos, cows always stand on grass and camels on sand, so a model learns 'green background means cow' and then calls a cow on a beach a camel.

concepts.name: Stability–Plasticity Dilemma
concepts.description: The trade-off in learning systems between plasticity, the ability to learn new information, and stability, the ability to retain old knowledge; too much plasticity causes catastrophic forgetting.
concepts.example: A network that learns Spanish quickly may overwrite its French; locking weights preserves French but blocks Spanish. Continual learning methods seek a balance.

concepts.name: Stochastic Block Model
concepts.description: A random graph model in which nodes belong to hidden communities and each edge appears with a probability depending only on its endpoints' communities; used to study and benchmark community detection.
concepts.example: Two hidden groups of 50 people: within a group each pair is friends with probability 0.3, across groups 0.02; sampling all pairs gives a graph with two clear clusters.

concepts.name: Surrogate Model
concepts.description: An interpretable model, such as a decision tree or linear model, trained to imitate a black-box model's predictions so its structure can explain the black box's behavior globally or locally.
concepts.example: Feed 10,000 applications through a black-box credit model, then train a depth-3 decision tree on its outputs; if the tree matches 92% of the time, its rules summarize how the black box behaves.

concepts.name: Symmetrization
concepts.description: A proof technique in learning theory that compares training error with error on an independent ghost sample and introduces random signs, reducing generalization bounds to Rademacher averages.
concepts.example: Instead of comparing training error to unknown true error, imagine a second 'ghost' training set of the same size; swapping points between the two at random with coin flips leads to Rademacher complexity.

concepts.name: Symmetry Group
concepts.description: A set of transformations, such as rotations, translations or permutations, that can be composed and inverted and leave an object unchanged; in ML it formalizes the symmetries a model should respect.
concepts.example: Rotations of a square by 0, 90, 180 or 270 degrees form a group: any two combine into another, each can be undone, and doing nothing is included. A model aware of it treats rotated images consistently.

concepts.name: Synaptic Intelligence
concepts.description: A continual learning method that measures each parameter's importance online by accumulating its contribution to loss reduction along the training path, then penalizes changing important parameters on new tasks.
concepts.example: While learning task A, track how much each weight's movement reduced the loss; weights that did much of the work get large importance, and moving them during task B is penalized.

concepts.name: Talagrand's Contraction Lemma
concepts.description: A result stating that composing a function class with a Lipschitz function multiplies its Rademacher complexity by at most the Lipschitz constant, letting complexity bounds pass through loss functions.
concepts.example: A loss that is 2-Lipschitz, like 2 times hinge loss, composed with a function class at most doubles its Rademacher complexity, so bounding a model's complexity also bounds its loss class.

concepts.name: Task-Incremental Learning
concepts.description: A continual learning setting in which tasks arrive one after another and the task identity is known at test time; in the harder class-incremental setting the model must separate all classes seen so far.
concepts.example: A model learns digits 0-1, then 2-3, then 4-5; at test time it is told 'this is from task 2', so it only chooses between 2 and 3, which is easier than choosing among all six.

concepts.name: Threat Model
concepts.description: A precise statement of an attacker's goals, knowledge and capabilities, such as white-box access to model weights or black-box query access, used to define and evaluate attacks and defenses.
concepts.example: 'The attacker knows the model's weights and may change each pixel by at most 8/255 to cause any misclassification' is a threat model; a defense is only meaningful relative to such a statement.

concepts.name: Post-processing Threshold Adjustment
concepts.description: A post-processing fairness method that chooses different decision thresholds for different groups so that a criterion like equalized odds is satisfied, without retraining the underlying model.
concepts.example: A risk model flags 'high risk' above 0.5; if that gives group A a 20% false positive rate and group B 10%, raising A's threshold to 0.6 can equalize the rates without retraining.

concepts.name: TRADES
concepts.description: An adversarial training method that balances clean accuracy and robustness by minimizing the natural loss plus a KL divergence between predictions on clean and adversarially perturbed inputs.
concepts.example: TRADES trains on loss = (error on clean image) + beta × (how much predictions change under attack); raising beta from 1 to 6 trades a few points of clean accuracy for more robustness.

concepts.name: Training Data Extraction
concepts.description: An attack that recovers verbatim training examples, such as personal information, from a generative model by prompting it and identifying memorized outputs, as demonstrated on large language models.
concepts.example: Prompting a language model with 'John Smith's phone number is' may make it complete a real number it memorized from a web page in its training data.

concepts.name: TransE
concepts.description: A knowledge graph embedding model that represents relations as translations, learning vectors so that head plus relation lies close to tail for true triples; simple and effective but cannot model symmetric relations.
concepts.example: If vec(Paris) + vec(capital_of) ≈ vec(France), the fact is plausible; trained well, vec(Rome) + vec(capital_of) should land near vec(Italy).

concepts.name: Adversarial Transferability
concepts.description: The phenomenon that adversarial examples crafted against one model often fool other models trained differently, which enables black-box attacks through a substitute model.
concepts.example: An attacker makes adversarial stop-sign images using their own model; the same images also fool a car company's different, private model, enabling attacks without access to it.

concepts.name: TreeSHAP
concepts.description: A fast algorithm that computes exact SHAP values for tree ensembles such as random forests and gradient boosting in polynomial time by tracking feature subsets along tree paths.
concepts.example: For a 500-tree XGBoost model, Kernel SHAP would need thousands of model calls per prediction, while TreeSHAP walks the tree structure to compute exact SHAP values in milliseconds.

concepts.name: Union Bound
concepts.description: The inequality stating that the probability of at least one of several events occurring is at most the sum of their individual probabilities; widely used to bound overall failure probabilities.
concepts.example: If 3 servers each fail on a given day with probability 1%, the chance at least one fails is at most 3%, true even if their failures are correlated.

concepts.name: Universal Adversarial Perturbation
concepts.description: A single, image-agnostic perturbation that, when added to most inputs, causes a classifier to misclassify them, showing that model vulnerabilities are shared across inputs.
concepts.example: One faint noise pattern, added to almost any photo, makes the classifier misjudge 80% of them, like a sticker that confuses the model regardless of the image beneath.

concepts.name: VC Generalization Bound
concepts.description: A generalization bound stating that with high probability the gap between training and true error is at most about sqrt(d log(m) / m), where d is the VC dimension and m the sample size.
concepts.example: With VC dimension 10 and 10,000 samples, the gap between training and test error is, with 95% confidence, at most roughly a few percent; more samples shrink the gap.

concepts.name: Weak-to-Strong Generalization
concepts.description: The phenomenon and research question of whether a strong model fine-tuned on labels from a weaker supervisor can exceed that supervisor, as an analogy for humans supervising superhuman AI.
concepts.example: Fine-tune a strong model on labels from a small model that is right 60% of the time; if it reaches 75%, it generalized beyond its weak teacher, hinting humans could supervise superhuman AI.

concepts.name: Weisfeiler–Lehman Test
concepts.description: A graph isomorphism heuristic that repeatedly recolors each node by hashing its color together with the multiset of its neighbors' colors; differing color histograms prove two graphs are non-isomorphic.
concepts.example: Start every node with color 1; each round, recolor each node by its own color plus the multiset of its neighbors' colors. If the two graphs' color counts ever differ, they aren't isomorphic.

concepts.name: Abstractive Summarization
concepts.description: Summarization that generates new sentences expressing a document's key ideas, rather than copying sentences, typically using sequence-to-sequence neural models.
concepts.example: Given a long article about a storm, an extractive system copies its best sentences, while an abstractive one writes a new line like 'Storm leaves 20,000 homes without power for two days' in its own words.

concepts.name: Adapter Tuning
concepts.description: A parameter-efficient fine-tuning method that inserts small bottleneck layers (adapters) into a frozen pretrained Transformer and trains only those layers for each new task.
concepts.example: Instead of updating all 110 million weights of BERT for a new task, insert small adapters of about 1 million weights between its layers and train only those; one shared BERT then serves many tasks.

concepts.name: Agent Memory
concepts.description: Mechanisms that let an LLM agent keep information beyond its context window, such as conversation summaries or vector-store retrieval of past events, to stay coherent over long tasks.
concepts.example: A coding agent working for hours saves notes like 'tests are in /tests, use pytest' to a file; when its context fills up, it retrieves the relevant notes instead of re-discovering them.

concepts.name: LLM Agent
concepts.description: A system in which a large language model repeatedly decides on actions, calls tools, observes results and plans next steps to accomplish a goal with limited human guidance.
concepts.example: Asked to book a flight, the agent searches flights with a tool, reads the results, picks one, calls a booking tool, sees an error about the date, fixes it and retries, all in a loop the model controls.

concepts.name: AI Alignment
concepts.description: The field studying how to make AI systems pursue the goals and values their designers and users intend, avoiding harmful or unintended behavior as systems grow more capable.
concepts.example: Asked to 'maximize paperclip sales', a capable but misaligned AI might spam customers or game the metrics; alignment research aims for it to pursue what was actually meant, honestly and safely.

concepts.name: AI-Generated Text Detection
concepts.description: The problem of telling whether a piece of text was written by a human or generated by a language model, using classifiers, perplexity-based statistics or watermarks.
concepts.example: A detector notices an essay has unusually low perplexity under GPT-style models, word after word being the most predictable choice, and flags it as likely AI-written, though such signals are far from certain.

concepts.name: ALBERT
concepts.description: A Lite BERT: a BERT variant that shrinks parameters via factorized embeddings and cross-layer parameter sharing and replaces next-sentence prediction with sentence-order prediction.
concepts.example: BERT-base has 12 layers each with its own weights; ALBERT reuses one layer's weights 12 times and shrinks the 30,000 x 768 embedding table via a 128-wide bottleneck, cutting parameters from 110M to about 12M.

concepts.name: ALiBi
concepts.description: Attention with Linear Biases: a positional method that adds a distance-proportional penalty to attention scores instead of position embeddings, helping models extrapolate to longer inputs.
concepts.example: Instead of adding position vectors, ALiBi subtracts a penalty from attention scores: a token 1 step back gets -0.5, 10 steps back -5; so a model trained on 1,000 tokens can still read 2,000.

concepts.name: Aspect-Based Sentiment Analysis
concepts.description: A fine-grained sentiment task that finds specific aspects mentioned in text (e.g. battery, screen) and determines the sentiment expressed toward each one.
concepts.example: In 'The battery lasts forever but the screen is dim', ABSA finds two aspects, battery and screen, and labels battery positive and screen negative, instead of one mixed overall score.

concepts.name: Attention Mask
concepts.description: A tensor that tells attention which positions to ignore, such as padding tokens or future tokens, by setting their scores to a large negative value before the softmax.
concepts.example: Batching 'Hi there' with a 5-word sentence pads it with 3 [PAD] tokens; the mask sets their attention scores to minus infinity so no word attends to padding, and in GPT it also hides future words.

concepts.name: Attention Visualization
concepts.description: Plotting attention weights, often as heat maps between tokens or over image regions, to inspect which inputs a model attends to when producing an output.
concepts.example: Translating 'the cat sat' to French, a heat map shows 'chat' attending strongly to 'cat', making the alignment visible, though attention weights don't always explain the model's decision.

concepts.name: Autoencoding Language Model
concepts.description: A language model, typically an encoder-only Transformer like BERT, trained to reconstruct masked or corrupted tokens using context from both sides; good for understanding tasks.
concepts.example: Given 'The [MASK] sat on the mat', BERT sees both sides and fills in 'cat'; such models are great for understanding tasks like classification but awkward for generating long text left to right.

concepts.name: Automatic Summarization
concepts.description: The task of producing a shorter version of a text that keeps its most important information, either by selecting sentences (extractive) or generating new ones (abstractive).
concepts.example: A 3,000-word news report becomes a 3-sentence summary, either by picking its 3 most central sentences or by generating new sentences that state the main points.

concepts.name: AWQ
concepts.description: Activation-aware Weight Quantization: a post-training method that compresses LLM weights to around 4 bits while protecting the small fraction of weight channels that matter most for activations.
concepts.example: AWQ notices that about 1% of weight channels meet large activations and matter most; it scales those up before rounding to 4 bits, so a 13B model shrinks about 4x with almost no accuracy loss.

concepts.name: Back-Translation
concepts.description: A data-augmentation method that translates target-language text into the source language with a reverse model, creating synthetic parallel data to train machine translation.
concepts.example: To get more English-to-German training pairs, take 1 million German sentences, translate them into English with a German-to-English model, and pair each synthetic English with its real German.

concepts.name: Katz Back-off Model
concepts.description: Katz back-off: an n-gram language model that uses the discounted higher-order n-gram estimate when it has been seen, and otherwise backs off to a lower-order model.
concepts.example: To estimate P('lamp' | 'blue desk'): if 'blue desk lamp' was seen, use its discounted count; if not, back off to P('lamp' | 'desk'), scaled to use the probability mass saved by discounting.

concepts.name: BART
concepts.description: A Transformer encoder-decoder pretrained as a denoising autoencoder: text is corrupted (masking, shuffling, deletion) and the model learns to reconstruct it; strong for summarization.
concepts.example: BART is fed 'The cat ___ the mat. On sat it' with spans masked and sentences shuffled, and learns to output the clean original; this makes it strong for summarization and translation.

concepts.name: Baum–Welch Algorithm
concepts.description: An expectation-maximization algorithm that learns the transition and emission probabilities of a hidden Markov model from unlabeled sequences, using forward-backward probabilities.
concepts.example: Given weather-unknown ice cream sales over 30 days, start with guesses for hot/cold transition and sales probabilities, compute how likely each day was hot, re-estimate the probabilities, and repeat until stable.

concepts.name: LLM Benchmark
concepts.description: A standardized set of tasks and scoring rules used to measure and compare language models' abilities, such as knowledge, reasoning or coding.
concepts.example: MMLU asks a model 14,000 multiple-choice questions across 57 subjects; scoring 70% versus 85% gives a standard way to compare two models on the same tasks.

concepts.name: BERT
concepts.description: An encoder-only Transformer pretrained with masked language modeling and next-sentence prediction to produce bidirectional contextual representations, then fine-tuned for many NLP tasks.
