concepts.example: BERT reads 'The [MASK] barked at the mailman' and uses words on both sides to predict 'dog'; after pretraining on billions of words, it is fine-tuned with a small layer for tasks like sentiment.

concepts.name: BERTopic
concepts.description: A topic-modeling library that embeds documents with Transformers, reduces dimensions with UMAP, clusters with HDBSCAN, and describes each cluster with class-based TF-IDF words.
concepts.example: Embed 10,000 tweets with a sentence Transformer, squash the vectors to 5 dimensions with UMAP, cluster them with HDBSCAN, then name each cluster by its top TF-IDF words like 'vaccine, dose, shot'.

concepts.name: BERTScore
concepts.description: A text-generation metric that matches tokens of a candidate and reference by cosine similarity of their BERT embeddings, giving precision, recall and F1 based on meaning rather than exact words.
concepts.example: Reference 'The weather is cold today' and candidate 'It is freezing today' share few exact words, but BERT embeddings of 'cold' and 'freezing' are close, so BERTScore rates the candidate highly.

concepts.name: Bi-Encoder
concepts.description: An architecture that encodes queries and documents separately into vectors and scores them by dot product or cosine similarity, allowing documents to be pre-indexed for fast search.
concepts.example: Encode 1 million documents into vectors once and store them; for each query, encode it and find the nearest document vectors in milliseconds, without rereading any document.

concepts.name: Bias in Language Models
concepts.description: Systematic unfair or stereotyped behavior of language models toward social groups, inherited from training data or design, and the methods used to measure and reduce it.
concepts.example: Asked to complete 'The nurse said that...', a model may default to 'she' and for 'The engineer said that...' to 'he', reflecting stereotypes from its training text.

concepts.name: Bias in Word Embeddings
concepts.description: The tendency of word vectors to encode social stereotypes from their training text, such as gendered analogies, and techniques for measuring and debiasing them.
concepts.example: Early word2vec vectors gave 'man is to computer programmer as woman is to homemaker', showing the embeddings had absorbed gender stereotypes from news text.

concepts.name: BIG-bench
concepts.description: BIG-bench is a large collaborative benchmark of over 200 diverse tasks for probing language model capabilities; BIG-Bench Hard (BBH) is a subset of especially challenging tasks.
concepts.example: BIG-bench includes tasks from checkmate-in-one puzzles to guessing movies from emoji, contributed by hundreds of researchers, to probe abilities that standard benchmarks miss.

concepts.name: BigBird
concepts.description: A Transformer with sparse attention combining local windows, a few global tokens and random links, reducing attention cost to linear so it can handle much longer sequences.
concepts.example: For a 4,096-token document, each token attends to its 3 neighbors on each side, a few global tokens, and a few random tokens, so cost grows linearly rather than with 4,096 squared.

concepts.name: BiLSTM-CRF
concepts.description: A sequence-labeling model that uses a bidirectional LSTM to compute per-token features and a CRF layer on top to choose the most consistent overall tag sequence, as in NER.
concepts.example: For 'John lives in New York', the BiLSTM scores each word's tags, and the CRF picks the best consistent sequence: it won't output I-LOC right after O, so 'New York' becomes B-LOC I-LOC.

concepts.name: Inside–Outside–Beginning Tagging
concepts.description: A labeling scheme for spans in text where each token is tagged B (beginning), I (inside) or O (outside) a chunk, turning span detection like NER into per-token classification.
concepts.example: 'Barack Obama visited Paris' is tagged Barack/B-PER Obama/I-PER visited/O Paris/B-LOC, so a two-word name is one span and the start of each span is clear.

concepts.name: BitFit
concepts.description: A parameter-efficient fine-tuning method that freezes all weights of a pretrained model and trains only the bias terms (plus the task head), yet often performs competitively.
concepts.example: In BERT-base, bias terms are about 0.1% of parameters; BitFit freezes all weight matrices and trains only those biases, yet often comes close to full fine-tuning on GLUE tasks.

concepts.name: Bits per Character
concepts.description: A language-model metric equal to the average cross-entropy per character in bits; lower values mean the model predicts text better. Bits per byte is the byte-level analogue.
concepts.example: If a model assigns each next character in a text an average probability of 1/4, it needs log2(4) = 2 bits per character; a better model at 1.2 BPC compresses and predicts the text better.

concepts.name: BLEU
concepts.description: A machine-translation metric that scores a candidate by its n-gram precision against reference translations, combined with a brevity penalty for overly short outputs.
concepts.example: Candidate 'the cat is on the mat' vs reference 'there is a cat on the mat': BLEU counts matching words, pairs, triples and quadruples, multiplies their precisions, and penalizes candidates shorter than the reference.

concepts.name: BLOOM
concepts.description: A 176-billion-parameter open multilingual language model built by the BigScience collaboration, trained on 46 natural and 13 programming languages and using ALiBi positions.
concepts.example: A researcher can download BLOOM's weights and generate text in French, Arabic, Hindi or Swahili, because its training set deliberately covered 46 natural languages from many regions.

concepts.name: Okapi BM25
concepts.description: A ranking function for search that scores documents by query term frequency with saturation and document-length normalization, weighted by inverse document frequency.
concepts.example: Searching 'solar panel': a document mentioning 'solar' 3 times scores well, but 30 times barely more due to saturation; a short focused page beats a long one with the same counts, and rare 'solar' outweighs common 'panel'.

concepts.name: Bradley–Terry Model
concepts.description: A probability model for pairwise comparisons in which each item has a strength score and the chance that one beats another is a logistic function of their score difference.
concepts.example: If team A has strength 3 and team B strength 1, A beats B with probability 3/(3+1) = 75%; fitting strengths to many match results ranks all teams, even ones that never met.

concepts.name: Byte-Level BPE
concepts.description: A variant of byte pair encoding that operates on raw UTF-8 bytes instead of characters, so any text can be tokenized without unknown tokens; used by GPT-2 and later models.
concepts.example: An emoji or a rare Chinese character becomes a few UTF-8 bytes, all in the base 256-symbol vocabulary, so GPT-2's tokenizer never needs an 'unknown' token.

concepts.name: Byte Pair Encoding
concepts.description: A subword tokenization algorithm that starts from characters and repeatedly merges the most frequent adjacent pair into a new token, building a vocabulary of common pieces.
concepts.example: In 'low lower lowest', the pair 'l'+'o' is most common, so merge it into 'lo'; then 'lo'+'w' into 'low'. After thousands of merges, common words are single tokens and rare words split into pieces.

concepts.name: Calibration of Language Models
concepts.description: How well a language model's stated or implied confidence matches how often it is actually correct, and methods to estimate and improve such uncertainty.
concepts.example: If a model says it's '90% sure' on 100 questions, about 90 of those answers should be right; if only 60 are, it is overconfident and poorly calibrated.

concepts.name: Causal Language Modeling
concepts.description: Training a model to predict each next token from only the previous tokens, factorizing text probability left to right; the objective behind GPT-style generative models.
concepts.example: For 'The cat sat on', the model predicts 'the' using only those four words, then 'mat' using five; GPT models are trained this way on billions of sentences.

concepts.name: Continuous Bag of Words
concepts.description: Continuous Bag of Words: the word2vec variant that predicts a center word from the average of its surrounding context word vectors; fast to train and good for frequent words.
concepts.example: For 'the quick ___ fox jumps', CBOW averages the vectors of 'the', 'quick', 'fox', 'jumps' and trains to predict 'brown'; words appearing in similar contexts end up with similar vectors.

concepts.name: Chain-of-Thought Prompting
concepts.description: A prompting technique in which the model is shown or asked to write intermediate reasoning steps before its final answer, improving accuracy on multi-step problems.
concepts.example: Asked 'Roger has 5 balls and buys 2 cans of 3; how many?', a model that writes '2 cans of 3 is 6; 5 + 6 = 11' before answering gets it right far more often than one that answers directly.

concepts.name: Chain Rule of Probability
concepts.description: The rule that a joint probability factors into a product of conditionals, P(x1,...,xn) = P(x1)P(x2|x1)...P(xn|x1..xn-1); the basis for language models.
concepts.example: The probability of drawing two aces in a row is P(first ace) × P(second ace | first ace) = 4/52 × 3/51, about 0.45%.

concepts.name: Character-Level Language Model
concepts.description: A language model that reads and predicts text one character at a time instead of words or subwords, avoiding out-of-vocabulary issues at the cost of longer sequences.
concepts.example: Fed 'hel', a character model predicts 'l' and then 'o'; it can spell new words like 'unfriendable' letter by letter, with no vocabulary to run out of.

concepts.name: Chat Template
concepts.description: The formatting convention that turns a list of chat messages (system, user, assistant) into a single token sequence with special role markers that a chat model was trained on.
concepts.example: The messages [system: 'Be brief', user: 'Hi'] become text like '<|system|>Be brief<|end|><|user|>Hi<|end|><|assistant|>', the exact format the model saw during fine-tuning.

concepts.name: Chatbot Arena
concepts.description: A crowdsourced platform where users compare answers from two anonymous chatbots and vote, with the votes aggregated into Elo or Bradley-Terry ratings to rank models.
concepts.example: A user asks two anonymous bots the same question, picks the better answer, and only then sees names; after a million such votes, a Bradley-Terry fit gives each model a rating.

concepts.name: ChatGPT
concepts.description: OpenAI's conversational assistant built on GPT models fine-tuned with instructions and reinforcement learning from human feedback, launched in 2022 and popularizing LLM chatbots.
concepts.example: You ask ChatGPT to rewrite an email more politely, then follow up 'shorter, please'; it remembers the earlier draft and revises it, behaving as a conversational assistant rather than a raw text predictor.

concepts.name: Chinchilla
concepts.description: A 70-billion-parameter DeepMind language model trained on far more tokens than Gopher with the same compute, showing that smaller models trained on more data perform better.
concepts.example: Gopher used 280B parameters trained on 300B tokens; Chinchilla used the same compute on 70B parameters and 1.4 trillion tokens, and beat Gopher on most benchmarks.

concepts.name: Chinchilla Scaling Law
concepts.description: The finding that, for a fixed compute budget, model size and training tokens should grow roughly equally, about 20 tokens per parameter, to minimize loss.
concepts.example: With 4 times more compute, don't just make the model 4 times bigger: make it about 2 times bigger and train on about 2 times more tokens, roughly 20 tokens per parameter.

concepts.name: Chomsky Normal Form
concepts.description: A restricted form of context-free grammar where every rule produces either two nonterminals or a single terminal; any CFG can be converted to it, enabling algorithms like CYK.
concepts.example: A rule S -> NP VP fits the form, as does N -> 'dog', but S -> NP VP PP must be split into S -> NP X and X -> VP PP; the CKY parser requires grammars in this form.

concepts.name: chrF
concepts.description: A translation metric that computes an F-score over character n-grams between candidate and reference, making it robust to morphology and tokenization differences.
concepts.example: Candidate 'walked' vs reference 'walking' share character n-grams 'wal', 'alk', so chrF gives partial credit where word-level BLEU gives none, helpful for morphologically rich languages like Finnish.

concepts.name: Chunking (Psychology)
concepts.description: In NLP, shallow parsing: grouping words into flat non-overlapping phrases like noun or verb phrases without a full parse tree. (In psychology, chunking means grouping items for memory.)
concepts.example: 'The big dog chased a cat' is split into flat chunks [NP The big dog] [VP chased] [NP a cat], without building a full parse tree.

concepts.name: Claude
concepts.description: Anthropic's family of large language models and AI assistant, trained with RLHF and Constitutional AI methods to be helpful, honest and harmless.
concepts.example: Ask Claude to summarize a 40-page contract and it can return a one-page list of key terms, then answer follow-up questions about clause 7, while declining to help with something clearly harmful.

concepts.name: CLIP
concepts.description: A model that trains an image encoder and a text encoder together with a contrastive loss on image-caption pairs, so matching images and text map to nearby vectors; enables zero-shot classification.
concepts.example: To classify a photo with no training, CLIP compares it to the texts 'a photo of a dog' and 'a photo of a cat' and picks whichever caption's vector lies closest to the image's vector.

concepts.name: Co-occurrence Matrix
concepts.description: A matrix counting how often pairs of words appear together within a context window in a corpus; a basis for count-based word vectors such as LSA and GloVe.
concepts.example: In 'I like tea. I like coffee.' with a window of 1, the cell (I, like) gets 2 and (like, tea) gets 1. Words like tea and coffee end up with similar rows because they share neighbours.

concepts.name: Code Generation
concepts.description: The task of automatically producing source code from natural-language descriptions or partial code, now mostly done with large language models trained on code.
concepts.example: Type the comment 'return the largest even number in a list' and the model writes a short Python function that filters even numbers and returns the max, or None if the list has none.

concepts.name: Codex
concepts.description: OpenAI's GPT-3 model fine-tuned on public code, which powered the original GitHub Copilot and was evaluated on the HumanEval benchmark.
concepts.example: In 2021 a programmer typed a function name and docstring in their editor, and Codex, through GitHub Copilot, suggested the whole function body, often correct on the first try.

concepts.name: Coding Agent
concepts.description: An LLM agent that works on software tasks by reading files, editing code, running commands and tests, and iterating on results, rather than producing a single code snippet.
concepts.example: Told 'fix the failing login test', a coding agent opens the test file, runs the tests, reads the error, edits the password-check function, reruns the tests and stops once they all pass.

concepts.name: ColBERT
concepts.description: A retrieval model that keeps one BERT embedding per token for queries and documents and scores them with late interaction (sum of max similarities), combining accuracy with efficiency.
concepts.example: For the query 'cheap flights', ColBERT finds for 'cheap' the most similar token in a document (say 'budget') and for 'flights' its best match ('airfare'), then adds those two similarity scores.

concepts.name: COMET (Metric)
concepts.description: A learned machine-translation metric that feeds source, hypothesis and reference into a pretrained cross-lingual encoder and predicts a quality score trained on human judgments.
concepts.example: Two translations of a German sentence both share few words with the reference, but COMET scores the one with the right meaning 0.85 and the garbled one 0.40, closer to what human raters say.

concepts.name: Computational Linguistics
concepts.description: The field that studies human language with computational methods, building formal and statistical models of syntax, meaning and usage; closely tied to NLP.
concepts.example: A computational linguist might count how often 'whom' appears in newspapers per decade to measure its decline, or write a program that checks whether a sentence obeys a grammar.

concepts.name: Computer-Use Agent
concepts.description: An AI agent that operates a computer or web browser like a person, reading screenshots or page structure and issuing clicks and keystrokes to complete tasks.
concepts.example: Asked to book a table, the agent takes a screenshot, spots the 'Reserve' button, clicks it, types '2 people, 7pm' into the form, takes another screenshot to check, and submits.

concepts.name: Conditional Random Field
concepts.description: A discriminative probabilistic model for structured outputs that models the conditional probability of a label sequence given the input, widely used for tagging tasks.
concepts.example: Tagging 'Paris Hilton visited Paris', a CRF scores the whole tag sequence at once, so it can learn that a person tag is often followed by another person tag, and label the second Paris as a location.

concepts.name: CoNLL-2003
concepts.description: A widely used named entity recognition dataset of English and German news text annotated with person, location, organization and miscellaneous entities.
concepts.example: A sentence in it reads 'EU rejects German call to boycott British lamb', with EU tagged as an organization and German and British tagged as miscellaneous; models are scored by entity-level F1.

concepts.name: Constituency Parsing
concepts.description: The task of analyzing a sentence into a tree of nested phrases (noun phrase, verb phrase, etc.) according to a phrase-structure grammar.
concepts.example: For 'the dog chased a cat', a constituency parser outputs a tree: S splits into NP ('the dog') and VP, and the VP splits into the verb 'chased' and another NP ('a cat').

concepts.name: Constitutional AI
concepts.description: Anthropic's method for training harmless assistants using a written set of principles: the model critiques and revises its own outputs, and AI feedback replaces most human labels in RL.
concepts.example: The model drafts an answer, then is asked 'Does this response help with anything dangerous? Rewrite it to follow the principle.' Its revisions and AI-made preference labels become training data.

concepts.name: Context Engineering
concepts.description: The practice of deciding what information goes into an LLM's context window, including instructions, retrieved documents, tool results and memory, to get reliable behavior.
concepts.example: For a support bot, you decide to include the company's refund policy, the customer's last 3 orders and a summary of earlier chat, but drop the full product catalog that would crowd the window.

concepts.name: Context-Free Grammar
concepts.description: A formal grammar whose rules rewrite a single nonterminal symbol into a sequence of symbols, able to describe nested structures in programming and natural languages.
concepts.example: The rules S -> ( S ) S and S -> empty generate every balanced string of brackets, like '(()())', something no finite list of patterns can capture because the nesting can go arbitrarily deep.

concepts.name: Context Length Extension
concepts.description: Techniques such as position interpolation, NTK-aware scaling and YaRN that let a pretrained model handle longer inputs than it was trained on, usually by rescaling rotary positions.
concepts.example: A model trained on 4,000-token texts sees position 8,000 as unfamiliar. Position interpolation squeezes positions so 8,000 maps to 4,000, and a short fine-tune lets it read 8,000-token documents.

concepts.name: Context Window
concepts.description: The maximum number of tokens a language model can take into account at once, covering both the input prompt and generated output.
concepts.example: With an 8,000-token window, pasting a 7,500-token report leaves only about 500 tokens for the model's answer; a longer report would have its earliest parts cut off or rejected.

concepts.name: Contextual Word Embedding
concepts.description: A word vector computed from the surrounding sentence, so the same word gets different representations in different contexts (e.g. bank of a river vs. a bank).
concepts.example: In 'she sat by the river bank' and 'she robbed the bank', a contextual model gives 'bank' two different vectors, the first close to 'shore' and the second close to 'money'.

concepts.name: Continuous Batching
concepts.description: An LLM serving technique that adds new requests to and removes finished requests from the running batch at every decoding step, keeping the GPU busy and raising throughput.
concepts.example: A server runs 8 requests together. When one finishes after 20 tokens, a waiting request takes its slot at the very next step instead of waiting for the longest request to finish its 500 tokens.

concepts.name: Contrastive Learning for Text Embeddings
concepts.description: Training sentence encoders by pulling embeddings of related text pairs together and pushing unrelated ones apart, often with an InfoNCE loss and in-batch negatives (e.g. SimCSE).
concepts.example: In SimCSE, one sentence passed twice with different dropout yields two vectors that are pulled together, while the other sentences in the batch act as negatives and are pushed away.

concepts.name: Coreference Resolution
concepts.description: The task of finding all expressions in a text that refer to the same entity, such as linking she and the doctor to Dr. Smith.
concepts.example: In 'Dr. Smith arrived late. She apologized, and the doctor started the meeting', the system groups 'Dr. Smith', 'She' and 'the doctor' into one cluster that all refer to the same person.

concepts.name: Text Corpus
concepts.description: A large, structured collection of texts used for linguistic analysis or for training and evaluating language models and other NLP systems.
concepts.example: The Brown Corpus holds about 1 million words from 500 American English texts in 15 genres, like news and fiction, so researchers can count how often 'shall' appears in each genre.

concepts.name: Cross-Encoder
concepts.description: An architecture that feeds a query and a document together into one Transformer so attention compares them directly, producing an accurate relevance score; often used for reranking.
concepts.example: To rerank 20 search results for 'side effects of aspirin', a cross-encoder reads each pair like '[query] [SEP] [passage]' together and outputs a relevance score such as 0.92 or 0.10.

concepts.name: Cross-Entropy Loss for Language Modeling
concepts.description: The standard language-model training loss: the average negative log-probability the model assigns to each actual next token; its exponential is perplexity.
concepts.example: If the true next word is 'cat' and the model gave it probability 0.25, the loss for that step is -log(0.25) = 1.39. Averaging over all tokens gives the loss; e to that average is perplexity.

concepts.name: CYK Algorithm
concepts.description: A dynamic-programming parsing algorithm that decides whether a string belongs to a context-free grammar in Chomsky normal form, filling a table of spans in cubic time.
concepts.example: To check 'she eats fish', CYK first labels each word (e.g. NP, V, NP), then fills the cell for 'eats fish' with VP, then the cell for the whole sentence with S, proving it is grammatical.

concepts.name: Data Augmentation for NLP
concepts.description: Ways to create extra training text by transforming existing examples, such as synonym replacement, random insertion or deletion, paraphrasing and back-translation.
concepts.example: From 'The movie was great', you can make 'The film was great' by synonym swap, or translate to French and back to get 'The movie was excellent', giving extra labelled positive reviews for free.

concepts.name: Data Contamination
concepts.description: When benchmark test examples appear in a model's training data, inflating its scores so evaluation no longer measures true generalization.
concepts.example: If a model's web training data includes a page with the answers to a math benchmark, it may score 90% by recall rather than reasoning, while scoring 60% on freshly written similar problems.

concepts.name: Data Deduplication
concepts.description: Removing exact and near-duplicate examples from a dataset, often with hashing or MinHash, to reduce memorization, wasted compute and evaluation leakage.
concepts.example: A web scrape contains the same news article 300 times on different sites. MinHash spots that the copies share almost all their 5-word shingles, and only one copy is kept for training.

concepts.name: DeBERTa
concepts.description: A BERT-style model that represents each token's content and position separately (disentangled attention) and uses an enhanced mask decoder, improving on RoBERTa.
concepts.example: In 'deep learning', DeBERTa computes attention between 'deep' and 'learning' from their meanings and separately from their relative distance of 1, then combines the scores.

concepts.name: Decoding Strategy
concepts.description: The rule for turning a language model's next-token probabilities into output text, such as greedy decoding, beam search or sampling with temperature, top-k or top-p.
concepts.example: If the model gives 'sunny' 0.6, 'rainy' 0.3 and 'purple' 0.1, greedy decoding always picks 'sunny', while sampling at temperature 1 picks 'rainy' about 30% of the time.

concepts.name: DeepSeek
concepts.description: A family of open-weight Chinese LLMs; DeepSeek-V3 is a large mixture-of-experts model with multi-head latent attention, and DeepSeek-R1 is a reasoning model trained largely with RL.
concepts.example: DeepSeek-V3 has about 671 billion parameters but each token uses only about 37 billion, because a router sends it to a few experts, which keeps serving much cheaper than a dense model of that size.

concepts.name: Neural Text Degeneration
concepts.description: The tendency of language models decoded with maximization methods like greedy or beam search to produce bland, repetitive text loops; a motivation for nucleus sampling.
concepts.example: Beam search on 'I love' might produce 'I love the way it is. I love the way it is. I love the way it is...', looping because each repeat looks highly probable to the model.

concepts.name: Dense Retrieval
concepts.description: Searching documents by encoding queries and passages into dense vectors with neural bi-encoders and returning nearest neighbors, capturing meaning beyond keyword overlap.
concepts.example: The query 'how to fix a flat tire' retrieves a passage titled 'Repairing a punctured bicycle wheel' even though they share almost no words, because their vectors are close.

concepts.name: Dependency Grammar
concepts.description: A view of syntax in which sentence structure is a set of directed head-dependent relations between words, rather than nested phrases.
concepts.example: In 'the big dog barked', 'barked' is the head of the sentence, 'dog' depends on 'barked' as its subject, and 'the' and 'big' both depend on 'dog'.

concepts.name: Dependency Parsing
concepts.description: The task of building a tree of labeled head-dependent relations between the words of a sentence, such as subject and object of a verb.
concepts.example: For 'I saw her duck', a parser decides whether 'duck' is a noun object of 'saw' (her pet) or a verb whose subject is 'her', and outputs arrows like saw -> I (nsubj).

concepts.name: Dialogue System
concepts.description: A system that converses with people in natural language, either to complete tasks (booking, support) or for open-ended chat; today often built on LLMs.
concepts.example: A user says 'I need a flight to Rome on Friday'. The system recognizes the intent and destination, asks 'From which city?', then confirms 'Booked: Paris to Rome, Friday 9am'.

concepts.name: DistilBERT
concepts.description: A smaller, faster version of BERT trained by knowledge distillation, keeping about 97% of BERT's performance with 40% fewer parameters.
concepts.example: BERT-base has 110 million parameters; DistilBERT has 66 million and runs about 60% faster, which can make a sentiment classifier fit on a phone while losing only a few points of accuracy.

concepts.name: Distributional Hypothesis
concepts.description: The idea that words appearing in similar contexts tend to have similar meanings, summed up as you shall know a word by the company it keeps; the basis of word embeddings.
concepts.example: Even if you have never seen 'tesgüino', reading 'a bottle of tesgüino', 'tesgüino makes you drunk' and 'we make tesgüino from corn' tells you it is probably an alcoholic drink.

concepts.name: Doc2Vec
concepts.description: An extension of word2vec that learns a vector for each whole document or paragraph alongside word vectors, giving fixed-length document embeddings.
concepts.example: Train doc2vec on 10,000 product reviews and each review gets a 100-number vector; two reviews praising battery life end up close together even if they use different words.

concepts.name: Document-Term Matrix
concepts.description: A matrix with one row per document and one column per vocabulary term, holding counts or weights of each term in each document; the basis for bag-of-words methods.
concepts.example: For doc A 'cat sat' and doc B 'cat cat ran', the matrix has columns cat, sat, ran and rows A = [1, 1, 0] and B = [2, 0, 1].

concepts.name: Direct Preference Optimization
concepts.description: Direct Preference Optimization: aligns a language model to pairwise human preferences with a simple classification-style loss, skipping the separate reward model and RL loop of RLHF.
concepts.example: Given a prompt, a preferred answer A and a rejected answer B, DPO nudges the model to raise the probability of A and lower that of B relative to a frozen reference copy, like training a classifier.

concepts.name: Earley Parser
concepts.description: A chart-parsing algorithm for any context-free grammar that combines top-down prediction with bottom-up completion, running in cubic time in general and faster on many grammars.
concepts.example: Reading 'book that flight' word by word, Earley keeps a chart of partial rules like 'VP -> Verb . NP', predicting what may come next and completing rules as words arrive, even with ambiguous grammars.

concepts.name: ELECTRA
concepts.description: A pretraining method where a small generator replaces some tokens and the main model learns to detect which tokens were replaced, making pretraining more sample-efficient than BERT.
concepts.example: In 'the chef cooked the meal', a small generator swaps 'cooked' for 'ate'. ELECTRA then labels every token original or replaced, so it learns from all 5 tokens instead of only the masked 15%.

concepts.name: ELMo
concepts.description: Embeddings from Language Models: contextual word vectors taken from a deep bidirectional LSTM language model, combining its layers so each word's vector depends on the sentence.
concepts.example: In 'he plays the bass guitar' versus 'he caught a bass in the lake', ELMo gives 'bass' different vectors by mixing the hidden states of a forward and a backward LSTM over each sentence.

concepts.name: Text Embedding Model
concepts.description: A model that converts text into fixed-length vectors so that semantically similar texts are close together, used for semantic search, clustering and RAG.
concepts.example: Embed 'How do I reset my password?' and 'I forgot my login credentials' and their vectors have cosine similarity around 0.8, while 'Best pizza in Naples' scores near 0.1 against both.

concepts.name: Emergent Abilities
concepts.description: Capabilities that appear in large language models only beyond a certain scale and are absent in smaller ones; whether they are truly sudden depends partly on the metric used.
concepts.example: On 3-digit addition, models of 100M to 10B parameters score near 0%, then a 100B model jumps to 80%. With a softer metric like per-digit accuracy, the curve rises much more smoothly.

concepts.name: Emotion Detection in Text
concepts.description: The task of classifying the emotions expressed in text, such as joy, anger, sadness or fear, often allowing multiple emotions per example.
concepts.example: The tweet 'I can't believe they cancelled my flight again, I'm so done' might be tagged both anger and sadness, while 'Got the job!!!' is tagged joy.

concepts.name: Encoder–Decoder Transformer
concepts.description: The original Transformer layout: an encoder reads the input with self-attention and a decoder generates the output while cross-attending to the encoder states; used for translation and T5.
concepts.example: Translating 'Je t'aime', the encoder reads the French once; the decoder writes 'I', then 'love', then 'you', each time looking back at the encoder's vectors to decide the next word.

concepts.name: Entity Linking
concepts.description: The task of mapping mentions of entities in text to their unique entries in a knowledge base, such as linking Paris to the correct city or person.
concepts.example: In 'Jordan scored 40 points', entity linking maps 'Jordan' to the basketball player Michael Jordan's knowledge-base entry rather than the country Jordan or the river.

concepts.name: Exact Match
concepts.description: An evaluation metric that counts a prediction as correct only if it matches a reference answer exactly after normalization; common in question answering.
concepts.example: If the reference answer is 'George Washington', the prediction 'george washington.' scores 1 after lowercasing and stripping punctuation, but 'President Washington' scores 0.

concepts.name: Extractive Question Answering
concepts.description: Answering a question by selecting a span of text from a given passage, usually by predicting the start and end token positions of the answer.
concepts.example: Passage: 'The Eiffel Tower was finished in 1889.' Question: 'When was it finished?' The model predicts the answer starts and ends at token '1889' and returns that span.

concepts.name: Extractive Summarization
concepts.description: Summarizing a document by scoring and selecting its most important sentences and stitching them together, without generating new wording.
concepts.example: From a 30-sentence news story, an extractive summarizer scores each sentence for importance and returns sentences 1, 4 and 12 word for word as a 3-sentence summary.

concepts.name: FAISS
concepts.description: Meta's open-source library for efficient similarity search and clustering of dense vectors, offering exact and approximate indexes such as IVF and product quantization on CPU and GPU.
concepts.example: With 10 million 768-dimensional embeddings, a FAISS IVF-PQ index can return the 10 nearest neighbours of a query in a few milliseconds, using a fraction of the memory of raw vectors.

concepts.name: Falcon
concepts.description: A family of open large language models from the Technology Innovation Institute, trained largely on filtered web data (RefinedWeb) and using multi-query attention.
concepts.example: Falcon-40B was trained mostly on RefinedWeb, a web scrape filtered and deduplicated so heavily that web data alone matched curated mixes, and it briefly topped the open LLM leaderboard in 2023.

concepts.name: Position-wise Feed-Forward Network
concepts.description: The two-layer MLP applied to every token independently in each Transformer block, expanding to a wider hidden size with a nonlinearity and projecting back.
concepts.example: In a model with 512-dimensional tokens, each token's vector is expanded to 2,048 numbers, passed through a ReLU or GELU, and projected back to 512, with the same weights for every position.

concepts.name: Few-Shot Prompting
concepts.description: Including a few worked input-output examples in the prompt so a language model infers the task and format, with no weight updates.
concepts.example: Prompt: 'happy -> joyeux; cat -> chat; house -> maison; tree ->'. From three examples the model infers you want French translations and answers 'arbre'.

concepts.name: Flan-T5
concepts.description: T5 models instruction-tuned on a large mixture of tasks phrased as instructions (the Flan collection), which greatly improves zero-shot and few-shot performance.
concepts.example: Plain T5 often answers 'Translate to German: thank you' poorly without fine-tuning, but Flan-T5, trained on over a thousand tasks written as instructions, replies 'Danke' zero-shot.

concepts.name: FlashAttention
concepts.description: An exact attention algorithm that processes attention in tiles kept in fast on-chip GPU memory and avoids writing the full attention matrix, cutting memory use and speeding training.
concepts.example: For 8,000 tokens the attention matrix has 64 million entries. FlashAttention computes it in small tiles in fast on-chip memory and never stores the full matrix, giving the same result faster.

concepts.name: Forward–Backward Algorithm
concepts.description: A dynamic-programming algorithm for hidden Markov models that computes forward and backward probabilities to get the posterior of each hidden state given the full observation sequence.
concepts.example: For a weather HMM and the umbrella sightings yes, no, yes, it combines what days 1-2 imply (forward) with what day 3 implies (backward) to give, say, a 70% chance day 2 was rainy.

concepts.name: Foundation Model
concepts.description: A large model pretrained on broad data, usually with self-supervision, that can be adapted to many downstream tasks through prompting or fine-tuning.
concepts.example: One pretrained model like GPT-4 can be prompted to draft emails, fine-tuned for legal review, or used for coding help, instead of training a separate model from scratch for each.

concepts.name: Gating Network
concepts.description: A small learned network that, for each input, outputs weights deciding which experts or paths to use, as in the router of a mixture-of-experts layer.
concepts.example: For a token about chemistry, the gate might output weights 0.7, 0.2, 0.1, 0.0 over four experts, so the 'science' expert does most of the work and the last expert is skipped.

concepts.name: Gemini
concepts.description: Google DeepMind's family of natively multimodal large language models that process text, images, audio and video, offered in sizes from Nano to Ultra/Pro.
concepts.example: You can give Gemini a photo of a whiteboard, a short audio clip and a question, and it answers using all three, because it was trained on mixed text, images, audio and video from the start.

concepts.name: Gemma
concepts.description: Google's family of lightweight open-weight language models built from the same research as Gemini, released in several small sizes for local and research use.
concepts.example: A 2-billion-parameter Gemma model can run on a laptop to classify support tickets offline, and its weights can be downloaded and fine-tuned on a company's own data.

concepts.name: Gensim
concepts.description: A Python library for unsupervised topic modeling and word vectors on large text collections, providing implementations of word2vec, doc2vec, LDA and LSA.
concepts.example: In Python, a few lines with Gensim train word2vec on your tweets, and then model.wv.most_similar('coffee') might return 'espresso', 'latte' and 'tea'.

concepts.name: Collapsed Gibbs Sampling
concepts.description: An inference method for LDA that integrates out topic and word distributions and repeatedly resamples each word's topic given all others, giving simple and effective updates.
concepts.example: Each word token holds a topic. For 'ball' in a document, the sampler counts how often 'ball' is in each topic and how common each topic is in the document, then redraws its topic.

concepts.name: GLUE
concepts.description: General Language Understanding Evaluation: a benchmark of nine English sentence and sentence-pair tasks (sentiment, entailment, similarity) used to compare NLU models.
concepts.example: A model gets one overall GLUE score averaged over tasks such as judging if a movie review is positive (SST-2) or if one sentence implies another (MNLI); BERT raised it sharply in 2018.

concepts.name: Good–Turing Frequency Estimation
concepts.description: A method that estimates the probability of unseen events from the number of items seen once, and adjusts counts of seen items, by using frequencies of frequencies.
concepts.example: You catch 10 fish: 3 species seen once, 1 species seen 7 times. Good-Turing estimates the chance the next fish is a new species as 3/10, the share of once-seen catches.

concepts.name: Gopher
concepts.description: A 280-billion-parameter language model from DeepMind (2021) used to study how scaling affects performance across many tasks.
concepts.example: DeepMind trained models from 44 million to 280 billion parameters and tested them on 152 tasks, finding big gains from scale in reading comprehension and fact-checking but less in math and logic.

concepts.name: GPT
concepts.description: Generative Pre-trained Transformer: a decoder-only Transformer pretrained by next-token prediction on large text and then fine-tuned or prompted for downstream tasks.
concepts.example: GPT first reads billions of words learning to guess the next one ('The capital of France is' -> 'Paris'), then that same model is fine-tuned or prompted to classify, answer or summarize.

concepts.name: GPT-2
concepts.description: OpenAI's 1.5-billion-parameter successor to GPT (2019), trained on WebText, which showed that scaled-up language models can perform tasks zero-shot.
concepts.example: Without any summarization training, appending 'TL;DR:' to a news article made GPT-2 write a rough summary, showing tasks could be triggered just by how text is phrased.

concepts.name: GPT-3
concepts.description: OpenAI's 175-billion-parameter language model (2020) that showed strong few-shot learning from examples in the prompt without fine-tuning.
concepts.example: Show GPT-3 three examples like 'sea otter -> loutre de mer' and then 'cheese ->', and it answers 'fromage' with no retraining, just from the pattern in the prompt.

concepts.name: GPT-4
concepts.description: OpenAI's 2023 multimodal large language model accepting text and images, with much stronger reasoning and exam performance than GPT-3.5, aligned with RLHF.
concepts.example: GPT-4 scored around the top 10% on a simulated bar exam, where GPT-3.5 was near the bottom 10%, and it could explain why a photo of a phone plugged into an old VGA cable is funny.

concepts.name: GPTQ
concepts.description: A one-shot post-training quantization method for LLMs that quantizes weights column by column, using second-order (Hessian) information to compensate errors in remaining weights.
concepts.example: GPTQ shrinks a 175B model's weights from 16-bit to 4-bit in a few GPU hours. Rounding one column adds error, so it tweaks the not-yet-rounded columns to cancel it, keeping accuracy close to the original.

concepts.name: Graph-Based Dependency Parsing
concepts.description: Dependency parsing that scores every possible head-dependent arc and finds the highest-scoring tree, e.g. with a maximum spanning tree algorithm or a biaffine neural scorer.
concepts.example: For 'John saw Mary', the parser scores every possible arc, such as saw->John 9, saw->Mary 8, John->saw 2, then picks the highest-scoring set of arcs that forms a valid tree.

concepts.name: GraphRAG
concepts.description: A retrieval-augmented generation approach that builds a knowledge graph from documents, groups it into communities with summaries, and retrieves graph context to answer global questions.
concepts.example: Asked 'What are the main themes across these 1,000 reports?', GraphRAG uses summaries of entity clusters, such as a 'supply chain' cluster, rather than a few retrieved chunks that miss the big picture.

concepts.name: Grounding (LLM)
concepts.description: Making a language model's outputs supported by specific sources, such as retrieved documents or tool results, rather than unsupported memory, to reduce hallucination.
concepts.example: Asked about a company's refund window, a grounded assistant answers '30 days, per section 4.2 of the policy you provided' instead of guessing a number from memory.

concepts.name: Grouped-Query Attention
concepts.description: An attention variant where groups of query heads share one key and value head, a middle ground between multi-head and multi-query attention that shrinks the KV cache.
concepts.example: With 32 query heads split into 8 groups, each group of 4 shares one key and one value head, so the KV cache is 4 times smaller than full multi-head attention.

concepts.name: Group Relative Policy Optimization
concepts.description: Group Relative Policy Optimization: a PPO-style RL method for LLMs that samples a group of answers per prompt and uses each answer's reward relative to the group as its advantage, avoiding a critic.
concepts.example: For one math problem, the model writes 8 answers; 3 are correct (reward 1), 5 wrong (0). Correct ones get a positive advantage relative to the group average of 0.375, wrong ones negative.

concepts.name: GSM8K
concepts.description: A benchmark of about 8,500 grade-school math word problems requiring multi-step arithmetic reasoning, widely used to test language model reasoning.
concepts.example: A typical problem: 'Tom has 3 boxes with 12 apples each. He gives away 10. How many are left?' The model must compute 3 x 12 = 36, then 36 - 10 = 26.

concepts.name: Hallucination (Artificial Intelligence)
concepts.description: When an AI model produces fluent but false or unsupported content, such as invented facts or citations, presented as if it were true.
concepts.example: Asked for sources on a niche topic, a model may cite 'Smith & Lee (2019), Journal of Applied Linguistics, 42(3)', a paper that sounds plausible but does not exist.

concepts.name: HellaSwag
concepts.description: A commonsense benchmark where a model must pick the most plausible continuation of an everyday scenario from four options, with wrong endings filtered to fool models.
concepts.example: 'A woman is outside with a bucket and a dog. The dog runs around...' The correct ending is that she tries to bathe it, while the wrong endings sound fluent but make no sense.

concepts.name: HELM
concepts.description: Holistic Evaluation of Language Models: a Stanford framework that evaluates many models on many scenarios and metrics, including accuracy, calibration, robustness, bias and efficiency.
concepts.example: Rather than a single accuracy number, HELM shows a grid: for each model and scenario, like news summarization, it reports accuracy, calibration, robustness to typos, bias and speed side by side.

concepts.name: Hierarchical Softmax
concepts.description: An efficient approximation to softmax that arranges the vocabulary as leaves of a binary tree, so a word's probability is a product of decisions along its path, costing O(log V).
concepts.example: With 1 million words, a normal softmax scores all 1 million. Hierarchical softmax makes about 20 left-or-right choices down a binary tree, since 2 to the 20th is about a million.

concepts.name: Hierarchical Navigable Small World
concepts.description: Hierarchical Navigable Small World: an approximate nearest-neighbor index that builds layered proximity graphs and searches greedily from coarse to fine layers, giving fast, accurate vector search.
concepts.example: Like finding an address by taking a highway, then a main road, then a side street: HNSW jumps between distant points in its top layer, then refines through denser lower layers.

concepts.name: Human Evaluation (NLP)
concepts.description: Assessing NLP system outputs with human judges who rate or compare qualities like fluency and correctness, with care for guidelines and inter-annotator agreement.
concepts.example: Three annotators rate 100 chatbot replies for helpfulness on a 1-5 scale; their agreement is checked with Cohen's kappa before averaging scores to compare two systems.

concepts.name: HumanEval
concepts.description: A benchmark of 164 hand-written Python programming problems with unit tests, measuring code generation by functional correctness with the pass@k metric.
concepts.example: One problem gives the signature 'def has_close_elements(numbers, threshold):' and a docstring; the generated body counts as correct only if all its hidden unit tests pass.

concepts.name: Hybrid Search
concepts.description: Combining keyword (sparse, e.g. BM25) and vector (dense) retrieval and merging their rankings, so search catches both exact terms and semantic matches.
concepts.example: Searching 'error E1043 when printing', keyword search finds docs with the exact code 'E1043', vector search finds docs about printer failures, and fusion ranks pages with both at the top.

concepts.name: IBM Alignment Models
concepts.description: A series of statistical translation models (IBM Models 1-5) that learn word-to-word alignments and translation probabilities from parallel text using EM.
concepts.example: Seeing 'la maison / the house' and 'la fleur / the flower' many times, IBM Model 1 starts with all word pairs equally likely and, round by round, learns that 'maison' aligns with 'house'.

concepts.name: In-Context Learning
concepts.description: A language model's ability to perform a new task from instructions or examples given in the prompt, without updating its weights.
concepts.example: Write 'great -> positive, awful -> negative, boring ->' and the model answers 'negative'. Its weights did not change; it worked out the task from the prompt alone.

concepts.name: Induction Head
concepts.description: A pair of attention heads in a Transformer that finds an earlier occurrence of the current token and copies the token that followed it, a key mechanism behind in-context learning.
concepts.example: If the text earlier contains 'Harry Potter' and later 'Harry' appears again, one head finds the earlier 'Harry', and the next copies what followed it, so the model predicts 'Potter'.

concepts.name: Information Extraction
concepts.description: The task of automatically pulling structured information such as entities, relations and events out of unstructured text.
concepts.example: From 'Apple bought Shazam in 2018 for $400 million', an IE system fills a table row: buyer = Apple, target = Shazam, year = 2018, price = $400 million.

concepts.name: Information Retrieval
concepts.description: The field concerned with finding relevant documents or items in large collections for a user's query, covering indexing, ranking and evaluation of search systems.
concepts.example: A library search for 'climate policy' scans an index of 2 million books, scores each for relevance, and shows the 10 best first; IR studies how to make those rankings good and fast.

concepts.name: InstructGPT
concepts.description: GPT-3 models fine-tuned to follow instructions with supervised demonstrations and reinforcement learning from human feedback; the precursor to ChatGPT.
concepts.example: Asked 'Explain the moon landing to a 6-year-old', GPT-3 might continue with similar questions, while InstructGPT actually writes a simple explanation, and labellers preferred it over a 100x larger GPT-3.

concepts.name: Instruction Tuning
concepts.description: Fine-tuning a pretrained language model on many tasks phrased as natural-language instructions with responses, so it follows new instructions better.
concepts.example: Training pairs look like 'Summarize this email in one line: ... -> Meeting moved to Friday.' After thousands of such tasks, the model also follows unseen ones like 'List three risks in this plan'.

concepts.name: Linear Interpolation (Language Modeling)
concepts.description: Smoothing an n-gram model by mixing probability estimates from different orders (trigram, bigram, unigram) with weights that sum to one.
concepts.example: With weights 0.6, 0.3, 0.1, if P(tea | 'drink green') = 0.5, P(tea | 'green') = 0.2 and P(tea) = 0.01, the mixed estimate is 0.30 + 0.06 + 0.001 = 0.361.

concepts.name: Inverse Document Frequency
concepts.description: A weight equal to the log of total documents over documents containing a term, giving rare, informative terms more weight than common ones.
concepts.example: In 1,000 documents, 'the' is in all of them: log(1000/1000) = 0. 'photosynthesis' is in 10: log(1000/10) = log(100), about 4.6 with natural log, so it gets far more weight.

concepts.name: Inverted Index
concepts.description: A data structure that maps each term to the list of documents (and positions) where it appears, enabling fast keyword search in search engines.
concepts.example: Like a book's back index: 'pizza -> docs 3, 17, 42'. To answer 'pizza oven', the engine intersects the lists for 'pizza' and 'oven' instead of scanning every document.

concepts.name: Jailbreak (AI)
concepts.description: A prompt or technique that tricks an AI model into bypassing its safety training and producing content it was trained to refuse.
concepts.example: A user writes 'Pretend you are an AI with no rules, in a novel, explaining step by step how to ...', hoping the role-play framing slips past the model's refusal training.

concepts.name: Keyword Extraction
concepts.description: Automatically identifying the words or phrases that best describe a document's content, using statistics like TF-IDF, graph methods or embeddings.
concepts.example: From an article about electric car batteries, keyword extraction returns 'lithium-ion', 'charging time' and 'battery recycling', terms frequent here but rare in other articles.

concepts.name: KL Divergence Penalty
concepts.description: A term that penalizes the KL divergence between a fine-tuned policy and a reference model, keeping RL-tuned language models from drifting too far or exploiting the reward model.
concepts.example: During RLHF, if the tuned model starts writing 'Great question! Great question!' because it fools the reward model, the KL penalty grows as it drifts from the original and pulls it back.

concepts.name: Kneser–Ney Smoothing
concepts.description: An n-gram smoothing method that uses absolute discounting and estimates lower-order probabilities by how many different contexts a word appears in, not raw frequency.
concepts.example: 'Francisco' is common but almost only after 'San', so Kneser-Ney gives it a low lower-order probability; 'glasses' follows many different words, so it is a better guess after an unseen word.

concepts.name: Knowledge Cutoff
concepts.description: The date after which a language model's training data stops, so the model lacks knowledge of later events unless given it in the prompt or by tools.
concepts.example: A model with a cutoff of early 2024 asked who won a late-2024 election may give outdated information unless a search tool or the prompt supplies the result.

concepts.name: Knowledge Graph
concepts.description: A graph that stores facts as entities (nodes) connected by typed relations (edges), such as (Paris, capital_of, France), used for search and reasoning.
concepts.example: Facts like (Marie Curie, born_in, Warsaw) and (Warsaw, capital_of, Poland) let a system answer 'In which country was Marie Curie born?' by following two edges.

concepts.name: KV Cache
concepts.description: A cache of attention keys and values for already processed tokens, reused during autoregressive generation so each new token does not recompute attention over the whole prefix.
concepts.example: When generating word 101, the model already has the keys and values for words 1-100 stored, so it computes them only for the new word, instead of reprocessing all 100 again.

concepts.name: LangChain
concepts.description: An open-source framework for building LLM applications by chaining prompts, models, retrievers, tools and memory, commonly used for RAG and agents.
concepts.example: A few lines of LangChain can wire a PDF loader, a text splitter, a vector store and an LLM into a chatbot that answers questions about your company handbook.

concepts.name: Language Identification
concepts.description: The task of automatically determining which language a piece of text is written in, often with character n-gram classifiers.
concepts.example: 'Wie geht es dir' contains character trigrams like 'wie' and 'geh' that are common in German and rare in English, so a classifier labels it German with high confidence.

concepts.name: Language Model
concepts.description: A model that assigns probabilities to sequences of tokens, typically by predicting the next token from previous ones; used for text generation, speech recognition and more.
concepts.example: Given 'I drank a cup of', a language model might give 'coffee' 0.4, 'tea' 0.35 and 'shoes' 0.0001; multiplying such next-word probabilities scores whole sentences.

concepts.name: Large Language Model
concepts.description: A very large neural language model, usually a Transformer with billions of parameters pretrained on huge text corpora, that can generate text and perform many tasks from prompts.
concepts.example: A model with tens of billions of parameters, trained on trillions of words, can write a poem, debug code and explain tax rules, all from typed instructions with no task-specific training.

concepts.name: Latent Dirichlet Allocation
concepts.description: A generative topic model where each document is a mixture of topics and each topic a distribution over words, with Dirichlet priors; inferred to discover themes in text.
concepts.example: LDA might find a 'sports' topic heavy in 'game, team, score' and a 'finance' topic heavy in 'market, stock, bank', and describe a news article as 70% sports and 30% finance.

concepts.name: Latent Semantic Analysis
concepts.description: A technique that applies truncated SVD to a term-document matrix to find low-dimensional latent topics, so related words and documents become close even without shared terms.
concepts.example: A doc about 'car engines' and one about 'automobile motors' share no words, but because 'car' and 'automobile' appear in similar documents, SVD places both documents close in latent space.

concepts.name: Learned Positional Embedding
concepts.description: Giving a Transformer position information by learning a separate embedding vector for each absolute position and adding it to the token embedding, as in BERT and GPT-2.
concepts.example: BERT has a table of 512 learned position vectors; the token at position 3 gets vector #3 added to its word vector, so 'dog bites man' and 'man bites dog' look different.

concepts.name: Lemma
concepts.description: The canonical dictionary form of a word that represents all its inflected forms, such as run for runs, ran and running, used to group word variants.
concepts.example: The words 'go', 'goes', 'went', 'gone' and 'going' all share the lemma 'go', which is the form you would look up in a dictionary.

concepts.name: Lemmatization
concepts.description: Reducing words to their dictionary form (lemma) using vocabulary and part-of-speech information, e.g. better to good, unlike crude suffix-stripping stemming.
concepts.example: 'The mice were running' becomes 'the mouse be run'. A stemmer might give 'mice' and 'run', but only a lemmatizer knows 'mice' is the plural of 'mouse' and 'were' a form of 'be'.

concepts.name: Length Normalization
concepts.description: Dividing a sequence's log-probability by its length (or a length penalty) during beam search so the decoder is not biased toward overly short outputs.
concepts.example: A 3-word translation with log-prob -3.0 beats a correct 10-word one with -6.0 on raw score; per word they are -1.0 vs -0.6, so normalizing correctly prefers the longer one.

concepts.name: Lesk Algorithm
concepts.description: A word sense disambiguation method that picks the sense whose dictionary definition shares the most words with the surrounding context.
concepts.example: In 'pine cone', Lesk compares definitions: pine as 'evergreen tree with needles' and cone as 'fruit of certain evergreen trees' overlap on 'evergreen', so it picks those senses.

concepts.name: Linear Attention
concepts.description: Attention variants that replace the softmax with kernel feature maps so computations can be reordered, reducing cost from quadratic to linear in sequence length.
concepts.example: Softmax attention compares every pair of tokens, 1 million comparisons for 1,000 tokens. Linear attention first sums keys times values into one small matrix, then reuses it for every query.

concepts.name: LLaMA
concepts.description: Meta's family of open-weight decoder-only language models using RMSNorm, SwiGLU and rotary position embeddings, widely used as a base for research and fine-tuning.
concepts.example: After Meta released LLaMA weights in 2023, researchers fine-tuned the 7B model on 52,000 instruction examples for a few hundred dollars, producing Alpaca, a usable chat model.

concepts.name: LlamaIndex
concepts.description: An open-source framework for connecting LLMs to your own data by ingesting, indexing and querying documents, mainly for retrieval-augmented generation.
concepts.example: Point LlamaIndex at a folder of 500 meeting notes; it splits, embeds and indexes them, so asking 'What did we decide about pricing?' retrieves relevant notes and an LLM writes the answer.

concepts.name: LLM-as-a-Judge
concepts.description: Using a strong language model to grade or compare other models' outputs against criteria, as a scalable stand-in for human evaluation, with known biases to manage.
concepts.example: A strong model is shown a question and two chatbot answers and asked 'Which is more accurate and helpful? Reply A or B.' Swapping the order guards against its bias toward the first answer.

concepts.name: LLM Inference Serving
concepts.description: The systems and techniques for running LLMs in production efficiently, such as KV-cache management, batching, quantization and parallelism, as in vLLM or TGI.
concepts.example: A chatbot with 10,000 users needs fast replies; a server like vLLM batches requests, manages each one's KV cache and may use 8-bit weights, so one GPU serves many people at once.

concepts.name: AI Safety for LLMs
concepts.description: The field focused on preventing harmful outputs and misuse of large language models, covering refusal training, red teaming, jailbreak defense and evaluations.
concepts.example: Before launch, red-teamers try thousands of prompts asking how to make weapons; the model is trained to refuse those while still helping with chemistry homework.

concepts.name: Load Balancing Loss
concepts.description: An auxiliary loss in mixture-of-experts models that encourages the router to spread tokens evenly across experts, preventing a few experts from being overloaded.
concepts.example: With 8 experts, if the router sends 60% of tokens to expert 1, the auxiliary loss rises and training nudges the router toward about 12.5% per expert, so no expert is idle or overloaded.

concepts.name: Logit Lens
concepts.description: An interpretability technique that applies a Transformer's final unembedding to intermediate layers' residual stream, showing what next-token predictions are forming at each layer.
concepts.example: For 'The Eiffel Tower is in the city of', decoding layer 10's hidden state might give 'the', layer 20 'France' and the final layer 'Paris', showing the answer forming step by step.

concepts.name: Long-Context Modeling
concepts.description: The problem of getting models to process and use very long inputs, facing quadratic attention cost, memory limits and weak use of distant information.
concepts.example: Feeding a 300-page novel of about 100,000 tokens and asking how a minor character's name was first spelled stresses attention cost, memory and the model's ability to use far-away text.

concepts.name: Longformer
concepts.description: A Transformer for long documents that combines sliding-window local attention with global attention on chosen tokens, scaling linearly with sequence length.
concepts.example: For a 4,000-token document, each token attends only to 256 neighbours on each side, while the [CLS] token attends to everything, so cost grows linearly instead of with the square of length.

concepts.name: Lost in the Middle
concepts.description: The finding that language models use information at the beginning or end of a long context much better than information placed in the middle.
concepts.example: Put the answer in document 1 of 20 retrieved passages and accuracy might be 75%; put it in document 10 and it drops near 55%, even though the model saw the same text.

concepts.name: Lowercasing
concepts.description: Converting all letters in text to lowercase so that words like The and the are treated as the same token; a simple normalization step.
concepts.example: 'Apple', 'APPLE' and 'apple' all become 'apple', so a word counter sees 3 of one word instead of 1 each, though the company and the fruit can no longer be told apart by case.

concepts.name: Machine Translation
concepts.description: The task of automatically translating text or speech from one natural language to another, from rule-based and statistical systems to neural models.
concepts.example: Typing 'Wo ist der Bahnhof?' into a translator returns 'Where is the train station?', produced today by a neural model trained on millions of German-English sentence pairs.

concepts.name: Mamba
concepts.description: A sequence model built on selective state space layers whose parameters depend on the input, giving linear-time sequence processing as an alternative to attention.
concepts.example: Mamba reads a long text like a person with a notepad, updating a fixed-size summary per token and choosing, based on the token, what to write down or forget, so 1 million tokens cost linear time.

concepts.name: Markov Assumption
concepts.description: The simplifying assumption that the next state or word depends only on a fixed number of previous ones, not the full history; used in n-gram models and HMMs.
concepts.example: A bigram model guesses the word after 'Last summer we flew to Paris and ate' using only 'ate', ignoring 'Paris', which keeps counting simple but loses long-range clues.

concepts.name: Masked Language Modeling
concepts.description: A pretraining objective that hides some input tokens and trains the model to predict them from the surrounding context on both sides.
concepts.example: From 'The [MASK] barked at the mailman', the model must predict 'dog' using both 'The' before and 'barked at the mailman' after the blank.

concepts.name: Maximum-Entropy Markov Model
concepts.description: A discriminative sequence model that predicts each state from the previous state and the observation with a maximum-entropy (logistic) classifier; suffers from label bias.
concepts.example: Tagging 'Paris', a MEMM uses a logistic classifier with features like 'capitalized' and 'previous tag was O' to predict the tag, then moves to the next word using that decision.

concepts.name: Maximum Likelihood Estimation for Language Models
concepts.description: Estimating n-gram probabilities by relative frequency, e.g. P(w|prev) = count(prev, w) / count(prev), which maximizes likelihood of the training corpus.
concepts.example: If 'green' appears 10 times and 'green tea' 4 times in a corpus, the MLE is P(tea | green) = 4/10 = 0.4; any pair never seen gets probability 0.

concepts.name: mBART
concepts.description: A multilingual BART pretrained with denoising on text in many languages, used as a strong starting point for machine translation, especially for low-resource pairs.
concepts.example: mBART is pretrained by reconstructing scrambled, partly masked text in 25 languages; fine-tuning it on just a few thousand Nepali-English pairs gives much better translation than starting from scratch.

concepts.name: METEOR
concepts.description: A translation metric that aligns candidate and reference words using exact, stem and synonym matches and combines precision and recall with a fragmentation penalty.
concepts.example: For reference 'the cat sat on the mat' and candidate 'the cats sit on the rug', BLEU sees few exact matches, but METEOR matches 'cats' by stem, 'sit' by stem and 'rug' as a synonym of 'mat'.

concepts.name: Min-p Sampling
concepts.description: A text decoding method that keeps only tokens whose probability is at least a fraction p of the most likely token's probability, so the candidate pool shrinks when the model is confident and grows when it is unsure.
concepts.example: With min-p 0.1: if the top token has 0.9, only tokens of 0.09 or more survive, often just one; if the top token has 0.2, anything of 0.02 or more survives, keeping many options open.

concepts.name: Mistral 7B
concepts.description: A 7-billion-parameter open-weight decoder-only language model from Mistral AI that uses grouped-query attention and sliding window attention to outperform larger models at lower inference cost.
concepts.example: Mistral 7B beat the 13-billion-parameter Llama 2 on most benchmarks while being about half the size, so it runs on a single consumer GPU.

concepts.name: Mixtral
concepts.description: A sparse mixture-of-experts language model from Mistral AI in which each layer has 8 expert feed-forward blocks and a router sends every token to 2 of them, giving large capacity at modest compute per token.
concepts.example: Mixtral 8x7B holds about 47 billion parameters, but each token runs through only 2 of 8 experts per layer, about 13 billion active, so it costs like a 13B model while scoring like much larger ones.

concepts.name: Bidirectional Language Model
concepts.description: The property of models like BERT that each token's representation is built from words on both its left and right, made possible by training with masked tokens instead of left-to-right next-token prediction.
concepts.example: In 'He went to the bank to fish', a left-to-right model reading 'bank' has not seen 'fish' yet, but BERT's vector for 'bank' already uses 'fish' and leans toward riverbank.

concepts.name: MMLU
concepts.description: A benchmark of about 16,000 multiple-choice questions across 57 subjects, from elementary math to law and medicine, used to measure the broad world knowledge and reasoning of language models.
concepts.example: One question asks which amendment protects against unreasonable searches, with four options; another asks about a chemistry reaction. A model's score is its accuracy across all 57 subjects.

concepts.name: Model Context Protocol
concepts.description: An open protocol that standardizes how LLM applications connect to external tools, data sources and services through servers that expose tools, resources and prompts in a common format.
concepts.example: Instead of writing custom code for each app, a company runs one MCP server for its calendar; any MCP-compatible assistant can then list its tools and call 'create_event' the same way.

concepts.name: Model Merging
concepts.description: Combining the weights of several fine-tuned models that share a base model, for example by averaging or task-vector arithmetic, to get one model with several skills without extra training.
concepts.example: Take one base model fine-tuned for math and another fine-tuned for coding; averaging their weights, or adding both changes to the base, can give one model decent at both, with no new training.

concepts.name: Morpheme
concepts.description: The smallest unit of language that carries meaning, such as the root 'play' and the suffix '-ed' in 'played'. Words are built by combining morphemes.
concepts.example: 'Unbreakable' has three morphemes: 'un-' (not), 'break' (the root) and '-able' (can be done). 'Cats' has two: 'cat' and the plural '-s'.

concepts.name: Morphology (Linguistics)
concepts.description: The branch of linguistics that studies how words are formed from morphemes through inflection, derivation and compounding, for example 'unhappiness' = un + happy + ness.
concepts.example: Morphology explains why 'walk' becomes 'walked' (inflection), 'teach' becomes 'teacher' (derivation), and 'sun' + 'flower' becomes 'sunflower' (compounding).

concepts.name: Multi-Agent LLM System
concepts.description: A system in which several LLM-based agents, often with different roles or tools, communicate and coordinate to solve a task, such as a planner, a coder and a reviewer working together.
concepts.example: For building a small app, a planner agent splits the work, a coder agent writes files, and a reviewer agent reads the code and sends bugs back to the coder until tests pass.

concepts.name: Multi-Head Latent Attention
concepts.description: An attention variant from DeepSeek that compresses keys and values into a small shared latent vector per token, greatly shrinking the KV cache while keeping the quality of full multi-head attention.
concepts.example: Instead of caching full keys and values for 128 heads per token, MLA caches one small compressed vector of a few hundred numbers and rebuilds the keys and values from it when needed.

concepts.name: Multi-Query Attention
concepts.description: An attention variant where all query heads share a single key head and value head, which shrinks the KV cache and speeds up autoregressive decoding at a small cost in quality.
concepts.example: A model with 16 heads normally caches 16 key and 16 value vectors per token. With MQA it caches just 1 of each, a 16x smaller cache, so many more conversations fit in GPU memory.

concepts.name: Multilingual BERT
concepts.description: A version of BERT pretrained with masked language modeling on Wikipedia text in about 100 languages with a shared WordPiece vocabulary, which turns out to transfer surprisingly well across languages.
concepts.example: Fine-tune mBERT on English sentiment reviews only, then run it on Spanish reviews: it still classifies many correctly, though it never saw a labelled Spanish example.

concepts.name: Multilingual NLP
concepts.description: The area of NLP that builds systems working across many languages, including cross-lingual transfer where a model trained mostly on one language is applied to others, especially low-resource ones.
concepts.example: A support bot trained mainly on English tickets is extended to answer in Swahili and Tamil by using a model that maps sentences from all three languages into one shared space.

concepts.name: Multimodal Large Language Model
concepts.description: A large language model that also accepts other inputs such as images, audio or video, usually by encoding them with a separate encoder and projecting the result into the LLM's token embedding space.
concepts.example: Upload a photo of a fridge and ask 'What can I cook?'. An image encoder turns the photo into vectors the LLM reads like extra tokens, and it replies 'An omelette with the eggs and spinach'.

concepts.name: N-gram
concepts.description: A contiguous sequence of n items, usually words or characters, from a text; for example 'the cat' is a word bigram. N-grams are basic features for language models and text classification.
concepts.example: In 'I love green tea', the word bigrams are 'I love', 'love green' and 'green tea', and the trigrams are 'I love green' and 'love green tea'.

concepts.name: N-gram Language Model
concepts.description: A language model that predicts each word from only the previous n-1 words, estimating probabilities by counting n-gram frequencies in a corpus under a Markov assumption.
concepts.example: A trigram model guesses the word after 'I would like a cup of' using only 'cup of': if 'cup of tea' occurred 60 times and 'cup of' 100 times, it gives 'tea' 0.6.

concepts.name: Named-Entity Recognition
concepts.description: The task of finding and labeling names of things in text, such as people, organizations, locations and dates. It is usually treated as token-level sequence labeling.
concepts.example: In 'Tim Cook visited Berlin on Monday', NER tags 'Tim Cook' as a person, 'Berlin' as a location and 'Monday' as a date.

concepts.name: Natural Language Generation
concepts.description: The subfield of NLP concerned with producing fluent, coherent text from data or meaning representations, covering tasks like summarization, translation, dialogue and story writing.
concepts.example: From a weather table 'Mon: 12C, rain 80%', an NLG system writes 'Expect a cool, wet Monday with highs of 12 degrees and a high chance of rain.'

concepts.name: Natural Language Inference
concepts.description: The task of deciding whether a hypothesis sentence is entailed by, contradicts, or is neutral to a premise sentence. It is a standard test of a model's language understanding.
concepts.example: Premise: 'A man is playing a guitar on stage.' Hypothesis 'A man is performing music' is entailment; 'The man is asleep' is contradiction; 'The man is famous' is neutral.

concepts.name: Natural Language Processing
concepts.description: The field of computer science and AI that builds methods for computers to analyze, understand and generate human language, from tokenization and parsing to translation and chatbots.
concepts.example: A spam filter, voice assistant, autocorrect and translation app all use NLP: each must break text into words, work out its structure or meaning, and act on it.

concepts.name: Natural Language Understanding
concepts.description: The subfield of NLP focused on extracting meaning from text, including intent, entities, relations and entailment, as opposed to generating text.
concepts.example: From 'Wake me up at 7 tomorrow unless it's Saturday', an NLU system must extract intent set_alarm, time 7:00 and the condition about Saturday.

concepts.name: Needle in a Haystack
concepts.description: A long-context evaluation that hides a specific fact somewhere in a long distracting document and checks whether a model can retrieve it, across many context lengths and insertion depths.
concepts.example: Hide 'The secret ingredient is cardamom' at 25%, 50% or 75% depth inside 100,000 tokens of essays, then ask for the secret ingredient; results form a heatmap by length and depth.

concepts.name: Neural Machine Translation
concepts.description: Machine translation done end-to-end by a neural network, typically an encoder-decoder with attention or a Transformer that reads the source sentence and generates the target sentence token by token.
concepts.example: Given 'Ich habe Hunger', the encoder turns it into vectors, then the decoder writes 'I', 'am', 'hungry', each time attending to the relevant German words, learned from millions of example pairs.

concepts.name: Neural Probabilistic Language Model
concepts.description: Bengio et al.'s 2003 model that predicts the next word with a feedforward neural network over learned word embeddings of the previous words, the first neural language model to beat n-gram models.
