concepts.description: In linear programming, a feasible point obtained by setting the non-basic variables to zero and solving for the basic ones; geometrically a vertex of the feasible polyhedron that the simplex method visits.
concepts.example: With constraints x + y + s1 = 4 and x + 3y + s2 = 6, set y = s1 = 0 and solve to get x = 4, s2 = 2, a corner point (4, 0). The simplex method moves between such corners.

concepts.name: Basis Pursuit
concepts.description: The problem of finding the solution of an underdetermined linear system with the smallest L1 norm, a convex substitute for seeking the sparsest solution; central to compressed sensing.
concepts.example: The equation x1 + 2x2 = 2 has infinitely many solutions; minimizing |x1| + |x2| picks (0, 1), which has a single nonzero entry, the sparsest answer.

concepts.name: Bayesian Optimization
concepts.description: A strategy for optimizing expensive black-box functions that fits a probabilistic surrogate, usually a Gaussian process, and picks the next point to evaluate by maximizing an acquisition function.
concepts.example: Tuning a model's learning rate where each trial takes 2 hours: after 5 trials, a Gaussian process guesses where the best value probably lies and how unsure it is, and suggests the next most promising trial.

concepts.name: BCH Code
concepts.description: A family of cyclic error-correcting codes built from polynomials over finite fields, designed so the number of correctable bit errors can be chosen precisely; used in storage and digital broadcasting.
concepts.example: A (15, 7) BCH code turns 7 data bits into 15 transmitted bits and is guaranteed to fix any 2 flipped bits; QR codes use a BCH code to protect their format information.

concepts.name: Broyden–Fletcher–Goldfarb–Shanno Algorithm
concepts.description: A quasi-Newton optimization method that builds an approximation to the inverse Hessian from successive gradient differences, giving fast superlinear convergence without computing second derivatives.
concepts.example: Instead of computing the full Hessian at every step, BFGS watches how the gradient changed after each step and updates its curvature estimate, like learning a road's bends by driving it.

concepts.name: BIBO Stability
concepts.description: A system is BIBO stable if every bounded input produces a bounded output; for linear time-invariant systems this holds exactly when the impulse response is absolutely summable or integrable.
concepts.example: A filter with impulse response 0.5^n is stable because 1 + 0.5 + 0.25 + ... = 2 is finite; one with response 1.1^n blows up even for a gentle bounded input.

concepts.name: Bilinear Transform
concepts.description: A mapping s = (2/T)(z-1)/(z+1) that converts a continuous-time filter's transfer function into a discrete-time one, preserving stability while warping the frequency axis.
concepts.example: To make a digital version of an analog audio filter, replace every s in its formula with (2/T)(z - 1)/(z + 1); a stable analog filter always becomes a stable digital one.

concepts.name: Binary Erasure Channel
concepts.description: A channel model where each transmitted bit is either received correctly or erased (marked as unknown) with probability p; its capacity is 1 - p bits per channel use.
concepts.example: With erasure probability 0.2, sending 1 0 1 1 0 might arrive as 1 ? 1 1 0; the receiver knows exactly which bits were lost, and the capacity is 1 - 0.2 = 0.8 bits per use.

concepts.name: Binary Integer Programming
concepts.description: An integer program in which every decision variable is restricted to 0 or 1, used to model yes/no choices such as selecting items, facilities or routes; NP-hard in general.
concepts.example: Choosing which of 5 projects to fund with a 10-million budget: each x_i is 1 (fund) or 0 (don't), maximize total value subject to the costs summing to at most 10.

concepts.name: Binary Symmetric Channel
concepts.description: A channel model in which each transmitted bit is independently flipped with a fixed crossover probability p; its capacity is 1 - H(p), where H is the binary entropy function.
concepts.example: With crossover p = 0.1, each sent bit has a 10% chance of arriving flipped; the capacity is 1 - H(0.1), about 1 - 0.47 = 0.53 bits per use.

concepts.name: Bit
concepts.description: The basic unit of information: the amount gained by learning the outcome of a fair yes/no choice, measured with base-2 logarithms; using natural logarithms gives the nat instead.
concepts.example: Learning the result of a fair coin flip gives 1 bit; guessing a number from 1 to 8 takes 3 yes/no questions, so it gives log2(8) = 3 bits.

concepts.name: Blahut–Arimoto Algorithm
concepts.description: An iterative alternating-maximization algorithm that numerically computes the capacity of a discrete memoryless channel or the rate-distortion function of a source.
concepts.example: For a channel with no simple formula, start with equal input probabilities, compute how well each input is distinguished at the output, shift probability toward the better inputs, and repeat until the rate stops growing.

concepts.name: Bland's Rule
concepts.description: A pivoting rule for the simplex method that always picks the lowest-indexed eligible entering and leaving variables, which provably prevents cycling on degenerate problems.
concepts.example: If x2 and x5 could both enter the basis, Bland's rule picks x2, the lower index, and breaks ties for leaving the same way; this simple habit guarantees the simplex method never cycles forever.

concepts.name: Block Code
concepts.description: An error-correcting code that encodes each fixed-length block of k message symbols into a codeword of n symbols, adding n - k redundant symbols to detect or fix errors.
concepts.example: A repetition code turns each 1-bit block into 3 bits, so 1 becomes 111; if noise changes it to 101, a majority vote still recovers 1.

concepts.name: Branch and Bound
concepts.description: An exact method for discrete optimization that splits the problem into subproblems in a search tree and discards branches whose bound shows they cannot beat the best solution found so far.
concepts.example: Packing a knapsack: split into 'take item 1' and 'skip item 1'. If the best possible value of a branch, even with fractional items, is below a packing you already found, discard the whole branch unexplored.

concepts.name: Branch and Cut
concepts.description: A method for integer programs that combines branch and bound with cutting planes, adding valid inequalities at tree nodes to tighten LP relaxations and prune more of the search.
concepts.example: While branching on an integer program, the solver notices the LP relaxation's answer x = 2.5 violates a valid inequality like x <= 2 and adds that cut, tightening the bound before branching further.

concepts.name: Broyden's Method
concepts.description: A quasi-Newton method for solving systems of nonlinear equations that updates an approximate Jacobian with a cheap rank-one correction at each step instead of recomputing it.
concepts.example: Solving two nonlinear equations in two unknowns, Broyden computes the Jacobian once, then after each step adjusts it so it matches the latest change in x and in f(x), skipping costly recomputation.

concepts.name: Butterworth Filter
concepts.description: A classic filter design with a maximally flat magnitude response in the passband (no ripple), trading this smoothness for a gentler roll-off than Chebyshev or elliptic filters.
concepts.example: A 2nd-order Butterworth low-pass at 1 kHz passes 100 Hz and 500 Hz almost equally with no wiggles, is down 3 dB at 1 kHz, and falls off by about 12 dB per octave beyond.

concepts.name: Causal System
concepts.description: A system is causal if its output at any time depends only on present and past inputs, never on future ones; this is required for real-time processing.
concepts.example: A filter computing y[n] = (x[n] + x[n-1]) / 2 is causal, using now and the past; one using x[n+1] is not and can't run live, though it can run on a recorded file.

concepts.name: Central Path
concepts.description: In interior-point methods, the curve traced by minimizers of the barrier-augmented objective as the barrier weight shrinks to zero; it leads through the feasible interior to the optimal solution.
concepts.example: Minimizing x subject to x >= 0 with a barrier: minimize t*x - log(x), giving x = 1/t. As t grows from 1 to 10 to 100, the points 1, 0.1, 0.01 trace the central path toward the optimum 0.

concepts.name: Chain Rule for Entropy
concepts.description: The identity H(X, Y) = H(X) + H(Y | X), and its extension to many variables, which splits the joint entropy of several random variables into a sum of conditional entropies.
concepts.example: Two fair coins, the second always equal to the first: H(X) = 1 bit and H(Y given X) = 0, so H(X, Y) = 1 + 0 = 1 bit, not 2.

concepts.name: Channel Capacity
concepts.description: The maximum rate, in bits per channel use, at which information can be sent over a noisy channel with arbitrarily small error, equal to the maximum mutual information between input and output.
concepts.example: A channel that flips 11% of bits has capacity about 0.5 bits per use, so with good coding you can reliably send about 500 information bits for every 1,000 bits transmitted, but no more.

concepts.name: Chebyshev Filter
concepts.description: A filter design that allows equal-sized ripple in the passband (type I) or stopband (type II) in exchange for a steeper roll-off than a Butterworth filter of the same order.
concepts.example: Compared with a Butterworth of the same order, a type I Chebyshev lets the passband ripple by, say, 0.5 dB, but in return cuts off much more sharply just past the cutoff.

concepts.name: Circular Convolution
concepts.description: Convolution of finite-length sequences where indices wrap around modulo the length N; it is what multiplying DFTs computes, so zero-padding is needed to obtain ordinary linear convolution.
concepts.example: Circularly convolving [1, 2, 3] with [0, 1, 0] shifts it with wraparound to [3, 1, 2]: the last element wraps to the front instead of falling off.

concepts.name: CMA-ES
concepts.description: An evolution strategy for black-box continuous optimization that samples candidates from a multivariate Gaussian and adapts its mean and covariance matrix toward successful search directions.
concepts.example: To tune 10 parameters, CMA-ES samples 20 candidates from a cloud, keeps the best 10, moves the cloud's center toward them and stretches its shape along directions that worked, repeating each generation.

concepts.name: Code Rate
concepts.description: The fraction k/n of a code's transmitted symbols that carry actual information, the rest being redundancy; lower rates give more protection against errors at the cost of throughput.
concepts.example: A (7, 4) Hamming code sends 7 bits for every 4 data bits, a rate of 4/7, about 0.57; a 3-times repetition code has rate 1/3, more robust but slower.

concepts.name: Coding Theory
concepts.description: The study of codes for reliable and efficient representation and transmission of data, including error-correcting codes and compression, built on information theory and algebra.
concepts.example: A CD still plays with a scratch because coding theory adds clever redundancy; Reed-Solomon codes can rebuild thousands of missing bits from the extra data.

concepts.name: Column Generation
concepts.description: A method for linear programs with huge numbers of variables that solves a restricted master problem and adds only columns with negative reduced cost, found by solving a pricing subproblem.
concepts.example: In cutting paper rolls, there are billions of possible cutting patterns; column generation starts with a few, solves the LP, then uses the dual prices to find one new pattern that would improve it, and repeats.

concepts.name: Combinatorial Optimization
concepts.description: The field of finding the best solution among a finite but typically enormous set of discrete options, such as routes, schedules or matchings, using exact, approximate and heuristic methods.
concepts.example: Finding the shortest route visiting 15 cities means choosing among about 43 billion distinct tours; combinatorial optimization finds the best without checking them one by one.

concepts.name: Communication Channel
concepts.description: The medium or abstract model through which a signal travels from sender to receiver; in information theory it is described by the probabilities of each output given each input, capturing noise.
concepts.example: Sending a text message over Wi-Fi: the radio link is the channel, and noise may turn the bit you sent as 1 into a received 0 with some probability, described by P(output given input).

concepts.name: Complementary Slackness
concepts.description: The optimality condition that for each inequality constraint either the constraint is tight or its dual variable is zero, linking optimal primal and dual solutions in LP and in the KKT conditions.
concepts.example: If a factory's optimal plan leaves 5 hours of machine time unused, that constraint's dual price is 0; an extra hour would be worthless. A resource that is fully used can have a positive price.

concepts.name: Complex Exponential
concepts.description: The function e^(iwt) = cos(wt) + i sin(wt) given by Euler's formula, a rotating unit phasor that represents a pure sinusoid and is the building block of Fourier analysis.
concepts.example: e^(i*pi/2) = cos(90 deg) + i sin(90 deg) = i: the point one quarter turn around the unit circle. As t grows, e^(iwt) spins around the circle w radians per second.

concepts.name: Compressed Sensing
concepts.description: A framework for recovering sparse signals from far fewer linear measurements than classical sampling requires, by solving L1-minimization problems under conditions like the restricted isometry property.
concepts.example: A medical MRI image that is sparse in the wavelet domain can be rebuilt from about a quarter of the usual measurements, cutting scan time, by solving for the sparsest image matching them.

concepts.name: Conditional Entropy
concepts.description: H(Y | X), the average uncertainty remaining about Y once X is known; it equals the joint entropy minus H(X) and is zero when Y is completely determined by X.
concepts.example: Tomorrow's weather has 1 bit of uncertainty, but if you know today's weather and it usually persists, the leftover uncertainty H(tomorrow given today) might be only 0.5 bits.

concepts.name: Conditional Mutual Information
concepts.description: I(X; Y | Z), the information X and Y share once Z is known, computed as the average mutual information given each value of Z; used in chain rules and feature selection.
concepts.example: Ice cream sales and drownings share information, but once you know the temperature Z, they share almost none: I(sales; drownings given temperature) is near 0.

concepts.name: Conic Optimization
concepts.description: Optimization of a linear objective over the intersection of an affine set with a convex cone, a unifying form covering linear, second-order cone and semidefinite programming.
concepts.example: Linear programs use the nonnegative orthant cone, second-order cone programs use the ice-cream cone, and semidefinite programs use the cone of positive semidefinite matrices; all are conic programs.

concepts.name: Constrained Optimization
concepts.description: Optimizing an objective function while requiring the solution to satisfy equality or inequality constraints, handled with tools like Lagrange multipliers, KKT conditions and penalty methods.
concepts.example: Maximize the area of a rectangular garden with 40 m of fence: the constraint 2w + 2h = 40 forces a square, 10 x 10 m, with area 100 m^2.

concepts.name: Constraint (Optimization)
concepts.description: A condition, written as an equation or inequality on the decision variables, that every solution of an optimization problem must satisfy, such as a budget limit or nonnegativity.
concepts.example: In a diet plan, 'total calories <= 2,000' and 'protein >= 50 g' are constraints; any meal plan breaking one is not allowed, however cheap it is.

concepts.name: Constraint Qualification
concepts.description: A regularity condition on the constraints, such as linear independence of active constraint gradients (LICQ) or Slater's condition, that guarantees the KKT conditions hold at an optimum.
concepts.example: Minimize x subject to x^2 <= 0: the only feasible point is 0, but the constraint's gradient there is 0, so LICQ fails and the KKT conditions have no multipliers even at the optimum.

concepts.name: Continuous-Time Signal
concepts.description: A signal defined at every instant of a continuous range of time, such as a voltage or a sound pressure wave, modeled as a function of a real-valued time variable.
concepts.example: The temperature in a room exists at every instant, at 3:00, 3:00:00.5 and every moment in between, so it is a continuous-time signal; a thermometer logging once a minute makes a discrete one.

concepts.name: Continuous Wavelet Transform
concepts.description: A transform that correlates a signal with scaled and shifted copies of a mother wavelet over a continuum of scales, giving a detailed time-scale picture for analyzing transient features.
concepts.example: Analyzing a bird song, stretched wavelets match the long low notes and squeezed wavelets match short high chirps, showing which pitch occurs when, like a musical score.

concepts.name: Convex Analysis
concepts.description: The branch of mathematics studying convex sets and convex functions, including separation theorems, subgradients, conjugate functions and duality; the theoretical basis of convex optimization.
concepts.example: Convex analysis explains why the bowl-shaped f(x) = |x| has a subgradient at its corner, any slope from -1 to 1, so optimality there can be checked even without a derivative.

concepts.name: Convex Combination
concepts.description: A weighted sum of points whose weights are nonnegative and add up to one; it describes every point on the segment or polygon between them and is the basis for defining convex sets.
concepts.example: 0.25 x (0, 0) + 0.75 x (4, 8) = (3, 6), a point three-quarters of the way along the segment; a mix of 30% coffee and 70% milk is a convex combination of the two.

concepts.name: Convex Cone
concepts.description: A set closed under addition and nonnegative scaling, so it contains every nonnegative combination of its points; examples include the nonnegative orthant and the cone of PSD matrices.
concepts.example: The set of points with x >= 0 and y >= 0, the first quadrant, is a convex cone: add two such points or multiply one by 3, and you are still in the quadrant.

concepts.name: Convex Conjugate
concepts.description: For a function f, the function f*(y) = sup over x of (y.x - f(x)), which encodes f through its supporting hyperplanes; it underlies Fenchel duality and many dual optimization methods.
concepts.example: For f(x) = x^2 / 2, the conjugate is f*(y) = max over x of (yx - x^2/2), reached at x = y, giving y^2 / 2: this function is its own conjugate.

concepts.name: Convex hull
concepts.description: The smallest convex set containing a given set of points, equivalently all their convex combinations; for points in the plane it is the polygon a stretched rubber band would form around them.
concepts.example: Hammer nails into a board at random spots and stretch a rubber band around all of them; when it snaps tight, the band's shape is the convex hull. Nails inside the band don't touch it, only the outermost ones become corners.

concepts.name: Convex Optimization
concepts.description: The study of minimizing convex functions over convex sets, where every local minimum is global; it includes LP, QP, SOCP and SDP and admits efficient, reliable algorithms.
concepts.example: Choosing how to split a $1000 budget across ads to minimize a bowl-shaped cost: because the cost is convex and the budget rules form a convex set, any split you can't improve locally is guaranteed to be the best possible.

concepts.name: Convolution Theorem
concepts.description: The result that the Fourier transform of a convolution equals the pointwise product of the Fourier transforms, and vice versa, letting convolutions be computed quickly via the FFT.
concepts.example: Blurring a 1-million-sample audio clip with a long filter directly takes about a trillion multiplications; transforming both with an FFT, multiplying them point by point and transforming back takes only tens of millions.

concepts.name: Convolutional Code
concepts.description: An error-correcting code that produces output bits as sliding combinations of the current and recent input bits using shift registers, typically decoded with the Viterbi algorithm.
concepts.example: A rate-1/2 encoder remembers the last 2 input bits; for each new bit it outputs two bits, each the XOR of a different subset of the current and remembered bits, so every input bit influences several outputs in a row.

concepts.name: Cooley–Tukey FFT Algorithm
concepts.description: The most common FFT algorithm, which recursively splits a length-N DFT into smaller DFTs, for example over even and odd indices, to compute it in O(N log N) instead of O(N^2) operations.
concepts.example: An 8-point DFT is split into two 4-point DFTs (even and odd samples), each split into two 2-point DFTs, then results are recombined with twiddle factors: about 8 x 3 = 24 steps instead of 64.

concepts.name: Coordinate Descent
concepts.description: An optimization algorithm that minimizes a multivariable function by repeatedly optimizing along one coordinate (or block) at a time while holding the others fixed; popular for lasso.
concepts.example: To minimize f(x, y) = x^2 + xy + y^2 starting at (1, 1): fix y = 1 and choose the best x (-0.5), then fix that x and choose the best y (0.25), and keep alternating; the point zigzags toward the minimum at (0, 0).

concepts.name: Cross-Correlation
concepts.description: A measure of similarity between two signals as a function of the time shift applied to one of them, used to estimate delays, detect templates and match patterns.
concepts.example: Two microphones hear the same clap, one 3 ms later; sliding one recording against the other and scoring how well they match, the score peaks at a 3 ms shift, revealing the delay and hence the direction of the sound.

concepts.name: Cross-Entropy
concepts.description: H(p, q) = -sum p(x) log q(x), the average number of bits needed to encode samples from p with a code optimized for q; it equals entropy plus KL divergence and is a standard ML loss.
concepts.example: If the true weather is sunny 90% of the time but your model says 50%, each sunny day costs you -log2(0.5) = 1 bit instead of about 0.15 bits; averaged over days, that mismatch shows up as cross-entropy larger than the true entropy.

concepts.name: Cutting-Plane Method
concepts.description: An optimization approach that repeatedly solves a relaxation and adds linear inequalities (cuts), such as Gomory cuts, that remove the current fractional point without excluding feasible solutions.
concepts.example: An integer program's LP relaxation says x = 2.5; a cut such as x <= 2 removes that fractional point but no integer solutions, and re-solving with the cut pushes the answer toward a true integer optimum.

concepts.name: CVX
concepts.description: A family of modeling tools (CVX for MATLAB, CVXPY for Python) that let users write convex optimization problems in natural math syntax, check convexity, and pass them to numerical solvers.
concepts.example: In CVXPY you can write minimize(norm(A @ x - b)) subject to x >= 0 almost exactly as on paper; the tool checks the problem is convex and passes it to a solver, returning the optimal x in a few lines of code.

concepts.name: Cyclic Redundancy Check
concepts.description: An error-detecting code that appends the remainder of dividing the message, treated as a binary polynomial, by a fixed generator polynomial; widely used in networks and storage.
concepts.example: Message 1101 with divisor 1011 (x^3 + x + 1): append three zeros to get 1101000, divide using XOR, and the remainder 001 is appended to send 1101001; the receiver divides again and any nonzero remainder flags an error.

concepts.name: Damped Newton Method
concepts.description: Newton's method for optimization with the step length chosen by a line search instead of always taking the full Newton step, which makes it converge from starting points far from the solution.
concepts.example: Far from the minimum of a curvy function, a full Newton step might overshoot to a worse point; damped Newton tries the full step, and if the value doesn't drop enough it halves the step, then halves again, until it does.

concepts.name: Data Compression
concepts.description: The field of encoding information in fewer bits than the original representation, either exactly (lossless, e.g. gzip) or approximately (lossy, e.g. JPEG), by exploiting redundancy.
concepts.example: A text with lots of 'the' can store each 'the' as a short code instead of 24 bits; a photo can drop fine detail the eye can't see. A 10 MB file squeezed to 2 MB is 5:1 compression.

concepts.name: Data Processing Inequality
concepts.description: The theorem that processing data cannot create information: if X, Y, Z form a Markov chain X -> Y -> Z, then I(X; Z) <= I(X; Y).
concepts.example: Photograph a scene (X), then make a blurry photocopy of the photo (Z via Y); no clever editing of the photocopy can reveal more about the scene than the original photo did.

concepts.name: Daubechies Wavelet
concepts.description: A family of orthogonal, compactly supported wavelets with the most vanishing moments possible for their length, widely used in the discrete wavelet transform and image compression.
concepts.example: Haar wavelets represent a smooth ramp with a staircase of jumps, but the 4-tap Daubechies D4 wavelet represents straight-line pieces with almost-zero detail coefficients, so smooth images compress much better.

concepts.name: Decibel
concepts.description: A logarithmic unit expressing the ratio of two power levels as 10 log10(P1/P2), or 20 log10 for amplitude ratios; used for signal strength, gain and sound levels.
concepts.example: Doubling power adds about 3 dB, since 10 log10(2) is about 3; a sound 1000 times more powerful than another is 30 dB louder. Doubling amplitude gives 20 log10(2), about 6 dB.

concepts.name: Decision Variable
concepts.description: An unknown quantity in an optimization problem whose value the solver chooses, such as how much of each product to make; the objective and constraints are written in terms of these.
concepts.example: A bakery deciding how many loaves (x) and cakes (y) to bake tomorrow: x and y are the decision variables, and the optimizer picks values like x = 40, y = 12 to maximize profit.

concepts.name: Degeneracy (Linear Programming)
concepts.description: A situation in linear programming where a basic feasible solution has a basic variable equal to zero, so simplex pivots can make no progress and the method may cycle.
concepts.example: In 2D, if three constraint lines meet at a single corner, simplex may pivot between different bases describing that same corner, making steps with zero improvement and, without care, even cycling forever.

concepts.name: Derivative-Free Optimization
concepts.description: Optimization methods that use only function evaluations, not gradients, suited to noisy, discontinuous or black-box objectives; includes Nelder-Mead, pattern search and evolutionary methods.
concepts.example: Tuning an oven's temperature and baking time to get the tastiest cake: you can only bake and taste, not compute a gradient, so you try settings, compare scores and move toward better ones.

concepts.name: Descent Direction
concepts.description: A vector along which a function decreases for small enough steps, meaning its directional derivative is negative; gradient-based methods choose such a direction at every iteration.
concepts.example: On f(x, y) = x^2 + y^2 at (1, 1), the gradient is (2, 2); the direction (-1, 0) has dot product -2 with it, so stepping a little that way lowers f, making it a descent direction.

concepts.name: Davidon–Fletcher–Powell Formula
concepts.description: The first quasi-Newton update, which builds a rank-two approximation of the inverse Hessian from step and gradient differences; it has largely been superseded by the more robust BFGS update.
concepts.example: After each step s and gradient change y, DFP adds two rank-one corrections to its inverse-Hessian guess so it maps y back to s; on a quadratic in n variables with exact line searches it recovers the true inverse Hessian in n steps.

concepts.name: Differential Entropy
concepts.description: The extension of entropy to continuous random variables, h(X) = -integral of p(x) log p(x) dx; unlike discrete entropy it can be negative and changes when the variable is rescaled.
concepts.example: A uniform distribution on [0, 1/2] has differential entropy log2(1/2) = -1 bit, which is negative, unlike any discrete entropy; a uniform on [0, 4] has +2 bits.

concepts.name: Differential Evolution
concepts.description: A population-based optimizer for continuous problems that creates trial solutions by adding scaled differences between random population members to another member, keeping improvements.
concepts.example: For a population of candidate vectors, pick three others A, B, C and form the mutant A + 0.8(B - C); mix it with the current vector and keep whichever scores better, so step sizes adapt to the population's spread.

concepts.name: Digital Signal Processing
concepts.description: The field of analyzing and modifying signals that have been sampled and quantized into numbers, using algorithms such as the FFT and digital filters running on computers and DSP chips.
concepts.example: A phone samples your voice 16,000 times a second, then runs number-crunching filters to cancel echo and noise before compressing it, all done with arithmetic on the sample values.

concepts.name: Dirac Delta Function
concepts.description: An idealized function that is zero everywhere except at zero yet integrates to one, modeling an instantaneous impulse; convolving any signal with it leaves the signal unchanged.
concepts.example: Model a hammer tap as a force spike so short and strong that only its total impulse matters: the delta is zero everywhere except time 0, yet integrating it gives 1, and integrating f(t) times delta(t) just picks out f(0).

concepts.name: Discrete Cosine Transform
concepts.description: A transform that expresses a finite sequence as a sum of cosines at different frequencies; it packs most energy into few coefficients, making it the core of JPEG and MP3 compression.
concepts.example: Run an 8-pixel row of a smooth sky (all near 200) through a DCT: the first coefficient holds nearly everything and the other seven are close to zero, which is why JPEG can discard them cheaply.

concepts.name: Discrete-Time Fourier Transform
concepts.description: The Fourier transform of a discrete-time sequence, giving a continuous, 2pi-periodic function of frequency that describes the sequence's spectral content.
concepts.example: The sequence 1, 1 (two samples) has DTFT 1 + e^(-iw): magnitude 2 at w = 0 and 0 at w = pi, revealing it as a simple low-pass averager; the curve repeats every 2pi.

concepts.name: Discrete-Time Signal
concepts.description: A signal defined only at discrete, usually equally spaced time instants and represented as a sequence of numbers, such as the samples a computer stores from an audio recording.
concepts.example: A thermometer logging temperature every hour gives 21, 20, 19, 22, ... : a list of numbers at times 0, 1, 2, 3 hours, with no values in between.

concepts.name: Discrete Wavelet Transform
concepts.description: A transform that decomposes a signal into wavelet coefficients at dyadic scales by repeated low-pass and high-pass filtering with downsampling; used in JPEG 2000 compression and denoising.
concepts.example: For 4 samples 6, 4, 5, 3, the Haar DWT takes pairwise averages (5, 4) and differences (1, 1), then repeats on the averages: 4.5 and 0.5. Small differences can be dropped for compression.

concepts.name: Downsampling
concepts.description: Reducing a discrete signal's sampling rate by keeping only every M-th sample, usually after low-pass filtering to prevent aliasing; used to save computation and storage.
concepts.example: Turning 48 kHz audio into 16 kHz keeps every 3rd sample; first a low-pass filter removes content above 8 kHz so it doesn't fold down into audible false tones.

concepts.name: Dual Ascent
concepts.description: An algorithm that solves a constrained problem by gradient ascent on the dual function: minimize the Lagrangian for fixed multipliers, then update the multipliers along the constraint residual.
concepts.example: Pricing shared bandwidth: the network posts a price, each user picks its usage to minimize cost plus price times usage, and the price rises if demand exceeds capacity or falls otherwise, until supply meets demand.

concepts.name: Dual Norm
concepts.description: For a norm, the dual norm of y is the maximum of y.x over all x with norm at most one; for example the L1 and L-infinity norms are duals of each other and the L2 norm is its own dual.
concepts.example: The dual of the L1 norm is the max norm: for y = (3, -5), the largest y.x over vectors with |x1| + |x2| <= 1 is 5, achieved at x = (0, -1), which equals max(|3|, |-5|).

concepts.name: Dual Problem
concepts.description: An optimization problem derived from a primal problem, typically via Lagrange multipliers, whose optimal value bounds the primal's; solving it can be easier and gives sensitivity information.
concepts.example: A factory maximizing profit from limited wood and labour has a dual: what minimum prices per unit of wood and labour would make selling the resources at least as good as making products? That minimum equals the best profit.

concepts.name: Dual Simplex Method
concepts.description: A variant of the simplex method that keeps the solution dual feasible while working toward primal feasibility; very useful for re-solving after constraints are added, as in branch and bound.
concepts.example: After adding a new constraint like x <= 3 that the current optimum violates, dual simplex starts from the old basis, still optimal-looking but infeasible, and pivots to restore feasibility, usually in just a few steps.

concepts.name: Duality Gap
concepts.description: The difference between the primal objective value and the dual objective value; it is nonnegative by weak duality, zero under strong duality, and commonly used as a stopping criterion.
concepts.example: If a feasible delivery plan costs 105 and the dual gives a lower bound of 100, the gap is 5, so the plan is at most 5 above optimal; a solver can stop once the gap drops below a tolerance.

concepts.name: Duality (Optimization)
concepts.description: The principle that every optimization problem has an associated dual problem that bounds its optimal value, revealing the prices of constraints and enabling alternative algorithms.
concepts.example: To prove 100 is the minimum cost of a diet, exhibit dual prices showing no diet can cost less; a matching pair of primal solution and dual bound certifies optimality without searching further.

concepts.name: Dynamic Programming
concepts.description: A technique that solves problems by breaking them into overlapping subproblems, solving each once and storing the results; it relies on optimal substructure and is captured by the Bellman equation.
concepts.example: Computing the 50th Fibonacci number naively makes over 10 billion recursive calls; storing each F(n) the first time it's computed needs only 50 additions.

concepts.name: Ellipsoid Method
concepts.description: A convex optimization algorithm that encloses the solution in an ellipsoid and repeatedly shrinks it using a cut through its center; it gave the first proof that LP is solvable in polynomial time.
concepts.example: Start with a big ellipse known to contain the answer; query its centre, use a separating line to discard the bad half, wrap a smaller ellipse around the good half, and repeat; the volume shrinks by a fixed factor each step.

concepts.name: Elliptic Filter
concepts.description: A filter design with equal ripple in both passband and stopband, achieving the sharpest transition for a given order at the cost of ripple and nonlinear phase; also called a Cauer filter.
concepts.example: To pass up to 1 kHz (1 dB ripple) yet cut 40 dB by 1.1 kHz, an elliptic filter needs about order 7, a Chebyshev about 14 and a Butterworth over 50, at the price of ripple in both bands.

concepts.name: Entropy Rate
concepts.description: The average entropy per symbol of a stochastic process in the limit of long sequences; it measures how much new information each symbol adds and bounds how well the source can be compressed.
concepts.example: English text has about 4.7 bits per letter if letters were random, but because letters depend on earlier ones, the entropy rate is estimated near 1 to 1.5 bits per letter, which is why text compresses well.

concepts.name: Envelope Theorem
concepts.description: A result stating that the derivative of an optimal value with respect to a parameter equals the partial derivative of the objective (or Lagrangian) at the optimum, ignoring how the optimizer moves.
concepts.example: A firm's maximum profit depends on the output price p; if it sells q* units at the optimum, raising p by $1 raises max profit by about q*, without recomputing how the firm reoptimizes.

concepts.name: Epigraph
concepts.description: The set of points lying on or above the graph of a function, {(x, t) : f(x) <= t}; a function is convex exactly when its epigraph is a convex set.
concepts.example: For f(x) = x^2, the epigraph is the inside of the U-shaped cup including its rim, like the water you could pour into it; the cup holds water without leaking through any chord, which is exactly why x^2 is convex.

concepts.name: Equality Constraint
concepts.description: A constraint requiring a function of the decision variables to equal a fixed value, h(x) = 0, such as a budget that must be spent exactly; it restricts solutions to a surface.
concepts.example: Splitting exactly $500 between stocks x and bonds y imposes x + y = 500: every allowed plan lies on that line, unlike a cap x + y <= 500 which allows spending less.

concepts.name: Error Correction Code
concepts.description: A scheme that adds structured redundancy to data so the receiver can detect and correct errors introduced by noise, as in Hamming, Reed-Solomon and LDPC codes.
concepts.example: Send each bit three times: 1 becomes 111. If noise flips one copy to 101, the receiver takes the majority vote and still reads 1, fixing the error at the cost of tripling the data.

concepts.name: Error Detection and Correction
concepts.description: The set of techniques for detecting and fixing errors in transmitted or stored data by adding redundancy, from simple parity bits and checksums to full error-correcting codes.
concepts.example: Bank card numbers end with a check digit: if you mistype one digit, the arithmetic check fails and the form rejects it immediately, detecting the error with a single extra digit.

concepts.name: Evolutionary Algorithm
concepts.description: A family of optimization algorithms inspired by natural evolution that improve a population of candidate solutions through selection, recombination and mutation over many generations.
concepts.example: To design an antenna, start with 100 random shapes, test each, keep the best 20, make new shapes by mixing and slightly mutating them, and repeat for hundreds of generations until performance stops improving.

concepts.name: f-Divergence
concepts.description: A general family of measures of difference between probability distributions, D_f(P||Q) = E_Q[f(dP/dQ)] for convex f with f(1) = 0; it includes KL, total variation, chi-squared and Hellinger.
concepts.example: Choosing f(t) = t log t gives KL divergence, f(t) = |t - 1|/2 gives total variation distance, and f(t) = (sqrt(t) - 1)^2 gives squared Hellinger distance: one formula, many distances.

concepts.name: Fano's Inequality
concepts.description: An inequality bounding the probability of error when guessing X from Y in terms of the conditional entropy H(X | Y); it is a key tool for proving converse coding theorems and lower bounds.
concepts.example: If you guess one of 1024 equally likely files from a corrupted copy and conditional uncertainty H(X|Y) is still 5 bits, Fano shows the guess is wrong with probability at least about (5 - 1)/10 = 40%.

concepts.name: Farkas' Lemma
concepts.description: A theorem of the alternative: either the system Ax = b, x >= 0 has a solution, or some y satisfies A^T y >= 0 and b.y < 0, but never both; it underlies LP duality.
concepts.example: Either you can mix nonnegative amounts of two juices to hit an exact target sugar and vitamin content, or there exist prices that rate both juices as at least zero but the target as negative, proving it impossible; never both.

concepts.name: Feasible Region
concepts.description: The set of all points that satisfy every constraint of an optimization problem; any optimum must lie in it, and for linear programs it is a convex polyhedron.
concepts.example: With constraints x >= 0, y >= 0 and x + y <= 10, the feasible region is a triangle with corners (0,0), (10,0) and (0,10); any plan outside that triangle breaks a rule.

concepts.name: Fenchel Duality
concepts.description: A duality theorem stating that minimizing f(x) + g(Ax) can be matched by a dual problem in terms of the convex conjugates of f and g, with equal optimal values under mild conditions.
concepts.example: To denoise a signal by minimizing a data-fit term f(x) plus a penalty g(Dx) on its differences, Fenchel duality gives an equivalent problem in the conjugates of f and g that is often easier, and the two optimal values match.

concepts.name: Filter Bank
concepts.description: An array of filters that splits a signal into several frequency subbands, which can be processed separately and recombined; used in audio coding, wavelets and mel-spectrogram features.
concepts.example: A music equalizer splits sound into 10 bands (bass, mid, treble, ...), lets you boost or cut each one, then adds the bands back together.

concepts.name: Filter Design
concepts.description: The task of choosing filter coefficients so the frequency response meets specifications such as passband ripple, stopband attenuation and cutoff, using methods like windowing or Parks-McClellan.
concepts.example: Spec: keep 0-3 kHz within 1 dB, suppress 4 kHz and up by 60 dB, at 16 kHz sampling. A design tool then finds, say, a 50-tap FIR or an 8th-order IIR meeting that.

concepts.name: Filter (Signal Processing)
concepts.description: A system that modifies a signal by removing or emphasizing certain frequency components or features, for example removing noise, isolating a band or smoothing; it can be analog or digital.
concepts.example: A bass knob on a stereo is a filter: turning it down weakens the low frequencies while leaving voices and cymbals mostly unchanged.

concepts.name: Finite Impulse Response Filter
concepts.description: A digital filter whose output is a weighted sum of a finite number of recent inputs, so its impulse response ends after finitely many samples; always stable and able to have exactly linear phase.
concepts.example: A 3-tap FIR with weights 0.25, 0.5, 0.25 outputs a weighted average of the current and two previous samples; feed it a single 1 and it outputs 0.25, 0.5, 0.25, then zeros forever.

concepts.name: First-Order Optimality Condition
concepts.description: The requirement that the gradient of a differentiable function is zero at an unconstrained local optimum; with constraints it generalizes to the Karush-Kuhn-Tucker conditions.
concepts.example: For f(x) = (x - 3)^2, the derivative 2(x - 3) is zero only at x = 3, so that's the only candidate minimum; for x^3 the derivative is zero at 0 too, showing the condition is necessary but not sufficient.

concepts.name: Fast Iterative Shrinkage-Thresholding Algorithm
concepts.description: An accelerated proximal gradient method that adds Nesterov-style momentum to iterative shrinkage-thresholding, improving the convergence rate from O(1/k) to O(1/k^2) for problems like lasso.
concepts.example: For a sparse regression problem, plain ISTA's error might shrink like 1/k, needing about 1000 steps for 0.001 accuracy; FISTA adds a momentum push and shrinks error like 1/k^2, needing only about 30.

concepts.name: Frank–Wolfe Algorithm
concepts.description: A projection-free constrained optimization method that at each step minimizes a linear approximation of the objective over the feasible set and then moves part of the way toward that point.
concepts.example: To minimize over the triangle of probability vectors in 3D, Frank-Wolfe finds which corner best decreases the linear approximation, then moves a fraction of the way toward it, so iterates stay feasible without any projection.

concepts.name: Frequency
concepts.description: How many times a repeating event or oscillation occurs per unit of time, measured in hertz (cycles per second); it is the reciprocal of the period of the oscillation.
concepts.example: A guitar's A string vibrates back and forth 110 times per second, so its frequency is 110 Hz; the A one octave higher vibrates twice as often, at 220 Hz.

concepts.name: Frequency Response
concepts.description: How a linear time-invariant system scales and phase-shifts a sinusoidal input at each frequency, often displayed as magnitude and phase curves in a Bode plot.
concepts.example: Play pure tones through a speaker: at 1 kHz the output is as loud as the input, at 50 Hz it's half as loud and slightly delayed. Plotting gain and phase shift for every tone gives its frequency response.

concepts.name: Gauss–Newton Algorithm
concepts.description: A method for nonlinear least squares that linearizes the residuals at each step and solves the resulting linear least-squares problem, approximating the Hessian by J^T J.
concepts.example: Fitting y = a e^(bx) to data: at the current a, b, approximate the curve by a straight-line (linear) model in a and b, solve that linear least-squares fit for a correction, update, and repeat until the fit settles.

concepts.name: Genetic Algorithm
concepts.description: An evolutionary algorithm that encodes candidate solutions as chromosomes, often bit strings, and evolves them using fitness-based selection, crossover and mutation.
concepts.example: Encode a packing plan as a bit string like 1011001; combine two good parents by taking the first half of one and second half of the other, flip an occasional bit as mutation, and keep the best children.

concepts.name: Geometric Programming
concepts.description: An optimization problem with posynomial objective and constraints that becomes convex after a logarithmic change of variables; used in circuit design and engineering sizing problems.
concepts.example: Designing a box with volume at least 1 m^3 to minimize surface area 2(xy + yz + xz): writing x = e^u etc. and taking logs turns this posynomial problem into a convex one solvable to global optimality.

concepts.name: Gibbs' Inequality
concepts.description: The result that for distributions p and q, -sum p log p <= -sum p log q, with equality only when p = q; equivalently, the KL divergence is never negative.
concepts.example: A fair coin has entropy 1 bit; coding it with a code designed for a 90/10 coin costs on average 0.5(0.15) + 0.5(3.32), about 1.74 bits, more than 1, as Gibbs' inequality guarantees.

concepts.name: Global Optimum
concepts.description: The best objective value over the entire feasible set, as opposed to a local optimum that is only best among nearby points; for convex problems every local optimum is global.
concepts.example: A hiker in fog might stop on a small hilltop, a local optimum, while the true global optimum is Everest; for cost minimization, the global optimum is the cheapest feasible plan of all.

concepts.name: Golden-Section Search
concepts.description: A method for finding the minimum of a unimodal function on an interval by repeatedly shrinking the interval with points placed at golden-ratio proportions, reusing one evaluation each step.
concepts.example: To find the lowest point of a valley on [0, 1], evaluate at 0.382 and 0.618; whichever is higher, drop the outer part beyond it. The kept point lands at a golden position in the new interval, so each step needs one new evaluation.

concepts.name: Gradient Descent
concepts.description: An iterative optimization algorithm that moves parameters a small step in the direction of the negative gradient to reduce a function; the basic method for training most machine learning models.
concepts.example: Minimizing f(x) = x^2 from x = 4 with step 0.1: the slope is 8, so move to 4 - 0.8 = 3.2, then 2.56, 2.05, and so on, shrinking by 20% each step toward 0.

concepts.name: Greedy Randomized Adaptive Search Procedure
concepts.description: A metaheuristic that repeatedly builds a solution with a randomized greedy procedure and then improves it with local search, keeping the best solution found across all iterations.
concepts.example: For a delivery route, repeatedly build a tour by choosing randomly among the 3 nearest unvisited stops, then polish it with local swaps; after 100 such runs, keep the best tour found.

concepts.name: Greedy Algorithm
concepts.description: An approach that builds a solution step by step, always taking the choice that looks best right now; it is optimal for problems with the greedy-choice property, such as Huffman coding.
concepts.example: Making 63 cents with US coins: take the biggest coin that fits each time: 25, 25, 10, 1, 1, 1, for six coins, which is optimal. With coins 1, 3 and 4, greedy makes 6 as 4+1+1 instead of the better 3+3.

concepts.name: Haar Wavelet
concepts.description: The simplest wavelet, a square step that is +1 on the first half of its interval and -1 on the second; it computes local averages and differences and is the standard introduction to the DWT.
concepts.example: The Haar transform of 9, 7 is the average 8 and the half-difference 1; a flat region like 5, 5 gives difference 0, so only edges and changes produce nonzero detail.

concepts.name: Half-Space
concepts.description: The set of points on one side of a hyperplane, {x : a.x <= b}; halfspaces are convex, and intersecting finitely many of them gives a polyhedron such as an LP's feasible region.
concepts.example: The inequality x + y <= 4 splits the plane along a line: every point below-left of it, like (1, 1), is in the halfspace; (3, 3) is not. Stacking such cuts carves out polygons.

concepts.name: Hamming Code
concepts.description: A family of linear error-correcting codes that place parity bits at power-of-two positions so any single-bit error can be located and corrected, e.g. the Hamming(7,4) code.
concepts.example: Hamming(7,4) sends 4 data bits with 3 parity bits at positions 1, 2 and 4; if bit 6 flips, the failing parity checks read 110 in binary, which is 6, pointing straight at the bad bit.

concepts.name: Hamming Distance
concepts.description: The number of positions at which two equal-length strings or bit vectors differ; it counts how many errors turn one codeword into another and determines a code's correction power.
concepts.example: The words karolin and kathrin differ in 3 positions (r/t, o/h, l/r), so their Hamming distance is 3; the bit strings 1011 and 1001 differ in one position, distance 1.

concepts.name: Heuristic
concepts.description: A practical rule or method that finds good-enough solutions quickly without guaranteeing optimality, used when exact methods are too slow, as in many routing and scheduling problems.
concepts.example: To plan a 50-city tour, 'always drive to the nearest unvisited city' gives a decent route in seconds, though often about 25% longer than the best, which could take far longer to find.

concepts.name: High-Pass Filter
concepts.description: A filter that passes frequencies above a cutoff and attenuates lower ones, removing slow drifts or DC offset and emphasizing rapid changes such as edges in images.
concepts.example: A recording has a slow 0.5 Hz drift from a sensor warming up; a high-pass filter at 1 Hz removes the drift but keeps the 100 Hz heartbeat or voice signal riding on it.

concepts.name: Hilbert Transform
concepts.description: A linear operator that shifts every frequency component of a signal by 90 degrees; combining a signal with its Hilbert transform gives the analytic signal, used for instantaneous amplitude and phase.
concepts.example: The Hilbert transform of cos t is sin t; combining them as cos t + i sin t = e^(it) gives an analytic signal whose magnitude is a steady 1, revealing the envelope of an AM radio wave.

concepts.name: Hill Climbing
concepts.description: A local search algorithm that starts from a solution and repeatedly moves to a better neighboring solution until no neighbor improves, often getting stuck at a local optimum.
concepts.example: Solving 8-queens: start with a random board, move one queen within its column to reduce the number of attacking pairs, and repeat; you may stall at a board where no single move helps, a local optimum.

concepts.name: Huffman Coding
concepts.description: A lossless compression algorithm that builds an optimal prefix code by repeatedly merging the two least frequent symbols into a tree, giving shorter codewords to more common symbols.
concepts.example: Letters A (50%), B (25%), C (12.5%), D (12.5%): merge C and D, then that with B, then with A, giving codes A=0, B=10, C=110, D=111, averaging 1.75 bits instead of 2.

concepts.name: Hungarian Algorithm
concepts.description: A polynomial-time algorithm that solves the assignment problem, finding a minimum-cost perfect matching in a bipartite graph by adjusting dual potentials and following augmenting paths.
concepts.example: Assign 3 workers to 3 jobs with a cost table: subtract each row's minimum, then each column's minimum, and find a set of independent zeros; if needed, adjust and repeat. The zeros mark the cheapest assignment.

concepts.name: Hyperplane
concepts.description: A flat subspace one dimension lower than its surrounding space, defined by a.x = b, such as a line in 2D or a plane in 3D; it splits the space into two halves.
concepts.example: In 3D, the equation x + 2y + 3z = 6 is a flat plane crossing the axes at x = 6, y = 3 and z = 2; in 2D, x + y = 1 is a line. Both are hyperplanes.

concepts.name: Digital Image Processing
concepts.description: The field of applying algorithms to digital images to enhance, restore, analyze or compress them, using operations such as filtering, transforms, morphology and segmentation.
concepts.example: Sharpening a blurry photo, removing red-eye, or detecting faces: each treats the picture as a grid of numbers and applies operations like blurring kernels or edge detectors to it.

concepts.name: Impulse Response
concepts.description: The output of a system when its input is a unit impulse; for a linear time-invariant system it fully characterizes the system, since any output is the input convolved with it.
concepts.example: Clap once in a cathedral and record the echo that follows: that recording is the hall's impulse response, and convolving any dry recording with it makes it sound as if it were played there.

concepts.name: Indicator Function (Convex Analysis)
concepts.description: In convex analysis, the function equal to 0 on a set C and +infinity outside it; adding it to an objective encodes the constraint x in C, and its proximal operator is projection onto C.
concepts.example: To restrict x to [0, 1] while minimizing f, minimize f(x) + I(x) instead, where I is 0 inside [0, 1] and infinity outside; any outside point costs infinitely much, so the constraint is enforced automatically.

concepts.name: Inequality Constraint
concepts.description: A constraint requiring a function of the decision variables to be at most (or at least) a bound, g(x) <= 0, such as a capacity limit; at the solution it may be active or slack.
concepts.example: A diet must contain at least 50 g of protein: 10x + 20y >= 50 for x eggs and y servings of fish. Plans with more protein are fine; it only rules out too little.

concepts.name: Infinite Impulse Response Filter
concepts.description: A digital filter that feeds back past outputs as well as inputs, so its impulse response can last forever; it achieves sharp responses with few coefficients but can become unstable.
concepts.example: The filter y[n] = 0.5 y[n-1] + x[n] responds to a single 1 with 1, 0.5, 0.25, 0.125, ... halving forever but never reaching zero, using just one multiply per sample.

concepts.name: Information Bottleneck Method
concepts.description: A method for finding a compressed representation T of an input X that keeps as much information as possible about a target Y, trading off I(X; T) against I(T; Y).
concepts.example: Summarize thousands of emails (X) into a few clusters (T) so that the clusters still predict spam or not (Y) well: squeeze out details like greetings that tell nothing about Y and keep words that do.

concepts.name: Information Theory
concepts.description: The mathematical study of quantifying, storing and communicating information, founded by Shannon, with core ideas such as entropy, mutual information, channel capacity and coding limits.
concepts.example: A fair coin flip carries 1 bit, a fair die about 2.58 bits. Information theory explains why a ZIP file can't shrink random data and how fast a Wi-Fi link with given noise can possibly send data.

concepts.name: Integer Programming
concepts.description: Optimization of a linear objective under linear constraints where some or all variables must take integer values; NP-hard in general and solved with branch and bound and cutting planes.
concepts.example: Choosing how many trucks (x) and vans (y) to buy: x = 2.7 trucks is meaningless, so x and y must be whole numbers; rounding the LP answer may break a constraint or miss the true best plan.

concepts.name: Interior-Point Method
concepts.description: A class of algorithms for linear and convex optimization that travel through the interior of the feasible region, using barrier functions and Newton steps to reach the optimum in polynomial time.
concepts.example: Instead of walking around the edges of the feasible polygon like simplex, an interior-point method cuts through the middle, following a smooth path that approaches the optimal corner as a barrier weight shrinks.

concepts.name: Iterated Local Search
concepts.description: A metaheuristic that alternates local search with random perturbations of the current local optimum, escaping it to explore new regions while remembering the best solution found.
concepts.example: For a route, run local search to a good tour, then shake it by swapping a few distant segments, run local search again, and keep the new tour if it's better; repeat dozens of times.

concepts.name: Jensen–Shannon Divergence
concepts.description: A symmetric, bounded measure of difference between distributions: the average KL divergence of each from their mixture; its square root is a metric and it appears in the original GAN analysis.
concepts.example: For P = (1, 0) and Q = (0, 1), the mixture M is (0.5, 0.5); each distribution is 1 bit away from M in KL terms, so JS = 1 bit, the maximum possible, whereas KL(P||Q) would be infinite.

concepts.name: Joint Entropy
concepts.description: H(X, Y), the entropy of a pair of random variables taken together, measuring the total uncertainty in both; it is at most H(X) + H(Y), with equality when they are independent.
concepts.example: Two independent fair coins have joint entropy 2 bits (four equally likely outcomes); if the second always copies the first, there are only two outcomes and the joint entropy is just 1 bit.

concepts.name: Karmarkar's Algorithm
concepts.description: A 1984 interior-point algorithm that solves linear programs in polynomial time using projective transformations, which sparked the development of practical interior-point methods.
concepts.example: In 1984 Karmarkar showed an LP could be solved by stepping through the interior, and repeatedly re-centring the current point with a projective transformation, in provably polynomial time and fast in practice.

concepts.name: Karush–Kuhn–Tucker Conditions
concepts.description: First-order necessary conditions for an optimum of a problem with inequality and equality constraints: stationarity of the Lagrangian, feasibility, nonnegative multipliers and complementary slackness.
concepts.example: Minimize x^2 subject to x >= 1: at x = 1 the gradient 2 is balanced by a multiplier 2 on the active constraint, satisfying stationarity, feasibility, nonnegative multiplier and complementary slackness.

concepts.name: Knapsack Problem
concepts.description: The problem of choosing items, each with a weight and a value, to maximize total value without exceeding a weight limit; NP-hard but solvable in pseudo-polynomial time by dynamic programming.
concepts.example: A backpack holds 10 kg; items are a 6 kg tent worth 30, a 5 kg stove worth 20 and a 4 kg camera worth 18. Taking the tent and camera gives 48, the best possible; a table over capacities 0-10 kg finds this.

concepts.name: Kolmogorov Complexity
concepts.description: The length of the shortest computer program that outputs a given string, measuring its intrinsic information content; it is uncomputable but underpins algorithmic information theory.
concepts.example: The string 'ab' repeated 500 times is 1000 characters but can be produced by a short program like print('ab'*500); a truly random 1000-character string needs a program about as long as itself.

concepts.name: Kraft–McMillan Inequality
concepts.description: The condition that the sum of 2^(-l_i) over codeword lengths l_i is at most 1, which must hold for a prefix code, or any uniquely decodable binary code, with those lengths to exist.
concepts.example: Codeword lengths 1, 2, 3, 3 give 1/2 + 1/4 + 1/8 + 1/8 = 1, so a prefix code exists (0, 10, 110, 111); lengths 1, 1, 2 give 1.25 > 1, so no uniquely decodable code can have them.

concepts.name: Limited-Memory BFGS
concepts.description: A memory-efficient variant of BFGS that stores only the last few step and gradient-difference pairs to apply its inverse Hessian approximation, suited to problems with millions of variables.
concepts.example: Training a model with 10 million parameters, full BFGS would need a 10M x 10M matrix; L-BFGS keeps only the last 10 step and gradient-change pairs, about 200 million numbers, and still gets curvature-aware steps.

concepts.name: Lagrangian Duality
concepts.description: Building a dual problem by minimizing the Lagrangian over the primal variables to obtain a dual function, which is then maximized over the multipliers to bound the primal optimum.
concepts.example: Minimize x^2 subject to x >= 1: the Lagrangian x^2 + lambda(1 - x) is minimized at x = lambda/2, giving dual function lambda - lambda^2/4; its maximum, at lambda = 2, is 1, matching the primal optimum.

concepts.name: Lagrangian
concepts.description: The function L(x, lambda) = f(x) + sum of lambda_i g_i(x) that combines an objective with its constraints weighted by Lagrange multipliers; its stationary points characterize constrained optima.
concepts.example: Maximize xy subject to x + y = 10: form L = xy - lambda(x + y - 10); setting its derivatives to zero gives y = lambda, x = lambda, so x = y = 5 with lambda = 5.

concepts.name: Lagrangian Relaxation
concepts.description: A technique that moves hard constraints into the objective with penalty multipliers, producing an easier problem whose solution bounds the original; widely used in integer programming.
concepts.example: In a delivery problem, the rule that each truck carries at most 10 tons ties everything together; move it into the cost with a price per extra ton, and the problem splits into easy per-truck pieces giving a lower bound.

concepts.name: Least Mean Squares Filter
concepts.description: An adaptive filter that adjusts its weights by stochastic gradient descent on the squared error between its output and a desired signal; used for echo cancellation and noise removal.
concepts.example: A noise-cancelling headset measures background hum, filters it with adjustable weights, and subtracts it from the voice microphone; after each sample, weights are nudged to shrink the leftover hum.

concepts.name: Lempel–Ziv–Welch
concepts.description: A dictionary-based lossless compression algorithm that builds a table of previously seen strings on the fly and replaces repeats with table indices; used in GIF images and Unix compress.
concepts.example: Encoding ABABABA: output A and store AB, output B and store BA, output AB and store ABA, then output ABA. Seven letters become four codes, and the decoder rebuilds the same dictionary.

concepts.name: Levenberg–Marquardt Algorithm
concepts.description: A nonlinear least-squares method that blends Gauss-Newton steps with gradient descent through an adaptive damping term, giving robust convergence for curve fitting.
concepts.example: Fitting a curve to data: when steps make the fit worse, the algorithm raises its damping and takes cautious gradient-descent-like steps; when steps succeed, it lowers the damping and moves like fast Gauss-Newton.

concepts.name: Line Search
concepts.description: A step in iterative optimization that, given a search direction, decides how far to move along it, either exactly or approximately using rules such as Armijo backtracking.
concepts.example: Having chosen to walk downhill due east, a line search tries step 1, finds the function went up, tries 0.5, finds it decreased enough, and accepts that step, as in backtracking with the Armijo rule.

concepts.name: Linear Code
concepts.description: An error-correcting code whose codewords form a vector subspace over a finite field, so it can be described by a generator matrix and checked or decoded with a parity-check matrix.
concepts.example: In the even-parity code on 3 bits, codewords are 000, 011, 101, 110; XOR any two, like 011 + 101 = 110, and you get another codeword, so the codewords form a subspace.

concepts.name: Linear Predictive Coding
concepts.description: A technique that models each signal sample as a linear combination of past samples, fitting the coefficients by least squares; linear predictive coding is widely used to compress and analyze speech.
concepts.example: For a smooth sine wave, predicting each sample as 1.9 times the previous minus the one before works almost perfectly; speech codecs send such coefficients instead of raw samples, saving many bits.

concepts.name: Linear Programming
concepts.description: Optimizing a linear objective subject to linear equality and inequality constraints; solved efficiently by simplex or interior-point methods, it models planning, logistics and resource allocation.
concepts.example: A farmer has 100 acres and $1000; wheat earns $40 per acre and costs $5, corn earns $60 and costs $15. Choosing acres to maximize profit under these linear limits is an LP, and its optimum sits at a corner of the feasible region.

concepts.name: Linear Programming Duality
concepts.description: The theorem that every linear program has a dual LP whose optimal value equals the primal's when either is feasible and bounded, with dual variables acting as shadow prices of the constraints.
concepts.example: Maximizing a bakery's profit from flour and sugar has a dual asking the lowest fair prices for flour and sugar; strong duality says the best profit and the lowest total resource value come out equal.

concepts.name: Linear Time-Invariant System
concepts.description: A system that is linear (obeys superposition) and time-invariant (shifting the input shifts the output), so its behavior is fully described by its impulse response or transfer function.
concepts.example: A guitar amp approximates an LTI system: playing twice as loud gives output twice as loud, two notes together give the sum of their outputs, and playing a note later just delays the output.

concepts.name: Lipschitz Continuous Gradient
concepts.description: A function is L-smooth if its gradient changes at most L times as fast as its input, |grad f(x) - grad f(y)| <= L|x - y|; this bounds safe step sizes in gradient methods.
concepts.example: For f(x) = 3x^2 the gradient 6x changes at most 6 times as fast as x, so L = 6; gradient descent with step size 1/L = 1/6 is then guaranteed to decrease f every step.

concepts.name: Local Search (Optimization)
concepts.description: A family of optimization heuristics that start from a candidate solution and repeatedly move to a neighboring solution, where neighbors are defined by small changes such as 2-opt edge swaps.
concepts.example: Scheduling exams: start with any timetable, then repeatedly swap two exams' time slots if that reduces conflicts, stopping when no single swap helps.

concepts.name: Logarithmic Barrier Function
concepts.description: The function -sum of log(-g_i(x)), which grows to infinity at the boundary of inequality constraints; adding it to the objective keeps iterates strictly feasible in interior-point methods.
concepts.example: To keep x below 5, add -log(5 - x) to the objective: at x = 4 it's 0, at x = 4.99 about 4.6, and it shoots to infinity as x nears 5, so the minimizer never crosses.

concepts.name: Lossless Compression
concepts.description: Compression that lets the original data be reconstructed exactly from the compressed form, as in ZIP, PNG or FLAC; the best achievable size is limited by the source's entropy.
concepts.example: The text AAAAABBB can be stored as 5A3B and expanded back to exactly AAAAABBB; ZIP does the same trick at scale, so software and spreadsheets come back byte-for-byte identical.

concepts.name: Lossy Compression
concepts.description: Compression that discards information judged unimportant, so data can only be approximately reconstructed, achieving much smaller sizes for images, audio and video as in JPEG and MP3.
concepts.example: A 30 MB raw photo saved as a JPEG might be 3 MB; it throws away fine color detail people barely notice, so the result looks the same but can't be restored exactly.

concepts.name: Low-Density Parity-Check Code
concepts.description: A linear error-correcting code defined by a sparse parity-check matrix and decoded iteratively with belief propagation, performing close to the Shannon limit; used in 5G and Wi-Fi.
concepts.example: A code with 1000 bits might have parity checks that each involve only 6 bits; the decoder passes beliefs between bits and checks for a few dozen rounds, fixing errors near Shannon's limit, as in Wi-Fi and 5G.

concepts.name: Low-Pass Filter
concepts.description: A filter that passes frequencies below a cutoff and attenuates higher ones, smoothing a signal and removing fast noise; also applied before sampling to prevent aliasing.
concepts.example: Smoothing a jittery GPS speed reading by averaging recent values is low-pass filtering: the slow trend of your trip survives, while rapid second-to-second wobble is removed.

concepts.name: Linear Programming Relaxation
concepts.description: Dropping the integrality requirements of an integer program to get a linear program, whose optimum bounds the integer optimum and guides branching or rounding to integer solutions.
concepts.example: If an integer program allows x = 0 or 1 but the relaxation picks x = 0.6 with value 47, the true best integer value can be at most 47 (for maximization), a bound used to prune branch-and-bound.

concepts.name: Matched Filter
concepts.description: The linear filter that maximizes the signal-to-noise ratio for detecting a known waveform in additive white noise, implemented by correlating the received signal with the template.
concepts.example: A radar sends a known chirp; sliding a template of that chirp along the noisy echo and summing products produces a sharp peak at the echo's delay, even when the echo is buried in noise.

concepts.name: Matching Pursuit
concepts.description: A greedy algorithm that approximates a signal as a sparse combination of dictionary atoms by repeatedly picking the atom most correlated with the residual; OMP re-fits all chosen atoms each step.
concepts.example: To approximate a sound with 3 notes from a dictionary of pure tones, pick the tone best matching the sound, subtract its share, pick the best match to what's left, and so on, three times.

concepts.name: Mathematical Optimization
concepts.description: The field of choosing the best element from a set of options according to an objective, covering continuous, discrete, convex and nonconvex problems; it underlies ML training and operations research.
concepts.example: Choosing the cheapest route through a city, the right mix of investments, or the weights of a neural network are all optimization: pick options from what's allowed to make some score as good as possible.

concepts.name: Maximum Flow Problem
concepts.description: The problem of sending as much flow as possible from a source to a sink through a network whose edges have capacities; solved by Ford-Fulkerson-type algorithms and dual to the minimum cut.
concepts.example: Water flows from a reservoir to a city through pipes rated 5, 3 and 4 units; the most that can reach the city equals the capacity of the narrowest cut of pipes separating them.

concepts.name: Median Filter
concepts.description: A nonlinear filter that replaces each sample or pixel with the median of its neighborhood, removing impulsive salt-and-pepper noise while preserving edges better than averaging.
concepts.example: The samples 3, 4, 99, 5, 4 contain a spike; a 3-point median replaces 99 with the median of 4, 99, 5, which is 5, removing the spike, while a mean would give 36.

concepts.name: Mel-Frequency Cepstrum
concepts.description: A representation of short-term audio spectra on the perceptual mel scale, computed by taking the log of mel filter bank energies and applying a DCT; MFCCs are classic speech features.
concepts.example: For speech recognition, chop audio into 25 ms frames, take each spectrum, sum it in about 26 mel-spaced bands, take logs, then a DCT; the first 13 numbers (MFCCs) summarize the vowel's shape.

concepts.name: Metaheuristic
concepts.description: A high-level, problem-independent strategy for guiding heuristics through large search spaces, such as simulated annealing, genetic algorithms and tabu search, balancing exploration and exploitation.
concepts.example: Simulated annealing for timetabling sometimes accepts a worse timetable on purpose, like shaking a box of marbles to settle them better, letting the search escape traps a plain local search would get stuck in.

concepts.name: Minimax Theorem
concepts.description: Von Neumann's theorem that in finite two-player zero-sum games with mixed strategies, the max-min and min-max values are equal, so every such game has a well-defined value.
concepts.example: In rock-paper-scissors, playing each move 1/3 of the time guarantees an expected payoff of 0 against anyone, and the opponent's same strategy holds you to 0, so max-min equals min-max equals 0.

concepts.name: Minimum-Cost Flow Problem
concepts.description: The problem of sending a required amount of flow through a capacitated network at the lowest total cost, generalizing shortest path, maximum flow, assignment and transportation problems.
concepts.example: Ship 20 tons from two warehouses to three stores along roads with limits and per-ton costs; the cheapest plan might send 12 tons via one road and split the rest, rather than using only the shortest road.

concepts.name: Minimum Description Length
concepts.description: The principle that the best model for data gives the shortest total description of the model plus the data encoded with it, formalizing Occam's razor for model selection.
concepts.example: Fitting 20 points, a straight line costs few bits to describe but leaves big errors to encode; a degree-19 polynomial fits exactly but costs many bits itself; MDL picks the model with the smallest total.

concepts.name: Mirror Descent
concepts.description: A generalization of gradient descent that takes steps in a dual space defined by a mirror map and its Bregman divergence, adapting to the geometry of the constraint set such as the probability simplex.
concepts.example: Optimizing a probability vector (3 options), mirror descent with an entropy mirror map updates weights multiplicatively, e.g. w_i times e^(-step x gradient_i), then renormalizes, so weights stay positive and sum to 1.

concepts.name: Mixed-Integer Linear Programming
concepts.description: A linear program in which some variables must be integers while others are continuous; the standard model for scheduling, routing and planning problems, solved by branch and cut.
concepts.example: Deciding whether to open each warehouse (yes/no, integer) and how many tons to ship from each (continuous), with costs and capacities linear, is a MILP solved by tools like Gurobi or CBC.

concepts.name: Modulation
concepts.description: Varying a property of a carrier wave, such as its amplitude (AM), frequency (FM) or phase, to encode an information signal for transmission over radio or other channels.
concepts.example: AM radio station at 1000 kHz: your voice (around 1 kHz) changes the strength of a 1000 kHz carrier wave; FM instead nudges the carrier's frequency up and down with the voice.

concepts.name: Momentum Method
concepts.description: A gradient descent variant that accumulates a velocity as a decaying sum of past gradients and steps along it, damping oscillations and speeding progress along consistent directions.
concepts.example: Like a ball rolling down a narrow valley: plain gradient descent zigzags between the walls, but momentum averages recent gradients so the side-to-side pushes cancel and the downhill pushes add up, speeding progress.

concepts.name: Moving Average Filter
concepts.description: A simple low-pass FIR filter that outputs the average of the last N input samples, smoothing out short-term fluctuations in signals such as sensor readings or prices.
concepts.example: Daily step counts 4000, 9000, 5000, 8000 smoothed with a 2-day moving average give 6500, 7000, 6500, damping the day-to-day swings to show the trend.

concepts.name: Multi-Objective Optimization
concepts.description: Optimization of several conflicting objectives at once, such as cost and quality, where no single best solution exists and the goal is the set of Pareto-optimal trade-offs.
concepts.example: Choosing a car to minimize both price and fuel use: a $20k car at 8 L/100km and a $30k car at 5 L/100km are both reasonable; neither beats the other on both, so you get a set of trade-offs, not one winner.

concepts.name: Multiresolution Analysis
concepts.description: A framework that represents a signal as nested approximations at successively coarser scales plus detail spaces, providing the mathematical basis for constructing orthogonal wavelets.
concepts.example: Like a map app: a country view, then each zoom level adds the details missing from the coarser map; the full-detail map equals the coarse view plus all the detail layers.

concepts.name: Mutual Information
