concepts.description: I(X; Y), the amount of information one random variable reveals about another, equal to H(X) - H(X | Y); it is zero exactly when the variables are independent.
concepts.example: Knowing today's weather tells you a lot about whether people carry umbrellas: if umbrella-carrying has 1 bit of uncertainty and only 0.3 bits remain once you know the weather, the mutual information is 0.7 bits.

concepts.name: Nelder–Mead Method
concepts.description: A derivative-free optimizer that moves a simplex of n+1 points through the search space by reflection, expansion, contraction and shrink steps; easy to use but without strong guarantees.
concepts.example: In 2D it keeps a triangle of 3 points; it reflects the worst corner through the opposite side, stretching further if that helps or shrinking the triangle if not, so the triangle tumbles downhill toward the minimum.

concepts.name: Nesterov Accelerated Gradient
concepts.description: A momentum method that evaluates the gradient at a look-ahead point after the momentum step, achieving the optimal O(1/k^2) convergence rate for smooth convex problems.
concepts.example: Like a skier who looks at the slope where momentum will carry them, not where they stand: compute the gradient at the look-ahead point, so you brake earlier before overshooting a valley.

concepts.name: Newton's Method in Optimization
concepts.description: An optimization algorithm that uses the gradient and Hessian to fit a local quadratic model and jump to its minimum at each step, converging quadratically near a solution.
concepts.example: For f(x) = x^2 - 4x, at x = 0 the slope is -4 and the curvature is 2; Newton jumps by 4/2 = 2 to x = 2, the exact minimum in one step, since f is a quadratic.

concepts.name: Noisy-Channel Coding Theorem
concepts.description: Shannon's theorem that reliable communication over a noisy channel is possible at any rate below the channel capacity, with error probability arbitrarily small, and impossible above it.
concepts.example: A channel that flips 11% of bits has capacity about 0.5 bits per use; Shannon proved you can send 0.49 bits per use with error rate as tiny as you like using long codes, but never reliably above 0.5.

concepts.name: Nonlinear Conjugate Gradient Method
concepts.description: An extension of the conjugate gradient method to general nonlinear functions that mixes the current gradient with the previous direction using formulas like Fletcher-Reeves or Polak-Ribiere.
concepts.example: Minimizing the Rosenbrock banana function, steepest descent zigzags for thousands of steps along the curved valley; nonlinear CG mixes in the previous direction (e.g. Fletcher-Reeves) and follows the valley far faster.

concepts.name: Nonlinear Least Squares
concepts.description: Fitting model parameters by minimizing the sum of squared residuals when the model is nonlinear in the parameters, as in curve fitting; solved iteratively by Gauss-Newton or Levenberg-Marquardt.
concepts.example: Fitting a cooling curve T = 20 + a e^(-kt) to temperature readings: k sits inside the exponent, so the error isn't a simple quadratic in the parameters, and you must iterate to find the best a and k.

concepts.name: Nonlinear Programming
concepts.description: The field of optimization problems whose objective or constraints are nonlinear, studied through optimality conditions like KKT and methods such as SQP and interior-point algorithms.
concepts.example: Designing a soda can that holds 330 ml with the least metal: surface area 2 pi r^2 + 2 pi r h and volume pi r^2 h = 330 are nonlinear, giving an optimal height about equal to the diameter.

concepts.name: Nyquist Rate
concepts.description: Twice the highest frequency present in a signal, the minimum sampling rate that avoids aliasing; the related Nyquist frequency is half the sampling rate, the highest frequency it can represent.
concepts.example: Human hearing tops out near 20 kHz, so audio's Nyquist rate is about 40 kHz; CDs sample at 44.1 kHz, just above it, leaving room for the anti-aliasing filter.

concepts.name: Nyquist–Shannon Sampling Theorem
concepts.description: The theorem that a band-limited signal can be perfectly reconstructed from its samples if the sampling rate exceeds twice its highest frequency, using sinc interpolation.
concepts.example: A sound containing only frequencies below 4 kHz is fully captured by more than 8,000 samples per second; sinc interpolation recreates the exact continuous wave between samples, losing nothing.

concepts.name: Objective Function
concepts.description: The function an optimization problem seeks to minimize or maximize, such as cost, error or profit, expressed in terms of the decision variables; in machine learning it is usually the loss.
concepts.example: A delivery company deciding routes measures cost = 0.5 x kilometres driven + 20 x hours of overtime; that formula is the objective function the optimizer tries to make as small as possible.

concepts.name: Online Convex Optimization
concepts.description: A sequential setting where a learner picks a point, then an adversary reveals a convex loss, over many rounds; algorithms such as online gradient descent aim for low regret against the best fixed point.
concepts.example: Each day you split money across 3 stocks before prices move, then see the loss; with online gradient descent, after 1000 days your total loss is close to that of the best fixed split chosen in hindsight.

concepts.name: Operations Research
concepts.description: The discipline of applying mathematical modeling, optimization, probability and simulation to improve decisions in areas like logistics, scheduling, supply chains and resource allocation.
concepts.example: An airline uses OR to decide which crews fly which flights, how many seats to sell at each price, and how to reroute after a storm, saving millions each year.

concepts.name: Optimal Control
concepts.description: The field of finding control inputs over time that steer a dynamical system while minimizing a cost, using tools such as Pontryagin's principle, dynamic programming and LQR.
concepts.example: Landing a rocket using the least fuel: choose the thrust at every moment so the rocket's motion, given by physics equations, ends at the pad with zero speed, minimizing total fuel burned.

concepts.name: Pareto Efficiency
concepts.description: A state where no objective can be improved without making another worse. The set of all such trade-off solutions is the Pareto front, central to multi-objective optimization and economics.
concepts.example: Laptops: A ($800, 2 kg), B ($1000, 1.2 kg), C ($1100, 1.5 kg). C is worse than B on both, so it's dominated; A and B are Pareto efficient because each is better on one criterion.

concepts.name: Parity Bit
concepts.description: An extra bit added to a group of bits so the total number of 1s is even (or odd). It lets a receiver detect any single-bit transmission error, though it cannot locate or fix it.
concepts.example: Send 1011 with even parity: it has three 1s, so append a 1 to get 10111. If one bit flips in transit, the receiver counts an odd number of 1s and knows something is wrong.

concepts.name: Parseval's Theorem
concepts.description: States that a signal's total energy is the same whether computed in the time domain or the frequency domain: the sum (or integral) of |x|^2 equals that of its Fourier transform's |X|^2, up to scaling.
concepts.example: The sequence 1, 1, 0, 0 has energy 2; its 4-point DFT is 2, 1-i, 0, 1+i, with squared magnitudes summing to 8, and 8/4 = 2, the same energy computed in the frequency domain.

concepts.name: Particle Swarm Optimization
concepts.description: A population-based optimizer where candidate solutions ('particles') move through the search space, each pulled toward its own best position and the swarm's best position found so far. Needs no gradients.
concepts.example: Picture 30 birds searching a field for food: each flies with some inertia, partly toward the best spot it has found and partly toward the best spot any bird has found, so the flock converges on good areas.

concepts.name: Pattern Search
concepts.description: A family of derivative-free optimizers that probe the objective at points along a set of directions around the current point, move if one is better, and shrink the step size when none is.
concepts.example: Starting at (0, 0) with step 1, test the four points (+-1, 0) and (0, +-1); move to any that improves, otherwise halve the step and try again, until the step is tiny.

concepts.name: Penalty Method
concepts.description: Solves a constrained problem by adding a term to the objective that penalizes constraint violations, then solving a sequence of unconstrained problems with an increasing penalty weight.
concepts.example: To minimize x^2 subject to x = 1, minimize x^2 + mu(x - 1)^2 instead: with mu = 1 the answer is 0.5, with mu = 100 it's about 0.99, approaching 1 as mu grows.

concepts.name: Perplexity
concepts.description: A measure of how well a probability model predicts a sample, equal to the exponential of the average negative log-likelihood (cross-entropy). Lower is better; widely used to evaluate language models.
concepts.example: If a language model has cross-entropy 3 bits per word, its perplexity is 2^3 = 8: it is as uncertain as if choosing uniformly among 8 words at each step.

concepts.name: Phase (Waves)
concepts.description: The position within one cycle of a periodic wave at a given time, usually expressed as an angle. A phase shift moves a wave left or right in time without changing its shape or frequency.
concepts.example: Two identical sine waves, one starting a quarter cycle later, differ in phase by 90 degrees (pi/2 radians); two waves half a cycle apart, 180 degrees, cancel each other completely when added.

concepts.name: Polar Code
concepts.description: An error-correcting code that uses channel polarization: recursively combining channel copies makes some bit-channels nearly perfect and others useless, and data is sent only on the good ones. Provably achieves capacity; used in 5G.
concepts.example: After repeatedly combining and splitting 1024 copies of a noisy channel, some synthetic channels become almost perfect and others almost useless; data goes on the good ones and fixed known bits on the bad ones, as in 5G control channels.

concepts.name: Poles and Zeros
concepts.description: The values of the complex variable where a system's transfer function becomes infinite (poles) or zero (zeros). Their locations determine a system's stability and frequency response.
concepts.example: The filter H(z) = (z - 1)/(z - 0.9) has a zero at z = 1, blocking DC completely, and a pole at 0.9, inside the unit circle, so the filter is stable and passes higher frequencies.

concepts.name: Polyhedron (Optimization)
concepts.description: The set of points satisfying a finite number of linear inequalities, i.e. an intersection of halfspaces. A bounded polyhedron is a polytope; the feasible region of a linear program is a polyhedron.
concepts.example: The constraints x >= 0, y >= 0, x <= 3, y <= 2 describe a rectangle; it is a polyhedron, the intersection of 4 halfspaces, and every LP over it has an optimum at one of its 4 corners.

concepts.name: Positive-Definite Matrix
concepts.description: A symmetric matrix A with x^T A x > 0 for every nonzero vector x, equivalently all eigenvalues positive. Semidefinite allows >= 0. Such matrices appear as covariances, Hessians at minima and kernels.
concepts.example: The matrix [[2, 0], [0, 3]] gives x^T A x = 2x^2 + 3y^2, positive for every nonzero (x, y), like a bowl opening upward; [[1, 0], [0, -1]] gives x^2 - y^2, a saddle, so it isn't.

concepts.name: Positive Semidefinite Cone
concepts.description: The set of all symmetric positive semidefinite matrices of a given size. It is a closed convex cone and serves as the feasible region of semidefinite programs.
concepts.example: Averaging two covariance matrices, or scaling one by 3, always gives another valid covariance matrix; that's why the PSD matrices form a convex cone.

concepts.name: Prefix Code
concepts.description: A code in which no codeword is the beginning of another, so an encoded message can be decoded symbol by symbol without separators. Huffman codes are the classic example.
concepts.example: With codes A = 0, B = 10, C = 11, the bits 010110 decode uniquely as 0|10|11|0 = ABCA, because no codeword starts another; phone numbers work similarly, with no number the start of another.

concepts.name: Primal-Dual Interior-Point Method
concepts.description: An interior-point method that updates primal and dual variables together, taking Newton steps on perturbed KKT conditions to follow the central path. The workhorse of modern LP and conic solvers.
concepts.example: Modern LP solvers update the production plan and resource prices together, each step a Newton step toward satisfying the optimality equations with a shrinking slack, typically solving huge LPs in 20-50 iterations.

concepts.name: Projected Gradient Descent
concepts.description: Gradient descent for constrained problems: take an ordinary gradient step, then project the result back onto the feasible set. Also the basis of the PGD adversarial attack.
concepts.example: To minimize a function with x confined to [0, 1]: from x = 0.9 a gradient step lands at 1.2, so projection snaps it back to 1, the nearest allowed point, and the iteration continues.

concepts.name: Projection onto a Convex Set
concepts.description: The map sending a point to the closest point in a convex set. For closed convex sets this closest point exists and is unique, making projection a basic building block of constrained optimization.
concepts.example: Projecting the point (3, 4) onto the unit disk gives (0.6, 0.8): scale it toward the origin until its length is 1. A point already inside the disk projects to itself.

concepts.name: Proximal Gradient Method
concepts.description: Minimizes a sum of a smooth function and a nonsmooth one by taking a gradient step on the smooth part, then applying the proximal operator of the nonsmooth part. ISTA for lasso is the classic case.
concepts.example: For LASSO, take a gradient step on the squared error, then apply soft-thresholding: shrink every coefficient toward 0 by a fixed amount, setting small ones exactly to zero, and repeat.

concepts.name: Proximal Operator
concepts.description: For a function f, prox_f(v) is the point minimizing f(x) plus half the squared distance to v. It generalizes projection; for the L1 norm it is soft-thresholding.
concepts.example: The prox of t|x| at v = 3 with t = 1 is 2: the point balancing being near 3 against a small |x|; at v = 0.5 it is 0. This soft-thresholding is what makes LASSO produce exact zeros.

concepts.name: Quadratic Programming
concepts.description: Optimizing a quadratic objective subject to linear equality and inequality constraints. Convex QPs are solved efficiently and arise in SVM training, portfolio optimization and MPC.
concepts.example: Choosing portfolio weights that sum to 1 and are nonnegative to minimize risk w^T C w, where C is the covariance matrix: a quadratic objective with linear constraints, i.e. Markowitz's QP.

concepts.name: Quadratically Constrained Quadratic Program
concepts.description: An optimization problem with a quadratic objective and quadratic constraints. It is convex only when all the quadratic forms are positive semidefinite; otherwise it is NP-hard in general.
concepts.example: Minimizing portfolio risk while requiring the tracking error versus a benchmark to stay below a set level: both the objective and the constraint are quadratic, a QCQP that's convex if the matrices are PSD.

concepts.name: Quantization (Signal Processing)
concepts.description: Mapping a continuous range of amplitudes to a finite set of levels, as in analog-to-digital conversion. The rounding introduces quantization error, often modeled as additive noise.
concepts.example: A 3-bit converter has 8 levels for 0-8 V; a reading of 5.7 V is rounded down to level 5, an error of 0.7 V. With 16 bits there are 65,536 levels and the error becomes tiny.

concepts.name: Quasi-Newton Method
concepts.description: Optimization methods that mimic Newton's method but build an approximation to the Hessian (or its inverse) from successive gradient differences, avoiding second derivatives. BFGS is the best known.
concepts.example: Rather than computing a 1000 x 1000 Hessian each step, BFGS watches how the gradient changed after each step and refines a curvature estimate, getting Newton-like speed at far lower cost.

concepts.name: Quasiconvex Function
concepts.description: A function whose sublevel sets are all convex. It generalizes convexity; quasiconvex functions can be minimized by bisection over convex feasibility problems.
concepts.example: The function sqrt(|x|) is not convex (its graph bends the wrong way), but every set where it's at most c is an interval, so it's quasiconvex and has no false local minima to get stuck in.

concepts.name: Rate–Distortion Theory
concepts.description: The branch of information theory giving the minimum bit rate needed to describe a source with expected distortion at most D. Its rate-distortion function sets the limit of lossy compression.
concepts.example: To store a Gaussian signal with variance 1 at mean squared error 0.25, you need at least 0.5 log2(1/0.25) = 1 bit per sample; halving the allowed distortion costs another half bit.

concepts.name: Reed–Solomon Code
concepts.description: An error-correcting code that treats data as coefficients or values of a polynomial over a finite field and sends extra evaluations. It corrects burst errors; used in CDs, QR codes and storage.
concepts.example: Encode 3 numbers as the values of a degree-2 polynomial at 7 points; any 3 correct values pin down the polynomial, so up to 4 lost values, or 2 wrong ones, can be recovered. CDs and QR codes use this.

concepts.name: Region of Convergence
concepts.description: The set of complex values for which a Z-transform or Laplace transform sum or integral converges. Together with the formula it uniquely determines the signal and reveals causality and stability.
concepts.example: The sequence 0.5^n for n >= 0 has Z-transform 1/(1 - 0.5/z), but only for |z| > 0.5; the ROC tells you whether that formula describes this sequence or a different, left-sided one.

concepts.name: Rényi Entropy
concepts.description: A one-parameter family of entropies, H_alpha = log(sum p_i^alpha)/(1-alpha), that includes Shannon entropy as alpha -> 1, plus min-entropy and collision entropy as other special cases.
concepts.example: For a coin with p = 0.9, Shannon entropy is 0.47 bits, collision entropy (alpha = 2) is -log2(0.82) = 0.29 bits, and min-entropy is -log2(0.9) = 0.15 bits: larger alpha focuses on the likeliest outcome.

concepts.name: Restricted Isometry Property
concepts.description: A matrix has RIP if it nearly preserves the length of every sparse vector. It guarantees that sparse signals can be exactly recovered from few measurements by L1 minimization in compressed sensing.
concepts.example: A random 100 x 1000 matrix maps 1000-dimensional vectors with at most 10 nonzeros to 100 numbers while keeping their lengths within, say, 10%, so such sparse vectors can be recovered from just 100 measurements.

concepts.name: Revised Simplex Method
concepts.description: A version of the simplex algorithm that keeps only a factorization of the current basis matrix instead of the full tableau, making each iteration much cheaper on large, sparse linear programs.
concepts.example: For an LP with 10,000 variables but only 100 constraints, the revised method stores an LU factorization of the 100 x 100 basis and computes only the columns it needs, instead of updating a 100 x 10,000 tableau.

concepts.name: Robust Optimization
concepts.description: Optimization under uncertainty where constraints must hold for every parameter value in an uncertainty set, giving a worst-case guarantee. Often reformulated as a tractable convex problem.
concepts.example: A shipping plan where each truck's travel time could be up to 20% longer than expected: a robust plan meets every deadline in the worst case within that range, not just on average.

concepts.name: Run-Length Encoding
concepts.description: A simple lossless compression method that replaces runs of repeated symbols with one symbol and a count, e.g. AAAABB becomes 4A2B. Effective for data with long repeated runs.
concepts.example: A row of a black-and-white fax WWWWWWWWBBBWWWW becomes 8W3B4W, 6 characters instead of 15; but text without runs, like ABCD, would grow to 1A1B1C1D.

concepts.name: Sampling (Signal Processing)
concepts.description: Converting a continuous-time signal into a discrete sequence by measuring it at regular intervals. The sampling rate determines which frequencies can be captured without aliasing.
concepts.example: A movie camera samples a scene 24 times per second; a wagon wheel spinning faster than 12 turns per second can appear to rotate backward, because the sampling was too slow.

concepts.name: Secant Condition
concepts.description: The requirement in quasi-Newton methods that the new Hessian approximation B satisfy B s = y, where s is the step and y the change in gradient, so it matches the observed curvature.
concepts.example: In 1D the condition reduces to the secant slope: if the gradient goes from 2 to 8 when x goes from 1 to 3, the curvature estimate is (8 - 2)/(3 - 1) = 3.

concepts.name: Second-Order Cone
concepts.description: The convex cone of points (x, t) with ||x||_2 <= t, shaped like an ice-cream cone. It is the building block of second-order cone programming.
concepts.example: In 3D, the points (x, y, t) with sqrt(x^2 + y^2) <= t form an ice-cream cone opening upward: at height t = 2 the slice is a disk of radius 2.

concepts.name: Second-Order Cone Programming
concepts.description: Convex optimization with a linear objective and constraints requiring affine expressions to lie in second-order cones. It covers LPs, convex QPs and robust LPs and is solved by interior-point methods.
concepts.example: Placing a warehouse to minimize the total straight-line distance to 5 stores: each distance is a norm, so this becomes an SOCP that interior-point solvers handle exactly.

concepts.name: Second-Order Optimality Condition
concepts.description: Conditions on the Hessian at a stationary point: a positive definite Hessian guarantees a strict local minimum, while a local minimum requires it to be positive semidefinite.
concepts.example: f(x, y) = x^2 + y^2 has zero gradient at the origin and Hessian [[2, 0], [0, 2]], positive definite, so it's a minimum; x^2 - y^2 also has zero gradient there but a mixed-sign Hessian, so it's a saddle.

concepts.name: Self-Concordant Function
concepts.description: A convex function whose third derivative is bounded by its second derivative to the 3/2 power. This makes Newton's method's behavior affine-invariant and underpins interior-point complexity bounds.
concepts.example: For f(x) = -log x, the third derivative magnitude 2/x^3 equals 2 times (1/x^2)^(3/2), satisfying the bound exactly; that's why log barriers make Newton's method converge in a predictable number of steps.

concepts.name: Information Content
concepts.description: The surprise of observing an outcome with probability p, defined as -log p. Rare events carry more information; the average self-information over outcomes is the entropy.
concepts.example: A fair coin landing heads (p = 1/2) carries 1 bit of surprise; rolling a six (p = 1/6) carries about 2.58 bits; a sure event carries 0 bits.

concepts.name: Semidefinite Programming
concepts.description: Optimizing a linear function of a symmetric matrix variable subject to linear constraints and the requirement that the matrix be positive semidefinite. Generalizes LP; used for relaxations like Max-Cut.
concepts.example: Finding the largest cut in a graph is hard, but relaxing it to an SDP over a PSD matrix gives the Goemans-Williamson algorithm, guaranteed within about 88% of the best cut.

concepts.name: Sensitivity Analysis (Linear Programming)
concepts.description: Studying how an LP's optimal solution and value change when objective coefficients or constraint bounds change, and over what ranges the current optimal basis stays optimal.
concepts.example: If a factory's optimal plan stays the same as long as chair profit is between $30 and $50, a manager knows a $5 price change from $40 needs no replanning.

concepts.name: Separating Hyperplane Theorem
concepts.description: States that two disjoint convex sets can be separated by a hyperplane, with each set on a different side. It is a key tool behind duality theory and linear classifiers.
concepts.example: Two non-overlapping circles on a plane can always be split by a straight line; for an L-shape and a point tucked in its corner, which isn't convex, no line may work.

concepts.name: Sequential Quadratic Programming
concepts.description: Solves nonlinear constrained problems by repeatedly solving a quadratic program built from a quadratic model of the Lagrangian and linearized constraints, essentially Newton's method on the KKT conditions.
concepts.example: To design a lightweight bracket under stress limits, SQP builds a quadratic model of the weight and linearized stress constraints at the current design, solves that QP for a step, and repeats.

concepts.name: Shadow Price
concepts.description: The rate at which the optimal objective value would improve per unit increase in a constraint's right-hand side. In LP it equals the optimal dual variable for that constraint.
concepts.example: If one extra hour of oven time would raise a bakery's maximum profit by $12, the oven's shadow price is $12/hour, so renting extra oven time for less than $12/hour is worth it.

concepts.name: Shannon–Fano Coding
concepts.description: An early prefix-code construction that sorts symbols by probability and recursively splits them into two groups of nearly equal probability, assigning 0 and 1. Simple but not always optimal like Huffman.
concepts.example: Symbols A 0.4, B 0.3, C 0.2, D 0.1: split into {A} and {B, C, D}, then {B} and {C, D}, giving A = 0, B = 10, C = 110, D = 111, roughly matching code lengths to surprise.

concepts.name: Shannon–Hartley Theorem
concepts.description: Gives the capacity of a band-limited channel with Gaussian noise: C = B log2(1 + S/N) bits per second. It sets the maximum error-free data rate for a given bandwidth and SNR.
concepts.example: A phone line with 3 kHz bandwidth and signal-to-noise ratio 1000 (30 dB) has capacity 3000 x log2(1001), about 30,000 bits per second, roughly where dial-up modems topped out.

concepts.name: Short-Time Fourier Transform
concepts.description: Computes Fourier transforms over short, overlapping windowed segments of a signal, showing how its frequency content changes over time. The basis of spectrograms in audio and speech processing.
concepts.example: Split a song into 50 ms windows and Fourier-transform each one: stacking them over time gives a spectrogram showing the melody rising and falling, which a single transform of the whole song can't show.

concepts.name: Signal
concepts.description: A function that conveys information, typically a quantity varying over time or space, such as an audio waveform, an image or a sensor reading. Can be continuous or discrete.
concepts.example: A recording of your voice is a signal: air pressure as a function of time. A photo is a signal too: brightness as a function of position.

concepts.name: Signal Processing
concepts.description: The field of analyzing, transforming and synthesizing signals such as audio, images and sensor data, using tools like filtering, Fourier analysis and sampling.
concepts.example: Noise-cancelling headphones record the hum around you, work out which frequencies it contains, and play the opposite wave so the hum cancels while your music passes through untouched.

concepts.name: Signal-to-Noise Ratio
concepts.description: The ratio of the power of a meaningful signal to the power of background noise, usually given in decibels. Higher SNR means a cleaner signal and more reliable communication.
concepts.example: If a voice on a phone line carries 100 times more power than the static behind it, the SNR is 100, or 20 dB; at 1 dB the voice and hiss are almost equally loud and words get lost.

concepts.name: Simplex Algorithm
concepts.description: Dantzig's algorithm for linear programming that moves from vertex to adjacent vertex of the feasible polyhedron, each time improving the objective, until no improving edge remains.
concepts.example: To maximise profit from making chairs and tables under wood and labour limits, start at the corner 'make nothing', then hop to a neighbouring corner of the feasible region that earns more, and stop when no neighbour is better.

concepts.name: Simulated Annealing
concepts.description: A metaheuristic that explores solutions randomly, sometimes accepting worse moves with probability exp(-delta/T); the temperature T is slowly lowered, helping escape local optima.
concepts.example: Looking for the lowest valley in hilly fog, you sometimes walk uphill on purpose early on; at temperature 10 an uphill step of 5 is accepted with probability e^-0.5, about 61%, but once T drops to 1 that chance falls to under 1%.

concepts.name: Sinc Function
concepts.description: The function sinc(x) = sin(x)/x (or sin(pi x)/(pi x) normalized), equal to 1 at zero. It is the Fourier transform of a rectangular pulse and the ideal interpolation kernel for sampled signals.
concepts.example: sinc(x) = sin(x)/x is 1 at x = 0 and then ripples with shrinking height: at x = pi it is 0, and around x = 4.5 it dips to about -0.22, like a stone's ripple dying out.

concepts.name: Sinusoidal Wave
concepts.description: A smooth periodic wave of the form A sin(2 pi f t + phi), defined by amplitude, frequency and phase. Sinusoids are the basic building blocks of Fourier analysis.
concepts.example: Mains electricity in Europe is a sinusoid with amplitude about 325 volts and frequency 50 Hz: the voltage swings smoothly up and down 50 times every second, forever repeating the same shape.

concepts.name: Slack Variable
concepts.description: A nonnegative variable added to an inequality constraint to turn it into an equality, measuring how far the constraint is from being tight. A surplus variable does the same for >= constraints.
concepts.example: The constraint 'wood used: 3x + 2y <= 12' becomes 3x + 2y + s = 12 with s >= 0. If you plan to use 10 boards, the slack s = 2 is the wood left over.

concepts.name: Slater's Condition
concepts.description: A constraint qualification for convex problems: if some point strictly satisfies all inequality constraints, then strong duality holds and the KKT conditions are necessary for optimality.
concepts.example: For minimising x^2 subject to x >= 1, the point x = 2 satisfies the constraint strictly (2 > 1), so Slater holds and the dual problem is guaranteed to give the same optimal value, 1.

concepts.name: Shannon's Source Coding Theorem
concepts.description: Shannon's theorem that a source cannot be losslessly compressed below its entropy in bits per symbol on average, and that rates arbitrarily close to the entropy are achievable.
concepts.example: A biased coin landing heads 90% of the time has entropy about 0.47 bits per flip, so a long record of 1000 flips can be squeezed to roughly 470 bits but no lossless method can average less.

concepts.name: Sparse Representation
concepts.description: Expressing a signal as a combination of only a few elements from a basis or overcomplete dictionary. Used for compression, denoising and compressed sensing; dictionary learning fits the dictionary to data.
concepts.example: A photo of a mostly blue sky can be described by a few smooth wavelet pieces plus a handful for the bird in it; storing those 50 coefficients instead of a million pixels is a sparse representation.

concepts.name: Spectral Leakage
concepts.description: The smearing of a sinusoid's energy into neighboring frequency bins when a DFT is taken over a segment that does not contain a whole number of periods. Reduced by applying window functions.
concepts.example: A 10.5 Hz tone analysed with a DFT whose bins sit at 10 Hz and 11 Hz cannot land in one bin, so its energy spills into 10, 11 and smaller amounts into 9, 12 and beyond.

concepts.name: Spectrogram
concepts.description: An image of a signal's frequency content over time, with time on one axis, frequency on the other and intensity as magnitude. Usually computed via the STFT; common input for audio models.
concepts.example: In a spectrogram of birdsong, each chirp shows up as a bright diagonal streak rising from 2 kHz to 5 kHz over a fraction of a second, so you can literally see the pitch sweep.

concepts.name: Symmetric Rank-One Update
concepts.description: A quasi-Newton update that adds a symmetric rank-one correction to the Hessian approximation so it satisfies the secant condition. Unlike BFGS it can capture indefinite curvature.
concepts.example: If the current Hessian guess predicts the gradient should change by 3 but it actually changed by 5, SR1 adds one rank-one correction so the updated matrix reproduces that change of 5 exactly.

concepts.name: Standard Form (Linear Programming)
concepts.description: A canonical way of writing a linear program: minimize c^T x subject to Ax = b and x >= 0. Any LP can be converted to it using slack variables and variable splitting; the simplex method works on it.
concepts.example: Maximise x + y with x + y <= 4 becomes: minimise -x - y with x + y + s = 4 and x, y, s >= 0. Same problem, written in the one shape that solvers expect.

concepts.name: Stationary Point
concepts.description: A point where a differentiable function's derivative or gradient is zero. It can be a local minimum, local maximum or saddle point; finding one is the goal of first-order optimization.
concepts.example: For f(x) = x^3 - 3x the derivative 3x^2 - 3 is zero at x = 1 (a local minimum) and x = -1 (a local maximum), while f(x) = x^3 has a stationary point at 0 that is neither.

concepts.name: Statistical Signal Processing
concepts.description: The study of signals as random processes, using estimation and detection theory to extract information from noisy data, e.g. in radar, communications and audio.
concepts.example: A radar receiver must decide whether a faint echo buried in random noise means a plane is there, and if so estimate its distance; treating noise as random lets you choose the decision threshold optimally.

concepts.name: Step Size
concepts.description: The scalar that sets how far an iterative optimizer moves along its search direction each step; called the learning rate in machine learning. Too large diverges, too small converges slowly.
concepts.example: Minimising f(x) = x^2 from x = 4 with gradient 8: a step size of 0.1 moves to 3.2, a careful approach; a step size of 1 jumps to -4 and you bounce back and forth forever.

concepts.name: Stochastic Gradient Descent
concepts.description: Gradient descent that updates parameters using the gradient on a single random example or small mini-batch instead of the full dataset. Noisy but cheap; the standard way to train neural networks.
concepts.example: Instead of tasting the whole pot of soup before each adjustment, you taste one spoonful and adjust; each taste is noisy, but you make far more adjustments and still end up near the right seasoning.

concepts.name: Stochastic Optimization
concepts.description: Optimization where the objective or constraints involve randomness or are only accessible through noisy samples, e.g. minimizing an expected loss. Includes SGD and stochastic approximation methods.
concepts.example: Choosing how many umbrellas to stock without knowing tomorrow's weather: you pick the number that maximises average profit over many simulated rainy and dry days.

concepts.name: Strictly Convex Function
concepts.description: A function whose graph lies strictly below every chord between two distinct points. A strictly convex function has at most one minimizer.
concepts.example: f(x) = x^2 is strictly convex: the straight line from (-1, 1) to (1, 1) passes above the curve at every point in between, e.g. 1 versus 0 at x = 0. A straight line f(x) = x is convex but not strictly.

concepts.name: Strong Duality
concepts.description: The property that the optimal values of a primal problem and its dual are equal, i.e. the duality gap is zero. It holds for linear programs and for convex problems satisfying conditions like Slater's.
concepts.example: A factory's minimum production cost is 500, and the best lower bound from pricing its resources (the dual) is also 500; when these meet exactly, as they do for feasible linear programs, strong duality holds.

concepts.name: Strongly Convex Function
concepts.description: A function that stays at least a quadratic bowl above its tangent planes: f(y) >= f(x) + grad f(x)^T (y-x) + (m/2)||y-x||^2. It guarantees a unique minimum and linear convergence of gradient descent.
concepts.example: f(x) = x^2 is strongly convex with constant 2: it curves upward at least that much everywhere. f(x) = x^4 is strictly convex but not strongly, since it is nearly flat near zero.

concepts.name: Subgradient
concepts.description: A generalization of the gradient to nondifferentiable convex functions: any vector g whose linear lower bound f(x) + g^T(y-x) touches f at x. The set of all of them is the subdifferential.
concepts.example: f(x) = |x| has no derivative at 0, but any slope between -1 and 1 gives a line through the origin that stays below the V shape, so every g in [-1, 1] is a subgradient there.

concepts.name: Subgradient Method
concepts.description: An iterative method for nondifferentiable convex functions that steps along a negative subgradient with diminishing step sizes. Simple and widely applicable but converges slowly.
concepts.example: To minimise |x - 3| from x = 0, step against the subgradient -1 with step sizes 1, 1/2, 1/3, and so on; you overshoot and oscillate around 3, but the shrinking steps settle you there.

concepts.name: Sublevel Set
concepts.description: For a function f and value c, the set of points where f(x) <= c. Every sublevel set of a convex function is convex, which is why sublevel sets define quasiconvexity.
concepts.example: For f(x, y) = x^2 + y^2 and c = 4, the sublevel set is the filled disk of radius 2: all points whose height on the bowl is at most 4.

concepts.name: Supporting Hyperplane
concepts.description: A hyperplane that touches a set at a boundary point while the whole set lies on one side of it. Every boundary point of a convex set has at least one.
concepts.example: Rest a ruler against a ball on a table: the ruler touches the ball at one point while the whole ball stays on one side. In 2D, the line y = 1 supports the unit disk at (0, 1).

concepts.name: Tabu Search
concepts.description: A local-search metaheuristic that keeps a short-term memory (tabu list) of recent moves or solutions and forbids revisiting them, letting the search escape local optima and avoid cycling.
concepts.example: Planning a delivery route, after swapping cities 3 and 7 you forbid swapping them back for the next 5 moves; this keeps the search from undoing its own changes and pushes it into new territory.

concepts.name: Time-Frequency Analysis
concepts.description: The study of signals whose frequency content changes over time, using joint time-frequency representations such as the short-time Fourier transform, wavelets and spectrograms.
concepts.example: Music changes key and tempo, so one overall spectrum blurs it all together; time-frequency analysis shows which notes play when, like a piano roll showing a melody rising over 10 seconds.

concepts.name: Total Unimodularity
concepts.description: A matrix is totally unimodular if every square submatrix has determinant 0, +1 or -1. Then an LP with integer data has integer vertex solutions, so the integer program can be solved as an LP.
concepts.example: Assignment problems have constraint matrices made of 0s and 1s whose square submatrices all have determinant 0 or +-1, so solving the plain LP already gives whole-number answers such as worker 2 to job 5.

concepts.name: Transfer Function
concepts.description: The ratio of the Laplace or Z-transform of a linear time-invariant system's output to that of its input. It fully characterizes the system and encodes its frequency response.
concepts.example: A simple RC low-pass filter has transfer function H(s) = 1/(1 + RCs); plug in a frequency and it tells you how much that tone is weakened, e.g. halved in amplitude well above the cut-off.

concepts.name: Transportation Problem
concepts.description: Finding the cheapest way to ship goods from a set of suppliers to a set of consumers, meeting supplies and demands. A special linear program with integral solutions and efficient specialized algorithms.
concepts.example: Two bakeries make 30 and 20 loaves; three shops need 10, 25 and 15. Choosing how many loaves go along each of the six routes to minimise total delivery cost is a transportation problem.

concepts.name: Traveling Salesman Problem
concepts.description: Find the shortest route that visits every city exactly once and returns to the start. A classic NP-hard problem studied with exact, approximation and heuristic algorithms.
concepts.example: With 5 cities there are only 12 different round trips to check, but with 20 cities there are about 60 quadrillion, which is why finding the shortest tour quickly becomes infeasible by brute force.

concepts.name: Trust Region Method
concepts.description: An optimization strategy that minimizes a local quadratic model within a region where the model is trusted, then grows or shrinks that region depending on how well the model predicted the actual decrease.
concepts.example: Using a road map you only trust within 1 km, you plan the best move inside that circle; if the move works as well as predicted you trust the map out to 2 km next time, otherwise you shrink to 500 m.

concepts.name: Turbo Code
concepts.description: An error-correcting code made of two convolutional encoders joined by an interleaver, decoded by iteratively exchanging soft probabilities between two decoders. Came close to Shannon capacity; used in 3G/4G.
concepts.example: Two puzzle solvers each work on a scrambled copy of the same crossword, swap hints about which letters they're confident in, and repeat; after a few rounds they agree on nearly every letter.

concepts.name: Typical Set
concepts.description: For long i.i.d. sequences, the set of sequences whose probability is close to 2^(-nH). It contains almost all the probability mass yet only about 2^(nH) sequences, which is why compression to entropy works.
concepts.example: Flip a coin with P(heads) = 0.9 a thousand times: you will almost surely get around 900 heads, and the sequences with about that count make up the typical set, even though the all-heads sequence is individually most likely.

concepts.name: Gabor Limit
concepts.description: The limit that a signal cannot be sharply localized in both time and frequency: the product of its time spread and frequency spread is bounded below. Gaussian pulses achieve the minimum.
concepts.example: A short click lasting 1 ms contains a broad smear of frequencies, while a pure pitch you can identify exactly must last a long time; squeezing a sound in time always spreads it in frequency.

concepts.name: Unconstrained Optimization
concepts.description: Minimizing or maximizing a function over all of its domain with no constraints on the variables. Solved by methods such as gradient descent, Newton's method and quasi-Newton methods.
concepts.example: Find the x that minimises f(x) = (x - 3)^2 + 1 with x allowed to be any real number: set the derivative 2(x - 3) to zero and get x = 3, with minimum value 1.

concepts.name: Upsampling
concepts.description: Increasing a signal's sampling rate by inserting new samples between existing ones, typically zeros followed by a low-pass interpolation filter. In images and neural networks it enlarges feature maps.
concepts.example: To double a 22 kHz audio clip to 44 kHz, insert a zero between every pair of samples, then low-pass filter so the zeros are filled with smooth in-between values.

concepts.name: Variable Neighborhood Search
concepts.description: A metaheuristic that systematically switches between several neighborhood structures, moving to a larger neighborhood when local search gets stuck and back to the first after an improvement.
concepts.example: In scheduling, first try swapping two adjacent jobs; if that cannot improve things, try swapping any two jobs, then moving blocks of three; as soon as something improves, go back to the smallest swaps.

concepts.name: Stochastic Variance Reduced Gradient
concepts.description: SGD variants such as SVRG and SAGA that correct each stochastic gradient using stored or periodically computed full gradients, reducing noise and achieving linear convergence on strongly convex finite sums.
concepts.example: SVRG periodically computes the exact full-data gradient and then corrects each noisy single-example gradient by the difference, so steps stay cheap but much less jittery, allowing a constant step size.

concepts.name: Viterbi Algorithm
concepts.description: A dynamic programming algorithm that finds the most likely sequence of hidden states in a hidden Markov model given observations. Used in speech recognition, tagging and decoding convolutional codes.
concepts.example: Given that a friend reported walk, shop, clean on three days, Viterbi finds the single most likely weather sequence, such as sunny, rainy, rainy, by keeping only the best path into each state at each day.

concepts.name: Wavelet
concepts.description: A brief, oscillating, localized function; scaled and shifted copies of a mother wavelet form a basis for analyzing signals at multiple resolutions in both time and frequency.
concepts.example: A wavelet is like a short musical 'blip'; sliding stretched and squeezed copies along a recording reveals both what pitch appears and exactly when, such as a sudden click at 2.3 seconds.

concepts.name: Weak Duality
concepts.description: The fact that the optimal value of the dual problem is always a lower bound on that of a primal minimization problem. It holds for every optimization problem, convex or not.
concepts.example: If a primal cost-minimisation problem has a feasible plan costing 100 and the dual has a feasible value of 80, weak duality guarantees the true minimum cost lies between 80 and 100.

concepts.name: Whittaker–Shannon Interpolation Formula
concepts.description: Reconstructs a band-limited continuous signal exactly from its samples by summing shifted sinc functions weighted by the sample values, provided sampling is above the Nyquist rate.
concepts.example: Given samples of a band-limited tone taken 8000 times a second, place a sinc pulse at each sample scaled by its value and add them all; the sum passes through every sample and recreates the smooth wave in between.

concepts.name: Wiener Filter
concepts.description: The linear filter that minimizes the mean squared error between its output and a desired signal, given the signal and noise statistics. Used for denoising and deblurring.
concepts.example: Cleaning a hissy recording: at frequencies where the voice is much stronger than the hiss the filter lets sound through almost fully, while where hiss dominates it turns the volume down, minimising average error.

concepts.name: Wiener–Khinchin Theorem
concepts.description: States that the power spectral density of a wide-sense stationary process is the Fourier transform of its autocorrelation function, linking time-domain correlation and frequency content.
concepts.example: Hum at 50 Hz makes a recording's autocorrelation repeat every 20 ms; Fourier transforming that autocorrelation gives a power spectrum with a sharp spike at 50 Hz.

concepts.name: Window Function
concepts.description: A function, such as the Hann or Hamming window, that tapers a signal segment toward zero at its ends before a Fourier transform to reduce spectral leakage. (In SQL, a window function computes over related rows.)
concepts.example: Before a DFT, multiply a 1024-sample chunk by a Hann window, which rises smoothly from 0 to 1 and back to 0; this removes the abrupt jumps at the edges that would otherwise smear the spectrum.

concepts.name: Wolfe Conditions
concepts.description: Two inequalities used to accept a step size in inexact line search: the Armijo condition requires sufficient decrease in the objective, and the curvature condition rules out steps that are too short.
concepts.example: Searching along a downhill direction, a step is accepted if it lowers the function enough (say at least 0.01% of what the slope promised) and if the slope has flattened enough that a longer step would not gain much more.

concepts.name: Z-Transform
concepts.description: Converts a discrete-time signal x[n] into a function of a complex variable z, X(z) = sum x[n] z^-n. It turns convolution into multiplication and is used to analyze digital filters and systems.
concepts.example: The sequence 1, 1/2, 1/4, 1/8, ... has Z-transform 1 + (1/2)z^-1 + (1/4)z^-2 + ... = 1/(1 - 0.5 z^-1), turning an infinite list into one compact fraction.

concepts.name: A/B Testing
concepts.description: A randomized experiment comparing two versions of something, such as a web page, by showing each to a random group of users and testing whether a metric differs significantly between them.
concepts.example: An online shop shows a green Buy button to a random half of 10,000 visitors and a blue one to the other half; 5.2% versus 4.6% buy, and a test checks whether that gap is bigger than chance would produce.

concepts.name: Absorbing Markov Chain
concepts.description: A Markov chain with at least one absorbing state that, once entered, is never left, and where every state can reach one; used to compute absorption probabilities and expected time to absorption.
concepts.example: In Snakes and Ladders, the final square is absorbing: once you land on it you stay. Every other square is transient, and the chain lets you compute the expected number of turns until a game ends.

concepts.name: Adjusted R-Squared
concepts.description: A version of R-squared that penalizes adding predictors, rising only when a new variable improves the fit more than chance would, which makes it useful for comparing regression models.
concepts.example: With 20 data points, adding a random useless predictor nudges R-squared from 0.700 to 0.705, but adjusted R-squared drops from about 0.68 to 0.67, flagging that the new variable doesn't earn its place.

concepts.name: Admissible Decision Rule
concepts.description: A decision rule or estimator is admissible if no other rule has risk that is at least as small for every parameter value and strictly smaller for some; inadmissible rules are dominated.
concepts.example: An estimator that always guesses 0 is admissible for a normal mean under squared error: nothing beats it when the true mean is exactly 0. A rule worse than another everywhere, like the sample mean plus 1, is inadmissible.

concepts.name: Akaike Information Criterion
concepts.description: A model selection score equal to 2k minus twice the maximized log-likelihood, where k is the number of parameters; lower AIC means a better balance of fit and complexity.
concepts.example: Model A has 3 parameters and log-likelihood -100, so AIC = 6 + 200 = 206; model B has 5 parameters and log-likelihood -99, so AIC = 208. The extra fit of B isn't worth its two extra parameters, so A wins.

concepts.name: Almost Sure Convergence
concepts.description: A sequence of random variables converges almost surely if, with probability one, the sequence of observed values converges to the limit; it is the strongest common mode of convergence.
concepts.example: Keep flipping a fair coin and track the fraction of heads: apart from a probability-zero set of freak sequences like all heads, every run of flips has its running fraction actually settle at 0.5.

concepts.name: Alternative Hypothesis
concepts.description: In hypothesis testing, the claim that contradicts the null hypothesis, such as that an effect or difference exists; data evidence against the null is taken as support for it.
concepts.example: Testing a new fertiliser, the null says plant height is unchanged; the alternative says plants grow taller with it. Evidence against the null is counted as support for this alternative.

concepts.name: Analysis of Variance
concepts.description: A statistical method that tests whether the means of several groups differ by comparing variance between groups to variance within groups using an F-test.
concepts.example: Three teaching methods give class averages of 70, 72 and 85. ANOVA compares how far apart those averages are with how much students vary within each class to judge whether the methods truly differ.

concepts.name: Ancillary Statistic
concepts.description: A statistic whose distribution does not depend on the unknown parameter, so on its own it carries no information about the parameter but can help in conditional inference.
concepts.example: For data from a normal with unknown mean and known spread, the sample range (largest minus smallest) has the same distribution whatever the mean is, so on its own it says nothing about the mean.

concepts.name: Analysis of Covariance
concepts.description: Analysis of covariance: a blend of ANOVA and regression that compares group means while adjusting for one or more continuous covariates, increasing precision and controlling for baseline differences.
concepts.example: Comparing exam scores across three teaching methods while accounting for each student's prior-year grade: a method may look better only because its students were stronger to begin with, and ANCOVA adjusts for that.

concepts.name: Anderson–Darling Test
concepts.description: A goodness-of-fit test that checks whether a sample comes from a given distribution, comparing the empirical and theoretical CDFs with extra weight on the tails; often used to test normality.
concepts.example: To check whether 50 measured bolt lengths are normal, compare their step-shaped empirical CDF with the normal CDF; Anderson-Darling weights disagreements in the tails heavily, catching too many extreme bolts.

concepts.name: Approximate Bayesian Computation
concepts.description: A likelihood-free Bayesian method that simulates data from the model under sampled parameters and keeps those whose simulated summaries are close to the observed data, approximating the posterior.
concepts.example: To estimate a disease's infection rate, guess a rate, simulate an outbreak, and keep the guess only if the simulated case count is close to the real 120 cases; the kept guesses approximate the posterior.

concepts.name: Autoregressive Conditional Heteroskedasticity
concepts.description: Time series models (ARCH and its generalization GARCH) in which the variance of today's shock depends on past squared shocks and past variances, capturing volatility clustering in financial data.
concepts.example: Stock returns are calm for weeks, then a crash day is followed by several wild days; an ARCH model makes today's variance grow with yesterday's squared return, reproducing such volatility clusters.

concepts.name: Autoregressive Integrated Moving Average
concepts.description: A time series model that differences a series to make it stationary and then models it with autoregressive and moving-average terms; ARIMA(p, d, q) is a standard forecasting tool.
concepts.example: Monthly sales that rise steadily have a trend; differencing them once gives month-to-month changes, which hover around a constant, and an ARMA model on those changes is an ARIMA(p,1,q) model.

concepts.name: ARIMAX Model
concepts.description: An ARIMA model extended with external explanatory variables, so the forecast depends both on the series' own past and on other inputs such as prices or holidays.
concepts.example: Forecasting ice-cream sales from both last week's sales and tomorrow's predicted temperature: the ARIMA part captures sales patterns while temperature enters as an external regressor.

concepts.name: Autoregressive–Moving-Average Model
concepts.description: A model for stationary time series combining an autoregressive part (dependence on past values) and a moving-average part (dependence on past random shocks).
concepts.example: Daily temperature anomalies: today's anomaly is partly yesterday's (AR part, e.g. 0.6 times yesterday) plus a lingering effect of yesterday's random weather shock (MA part).

concepts.name: Asymptotic Normality of the MLE
concepts.description: The result that, under regularity conditions, the maximum likelihood estimator is approximately normally distributed for large samples, centered at the true parameter with variance given by the inverse Fisher information.
concepts.example: Estimate a coin's heads probability from 400 flips with true p = 0.5: the MLE, the fraction of heads, varies across experiments like a bell curve centred at 0.5 with standard deviation 0.025.

concepts.name: Augmented Dickey–Fuller Test
concepts.description: A unit root test for time series that extends the Dickey-Fuller test with lagged differences to absorb autocorrelation, used to check whether a series is non-stationary.
concepts.example: Testing whether a stock price wanders like a random walk: ADF regresses daily changes on yesterday's price plus several past changes, so short-term momentum doesn't fool the unit root test.

concepts.name: Autocorrelation
concepts.description: The correlation of a time series with a lagged copy of itself, measuring how strongly past values relate to current ones; the autocorrelation function shows this across lags.
concepts.example: Daily temperatures have high autocorrelation at lag 1, around 0.8, since a hot day usually follows a hot day, but correlation near 0 with the temperature six months earlier after removing seasons.

concepts.name: Durbin–Watson Statistic
concepts.description: The Durbin-Watson statistic tests whether the residuals of a regression are correlated with their immediate predecessors; values near 2 suggest no first-order autocorrelation.
concepts.example: A Durbin-Watson value near 2 means residuals are uncorrelated; a value of 0.5 in a regression of monthly sales means each error resembles the previous one, so the model is missing a time pattern.

concepts.name: Autocovariance
concepts.description: The covariance between a stochastic process and itself at two different times, which for a stationary series depends only on the lag between them.
concepts.example: For daily temperature, the autocovariance at lag 1 measures how yesterday's deviation from average and today's move together; positive values mean warm days tend to follow warm days.

concepts.name: Autoregressive Model
concepts.description: A time series model in which each value is a linear combination of a fixed number of its own past values plus random noise; AR(p) uses the previous p values.
concepts.example: An AR(1) model for monthly inflation might say this month = 0.5 + 0.7 times last month + noise; if last month was 3%, the forecast is 2.6%.

concepts.name: Bandwidth Selection (Kernel Density Estimation)
concepts.description: Choosing the smoothing parameter of a kernel density estimator; too small gives a spiky estimate and too large over-smooths, so rules of thumb or cross-validation are used.
concepts.example: Estimating the distribution of 200 adult heights with a 0.5 cm bandwidth gives a jagged comb of spikes; with 30 cm it is one shapeless blob; something like 4 cm reveals the real two-peaked shape.

concepts.name: Bartlett's Test
concepts.description: A hypothesis test of whether several groups have equal variances, assuming the data are normal; it is often run before ANOVA to check its equal-variance assumption.
concepts.example: Before running ANOVA on three fertilisers, Bartlett's test checks whether plant heights spread equally in each group, since sample variances of 4, 5 and 20 would violate ANOVA's assumption.

concepts.name: Base Rate Fallacy
concepts.description: The error of ignoring how common something is overall when judging a specific case, for example trusting a positive test for a rare disease without accounting for the many false positives.
concepts.example: A disease affects 1 in 1000 people and a test is 99% accurate. Out of 1000 people, about 10 healthy people test positive alongside the 1 sick person, so a positive result means only about a 9% chance of disease.

concepts.name: Bayes Estimator
concepts.description: An estimator that minimizes expected loss under the posterior distribution, such as the posterior mean for squared error loss; its average risk under the prior is the Bayes risk.
concepts.example: After a coin's posterior for heads-probability becomes a Beta(8, 4), the Bayes estimate under squared error is the posterior mean 8/12 = 0.67; under absolute error it would be the posterior median instead.

concepts.name: Bayes Factor
concepts.description: The ratio of the marginal likelihoods of the data under two competing models, used in Bayesian statistics to quantify how much the evidence favours one model over the other.
concepts.example: If observed data are 10 times more probable under 'the coin is biased' than under 'the coin is fair', the Bayes factor is 10, which shifts the odds for bias up tenfold whatever the starting odds were.

concepts.name: Bayes' Theorem
concepts.description: A formula for updating probabilities with evidence: P(A|B) = P(B|A) P(A) / P(B); it turns a prior belief into a posterior belief and underlies Bayesian inference.
concepts.example: 1% of emails are spam; 'free money' appears in 60% of spam and 1% of normal mail. Seeing the phrase, P(spam) = 0.6 x 0.01 / (0.6 x 0.01 + 0.01 x 0.99), about 38%.

concepts.name: Bayesian Hierarchical Modeling
concepts.description: Bayesian models with multiple levels of parameters, where group-level parameters are themselves drawn from shared distributions, letting groups borrow strength and partially pool information.
concepts.example: Estimating each hospital's success rate: a small hospital with 3 of 3 successes is not judged perfect, because all hospitals share a common distribution that pulls its estimate towards the overall average.

concepts.name: Bayesian Information Criterion
concepts.description: A model selection score equal to k ln(n) minus twice the maximized log-likelihood; compared with AIC it penalizes extra parameters more heavily as sample size grows.
concepts.example: With 100 data points, BIC charges ln(100), about 4.6, per parameter versus AIC's 2, so a model with 2 extra parameters must improve twice the log-likelihood by over 9 rather than 4 to be preferred.

concepts.name: Bayesian Linear Regression
concepts.description: Linear regression treated in Bayesian terms: a prior is placed on the weights and combined with the data to give a posterior distribution over weights and predictions with uncertainty.
concepts.example: Fitting house price against size with only 5 sales, a prior that the price per square metre is around 3000 keeps the slope reasonable, and the posterior gives a range of plausible slopes rather than one number.

concepts.name: Bayesian Network
concepts.description: A directed acyclic graph whose nodes are random variables and whose edges encode conditional dependencies, compactly representing a joint distribution as a product of local conditionals.
concepts.example: A network with arrows Rain -> Wet grass <- Sprinkler lets you reason that seeing wet grass and learning the sprinkler was on makes rain less likely, the 'explaining away' effect.

concepts.name: Bayesian Statistics
concepts.description: An approach to statistics that treats unknown parameters as random, represents beliefs with probability distributions, and updates them with data via Bayes' theorem.
concepts.example: Starting with a belief that a new drug works for about 50% of patients, then seeing 18 of 20 recover, you update to a belief concentrated around 85% while still expressing remaining uncertainty.

concepts.name: Benjamini–Hochberg Procedure
concepts.description: A step-up method for multiple testing that controls the false discovery rate by sorting p-values and rejecting all hypotheses up to the largest k with p(k) <= kq/m.
concepts.example: With 10 p-values sorted, compare the k-th smallest to 0.05 x k/10; find the largest k where p fits under its line, say k = 3, and declare those 3 tests discoveries.

concepts.name: Bernoulli Distribution
concepts.description: The distribution of a single trial with two outcomes, 1 with probability p and 0 with probability 1-p, such as one coin flip; it is the building block of the binomial distribution.
concepts.example: A free throw by a player who scores 70% of the time is a Bernoulli trial: X = 1 with probability 0.7 and X = 0 with probability 0.3, so its mean is 0.7.

concepts.name: Berry–Esseen Theorem
concepts.description: A quantitative central limit theorem bounding how far the distribution of a standardized sample mean can be from the normal distribution, with error shrinking like 1/sqrt(n).
concepts.example: For averages of 100 fair coin flips the theorem guarantees the normal approximation's CDF is off by at most a few percent anywhere, and the error shrinks like 1 over the square root of n.

concepts.name: Bessel's Correction
concepts.description: Using n-1 instead of n in the denominator of the sample variance, which removes the bias that arises because deviations are measured from the sample mean rather than the true mean.
concepts.example: Samples 2, 4, 6 have mean 4; squared deviations sum to 8. Dividing by 3 gives 2.67, but dividing by n - 1 = 2 gives 4, correcting for the sample mean sitting closer to the data than the true mean does.

concepts.name: Beta-Binomial Distribution
concepts.description: The distribution of the number of successes in n trials when the success probability itself is drawn from a beta distribution; it models overdispersed count data.
concepts.example: Basketball players' free-throw rates vary, so pick a random player (rate from a beta) and count makes in 10 throws; the counts are more spread out than a binomial with the average rate would predict.

concepts.name: Beta-Binomial Model
concepts.description: The Bayesian model pairing a beta prior with binomial (or Bernoulli) data, which gives a beta posterior in closed form; it is the classic example of conjugacy.
concepts.example: Start with a Beta(1, 1) prior on a coin's heads rate, observe 7 heads and 3 tails, and the posterior is simply Beta(8, 4): add the heads and tails to the two parameters.

concepts.name: Beta Distribution
concepts.description: A continuous distribution on the interval [0, 1] with two shape parameters, often used to model probabilities and proportions and as a prior for a Bernoulli success rate.
concepts.example: A batter with 30 hits in 100 at-bats can be described by a Beta(30, 70) for their true hit rate, which peaks near 0.3 and narrows as more at-bats are added.

concepts.name: Bias of an Estimator
concepts.description: The difference between an estimator's expected value and the true parameter it estimates; an estimator with zero bias is called unbiased.
concepts.example: Estimating a population's average height, a tape measure that always reads 2 cm too high gives an estimator whose average is 2 cm above the truth: bias of +2 cm, however many people you measure.

concepts.name: Bias-Variance Tradeoff
concepts.description: The tension in model fitting between bias (error from overly simple assumptions) and variance (sensitivity to the training sample); expected squared error decomposes into bias squared, variance and noise.
concepts.example: Darts: a player who always hits the same spot left of the bullseye has high bias, low variance; one scattered all around the bullseye has low bias, high variance. Flexible models tend toward the second.

concepts.name: Binomial Distribution
concepts.description: The distribution of the number of successes in n independent trials each with success probability p, such as counting heads in n coin flips.
concepts.example: Flip a fair coin 4 times: the number of heads is binomial with P(2 heads) = 6 x (1/2)^4 = 6/16, since 6 orderings like HHTT and HTHT each have probability 1/16.

concepts.name: Binomial Test
concepts.description: An exact hypothesis test of whether the observed proportion of successes in binary trials is consistent with a hypothesized probability, using the binomial distribution directly.
concepts.example: A coin gives 9 heads in 10 flips. If it were fair, the chance of 9 or more heads is 11/1024, about 1%, so a one-sided binomial test rejects fairness at the 5% level.

concepts.name: Birth–Death Process
concepts.description: A continuous-time Markov chain on counts where the state can only go up by one (a birth) or down by one (a death); used for populations and queues.
concepts.example: The number of customers in a shop: someone arrives (+1) or leaves (-1), never two at once. Arrival and departure rates determine how crowded the shop gets on average.

concepts.name: Birthday Problem
concepts.description: The question of how many people are needed before two likely share a birthday; surprisingly only 23 give over a 50% chance, illustrating how fast collision probabilities grow.
concepts.example: With 23 people, there are 253 different pairs, each with a 1/365 chance of sharing a birthday, so the probability that at least one pair matches is about 50.7%.

concepts.name: Bivariate Normal Distribution
concepts.description: The joint normal distribution of two random variables, described by two means, two variances and a correlation; its density contours are ellipses.
concepts.example: Heights and weights of adults form an oval cloud: each is roughly bell-shaped, and with a correlation around 0.5 the cloud tilts so taller people tend to be heavier.

concepts.name: Blinded Experiment
concepts.description: Keeping participants, and in double-blind studies also the researchers, unaware of who receives which treatment, so that expectations cannot bias the outcomes of an experiment.
concepts.example: In a headache pill trial, patients get identical-looking real or sugar pills and doctors don't know which; this stops hopes or expectations from skewing reported pain.

concepts.name: Block Bootstrap
concepts.description: A bootstrap variant for dependent data such as time series that resamples contiguous blocks of observations instead of single points, preserving short-range dependence.
concepts.example: Resampling single days of temperature would scramble warm and cold spells; instead resample whole 7-day blocks, keeping each week's day-to-day dependence inside the block.

concepts.name: Blocking (Statistics)
concepts.description: Grouping experimental units into blocks that are similar (for example by field or day) and randomizing treatments within each block, which removes block-to-block variation from the comparison.
concepts.example: Testing two fertilisers across 5 fields that differ in soil, put both fertilisers in each field; comparing within fields removes soil differences from the comparison.

concepts.name: Bonferroni Correction
concepts.description: A simple multiple-testing fix that controls the family-wise error rate by testing each of m hypotheses at level alpha/m instead of alpha.
concepts.example: Running 20 tests at the usual 0.05 level, you'd expect about one false positive by chance; Bonferroni tests each at 0.05/20 = 0.0025, keeping the chance of any false positive under 5%.

concepts.name: Bootstrap Confidence Interval
concepts.description: A confidence interval built from the bootstrap distribution of a statistic, for example using its percentiles or the bias-corrected and accelerated (BCa) method, without assuming normality.
concepts.example: Resample 50 house prices with replacement 2000 times, compute the median each time, and take the 2.5th and 97.5th percentiles of those medians as a 95% interval for the true median price.

concepts.name: Bootstrapping (Statistics)
concepts.description: A resampling method that estimates the sampling distribution of a statistic by repeatedly drawing samples with replacement from the observed data and recomputing the statistic.
concepts.example: You have 30 measurements but want to know how much their mean would wobble with new data: draw 30 values from your own sample with replacement, compute the mean, repeat 1000 times, and look at the spread.

concepts.name: Borel–Cantelli Lemma
concepts.description: A result stating that if the probabilities of a sequence of events have a finite sum, then with probability one only finitely many of the events occur; a partial converse holds for independent events.
concepts.example: If on day n your bike has a 1/n^2 chance of a flat tyre, these probabilities sum to about 1.64, so with probability one you only ever get finitely many flats.

concepts.name: Box–Jenkins Method
concepts.description: A systematic approach to time series modelling: identify an ARIMA model from autocorrelation plots, estimate its parameters, check the residuals, and iterate before forecasting.
concepts.example: Looking at airline passenger data, you spot from autocorrelation plots that an ARIMA(0,1,1) fits, estimate its parameter, check the leftover errors look random, then forecast next year.

concepts.name: Box–Muller Transform
concepts.description: A method that turns two independent uniform random numbers into two independent standard normal random numbers using a logarithm, square root and sine and cosine.
concepts.example: Take two uniform numbers, say 0.5 and 0.25: compute sqrt(-2 ln 0.5), about 1.18, times cos(2pi x 0.25) = 0 and sin = 1, giving the normal pair 0 and 1.18.

concepts.name: Box Plot
concepts.description: A chart that summarizes a numeric variable with a box spanning the first to third quartile, a line at the median, and whiskers and dots showing spread and outliers.
concepts.example: Test scores with quartiles 60, 72 and 85 make a box from 60 to 85 with a line at 72; whiskers reach the lowest and highest typical scores, and a single 15 shows up as an outlier dot.

concepts.name: Branching Process
concepts.description: A stochastic process in which each individual independently produces a random number of offspring; the Galton-Watson process asks, for example, whether a family line dies out.
concepts.example: Each person with a surname has 0, 1 or 2 sons with equal chance, so 1 son on average; even then the name eventually dies out with probability 1, as each generation is random.

concepts.name: Breusch–Pagan Test
concepts.description: A test for heteroscedasticity in linear regression that regresses the squared residuals on the predictors and checks whether they explain a significant part of the variance.
concepts.example: In a regression of spending on income, if the squared residuals grow with income, the BP test's auxiliary regression picks that up and flags that error spread is not constant.

concepts.name: Canonical Correlation
concepts.description: A technique that finds pairs of linear combinations of two sets of variables that are maximally correlated with each other, revealing the shared structure between the two sets.
concepts.example: With students' reading and writing scores on one side and maths and science on the other, canonical correlation finds the weighted verbal score and weighted quantitative score that correlate the most.

concepts.name: Case–Control Study
concepts.description: An observational study that starts from people with an outcome (cases) and without it (controls) and looks back at their past exposures; it is efficient for rare diseases.
concepts.example: To study a rare cancer, researchers find 200 patients who have it and 400 similar people who don't, then ask everyone about past pesticide exposure; 30% versus 10% exposed hints at a link.

concepts.name: Categorical Distribution
concepts.description: The distribution of a single trial with k possible outcomes, each with its own probability; it generalizes the Bernoulli distribution and is what a softmax classifier outputs.
concepts.example: Rolling a loaded die where face 6 has probability 0.5 and faces 1 to 5 have 0.1 each is one draw from a categorical distribution with six categories.

concepts.name: Categorical Variable
concepts.description: A variable that takes one of a limited set of labels or categories, such as colour or country, rather than a numeric quantity; it may be nominal or ordinal.
concepts.example: Blood type (A, B, AB, O) is categorical: you can count how many people have each type, but averaging 'A' and 'O' makes no sense.

concepts.name: Cauchy Distribution
concepts.description: A bell-shaped but very heavy-tailed continuous distribution, the ratio of two independent standard normals, whose mean and variance are undefined; it breaks the law of large numbers.
concepts.example: Shine a spinning laser at a wall at a random angle: where the spot lands follows a Cauchy distribution, and averaging a million landing spots is no more precise than a single one, because it has no mean.

concepts.name: Causal Inference
concepts.description: The field concerned with estimating cause-and-effect relationships from data, using experiments, potential outcomes and causal graphs to separate causation from mere correlation.
concepts.example: Coffee drinkers may have more heart disease, but smokers also drink more coffee; causal inference asks what would happen if the same people drank coffee versus not, adjusting for smoking.

concepts.name: Censoring (Statistics)
concepts.description: A situation where a value is only partially known, for example when a patient leaves a study before an event happens, so we know only that the event time exceeds some value.
concepts.example: In a 5-year study of light-bulb lifetimes, a bulb still working at the end is censored: we know it lasted at least 5 years, but not its true lifetime. Throwing it away would bias results.

concepts.name: Central Limit Theorem
concepts.description: The theorem that the suitably scaled sum or mean of many independent, identically distributed random variables with finite variance is approximately normally distributed, whatever their original distribution.
concepts.example: A single die roll is flat, equally likely 1 to 6, yet the average of 50 rolls is bell-shaped around 3.5; the more dice you average, the closer to a normal curve it gets.

concepts.name: Central Moment
concepts.description: The expected value of a power of a random variable's deviation from its mean, E[(X-mu)^k]; the second is the variance and higher ones relate to skewness and kurtosis.
concepts.example: Data 1, 2, 3, 6 have mean 3; deviations -2, -1, 0, 3 give second central moment (4+1+0+9)/4 = 3.5, the variance, and third central moment (-8-1+0+27)/4 = 4.5, showing right skew.

concepts.name: Central Tendency
concepts.description: The idea of a typical or central value of a dataset or distribution, summarized by measures such as the mean, median and mode.
concepts.example: Salaries of 9 staff at 40k and a boss at 400k give a mean of 76k but a median of 40k; both summarise the 'centre', but the median better describes a typical employee here.

concepts.name: Chapman–Kolmogorov Equation
