concepts.description: The identity that the probability of moving between two states over a combined time span equals the sum over intermediate states of products of shorter transition probabilities.
concepts.example: To find the chance of going from Sunny to Rainy in two days, add up Sunny->Sunny->Rainy and Sunny->Rainy->Rainy (and every other middle state); in matrix terms, the two-step matrix is P times P.

concepts.name: Characteristic Function (Probability Theory)
concepts.description: The expected value of e^{itX} for a random variable X, i.e. the Fourier transform of its distribution; it always exists and uniquely determines the distribution.
concepts.example: For a fair coin X in {0, 1}, the characteristic function is (1 + e^{it})/2; for the sum of 10 independent flips it is simply that raised to the 10th power, which is why sums are easy to handle.

concepts.name: Chebyshev's Inequality
concepts.description: A bound stating that the probability a random variable lies more than k standard deviations from its mean is at most 1/k^2, for any distribution with finite variance.
concepts.example: Exam scores have mean 70 and standard deviation 10, with no other information; Chebyshev guarantees that at most 1/4 of students scored below 50 or above 90, since that is 2 standard deviations.

concepts.name: Chernoff Bound
concepts.description: An exponentially decreasing bound on the tail probability of a sum of independent random variables, obtained by applying Markov's inequality to the moment generating function.
concepts.example: Flip a fair coin 1000 times: Chebyshev says at least 600 heads has probability at most 2.5%, but a Chernoff bound gives below about 1 in 200 million, since tails of sums shrink exponentially.

concepts.name: Chi-Squared Distribution
concepts.description: The distribution of a sum of squares of k independent standard normal variables; it is used in tests of variance, goodness of fit and independence.
concepts.example: Draw 3 standard normal numbers, square them and add, e.g. 1.0^2 + 0.5^2 + 1.5^2 = 3.5; repeating gives a chi-squared distribution with 3 degrees of freedom, whose average is 3.

concepts.name: Chi-Squared Test
concepts.description: A family of tests using the chi-squared statistic to compare observed and expected counts, checking goodness of fit or independence between categorical variables.
concepts.example: Roll a die 60 times expecting 10 of each face. Observing 5, 8, 9, 12, 11, 15, add up (observed - expected)^2 / expected to get 6.0, compared against a chi-squared distribution to judge fairness.

concepts.name: Clopper–Pearson Interval
concepts.description: An exact confidence interval for a binomial proportion obtained by inverting binomial tests; it guarantees at least the nominal coverage but is conservative.
concepts.example: After 0 failures in 20 tests of a part, the 95% Clopper-Pearson interval for the failure rate is 0 to about 0.17; it never claims a rate of exactly zero, and it is guaranteed not to undercover.

concepts.name: Cluster Sampling
concepts.description: A sampling method that divides the population into groups such as schools or towns, randomly selects some groups, and then studies all or many members of the chosen groups.
concepts.example: Instead of listing all pupils in a country, pick 20 schools at random and survey every pupil in those schools; cheaper, but pupils within one school tend to be alike.

concepts.name: Cochran–Mantel–Haenszel Test
concepts.description: A test of association between a binary exposure and outcome across several strata of 2x2 tables, giving a pooled odds ratio while controlling for a confounding variable.
concepts.example: Testing whether a drug helps across 4 hospitals, each with its own 2x2 table of drug versus outcome, CMH combines them into one test and pooled odds ratio while respecting hospital differences.

concepts.name: Coefficient of Determination
concepts.description: R-squared: the proportion of the variance in the response that a regression model explains, computed as one minus the residual sum of squares over the total sum of squares.
concepts.example: If house prices vary with total variance 100 and the residuals from a regression on size have variance 30, then R-squared = 1 - 30/100 = 0.7: size explains 70% of the variation.

concepts.name: Coefficient of Variation
concepts.description: The ratio of the standard deviation to the mean, a unit-free measure of relative spread that lets you compare variability across quantities measured on different scales.
concepts.example: Mice weigh 25 g with SD 5 g (CV 20%), elephants 5000 kg with SD 500 kg (CV 10%); the elephants vary more in kilograms, but mice vary more relative to their size.

concepts.name: Cohen's d
concepts.description: An effect size for the difference between two group means, expressed as that difference divided by a pooled standard deviation; values around 0.2, 0.5 and 0.8 are called small, medium and large.
concepts.example: A study method raises scores from 70 to 75 when scores have a standard deviation of 10, so d = 5/10 = 0.5, conventionally a medium effect.

concepts.name: Cohort Study
concepts.description: An observational study that follows a group of people with and without an exposure forward in time to see who develops an outcome, allowing estimation of relative risk.
concepts.example: Researchers follow 10,000 people for 20 years, noting who smokes, and see 15% of smokers versus 2% of non-smokers develop a disease, a relative risk of 7.5.

concepts.name: Cointegration
concepts.description: A property of non-stationary time series that move together so that some linear combination of them is stationary, indicating a long-run equilibrium relationship; tested with Engle-Granger or Johansen.
concepts.example: A drunk walking a dog: both wander unpredictably, but the leash keeps them close; their distance apart is stable even though each path drifts. Share prices of two similar companies can behave like that.

concepts.name: Counting Principles
concepts.description: Basic rules for counting arrangements and selections, including the rule of product, permutations and combinations, which are needed to compute probabilities of discrete events.
concepts.example: With 3 shirts and 4 trousers there are 3 x 4 = 12 outfits; choosing 2 friends out of 5 for a trip gives 10 combinations, since order doesn't matter.

concepts.name: Completeness (Statistics)
concepts.description: A statistic is complete if no non-trivial function of it has expected value zero for every parameter value; completeness plus sufficiency yields unique best unbiased estimators.
concepts.example: For coin flips, the number of heads is complete: the only function of it that averages to zero for every heads probability is zero itself, so any unbiased estimator based on it is unique.

concepts.name: Compound Poisson Process
concepts.description: A process where events arrive as a Poisson process and each event adds an independent random amount, such as insurance claims of random sizes arriving over time.
concepts.example: Insurance claims arrive about 3 per day at random, each of random size; the total paid out by day 10 is a compound Poisson process, with average 30 times the average claim.

concepts.name: Concentration Inequality
concepts.description: A bound showing that a random quantity, such as a sum or average of many independent variables, is very likely to be close to its expected value; examples are Hoeffding and Chernoff bounds.
concepts.example: Averaging 10,000 fair coin flips, a concentration inequality guarantees the fraction of heads is between 0.48 and 0.52 except with probability below 0.07%, without needing exact distributions.

concepts.name: Conditional Expectation
concepts.description: The expected value of a random variable given information about another, E[X | Y], which is itself a function of Y; it is the best mean-squared-error predictor of X from Y.
concepts.example: Two dice: given that the first shows 4, the expected total is 4 + 3.5 = 7.5. Over all possible first rolls, E[total | first] is first + 3.5, itself a random quantity.

concepts.name: Conditional Independence
concepts.description: Two random variables are conditionally independent given a third if, once the third is known, learning one gives no further information about the other; key to graphical models.
concepts.example: Children's shoe size and reading skill are correlated, but once you know their age, shoe size tells you nothing more about reading; they are independent given age.

concepts.name: Conditional Probability
concepts.description: The probability of an event given that another event has occurred, P(A|B) = P(A and B) / P(B); it formalizes updating probabilities with new information.
concepts.example: In a deck, P(king) = 4/52; given the card is a face card, there are 12 possibilities, 4 of them kings, so P(king | face card) = 4/12 = 1/3.

concepts.name: Conditional Probability Distribution
concepts.description: The probability distribution of one random variable when another is fixed at a given value, obtained by dividing the joint distribution by the marginal.
concepts.example: Among 100 people, 40 tall and 60 short; of the 40 tall, 30 play basketball. The distribution of basketball playing given tall is 75% yes, 25% no.

concepts.name: Confidence Interval
concepts.description: A range computed from sample data that, under repeated sampling, would contain the true parameter a specified proportion of the time, such as 95%.
concepts.example: A poll of 1000 voters finds 52% support with standard error 1.6%; the 95% interval is 52 plus or minus about 3.1, so roughly 49% to 55%.

concepts.name: Confidence Level
concepts.description: The long-run proportion of confidence intervals, built by a given procedure, that would contain the true parameter, commonly 90%, 95% or 99%.
concepts.example: If 100 researchers each build a 95% confidence interval from their own sample, about 95 of the intervals will contain the true value and about 5 will miss.

concepts.name: Confirmatory Factor Analysis
concepts.description: A method that tests whether data fit a pre-specified factor structure, in which particular observed variables are assumed to load on particular latent factors.
concepts.example: A survey with 6 questions is designed so 3 measure anxiety and 3 measure depression; CFA tests whether responses really fit that two-factor plan rather than discovering structure freely.

concepts.name: Confounding
concepts.description: A distortion of the apparent effect of an exposure on an outcome caused by a third variable that influences both, so the association does not reflect causation.
concepts.example: Ice cream sales and drownings rise together, but hot weather drives both; temperature is a confounder, and ignoring it makes ice cream look dangerous.

concepts.name: Conjugate Prior
concepts.description: A prior distribution that, combined with a given likelihood, produces a posterior in the same family, such as a beta prior for binomial data, making Bayesian updating analytic.
concepts.example: With a Beta(2, 2) prior on a coin's heads rate and 5 heads in 5 flips, the posterior is Beta(7, 2), still a beta, found by simple addition, no integration needed.

concepts.name: Consistent Estimator
concepts.description: An estimator that converges in probability to the true parameter as the sample size grows, so with enough data it becomes arbitrarily accurate.
concepts.example: The sample average of die rolls is consistent for 3.5: after 10 rolls it may be 4.2, after 10,000 almost surely within 0.05 of 3.5.

concepts.name: Contingency Table
concepts.description: A table that counts how often each combination of categories of two or more categorical variables occurs, used to examine association between them.
concepts.example: A 2x2 table of 100 people: smokers with cough 20, smokers without 10, non-smokers with cough 15, non-smokers without 55. It shows at once how smoking and coughing go together.

concepts.name: Continuous Mapping Theorem
concepts.description: The result that applying a continuous function to a sequence of random variables preserves convergence in distribution, in probability and almost surely.
concepts.example: If the sample mean converges to 5, then the sample mean squared converges to 25, and its logarithm to ln 5, because squaring and logs are continuous.

concepts.name: Continuous Random Variable
concepts.description: A random variable that can take any value in an interval, described by a probability density function, so the probability of any single exact value is zero.
concepts.example: A person's exact height is continuous: P(height between 170 and 171 cm) might be 5%, but the chance of exactly 170.000... cm is zero.

concepts.name: Continuous-Time Markov Chain
concepts.description: A Markov process on discrete states that can jump at any moment in time, with exponentially distributed holding times governed by transition rates.
concepts.example: A machine switches between working and broken at random times: it works for an exponentially distributed time averaging 100 hours, then is repaired in about 5 hours, and so on.

concepts.name: Continuous Uniform Distribution
concepts.description: The distribution that assigns equal density to every value in an interval [a, b], so all equal-length sub-intervals are equally likely; it is the basis of random number generation.
concepts.example: A bus arrives every 10 minutes and you show up at a random time, so your waiting time is uniform on [0, 10]: the chance of waiting under 3 minutes is 3/10, and on average you wait 5.

concepts.name: Convenience Sampling
concepts.description: A non-probability sampling method that selects whoever is easiest to reach, such as passers-by or volunteers, which is cheap but often produces biased samples.
concepts.example: Surveying shoppers at one mall on a weekday afternoon to learn a city's opinion is convenient but skews toward people who are free then and live nearby.

concepts.name: Convergence in Distribution
concepts.description: A sequence of random variables converges in distribution if their CDFs converge to a limiting CDF at all continuity points; it is the mode of convergence in the central limit theorem.
concepts.example: The number of heads in n fair flips, standardised, has a CDF that gets closer to the normal CDF as n grows, even though the count is always a whole number.

concepts.name: Convergence in Probability
concepts.description: A sequence of random variables converges in probability to a limit if, for every tolerance, the probability that they differ by more than that tolerance goes to zero.
concepts.example: The proportion of heads in n fair flips converges in probability to 0.5: the chance it is off by more than 0.01 shrinks toward zero as n grows.

concepts.name: Convergence of Random Variables
concepts.description: The various senses in which a sequence of random variables can approach a limit, including almost surely, in probability, in mean and in distribution.
concepts.example: As you flip more coins, the running fraction of heads approaches 0.5 in several senses: its spread shrinks, almost every run settles there, and its distribution clusters there.

concepts.name: Convolution of Probability Distributions
concepts.description: The distribution of the sum of two independent random variables, obtained by convolving their probability mass or density functions.
concepts.example: Two dice: P(total 4) sums P(first)P(second) over pairs (1,3), (2,2), (3,1), giving 3/36. That sliding sum over all ways is the convolution of the two distributions.

concepts.name: Cook's Distance
concepts.description: A regression diagnostic that measures how much all fitted values change when a single observation is removed, flagging influential points that combine high leverage and large residuals.
concepts.example: In a regression of 30 houses, one mansion has huge size and a low price; removing it shifts the fitted line visibly, giving it a large Cook's distance, while removing a typical house barely matters.

concepts.name: Copula (Probability Theory)
concepts.description: A multivariate distribution with uniform marginals that describes the dependence structure between random variables separately from their individual distributions, per Sklar's theorem.
concepts.example: Two stocks' returns each look normal, but they crash together far more than a normal model predicts; a copula lets you keep the normal marginals and swap in a dependence structure with joint crashes.

concepts.name: Correlation
concepts.description: A measure of how strongly two variables move together, scaled to lie between -1 and 1; positive values mean they rise together and negative values mean one rises as the other falls.
concepts.example: Hours studied and exam scores might have correlation 0.8, a strong positive link; shoe size and exam scores, near 0; hours of TV and scores, perhaps -0.3.

concepts.name: Correlation Matrix
concepts.description: A symmetric matrix whose (i, j) entry is the correlation between variables i and j, with ones on the diagonal; it summarizes pairwise linear relationships in a dataset.
concepts.example: For height, weight and age, a 3x3 correlation matrix might show 0.7 between height and weight, 0.1 with age, and 1s along the diagonal since each variable correlates perfectly with itself.

concepts.name: Correlation Does Not Imply Causation
concepts.description: The principle that two variables being associated does not prove one causes the other, since the link may come from confounding, reverse causation or chance.
concepts.example: Cities with more firefighters have more fire damage, but firefighters don't cause damage: big fires bring both. Association alone can't tell you which way, if any, cause runs.

concepts.name: Correspondence Analysis
concepts.description: A dimensionality reduction technique for contingency tables that maps the rows and columns of categorical data into a low-dimensional space so associations can be visualized.
concepts.example: Survey results tabulating eye colour against hair colour can be drawn on a 2D map where blue eyes sit near blond hair and brown eyes near black hair, showing which categories go together.

concepts.name: Covariance
concepts.description: A measure of how two random variables vary together, E[(X - E[X])(Y - E[Y])]; it is positive when they tend to rise together and negative when they move oppositely.
concepts.example: Heights 160, 170, 180 and weights 55, 65, 75 have mean deviations -10, 0, 10 for both, so covariance is (100 + 0 + 100)/3 = 66.7: positive, since they rise together.

concepts.name: Proportional Hazards Model
concepts.description: A survival regression model in which covariates multiply an unspecified baseline hazard, so hazard ratios between subjects stay constant over time; fit by partial likelihood.
concepts.example: If smokers' hazard of heart attack is 2 times non-smokers' at every age, Cox regression estimates that factor of 2 without needing to know the shape of the risk over age.

concepts.name: Cramér–Rao Bound
concepts.description: A lower bound on the variance of any unbiased estimator, equal to the inverse of the Fisher information; an estimator that attains it is efficient.
concepts.example: Estimating a coin's heads chance near 0.5 from 100 flips, no unbiased estimator can have standard deviation below 0.05; the sample proportion achieves exactly that.

concepts.name: Credible Interval
concepts.description: A Bayesian interval that contains the unknown parameter with a stated posterior probability, such as 95%, given the data and prior.
concepts.example: After seeing data, a 95% credible interval of 0.6 to 0.8 for a drug's cure rate means you believe the rate is in there with 95% probability, a direct statement confidence intervals don't make.

concepts.name: Critical Value
concepts.description: The threshold value of a test statistic beyond which the null hypothesis is rejected at a given significance level; the values beyond it form the rejection region.
concepts.example: In a two-sided z-test at the 5% level, the critical values are -1.96 and 1.96; a test statistic of 2.3 lies beyond them, so the null is rejected.

concepts.name: Cronbach's Alpha
concepts.description: A reliability coefficient measuring the internal consistency of a set of test or survey items, based on how much their scores covary relative to their total variance.
concepts.example: A 5-question 'job satisfaction' survey where people who agree with one question tend to agree with the others has high alpha, say 0.85; random questions would give alpha near 0.

concepts.name: Cross-Validation
concepts.description: A model evaluation technique that splits the data into k folds, trains on k-1 of them and tests on the remaining one in rotation, then averages the scores to estimate performance on unseen data.
concepts.example: With 100 examples and 5 folds, train on 80 and test on the other 20, rotating five times so every example is tested once; averaging the five scores, say 82%, 85%, 80%, 84%, 79%, gives 82%.

concepts.name: Cumulant
concepts.description: Quantities derived from the logarithm of the moment generating function; the first three are the mean, variance and third central moment, and cumulants add for independent variables.
concepts.example: For a normal distribution, the first two cumulants are the mean and variance and every higher cumulant is zero; a nonzero third cumulant therefore signals skewness away from normality.

concepts.name: Cumulative Distribution Function
concepts.description: The function F(x) = P(X <= x) giving the probability that a random variable takes a value at most x; it fully describes any distribution.
concepts.example: For one fair die, F(2) = P(roll <= 2) = 2/6 and F(6) = 1; the CDF climbs in steps of 1/6 at each face.

concepts.name: Data Transformation (Statistics)
concepts.description: Applying a function such as a logarithm, square root or Box-Cox power to every value of a variable to make data more symmetric, stabilize variance or linearize relationships.
concepts.example: Incomes of 20k, 40k, 80k and 2 million are badly skewed; taking log10 gives about 4.3, 4.6, 4.9 and 6.3, which are far easier to plot and model.

concepts.name: De Finetti's Theorem
concepts.description: The theorem that an infinite exchangeable sequence of random variables behaves as if it were drawn i.i.d. given some latent parameter with a prior, which justifies Bayesian modelling.
concepts.example: If you'd judge any reordering of an infinite run of coin flips equally likely, de Finetti says it is as if nature first picked a hidden bias p at random and then flipped independently with that p.

concepts.name: De Moivre–Laplace Theorem
concepts.description: The special case of the central limit theorem stating that a binomial distribution with many trials is well approximated by a normal distribution with the same mean and variance.
concepts.example: The chance of 55 or more heads in 100 fair flips can be approximated by a normal with mean 50 and standard deviation 5: about 18%, close to the exact binomial 18.4%.

concepts.name: Statistical Decision Theory
concepts.description: The framework for choosing actions or estimators under uncertainty by minimizing expected loss (risk), covering concepts like Bayes rules, minimax rules and admissibility.
concepts.example: A doctor deciding whether to treat: missing a disease costs much more than an unnecessary treatment, so decision theory may say treat when P(disease) is only 20%, minimising expected loss.

concepts.name: Degrees of Freedom (Mechanics)
concepts.description: The number of independent values that are free to vary in a calculation or system; in statistics it determines the shape of t, chi-squared and F distributions.
concepts.example: If 3 numbers must average 10, you can choose the first two freely, say 8 and 15, but the third is forced to be 7; only 2 of the 3 values are free, so there are 2 degrees of freedom.

concepts.name: Delta Method
concepts.description: A technique for approximating the distribution and variance of a smooth function of an estimator using a first-order Taylor expansion, giving an asymptotically normal result.
concepts.example: If the sample mean of 100 values is about 4 with standard error 0.2, the standard error of its square root is about 0.2 x 1/(2 sqrt 4) = 0.05.

concepts.name: Descriptive Statistics
concepts.description: The branch of statistics that summarizes and describes data with numbers such as the mean, median and standard deviation and with charts such as histograms.
concepts.example: Summarising a class's test scores as mean 72, median 75, range 40 to 98 and standard deviation 12 is descriptive statistics: no conclusions beyond the data, just a clear picture.

concepts.name: Design Effect
concepts.description: The ratio of an estimator's variance under a complex survey design, such as cluster sampling, to its variance under simple random sampling of the same size.
concepts.example: Surveying 20 pupils from each of 50 schools gives 1000 pupils, but because classmates are similar the variance may be twice that of a simple random sample: design effect 2, like having only 500 independent pupils.

concepts.name: Design Matrix
concepts.description: The matrix of predictor values in a regression, with one row per observation and one column per feature, often including a column of ones for the intercept.
concepts.example: For 3 houses with sizes 50, 80, 120 and 1, 2, 3 bedrooms, the design matrix has 3 rows like [1, 50, 1], [1, 80, 2], [1, 120, 3], where the first column of 1s gives the intercept.

concepts.name: Design of Experiments
concepts.description: The field of planning experiments so they answer questions efficiently and without bias, using principles such as randomization, replication and blocking.
concepts.example: To test 2 fertilisers and 2 watering levels, a 2x2 factorial design tries all 4 combinations, randomly assigned to plots, letting you see each effect and their interaction from one experiment.

concepts.name: Detailed Balance
concepts.description: A condition on a Markov chain stating that, at stationarity, the probability flow from each state to another equals the flow back; it ensures a target distribution is stationary in MCMC.
concepts.example: Two rooms with 30 people in A and 10 in B are balanced if 10% of A moves to B each hour (3 people) while 30% of B moves to A (3 people): each pair of rooms swaps equal numbers.

concepts.name: Deviance (Statistics)
concepts.description: A goodness-of-fit measure for models fit by maximum likelihood, equal to twice the difference in log-likelihood between a saturated model and the fitted model; it generalizes residual sum of squares.
concepts.example: A logistic regression with deviance 120 versus a saturated model, and 100 after adding a predictor, shows a drop of 20 for one parameter, strong evidence the predictor helps.

concepts.name: Dickey–Fuller Test
concepts.description: A hypothesis test for whether an autoregressive time series has a unit root, meaning it is non-stationary like a random walk.
concepts.example: Regress today's change in a stock price on yesterday's price; if the coefficient is close to zero, the price wanders like a random walk (unit root) rather than pulling back to an average.

concepts.name: Difference in Differences
concepts.description: A causal inference method comparing the change in outcome over time in a treated group with the change in an untreated group, assuming they would otherwise follow parallel trends.
concepts.example: City A raised its minimum wage; jobs there went from 100 to 98, while in similar City B jobs went from 100 to 95. The estimated effect is (98 - 100) - (95 - 100) = +3 jobs.

concepts.name: Differencing (Time Series)
concepts.description: Transforming a time series by taking differences between consecutive values (or values a season apart) to remove trends or seasonality and make it stationary.
concepts.example: A series 10, 12, 14, 16, 18 has a clear upward trend; differencing gives 2, 2, 2, 2, which is flat and stationary.

concepts.name: Dirichlet Distribution
concepts.description: A distribution over probability vectors, i.e. vectors of positive numbers that sum to one, generalizing the beta distribution; it is the conjugate prior for categorical data.
concepts.example: To model uncertainty about a die's three-way loading among red, green, blue faces, a Dirichlet(10, 10, 10) gives vectors like (0.31, 0.36, 0.33), always summing to 1 and clustered near equal.

concepts.name: Dirichlet Process
concepts.description: A distribution over probability distributions used as a nonparametric Bayesian prior, allowing a model such as a mixture to use as many clusters as the data support; described by the Chinese restaurant process.
concepts.example: Restaurant analogy: each new customer joins an existing table with probability proportional to its size, or opens a new table; the number of tables, or clusters, grows with the customers.

concepts.name: Discrete Random Variable
concepts.description: A random variable that takes a countable set of values, such as the result of a die roll, described by a probability mass function.
concepts.example: The number of heads in 3 coin flips takes only the values 0, 1, 2 or 3, with probabilities 1/8, 3/8, 3/8 and 1/8.

concepts.name: Discrete Uniform Distribution
concepts.description: The distribution that gives each of a finite set of values the same probability, such as each face of a fair die having probability one sixth.
concepts.example: Rolling a fair die, each face 1 to 6 has probability 1/6; picking a random card's position from 1 to 52 is also discrete uniform.

concepts.name: Duality Between Hypothesis Tests and Confidence Intervals
concepts.description: The correspondence that a confidence interval contains exactly the parameter values that a hypothesis test at the matching level would not reject, so each can be built from the other.
concepts.example: If a 95% confidence interval for the average weight is 68 to 74 kg, then a 5%-level test would reject the claim that the mean is 75 kg and not reject 70 kg.

concepts.name: Dummy Variable
concepts.description: A 0/1 variable that indicates whether an observation belongs to a category, letting categorical predictors be used in regression and other numeric models.
concepts.example: To include colour (red, green, blue) in a regression, add two 0/1 columns, 'is green' and 'is blue'; red is the baseline when both are 0.

concepts.name: Dunnett's Test
concepts.description: A multiple comparison procedure that compares each of several treatment groups with a single control group while controlling the family-wise error rate.
concepts.example: A lab compares 4 new drugs to a placebo: Dunnett's test makes just those 4 comparisons with the control, keeping the overall false positive rate at 5% and giving more power than testing all pairs.

concepts.name: Effect Size
concepts.description: A quantitative measure of the magnitude of a difference or relationship, such as Cohen's d or a correlation, which, unlike a p-value, does not depend on sample size.
concepts.example: With a huge sample, a diet might cause a statistically significant weight loss of 0.2 kg, which is real but tiny; an effect size tells you how much it matters, not just whether it exists.

concepts.name: Efficiency (Statistics)
concepts.description: A measure of an estimator's quality comparing its variance with the smallest achievable variance; an efficient estimator attains the Cramer-Rao bound.
concepts.example: For normal data, the sample median has about 64% the efficiency of the mean: you would need roughly 157 observations with the median to match the precision of the mean from 100.

concepts.name: Elastic Net Regularization
concepts.description: A regularization penalty that mixes the L1 (lasso) and L2 (ridge) penalties, producing sparse models while handling groups of correlated features better than lasso alone.
concepts.example: Predicting house price with two nearly identical features, lasso may arbitrarily keep one; elastic net mixes in ridge so both get similar weights, while still zeroing out irrelevant features.

concepts.name: Empirical Distribution Function
concepts.description: The step function that, at each value x, gives the fraction of sample observations that are at most x; it estimates the true cumulative distribution function.
concepts.example: For the sample 3, 5, 5, 9, the EDF is 0 below 3, steps to 1/4 at 3, jumps to 3/4 at 5, and reaches 1 at 9.

concepts.name: 68–95–99.7 Rule
concepts.description: The rule that for a normal distribution about 68%, 95% and 99.7% of values fall within one, two and three standard deviations of the mean.
concepts.example: Adult heights with mean 170 cm and SD 10 cm: about 68% of people are between 160 and 180 cm, 95% between 150 and 190 cm, and almost everyone (99.7%) between 140 and 200 cm.

concepts.name: Endogeneity
concepts.description: A problem in regression where an explanatory variable is correlated with the error term, due to omitted variables, measurement error or simultaneity, which biases estimates.
concepts.example: Regress wages on years of schooling while ignoring ability: smarter people both study longer and earn more, so schooling is tangled up with the hidden ability in the error term and its effect looks bigger than it really is.

concepts.name: Entropy
concepts.description: Shannon entropy measures the average uncertainty or information content of a random variable, H(X) = -sum p(x) log p(x); it sets the limit on lossless compression.
concepts.example: A fair coin has entropy 1 bit: each flip is a full surprise. A coin landing heads 99% of the time has only about 0.08 bits, so a long sequence of its flips can be compressed to a tiny fraction of its length.

concepts.name: Ergodic Theorem
concepts.description: The theorem that for an ergodic process, time averages along a single long trajectory converge to averages over the stationary distribution; it justifies MCMC estimates.
concepts.example: Follow one random surfer clicking links for a million steps and count how often they land on each page; those time fractions match the long-run page probabilities, which is why one long MCMC run can estimate averages.

concepts.name: Ergodicity
concepts.description: The property of a Markov chain or process that it eventually explores the whole state space so long-run time averages equal ensemble averages; for chains it means irreducible and aperiodic.
concepts.example: A mouse wandering a maze where every room connects to every other eventually visits all rooms in stable proportions. If the maze split into two sealed halves, or the mouse alternated rooms in a strict rhythm, that would fail.

concepts.name: Erlang Distribution
concepts.description: The distribution of the sum of k independent exponential random variables with the same rate, modelling the waiting time until the k-th event; a gamma distribution with integer shape.
concepts.example: Calls arrive at a help desk at 2 per minute on average. The waiting time until the 3rd call is Erlang with k=3 and rate 2, averaging 3/2 = 1.5 minutes: three exponential waits stacked end to end.

concepts.name: Errors and Residuals
concepts.description: An error is the deviation of an observation from the unobservable true value, while a residual is its deviation from the fitted model's prediction, which we can compute.
concepts.example: If the true average height of men is 175 cm and a man is 180 cm, his error is +5. If your sample's average is 177, his residual is +3: computed from the sample estimate, since the true value is unknown.

concepts.name: Errors-in-Variables Model
concepts.description: Regression models that account for measurement error in the explanatory variables, which otherwise biases ordinary least squares slopes toward zero (attenuation).
concepts.example: Measure people's daily calorie intake with noisy food diaries and regress weight on it: the noise flattens the fitted slope toward zero. Errors-in-variables models correct for that attenuation using the known noise level.

concepts.name: Estimator
concepts.description: A rule or formula that computes an estimate of an unknown population parameter from sample data, such as the sample mean estimating the population mean.
concepts.example: To estimate the average age in a town, survey 50 people and average their ages. The rule 'add up the sample and divide by n' is the estimator; the number it gives, say 38.2, is the estimate.

concepts.name: Event (Probability Theory)
concepts.description: In probability, an event is a set of outcomes of a random experiment, i.e. a subset of the sample space, to which a probability is assigned.
concepts.example: Roll a die: the sample space is {1,2,3,4,5,6}. 'Rolling an even number' is the event {2,4,6}, and its probability is 3/6 = 1/2 because it contains three of the six equally likely outcomes.

concepts.name: Expectation–Maximization Algorithm
concepts.description: An iterative algorithm for maximum likelihood with latent variables that alternates an E-step, computing expected latent assignments, and an M-step, re-estimating parameters; used for Gaussian mixtures.
concepts.example: Given heights of mixed men and women without labels, guess the two group averages, compute each person's probability of being in each group (E-step), recompute averages using those weights (M-step), and repeat until stable.

concepts.name: Expected Value
concepts.description: The probability-weighted average of all possible values of a random variable, representing its long-run average outcome over many repetitions.
concepts.example: A game pays $10 with probability 0.2 and $0 otherwise. Its expected value is 0.2 x 10 = $2, so if you played thousands of times your average winnings per game would settle near $2.

concepts.name: Exponential Distribution
concepts.description: A continuous distribution of waiting times between events in a Poisson process, with density lambda e^{-lambda x}; it is the only memoryless continuous distribution.
concepts.example: If a bus arrives on average every 10 minutes at random, the wait until the next one is exponential with mean 10. The chance of waiting more than 20 minutes is e^(-2), about 13.5%.

concepts.name: Exponential Family
concepts.description: A broad class of distributions whose density can be written as exp(natural parameter times sufficient statistic minus a log-normalizer); it includes the normal, Poisson, binomial and gamma and underlies GLMs and conjugate priors.
concepts.example: The Bernoulli, Poisson, normal and gamma distributions all fit one template, exp(parameter x statistic - normalizer). Because they share it, one set of tools, such as GLMs and conjugate priors, works for all of them at once.

concepts.name: Exponential Smoothing
concepts.description: A forecasting method that predicts the next value as a weighted average of past observations with weights decaying exponentially into the past; Holt and Holt-Winters variants add trend and seasonality.
concepts.example: With smoothing factor 0.3, if yesterday's forecast was 100 and today's sales were 110, tomorrow's forecast is 0.3 x 110 + 0.7 x 100 = 103. Older data still counts, but its weight shrinks by 0.7 each day.

concepts.name: Extreme Value Theory
concepts.description: The branch of statistics that models the behaviour of the largest or smallest values in data, such as maxima of rainfall or financial losses, to estimate the probability of rare extreme events.
concepts.example: An engineer building a sea wall cares not about average waves but about the biggest wave in 100 years. Extreme value theory fits the yearly maximum wave heights to estimate how high a once-a-century wave could be.

concepts.name: F-Distribution
concepts.description: The continuous distribution of the ratio of two independent chi-squared variables each divided by its degrees of freedom; it is the reference distribution for ANOVA and F-tests comparing variances.
concepts.example: Take two independent normal samples, compute each one's sample variance divided by the true variance, and take their ratio. Repeating this many times gives an F distribution; values near 1 are common, large ones are rare.

concepts.name: F-Test
concepts.description: Any hypothesis test whose test statistic follows an F-distribution under the null, commonly used to compare nested regression models or test whether group means differ in ANOVA.
concepts.example: Comparing average test scores across three teaching methods, ANOVA computes F = (variation between groups) / (variation within groups). An F of 8 with 10 students per group is far above what chance gives, so the methods likely differ.

concepts.name: F-Test of Equality of Variances
concepts.description: A test of whether two normal populations have equal variances, computed as the ratio of the two sample variances and compared to an F-distribution; it is very sensitive to non-normality.
concepts.example: Machine A's bolts have sample variance 4 and machine B's have 1, with 15 bolts each. F = 4/1 = 4, well beyond what the F distribution with 14 and 14 degrees of freedom usually gives, suggesting A is less consistent.

concepts.name: Factor Analysis
concepts.description: A latent-variable method that explains correlations among many observed variables through a smaller number of unobserved factors plus variable-specific noise, used in psychometrics and survey analysis.
concepts.example: Scores on vocabulary, reading and spelling tests are all strongly correlated. Factor analysis explains this by one hidden 'verbal ability' factor that each test measures with some noise of its own.

concepts.name: Factorial Experiment
concepts.description: An experimental design that tests every combination of the levels of two or more factors, letting researchers estimate each factor's main effect and the interactions between factors efficiently.
concepts.example: Testing fertilizer (yes/no) and watering (low/high) on tomatoes, you grow plants under all 4 combinations. This reveals whether fertilizer helps more when watering is high, which separate one-at-a-time tests would miss.

concepts.name: False Discovery Rate
concepts.description: The expected proportion of false positives among all hypotheses declared significant; controlling it, e.g. with the Benjamini-Hochberg procedure, is a less strict alternative to familywise error control in many tests.
concepts.example: A lab tests 1,000 genes and flags 100 as significant. Controlling FDR at 5% means that, on average, no more than about 5 of those 100 flagged genes are false alarms.

concepts.name: Family-Wise Error Rate
concepts.description: The probability of making at least one false rejection (type I error) when testing a whole family of hypotheses; methods like Bonferroni and Holm keep it below a chosen level.
concepts.example: Run 20 independent tests at the 5% level when all nulls are true and the chance of at least one false alarm is 1 - 0.95^20, about 64%. FWER control keeps that overall chance at 5%.

concepts.name: Feature Scaling
concepts.description: Rescaling numeric features to comparable ranges, for example standardizing to zero mean and unit variance or min-max scaling to [0,1], so distance-based and gradient-based models treat features fairly.
concepts.example: Predicting house prices from size (500 to 5,000 sq ft) and bedrooms (1 to 5), size dominates distance-based methods. Standardizing both to mean 0 and SD 1 puts them on an equal footing.

concepts.name: Filtration (Probability Theory)
concepts.description: An increasing family of sigma-algebras indexed by time that represents the information available up to each moment; it is used to define adapted processes, martingales and stopping times.
concepts.example: In a stock price model, the filtration at Monday includes all prices up to Monday; by Tuesday it includes Tuesday's price too. Information only accumulates; nothing is ever forgotten.

concepts.name: Finite Population Correction
concepts.description: A factor sqrt((N-n)/(N-1)) applied to standard errors when sampling without replacement from a finite population, reducing variance when the sample is a large fraction of the population.
concepts.example: Survey 400 of a school's 500 students and the standard error shrinks by sqrt(100/499), about 0.45. You have seen most of the population, so there is much less left to be uncertain about.

concepts.name: Fisher Information
concepts.description: A measure of how much information an observation carries about an unknown parameter, defined as the variance of the score (or expected negative curvature of the log-likelihood); it sets the Cramér-Rao bound.
concepts.example: For one coin flip with bias p, the Fisher information is 1/(p(1-p)): 4 at p = 0.5 but about 11 at p = 0.1. Near the extremes each flip pins p down more precisely.

concepts.name: Fisher–Neyman Factorization Theorem
concepts.description: A theorem stating that a statistic is sufficient for a parameter exactly when the likelihood factors into a part depending on the data only through that statistic and a part not depending on the parameter.
concepts.example: For 10 coin flips, the likelihood is p^k (1-p)^(10-k), where k is the number of heads. Because it depends on the data only through k, the theorem says k alone is sufficient for p.

concepts.name: Fisher–Tippett–Gnedenko Theorem
concepts.description: The central result of extreme value theory: properly normalized maxima of i.i.d. samples, if they converge, must converge to a Gumbel, Fréchet or Weibull distribution, i.e. the generalized extreme value family.
concepts.example: Whether daily rainfall is exponential, Pareto or uniform, the yearly maximum, once rescaled, settles into one of just three shapes: Gumbel, Frechet or Weibull. It is a central limit theorem for maxima.

concepts.name: Fisher's Exact Test
concepts.description: A test of association between two categorical variables in a 2x2 contingency table that computes exact p-values from the hypergeometric distribution, useful when sample sizes are small.
concepts.example: In a tea-tasting trial, a lady identifies all 4 milk-first cups among 8. The chance of doing so by luck is 1 out of C(8,4) = 70, about 1.4%, an exact p-value with no approximation.

concepts.name: Five-Number Summary
concepts.description: A compact description of a dataset using its minimum, first quartile, median, third quartile and maximum; it is the basis of the box plot and summarizes center and spread robustly.
concepts.example: For test scores 50, 60, 65, 70, 75, 80, 95: min 50, Q1 60, median 70, Q3 80, max 95. These five numbers show the centre, spread and range at a glance and draw a box plot.

concepts.name: Fixed Effects Model
concepts.description: A regression model treating group-specific intercepts as fixed unknown parameters, commonly used with panel data to control for all time-invariant characteristics of each unit.
concepts.example: Studying how police numbers affect crime across 50 cities over 10 years, giving each city its own intercept removes stable differences like city culture, so only changes within each city drive the estimate.

concepts.name: Forecasting
concepts.description: The task of predicting future values of a quantity, typically a time series, from its past and related information, along with quantifying the uncertainty of those predictions.
concepts.example: A shop that sold 100, 110, 120 and 130 umbrellas in the past four months might forecast 140 next month by extending the trend, then adjust upward because rainy season is starting.

concepts.name: Fractional Factorial Design
concepts.description: An experimental design that runs only a carefully chosen fraction of all factor-level combinations, trading the ability to separate some high-order interactions (aliasing) for far fewer runs.
concepts.example: Testing 7 two-level factors fully needs 2^7 = 128 runs. A carefully chosen 1/16 fraction of 8 runs still estimates all 7 main effects, at the cost of mixing them up with interactions.

concepts.name: Frequency Distribution
concepts.description: A table or summary showing how often each value or range of values occurs in a dataset; it is the starting point for histograms and descriptive statistics.
concepts.example: Asking 20 people how many pets they own gives: 0 pets (8 people), 1 pet (7), 2 pets (4), 3 pets (1). This table turns a jumble of answers into a clear picture of what is common.

concepts.name: Frequentist Inference
concepts.description: The school of statistical inference that interprets probability as long-run frequency and evaluates procedures by their behaviour over repeated samples, using tools like p-values and confidence intervals.
concepts.example: A frequentist 95% confidence interval means: if we repeated the study many times, 95% of the intervals built this way would contain the true value. It is a claim about the method, not about this one interval.

concepts.name: Friedman Test
concepts.description: A nonparametric alternative to repeated-measures ANOVA that ranks values within each block or subject and tests whether several treatments differ systematically.
concepts.example: Ten tasters rank three colas from 1 to 3. The Friedman test checks whether some cola consistently gets better ranks across tasters, without assuming the scores are normal.

concepts.name: G-Test
concepts.description: A likelihood-ratio test for goodness of fit or independence in contingency tables, using the statistic 2 sum O ln(O/E), which is approximately chi-squared distributed like Pearson's test.
concepts.example: Expecting 50/50 boys and girls in 100 births but seeing 60 boys and 40 girls, G = 2[60 ln(60/50) + 40 ln(40/50)], about 4.03, which is compared with a chi-squared distribution with 1 degree of freedom.

concepts.name: Gambler's Ruin
concepts.description: A classic random-walk problem in which a gambler bets repeatedly until reaching a target or going broke; it asks for the probability of ruin and expected duration of play.
concepts.example: Start with $3, bet $1 on fair coin flips, and stop at $0 or $10. The chance of reaching $10 is 3/10. With even a slight house edge, that chance drops sharply.

concepts.name: Gamma Distribution
concepts.description: A continuous distribution on positive numbers with shape and rate parameters, modeling waiting times for several Poisson events; it generalizes the exponential and chi-squared distributions.
concepts.example: If customers arrive at 4 per hour, the waiting time until the 5th customer is gamma with shape 5 and rate 4, averaging 5/4 = 1.25 hours. A non-integer shape generalizes this to flexible skewed positive data.

concepts.name: Gauss–Markov Theorem
concepts.description: The theorem that, under linear model assumptions with uncorrelated homoscedastic zero-mean errors, ordinary least squares gives the best (lowest-variance) linear unbiased estimator of the coefficients.
concepts.example: Among all ways to estimate a line's slope that are linear in the data and unbiased, ordinary least squares has the smallest variance, as long as errors are uncorrelated with equal spread.

concepts.name: Gaussian Mixture Model
concepts.description: A probabilistic model representing a distribution as a weighted sum of several Gaussian components, typically fitted with expectation-maximization and used for soft clustering and density estimation.
concepts.example: Heights of a mixed crowd form a two-humped curve. A GMM models it as 50% of a bell at 163 cm plus 50% of a bell at 177 cm, and can say how likely each person belongs to each group.

concepts.name: Gaussian Process
concepts.description: A distribution over functions in which any finite set of function values is jointly Gaussian, specified by a mean and a kernel covariance function; it enables nonparametric regression with uncertainty.
concepts.example: Knowing the temperature at 9am and noon, a GP predicts 10:30 as roughly in between with a narrow error band, and widens the band at 6pm where there is no nearby data.

concepts.name: Generalized Additive Model
concepts.description: A regression model in which the link-transformed mean is a sum of smooth nonlinear functions of each predictor, usually splines, combining flexibility with interpretability.
concepts.example: Predicting ice cream sales from temperature, a GAM can learn that sales rise steeply from 15 to 30 degrees and then flatten, instead of forcing a straight line, while still adding up each predictor's own curve.

concepts.name: Generalized Extreme Value Distribution
concepts.description: A three-parameter family unifying the Gumbel, Fréchet and Weibull distributions, used to model block maxima such as annual peak floods.
concepts.example: Fitting the GEV to 50 years of annual maximum river levels gives one curve whose shape parameter says whether floods have a hard upper limit, Gumbel-like tails, or very heavy tails.

concepts.name: Generalized Least Squares
concepts.description: A regression method for errors that are correlated or have unequal variances, weighting the least-squares problem by the inverse error covariance matrix to obtain efficient estimates.
concepts.example: When combining survey results where some regions' data is far noisier, GLS gives noisy observations less weight and accounts for correlated neighbours, giving more precise coefficients than plain OLS.

concepts.name: Generalized Linear Model
concepts.description: A family of regression models linking a linear predictor to the mean of an exponential-family response through a link function, covering linear, logistic and Poisson regression.
concepts.example: To model the number of insurance claims, a Poisson GLM says log(expected claims) = a + b x age. The log link keeps predictions positive while the right-hand side stays a simple linear formula.

concepts.name: Generalized Method of Moments
concepts.description: An estimation technique that chooses parameters to make sample averages of moment conditions as close to zero as possible, weighted optimally; widely used in econometrics.
concepts.example: With more valid instruments than unknowns, you cannot make all sample moment conditions exactly zero. GMM picks the parameters making them jointly as close to zero as possible, weighting the most reliable conditions most.

concepts.name: Geometric Brownian Motion
concepts.description: A continuous-time process whose logarithm follows Brownian motion with drift, so values stay positive and grow exponentially on average; it is the standard model for stock prices in Black-Scholes.
concepts.example: A $100 stock growing 8% a year on average with 20% volatility follows GBM: its price wiggles randomly but proportionally, so it can never fall below zero, and its log price behaves like a random walk.

concepts.name: Geometric Distribution
concepts.description: The discrete distribution of the number of independent Bernoulli trials needed to get the first success; it is the only memoryless discrete distribution.
concepts.example: Rolling a die until you get a six: the chance it takes exactly 3 rolls is (5/6)^2 x 1/6, about 11.6%, and on average it takes 6 rolls.

concepts.name: Geometric Mean
concepts.description: The n-th root of the product of n positive numbers, equivalently the exponential of the mean log; it is the right average for growth rates and ratios.
concepts.example: An investment grows 50% one year and falls 50% the next: 1.5 x 0.5 = 0.75. The geometric mean growth factor is sqrt(0.75), about 0.866, a 13.4% yearly loss, while the arithmetic mean wrongly says 0%.

concepts.name: Gibbs Sampling
concepts.description: An MCMC algorithm that samples from a joint distribution by repeatedly drawing each variable from its conditional distribution given the current values of all others.
concepts.example: To sample (height, weight) pairs, start at any point, draw a new height given the current weight, then a new weight given that height, and repeat. After many steps the pairs follow the joint distribution.

concepts.name: Glivenko–Cantelli Theorem
concepts.description: The theorem that the empirical distribution function converges uniformly and almost surely to the true CDF as sample size grows, sometimes called the fundamental theorem of statistics.
concepts.example: Draw 10 random numbers and plot the fraction below each value: a jagged staircase. With 10,000 draws the staircase hugs the true CDF everywhere, and the worst gap shrinks to zero as n grows.

concepts.name: Goodness of Fit
concepts.description: How well a statistical model or assumed distribution matches observed data, assessed by measures such as R-squared or tests like chi-squared and Kolmogorov-Smirnov.
concepts.example: You suspect a die is loaded and roll it 600 times expecting 100 of each face. If you get 150 sixes and 70 ones, a goodness-of-fit test says the fair-die model fits the data poorly.

concepts.name: Granger Causality
concepts.description: A test of whether past values of one time series improve prediction of another beyond that series' own past; it captures predictive, not true, causality.
concepts.example: If last month's ad spending helps predict this month's sales better than past sales alone, ads Granger-cause sales. It shows predictive lead, not proof that ads truly cause sales.

concepts.name: Grubbs's Test
concepts.description: A test for a single outlier in an approximately normal sample, based on the largest absolute deviation from the mean divided by the sample standard deviation.
concepts.example: Lab measurements of 9.8, 10.1, 10.0, 9.9 and 14.2: the 14.2 is about 1.8 standard deviations from the mean, the most possible with only 5 points. Grubbs' test checks whether that is too extreme for normal data and flags it.

concepts.name: Gumbel Distribution
concepts.description: A continuous distribution for the maximum of many samples from light-tailed distributions such as the normal or exponential; it is the type I extreme value distribution.
concepts.example: Daily rainfall is light-tailed, so the wettest day of each year follows roughly a Gumbel distribution. Engineers use it to estimate the 100-year storm when designing drains.

concepts.name: Hamiltonian Monte Carlo
concepts.description: An MCMC method that treats parameters as particles moving under Hamiltonian dynamics, using the log-density gradient to make distant, high-acceptance proposals in high dimensions.
concepts.example: Imagine a frictionless puck gliding over a landscape where valleys are high-probability regions. Giving it a random push and letting it slide lets the sampler travel far yet still land in likely places.

concepts.name: Harmonic Mean
concepts.description: The reciprocal of the average of reciprocals of positive numbers; it is the right average for rates such as speeds and is used to define the F1 score.
concepts.example: Drive 60 km at 30 km/h and return at 60 km/h. The average speed is not 45 but the harmonic mean, 2/(1/30 + 1/60) = 40 km/h, because you spend longer at the slow speed.

concepts.name: Hazard Function
concepts.description: The instantaneous rate at which an event occurs at time t given survival up to t, equal to the density divided by the survival function; central to survival analysis.
concepts.example: For light bulbs, the hazard at 1,000 hours is the chance per hour that a bulb still working at 1,000 hours fails right then. A rising hazard means bulbs wear out; a constant hazard means failure is pure chance.

concepts.name: Heavy-Tailed Distribution
concepts.description: A distribution whose tails decay more slowly than an exponential, so extreme values are far more likely than under a normal; examples include Pareto, Cauchy and Student t.
concepts.example: City populations are heavy-tailed: most towns are small, but a few cities have millions. Under a normal curve, a city 100 times the average would be essentially impossible; here it is routine.

concepts.name: Heteroscedasticity
concepts.description: The situation where the variance of regression errors changes across observations or predictor values, violating OLS assumptions and making standard errors unreliable.
concepts.example: Regress spending on income: low earners all spend similarly, but high earners vary hugely, some saving, some splurging. The scatter fans out like a cone as income grows.

concepts.name: Heteroscedasticity-Consistent Standard Errors
concepts.description: Standard errors for regression coefficients, such as White's sandwich estimator, that remain valid when error variance differs across observations.
concepts.example: When predicting spending from income where rich people's spending varies far more, the usual standard errors are too small. White's robust standard errors correct this, giving honest confidence intervals.

concepts.name: Hidden Markov Model
concepts.description: A model where a hidden Markov chain of states generates observed outputs; algorithms like forward-backward and Viterbi infer hidden states, used in speech and sequence analysis.
concepts.example: You cannot see the weather in a distant city, but you see whether a friend there carries an umbrella each day. An HMM uses those umbrella sightings to infer the likely sequence of rainy and sunny days.

concepts.name: Hierarchical Clustering
concepts.description: A clustering approach that builds a tree of nested clusters by repeatedly merging the closest groups (agglomerative) or splitting groups (divisive), visualized as a dendrogram.
concepts.example: Start with each animal as its own group, merge the most similar pair (wolf and dog), then the next (cat and lion), and so on. The resulting tree shows both small and large groupings at once.

concepts.name: Highest Posterior Density Interval
concepts.description: The narrowest Bayesian credible interval containing a given posterior probability, where every point inside has higher posterior density than every point outside.
concepts.example: For a skewed posterior on a disease rate peaking at 2%, the 95% HPD might run from 0.5% to 5%, including the peak, whereas an equal-tailed interval could exclude values more likely than some it includes.

concepts.name: Histogram
concepts.description: A chart that groups numeric data into adjacent bins and draws a bar for each bin whose height shows how many values fall in it, revealing the data's shape.
concepts.example: Bin 30 exam scores into 50-59, 60-69, 70-79, 80-89 and 90-99 and draw a bar for each count. A tall bar at 70-79 and short bars at the ends show at a glance that scores cluster in the middle.

concepts.name: Hodges–Lehmann Estimator
concepts.description: A robust estimator of location, or of a shift between two samples, equal to the median of all pairwise averages (or pairwise differences); it pairs naturally with rank tests.
concepts.example: For data 1, 2, 3, 100, the mean is 26.5 but the median of all pairwise averages (Walsh averages) is 2.5, barely moved by the wild 100 yet using more information than the median alone.

concepts.name: Hoeffding's Inequality
concepts.description: A concentration bound stating that the mean of independent bounded random variables deviates from its expectation by more than t with probability at most exp(-2nt^2/(b-a)^2).
concepts.example: Flip a fair coin 1,000 times. Hoeffding guarantees the chance the fraction of heads is off by more than 0.05 is at most 2e^(-5), about 1.3%, with no assumption beyond independence and bounded values.

concepts.name: Holm–Bonferroni Method
concepts.description: A step-down multiple-testing procedure that sorts p-values and compares the k-th smallest to alpha/(m-k+1), controlling familywise error with more power than plain Bonferroni.
concepts.example: With 3 p-values 0.01, 0.02, 0.04 at alpha 0.05: compare 0.01 with 0.05/3 (reject), 0.02 with 0.05/2 (reject), 0.04 with 0.05/1 (reject). Plain Bonferroni would reject only the first.

concepts.name: Homoscedasticity
concepts.description: The assumption that the error terms in a model have the same variance across all observations and predictor values, required for ordinary least squares standard errors to be valid.
concepts.example: Predicting test scores from study hours, if students' scores scatter about plus or minus 5 points around the line whether they studied 1 hour or 10, the errors are homoscedastic.

concepts.name: Horvitz–Thompson Estimator
concepts.description: An unbiased estimator of a population total that weights each sampled value by the inverse of its probability of selection, the basis of inverse probability weighting.
concepts.example: If a big farm had a 50% chance of being sampled and a small farm a 10% chance, each sampled big farm stands in for 2 farms and each small one for 10. Summing value x (1/probability) estimates the total.

concepts.name: Hotelling's T-Squared Distribution
concepts.description: A multivariate generalization of Student's t used to test whether the mean vector of multivariate normal data equals a hypothesized vector or differs between two groups.
concepts.example: Testing whether a factory's bolts match target length and diameter together, Hotelling's T-squared handles both at once and accounts for the correlation between them, rather than running two separate t-tests.

concepts.name: Hypergeometric Distribution
concepts.description: The discrete distribution of the number of successes when drawing a fixed number of items without replacement from a finite population containing a known number of successes.
concepts.example: A box has 5 red and 15 blue balls; draw 4 without replacement. The chance of exactly 2 red is C(5,2) x C(15,2) / C(20,4) = 10 x 105 / 4845, about 21.7%.

concepts.name: Identifiability
concepts.description: A property of a statistical model meaning different parameter values always produce different data distributions, so parameters can in principle be learned uniquely from enough data.
concepts.example: If a model says y = (a + b) x, data can reveal the sum a + b = 5 but never whether a=2, b=3 or a=4, b=1. Such a model is not identifiable, so no amount of data pins down a and b.

concepts.name: Independent and Identically Distributed Random Variables
concepts.description: A collection of random variables that are mutually independent and share the same probability distribution; it is the standard assumption behind most basic statistics and ML theory.
concepts.example: Rolling the same fair die 10 times gives iid outcomes: each roll follows the same 1-to-6 distribution and none affects another. Drawing cards without replacement is not iid, because each draw changes the deck.

concepts.name: Importance Sampling
concepts.description: A Monte Carlo technique that estimates expectations under one distribution by sampling from another and reweighting samples by the density ratio, used to reduce variance or handle hard targets.
concepts.example: To estimate the chance of a rare loss over $1 million, simulate from a distribution where big losses are common, then down-weight each sample by how much more likely it was than under the real model.

concepts.name: Independence (Probability Theory)
concepts.description: Two events or random variables are independent when knowing one gives no information about the other, so their joint probability equals the product of their individual probabilities.
concepts.example: Flipping a coin and rolling a die: P(heads and 6) = 1/2 x 1/6 = 1/12. Knowing the coin landed heads does not change the chance of a 6 at all.

concepts.name: Independent Component Analysis
concepts.description: A method that separates a multivariate signal into statistically independent, non-Gaussian source components, classically used for blind source separation like the cocktail party problem.
concepts.example: At a party, two microphones each record a mix of two people talking. ICA unmixes the recordings into the two separate voices by finding the most independent, non-Gaussian signals.

concepts.name: Statistical Inference
concepts.description: The branch of statistics that draws conclusions about a population from a sample, using estimation, confidence intervals and hypothesis tests to quantify uncertainty.
concepts.example: Polling 1,000 voters and finding 52% support a candidate, inferential statistics says the true support among millions of voters is likely between 49% and 55%.

concepts.name: Influential Observation
concepts.description: A data point whose removal would substantially change a fitted regression model, often combining high leverage with a large residual; measured by Cook's distance.
concepts.example: In a plot of 20 points showing no trend, one point far to the right and far above can single-handedly tilt the fitted line steeply upward. Removing it flattens the line: it is influential.

concepts.name: Instrumental Variables Estimation
concepts.description: An estimation approach for causal effects when a regressor is endogenous, using an instrument that affects the outcome only through that regressor; two-stage least squares is the common form.
concepts.example: To find whether more schooling raises earnings, use distance to the nearest college as an instrument: it affects how much people study but plausibly not their earnings directly, isolating schooling's true effect.

concepts.name: Interaction (Statistics)
concepts.description: An interaction occurs when the effect of one variable on an outcome depends on the value of another variable, modeled for example by product terms in regression.
concepts.example: A drug lowers blood pressure by 10 points in young patients but 20 in older ones. The drug's effect depends on age, which is an interaction between drug and age.

concepts.name: Interquartile Range
concepts.description: The difference between the third and first quartiles of a dataset, measuring the spread of the middle 50% of values; it is robust to outliers.
concepts.example: For salaries where Q1 is $40k and Q3 is $70k, the IQR is $30k: the middle half of workers earn within that $30k span, and a CEO earning $5M does not change it.

concepts.name: Interval Estimation
concepts.description: Estimating an unknown parameter by a range of plausible values, such as a confidence or credible interval, rather than a single number, to convey uncertainty.
concepts.example: Instead of saying 'the average commute is 27 minutes', say 'it is between 24 and 30 minutes with 95% confidence', which tells readers how precise the estimate really is.

concepts.name: Intraclass Correlation
concepts.description: A measure of how strongly units in the same group resemble each other, defined as between-group variance over total variance; used for rater reliability and clustered data.
concepts.example: If students in the same school score similarly, the ICC is high. An ICC of 0.3 means 30% of the total variation in scores lies between schools and 70% within them.

concepts.name: Invariance Property of the MLE
concepts.description: The property that if theta-hat is the maximum likelihood estimate of theta, then g(theta-hat) is the MLE of g(theta) for any function g.
concepts.example: If the MLE of a coin's probability of heads is 0.6, the MLE of its odds is simply 0.6/0.4 = 1.5. No new maximization is needed; just plug the estimate into the function.

concepts.name: Inverse-Gamma Distribution
concepts.description: The distribution of the reciprocal of a gamma random variable, defined on positive values; it is the conjugate prior for the variance of a normal distribution.
concepts.example: In a Bayesian model of measurement noise, putting an inverse-gamma prior on the variance means that after seeing data the posterior for the variance is again inverse-gamma, just with updated parameters.

concepts.name: Inverse Transform Sampling
concepts.description: A method that generates samples from any distribution by drawing a uniform random number and passing it through the inverse cumulative distribution function.
concepts.example: To simulate exponential waiting times with rate 2, draw a uniform U between 0 and 1 and compute -ln(1-U)/2. If U = 0.5, the sample is about 0.35, and repeating this produces genuine exponential samples.

concepts.name: Inverse-Wishart Distribution
concepts.description: A distribution over positive-definite matrices, the inverse of a Wishart-distributed matrix, used as the conjugate prior for a multivariate normal's covariance matrix.
concepts.example: Estimating how two stocks' returns vary and co-vary, an inverse-Wishart prior on their 2x2 covariance matrix combines with normal data to give an inverse-Wishart posterior, keeping updates simple.

concepts.name: Irreducible Markov Chain
concepts.description: A Markov chain is irreducible if every state can eventually be reached from every other state, so the whole chain forms a single communicating class.
concepts.example: A board game where from any square you can eventually reach any other is irreducible. If there were a trap region you could enter but never leave, the chain would not be irreducible.

concepts.name: Iteratively Reweighted Least Squares
concepts.description: An algorithm that fits models such as GLMs or robust regressions by repeatedly solving a weighted least-squares problem whose weights are updated from the current fit.
concepts.example: To fit a logistic regression, start with a guess, compute weights from the current fitted probabilities, solve a weighted least squares problem, and repeat. Usually a handful of rounds suffice.

concepts.name: Itô Calculus
concepts.description: The calculus of stochastic processes such as Brownian motion, defining integrals and differentials of random paths that are nowhere differentiable; used in finance and physics.
concepts.example: For Brownian motion W, ordinary calculus would say the integral of W dW is W^2/2, but Ito calculus gives W^2/2 - t/2. The extra term comes from the wild jaggedness of random paths.

concepts.name: Itô's Lemma
concepts.description: The stochastic chain rule: for a function of an Itô process, the differential includes an extra second-derivative term because Brownian increments have squared size dt.
concepts.example: If a stock follows GBM, Ito's lemma gives the dynamics of log price: the drift becomes mu - sigma^2/2. With 10% drift and 20% volatility, the log grows only 8% per year on average.

concepts.name: Jackknife Resampling
concepts.description: A resampling method that recomputes a statistic leaving out one observation at a time, using the variation among these estimates to estimate bias and standard error.
concepts.example: With 5 measurements, compute the mean 5 times, each time leaving one value out. How much those 5 means vary gives an estimate of the standard error without any formula.

concepts.name: James–Stein Estimator
concepts.description: An estimator that shrinks a vector of sample means toward a common point and, for three or more means, has lower total squared error than the sample means themselves (Stein's paradox).
concepts.example: Estimating 20 baseball players' batting averages, pulling each player's early-season average partway toward the group average predicts their season averages better in total than using each one raw.

concepts.name: Jarque–Bera Test
concepts.description: A test of normality based on whether the sample skewness and kurtosis match those of a normal distribution (0 and 3), often applied to regression residuals.
concepts.example: Daily stock returns with skewness -0.5 and kurtosis 8 give a huge JB statistic from 1,000 days of data, so normality is firmly rejected: the returns are too heavy-tailed.

concepts.name: Jeffreys Prior
concepts.description: A noninformative prior proportional to the square root of the determinant of the Fisher information, which stays consistent under reparameterization of the model.
concepts.example: For a coin's probability p, the Jeffreys prior is proportional to 1/sqrt(p(1-p)), a Beta(1/2,1/2). It gives the same inferences whether you parametrize by p or by the log-odds.

concepts.name: Joint Probability Distribution
concepts.description: The probability distribution describing two or more random variables together, giving the probability of each combination of their values.
concepts.example: Roll two dice: the joint distribution lists all 36 pairs, each with probability 1/36. It answers questions about both together, like P(first is 6 and sum is 10) = 1/36.

concepts.name: Kalman Filter
concepts.description: A recursive algorithm that estimates the hidden state of a linear system with Gaussian noise by alternating prediction and update steps, fusing a model with noisy measurements.
concepts.example: A GPS says your car is at 100 m (plus or minus 10) while your speed-based prediction says 106 m (plus or minus 5). The Kalman filter blends them, trusting the more precise one more, to about 104.8 m with less uncertainty than either.

concepts.name: Kaplan–Meier Estimator
concepts.description: A nonparametric estimate of the survival function from censored time-to-event data, multiplying the conditional survival probabilities at each observed event time.
concepts.example: Of 10 patients, 1 dies in month 2 and 2 in month 5, while 1 drops out in month 3. Survival is 9/10 after month 2, then 0.9 x 6/8 = 0.675 after month 5, since only 8 were still being followed.

concepts.name: Kendall Rank Correlation Coefficient
concepts.description: A rank correlation coefficient based on the proportion of concordant versus discordant pairs of observations, measuring how consistently two variables are ordered.
concepts.example: Two judges rank 4 singers. Of the 6 possible pairs of singers, if 5 are ordered the same way by both judges and 1 the opposite way, Kendall's tau is (5 - 1)/6, about 0.67.

concepts.name: Kernel Density Estimation
concepts.description: A nonparametric way to estimate a probability density by placing a smooth kernel, such as a Gaussian bump, on each data point and summing, with a bandwidth controlling smoothness.
concepts.example: With waiting times 2, 3 and 7 minutes, place a small bell curve on each point and add them up. The result is a smooth hill around 2 to 3 and a smaller bump at 7, unlike a blocky histogram.

concepts.name: Kullback–Leibler Divergence
concepts.description: A measure of how one probability distribution differs from a reference distribution, the expected log-ratio of their probabilities; it is nonnegative and asymmetric, widely used in ML.
concepts.example: If the truth is a fair coin but you model it as 90% heads, the KL divergence is 0.5 log2(0.5/0.9) + 0.5 log2(0.5/0.1), about 0.74 extra bits wasted per flip by using the wrong model.

concepts.name: Kolmogorov–Smirnov Test
concepts.description: A nonparametric test comparing a sample to a reference distribution, or two samples to each other, using the maximum distance between their cumulative distribution functions.
concepts.example: Plot the staircase CDF of 50 measured reaction times next to a normal CDF. If the largest vertical gap between them is 0.25, that is too big for 50 points, so the normal model is rejected.

concepts.name: KPSS Test
concepts.description: A unit-root test for time series whose null hypothesis is stationarity (around a level or trend), complementing the Dickey-Fuller test whose null is a unit root.
concepts.example: Run ADF and KPSS on a stock price: ADF fails to reject a unit root and KPSS rejects stationarity, so both point the same way, the series is non-stationary and should be differenced.

concepts.name: Kruskal–Wallis Test
