concepts.description: A rank-based nonparametric test of whether three or more independent groups come from the same distribution, the nonparametric counterpart of one-way ANOVA.
concepts.example: Comparing customer ratings at three cafes, pool all ratings, rank them, and check whether one cafe's ratings sit at consistently higher ranks, without assuming ratings are normally distributed.

concepts.name: Kurtosis
concepts.description: A measure of the tailedness of a distribution based on the standardized fourth central moment; excess kurtosis compares it to the normal distribution's value of 3.
concepts.example: Daily returns of two stocks may both have SD 1%, but one has mostly tiny moves and occasional 8% crashes. That stock has high kurtosis: its fat tails hide rare extreme events.

concepts.name: Lag Operator
concepts.description: An operator L that shifts a time series back one step, L x_t = x_{t-1}; it lets ARIMA and other time-series models be written compactly as polynomials in L.
concepts.example: If sales are 10, 12, 15, then applying L to the series gives the previous value at each time: L x3 = 12. An AR(1) model x_t = 0.5 x_{t-1} + e_t can be written neatly as (1 - 0.5L) x_t = e_t.

concepts.name: Laplace Approximation
concepts.description: Approximating a probability distribution, usually a posterior, by a Gaussian centered at its mode with covariance given by the inverse Hessian of the negative log density there.
concepts.example: A posterior for a coin's bias peaks at 0.7. Fit a bell curve centred at 0.7 whose width matches how sharply the log-posterior curves there; the bell then stands in for the exact posterior.

concepts.name: Laplace Distribution
concepts.description: A symmetric continuous distribution with a sharp peak and exponential tails on both sides, like two back-to-back exponentials; it corresponds to L1 loss and lasso priors.
concepts.example: If daily forecast errors are Laplace distributed, small errors are very common and the chance of a large error falls off exponentially in either direction: a sharp peak with heavier tails than the normal.

concepts.name: Lasso (Statistics)
concepts.description: Linear regression with an L1 penalty on the coefficients, which shrinks them and sets many exactly to zero, performing variable selection along with regularization.
concepts.example: Predicting house prices from 50 features, lasso might set 42 coefficients to exactly zero and keep only size, location and age. You get a simpler model that often predicts as well or better.

concepts.name: Latent Variable
concepts.description: A variable that is not directly observed but is inferred from other measured variables through a model, such as intelligence in psychometrics or a cluster label in a mixture model.
concepts.example: A person's 'intelligence' cannot be measured directly, but test scores in maths, reading and logic can. A model treats intelligence as a hidden variable that explains why those scores move together.

concepts.name: Latin Square Design
concepts.description: An experimental design arranging treatments in a grid so each appears exactly once in every row and column, controlling for two nuisance factors simultaneously.
concepts.example: Testing 4 tyre brands on 4 cars over 4 days, arrange them so each brand appears once per car and once per day. That way neither car differences nor day-to-day weather can bias the comparison.

concepts.name: Law of Large Numbers
concepts.description: The theorem that the average of many independent samples from a distribution converges to its expected value as the number of samples grows.
concepts.example: Flip a fair coin 10 times and you may get 7 heads (70%). Flip it 10,000 times and you will almost surely get very close to 50%. Averages settle down as samples grow.

concepts.name: Law of the Iterated Logarithm
concepts.description: A theorem giving the exact size of the largest fluctuations of a random walk: they grow like sqrt(2n log log n), lying between the scales of the LLN and the CLT.
concepts.example: After a million fair +1/-1 coin steps, a random walk's position typically sits within about 1,000 of zero. Its record highs over time reach about sqrt(2n log log n), roughly 2,300 at that point, and no more.

concepts.name: Law of the Unconscious Statistician
concepts.description: A rule for computing the expected value of g(X) directly from the distribution of X, by summing or integrating g(x) times the probability of x, without finding the distribution of g(X).
concepts.example: To find E[X^2] for a die roll, you need not work out the distribution of X^2. Just compute (1 + 4 + 9 + 16 + 25 + 36)/6, about 15.17, weighting each g(x) by P(X = x).

concepts.name: Law of Total Expectation
concepts.description: The rule that the expected value of X equals the expectation of its conditional expectation given Y, E[X] = E[E[X|Y]], allowing expectations to be computed by conditioning.
concepts.example: If 60% of employees are in Sales averaging $50k and 40% in Engineering averaging $80k, the company average is 0.6 x 50 + 0.4 x 80 = $62k: an average of group averages.

concepts.name: Law of Total Probability
concepts.description: The rule that the probability of an event equals the sum of its conditional probabilities over a partition of the sample space, each weighted by the probability of that part.
concepts.example: A factory gets 70% of parts from supplier A (2% defective) and 30% from B (5% defective). The overall defect rate is 0.7 x 0.02 + 0.3 x 0.05 = 2.9%.

concepts.name: Law of Total Variance
concepts.description: The decomposition Var(X) = E[Var(X|Y)] + Var(E[X|Y]), splitting total variance into average within-group variance and variance between group means.
concepts.example: Heights vary partly because men and women have different averages and partly because people vary within each sex. Total variance = average within-sex variance + variance of the two sex averages.

concepts.name: Lehmann–Scheffé Theorem
concepts.description: The theorem that an unbiased estimator that is a function of a complete sufficient statistic is the unique minimum-variance unbiased estimator.
concepts.example: For Poisson counts, the sample total is complete and sufficient, so the sample mean, being an unbiased function of it, is guaranteed to be the single best unbiased estimator of the rate.

concepts.name: Level of Measurement
concepts.description: A classification of variables as nominal, ordinal, interval or ratio according to what comparisons and arithmetic are meaningful, guiding which statistics apply.
concepts.example: Eye colour is nominal (no order), T-shirt size is ordinal (S < M < L), Celsius temperature is interval (20 is not twice 10), and weight is ratio (20 kg is twice 10 kg).

concepts.name: Levene's Test
concepts.description: A test of whether several groups have equal variances that runs an ANOVA on absolute deviations from group centers, making it less sensitive to non-normality than the F-test.
concepts.example: To check whether three classes have equally spread test scores, compute each student's distance from their class mean, then run an ANOVA on those distances. Large differences mean unequal spread.

concepts.name: Leverage (Statistics)
concepts.description: A measure of how far an observation's predictor values are from the others, given by the diagonal of the hat matrix; high-leverage points can strongly pull a regression fit.
concepts.example: In data on house sizes mostly between 1,000 and 2,000 sq ft, one 10,000 sq ft mansion has high leverage. It sits far from the rest, so the fitted line is forced to pass close to it.

concepts.name: Lévy Process
concepts.description: A continuous-time stochastic process with independent, stationary increments, a family that includes Brownian motion and Poisson processes and can model jumps.
concepts.example: Model an insurer's claims as small continuous fluctuations plus sudden jumps when a disaster strikes. A Levy process combines Brownian wiggles and Poisson-timed jumps, with each period behaving like any other.

concepts.name: Likelihood Function
concepts.description: The probability (or density) of the observed data viewed as a function of the model parameters, used to compare how well different parameter values explain the data.
concepts.example: You flip a coin 10 times and get 7 heads. The likelihood of p = 0.5 is C(10,7) 0.5^10, about 0.117, while for p = 0.7 it is about 0.267, so p = 0.7 explains the data better.

concepts.name: Likelihood-Ratio Test
concepts.description: A test comparing nested models by twice the log of the ratio of their maximized likelihoods, which under the null is approximately chi-squared distributed.
concepts.example: If adding 2 predictors raises the maximized log-likelihood from -120 to -114, the statistic is 2 x 6 = 12. Compared with chi-squared on 2 degrees of freedom, that gives p of about 0.0025, so the predictors help.

concepts.name: Lilliefors Test
concepts.description: A normality test based on the Kolmogorov-Smirnov statistic but with mean and variance estimated from the data, using adjusted critical values.
concepts.example: Testing whether 30 weights are normal, you estimate the mean and SD from the same data, which makes the fitted curve hug the data closely. Lilliefors adjusts the KS critical values so the test is not too lenient.

concepts.name: Lindeberg–Feller Central Limit Theorem
concepts.description: A version of the central limit theorem for independent but not identically distributed variables, holding when the Lindeberg condition ensures no single term dominates the variance.
concepts.example: Adding up many small, independent errors from different sources, each with its own distribution, still gives a nearly normal total, as long as no single source dominates the overall variance.

concepts.name: Linear Discriminant Analysis
concepts.description: A classification and dimensionality-reduction method that finds linear combinations of features that best separate classes, assuming Gaussian classes with a shared covariance.
concepts.example: Classifying flowers by petal length and width, LDA finds the single direction along which the species' averages are farthest apart relative to their spread, and splits the classes along it.

concepts.name: Linear Regression
concepts.description: A model that predicts a numeric outcome as a weighted sum of input features plus an intercept, with weights usually fitted by minimizing squared error (ordinary least squares).
concepts.example: Predicting house price as 50,000 + 200 x size + 10,000 x bedrooms, a 1,500 sq ft, 3-bed home gets 50,000 + 300,000 + 30,000 = $380,000. The weights are chosen to minimize squared errors.

concepts.name: Linearity of Expectation
concepts.description: The property that the expected value of a sum equals the sum of expected values, E[aX+bY] = aE[X]+bE[Y], holding even when the variables are dependent.
concepts.example: If 10 guests randomly take hats, each gets their own with probability 1/10, so the expected number of matches is 10 x 1/10 = 1. This works even though the matches are dependent.

concepts.name: Link Function
concepts.description: In a generalized linear model, the function connecting the mean of the response to the linear predictor, such as the logit for probabilities or the log for counts.
concepts.example: In logistic regression the logit link maps a probability of 0.8 to log(0.8/0.2), about 1.39, onto the unbounded scale where the linear predictor lives, so predictions always stay between 0 and 1.

concepts.name: Little's Law
concepts.description: A queueing result stating that the average number of items in a stable system equals the arrival rate times the average time each item spends in the system, L = lambda W.
concepts.example: A coffee shop serves 30 customers per hour and each spends 20 minutes (1/3 hour) inside on average. Then about 30 x 1/3 = 10 customers are in the shop at any moment.

concepts.name: Ljung–Box Test
concepts.description: A test of whether a time series, often model residuals, shows significant autocorrelation over a group of lags, using a weighted sum of squared sample autocorrelations.
concepts.example: After fitting a forecasting model, check whether its residuals' autocorrelations at lags 1 to 10 are jointly near zero. A large Q statistic means the model missed some pattern.

concepts.name: Local Regression
concepts.description: A nonparametric smoothing method (LOESS/LOWESS) that fits a weighted low-degree polynomial around each point using nearby data, producing a flexible curve through a scatter plot.
concepts.example: To smooth a noisy scatter of age versus income, at each age fit a small line using only nearby people, with closer ones weighted more. Joining these local fits gives a flexible curve.

concepts.name: Log-Likelihood
concepts.description: The natural logarithm of the likelihood function; it turns products over observations into sums, making maximization and derivatives far easier and numerically stable.
concepts.example: The likelihood of 100 coin flips is a product of 100 numbers below 1, about 10^-30, too tiny to handle well. Taking logs turns it into a sum of 100 terms, around -69, which is easy to compute and maximize.

concepts.name: Log-Normal Distribution
concepts.description: The distribution of a positive variable whose logarithm is normally distributed; it is right-skewed and models quantities formed by multiplying many factors, like incomes.
concepts.example: Incomes are often log-normal: their logs form a bell curve, but the incomes themselves are skewed, with most people earning moderate amounts and a long tail of very high earners.

concepts.name: Log-Rank Test
concepts.description: A nonparametric test comparing survival curves of two or more groups by comparing observed and expected numbers of events at each event time.
concepts.example: Comparing two cancer drugs, at each death time count how many deaths each group would expect given who is still at risk. If one group consistently has more deaths than expected, its survival is worse.

concepts.name: Logistic Distribution
concepts.description: A symmetric continuous distribution resembling the normal but with heavier tails, whose CDF is the logistic sigmoid; it underlies the logit model.
concepts.example: Its CDF is the familiar S-shaped sigmoid: at 0 it gives 0.5, at 2 about 0.88. It looks like a normal curve but with slightly heavier tails, and it underlies logistic regression's latent-variable view.

concepts.name: Logistic Regression
concepts.description: A classification model that predicts the probability of a binary outcome by passing a linear combination of features through the sigmoid function, fitted by maximum likelihood.
concepts.example: Predicting whether a student passes from hours studied, a model might give log-odds = -4 + 1 x hours. At 4 hours the log-odds are 0, so pass probability 50%; at 6 hours it rises to about 88%.

concepts.name: M-Estimator
concepts.description: A broad class of estimators defined by minimizing a sum of a chosen function of the data and parameter, generalizing maximum likelihood and enabling robust estimators like Huber's.
concepts.example: Instead of minimizing squared errors, which lets one outlier dominate, an M-estimator using Huber loss treats small errors as squared and large ones as linear, so a typo of 10,000 in the data barely moves the estimate.

concepts.name: Mahalanobis Distance
concepts.description: A distance between a point and a distribution that accounts for correlations and different scales by using the inverse covariance matrix; used in outlier detection and classification.
concepts.example: Height and weight are correlated, so a 190 cm, 50 kg person is unusual even though each value alone is plausible. Mahalanobis distance flags them as far from the crowd, while Euclidean distance would not.

concepts.name: Main Effect
concepts.description: The average effect of one factor on the response in an experiment or regression, averaged over the levels of the other factors.
concepts.example: In a study of fertilizer and water on plant growth, if fertilized plants grow 5 cm more on average across both watering levels, the main effect of fertilizer is 5 cm.

concepts.name: Mann–Whitney U Test
concepts.description: A nonparametric test of whether one of two independent samples tends to have larger values, based on the ranks of all observations; an alternative to the two-sample t-test.
concepts.example: Comparing reaction times of 5 coffee drinkers and 5 non-drinkers, rank all 10 times. If coffee drinkers take ranks 1 to 5, the groups clearly differ, and no normality assumption is needed.

concepts.name: Multivariate Analysis of Variance
concepts.description: An extension of ANOVA to several dependent variables at once, testing whether group mean vectors differ while accounting for correlations between the outcomes.
concepts.example: Testing whether three diets affect both weight loss and cholesterol, MANOVA tests both outcomes together, using their correlation, instead of running two separate ANOVAs.

concepts.name: Margin of Error
concepts.description: Half the width of a confidence interval, usually a critical value times the standard error, describing how far a survey estimate may plausibly be from the true value.
concepts.example: A poll says 52% support a policy with a margin of error of 3 points. The 95% confidence interval runs from 49% to 55%, so the support level cannot be called a clear majority.

concepts.name: Marginal Distribution
concepts.description: The distribution of a subset of random variables obtained from a joint distribution by summing or integrating out the other variables.
concepts.example: A table of students by gender and grade gives joint counts. Adding across genders gives the marginal distribution of grades alone, the totals written in the margin of the table.

concepts.name: Marginal Likelihood
concepts.description: The probability of the observed data under a model after integrating over its parameters weighted by the prior; it is used to compare Bayesian models and appears as the denominator of Bayes' rule.
concepts.example: Model A says a coin is fair; model B says its bias is anywhere from 0 to 1. After 10 heads in 10 flips, B's average likelihood over its prior is far higher, so the evidence favours B.

concepts.name: Markov Chain
concepts.description: A stochastic process that moves between states where the probability of the next state depends only on the current state, described by a transition matrix.
concepts.example: Weather where tomorrow is sunny with 80% chance after a sunny day and 40% after a rainy day is a Markov chain: tomorrow depends only on today, not on last week.

concepts.name: Markov Chain Monte Carlo
concepts.description: A family of algorithms that draw samples from a complex distribution by constructing a Markov chain whose stationary distribution is the target, used for Bayesian posterior inference.
concepts.example: To sample from a complicated posterior, build a random walk that moves toward likely areas more often. After a burn-in period, the places it visits are samples you can average to get estimates.

concepts.name: Markov Property
concepts.description: The property that the future of a process depends only on its present state and not on how it arrived there; the past is irrelevant once the present is known.
concepts.example: In Snakes and Ladders, your next position depends only on your current square and the die roll, not on how you got there. That memorylessness is the Markov property.

concepts.name: Markov's Inequality
concepts.description: A bound stating that for a nonnegative random variable X and a > 0, P(X >= a) <= E[X]/a; it is the simplest concentration inequality.
concepts.example: If the average salary in a company is $50k, then at most 1 in 5 employees can earn $250k or more, since 50/250 = 0.2. No other information about salaries is needed.

concepts.name: Martingale (Probability Theory)
concepts.description: A stochastic process whose expected next value, given all past information, equals its current value; it models a fair game and is central to probability theory and finance.
concepts.example: Your bankroll while betting $1 on fair coin flips is a martingale: with $50 now, your expected bankroll after the next flip is exactly $50, no matter what happened before.

concepts.name: Maximum a Posteriori Estimation
concepts.description: Estimating parameters by the value that maximizes the posterior distribution, combining the likelihood with a prior; it equals regularized maximum likelihood.
concepts.example: A coin lands heads 3 times in 3 flips: MLE says p = 1. With a Beta(2,2) prior favouring fairness, the posterior is Beta(5,2) and its peak, the MAP estimate, is 4/5 = 0.8, a more sensible guess.

concepts.name: Principle of Maximum Entropy
concepts.description: The principle that, among all distributions consistent with known constraints, one should choose the one with highest entropy, making the fewest extra assumptions.
concepts.example: If all you know about a die is that its average roll is 3.5, the maximum entropy choice is the uniform distribution. If you know the average is 4.5, it tilts the probabilities exponentially toward high faces and assumes nothing more.

concepts.name: Maximum Likelihood Estimation
concepts.description: Estimating model parameters by choosing the values that make the observed data most probable, i.e. maximizing the (log-)likelihood function.
concepts.example: You flip a coin 10 times and get 7 heads. Trying every p, the probability of seeing exactly that outcome is highest at p = 0.7, so 0.7 is the maximum likelihood estimate.

concepts.name: MCMC Convergence Diagnostics
concepts.description: Tools for checking whether MCMC chains have converged and mixed well, such as trace plots, the Gelman-Rubin R-hat statistic comparing chains, and effective sample size.
concepts.example: Run 4 MCMC chains from different starting points. If their trace plots overlap like fuzzy caterpillars and R-hat is about 1.00, they agree; if one chain is stuck elsewhere, R-hat climbs above 1.1.

concepts.name: McNemar's Test
concepts.description: A test for paired binary data, such as before-and-after outcomes on the same subjects, that compares the counts of discordant pairs in a 2x2 table.
concepts.example: 100 people answer a yes/no question before and after an ad. Only those who changed matter: if 20 switched from no to yes but only 5 from yes to no, McNemar's test says the ad shifted opinions.

concepts.name: Mean
concepts.description: The arithmetic average of a set of numbers, found by adding them up and dividing by how many there are; it is the most common measure of central tendency.
concepts.example: Five friends have $2, $4, $6, $8 and $10. The mean is (2 + 4 + 6 + 8 + 10) / 5 = $6: if they pooled their money and split it equally, each would get $6.

concepts.name: Mean Squared Error
concepts.description: The average of squared differences between predictions or estimates and true values; it penalizes large errors heavily and equals variance plus squared bias for estimators.
concepts.example: A forecaster predicts 20, 25 and 30 degrees when the actual temperatures are 22, 25 and 26. The errors are -2, 0 and 4, so MSE = (4 + 0 + 16) / 3, about 6.7; the big miss counts four times as much as the small one.

concepts.name: Median
concepts.description: The middle value of a sorted list of numbers (or the average of the two middle values), splitting the data in half; it is robust to outliers.
concepts.example: Salaries of $30k, $35k, $40k, $45k and $1M have a mean of $230k but a median of $40k, the middle value. The median better describes a typical worker because the millionaire does not drag it up.

concepts.name: Median Absolute Deviation
concepts.description: A robust measure of spread defined as the median of the absolute deviations of data points from their median, much less affected by outliers than the standard deviation.
concepts.example: For data 1, 2, 3, 4, 100, the median is 3 and the absolute deviations are 2, 1, 0, 1, 97. Their median, the MAD, is 1, while the standard deviation is over 40 because of the single outlier.

concepts.name: Memorylessness
concepts.description: A property of a distribution where the remaining waiting time does not depend on how long one has already waited; only the exponential and geometric distributions have it.
concepts.example: If light bulb lifetimes are exponential with mean 1,000 hours, a bulb that has already lasted 500 hours still expects 1,000 more. It does not 'age': the past tells you nothing about the remaining wait.

concepts.name: Meta-Analysis
concepts.description: A statistical method for combining results from multiple independent studies of the same question, weighting each study's effect size to obtain an overall estimate.
concepts.example: Five small trials found a drug lowers blood pressure by 3, 5, 4, 8 and 2 points. Meta-analysis weights larger, more precise trials more and combines them into one estimate with a much narrower interval.

concepts.name: Method of Moments (Statistics)
concepts.description: An estimation technique that sets sample moments, such as the sample mean and variance, equal to their theoretical expressions and solves for the parameters.
concepts.example: For data assumed uniform between 0 and b, the theoretical mean is b/2. If the sample mean is 4, set b/2 = 4 and solve: the estimate is b = 8.

concepts.name: Metropolis–Hastings Algorithm
concepts.description: An MCMC algorithm that proposes a new state from a proposal distribution and accepts it with a probability based on the ratio of target densities, so the chain samples the target.
concepts.example: Exploring a hilly landscape blindfolded, propose a random step: if it goes uphill (more probable) always take it; if downhill, take it only sometimes, with probability equal to the height ratio. Your footprints sample the landscape.

concepts.name: Minimal Sufficient Statistic
concepts.description: A sufficient statistic that is a function of every other sufficient statistic, giving the greatest possible data reduction without losing information about the parameter.
concepts.example: For coin flips, both the full sequence and the count of heads are sufficient, but the count is minimal: it compresses the data as much as possible without losing any information about p.

concepts.name: Minimax Estimator
concepts.description: An estimator chosen to minimize the worst-case risk over all possible parameter values, guarding against the least favourable situation.
concepts.example: Guessing a coin's bias from n flips, the plain proportion is risky near p = 0.5. The minimax estimator (heads + sqrt(n)/2) / (n + sqrt(n)) has the same risk for every p, the lowest possible worst case.

concepts.name: Minimum-Variance Unbiased Estimator
concepts.description: An unbiased estimator whose variance is no larger than that of any other unbiased estimator, for every value of the parameter.
concepts.example: For normal data, the sample mean is unbiased for the true mean and no other unbiased estimator has lower variance, so it is the MVUE. The sample median is also unbiased but noisier.

concepts.name: Missing Data
concepts.description: Values absent from a dataset; analysis depends on why they are missing (completely at random, at random, or not at random), which determines whether deletion or imputation is unbiased.
concepts.example: In a survey, high earners skip the income question more often. Simply averaging the answers given would underestimate income, because the data are not missing at random.

concepts.name: Mixed Model
concepts.description: A regression model containing both fixed effects shared by all observations and random effects that vary across groups, used for clustered, repeated or hierarchical data.
concepts.example: Testing a teaching method across 20 schools, a mixed model has a fixed effect for the method, shared everywhere, and a random effect letting each school have its own baseline score.

concepts.name: Markov Chain Mixing Time
concepts.description: The number of steps a Markov chain needs before its distribution is close, for example in total variation, to its stationary distribution regardless of starting state.
concepts.example: Shuffling a deck by riffle shuffles takes about 7 shuffles to look random, so 7 is roughly its mixing time. Shuffling by moving the top card to a random spot takes hundreds of moves.

concepts.name: Mixture Distribution
concepts.description: A distribution formed by randomly choosing one of several component distributions according to mixing weights, then drawing from it; its density is the weighted sum of the components.
concepts.example: Pick a fish: 70% chance it is a minnow (around 5 cm) and 30% a trout (around 40 cm). The lengths of fish caught form a mixture: a big hump near 5 cm and a smaller one near 40 cm.

concepts.name: Mode (Statistics)
concepts.description: The value that appears most often in a dataset, or where a probability density reaches its peak; it is the only central tendency measure usable for nominal data.
concepts.example: In a shoe store selling sizes 7, 8, 8, 9, 8, 10, 8, the mode is 8, the size to stock most of. For colours like red, blue, red, green, the mode is red: the only average that works for categories.

concepts.name: Model Selection
concepts.description: Choosing among candidate statistical or machine-learning models by balancing fit and complexity, using tools such as cross-validation, AIC, BIC or held-out performance.
concepts.example: Fitting polynomials of degree 1 to 10 to noisy data, degree 10 fits the training points perfectly but predicts poorly. Cross-validation picks degree 3, the best balance between fit and simplicity.

concepts.name: Moment-Generating Function
concepts.description: The function M(t) = E[e^{tX}] of a random variable, whose derivatives at zero give its moments and which uniquely determines the distribution when it exists.
concepts.example: For a fair coin X (0 or 1), M(t) = (1 + e^t)/2. Its derivative at t=0 is 1/2, the mean. For a sum of independent variables, just multiply their MGFs.

concepts.name: Moment (Mathematics)
concepts.description: The k-th moment of a distribution is the expected value of X^k (or of (X-c)^k); the first moment is the mean and the second central moment is the variance.
concepts.example: For a fair die, the first moment E[X] is 3.5 and the second moment E[X^2] is 91/6, about 15.17. The variance is 15.17 - 3.5^2, about 2.92, built directly from these moments.

concepts.name: Monte Carlo Method
concepts.description: A broad technique that estimates quantities such as integrals, probabilities or expectations by averaging the results of many random simulations.
concepts.example: To estimate pi, throw 10,000 random darts at a square containing a circle. If about 7,854 land inside, the circle's area fraction is pi/4, so pi is about 4 x 0.7854 = 3.14.

concepts.name: Monty Hall Problem
concepts.description: A probability puzzle in which a contestant picks one of three doors, the host opens a losing door, and switching wins with probability 2/3, illustrating conditional probability.
concepts.example: You pick door 1; the host, who knows where the car is, opens door 3 showing a goat. Switching to door 2 wins 2/3 of the time, because your first pick was right only 1/3 of the time.

concepts.name: Moving Average
concepts.description: A smoothing technique that replaces each point in a series with the average of a window of neighbouring or preceding points, revealing trends by reducing noise.
concepts.example: Daily sales of 10, 14, 12, 18, 16 give a 3-day moving average of 12, 14.67, 15.33. The day-to-day bumps smooth out and the upward trend becomes easier to see.

concepts.name: Moving-Average Model
concepts.description: A time-series model in which each value is a linear combination of the current and a finite number of past white-noise error terms; the MA part of ARMA models.
concepts.example: In an MA(1) model, today's value = shock today + 0.6 x yesterday's shock. A surprise sales spike echoes into tomorrow, then vanishes completely after that.

concepts.name: Multicollinearity
concepts.description: A situation in regression where predictors are highly correlated with one another, making coefficient estimates unstable and their standard errors large.
concepts.example: Predicting house price from both square feet and square metres, the two predictors carry the same information, so the model cannot tell which deserves the credit and the coefficients swing wildly between samples.

concepts.name: Multidimensional Scaling
concepts.description: A technique that places objects in a low-dimensional space so that their pairwise distances match given dissimilarities as closely as possible, used for visualization.
concepts.example: Given only the driving distances between 10 cities, MDS draws a 2D map placing the cities so their distances on the map match the driving distances as closely as possible.

concepts.name: Multinomial Distribution
concepts.description: The generalization of the binomial distribution to more than two outcomes, giving probabilities of the counts in each category over a fixed number of independent trials.
concepts.example: Roll a die 12 times: the probability of exactly two of each face is 12! / (2!)^6 x (1/6)^12, about 0.34%. It counts outcomes in several categories at once.

concepts.name: Multinomial Logistic Regression
concepts.description: An extension of logistic regression to more than two classes that models class probabilities with a softmax over linear scores, also called softmax regression.
concepts.example: Predicting whether a commuter takes car, bus or bike, the model gives each option a score from the features, then softmax turns scores like 2, 1, 0 into probabilities of about 67%, 24% and 9%.

concepts.name: Multiple Comparisons Problem
concepts.description: The increased chance of false positives when many hypothesis tests are performed at once, since each test has its own error rate; corrections like Bonferroni or FDR address it.
concepts.example: Test 20 jelly bean colours for a link to acne at the 5% level and, even if none has an effect, you expect one 'significant' result by chance, the infamous green jelly bean headline.

concepts.name: Multistage Sampling
concepts.description: A survey sampling method that selects large units first (e.g. regions), then samples smaller units within them in stages, reducing cost for spread-out populations.
concepts.example: To survey a country's households, randomly pick 20 provinces, then 5 towns in each, then 10 households per town. You never need a list of every household in the country.

concepts.name: Multivariate Normal Distribution
concepts.description: The generalization of the normal distribution to random vectors, defined by a mean vector and a covariance matrix; its density has elliptical contours.
concepts.example: Heights and weights of adults form a tilted oval-shaped cloud: both are normal on their own, and the tilt shows they are positively correlated. A mean vector and covariance matrix describe the whole cloud.

concepts.name: Multivariate Statistics
concepts.description: The branch of statistics that analyzes several variables simultaneously, studying their joint distribution and relationships, with methods such as PCA, MANOVA and factor analysis.
concepts.example: A doctor studies blood pressure, cholesterol and weight together, because they are linked. Analysing them jointly reveals patterns, like clusters of at-risk patients, that separate analyses would miss.

concepts.name: Negative Binomial Distribution
concepts.description: The discrete distribution of the number of failures before a fixed number of successes in Bernoulli trials; it also models overdispersed count data.
concepts.example: A basketball player who makes 60% of free throws keeps shooting until 3 makes. The number of misses before the 3rd make follows a negative binomial; on average there are 3 x 0.4/0.6 = 2 misses.

concepts.name: Negative Binomial Regression
concepts.description: A generalized linear model for count data whose variance exceeds its mean, using a negative binomial response to extend Poisson regression.
concepts.example: Modelling doctor visits per year, the mean is 3 but the variance is 15, far beyond what Poisson allows. Negative binomial regression adds a dispersion parameter, so standard errors are not falsely small.

concepts.name: Fisher Scoring
concepts.description: An iterative method for maximum likelihood that replaces the observed Hessian in Newton's method with the expected Fisher information, giving stable updates for GLMs.
concepts.example: Fitting a logistic regression, Fisher scoring takes Newton-like steps but uses the expected curvature of the log-likelihood instead of the observed one, which is more stable and here gives exactly IRLS.

concepts.name: Neyman–Pearson Lemma
concepts.description: The theorem that, for testing one simple hypothesis against another, the likelihood-ratio test is the most powerful test at any given significance level.
concepts.example: Testing whether a coin has p = 0.5 or p = 0.8, the lemma says the most powerful test simply rejects when the number of heads is large, i.e. when the likelihood ratio favours 0.8 enough.

concepts.name: No-U-Turn Sampler
concepts.description: An adaptive version of Hamiltonian Monte Carlo that automatically chooses trajectory length by stopping when the path starts doubling back, used by default in Stan and PyMC.
concepts.example: Instead of fixing how long the simulated puck glides, NUTS keeps extending its path until it starts heading back toward where it began, then stops. This avoids wasted steps without manual tuning.

concepts.name: Noncentral Chi-Squared Distribution
concepts.description: The distribution of a sum of squares of independent normal variables with nonzero means; it describes test statistics under the alternative and is used in power calculations.
concepts.example: If a test's effect is real, the squared z-statistic is no longer centred at zero. With a true effect of 2 standard errors, it is noncentral chi-squared with noncentrality 4, used to compute the test's power.

concepts.name: Nonlinear Regression
concepts.description: Regression in which the model is a nonlinear function of its parameters, such as exponential growth curves, fitted by iterative least-squares methods like Gauss-Newton.
concepts.example: Bacteria counts grow as y = a times e^(bt). Fitting a and b directly to the counts requires nonlinear methods, since b sits inside the exponent rather than multiplying a predictor.

concepts.name: Nonparametric Statistics
concepts.description: The branch of statistics using methods that make few assumptions about the form of the underlying distribution, such as rank tests, bootstrapping and kernel density estimation.
concepts.example: To compare two diets without assuming weight loss is bell-shaped, rank all 20 people's losses from 1 to 20 and check whether one diet's people hold mostly the high ranks. No distribution shape is ever assumed.

concepts.name: Participation Bias
concepts.description: Bias arising when people who decline to respond or participate in a survey or study differ systematically from those who do, distorting results.
concepts.example: A survey about working hours gets mailed to 1,000 people, but the busiest workers are too swamped to reply. The 300 answers that come back then make average working hours look lower than they really are.

concepts.name: Normal Distribution
concepts.description: The symmetric bell-shaped continuous distribution defined by a mean and standard deviation; it arises naturally via the central limit theorem and is the most used distribution in statistics.
concepts.example: Adult heights cluster around a mean of about 170 cm with a standard deviation of about 10 cm. Roughly 68% of people fall between 160 and 180 cm, 95% between 150 and 190, and very few are outside that.

concepts.name: Normality Test
concepts.description: A statistical test of whether data plausibly come from a normal distribution, such as Shapiro-Wilk, Anderson-Darling or Jarque-Bera, often used to check model assumptions.
concepts.example: Before running a t-test on 25 reaction times, run Shapiro-Wilk on them. A p-value of 0.40 means there is no strong evidence against normality, while 0.001 warns that the data are clearly skewed or heavy-tailed.

concepts.name: Nuisance Parameter
concepts.description: A parameter of a model that must be accounted for but is not of direct interest, such as the variance when testing a mean.
concepts.example: You want to know whether a new bulb lasts 1,000 hours on average, but you don't know how much lifetimes vary. That spread is a nuisance parameter: you must estimate it to get the test right, yet you don't care about its value.

concepts.name: Null Hypothesis
concepts.description: The default claim in a hypothesis test, typically of no effect or no difference, which is rejected only if the data provide strong enough evidence against it.
concepts.example: Testing whether a coin is fair, the null hypothesis is 'heads has probability 0.5'. Getting 52 heads in 100 flips fits it fine, while 85 heads would be strong evidence against it.

concepts.name: Observational Study
concepts.description: A study in which researchers measure subjects without assigning treatments, so associations can be found but causal conclusions are threatened by confounding.
concepts.example: Researchers note that coffee drinkers live longer, but nobody was assigned to drink coffee. Coffee drinkers might also be wealthier, so the study shows a link, not proof that coffee causes long life.

concepts.name: Odds
concepts.description: The ratio of the probability that an event happens to the probability that it does not, p/(1-p); used in gambling and as the basis of logistic regression.
concepts.example: If a team wins 3 games out of 4, its probability of winning is 0.75, but its odds are 3 to 1: three wins for every loss. A 50% chance is odds of 1 to 1, or 'evens'.

concepts.name: Odds Ratio
concepts.description: The ratio of the odds of an outcome in one group to the odds in another, measuring the strength of association between an exposure and a binary outcome.
concepts.example: Among smokers, 20 got sick and 80 didn't (odds 0.25); among non-smokers, 5 got sick and 95 didn't (odds about 0.053). The odds ratio is about 4.75, so smokers' odds of illness are nearly five times higher.

concepts.name: One- and Two-Tailed Tests
concepts.description: A one-tailed test looks for an effect in only one direction, putting all of alpha in one tail, while a two-tailed test considers deviations in either direction.
concepts.example: If you only care whether a new drug lowers blood pressure, a one-tailed test puts all 5% of alpha on the 'lower' side. If it might go either way, a two-tailed test splits 2.5% to each side, needing a bigger effect in either direction.

concepts.name: One-Sample t-Test
concepts.description: A test of whether the mean of a single sample differs from a hypothesized value, using the t-distribution because the population standard deviation is estimated.
concepts.example: A cereal box claims 500 g. You weigh 16 boxes and get a mean of 494 g with SD 12 g. The t-statistic is (494 - 500) / (12/4) = -2, which with 15 degrees of freedom gives a p-value around 0.06.

concepts.name: One-Way Analysis of Variance
concepts.description: A test of whether the means of three or more independent groups are all equal, comparing between-group variance to within-group variance with an F-statistic.
concepts.example: Three fertilisers are tried on 10 plants each. If the average heights differ a lot compared with how much plants vary within each group, the F-statistic is large and ANOVA concludes not all fertilisers are equal.

concepts.name: Optional Stopping Theorem
concepts.description: The theorem that, under suitable conditions, a martingale's expected value at a stopping time equals its starting value, so no stopping strategy can make a fair game favourable.
concepts.example: A gambler betting $1 on fair coin flips starts with $10 and quits on reaching $20 or going broke. Since the game is fair, the expected final fortune is still $10, so he reaches $20 with probability exactly 1/2.

concepts.name: Order Statistic
concepts.description: The k-th smallest value in a sample; the minimum, maximum and median are all order statistics. Their distributions underpin quantile estimates, ranges and many nonparametric methods.
concepts.example: Measure 5 runners' times: 12, 9, 15, 11, 10 seconds. Sorted, they are 9, 10, 11, 12, 15, so the 1st order statistic (minimum) is 9, the 3rd (median) is 11 and the 5th (maximum) is 15.

concepts.name: Ordinal Regression
concepts.description: Regression for an outcome with ordered categories (e.g. poor/fair/good), typically modelling cumulative probabilities with shared slopes and ordered cut-points, as in the ordered logit model.
concepts.example: Predicting hotel ratings of poor/fair/good/excellent from price and distance, ordinal regression models the chance of rating 'fair or worse', 'good or worse' and so on, keeping the natural order instead of treating the levels as unrelated.

concepts.name: Ornstein–Uhlenbeck Process
concepts.description: A mean-reverting continuous-time Gaussian process: a Brownian motion with a drift that pulls it back toward a long-run mean. Used for interest rates, physics and exploration noise in RL.
concepts.example: Picture a dog on an elastic leash tied to a post while it gets randomly jostled. It wanders, but the farther it strays the harder the leash pulls it back, so it keeps hovering near the post. Interest-rate models use this idea.

concepts.name: Outlier
concepts.description: A data point that lies unusually far from the rest of the data, caused by measurement error, data corruption or genuinely rare events. Outliers can distort means, variances and fitted models.
concepts.example: Household incomes on a street are mostly $40k-$70k, but one billionaire lives there. That one value is an outlier: it drags the average up to millions while the median barely moves.

concepts.name: Overdispersion
concepts.description: When observed count data are more variable than the assumed model allows, e.g. variance exceeding the mean under a Poisson model. Ignoring it understates standard errors; negative binomial models fix it.
concepts.example: A Poisson model for daily clinic visits predicts variance equal to the mean, say 10. If real counts swing between 2 and 30 with variance 40, the data are overdispersed and the Poisson model will understate uncertainty.

concepts.name: Data Dredging
concepts.description: Data dredging: trying many analyses, subsets or outcomes and reporting only those that reach statistical significance, which inflates false positives and produces unreliable findings.
concepts.example: A researcher tests whether jelly beans cause acne, finds nothing, then tests 20 colours separately. Green comes out at p = 0.04, and only green gets published, although one false hit in 20 tries is exactly what chance predicts.

concepts.name: P-Value
concepts.description: The probability, assuming the null hypothesis is true, of observing a test statistic at least as extreme as the one actually obtained. Small p-values count as evidence against the null hypothesis.
concepts.example: If a coin is fair, the chance of getting 9 or more heads (or 9 or more tails) in 10 flips is about 0.02. So seeing 9 heads gives p = 0.02: results this extreme would be rare if the coin were really fair.

concepts.name: Paired t-Test
concepts.description: A t-test comparing two measurements taken on the same subjects (e.g. before and after a treatment) by testing whether the mean of the paired differences is zero.
concepts.example: Eight people's blood pressure is measured before and after a drug. Instead of comparing two groups, take each person's difference (e.g. -5, -8, -2) and test whether the average difference is zero, which removes person-to-person variation.

concepts.name: Statistical Parameter
concepts.description: A numerical characteristic of a population or of a probability distribution, such as the population mean or variance, that is usually unknown and estimated from sample data.
concepts.example: The true average height of every adult in a country is a parameter: a fixed number we usually can't measure directly. The average of 500 sampled adults is only an estimate of it.

concepts.name: Parametric Bootstrap
concepts.description: A bootstrap variant that fits a parametric model to the data and then simulates new datasets from the fitted model, instead of resampling the observed points, to estimate uncertainty.
concepts.example: With 30 waiting times, fit an exponential distribution by MLE (say mean 4 minutes), then simulate 1,000 fake datasets of 30 from that fitted exponential. The spread of the statistic across those fakes estimates its uncertainty.

concepts.name: Parametric Model
concepts.description: A statistical model described by a fixed, finite number of parameters, such as a normal distribution with mean and variance. It contrasts with nonparametric models whose complexity grows with the data.
concepts.example: Saying 'exam scores are normal' is a parametric model: once you know just two numbers, the mean (say 70) and the SD (say 10), the whole distribution is fixed. Estimating those two numbers is all the fitting required.

concepts.name: Pareto Distribution
concepts.description: A heavy-tailed power-law distribution in which the probability of exceeding a value falls off as a power of that value; it models wealth, file sizes and the '80/20' rule.
concepts.example: In the classic '80/20 rule', 20% of people hold 80% of the wealth. A Pareto distribution produces this: most values are modest, but a few huge ones dominate, and the chance of exceeding a value shrinks like a power of that value.

concepts.name: Partial Autocorrelation Function
concepts.description: The correlation between a time series and its lag-k value after removing the effects of all shorter lags. Its cut-off pattern helps choose the order of an autoregressive model.
concepts.example: If today's temperature depends only on yesterday's, the lag-2 correlation is still positive because of the chain through yesterday. The partial autocorrelation at lag 2 removes that link and drops to about zero, revealing an AR(1) process.

concepts.name: Partial Correlation
concepts.description: The correlation between two variables after removing the linear effect of one or more control variables, computed by correlating the residuals of regressions on those controls.
concepts.example: Ice-cream sales and drownings are correlated, but both rise with temperature. Regress each on temperature, then correlate the leftovers: the partial correlation is near zero, showing the link was due to temperature.

concepts.name: Partial Least Squares Regression
concepts.description: A regression method that projects predictors and responses onto a few latent components chosen to maximise their covariance, useful when predictors are many and highly collinear.
concepts.example: Predicting sugar content from 500 near-infrared readings of fruit, PLS compresses the readings into a few components chosen specifically because they track sugar, then regresses sugar on just those few.

concepts.name: Principal Component Analysis
concepts.description: Principal Component Analysis finds orthogonal directions of maximal variance in data (eigenvectors of the covariance matrix) and projects onto the top ones to reduce dimensionality while keeping most variation.
concepts.example: Shoe size, height and arm length all rise together, so one direction, 'overall body size', captures most of their variation. PCA finds that direction first, letting three columns be summarised by roughly one number.

concepts.name: Pearson Correlation Coefficient
concepts.description: A number between -1 and 1 measuring the strength and direction of a linear relationship between two variables, computed as their covariance divided by the product of their standard deviations.
concepts.example: Hours studied and test scores for 5 students: (1,50), (2,60), (3,65), (4,80), (5,90). The points rise almost in a straight line, so r is about 0.99. If scores fell as hours rose, r would be near -1.

concepts.name: Pearson's Chi-Squared Test
concepts.description: A test that compares observed category counts with the counts expected under a hypothesis, using the sum of (observed-expected)^2/expected, to check goodness of fit or independence in contingency tables.
concepts.example: A die rolled 60 times should show each face about 10 times. If you see counts like 5, 8, 9, 10, 12, 16, sum (observed - 10)^2 / 10 over the faces; a large total suggests the die is loaded.

concepts.name: Percentile
concepts.description: The value below which a given percentage of the data falls; for example the 90th percentile exceeds 90% of observations. Percentiles summarise the shape and spread of a distribution.
concepts.example: If you scored 640 on an exam and that beat 90% of test-takers, you are at the 90th percentile. A baby at the 25th percentile for weight is heavier than a quarter of babies of the same age.

concepts.name: Periodicity (Markov Chain)
concepts.description: The period of a Markov chain state is the greatest common divisor of the possible return times to it; a chain is aperiodic when this is 1, a condition needed for convergence to a stationary distribution.
concepts.example: A chain that bounces between 'left' and 'right' each step can only return to 'left' after 2, 4, 6... steps, so its period is 2. Add a chance of staying put and returns in 1 step become possible, making it aperiodic.

concepts.name: Permutation Test
concepts.description: A nonparametric test that builds the null distribution of a statistic by repeatedly shuffling group labels and recomputing it, giving exact or approximate p-values without distributional assumptions.
concepts.example: Group A scored 5, 7, 9 and group B 2, 3, 4: a difference in means of 4. Shuffle the six scores into new groups of three thousands of times; if very few shuffles give a difference of 4 or more, the real gap is unlikely to be chance.

concepts.name: Pivotal Quantity
concepts.description: A function of the data and an unknown parameter whose distribution does not depend on that parameter, like the t-statistic; inverting it yields confidence intervals.
concepts.example: For normal data, (sample mean - true mean) divided by its standard error follows a t-distribution whatever the true mean is. Because that distribution is known, you can turn it around to get a confidence interval for the mean.

concepts.name: Point Estimation
concepts.description: Using sample data to compute a single best guess for an unknown parameter, such as the sample mean for the population mean, as opposed to giving a range of plausible values.
concepts.example: To guess the share of voters backing a candidate, poll 1,000 people and find 540 in favour. Your point estimate is 0.54: one single best number, with no range attached.

concepts.name: Poisson Distribution
concepts.description: A discrete distribution for the number of events in a fixed interval when events occur independently at a constant average rate; its mean and variance both equal the rate lambda.
concepts.example: A bakery gets 3 customers per 10 minutes on average. The Poisson gives the chance of exactly 0 customers in a 10-minute slot as e^-3, about 5%, and of exactly 3 as about 22%.

concepts.name: Poisson Limit Theorem
concepts.description: States that a binomial distribution with many trials and a small success probability, where n times p stays fixed, approaches a Poisson distribution; it explains why rare events follow Poisson counts.
concepts.example: A factory makes 10,000 chips, each faulty with probability 0.0003. The exact binomial count of faulty chips is fiddly, but it is almost identical to a Poisson with mean 3, so P(no faults) is about e^-3, roughly 5%.

concepts.name: Poisson Point Process
concepts.description: A random scatter of points in time or space where counts in disjoint regions are independent and Poisson distributed; in time, gaps between events are exponential. Models arrivals, calls and decays.
concepts.example: Raindrops landing on a paving slab at random: the number in any square follows a Poisson distribution, counts in non-overlapping squares are independent, and the waiting time between drops on a line is exponential.

concepts.name: Poisson Regression
concepts.description: A generalized linear model for count outcomes that assumes a Poisson response and models the log of its expected value as a linear function of predictors.
concepts.example: Model the number of bike accidents at a junction from traffic volume. With a log link, a coefficient of 0.1 for each extra 1,000 cars means expected accidents multiply by e^0.1, about 1.11, i.e. 11% more.

concepts.name: Polynomial Regression
concepts.description: Linear regression on powers of the input (x, x^2, x^3, ...) to fit curved relationships; it stays linear in the coefficients, so ordinary least squares still applies.
concepts.example: Fuel economy rises with speed up to about 80 km/h then falls. A straight line can't capture that, but fitting y = a + b*speed + c*speed^2 gives a curve that bends, and it is still solved with ordinary least squares.

concepts.name: Statistical Population
concepts.description: The complete set of individuals or items a study wants to draw conclusions about, such as all voters in a country, from which samples are drawn.
concepts.example: If a study asks 'how many hours do UK teenagers sleep?', the population is every teenager in the UK. The 2,000 teens actually surveyed are only a sample from it.

concepts.name: Post Hoc Analysis
concepts.description: Follow-up comparisons performed after an ANOVA finds an overall difference, to identify which specific groups differ while controlling the extra false positives from multiple tests.
concepts.example: ANOVA says four teaching methods don't all give equal scores, but not which differ. Post hoc tests then compare each pair, for example finding method C beats A and B while A and B are indistinguishable.

concepts.name: Posterior Predictive Distribution
concepts.description: The distribution of a new, unseen observation given observed data, obtained by averaging the likelihood over the posterior distribution of the parameters; used for prediction and model checking.
concepts.example: After seeing 7 heads in 10 flips of an unknown coin, you don't plug in one bias. You average over all plausible biases weighted by your posterior, which with a flat prior gives about a 67% chance the next flip is heads.

concepts.name: Posterior Probability
concepts.description: The updated probability of a hypothesis or parameter after observing data, obtained via Bayes' theorem by combining the prior with the likelihood of the data.
concepts.example: A disease affects 1% of people, and a test catches 90% of cases with a 5% false-positive rate. After a positive result, the posterior probability of disease is only about 15%, far below the 90% many people guess.

concepts.name: Power Analysis
concepts.description: Calculating the sample size needed to detect an effect of a given size with a chosen probability (power) and significance level, or the power achievable with a given sample.
concepts.example: To detect a 5-point improvement in test scores (SD 15) with 80% power at alpha 0.05, a power analysis says you need about 140 students per group. With only 30 per group you would usually miss the effect.

concepts.name: Prediction Interval
concepts.description: A range that, with a stated probability, will contain a future individual observation; it is wider than a confidence interval for the mean because it also covers individual noise.
concepts.example: From 50 adults you estimate mean height 170 cm with a 95% CI of 167-173. But the next single person you meet could easily be 155 or 185; the 95% prediction interval, roughly 150-190, covers individuals, not the average.

concepts.name: Principal Component Regression
concepts.description: Regression that first reduces predictors with PCA and then regresses the response on the leading principal components, handling multicollinearity at the cost of ignoring the response when choosing components.
concepts.example: Predicting house prices from 30 overlapping size measures (rooms, floor area, plot size...), PCR first squeezes them into, say, 3 principal components, then regresses price on those 3, avoiding wildly unstable coefficients.

concepts.name: Prior Predictive Distribution
concepts.description: The distribution of data implied by a Bayesian model before any data are seen, found by averaging the likelihood over the prior; used to check whether priors produce plausible data.
concepts.example: Before collecting data you believe a coin's heads rate is anywhere from 0 to 1 equally. Averaging over that belief, the prior predictive says every count of heads in 10 flips, from 0 to 10, is equally likely at 1/11 each.

concepts.name: Prior Probability
concepts.description: The probability assigned to a hypothesis or parameter before seeing the current data, encoding background knowledge or assumptions in Bayesian inference.
concepts.example: Before testing, a doctor knows a disease affects 1 in 1,000 people of your age. That 0.1% is the prior: your chance of having it before any test result is considered.

concepts.name: Probability
concepts.description: A number from 0 to 1 measuring how likely an event is, where 0 means impossible and 1 means certain; for equally likely outcomes it is favourable outcomes divided by total outcomes.
concepts.example: A standard die has 6 equally likely faces, 2 of which (5 and 6) are above 4. So the probability of rolling above 4 is 2/6 = 1/3, meaning about one roll in three over many rolls.

concepts.name: Probability Axioms
concepts.description: Kolmogorov's three axioms defining probability: probabilities are non-negative, the whole sample space has probability 1, and probabilities of disjoint events add.
concepts.example: For a die, each face's probability must be at least 0, all six must add to 1, and P(1 or 2) must equal P(1) + P(2) because they can't both happen. Every other probability rule follows from these three.

concepts.name: Probability Density Function
concepts.description: A function describing a continuous random variable whose integral over an interval gives the probability of landing in that interval; it is non-negative and integrates to 1.
concepts.example: If a bus arrives uniformly at random within 10 minutes, its density is a flat line at height 0.1. The chance it comes between minutes 2 and 5 is the area under that line: 3 x 0.1 = 0.3.

concepts.name: Probability Distribution
concepts.description: A description of how probability is spread across the possible values of a random variable, given by a mass function for discrete variables or a density function for continuous ones.
concepts.example: For the sum of two dice, the distribution lists each total's chance: 2 has 1/36, 7 has 6/36 (the most likely), and 12 has 1/36. Together the values cover all outcomes and add up to 1.

concepts.name: Probability-Generating Function
concepts.description: For a non-negative integer random variable, the power series G(s)=E[s^X] whose coefficients are its probabilities; derivatives give moments and products handle sums of independent variables.
concepts.example: For a fair coin's number of heads in one flip, G(s) = 0.5 + 0.5s. For two independent flips you multiply: (0.5 + 0.5s)^2 = 0.25 + 0.5s + 0.25s^2, and the coefficients are exactly P(0), P(1), P(2) heads.

concepts.name: Probability Mass Function
concepts.description: A function giving the probability that a discrete random variable equals each possible value; the probabilities are non-negative and sum to 1.
concepts.example: For a fair die, the PMF assigns 1/6 to each of 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6 and 0 to everything else. For a loaded die it might give 1/2 to six and 1/10 to each other face, still adding to 1.

concepts.name: Probability Measure
concepts.description: A measure on a sigma-algebra of events that assigns 1 to the whole space and is countably additive; it is the rigorous foundation of probability in measure theory.
concepts.example: Pick a point uniformly in a 1x1 square. The probability measure assigns each nice region its area, so a disk of area 0.2 gets 0.2, the whole square gets 1, and disjoint regions' measures add up.

concepts.name: Probability Space
concepts.description: The triple of a sample space, a sigma-algebra of events and a probability measure that formally defines a random experiment in measure-theoretic probability.
concepts.example: For one die roll: the sample space is {1,...,6}, the events are all subsets such as 'even' = {2,4,6}, and the measure gives each subset its size divided by 6. Those three pieces together form a probability space.

concepts.name: Probability Theory
concepts.description: The mathematical study of randomness, covering random variables, distributions, expectation, limit theorems and stochastic processes; it is the foundation of statistics and machine learning.
concepts.example: Probability theory answers questions like 'how many people must be in a room for a better-than-even chance two share a birthday?' (23) and 'why do averages of many dice rolls cluster tightly around 3.5?'.

concepts.name: Probit Model
concepts.description: A binary-outcome regression in which the probability of success is the standard normal CDF of a linear combination of predictors; similar to logistic regression but with a normal link.
concepts.example: To model whether a student passes based on study hours, a probit says P(pass) = Phi(-2 + 0.5 x hours). At 4 hours that's Phi(0) = 50%; at 6 hours Phi(1), about 84%.

concepts.name: Propensity Score Matching
concepts.description: A causal-inference method that estimates each unit's probability of receiving treatment from covariates, then matches or weights treated and untreated units with similar scores to reduce confounding.
concepts.example: To study a job-training programme people chose to join, estimate each person's probability of joining from age, education and past earnings. Then pair each trainee with a non-trainee with a similar score and compare their later earnings.

concepts.name: Pseudorandom Number Generator
concepts.description: A deterministic algorithm that produces a long sequence of numbers that look statistically random from an initial seed; used in simulation, sampling and initialising ML models.
concepts.example: A tiny generator: start at 7, then repeatedly compute next = (5 x current + 3) mod 16. It gives 6, 1, 8, 11, 10... which look jumbled but are fully determined by the seed, so rerunning with seed 7 repeats them exactly.

concepts.name: Q–Q Plot
concepts.description: A graph plotting the quantiles of a dataset against those of a reference distribution (or another dataset); points near a straight line indicate the distributions match, deviations reveal skew or heavy tails.
concepts.example: Sort 100 sample values and plot them against where a perfect normal would put the 1st, 2nd... 100th points. A straight diagonal line means normal; an upward curl at the right end means a heavier right tail.

concepts.name: Quadratic Discriminant Analysis
concepts.description: A generative classifier that models each class as a Gaussian with its own covariance matrix and assigns points by Bayes' rule, producing quadratic decision boundaries.
concepts.example: Classifying apples versus pears by weight and width: if pears vary much more in width than apples, QDA gives each fruit its own spread, so the boundary between them becomes a curve rather than a straight line.

concepts.name: Quantile
concepts.description: A cut point dividing a distribution so that a given fraction of values falls below it; the median is the 0.5 quantile and quartiles and percentiles are special cases.
concepts.example: In the data 1, 3, 4, 6, 8, 9, 12, 15, 20, the 0.5 quantile (median) is 8. The 0.25 quantile is around 4 and the 0.75 is around 12, so a quarter of values lie below 4 and a quarter above 12.

concepts.name: Quantile Function
concepts.description: The inverse of the cumulative distribution function: given a probability p it returns the value x below which a fraction p of the distribution lies. Used in inverse transform sampling.
concepts.example: For a uniform distribution on 0 to 10, the CDF at 3 is 0.3. The quantile function goes the other way: Q(0.3) = 3. Feeding it uniform random numbers is a standard way to simulate draws from any distribution.

concepts.name: Quantile Regression
concepts.description: Regression that models a chosen conditional quantile (such as the median or 90th percentile) of the response instead of its mean, by minimising an asymmetric absolute 'pinball' loss.
concepts.example: Ordinary regression predicts average delivery time from distance. Quantile regression at 0.9 predicts the time beaten by 90% of deliveries, e.g. 25 minutes at 5 km, which is what a 'guaranteed by' promise needs.

concepts.name: Quartile
concepts.description: The three values that split sorted data into four equal parts; the first and third quartiles bound the middle 50% of the data and define the interquartile range.
concepts.example: For the data 2, 4, 5, 7, 8, 10, 11, 13, the median is 7.5, the first quartile about 4.5 and the third about 10.5. So the middle half of the values lies between 4.5 and 10.5, an interquartile range of 6.

concepts.name: Queueing Theory
concepts.description: The mathematical study of waiting lines, modelling arrivals, service times and servers (e.g. the M/M/1 queue) to predict waiting times, queue lengths and utilisation.
concepts.example: A coffee shop gets 20 customers per hour and the barista serves 30 per hour. The M/M/1 model says the barista is busy 2/3 of the time and an average of 2 customers are in the shop (queue plus service).

concepts.name: Quota Sampling
concepts.description: A non-probability sampling method where researchers fill fixed quotas for subgroups (e.g. by age and gender) but choose individuals within each quota non-randomly.
concepts.example: A street interviewer is told to get 50 men and 50 women, half under 40. She approaches whoever passes by until each quota is filled, so the totals match the population but the choice within each group isn't random.

concepts.name: Random Effects Model
concepts.description: A model treating some effects, such as group-specific intercepts, as random draws from a distribution, letting estimates borrow strength across groups and account for within-group correlation.
concepts.example: Testing pupils in 30 schools, a random effects model treats each school's average as a draw from a bell curve of school averages. A school with only 5 pupils gets its estimate pulled toward the overall mean rather than trusted fully.

concepts.name: Random Variable
concepts.description: A function that assigns a number to each outcome of a random experiment, such as the sum of two dice; it lets us describe uncertain quantities with probability distributions.
concepts.example: Roll two dice and let X be their sum. X turns each outcome like (3,4) into a number, 7, so we can ask things like P(X = 7) = 6/36 or the average value of X, which is 7.

concepts.name: Random Walk
concepts.description: A process formed by summing random steps, such as moving +1 or -1 with fair coin flips; it models stock prices, diffusion and graph exploration, and converges to Brownian motion.
concepts.example: Start at 0 and flip a coin 10 times, stepping +1 for heads and -1 for tails. You might end at +2 or -4; on average you end at 0, but the typical distance from the start grows like the square root of the number of steps.

concepts.name: Randomization
concepts.description: Assigning experimental units to treatment or control by a chance mechanism, which balances known and unknown confounders on average and justifies causal conclusions.
concepts.example: For a trial of 100 patients, flip a coin for each one: heads gets the new drug, tails the old one. Since chance decides, older and younger, sicker and healthier patients end up roughly balanced in both groups.

concepts.name: Randomized Controlled Trial
concepts.description: An experiment where subjects are randomly assigned to treatment or control groups so differences in outcomes can be attributed to the treatment; A/B tests are the online version.
concepts.example: To test a vaccine, 30,000 volunteers are randomly split: half get it, half get a placebo. If 10 vaccinated and 100 placebo people get sick, the difference can be attributed to the vaccine, since the groups were alike otherwise.

concepts.name: Range (Statistics)
concepts.description: The difference between the largest and smallest values in a dataset, the simplest measure of spread, though very sensitive to outliers.
concepts.example: Daily high temperatures of 18, 21, 19, 25, 22 degrees have a range of 25 - 18 = 7 degrees. Add one freak 40-degree day and the range jumps to 22, showing how sensitive it is to a single extreme value.

concepts.name: Ranking (Statistics)
concepts.description: Replacing data values by their ranks (positions in sorted order) to build methods that are robust to outliers and need no distributional assumptions, as in Spearman correlation and Wilcoxon tests.
concepts.example: The values 3.1, 250, 7.4, 5.0 become ranks 1, 4, 3, 2. The huge 250 is just 'rank 4' now, so a single wild value can't distort a rank-based method the way it distorts a mean.

concepts.name: Rao–Blackwell Theorem
concepts.description: States that conditioning any estimator on a sufficient statistic gives a new estimator whose mean squared error is no larger, giving a recipe for improving estimators.
concepts.example: To estimate a coin's heads rate from 10 flips, the crude estimator 'was the first flip heads?' is unbiased but noisy. Averaging it given the total heads count gives the overall proportion of heads, which is far more precise.

concepts.name: Rayleigh Distribution
concepts.description: A continuous distribution for the magnitude of a 2D vector whose components are independent zero-mean normals with equal variance; it models wind speed and signal fading.
concepts.example: If a dart's horizontal and vertical misses from the bullseye are independent normals with SD 2 cm, its total distance from the centre follows a Rayleigh distribution, typically about 2.5 cm and never negative.

concepts.name: Recurrent and Transient States
concepts.description: A Markov chain state is recurrent if the chain returns to it with probability 1 and transient if it may never return; this classification governs long-run behaviour.
concepts.example: A drunkard taking random steps on a line or a flat grid is certain to get home eventually: those states are recurrent. In 3D, like a bird flying randomly, there's about a 66% chance it never returns, so its states are transient.

concepts.name: Regression
concepts.description: A family of methods for modelling how a numeric outcome depends on one or more input variables, used for prediction and for quantifying relationships.
concepts.example: A real-estate agent plots house prices against floor area and fits a line: price rises by about $2,000 per square metre. That relationship can then predict the price of an unlisted 90 m2 home.

concepts.name: Regression Diagnostics
concepts.description: Checks of whether a fitted regression meets its assumptions, using residual plots, leverage, Cook's distance and tests for heteroscedasticity, normality and multicollinearity.
concepts.example: After fitting a line, plot residuals against fitted values. A random cloud is good; a funnel shape means unequal variance, a U-shape means a missed curve, and one point with a huge Cook's distance may be single-handedly steering the fit.

concepts.name: Regression Discontinuity Design
concepts.description: A quasi-experimental method that estimates causal effects by comparing units just above and just below a cutoff that determines treatment, such as a test-score threshold for a scholarship.
concepts.example: Students scoring 80 or above win a scholarship. Comparing those who scored 79 with those who scored 80 gives near-identical students who differ only in getting the money, so any jump in later outcomes at 80 estimates its effect.

concepts.name: Regression Toward the Mean
concepts.description: The tendency for an extreme measurement to be followed by one closer to the average when the two are imperfectly correlated, which can masquerade as a treatment effect.
concepts.example: Pupils who scored highest on the first test tend to score a bit lower on the second, and the lowest scorers tend to improve, even with no teaching. Part of an extreme score was luck, and luck doesn't repeat reliably.

concepts.name: Rejection Sampling
concepts.description: A method for sampling from a hard target distribution: draw from an easier proposal that envelops it after scaling and accept each draw with probability equal to the ratio of target to scaled proposal.
concepts.example: To pick random points inside a heart shape, throw points uniformly into a rectangle around it and keep only those landing inside the heart. The kept points are uniform over the heart; the rest are rejected.

concepts.name: Relative Risk
concepts.description: The ratio of the probability of an outcome in an exposed group to that in an unexposed group; a value of 2 means the exposure doubles the risk.
concepts.example: If 12 of 1,000 smokers and 3 of 1,000 non-smokers develop a disease, the risks are 1.2% and 0.3%. The relative risk is 1.2 / 0.3 = 4, so smokers are four times as likely to get it.

concepts.name: Renewal Theory
concepts.description: The study of processes in which events recur with independent, identically distributed waiting times between them, generalising the Poisson process; it gives long-run rates and averages.
concepts.example: You replace a lightbulb each time it burns out, and lifetimes average 500 hours. Renewal theory says that in the long run you'll replace about 1 bulb per 500 hours, regardless of the lifetime distribution's shape.

concepts.name: Repeated Measures Design
concepts.description: An ANOVA design in which the same subjects are measured under several conditions or times, separating between-subject variability to give more powerful comparisons.
concepts.example: Ten runners are timed after three different diets, each runner trying all three. Repeated measures ANOVA compares the diets while removing the fact that some runners are simply faster than others.

concepts.name: Replication Crisis
concepts.description: The finding that many published scientific results, especially in psychology and medicine, fail to replicate, attributed to small samples, p-hacking, publication bias and low statistical power.
concepts.example: In a 2015 project repeating 100 psychology studies, only about 36% reproduced a significant result. Small samples plus selective reporting meant many original 'findings' were likely flukes.

concepts.name: Resampling (Statistics)
