concepts.description: Methods that repeatedly draw samples from the observed data, such as the bootstrap, jackknife and permutation tests, to estimate uncertainty or test hypotheses without strong assumptions.
concepts.example: With 20 measurements, draw 20 values from them with replacement and compute the median, then repeat 1,000 times. The spread of those 1,000 medians shows how uncertain the original median is, without any formula.

concepts.name: Reservoir Sampling
concepts.description: An algorithm that keeps a uniform random sample of k items from a stream of unknown length in one pass, replacing stored items with decreasing probability as new items arrive.
concepts.example: To pick 1 random tweet from a stream of unknown length, keep the first; when the n-th arrives, replace your pick with probability 1/n. At the end, each tweet had exactly the same chance of being the one kept.

concepts.name: Response Surface Methodology
concepts.description: A set of experimental-design and regression techniques that fit low-order polynomial models to explore how several factors affect a response and to find settings that optimise it.
concepts.example: A baker tests cakes at several oven temperatures and baking times, fits a curved surface of taste versus both factors, and follows it uphill to find the best combination, say 180 degrees for 35 minutes.

concepts.name: Ridge Regression
concepts.description: Linear regression with an L2 penalty on the coefficients, which shrinks them toward zero and stabilises estimates when predictors are correlated or numerous.
concepts.example: With two near-identical predictors, ordinary least squares might give coefficients of +50 and -48. Ridge adds a penalty on squared coefficient size, pulling them to something like +1 and +1, which predicts nearly as well and is far more stable.

concepts.name: Robust Regression
concepts.description: Regression methods that are less affected by outliers than least squares, for example using the Huber loss or iteratively reweighted least squares to downweight large residuals.
concepts.example: Fitting a line through 20 tidy points plus one wildly wrong data-entry value, least squares tilts toward the bad point. A Huber-loss fit penalises big residuals less steeply, so the line stays with the 20 good points.

concepts.name: Robust Statistics
concepts.description: The branch of statistics developing methods that remain reliable when data contain outliers or deviate from model assumptions, such as medians, trimmed means and M-estimators.
concepts.example: The salaries 30, 32, 35, 38, 1000 (in thousands) have a mean of 227 but a median of 35. The median is robust: one extreme value barely affects it, which makes it a safer summary of messy data.

concepts.name: Wald–Wolfowitz Runs Test
concepts.description: The Wald-Wolfowitz runs test checks whether a sequence of two-valued outcomes is random by comparing the number of runs (consecutive identical values) with what randomness would produce.
concepts.example: Coin flips HHHHHTTTTT have only 2 runs, and HTHTHTHTHT has 10; a random sequence of 5 H and 5 T usually has around 6. The runs test flags both extremes as suspiciously clumped or suspiciously alternating.

concepts.name: Sample Size Determination
concepts.description: Choosing how many observations to collect so that an estimate reaches a desired precision or a test reaches a desired power at a given significance level.
concepts.example: To estimate a vote share within plus or minus 3 points at 95% confidence, use n = 1.96^2 x 0.5 x 0.5 / 0.03^2, which is about 1,070 people. Halving the margin to 1.5 points needs four times as many, about 4,270.

concepts.name: Sample Space
concepts.description: The set of all possible outcomes of a random experiment, such as {heads, tails} for a coin flip or the six faces of a die.
concepts.example: Flipping two coins has the sample space {HH, HT, TH, TT}. The event 'exactly one head' is the subset {HT, TH}, so with equally likely outcomes its probability is 2/4 = 1/2.

concepts.name: Sample (Statistics)
concepts.description: A subset of a population that is actually observed or measured, used to draw conclusions about the whole population.
concepts.example: A factory makes 50,000 bolts a day; checking all of them is impractical, so inspectors measure 200 picked at random. Those 200 are the sample, used to judge the quality of all 50,000.

concepts.name: Sample Variance
concepts.description: An estimate of population variance from a sample, computed as the sum of squared deviations from the sample mean divided by n-1 (Bessel's correction) so that it is unbiased.
concepts.example: For the values 2, 4, 6, the mean is 4 and the squared deviations are 4, 0, 4, summing to 8. Dividing by n - 1 = 2 gives a sample variance of 4; dividing by 3 would systematically underestimate the population variance.

concepts.name: Sampling Bias
concepts.description: A systematic error where some members of the population are more likely to be included in a sample than others, so the sample misrepresents the population.
concepts.example: A phone poll calling only landlines in the daytime mostly reaches retirees, so it overstates views common among older people. Asking more people the same way doesn't fix it; the bias is in who can be reached.

concepts.name: Sampling Distribution
concepts.description: The probability distribution of a statistic, such as the sample mean, across all possible samples of a given size; it describes how the statistic varies from sample to sample.
concepts.example: Roll 2 dice and average them, over and over. Averages near 3.5 are common while 1 and 6 are rare (1/36 each). That pattern of averages, not the dice themselves, is the sampling distribution of the mean for n = 2.

concepts.name: Sampling Error
concepts.description: The difference between a sample statistic and the true population value that arises purely because only a sample, not the whole population, was observed.
concepts.example: If exactly 50% of voters back a candidate, a random poll of 1,000 might still find 48% or 52% just by luck of the draw. That 2-point gap is sampling error; it shrinks as the sample grows.

concepts.name: Sampling Frame
concepts.description: The actual list or procedure from which a sample is drawn, such as a voter register; mismatches between frame and target population cause coverage bias.
concepts.example: A survey of a town's residents draws names from the electoral register. Anyone not registered, such as recent arrivals or non-citizens, can never be picked, so the register is the frame and its gaps become blind spots.

concepts.name: Seasonal ARIMA
concepts.description: Seasonal ARIMA extends ARIMA with seasonal autoregressive, differencing and moving-average terms at a seasonal lag (e.g. 12 months) to model time series with repeating patterns.
concepts.example: Monthly ice-cream sales rise every summer and also trend upward over years. SARIMA handles both: ordinary ARIMA terms for month-to-month changes, plus seasonal terms linking each July to the previous July (lag 12).

concepts.name: Scatter Plot
concepts.description: A chart that plots pairs of values as points on two axes, revealing relationships, clusters and outliers between two numeric variables.
concepts.example: Plot 30 students with hours studied on the x-axis and exam score on the y-axis, one dot each. If the dots drift upward to the right, more study goes with higher scores, and a dot far from the cloud stands out as unusual.

concepts.name: Scheffé's Method
concepts.description: A multiple-comparison procedure after ANOVA that controls the family-wise error rate for all possible linear contrasts among group means, making it conservative but very flexible.
concepts.example: After ANOVA on four diets, you might ask 'is the average of diets A and B different from C?' as well as simple pairs. Scheffe's method lets you test any such contrast, even ones chosen after looking, while keeping overall error at 5%.

concepts.name: Score (Statistics)
concepts.description: The gradient of the log-likelihood with respect to the parameters; its expected value is zero at the true parameter and its variance is the Fisher information.
concepts.example: For 10 coin flips with 7 heads, the log-likelihood's slope with respect to p is 7/p - 3/(1 - p). At p = 0.5 the score is 14 - 6 = 8, positive, pointing toward larger p; at p = 0.7 it is zero, the MLE.

concepts.name: Score Test
concepts.description: A likelihood-based hypothesis test that uses the score (gradient of the log-likelihood) evaluated under the null hypothesis, so only the restricted model has to be fitted.
concepts.example: To test whether a coin is fair, you only need the slope of the log-likelihood at p = 0.5, not the fitted model. If that slope is steep relative to its expected variability, the data are pulling away from fairness.

concepts.name: Seasonality
concepts.description: Regular, repeating patterns in a time series tied to calendar periods, such as higher retail sales every December or daily traffic peaks.
concepts.example: A toy shop's sales spike every December and dip every January, year after year. That 12-month repeating pattern is seasonality; comparing December with November would misleadingly suggest a boom.

concepts.name: Sensitivity and Specificity
concepts.description: Sensitivity is the fraction of actual positives a test correctly flags (true positive rate); specificity is the fraction of actual negatives it correctly clears (true negative rate).
concepts.example: A COVID test detects 95 of 100 infected people (sensitivity 95%) and correctly clears 980 of 1,000 healthy people (specificity 98%). High sensitivity misses few cases; high specificity raises few false alarms.

concepts.name: Sequential Probability Ratio Test
concepts.description: Wald's test that examines data one observation at a time, updating a likelihood ratio and stopping as soon as it crosses an upper or lower threshold, often needing fewer samples than fixed designs.
concepts.example: Testing light bulbs one at a time, after each bulb you update how much more likely the data are under 'bad batch' than 'good batch'. If the ratio passes the upper boundary you reject, below the lower you accept, otherwise you test another bulb.

concepts.name: Shapiro–Wilk Test
concepts.description: A test of whether a sample comes from a normal distribution, based on how well the ordered sample values correlate with expected normal order statistics; widely used and powerful for small samples.
concepts.example: Sort 20 measurements and compare them with the values a perfect normal sample of 20 would be expected to have in order. If they line up closely, W is near 1; a W of 0.85 would signal the data are clearly non-normal.

concepts.name: Sigma-Algebra
concepts.description: A collection of subsets of a set that contains the whole set and is closed under complements and countable unions; it specifies which events can be assigned probabilities or measures.
concepts.example: For a coin, the sigma-algebra can be {empty, {H}, {T}, {H,T}}: every event you might ask about, closed under 'not' and 'or'. If you can ask about {H} you must also be able to ask about its complement {T}.

concepts.name: Sign Test
concepts.description: A simple nonparametric test of whether the median difference is zero, counting how many paired differences are positive and comparing that count with a Binomial(n, 0.5) distribution.
concepts.example: Ten patients rate pain before and after a treatment; 9 improve and 1 gets worse. If the treatment did nothing, each would go either way with probability 1/2, and 9 or more out of 10 has two-sided p of about 0.02.

concepts.name: Simple Linear Regression
concepts.description: Fitting a straight line y = a + b x to data with one predictor by least squares, estimating the intercept and slope that minimise the sum of squared residuals.
concepts.example: Fitting price against size for 5 flats gives price = 50 + 3 x size (in thousands and square metres). The intercept 50 is the base level and the slope 3 says each extra square metre adds about 3,000 to the price.

concepts.name: Simple Random Sample
concepts.description: A sample chosen so that every subset of the given size has the same chance of being selected, giving each population member an equal chance of inclusion.
concepts.example: Put all 500 students' names in a hat and draw 50. Every group of 50 is equally likely to be the chosen one, so each student has a 1 in 10 chance and no type of student is favoured.

concepts.name: Simpson's Paradox
concepts.description: A trend that appears within each of several groups reverses or disappears when the groups are combined, usually because of a confounding variable that differs between groups.
concepts.example: Hospital A has better survival than B for both mild and severe cases, yet worse survival overall. That happens because A takes most severe cases; mixing the groups hides the fact that A is better in each one.

concepts.name: Skewness
concepts.description: A measure of a distribution's asymmetry based on the third standardised moment; positive skew means a long right tail, negative skew a long left tail.
concepts.example: Household incomes have a long right tail: most families earn moderate amounts but a few earn enormous ones, so the mean exceeds the median and skewness is positive. Exam scores with most near 90 and a few failures are negatively skewed.

concepts.name: Slutsky's Theorem
concepts.description: States that if X_n converges in distribution to X and Y_n converges in probability to a constant c, then sums, products and ratios of them converge to the corresponding expressions in X and c.
concepts.example: The t-statistic swaps the unknown true SD for the sample SD. Because the sample SD converges in probability to the true SD, Slutsky's theorem says the t-statistic still converges to a standard normal for large samples.

concepts.name: Snowball Sampling
concepts.description: A non-probability sampling technique where existing participants recruit further participants from their contacts, useful for hard-to-reach populations but prone to bias.
concepts.example: To study people who use an underground music scene, a researcher interviews 3 known fans, then asks each to recommend others, who recommend more. The sample grows like a rolling snowball through social ties.

concepts.name: Spearman's Rank Correlation Coefficient
concepts.description: The Pearson correlation computed on the ranks of two variables, measuring how well their relationship is described by any monotonic function and resisting outliers.
concepts.example: Studying hours 1, 2, 3, 4, 5 against scores 10, 20, 40, 80, 160 is curved, so Pearson's r is below 1. Ranks are 1-5 for both, so Spearman's coefficient is exactly 1: the relationship is perfectly increasing.

concepts.name: Spectral Density
concepts.description: A function showing how the variance (power) of a stationary signal or time series is distributed across frequencies; it is the Fourier transform of the autocovariance function.
concepts.example: A temperature record sampled hourly has strong daily cycles and weaker yearly cycles. Its spectral density shows a tall peak at 1 cycle per day and a smaller one at 1 per year, revealing which rhythms carry most variance.

concepts.name: Standard Deviation
concepts.description: The square root of the variance, measuring how far data typically lie from the mean, in the same units as the data.
concepts.example: For the values 2, 4, 4, 4, 5, 5, 7, 9 the mean is 5 and the variance is 4, so the standard deviation is 2. Values typically sit about 2 units from the mean, in the same units as the data.

concepts.name: Standard Error
concepts.description: The standard deviation of an estimator's sampling distribution, quantifying how much the estimate would vary across repeated samples.
concepts.example: A poll of 1,000 finds 50% support. If repeated many times, results would scatter by about 1.6 points (sqrt(0.5 x 0.5 / 1000)). That 1.6-point spread is the standard error of the estimate.

concepts.name: Standard Error of the Mean
concepts.description: The standard deviation of the sample mean, equal to the population standard deviation divided by the square root of the sample size; it shrinks as more data are collected.
concepts.example: Individual heights vary with SD 10 cm. The mean of 25 people varies far less: 10 / sqrt(25) = 2 cm. With 100 people it drops to 1 cm, so quadrupling the sample halves the uncertainty.

concepts.name: Standard Normal Distribution
concepts.description: The normal distribution with mean 0 and standard deviation 1; any normal variable can be converted to it via z-scores, and its tables give probabilities for many tests.
concepts.example: IQ scores are normal with mean 100 and SD 15. Converting a score of 130 gives z = (130 - 100)/15 = 2, and a standard normal table says about 97.7% of people score below that.

concepts.name: State Space Model (Deep Learning)
concepts.description: A sequence model that maps inputs to outputs through a latent state evolving by learned linear dynamics, discretised for deep learning (as in S4) to capture very long-range dependencies efficiently.
concepts.example: A model like S4 or Mamba reads a long sequence token by token, updating a small hidden state with fixed linear rules. Because the rules are linear, training can process the whole sequence at once, and inference stays cheap like an RNN.

concepts.name: Stationary Process
concepts.description: A stochastic process is stationary when its statistical properties do not change over time; weak stationarity requires constant mean and variance and autocovariance depending only on lag.
concepts.example: Daily temperature deviations from the seasonal average bounce around zero with the same spread in any year: stationary. A company's share price drifting upward with growing swings is not, since its mean and variance change.

concepts.name: Stationary Distribution
concepts.description: A probability distribution over a Markov chain's states that stays unchanged after a transition (pi P = pi); under suitable conditions the chain converges to it from any start.
concepts.example: Weather moves sunny-to-rainy with probability 0.1 and rainy-to-sunny with 0.5. In the long run it's sunny 5/6 of the days and rainy 1/6, and applying one more day's transitions leaves those proportions unchanged.

concepts.name: Statistic
concepts.description: Any quantity computed from sample data, such as the sample mean, median or maximum, used to describe the sample or estimate population parameters.
concepts.example: From 5 test scores 70, 85, 90, 60, 95 you can compute many statistics: the mean 80, the median 85, the maximum 95. Each is a single number calculated purely from the sample, with no unknown inputs.

concepts.name: Statistical Dispersion
concepts.description: How spread out data values are around their center, measured by quantities such as range, interquartile range, variance and standard deviation.
concepts.example: Two classes both average 70 on a test. In one everyone scored 68-72; in the other scores range from 40 to 100. Measures of dispersion, like the range or SD, capture that difference the average hides.

concepts.name: Statistical Hypothesis Testing
concepts.description: A procedure for deciding whether data provide enough evidence to reject a null hypothesis in favour of an alternative, based on a test statistic and its distribution under the null.
concepts.example: To check if a new teaching method helps, assume it doesn't (the null). If test scores in the new class are so much higher that this would happen under 1% of the time by chance, reject the null and conclude the method works.

concepts.name: Statistical Model
concepts.description: A mathematical description of how data are generated, specifying a family of probability distributions for the observations, usually indexed by parameters.
concepts.example: Assume each customer's spending is independent and normal with an unknown mean and SD. That model lets you estimate the mean, quantify uncertainty and predict next week, even though it simplifies real behaviour.

concepts.name: Statistical Power
concepts.description: The probability that a test correctly rejects a false null hypothesis; it grows with sample size, effect size and significance level and equals one minus the Type II error rate.
concepts.example: If a drug truly lowers blood pressure by 5 points, a study of 20 patients might detect it only 30% of the time; with 200 patients, 90%. That chance of catching a real effect is the power.

concepts.name: Statistical Process Control
concepts.description: Using control charts and statistics to monitor a production process over time, flagging points beyond control limits (often mean plus or minus 3 standard deviations) as signs of a problem.
concepts.example: A bottling line fills 500 ml bottles with SD 2 ml. Control limits sit at 494 and 506 ml (3 SD). A bottle at 508 ml, or seven in a row above 500, signals the machine needs checking.

concepts.name: Statistical Significance
concepts.description: A result is statistically significant when its p-value falls below a pre-chosen threshold alpha (often 0.05), meaning it would be unlikely if the null hypothesis were true.
concepts.example: A study finds a new diet loses 1 kg more than control with p = 0.03. Since 0.03 < 0.05, it is statistically significant: unlikely to be just chance. It still says nothing about whether 1 kg matters in practice.

concepts.name: Statistics
concepts.description: The science of collecting, summarising, analysing and interpreting data, and of drawing conclusions under uncertainty; it underlies experiments, surveys and machine learning.
concepts.example: A school collects 500 students' exam scores, summarises them with an average and a chart, then asks whether a new tutoring scheme really raised scores or the change could be chance. Each step is part of statistics.

concepts.name: Stepwise Regression
concepts.description: Building a regression model by adding or removing predictors one at a time based on criteria such as p-values or AIC; simple but prone to overfitting and biased inference.
concepts.example: Start with no predictors for house prices, add whichever one lowers AIC most (say floor area), then the next best (location), and so on, removing any that stop helping. Stop when no change improves AIC.

concepts.name: Stochastic Differential Equation
concepts.description: A differential equation driven partly by random noise, typically Brownian motion, such as dX = mu dt + sigma dW; it models asset prices, physics and diffusion generative models.
concepts.example: A stock price grows at 5% a year on average but is jolted by random news every instant. An SDE writes this as change = 5% x price x dt + volatility x price x random shock, which is the model behind Black-Scholes.

concepts.name: Stochastic Process
concepts.description: A collection of random variables indexed by time or space, like daily stock prices or a random walk, describing how a random system evolves.
concepts.example: The temperature recorded at noon each day for a year is a stochastic process: 365 random values indexed by date. Today's value tells you something about tomorrow's, and the process describes how they jointly vary.

concepts.name: Stopping Time
concepts.description: A random time whose occurrence can be decided using only the information available up to that time, such as the first time a random walk hits a level; central to martingale theory.
concepts.example: 'Stop the first time the coin shows heads' is a stopping time: you know when to stop using only flips so far. 'Stop just before the last heads' is not, because deciding it requires seeing future flips.

concepts.name: Stratified Sampling
concepts.description: Dividing a population into non-overlapping subgroups (strata) and drawing a random sample from each, which ensures representation and usually reduces estimate variance.
concepts.example: A university has 70% undergrads and 30% postgrads. To survey 100 students, randomly choose 70 undergrads and 30 postgrads, guaranteeing both groups are represented in proportion instead of hoping a random draw gets it right.

concepts.name: Strong Law of Large Numbers
concepts.description: States that the sample average of i.i.d. random variables with finite mean converges almost surely to the true mean as the sample size grows.
concepts.example: Keep flipping a fair coin forever and track the fraction of heads. The strong law says that, with probability 1, this running fraction will eventually settle at 0.5 and stay arbitrarily close to it.

concepts.name: Structural Equation Modeling
concepts.description: A framework combining factor analysis and path analysis to model relationships among observed and latent variables through a system of simultaneous regression equations.
concepts.example: A researcher treats 'job satisfaction' as a hidden factor measured by 5 survey questions, and tests a path model where satisfaction drives loyalty, which drives sales, all estimated together in one model.

concepts.name: Student's t-Distribution
concepts.description: A bell-shaped distribution with heavier tails than the normal, indexed by degrees of freedom; it describes standardised sample means when the population variance is estimated from the data.
concepts.example: With only 5 measurements, the t-statistic uses an estimated SD, which adds uncertainty. So the 95% cut-off is 2.78 (t with 4 df) instead of 1.96; with 100 measurements it is about 1.98, almost normal.

concepts.name: Student's t-Test
concepts.description: A family of tests using the t-distribution to compare a sample mean with a value or two means with each other when the population variance is unknown.
concepts.example: To check if a new teaching method changes test averages, compare the class means relative to their standard error. A t-value of 2.5 with 30 degrees of freedom gives p of about 0.02, suggesting a real difference.

concepts.name: Sufficient Statistic
concepts.description: A statistic that captures all information in the sample about a parameter, so that given it, the remaining data carry no further information about the parameter.
concepts.example: For 10 coin flips, the total number of heads is sufficient for estimating p. Knowing whether the 7 heads came as HHHHHHHTTT or HTHTHHTHHH adds no information about the coin's bias.

concepts.name: Partition of Sums of Squares
concepts.description: Splitting the total sum of squared deviations from the mean into a part explained by the model and a residual part (SST = SSR + SSE), the basis of R-squared and ANOVA.
concepts.example: Exam scores vary with a total sum of squares of 1,000. A regression on hours studied explains 600 of it, leaving 400 in residuals. So 600 + 400 = 1,000, and R^2 = 600/1,000 = 0.6.

concepts.name: Survey Methodology
concepts.description: The field studying how to design and run surveys, covering sampling, questionnaire design, data collection modes, nonresponse and weighting, to produce accurate population estimates.
concepts.example: Asking 'Don't you agree taxes are too high?' nudges people toward yes. Survey methodology covers fixing such wording, choosing who to sample, whether to ask by phone or online, and chasing up non-responders.

concepts.name: Survey Weighting
concepts.description: Adjusting the weight of each survey respondent, through methods like post-stratification and raking, so that the weighted sample matches known population totals and corrects for unequal selection.
concepts.example: A poll ends up with 60% women though the population is 50% women. Give each woman a weight of 50/60, about 0.83, and each man 50/40 = 1.25, so the weighted sample matches the population on gender.

concepts.name: Survival Analysis
concepts.description: The statistical study of time until an event (death, failure, churn), handling censored observations with tools such as survival functions, hazard rates, Kaplan-Meier and Cox models.
concepts.example: In a 5-year cancer study, some patients are still alive at the end and some moved away. Survival analysis uses their partial follow-up instead of discarding them, for example with a Kaplan-Meier curve of the share surviving over time.

concepts.name: Survival Function
concepts.description: The probability that the time until an event exceeds t, S(t) = 1 - F(t), where F is the cumulative distribution function of the event time.
concepts.example: For light bulbs, S(1000 hours) = 0.8 means 80% still work after 1,000 hours. S starts at 1 at time 0 and only goes down, so S(2000) might be 0.4 and S(5000) close to 0.

concepts.name: Survivorship Bias
concepts.description: Drawing conclusions only from cases that passed some selection process, such as successful companies, while ignoring those that failed, which leads to overly optimistic or wrong conclusions.
concepts.example: In WWII, planes returning with bullet holes in the wings led some to armour the wings. Abraham Wald noted the planes hit in the engines never came back, so the engines were the places that needed armour.

concepts.name: Systematic Sampling
concepts.description: Selecting every k-th member from an ordered list after a random start; simple to carry out but biased if the list has a periodic pattern matching k.
concepts.example: From a list of 1,000 customers, pick a random start between 1 and 10, say 4, then take every 10th: 4, 14, 24... If the list alternated husband-wife, picking every even number could give all wives, showing the risk.

concepts.name: Test Statistic
concepts.description: A number computed from sample data, such as a t or chi-squared statistic, whose distribution under the null hypothesis is known and is used to decide whether to reject it.
concepts.example: To test if a coin is fair, flip it 100 times and count heads. That count is the test statistic: under the null it should be near 50, so a count of 70 is far into the tail and evidence against fairness.

concepts.name: Theil–Sen Estimator
concepts.description: A robust way to fit a line by taking the median of the slopes between all pairs of points; it tolerates up to about 29% outliers.
concepts.example: With 5 points you can draw 10 lines between pairs. Take their 10 slopes, say ranging from 1.2 to 2.1, plus one crazy slope of 40 from a typo, and use the median slope. The typo barely shifts the result.

concepts.name: Time Series
concepts.description: A sequence of observations recorded in time order, such as daily temperatures or monthly sales, where neighbouring values are typically dependent.
concepts.example: Your phone's daily step counts over a year form a time series: 365 values in date order. Weekends might be higher, winter lower, and today's count often resembles yesterday's.

concepts.name: Time Series Analysis
concepts.description: The field of methods for modelling, understanding and forecasting time-ordered data, including trend and seasonality decomposition, autocorrelation, ARIMA and state-space models.
concepts.example: To forecast electricity demand, an analyst removes the yearly trend, models daily and weekly cycles, checks whether leftover values are stationary, then fits a model using recent days' demand to predict tomorrow's.

concepts.name: Decomposition of Time Series
concepts.description: Splitting a time series into trend, seasonal and residual components, additively or multiplicatively, for example with classical moving averages or STL, to understand and forecast it.
concepts.example: Monthly airline passengers can be split into an upward trend (a 12-month moving average), a repeating summer peak (the seasonal part) and whatever wiggles remain (the residual). Adding the three back recovers the data.

concepts.name: Tolerance Interval
concepts.description: An interval that, with a stated confidence, contains at least a specified proportion of the population, used in quality control and engineering specifications.
concepts.example: A bolt maker says, with 95% confidence, at least 99% of all bolts are between 9.9 and 10.1 mm long. That is a tolerance interval: it bounds a proportion of the whole population, not one future bolt or the mean.

concepts.name: Transformation of Random Variables
concepts.description: Finding the distribution of Y = g(X) from that of X, for example by the CDF method or the change-of-variables formula that multiplies the density by the absolute Jacobian determinant.
concepts.example: If X is uniform on 0 to 1, what about Y = X^2? P(Y <= y) = P(X <= sqrt(y)) = sqrt(y), so Y has CDF sqrt(y): values near 0 become more common, since squaring shrinks small numbers.

concepts.name: Triangular Distribution
concepts.description: A continuous distribution defined by a minimum, a most likely value and a maximum, whose density rises linearly to a peak and falls linearly; used for rough estimates in risk analysis.
concepts.example: A project manager guesses a task takes at least 2 days, most likely 4, at most 10. The triangular distribution peaks at 4 and slopes to zero at 2 and 10, giving a mean of (2 + 4 + 10)/3, about 5.3 days.

concepts.name: Truncated Mean
concepts.description: The mean computed after discarding a fixed percentage of the smallest and largest values, giving a measure of center that is robust to outliers.
concepts.example: Olympic diving judges' scores 6.0, 7.5, 7.5, 8.0, 9.5: drop the highest and lowest and average the middle three to get 7.67. One biased judge giving 9.5 or 6.0 then can't sway the result.

concepts.name: Tukey's Range Test
concepts.description: Tukey's honestly significant difference test compares all pairs of group means after ANOVA using the studentised range distribution, controlling the family-wise error rate.
concepts.example: After ANOVA shows four fertilisers differ, Tukey's HSD compares all 6 pairs at once. It uses one critical difference, say 3.2 cm, so any pair of means differing by more than 3.2 cm is declared different, with overall error kept at 5%.

concepts.name: Two-Sample t-Test
concepts.description: A t-test comparing the means of two independent groups, testing whether their difference is zero; the classic version assumes equal variances in both groups.
concepts.example: Class A (20 pupils) averages 72 and class B (20 pupils) averages 66 on the same test. The two-sample t-test checks whether that 6-point gap is large compared with how much scores vary within classes.

concepts.name: Two-Way Analysis of Variance
concepts.description: An analysis of variance with two categorical factors that tests each factor's main effect and their interaction on a numeric outcome.
concepts.example: Crop yield is tested with 2 fertilisers and 3 watering levels. Two-way ANOVA asks whether fertiliser matters, whether watering matters, and whether a fertiliser works better only with heavy watering (an interaction).

concepts.name: Type I and Type II Errors
concepts.description: A Type I error rejects a true null hypothesis (false positive, rate alpha); a Type II error fails to reject a false null (false negative, rate beta). Reducing one usually increases the other.
concepts.example: A smoke alarm that rings when there is only burnt toast makes a Type I error (false alarm). One that stays silent during a real fire makes a Type II error (missed detection). Making it more sensitive trades one for the other.

concepts.name: Unbiased Estimator
concepts.description: An estimator whose expected value equals the parameter it estimates for every possible parameter value, so it is correct on average over repeated samples.
concepts.example: The average of a random sample is an unbiased estimator of the population mean: some samples overshoot, others undershoot, but on average over all possible samples it hits the true value exactly.

concepts.name: Uniformly Most Powerful Test
concepts.description: A test that has the highest power among all tests of the same size against every alternative in a composite hypothesis; it exists for one-sided tests in monotone likelihood ratio families.
concepts.example: Testing whether a normal mean is 0 against 'greater than 0', the test 'reject when the sample mean is large' is best for every possible positive mean at once. No other 5% test beats it anywhere, so it is uniformly most powerful.

concepts.name: Non-Informative Prior
concepts.description: A prior distribution chosen to have minimal influence on the posterior, such as a flat prior or the Jeffreys prior, used when little prior knowledge is available.
concepts.example: Estimating a coin's heads probability with no prior idea, you might use a flat prior giving every value from 0 to 1 equal weight. After 7 heads in 10 flips, the posterior is then driven almost entirely by the data.

concepts.name: Unit Root
concepts.description: A time series has a unit root when its autoregressive characteristic equation has a root equal to 1, making it non-stationary like a random walk with shocks that never fade.
concepts.example: In y_t = y_(t-1) + noise, each shock stays forever, so the series wanders like a random walk. In y_t = 0.5 y_(t-1) + noise, shocks fade by half each step. The first has a unit root; the second is stationary.

concepts.name: Variance
concepts.description: The average squared deviation of a random variable or dataset from its mean, measuring spread; its square root is the standard deviation.
concepts.example: For the values 2, 4, 6 the mean is 4. The squared deviations are 4, 0, 4, averaging 8/3, about 2.67. Spreading the values to 0, 4, 8 makes the variance 32/3, four times bigger.

concepts.name: Variance Inflation Factor
concepts.description: A diagnostic measuring how much a regression coefficient's variance is inflated by multicollinearity, equal to 1/(1 - R^2) from regressing that predictor on all others.
concepts.example: If floor area is predicted from the other house features with R^2 = 0.9, its VIF is 1/(1 - 0.9) = 10. That means its coefficient's variance is 10 times larger than if it were uncorrelated with the others.

concepts.name: Variational Inference
concepts.description: Approximate Bayesian inference that turns posterior computation into optimisation, fitting a simple distribution to the true posterior by maximising the evidence lower bound (minimising KL divergence).
concepts.example: Instead of computing an intractable posterior exactly, pick a simple family like a normal, and tune its mean and SD until it is as close as possible to the true posterior. Inference becomes an optimisation problem, often much faster than sampling.

concepts.name: Vector Autoregression
concepts.description: A multivariate time-series model in which each variable is regressed on lagged values of itself and of every other variable, capturing their dynamic interactions.
concepts.example: Model inflation and interest rates together: this quarter's inflation depends on last quarter's inflation and interest rate, and vice versa. A VAR estimates both equations jointly to forecast them and study how a shock to one spreads to the other.

concepts.name: Wald Interval
concepts.description: The simple confidence interval estimate plus or minus z times its standard error, e.g. p-hat +/- z*sqrt(p-hat(1-p-hat)/n) for a proportion; it performs poorly for small samples or extreme proportions.
concepts.example: In a poll of 100, 60 back a policy. The Wald interval is 0.6 +/- 1.96 x sqrt(0.6 x 0.4 / 100) = 0.6 +/- 0.096, about 50% to 70%. It's simple but becomes unreliable when the proportion is near 0 or 1.

concepts.name: Wald Test
concepts.description: A hypothesis test comparing an estimated parameter with its hypothesised value, scaled by its standard error; the squared statistic follows a chi-squared distribution asymptotically.
concepts.example: A logistic regression estimates a coefficient of 0.8 with standard error 0.3. The Wald statistic is 0.8/0.3, about 2.67, far enough from 0 to give p of about 0.008, so the predictor matters.

concepts.name: Weak Law of Large Numbers
concepts.description: States that the sample mean of i.i.d. random variables converges in probability to the true mean, so large samples give averages close to the expectation with high probability.
concepts.example: Flip a fair coin 10 times and getting 70% heads is common; with 10,000 flips, being off by even 2 points is extremely unlikely. The weak law says the chance of a large gap from 50% shrinks to zero as flips increase.

concepts.name: Weibull Distribution
concepts.description: A flexible continuous distribution for lifetimes and failure times whose shape parameter lets the hazard rate decrease, stay constant (exponential case) or increase over time.
concepts.example: Light bulbs with shape parameter less than 1 fail mostly early (defects); shape 1 gives constant risk like the exponential; above 1, risk grows with age as parts wear out. One family covers all three.

concepts.name: Weighted Arithmetic Mean
concepts.description: An average where each value is multiplied by a weight reflecting its importance and the sum is divided by the total weight, like a course grade combining exams of different weights.
concepts.example: A course grade counts homework 20%, midterm 30% and final 50%. Scores of 90, 70 and 80 give 0.2 x 90 + 0.3 x 70 + 0.5 x 80 = 79, not the plain average of 80.

concepts.name: Weighted Least Squares
concepts.description: Least squares in which each observation's squared residual is weighted, typically by the inverse of its variance, giving efficient estimates under heteroscedasticity.
concepts.example: Averaging lab results where some machines are much noisier than others, WLS gives each reading weight 1/variance. A reading with variance 4 counts a quarter as much as one with variance 1, so precise data drive the fit.

concepts.name: Welch's t-Test
concepts.description: A version of the two-sample t-test that does not assume equal variances, using separate variance estimates and adjusted degrees of freedom; usually the safer default.
concepts.example: Comparing commute times of 10 cyclists (SD 3 min) and 40 drivers (SD 15 min), the spreads clearly differ. Welch's test uses each group's own variance and adjusted degrees of freedom instead of pooling them.

concepts.name: White Noise
concepts.description: A sequence of uncorrelated random values with zero mean and constant variance, containing no predictable pattern; it is the building block of time-series models.
concepts.example: The hiss from an untuned radio, or a sequence of independent dice rolls minus 3.5, is white noise: every value has the same spread, averages zero, and knowing past values doesn't help predict the next.

concepts.name: White Test
concepts.description: A regression test for heteroscedasticity that regresses squared residuals on the predictors, their squares and cross-products, needing no assumption about the form of the variance.
concepts.example: After regressing wages on education, square the residuals and regress them on education and education squared. If that auxiliary R^2 times n is large on the chi-squared scale, error spread changes with education.

concepts.name: Wiener Process
concepts.description: Brownian motion: a continuous-time stochastic process with continuous paths and independent, normally distributed increments whose variance equals elapsed time; the core of stochastic calculus.
concepts.example: A pollen grain jiggling in water drifts randomly: over any 1 second its displacement is normal with variance proportional to 1 s, over 4 seconds four times that variance, and movements in separate intervals are independent.

concepts.name: Wilcoxon Signed-Rank Test
concepts.description: A nonparametric test for paired data that ranks the absolute differences and compares sums of ranks for positive and negative differences, an alternative to the paired t-test.
concepts.example: Paired differences of +1, -2, +4, +6, +8 have ranks 1, 2, 3, 4, 5 by absolute size. Positive ranks sum to 13 and negative ones to 2; such a lopsided split suggests the typical difference is above zero.

concepts.name: Wilks' Theorem
concepts.description: States that, under regularity conditions, twice the log-likelihood ratio between nested models follows a chi-squared distribution asymptotically, with degrees of freedom equal to the number of restrictions.
concepts.example: Comparing a model with 3 parameters to a nested one with 1, compute twice the log-likelihood gain. Wilks says this is roughly chi-squared with 2 degrees of freedom, so a value above 5.99 is significant at 5%.

concepts.name: Wilson Score Interval
concepts.description: A confidence interval for a binomial proportion obtained by inverting the score test; unlike the Wald interval it stays accurate near 0 or 1 and with small samples.
concepts.example: With 0 successes in 10 trials, the Wald interval collapses to [0, 0], which is absurd. The Wilson interval gives roughly [0, 0.28], sensibly allowing some chance of success.

concepts.name: Wishart Distribution
concepts.description: A distribution over symmetric positive-definite matrices, generalising the chi-squared distribution; it describes sample covariance matrices of multivariate normal data and serves as a conjugate prior.
concepts.example: Draw 20 random vectors from a 3-dimensional normal with mean zero and add up their outer products to form a 3x3 matrix. Repeat, and those matrices follow a Wishart distribution, the matrix version of a chi-squared.

concepts.name: Wold's Theorem
concepts.description: States that any weakly stationary time series can be written as a deterministic part plus an infinite moving average of white-noise innovations, justifying linear ARMA models.
concepts.example: Wold's theorem says any weakly stationary series, like monthly temperature anomalies, can be written as a weighted sum of today's and all past random shocks, plus a perfectly predictable part. That justifies MA and ARMA models.

concepts.name: Standard Score
concepts.description: The number of standard deviations a value lies above or below the mean, z = (x - mean)/sd; it puts values on a common scale for comparison.
concepts.example: In a test with mean 60 and SD 8, a score of 76 has z = (76 - 60)/8 = 2, two SDs above average. A height with z = 2 is equally unusual, so z-scores let you compare across different scales.

concepts.name: Z-Test
concepts.description: A hypothesis test that uses the standard normal distribution for its test statistic, appropriate when the population variance is known or the sample is large.
concepts.example: A machine should fill bags to 500 g with known SD 10 g. A sample of 25 averages 504 g, so z = (504 - 500)/(10/5) = 2, beyond 1.96, and the machine seems to overfill at the 5% level.

concepts.name: Zipf's Law
concepts.description: The empirical law that the frequency of an item is roughly inversely proportional to its rank, so the second most common word appears about half as often as the most common.
concepts.example: In English text, 'the' is the most common word, 'of' appears about half as often, and 'and' about a third as often. Frequency is roughly proportional to 1/rank, so a few words make up much of all text.

concepts.name: Abstraction (Computer Science)
concepts.description: Hiding implementation details behind a simpler interface so that code can be used and reasoned about at a higher level, as with functions, abstract data types, classes and APIs.
concepts.example: When you call sort(list), you don't care if it uses quicksort or merge sort; you just get a sorted list. That interface hides the details, so the implementation can change without breaking your code.

concepts.name: ACID
concepts.description: The four guarantees of reliable database transactions: atomicity (all or nothing), consistency (valid states), isolation (concurrent transactions don't interfere) and durability (committed data survives crashes).
concepts.example: Transferring $100 from savings to checking is two updates. Atomicity means both happen or neither; consistency keeps balances valid; isolation stops others seeing it half done; durability means a crash after commit doesn't lose it.

concepts.name: Aggregate Function
concepts.description: A function that summarizes many values into one, such as COUNT, SUM, AVG, MIN and MAX in SQL. Usually combined with GROUP BY to compute summaries per group.
concepts.example: In a table of orders, SELECT customer, SUM(amount) FROM orders GROUP BY customer collapses each customer's many rows into one total, such as Alice 120 and Bob 45. COUNT, AVG, MIN and MAX work the same way.

concepts.name: Amazon Redshift
concepts.description: Amazon's fully managed cloud data warehouse built on columnar storage and massively parallel processing, used to run SQL analytics over large datasets.
concepts.example: A retailer loads three years of sales, 2 billion rows, into Redshift. A query summing revenue by month reads only the date and amount columns, split across 8 nodes that each scan their share at the same time, so it returns in seconds.

concepts.name: Amazon S3
concepts.description: Amazon Simple Storage Service, a scalable object storage service that stores files as objects in buckets accessed over HTTP APIs. A common foundation for data lakes and backups.
concepts.example: Upload holiday.jpg into a bucket called my-photos and it gets an address like s3://my-photos/2024/holiday.jpg. Any program with permission can fetch it over HTTPS, and you pay only for the gigabytes stored and the requests made.

concepts.name: Amazon Web Services
concepts.description: Amazon's cloud computing platform offering on-demand compute, storage, databases, networking and machine learning services, billed by usage. The largest public cloud provider.
concepts.example: Instead of buying a server for a launch, a startup rents an EC2 machine for a few cents an hour, stores uploads in S3 and runs its database on RDS. When traffic spikes it adds 10 more machines, then switches them off afterwards.

concepts.name: Apache Airflow
concepts.description: An open-source workflow orchestration platform where data pipelines are defined in Python as DAGs of tasks, then scheduled, executed and monitored with retries and a web UI.
concepts.example: A nightly pipeline is written in Python as three tasks: download sales, clean them, load into the warehouse. Airflow runs them at 2 a.m. in that order, retries the download twice if the API fails, and shows green or red boxes in its web UI.

concepts.name: Apache Arrow
concepts.description: A language-independent columnar in-memory format for tabular data with libraries in many languages, enabling zero-copy sharing and fast analytics between tools like pandas, Spark and DuckDB.
concepts.example: A pandas table of 1 million prices can be handed to DuckDB or Polars without converting it: both read the same Arrow memory, where all prices sit side by side in one contiguous column, so no copy or re-encoding is needed.

concepts.name: Apache Avro
concepts.description: A row-oriented data serialization format that stores data in compact binary form along with a JSON schema, supporting schema evolution. Common with Kafka and Hadoop.
concepts.example: A user record {name: "Ann", age: 30} is written as a few compact bytes with no field names, plus a schema saying name is a string and age an int. A reader that later expects an extra email field with a default can still read the old file.

concepts.name: Apache Flink
concepts.description: An open-source distributed engine for stateful stream processing that handles unbounded event streams with low latency, event-time semantics and exactly-once state guarantees; it also runs batch jobs.
concepts.example: A bank streams card swipes into Flink, which keeps running state per card. If the same card is used in two countries within 10 minutes, Flink raises a fraud alert in milliseconds, even when some swipe events arrive late.

concepts.name: Apache Hadoop
concepts.description: An open-source framework for storing and processing very large datasets across clusters of commodity machines, combining the HDFS distributed file system, YARN resource manager and MapReduce.
concepts.example: To count words in 10 TB of web pages, Hadoop splits the files into 128 MB blocks stored on 100 cheap machines, sends the counting code to each machine, and then combines the partial counts into one total.

concepts.name: Apache Hive
concepts.description: A data warehouse system on top of Hadoop that lets users query huge datasets stored in HDFS or object storage with HiveQL, an SQL-like language compiled into distributed jobs.
concepts.example: An analyst writes SELECT country, COUNT(*) FROM clicks GROUP BY country over 5 TB of log files. Hive turns that SQL into distributed jobs over the files in HDFS, so no Java code is needed.

concepts.name: Apache Iceberg
concepts.description: An open table format for huge analytic datasets that adds database-like features such as ACID transactions, schema evolution, hidden partitioning and time travel on top of files in a data lake.
concepts.example: A sales table is just Parquet files on S3. Iceberg adds a metadata layer listing which files belong to each version, so you can add a column safely, have two writers commit without corrupting it, or query the table as it was last Tuesday.

concepts.name: Apache Kafka
concepts.description: A distributed event streaming platform that stores ordered, replicated logs of records in topics and lets many producers and consumers publish and read high-throughput real-time data streams.
concepts.example: An online shop writes every order to a Kafka topic called orders. The billing, shipping and analytics services each read the same stream at their own pace, and a new service added next month can replay orders from last week.

concepts.name: Apache Parquet
concepts.description: An open-source columnar file format that stores data column by column with compression and encoding, making analytic queries that read only a few columns much faster and cheaper.
concepts.example: A table has 50 columns and 100 million rows. To average one column, a CSV reader must read every byte, but with Parquet the reader jumps to that column's compressed chunks and might read 1/50th of the file.

concepts.name: Apache Spark
concepts.description: An open-source distributed computing engine that processes large datasets in memory across a cluster, offering APIs for SQL, DataFrames, streaming and machine learning in Python, Scala, Java and R.
concepts.example: To join 1 billion clicks with 10 million users, Spark splits both tables across 50 machines, keeps intermediate results in memory instead of writing them to disk, and returns a DataFrame you can query much like a pandas table.

concepts.name: API
concepts.description: An application programming interface is a defined set of functions, endpoints or protocols through which one piece of software can request services or data from another without knowing its internals.
concepts.example: A weather app does not measure the weather itself: it calls a weather service's API with GET /forecast?city=Paris and gets back {"temp": 18}. Like a restaurant menu, you order from the listed options without seeing the kitchen.

concepts.name: Asynchronous Programming
concepts.description: A programming style where tasks such as network or disk I/O are started and awaited without blocking, letting one thread juggle many operations, e.g. with async/await and event loops.
concepts.example: A program must download 10 web pages that each take 1 second. Done one after another that takes 10 seconds, but with async/await it starts all 10 requests, waits for them together, and finishes in about 1 second on a single thread.

concepts.name: API Authentication
concepts.description: The methods by which an API verifies who is calling it, such as API keys, tokens, or OAuth flows that grant limited, revocable access without sharing passwords.
concepts.example: To call a payment API, your server sends a header like Authorization: Bearer abc123. The API checks that token, sees it belongs to your shop and is allowed only to create charges, and rejects calls with a missing or expired token.

concepts.name: Bash (Unix Shell)
concepts.description: A widely used Unix shell and scripting language for running commands, chaining programs with pipes, manipulating files and automating tasks from the command line.
concepts.example: The one-liner cat access.log | grep 404 | wc -l reads a log file, keeps only lines containing 404, and counts them, chaining three small programs with pipes. Save such commands in a .sh file and you have a reusable script.

concepts.name: Batch Processing
concepts.description: Processing data in large, discrete chunks on a schedule rather than continuously, e.g. a nightly job that transforms the whole day's records; simple and efficient but higher latency than streaming.
concepts.example: A bank does not recompute its reports after every coffee purchase; at midnight a job takes all of that day's 2 million transactions, totals them per account, and writes the results in one go.

concepts.name: Big Data
concepts.description: The field dealing with datasets too large, fast or varied for a single machine or traditional database, using distributed storage and computation to collect, process and analyze them.
concepts.example: A ride-hailing app logs every car's GPS position each second: millions of rows per minute. That volume and speed overwhelm one database server, so the data is spread over a cluster of machines that store and analyse it in parallel.

concepts.name: BigQuery
concepts.description: Google Cloud's serverless, fully managed data warehouse that runs SQL queries over very large datasets using columnar storage and massive parallelism, billed by data scanned or compute used.
concepts.example: Run SELECT COUNT(*) on a public table with hundreds of millions of rows and BigQuery answers in seconds. There are no servers to set up; under on-demand pricing you pay for the bytes your query reads.

concepts.name: Boolean Data Type
concepts.description: A data type with only two values, true and false, used to represent the results of comparisons and logical conditions that control program flow.
concepts.example: The expression 7 > 3 evaluates to true and 2 == 5 to false. A variable is_logged_in = true can then drive an if statement, and true AND false gives false, just as in logic.

concepts.name: Boyce-Codd Normal Form
concepts.description: A stricter version of third normal form in which, for every non-trivial functional dependency X -> Y, X must be a superkey, eliminating remaining redundancy anomalies in a relational schema.
concepts.example: In a table (student, course, teacher), each teacher teaches one course, so teacher -> course, but teacher is not a key. The table can be in 3NF yet repeat course names; BCNF splits it into (teacher, course) and (student, teacher).

concepts.name: Broadcasting
concepts.description: A rule in array libraries like NumPy and PyTorch that automatically stretches arrays with compatible but different shapes so elementwise operations work without explicitly copying data.
concepts.example: Adding the row [10, 20, 30] to a 2x3 array [[1,2,3],[4,5,6]] gives [[11,22,33],[14,25,36]]: NumPy treats the single row as if it were copied onto every row, without actually making the copies.

concepts.name: C++
concepts.description: A compiled, statically typed general-purpose language extending C with classes, templates and manual memory control; it powers high-performance systems, game engines and ML library backends.
concepts.example: A game engine in C++ defines class Player with a position and a move() method, uses a template vector<Player> for a list of players, and manages raw memory for speed, all compiled to fast machine code before the game ships.

concepts.name: Cache (Computing)
concepts.description: A small, fast storage layer that keeps copies of frequently or recently used data so future requests are served faster than from the slower original source, such as memory or a database.
concepts.example: Your browser saves a site's logo the first time you visit; on the next visit it shows the saved copy instantly instead of downloading it again. A CPU does the same, keeping recently used memory in a tiny cache far faster than RAM.

concepts.name: CAP Theorem
concepts.description: A result stating that a distributed data store facing a network partition must choose between consistency (every read sees the latest write) and availability (every request gets a response).
concepts.example: Two bank servers in different cities lose their link. If a withdrawal arrives, one server can refuse it until the link returns (consistent but unavailable) or allow it and risk the other city showing an old balance (available but inconsistent).

concepts.name: Apache Cassandra
concepts.description: A distributed wide-column NoSQL database designed for high write throughput and availability with no single point of failure, using consistent hashing and tunable consistency.
concepts.example: A messaging app writes huge volumes of messages to Cassandra across 3 data centres. Any node can accept a write, each message is copied to 3 nodes, and if one data centre goes offline the app keeps working.

concepts.name: Change Data Capture
concepts.description: A technique that detects and streams row-level inserts, updates and deletes from a database (often by reading its transaction log) so downstream systems stay in sync in near real time.
concepts.example: When a customer changes their address in the shop's Postgres database, a CDC tool reads that UPDATE from the database's write-ahead log and sends an event to Kafka within a second, so the warehouse and search index update too.

concepts.name: Character Encoding
concepts.description: A scheme that maps characters to numbers and bytes so text can be stored and transmitted; Unicode assigns code points to characters and UTF-8 encodes them in one to four bytes.
concepts.example: The letter A is code point 65, stored as one byte in UTF-8, while the euro sign is code point 8364 and needs three bytes. Open a UTF-8 file as Latin-1 and "café" shows up as "cafÃ©".

concepts.name: CI/CD
concepts.description: Continuous integration and continuous delivery/deployment: automatically building and testing every code change and releasing passing versions quickly and reliably through automated pipelines.
concepts.example: A developer pushes a fix. Within minutes the CI server builds the app and runs 500 tests; if all pass, the CD pipeline deploys it to production automatically, and if one fails, the change is blocked and the developer is notified.

concepts.name: Class (Computer Programming)
concepts.description: A blueprint in object-oriented programming that defines the attributes (data) and methods (behavior) shared by all objects created from it.
concepts.example: A class Dog says every dog has a name and an age and can bark(). From that one blueprint you create rex = Dog("Rex", 3) and fido = Dog("Fido", 5), two separate objects with their own data but the same behaviour.

concepts.name: Client–Server Model
concepts.description: An architecture where clients send requests over a network to a server that provides a resource or service and returns responses, as in web browsers talking to web servers.
concepts.example: When you open a news site, your browser (the client) asks the site's server for the home page; the server builds it and sends it back. Thousands of browsers can ask the same server, like diners ordering from one kitchen.

concepts.name: Closure (Computer Programming)
concepts.description: A function bundled together with the variables from the scope where it was defined, so it can still access and remember those variables after the outer function has returned.
concepts.example: make_counter() creates count = 0 and returns an inner function that adds 1 to count and returns it. Call the returned function three times and you get 1, 2, 3: it still remembers count even though make_counter finished long ago.

concepts.name: Cloud Computing
concepts.description: Delivering computing resources such as servers, storage, databases and software over the internet on demand, paying only for what is used instead of owning hardware.
concepts.example: Instead of buying a 10,000 dollar server, a team rents virtual machines for cents an hour, runs a big job on 50 of them for one afternoon, then shuts them down and pays a few dollars, like using electricity from the grid.

concepts.name: Wide-Column Store
concepts.description: A NoSQL database that stores data in rows grouped into column families, where each row may have a different and very large set of columns, suited to sparse, high-volume data.
concepts.example: In a wide-column store, user 1 might have columns name and email while user 2 has name, phone and a column for each day they logged in. Rows are looked up by key and only the columns that exist are stored.

concepts.name: Column-Oriented DBMS
concepts.description: A way of storing tables column by column rather than row by row, so analytic queries scanning a few columns read less data and compress better.
concepts.example: A sales table has columns date, store, product and price. Stored by column, all prices sit together, so SUM(price) over 100 million rows reads just that one column, and long runs of similar values compress to a fraction of their size.

concepts.name: Command-Line Interface
concepts.description: A text-based way to interact with a computer by typing commands into a terminal, as opposed to clicking a graphical interface; essential for scripting and servers.
concepts.example: Instead of opening a file manager and dragging files, you type mkdir photos and then mv *.jpg photos to move every JPEG into a new folder in two short commands, which you can also save and repeat.

concepts.name: Common Table Expression
concepts.description: A named temporary result set defined with a WITH clause at the start of an SQL query, making complex queries more readable and enabling recursive queries.
concepts.example: WITH big_orders AS (SELECT * FROM orders WHERE total > 100) SELECT customer, COUNT(*) FROM big_orders GROUP BY customer names the filtered set first, so the main query reads top to bottom instead of nested brackets.

concepts.name: Compiler
concepts.description: A program that translates source code written in a high-level language into machine code or another lower-level form before the program is run.
concepts.example: You write x = 2 + 3 in C. The compiler checks it, works out that it is just 5, and outputs machine instructions the CPU can run directly, producing an executable that runs without the compiler present.

concepts.name: Concurrency (Computer Science)
concepts.description: The ability of a program to make progress on multiple tasks during overlapping time periods, through threads, processes or asynchronous code, which raises issues like race conditions.
concepts.example: A web server handles 100 visitors at once: while one request waits on the database, it works on another. Like a cook stirring soup, then chopping onions while it simmers, tasks overlap even if only one thing happens at a given instant.

concepts.name: Conda (Package Manager)
concepts.description: A cross-platform package and environment manager, popular in data science, that installs Python and non-Python dependencies and isolates them in separate environments.
concepts.example: Running conda create -n proj python=3.10 numpy cudatoolkit builds an isolated environment with exactly those versions, including non-Python libraries like CUDA, so it won't clash with another project needing Python 3.12.

concepts.name: Conditional (Computer Programming)
concepts.description: A programming construct such as if/else that runs different blocks of code depending on whether a Boolean condition is true or false.
concepts.example: if temperature > 30: print("Hot") else: print("Fine"). With temperature = 35 the comparison is true and "Hot" prints; with 20 it is false and the else branch runs.

concepts.name: Consensus (Computer Science)
concepts.description: A protocol that lets the nodes of a distributed system agree on a single value or sequence of operations even when some nodes fail or messages are delayed, as in Paxos and Raft.
concepts.example: Five servers store a bank's ledger. With Raft, they elect a leader; a new entry counts only once at least 3 of 5 have saved it, so even if two servers crash, the survivors still agree on the exact order of transactions.

concepts.name: Constructor (Object-Oriented Programming)
concepts.description: A special method of a class that runs when a new object is created, initializing its attributes, such as __init__ in Python.
concepts.example: When you write p = Point(3, 4), Python runs Point's __init__(self, x, y), which sets p.x = 3 and p.y = 4. Every new Point starts life with its coordinates already filled in.

concepts.name: Container Image
concepts.description: A read-only, layered package containing an application, its dependencies, libraries and configuration, from which identical containers can be started anywhere.
concepts.example: A Python web app's image bundles a slim Linux base layer, Python 3.11, the installed packages and the app code. Ship that one image and it runs the same on a laptop, a test server or 100 cloud machines.

concepts.name: Container Orchestration
concepts.description: The automated deployment, scaling, networking, health checking and recovery of many containers across a cluster of machines, done by systems such as Kubernetes.
concepts.example: An app runs as 20 containers across 5 servers. When traffic doubles, the orchestrator starts 20 more; when a server dies, it restarts its containers elsewhere and routes traffic around the failure, with no one paged at 3 a.m.

concepts.name: Containerization
concepts.description: Packaging an application with its dependencies into a lightweight, isolated container that shares the host operating system kernel, so it runs the same way on any machine.
concepts.example: An app needs Python 3.9 and a specific library version, but the server has Python 3.12. Packed in a container with its own dependencies, it runs anyway, starting in a second and sharing the host's kernel instead of booting a whole OS.

concepts.name: Context Manager
concepts.description: A Python object that sets up and tears down a resource around a block of code using the with statement, e.g. guaranteeing a file is closed even when an error occurs.
concepts.example: with open("data.txt") as f: text = f.read() opens the file, runs the block, and closes the file automatically when the block ends, even if reading raised an error halfway through.

concepts.name: Control Flow
concepts.description: The order in which a program's statements are executed, governed by sequential steps, conditionals, loops and function calls.
concepts.example: A recipe program runs step 1, then step 2, then checks "is the oven hot?" and either waits in a loop or continues, then calls a bake() function. That path through the code, not just its text order, is the control flow.

concepts.name: Central Processing Unit
concepts.description: The central processing unit is the main chip of a computer that executes program instructions, performing arithmetic, logic and control operations with a few powerful cores.
concepts.example: When you add two numbers in a spreadsheet, the CPU fetches the instruction from memory, decodes it as add, runs it in its arithmetic unit and stores the result, repeating billions of such steps every second.

concepts.name: Cron
concepts.description: A Unix job scheduler that runs commands or scripts automatically at fixed times or intervals specified by cron expressions, such as every night at 2 AM.
concepts.example: The line 0 2 * * * /home/me/backup.sh tells cron to run backup.sh at 2:00 a.m. every day; the five fields are minute, hour, day of month, month and day of week.

concepts.name: Cross Join
concepts.description: An SQL join that returns the Cartesian product of two tables, pairing every row of the first with every row of the second.
concepts.example: A table of 3 shirt sizes (S, M, L) cross-joined with 4 colours gives 12 rows, every size paired with every colour, which is handy for building a full product grid.

concepts.name: Comma-Separated Values
concepts.description: A plain-text file format storing tabular data where each line is a row and values are separated by commas; simple and universal but without types or schema.
concepts.example: A file with the lines name,age then Ann,30 then Bob,25 is a CSV: one header row and two data rows. Any spreadsheet can open it, but a value like "Smith, John" must be quoted because it contains a comma.

concepts.name: CUDA
concepts.description: NVIDIA's parallel computing platform and programming model that lets developers write code running on thousands of GPU threads, underpinning most deep learning libraries.
concepts.example: Adding two arrays of 1 million numbers, a CPU loop handles them a few at a time. With CUDA you write one small C++-style function and the GPU runs it across a million threads, one per element, thousands at once.

concepts.name: CUDA Kernel
concepts.description: A function launched on an NVIDIA GPU and executed in parallel by many threads, organized into blocks and grids, with threads scheduled in groups of 32 called warps.
concepts.example: A kernel add(a, b, c) computes c[i] = a[i] + b[i], where each thread works out its own i from its block and thread index. Launched with 4,096 blocks of 256 threads, it covers about a million elements in one launch.

concepts.name: Dagster
concepts.description: An open-source data orchestrator that models pipelines as software-defined assets with typed dependencies, scheduling, testing and lineage tracking.
concepts.example: Instead of describing steps, you declare assets: raw_orders, then cleaned_orders computed from raw_orders, then a daily_revenue table from that. Dagster figures out the order, can rerun only what's stale, and shows when each asset last updated.

concepts.name: Dask (Software)
concepts.description: A Python library for parallel and distributed computing that scales NumPy, pandas and custom workloads to multicore machines and clusters using lazily built task graphs.
concepts.example: A 50 GB CSV won't fit in pandas on a 16 GB laptop. With Dask you write nearly the same pandas code; Dask splits the file into chunks, builds a plan, and runs it in parallel on chunks only when you call .compute().

concepts.name: Data Cleaning
concepts.description: Detecting and correcting errors, inconsistencies, duplicates, missing values and outliers in a dataset so that analysis and models built on it are reliable.
concepts.example: A customer list has "NY", "New York" and "new york" in the city column, two copies of the same person, an age of 250, and blank emails. Cleaning standardizes the city, removes the duplicate, flags the age and decides what to do with blanks.

concepts.name: Data Definition Language
concepts.description: The subset of SQL used to define and change database structure, with commands such as CREATE, ALTER and DROP for tables, indexes and schemas.
concepts.example: CREATE TABLE users (id INT PRIMARY KEY, email TEXT) builds a new table, ALTER TABLE users ADD COLUMN age INT adds a column, and DROP TABLE users deletes it. These change the structure rather than editing individual rows.

concepts.name: Data Engineering
concepts.description: The field of designing and building systems that collect, store, transform and serve data reliably at scale, so analysts and ML models can use it.
concepts.example: An app's events, payments in Stripe and a CRM's contacts all need to end up as clean, joined tables for analysts by 8 a.m. A data engineer builds and maintains the pipelines, schedules and storage that make that happen every day.

concepts.name: Data Governance
concepts.description: The policies, roles and processes that define how an organization's data is owned, secured, documented, quality-checked and used in compliance with regulations.
concepts.example: A company decides that the finance team owns revenue data, that customer emails are tagged as personal and visible only to approved roles, and that each table has a documented definition. That rulebook and its enforcement is governance.

concepts.name: Data Ingestion
concepts.description: The process of importing data from sources such as databases, APIs, files or event streams into a storage or processing system, in batches or in real time.
concepts.example: Every hour a job pulls new rows from the sales database, downloads a CSV from a partner's SFTP site and reads click events from Kafka, landing all three in the data lake. That bringing-in step is ingestion.

concepts.name: Data Lake
concepts.description: A central repository that stores large amounts of raw data in its native formats, structured or not, usually on cheap object storage, to be processed later as needed.
concepts.example: A company dumps everything into cheap S3 storage as-is: JSON app logs, CSV exports, product photos, Parquet tables. Nothing is reshaped up front; analysts and ML jobs decide how to read it later.

concepts.name: Data Lakehouse
concepts.description: An architecture combining a data lake's cheap open-format storage with data warehouse features such as ACID transactions, schemas and fast SQL, using table formats like Delta Lake or Iceberg.
concepts.example: Raw and cleaned data stays as Parquet files on S3, but a table layer like Delta Lake adds transactions and schemas, so analysts run SQL dashboards and data scientists train models on the very same tables.

concepts.name: Data Lineage
concepts.description: A record of where data came from and every transformation and system it passed through, used for debugging, auditing, impact analysis and trust in data.
concepts.example: A dashboard's revenue number looks wrong. Lineage shows it comes from table daily_revenue, built from cleaned_orders, built from the raw Stripe feed, so you can trace the error back to a bad currency conversion two steps upstream.

concepts.name: Data Manipulation Language
concepts.description: The subset of SQL used to read and modify data inside tables, with statements such as SELECT, INSERT, UPDATE and DELETE.
concepts.example: INSERT INTO users VALUES (1, 'Ann') adds a row, UPDATE users SET name = 'Anna' WHERE id = 1 changes it, SELECT * FROM users reads it, and DELETE FROM users WHERE id = 1 removes it. The table structure never changes.

concepts.name: Data Mart
concepts.description: A smaller, subject-focused slice of a data warehouse built for one team or business area, such as sales or finance, to simplify and speed up its queries.
concepts.example: The company warehouse has data on sales, HR, inventory and finance. The marketing team gets a data mart with just campaigns, leads and web traffic, shaped for their questions and quick to query.

concepts.name: Data Parallelism
concepts.description: A way to train a model across many devices where each holds a full model copy, processes a different slice of the batch, and gradients are averaged (e.g. with all-reduce) before each update.
concepts.example: Train on 4 GPUs: each holds the same model and gets a different 32 images from a batch of 128. Each computes its own gradients, they average them with all-reduce, and all 4 apply the same update so the copies stay identical.

concepts.name: Partition (Database)
