concepts.description: Splitting a large table or dataset into smaller parts, for example by date or key, so queries can skip irrelevant data and work can be spread across machines.
concepts.example: A 5-year logs table is split into one partition per day. The query WHERE date = '2024-03-01' reads only that day's folder and skips the other 1,800, so it finishes far faster.

concepts.name: Data Pipeline
concepts.description: A sequence of automated steps that moves data from sources through transformations to destinations such as warehouses, dashboards or ML models.
concepts.example: Every night: pull yesterday's orders from the app database, remove test orders, convert currencies to dollars, and write the result into the warehouse. Like a factory line, each step's output feeds the next.

concepts.name: Data Quality
concepts.description: How fit data is for its use, measured by accuracy, completeness, consistency, timeliness and validity, and enforced with checks and tests in data pipelines.
concepts.example: Checks run each morning: no order total is negative, every order has a customer ID, row count is within 10% of yesterday's, and data arrived by 6 a.m. A failed check stops bad numbers from reaching the CEO's dashboard.

concepts.name: Data Skew
concepts.description: An imbalance in distributed processing where some partitions or keys hold far more data than others, so a few tasks run much longer and slow the whole job.
concepts.example: A job counts tweets by country across 100 workers. One worker gets all USA tweets, 40% of the data, and runs for an hour while the other 99 finish in 2 minutes, so the whole job waits on that one straggler.

concepts.name: Data Type
concepts.description: A classification of values, such as integers, floats, strings or Booleans, that determines what they can hold, how they are stored and which operations apply to them.
concepts.example: In Python, 5 is an int, 5.0 is a float and "5" is a string. 5 + 5 gives 10, but "5" + "5" gives "55", because the type decides what the + operation means.

concepts.name: Data Version Control
concepts.description: DVC is an open-source tool that versions large datasets and models alongside Git by storing small pointer files in the repository and the data itself in remote storage.
concepts.example: A 20 GB training set lives in S3, while Git stores only a tiny data.dvc file with its hash. Checking out last month's commit and running dvc pull brings back exactly the data that model was trained on.

concepts.name: Data Warehouse
concepts.description: A central database optimized for analytical queries that integrates cleaned, structured historical data from many sources, typically organized in star or snowflake schemas.
concepts.example: Sales, website and support data from three systems are cleaned and loaded each night into one warehouse. An analyst can then ask "revenue by region by month for 5 years" in a single SQL query without touching the live app.

concepts.name: Data Wrangling
concepts.description: Transforming raw data into a usable format by cleaning, reshaping, merging, filtering and enriching it, usually as a step before analysis or modeling.
concepts.example: A raw export has dates as text, prices with $ signs, and customers spread across two files. Wrangling parses the dates, strips the $ and converts to numbers, merges the files on customer ID, and pivots months into columns for a report.

concepts.name: Database
concepts.description: An organized collection of data stored electronically and managed so it can be efficiently queried, updated and kept consistent.
concepts.example: A library's database stores every book, member and loan. Asking "which books are overdue?" takes milliseconds, and two librarians lending books at the same time won't overwrite each other's records.

concepts.name: Database Index
concepts.description: A data structure, often a B-tree or hash table, that a database keeps alongside a table so it can locate rows matching a condition without scanning the whole table.
concepts.example: Finding user 'ann@x.com' in 10 million rows without an index means checking every row. With a B-tree index on email, the database walks down about 4 levels of the tree to the right row, like using a book's index.

concepts.name: Database Normalization
concepts.description: Organizing relational tables into normal forms to remove redundancy and update anomalies, by splitting data so each fact is stored in exactly one place.
concepts.example: Storing a customer's address on every order means updating 50 rows when they move. Normalization splits it into a customers table and an orders table that refers to customer_id, so the address lives in exactly one place.

concepts.name: Database Schema
concepts.description: The formal structure of a database: its tables, columns, data types, keys, constraints and relationships.
concepts.example: A shop's schema says: table customers(id INT primary key, name TEXT), table orders(id INT, customer_id INT referencing customers, total DECIMAL). It is the blueprint every row must fit.

concepts.name: Database Transaction
concepts.description: A group of database operations executed as a single unit that either fully succeeds or fully fails, preserving consistency even under concurrency or crashes.
concepts.example: Transferring 100 dollars runs two updates: subtract 100 from Alice and add 100 to Bob. Wrapped in one transaction, a crash between them rolls back the first update, so money never vanishes.

concepts.name: Databricks
concepts.description: A cloud data and AI platform built around Apache Spark that combines notebooks, Delta Lake storage, SQL warehousing and ML tooling in a unified lakehouse.
concepts.example: A team opens a Databricks notebook, reads Delta tables from cloud storage, runs a Spark job on a cluster that starts in minutes, trains a model on the result, and shares a SQL dashboard, all in one platform.

concepts.name: DataFrame
concepts.description: A two-dimensional table of data with labeled columns that can each have a different type, as provided by pandas, R and Spark, for filtering, grouping and transforming data.
concepts.example: A DataFrame with columns name (text), age (int) and score (float) holds three students in rows. You can write df[df.age > 20] to filter or df.score.mean() to average, like a spreadsheet you control with code.

concepts.name: Database Management System
concepts.description: Software such as PostgreSQL or MySQL that stores, retrieves, secures and manages data in databases, handling queries, transactions, concurrency and recovery.
concepts.example: PostgreSQL is a DBMS. When your app sends SELECT * FROM orders WHERE id = 5, Postgres plans the query, uses an index, checks your permissions, and makes sure another user's update doesn't corrupt the result.

concepts.name: dbt (Data Build Tool)
concepts.description: A tool that lets analysts transform data inside a warehouse by writing modular SQL SELECT models, with dependency graphs, tests and documentation managed as code.
concepts.example: An analyst writes models/revenue.sql as SELECT date, SUM(amount) FROM {{ ref('clean_orders') }} GROUP BY date. dbt sees it depends on clean_orders, builds that first inside the warehouse, then runs tests such as revenue never being null.

concepts.name: Debugging
concepts.description: The process of finding, understanding and fixing defects in a program, using techniques such as reading error messages, printing values, breakpoints and debuggers.
concepts.example: average([2, 4, 6]) returns 3 instead of 4. Printing inside the function shows the sum is 12, correct, but the divisor is 4. The loop counter started at 1 instead of 0, so you fix that off-by-one and rerun to confirm.

concepts.name: Declarative Programming
concepts.description: A paradigm where code describes what result is wanted rather than the step-by-step procedure to get it, as in SQL queries or configuration languages.
concepts.example: SELECT name FROM users WHERE age > 30 says what you want, not how to find it; the database chooses whether to scan or use an index. Ordering "a cappuccino" is declarative; giving the barista each step is imperative.

concepts.name: Python Decorator
concepts.description: A Python function that takes another function and returns a modified version of it, applied with @ syntax to add behavior like logging, caching or timing.
concepts.example: Writing @timer above def load_data() wraps load_data so every call prints how long it took. It is shorthand for load_data = timer(load_data), and the original function code stays untouched.

concepts.name: Delta Lake
concepts.description: An open-source storage layer that adds ACID transactions, schema enforcement, versioning and time travel to Parquet files in a data lake, commonly used with Spark.
concepts.example: A Spark job writing Parquet files to a lake crashes halfway. With plain Parquet, readers may see half the files; with Delta Lake the write only appears once its log entry commits, and you can even query the table as of yesterday.

concepts.name: Denormalization
concepts.description: Intentionally adding redundant data or combining tables in a database to reduce joins and speed up reads, at the cost of extra storage and harder updates.
concepts.example: A dashboard shows orders with customer names, needing a join on every load. Copying customer_name directly into the orders table makes reads join-free and fast, but now a name change must be updated in many rows.

concepts.name: Software Design Pattern
concepts.description: A reusable, named solution to a common software design problem, such as singleton, factory or observer, describing how classes and objects should interact.
concepts.example: The observer pattern: a weather station keeps a list of displays and notifies them all when the temperature changes. Whenever you need "tell everyone who cares when this changes", you reach for the same named solution.

concepts.name: DevOps
concepts.description: A set of practices and culture combining software development and IT operations to ship changes quickly and reliably through automation, CI/CD, monitoring and shared ownership.
concepts.example: Instead of developers handing a release to a separate ops team every three months, one team owns the app end to end: every merged change is tested and deployed automatically to the cloud, and the same people watch the alerts and fix outages.

concepts.name: Dimension Table
concepts.description: A table in a dimensional model that stores descriptive attributes, such as customer, product or date details, used to filter and group facts.
concepts.example: A product dimension has one row per product: product_key 17, name "Blue Mug", category "Kitchen", brand "Acme". Sales facts store only 17, and reports join to this table to group revenue by category or brand.

concepts.name: Dimensional Modeling
concepts.description: A data warehouse design method, popularized by Kimball, that organizes data into fact tables of measurable events surrounded by dimension tables of context, often as a star schema.
concepts.example: A store models sales as a star: a central fact table of sales (quantity, amount) surrounded by dimensions for date, product, store and customer. "Revenue by month by region" then becomes one simple join-and-group query.

concepts.name: Directed Acyclic Graph (Workflow)
concepts.description: A way of describing a workflow as tasks connected by directed dependencies with no cycles, so tools like Airflow can determine a valid execution order and run independent tasks in parallel.
concepts.example: Tasks: extract, clean, train, report. Clean depends on extract, train and report both depend on clean. Arrows only point forward and never loop back, so the scheduler can run train and report in parallel once clean finishes.

concepts.name: Distributed Computing
concepts.description: The field of systems in which multiple networked computers coordinate to solve a problem, dealing with communication, partial failures, consistency and scaling.
concepts.example: Counting words in a billion documents on one machine would take weeks. Split them across 1,000 machines, each counts its share, then the partial counts are added up over the network, and it finishes in an hour, if failures are handled.

concepts.name: Distributed Training
concepts.description: Training a machine learning model across multiple GPUs or machines, splitting data, model or both and synchronizing gradients, to train larger models faster.
concepts.example: A language model too slow to train on one GPU is trained on 64 GPUs over 8 machines. Each step, every GPU processes part of the batch or part of the model, and they exchange gradients over a fast network to stay in sync.

concepts.name: Docker (Software)
concepts.description: A popular platform for building, sharing and running containers, using Dockerfiles to define images and a runtime to launch isolated application containers.
concepts.example: Write a Dockerfile, run docker build -t myapp . to make an image, then docker run -p 8080:80 myapp to start it. A teammate pulls the same image from a registry and gets the identical app running in seconds.

concepts.name: Docker Compose
concepts.description: A Docker tool that defines and runs multi-container applications from a single YAML file listing services, networks and volumes, started with one command.
concepts.example: A docker-compose.yml lists three services: web (your app), db (postgres:16) and cache (redis). Running docker compose up starts all three on a shared network where web reaches the database simply at hostname db.

concepts.name: Dockerfile
concepts.description: A text file of instructions such as FROM, RUN, COPY and CMD that Docker follows step by step to build a container image.
concepts.example: FROM python:3.11-slim, then COPY requirements.txt ., then RUN pip install -r requirements.txt, then COPY . ., then CMD ["python", "app.py"]. Each line adds a layer, and Docker reuses unchanged layers to rebuild in seconds.

concepts.name: Document-Oriented Database
concepts.description: A NoSQL database that stores data as flexible, self-describing documents, usually JSON-like, allowing nested fields and varying structure, as in MongoDB.
concepts.example: MongoDB stores a user as one document: {name: "Ann", address: {city: "Oslo"}, orders: [{id: 1, total: 20}]}. Another user can have extra fields like phone, and the whole profile is read in one lookup without joins.

concepts.name: Duck Typing
concepts.description: A typing style where an object's suitability is determined by whether it has the needed methods and attributes rather than its declared type: if it quacks like a duck, treat it as one.
concepts.example: A function calls thing.read() on whatever it is given. A real file works, but so does a StringIO object or your own class with a read method; Python never checks the type, only that read exists. If it walks like a duck...

concepts.name: DuckDB
concepts.description: An in-process analytical SQL database, like SQLite for analytics, that runs fast columnar queries directly on local files such as Parquet and CSV and on pandas DataFrames.
concepts.example: In a Python notebook, duckdb.sql("SELECT city, AVG(price) FROM 'sales.parquet' GROUP BY city") runs straight on a 2 GB file in seconds. No server, no loading step, just a library inside your process.

concepts.name: Dynamic Typing
concepts.description: A type system where variable types are checked at runtime and a variable can hold values of different types over time, as in Python and JavaScript.
concepts.example: In Python, x = 5 then x = "hello" is fine: the variable just holds whatever value it was last given. But "5" + 3 only fails when that line actually runs, not before.

concepts.name: Elasticsearch
concepts.description: A distributed search and analytics engine built on Apache Lucene that indexes JSON documents with inverted indexes for fast full-text search, log analytics and aggregations.
concepts.example: An online shop indexes 2 million product descriptions. Typing "red running shoes" looks up each word in an inverted index, finds matching products in milliseconds, and ranks them by relevance, even with a typo like "runing" when fuzzy matching is on.

concepts.name: Extract, Load, Transform
concepts.description: Extract, Load, Transform: a data integration pattern that loads raw data into a powerful warehouse or lake first and transforms it there, typically with SQL.
concepts.example: Raw Salesforce and app tables are copied unchanged into Snowflake first. Later, SQL models inside the warehouse clean and join them, and if the logic changes you just rerun the SQL on the raw data already there.

concepts.name: Encapsulation (Computer Programming)
concepts.description: Bundling data with the methods that operate on it inside an object and hiding internal details behind a public interface, so other code cannot depend on or corrupt internal state.
concepts.example: A BankAccount keeps balance private and exposes deposit() and withdraw(), which refuses to go below zero. Other code can't set balance = -500 directly, so the rule can't be bypassed, and the internals can change freely.

concepts.name: Entity-Relationship Model
concepts.description: A conceptual way to design a database by describing entities, their attributes and the relationships between them, often drawn as an ER diagram before creating tables.
concepts.example: Designing a school database, you draw entities Student and Course, give Student attributes name and birthdate, and connect them with an "enrolls in" relationship that is many-to-many, before writing any table.

concepts.name: Extract, Transform, Load
concepts.description: Extract, Transform, Load: a data integration process that pulls data from sources, cleans and reshapes it, and loads it into a target such as a data warehouse.
concepts.example: Each night: extract orders from MySQL and refunds from a CSV, transform by converting currencies and removing test orders, then load the clean table into the warehouse. Only tidy data ever reaches the warehouse.

concepts.name: Event Stream Processing
concepts.description: Processing continuous streams of events, such as clicks or sensor readings, as they arrive, often through a durable log like Kafka, to react and compute results in near real time.
concepts.example: Every click on a shopping site becomes an event in a stream. A processor reads them as they arrive, keeps a running count of views per product over the last 5 minutes, and updates a "trending now" list in real time.

concepts.name: Event Time vs Processing Time
concepts.description: The distinction in stream processing between when an event actually happened and when the system processes it; watermarks estimate progress in event time to handle late data.
concepts.example: A phone records a step count at 9:00 but is offline until 9:30, when the event finally arrives. Its event time is 9:00 and its processing time 9:30; counting by event time puts it in the correct 9:00 window.

concepts.name: Eventual Consistency
concepts.description: A consistency model for replicated data in which, if no new updates are made, all replicas will eventually converge to the same value, though reads may briefly see stale data.
concepts.example: You update your profile photo; a friend in another region still sees the old one for a second or two until the change replicates. With no further updates, every copy ends up showing the new photo.

concepts.name: Exactly-Once Semantics
concepts.description: A delivery guarantee in messaging and stream processing that each record affects the result exactly once despite failures and retries, unlike at-most-once or at-least-once.
concepts.example: A payment event is processed, but the worker crashes before recording it, so the event is redelivered. With exactly-once processing, using idempotent writes or transactions, the customer is still charged once, not twice.

concepts.name: Exception Handling
concepts.description: A mechanism for detecting and responding to runtime errors, using constructs like try/except or try/catch to recover gracefully instead of crashing.
concepts.example: try: n = int(input_text) except ValueError: n = 0. If the user types "abc", int() raises an error, and instead of crashing the program jumps to the except block and uses 0.

concepts.name: Experiment Tracking
concepts.description: Systematically logging the code version, data, hyperparameters, metrics and artifacts of each ML training run so results can be compared and reproduced.
concepts.example: You train 30 models with different learning rates. A tracker like MLflow records each run's code commit, data version, learning rate, accuracy curve and saved model, so weeks later you can find which settings got 92% and rerun them.

concepts.name: Expression (Computer Science)
concepts.description: A combination of values, variables, operators and function calls that a program evaluates to produce a single value, such as 2 * x + 1.
concepts.example: In total = price * 3 + 2, the part price * 3 + 2 is an expression: with price = 4 it evaluates to 14. len("hi") > 1 is also an expression, evaluating to True.

concepts.name: Fact Table
concepts.description: The central table in a star schema that records measurable business events, such as sales amounts, with foreign keys pointing to dimension tables.
concepts.example: Each row of a sales fact table is one purchase: date_key 20240301, product_key 17, store_key 4, quantity 2, amount 19.98. Millions of such narrow rows are summed and grouped using the linked dimension tables.

concepts.name: FastAPI
concepts.description: A modern Python web framework for building APIs quickly, using type hints to validate requests, generate OpenAPI docs automatically and support async endpoints.
concepts.example: def get_item(item_id: int) decorated with @app.get("/items/{item_id}") is a full endpoint: FastAPI rejects /items/abc with a clear error because of the int hint, and generates interactive docs at /docs automatically.

concepts.name: Fault Tolerance
concepts.description: The ability of a system to keep working correctly when some of its components fail, achieved with redundancy, replication, retries and checkpointing.
concepts.example: A website runs on 3 servers behind a load balancer. One server's disk fails at noon; the balancer stops sending it traffic and the other two carry on, so visitors notice nothing.

concepts.name: File Format
concepts.description: A standard way of encoding information in a computer file, such as CSV, JSON, Parquet or PNG, defining how bytes map to data so programs can read and write it.
concepts.example: A PNG starts with 8 fixed signature bytes so programs know it's a PNG, then stores image chunks in a defined order. Rename it to .txt and it's still a PNG; the format is in the bytes, not the name.

concepts.name: Filter (Higher-Order Function)
concepts.description: A higher-order function that takes a predicate and a collection and returns only the elements for which the predicate is true.
concepts.example: filter(lambda n: n % 2 == 0, [1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6]) keeps only the items where the test is true, giving [2, 4, 6]. Like a sieve, the predicate decides what passes through.

concepts.name: First-Class Function
concepts.description: A language feature where functions are treated like any other value: they can be stored in variables, passed as arguments and returned from other functions.
concepts.example: In Python you can write shout = str.upper, then put shout in a list, pass it to another function, or return it, exactly as you would with a number. shout("hi") gives "HI".

concepts.name: First Normal Form
concepts.description: A relational table is in first normal form when every column holds single atomic values, with no repeating groups or lists inside a cell, and rows are uniquely identifiable.
concepts.example: A row (order 1, items "pen, ink, paper") breaks 1NF because one cell holds a list. Splitting it into three rows (order 1, pen), (order 1, ink), (order 1, paper) gives one atomic value per cell.

concepts.name: Flask (Web Framework)
concepts.description: A lightweight Python web framework for building web applications and APIs with minimal boilerplate, mapping URL routes to Python functions.
concepts.example: Five lines make a web app: create app = Flask(__name__), decorate def hello() with @app.route("/hello") and return "Hi!". Visiting /hello in a browser calls the function and shows its text.

concepts.name: For Loop
concepts.description: A loop that repeats a block of code once for each item in a sequence or for a counted number of iterations.
concepts.example: for name in ["Ann", "Bob", "Cy"]: print("Hi " + name) runs the print three times, once per name. for i in range(5) runs a block exactly 5 times, with i = 0, 1, 2, 3, 4.

concepts.name: Foreign Key
concepts.description: A column in one table whose values must match the primary key of another table, linking related rows and enforcing referential integrity.
concepts.example: An orders table has customer_id = 42, which must match a row with id 42 in customers. Trying to insert an order for customer 999, who doesn't exist, is rejected by the database.

concepts.name: Function (Computer Programming)
concepts.description: A named, reusable block of code that takes inputs as parameters, performs a task and optionally returns a value.
concepts.example: def area(w, h): return w * h. Now area(3, 4) gives 12 and area(5, 2) gives 10: you write the logic once, name it, and reuse it with different inputs, like a vending machine button.

concepts.name: Functional Dependency
concepts.description: A constraint in a relation where the value of one set of attributes uniquely determines another, written X -> Y; the basis for database normalization.
concepts.example: In a table of employees, employee_id -> name: knowing the ID tells you exactly one name. But name -/-> employee_id, since two people can be called Ann. These dependencies guide how to split tables.

concepts.name: Functional Programming
concepts.description: A paradigm that builds programs by composing pure functions, avoiding mutable state and side effects, and using higher-order functions like map, filter and reduce.
concepts.example: Instead of a loop that edits a running total, sum(map(lambda x: x * x, filter(is_even, nums))) composes small functions: keep evens, square them, add them. Nothing is modified along the way, so each piece is easy to test.

concepts.name: Garbage Collection (Computer Science)
concepts.description: Automatic memory management in which the runtime finds objects that are no longer reachable by the program and frees their memory, using reference counting or tracing.
concepts.example: In Python, a = [1, 2, 3] then a = None leaves the old list with no references. The runtime notices nothing can reach it any more and frees that memory, so you never call free() yourself.

concepts.name: Generator (Computer Programming)
concepts.description: A function that produces a sequence of values lazily, pausing at each yield and resuming on the next request, so large or infinite sequences use little memory.
concepts.example: def countdown(n): while n > 0: yield n; n -= 1. Calling countdown(3) does nothing yet; each next() resumes the function to give 3, then 2, then 1. A generator over a billion numbers uses almost no memory.

concepts.name: ggplot2
concepts.description: An R data visualization package based on the grammar of graphics, building plots by mapping data columns to aesthetics and layering geometries, scales and facets.
concepts.example: ggplot(cars, aes(x = weight, y = mpg, colour = cyl)) + geom_point() maps weight to x, mpg to y and cylinders to colour; adding + geom_smooth() layers a trend line on the same plot.

concepts.name: Git
concepts.description: A distributed version control system that records snapshots of a project's files as commits, letting developers branch, merge and collaborate on code history.
concepts.example: You edit three files and run git commit -m "Fix login". Git saves a snapshot; a week later you can see exactly what changed, undo it, or compare it, and a teammate's copy can merge your work with theirs.

concepts.name: Branching (Version Control)
concepts.description: An independent line of development in version control, implemented in Git as a movable pointer to a commit, used to work on features without affecting the main code.
concepts.example: On main, you run git switch -c new-header and start redesigning. Your commits go only to new-header while main stays untouched, so a hotfix can still ship from main the same afternoon.

concepts.name: Commit (Version Control)
concepts.description: A saved snapshot of the tracked files in a repository at a point in time, with a message, author and a link to its parent commit, forming the project's history.
concepts.example: After fixing a typo in README.md, you run git add README.md and git commit -m "Fix typo". Git stores a snapshot with your name, the time, the message and a link to the previous commit, identified by a hash like 3f2a9c1.

concepts.name: Merge (Version Control)
concepts.description: Combining the changes from two branches into one, creating a merge commit when histories diverge; conflicting edits to the same lines must be resolved by hand.
concepts.example: Ann adds a header on branch A, Bob fixes a footer on branch B. git merge B into A combines both changes; if both had edited the same line, Git would stop and ask which version to keep.

concepts.name: Git Rebase
concepts.description: A Git operation that moves or replays a branch's commits on top of another base commit, producing a linear history instead of a merge commit.
concepts.example: Your feature branch has 3 commits made from main last week, and main has moved on. git rebase main replays your 3 commits on top of the latest main, so history reads as a straight line with no merge commit.

concepts.name: GitHub
concepts.description: A web platform for hosting Git repositories that adds collaboration features such as pull requests, code review, issue tracking and Actions for CI/CD.
concepts.example: You push your Git repository to GitHub, a colleague opens a pull request with a fix, you review the diff line by line, automated tests run on it, and you click merge, all in the browser.

concepts.name: Global Interpreter Lock
concepts.description: A mutex in CPython that allows only one thread to execute Python bytecode at a time, simplifying memory management but limiting CPU-bound multithreading.
concepts.example: Running a CPU-heavy calculation on 4 threads in standard CPython takes about as long as on 1 thread, because only one thread may run Python bytecode at a time. Threads waiting on network I/O still overlap fine.

concepts.name: Google Cloud Platform
concepts.description: Google's suite of cloud computing services, including compute, storage, BigQuery and Vertex AI, for building and running applications and ML workloads.
concepts.example: A team stores images in Cloud Storage, runs its API on Cloud Run, analyses logs in BigQuery and trains a model on Vertex AI, all billed to one GCP project and controlled by the same permissions.

concepts.name: Google Colab
concepts.description: A free hosted Jupyter notebook service from Google that runs Python in the browser with access to GPUs and TPUs, popular for learning and prototyping ML.
concepts.example: Open a link in your browser, click Runtime > Change runtime type > GPU, and train a small neural network in a notebook without installing anything, then share it like a Google Doc.

concepts.name: General-Purpose Computing on GPUs
concepts.description: Using graphics processing units for general-purpose computation beyond graphics, exploiting their thousands of parallel cores for workloads like matrix math and deep learning.
concepts.example: Training an image model means multiplying huge grids of numbers. A GPU built to colour millions of pixels at once does those multiplications in parallel too, often dozens of times faster than a CPU.

concepts.name: Graphics Processing Unit
concepts.description: A graphics processing unit is a processor with thousands of simple cores designed for massively parallel computation, originally for graphics and now central to training neural networks.
concepts.example: Brightening a 4K photo means adjusting 8 million pixels with the same formula. A CPU's few powerful cores work through them in batches, while a GPU's thousands of simple cores process huge numbers of pixels at the same time.

concepts.name: GPU Memory
concepts.description: The dedicated high-bandwidth memory on a GPU, such as GDDR or HBM, that holds model weights, activations and data; its capacity and bandwidth often limit model size and speed.
concepts.example: A 7-billion-parameter model in 16-bit precision needs about 14 GB just for its weights. On a 24 GB GPU that leaves about 10 GB for activations and batches; training needs far more for gradients and optimizer state.

concepts.name: Graph (Abstract Data Type)
concepts.description: An abstract data type made of vertices and edges connecting them, stored in a computer as an adjacency list or adjacency matrix to model networks and relationships.
concepts.example: A friends network with Ann-Bob, Bob-Cy and Ann-Dee is stored as an adjacency list: Ann: [Bob, Dee], Bob: [Ann, Cy], Cy: [Bob], Dee: [Ann]. Listing Ann's friends is then a single lookup.

concepts.name: Graph Database
concepts.description: A database that stores data as nodes and relationships with properties, making it efficient to query highly connected data such as social networks or knowledge graphs.
concepts.example: To find friends of friends who like jazz, a graph database such as Neo4j starts at your node and hops along FRIEND edges twice, then checks LIKES edges, instead of joining big tables three times.

concepts.name: GraphQL
concepts.description: A query language and runtime for APIs that lets clients request exactly the fields they need from a typed schema in a single request, avoiding over- and under-fetching.
concepts.example: A mobile screen needs only a user's name and their last 3 post titles. One GraphQL query { user(id: 1) { name posts(last: 3) { title } } } returns exactly that, instead of several REST calls returning extra fields.

concepts.name: GROUP BY (SQL)
concepts.description: The SQL clause that groups rows sharing the same values in given columns so aggregate functions like COUNT or SUM are computed per group; HAVING filters the groups.
concepts.example: SELECT city, COUNT(*), AVG(age) FROM customers GROUP BY city turns 10,000 customer rows into one row per city, e.g. Paris, 1200, 34.5, with the count and average computed inside each group.

concepts.name: Group By
concepts.description: The split-apply-combine operation on a table: split rows into groups by key values, apply a function such as an aggregation to each group, and combine the results.
concepts.example: df.groupby("team")["score"].mean() splits players by team, averages scores within each group, and combines the results into one row per team: Red 8.5, Blue 7.2.

concepts.name: gRPC
concepts.description: A high-performance remote procedure call framework from Google that uses Protocol Buffers for compact messages and HTTP/2 for streaming, common for service-to-service calls.
concepts.example: A checkout service calls GetPrice(item_id=17) on a pricing service as if it were a local function. gRPC encodes the request in a small binary Protocol Buffers message and sends it over HTTP/2, faster than JSON over REST.

concepts.name: Hardware Acceleration
concepts.description: Using specialized hardware such as GPUs, TPUs or FPGAs to perform specific computations far faster or more efficiently than a general-purpose CPU.
concepts.example: Playing a 4K video on a laptop, the CPU alone might hit 100% and stutter. Handing decoding to the GPU's dedicated video unit makes playback smooth at a few percent CPU, and the battery lasts longer.

concepts.name: HDF5
concepts.description: A hierarchical binary file format and library for storing large numerical datasets, organizing arrays in groups with metadata, widely used in science and for saving model weights.
concepts.example: A climate file holds groups like /temperature/2023 containing a 365 x 180 x 360 array of floats. You can read just one day's 180 x 360 slice from a 50 GB file without loading the rest.

concepts.name: Hadoop Distributed File System
concepts.description: The Hadoop Distributed File System stores very large files by splitting them into blocks replicated across many machines, providing fault-tolerant, high-throughput access.
concepts.example: A 1 GB log file goes into HDFS as 8 blocks of 128 MB, each copied to 3 different machines. If one machine dies, every block still has 2 copies and HDFS quietly makes a new third.

concepts.name: Higher-Order Function
concepts.description: A function that takes other functions as arguments or returns a function as its result, such as map, filter and sorted with a key.
concepts.example: sorted(words, key=len) passes the function len into sorted, which uses it to sort by length. And make_multiplier(3) can return a new function that triples numbers; both are higher-order functions.

concepts.name: Scalability
concepts.description: Scalability is a system's ability to handle growing load; horizontal scaling adds more machines, while vertical scaling adds more CPU, memory or storage to a single machine.
concepts.example: A website slows down at 10,000 visitors. Vertical scaling buys a bigger server; horizontal scaling adds 4 more identical servers behind a load balancer, and can keep adding more as traffic grows.

concepts.name: HTTP
concepts.description: The Hypertext Transfer Protocol is the request-response protocol of the web, in which clients send methods like GET and POST to URLs and servers return status codes and content.
concepts.example: Your browser sends GET /index.html to example.com; the server replies 200 OK with the page's HTML. Submitting a form sends a POST, and a missing page returns 404 Not Found.

concepts.name: Hugging Face Transformers
concepts.description: A Python library providing thousands of pretrained Transformer models and tokenizers for text, vision and audio, with simple APIs to download, fine-tune and run them.
concepts.example: Three lines run sentiment analysis: from transformers import pipeline; clf = pipeline("sentiment-analysis"); clf("I love it") returns POSITIVE with about 0.99 score, using a pretrained model downloaded automatically.

concepts.name: Infrastructure as a Service
concepts.description: Infrastructure as a Service is a cloud model where providers rent virtual machines, storage and networks on demand, while users manage the operating system and software.
concepts.example: A company rents 4 virtual machines with 16 GB RAM each plus 1 TB of disk from a cloud provider. It installs its own OS, database and app; the provider handles only the physical hardware and network.

concepts.name: Idempotence
concepts.description: The property of an operation that applying it multiple times has the same effect as applying it once, making retries in APIs and data pipelines safe.
concepts.example: Pressing an elevator's call button 5 times calls the elevator once. Likewise, setting balance = 100 twice gives 100, but adding 10 twice gives a different result, so retrying the first is safe and the second is not.

concepts.name: Immutable Object
concepts.description: An immutable object's state cannot be changed after it is created; any modification produces a new object, which makes code safer to reason about and share across threads.
concepts.example: In Python, s = "cat" then s.upper() returns a new string "CAT" and leaves s as "cat". Tuples work the same way, so two parts of a program sharing one can never surprise each other.

concepts.name: Imperative Programming
concepts.description: A paradigm where programs are sequences of statements that explicitly change program state step by step, describing how to compute a result.
concepts.example: To sum a list imperatively: set total = 0, then for each number add it to total, then return total. Each statement changes the program's state step by step, like a recipe followed exactly.

concepts.name: Infrastructure as Code
concepts.description: Managing and provisioning servers, networks and cloud resources through version-controlled configuration files and tools like Terraform instead of manual setup.
concepts.example: A Terraform file declares 2 servers, a database and a load balancer. Running terraform apply creates them; changing 2 to 3 and reapplying adds one server, and the file's history in Git shows who changed what.

concepts.name: Inheritance (Object-Oriented Programming)
concepts.description: An object-oriented mechanism where a new class derives attributes and methods from an existing parent class, reusing and extending or overriding its behavior.
concepts.example: class Animal has name and eat(); class Dog(Animal) adds bark(). A Dog automatically gets name and eat() without rewriting them, and could override eat() if dogs eat differently.

concepts.name: Inner Join
concepts.description: An SQL join that returns only rows where the join condition matches in both tables, discarding rows without a partner.
concepts.example: Customers Ann, Bob and Cy; orders exist only for Ann and Bob. An inner join on customer_id returns rows for Ann and Bob with their orders, and Cy, with no orders, is left out.

concepts.name: Integer (Computer Science)
concepts.description: A data type representing whole numbers, stored in a fixed number of bits (or arbitrary precision in Python), with a limited range and possible overflow.
concepts.example: A signed 8-bit integer holds -128 to 127, so 127 + 1 overflows to -128 in languages like C. Python's int has arbitrary precision, so 2 ** 100 just works.

concepts.name: Interface (Object-Oriented Programming)
concepts.description: A contract specifying methods a class must implement without defining how, letting different classes be used interchangeably; in Python, abstract base classes play this role.
concepts.example: An interface Shape requires area(). Circle and Square each implement it their own way, so code that totals the area of a list of shapes calls shape.area() without caring which kind it is.

concepts.name: Interpreter (Computing)
concepts.description: A program that executes source code directly, statement by statement or via bytecode, rather than first compiling it into a standalone machine-code program.
concepts.example: Typing 2 + 3 into the Python prompt prints 5 immediately; there's no separate build step. The interpreter reads each statement (via bytecode) and executes it on the spot.

concepts.name: IPython
concepts.description: An enhanced interactive Python shell with tab completion, rich history, magic commands and object introspection; it is the kernel behind Jupyter notebooks.
concepts.example: In IPython, typing df. then Tab lists all methods, df? shows the docs, and %timeit sum(range(1000)) measures how fast the code runs, conveniences the plain python prompt lacks.

concepts.name: Isolation (Database Systems)
concepts.description: The ACID property describing how concurrent transactions see each other's changes, with levels like read committed, repeatable read and serializable trading safety for performance.
concepts.example: Transaction A reads a balance of 100, then B changes it to 50 and commits. Under read committed, A reading again sees 50; under repeatable read or snapshot isolation, A keeps seeing 100 until it ends.

concepts.name: Iterator
concepts.description: An object that produces the elements of a collection one at a time on request, keeping track of its position, as used by for loops in Python.
concepts.example: it = iter([10, 20, 30]); next(it) gives 10, next(it) gives 20, next(it) gives 30, and one more next raises StopIteration. A for loop does exactly this behind the scenes.

concepts.name: Java (Programming Language)
concepts.description: A statically typed, object-oriented language compiled to bytecode that runs on the Java Virtual Machine, widely used in enterprise systems and big data tools like Hadoop.
concepts.example: A Java program declares int count = 0; and String name = "Ann"; puts code in classes, and compiles to bytecode once. The same .class files then run on Windows, Mac or Linux through the JVM.

concepts.name: JavaScript
concepts.description: The programming language of the web browser, dynamically typed and event-driven, also used on servers via Node.js to build interactive websites and applications.
concepts.example: Clicking a "Like" button runs a JavaScript function in the browser that turns the heart red and sends a request to the server, without reloading the page. The same language can also run servers with Node.js.

concepts.name: JAX
concepts.description: A Google Python library combining a NumPy-like API with automatic differentiation, JIT compilation via XLA and vectorization, for high-performance ML research on GPUs and TPUs.
concepts.example: Write loss(w) with jax.numpy, then jax.grad(loss) gives its gradient function and jax.jit compiles it to fast GPU code. jax.vmap turns a function on one example into one over a whole batch.

concepts.name: Just-in-Time Compilation
concepts.description: Just-in-time compilation translates code into optimized machine code at runtime, right before or while it executes, combining interpreter flexibility with compiled speed.
concepts.example: A Python loop summing 10 million numbers takes about a second. Decorated with Numba's @jit, the first call compiles it to machine code and later calls run in milliseconds, because hot code no longer goes through the interpreter.

concepts.name: Join (SQL)
concepts.description: An SQL operation that combines rows from two or more tables based on a related column, such as matching foreign keys to primary keys.
concepts.example: A customers table (id 1 Ann, id 2 Bob) and orders table (order 10 for customer 1) are joined ON orders.customer_id = customers.id, producing the row: order 10, Ann.

concepts.name: JSON
concepts.description: JavaScript Object Notation is a lightweight text format representing data as nested key-value objects and arrays, widely used for web APIs and configuration.
concepts.example: {"name": "Ann", "age": 30, "pets": ["cat", "dog"]} is JSON: keys in quotes, values that can be strings, numbers, lists or nested objects. Almost every language and web API can read and write it.

concepts.name: Julia (Programming Language)
concepts.description: A high-level, dynamically typed language for scientific and numerical computing that uses JIT compilation and multiple dispatch to reach speeds close to C.
concepts.example: A scientist writes a simple loop in Julia to simulate 10 million particles. It reads like Python, but the first call compiles it to machine code, so it runs at speeds close to C.

concepts.name: Jupyter Notebook
concepts.description: A web-based interactive document that mixes live code cells, outputs, plots and text, widely used for data exploration, teaching and prototyping in Python.
concepts.example: In one cell you load a CSV and see the first rows below it; in the next you plot a chart that appears inline; between them a text cell explains your reasoning. Rerun any cell and only its output updates.

concepts.name: Kafka Topic and Partition
concepts.description: In Kafka, a topic is a named stream of records split into ordered, replicated partitions; consumers in a consumer group divide the partitions to read in parallel.
concepts.example: Topic orders has 3 partitions; orders for customer 42 always hash to partition 1, so they stay in order. A consumer group with 3 consumers gives each one partition, reading in parallel.

concepts.name: Kappa Architecture
concepts.description: A data processing architecture that handles both real-time and historical data with a single stream processing pipeline, reprocessing history by replaying the event log.
concepts.example: Instead of a nightly batch job plus a separate real-time job, everything runs as one streaming job over Kafka. To fix a bug or recompute history, you replay the stored event log through the corrected stream job.

concepts.name: Keras
concepts.description: A high-level deep learning API, now part of TensorFlow and also multi-backend, that lets users build and train neural networks by stacking layers with little code.
concepts.example: model = Sequential([Dense(64, activation="relu"), Dense(10, activation="softmax")]), then model.compile(...) and model.fit(x, y, epochs=5): a digit classifier in a few readable lines.

concepts.name: Key-Value Database
concepts.description: A NoSQL database that stores data as a collection of unique keys mapped to values, offering very fast lookups by key, as in Redis or DynamoDB.
concepts.example: Redis stores session:abc123 -> {user: 42}. Every request looks up the key directly and gets the value in well under a millisecond; there are no tables or joins, just keys and values.

concepts.name: Kubernetes
concepts.description: An open-source container orchestration system that automatically deploys, scales, load-balances and heals containerized applications across a cluster of machines.
concepts.example: You declare "run 5 copies of my-api image". Kubernetes places them across nodes, gives them one stable address with load balancing, restarts any that crash, and rolls out a new version one copy at a time.

concepts.name: Pod (Kubernetes)
concepts.description: The smallest deployable unit in Kubernetes: one or more tightly coupled containers that share networking and storage and are scheduled together on a node.
concepts.example: A pod runs a web server container plus a small sidecar that ships its logs. Both share the same IP address and a shared volume, and Kubernetes schedules, starts and restarts them as one unit.

concepts.name: Lambda Architecture
concepts.description: A data processing architecture combining a batch layer for accurate results over all historical data with a speed layer for low-latency real-time results, merged at query time.
concepts.example: A site counts page views two ways: a nightly batch job recomputes exact totals from all history, while a streaming job adds today's views in real time. Queries combine both for counts that are fresh and eventually exact.

concepts.name: Anonymous Function
concepts.description: An anonymous function defined inline without a name, typically short, used where a function is needed briefly, such as a sort key or a map argument.
concepts.example: sorted(people, key=lambda p: p.age) sorts by age using a tiny unnamed function written inline, rather than defining def get_age(p): return p.age elsewhere.

concepts.name: Lazy Evaluation
concepts.description: An evaluation strategy that delays computing an expression until its value is actually needed, saving work and enabling infinite or very large data structures.
concepts.example: range(1_000_000_000) in Python doesn't build a billion numbers; it produces each one only when the loop asks. If the loop breaks at 10, the other numbers are never computed.

concepts.name: Transformations and Actions (Spark)
concepts.description: In Spark, transformations like map and filter only build a plan of the computation, and nothing runs until an action like count or collect triggers optimized execution.
concepts.example: df.filter(df.age > 30).select("name") runs instantly because nothing is computed yet. Only df.count() triggers the job, letting Spark optimize the whole chain first, for example reading only the needed columns.

concepts.name: LightGBM
concepts.description: A fast gradient boosting library from Microsoft that uses histogram-based splits and leaf-wise tree growth, efficient on large tabular datasets.
concepts.example: On a 10-million-row table, LightGBM first buckets each feature into about 255 histogram bins, then grows each tree by splitting the leaf with the biggest gain, often training many times faster than older boosting libraries.

concepts.name: Linux
concepts.description: A free, open-source Unix-like operating system kernel and family of distributions that runs most servers, cloud machines and supercomputers.
concepts.example: Most of the web's servers run Linux. You SSH into one, type ls to list files and sudo apt install nginx to set up a web server, all from a terminal and all free and open source.

concepts.name: List (Abstract Data Type)
concepts.description: An ordered collection of elements that allows duplicates and access by position, implemented as an array or linked list; Python's list is a dynamic array.
concepts.example: shopping = ["milk", "eggs", "milk"] keeps order and allows duplicates. shopping[1] is "eggs", and append("bread") adds a fourth item at the end.

concepts.name: List Comprehension
concepts.description: A concise Python syntax for building a new list by applying an expression to each item of an iterable, optionally filtered by a condition, e.g. [x*x for x in xs if x > 0].
concepts.example: [x * x for x in range(6) if x % 2 == 0] builds [0, 4, 16] in one line: loop over 0 to 5, keep the even ones, square them. It replaces a 4-line for loop with append.

concepts.name: Load Balancing
concepts.description: Distributing incoming requests or work across multiple servers so no single machine is overloaded, improving throughput, latency and availability.
concepts.example: Requests to a site hit a load balancer that sends the first to server A, the next to B, then C, then A again. If B stops answering health checks, traffic goes only to A and C.

concepts.name: Loop (Computer Programming)
concepts.description: A control structure that repeats a block of code while a condition holds or for each item in a collection.
concepts.example: A loop prints "Hello" 5 times without writing the line 5 times; a while loop keeps asking for a password until it's correct. Repeating work is one of the most basic things a program does.

concepts.name: Map (Higher-Order Function)
concepts.description: A higher-order function that applies a given function to every element of a collection and returns a collection of the results.
concepts.example: map(lambda c: c * 9 / 5 + 32, [0, 100, 37]) converts each Celsius reading to Fahrenheit, giving 32, 212 and 98.6: one function applied to every element, producing a new collection.

concepts.name: MapReduce
concepts.description: A programming model for processing large datasets in parallel on a cluster: a map step emits key-value pairs, a shuffle groups them by key, and a reduce step aggregates each group.
concepts.example: Word count: the map step turns each line into pairs like (cat, 1), (dog, 1); the framework groups pairs by word; the reduce step sums each group to give (cat, 3), (dog, 5). Each step runs on many machines.

concepts.name: Matplotlib
concepts.description: The foundational Python plotting library for creating static, animated and interactive charts such as line plots, histograms and scatter plots.
concepts.example: import matplotlib.pyplot as plt; plt.plot([1, 2, 3], [2, 4, 9]); plt.title("Growth"); plt.show() draws a line chart of three points. The same library makes bar charts, histograms and scatter plots.

concepts.name: Memory Hierarchy
concepts.description: The layered organization of computer storage from small, fast registers and caches to larger, slower main memory and disk, exploited by programs that reuse nearby data.
concepts.example: A chef keeps salt within arm's reach (registers), spices on a nearby shelf (cache), bulk flour in the pantry (RAM) and extra sacks in the basement (disk). Reaching for salt takes a second; a basement trip takes minutes, so good cooks keep what they reuse close.

concepts.name: Memory Management
concepts.description: How a program or operating system allocates, tracks and frees memory, whether manually as in C or automatically with garbage collection.
concepts.example: In C you call malloc(100) to get 100 bytes for a list and must call free() when done, or the memory leaks. In Python you just build the list, and the garbage collector frees it once nothing refers to it any more.

concepts.name: Message Queue
concepts.description: A component that lets services communicate asynchronously by having producers place messages in a queue that consumers process later, decoupling and buffering them.
concepts.example: An online shop's checkout drops an 'order placed' message into a queue and replies to the customer instantly. Minutes later, the email service and the warehouse service pick up the message at their own pace, even if one was briefly down.

concepts.name: Metadata
concepts.description: Data that describes other data, such as a table's schema, owner, creation time or source; data catalogs organize metadata so datasets can be discovered and trusted.
concepts.example: A photo file holds the picture itself, but also a timestamp, camera model and GPS location. Those extra fields are metadata: they don't show the image, yet they let you search for 'photos from Paris in 2023'.

concepts.name: Method (Computer Programming)
concepts.description: A function defined inside a class that operates on an object's data, called on an instance, as in obj.method().
concepts.example: A BankAccount class might define deposit(amount). Calling acct.deposit(50) runs that function on acct's own balance, so two accounts each change only their own money even though they share the same method code.

concepts.name: Microservices
concepts.description: An architecture that builds an application as many small, independently deployable services, each owning one business capability and communicating over APIs.
concepts.example: Instead of one giant shopping app, the system splits into a login service, a catalog service and a payment service. The payment team can redeploy their service on Friday without touching or restarting the catalog.

concepts.name: Microsoft Azure
concepts.description: Microsoft's cloud computing platform providing virtual machines, storage, databases and AI services for building, deploying and managing applications.
concepts.example: A startup can rent a Linux virtual machine in Azure's West Europe region in a couple of minutes, store user uploads in Azure Blob Storage and pay only for the hours and gigabytes used, with no servers of its own.

concepts.name: Mixed-Precision Training
concepts.description: Training neural networks using lower-precision numbers such as FP16 or bfloat16 for most computations while keeping FP32 master weights, cutting memory and speeding up GPUs with little accuracy loss.
concepts.example: A model's matrix multiplies run in 16-bit numbers, roughly doubling speed and halving memory, while a 32-bit master copy of the weights collects the tiny updates like 0.0001 that would otherwise round away to nothing in 16 bits.

concepts.name: MLflow
concepts.description: An open-source platform for managing the machine learning lifecycle: logging experiments and metrics, packaging models, storing them in a model registry, and deploying them.
concepts.example: You train three versions of a churn model with different learning rates; MLflow logs each run's parameters and accuracy so you can compare them in a table, then register the best one as 'churn-model v3' for deployment.

concepts.name: MLOps
concepts.description: The practice of reliably building, deploying, monitoring and maintaining machine learning systems in production, combining ML with DevOps and data engineering methods.
concepts.example: A fraud model is retrained automatically every week on fresh data, tested against the current model, deployed only if it scores better, and monitored so an alert fires when its accuracy starts to drift down.

concepts.name: Model Parallelism
concepts.description: Splitting one neural network across several devices, either by dividing layers' tensors (tensor parallelism) or by placing consecutive layers on different devices (pipeline parallelism).
concepts.example: A model needs 80 GB but each GPU has 40 GB, so you put layers 1-12 on GPU A and layers 13-24 on GPU B. Activations flow from A to B on the forward pass and gradients flow back from B to A.

concepts.name: Model Serving
concepts.description: Running a trained model behind an interface, usually a network API, so applications can send inputs and receive predictions with acceptable latency and throughput.
concepts.example: A trained spam classifier runs behind an endpoint: the email app sends a POST request with an email's text and gets back {"spam": 0.97} in 20 milliseconds, thousands of times per second.

concepts.name: MongoDB
concepts.description: A popular document-oriented NoSQL database that stores records as flexible JSON-like documents instead of rows in fixed tables.
concepts.example: A blog stores each post as one document: {title: 'Hello', tags: ['intro'], comments: [{user: 'ann', text: 'Nice'}]}. A newer post can add a 'video' field without changing any table schema.

concepts.name: MySQL
concepts.description: A widely used open-source relational database management system that stores data in tables and is queried with SQL.
concepts.example: A web shop keeps customers and orders tables in MySQL, and the site runs SELECT * FROM orders WHERE customer_id = 42 to show one customer's order history.

concepts.name: NCCL
concepts.description: NVIDIA's library of fast GPU-to-GPU communication routines such as all-reduce and broadcast, used to synchronize gradients in multi-GPU distributed training.
concepts.example: Eight GPUs each compute gradients on their own batch; an NCCL all-reduce sums the eight gradient arrays and gives every GPU the same total, using fast NVLink connections so it takes milliseconds.

concepts.name: NumPy Array
concepts.description: NumPy's core n-dimensional array: a fixed-type, contiguous block of numbers with a shape, supporting fast element-wise math, slicing and broadcasting.
concepts.example: np.array([[1, 2, 3], [4, 5, 6]]) has shape (2, 3) and an integer dtype. Writing a * 10 multiplies all six numbers at once in compiled code, with no Python loop.

concepts.name: Neo4j
concepts.description: A graph database that stores data as nodes and relationships and is queried with the Cypher language, suited to highly connected data like social networks.
concepts.example: A social network stores people as nodes and FRIENDS_WITH as relationships. The Cypher query MATCH (a:Person {name:'Ann'})-[:FRIENDS_WITH*2]-(fof) RETURN fof finds friends of friends without any joins.

concepts.name: NoSQL
concepts.description: A family of non-relational databases (document, key-value, column-family, graph) that trade fixed schemas and joins for flexibility and horizontal scalability.
concepts.example: A shopping cart stored in a key-value store is just key 'cart:42' mapped to a blob of items, read in one fast lookup. There's no fixed table schema and it scales across many servers, but complex joins are harder.

concepts.name: Null (SQL)
concepts.description: A special SQL marker meaning a value is missing or unknown; comparisons with NULL yield unknown, so it needs IS NULL checks and three-valued logic.
concepts.example: If Bob's phone is NULL, then WHERE phone = NULL matches nothing, not even Bob, because comparing to unknown gives unknown. You must write WHERE phone IS NULL to find him.

concepts.name: NumPy
concepts.description: The fundamental Python library for numerical computing, providing fast n-dimensional arrays, vectorized math, linear algebra and random number generation.
concepts.example: To convert 1 million temperatures from Celsius to Fahrenheit, temps * 9/5 + 32 on a NumPy array runs in a few milliseconds, while a plain Python loop over a list takes roughly a hundred times longer.

concepts.name: Object (Computer Science)
concepts.description: A bundle of data (attributes) and behaviour (methods) in a program; in object-oriented languages an object is an instance created from a class.
concepts.example: A Dog object might hold name='Rex' and age=3 and also know how to bark(). Rex and another dog object, Fido, have separate data but the same behaviour.

concepts.name: Object-Oriented Programming
concepts.description: A programming paradigm that organizes code into objects combining data and methods, using classes, encapsulation, inheritance and polymorphism.
concepts.example: A drawing app has a Shape class with Circle and Square subclasses. Each knows how to draw() itself, so the app just loops over shapes calling draw() without caring which kind each one is.

concepts.name: Object Storage
concepts.description: A storage architecture that keeps data as objects (blobs with metadata and a unique key) in a flat namespace, used by cloud services like Amazon S3.
concepts.example: Uploading cat.jpg to Amazon S3 under the key 'photos/2024/cat.jpg' stores it as one object with metadata like content-type. You fetch it by that key over HTTP; you can't edit a few bytes in the middle, only replace the whole object.

concepts.name: Online Analytical Processing
concepts.description: Online analytical processing: systems and techniques for fast multidimensional analysis of large historical data, such as slicing and aggregating sales by region and month.
concepts.example: A sales cube lets an analyst see revenue by region and month, then drill from 'Europe, 2024' down to 'France, March' in a second, because totals are pre-aggregated across those dimensions.

concepts.name: Online Transaction Processing
concepts.description: Online transaction processing: database workloads made of many small, concurrent read and write transactions, like orders or payments, that must stay consistent.
concepts.example: An ATM withdrawal is a typical OLTP transaction: read one account's balance, subtract 50, insert a transaction row, commit. A bank handles thousands of these small operations per second.

concepts.name: ONNX
concepts.description: Open Neural Network Exchange, an open format for representing trained models as computation graphs so they can move between frameworks and run on optimized runtimes.
concepts.example: You train an image model in PyTorch, export it to model.onnx, and then run it in a C# app with ONNX Runtime or on a phone, without needing PyTorch installed there.

concepts.name: Operator (Computer Programming)
concepts.description: A symbol or keyword such as +, == or and that performs an operation on one or more values (operands) and produces a result in a program.
concepts.example: In x = 7 + 3 * 2, the operators * and + combine values, giving 13 because * goes first. In score >= 50 and passed, >= compares and 'and' combines two true/false values.

concepts.name: Apache ORC
concepts.description: Apache ORC (Optimized Row Columnar), a columnar file format for Hadoop-era data lakes with compression, stripes and built-in indexes for fast analytic queries.
concepts.example: A Hive table of 1 billion web events stored as ORC lets a query that needs only 'country' read just that column, and stripe statistics let it skip whole stripes whose date range can't match the filter.

concepts.name: ORDER BY
concepts.description: The SQL clause that sorts query results by one or more columns in ascending or descending order.
concepts.example: SELECT name, score FROM players ORDER BY score DESC returns Ana 95, Ben 88, Cy 70: the highest score first. Adding ', name' breaks ties alphabetically.

concepts.name: Object-Relational Mapping
concepts.description: Object-relational mapping: a technique and libraries (e.g. SQLAlchemy) that map database tables to classes so programs can read and write rows as objects instead of raw SQL.
concepts.example: With SQLAlchemy you write user = User(name='Ann'); session.add(user); session.commit(), and the library generates INSERT INTO users (name) VALUES ('Ann') for you.

concepts.name: Outer Join
concepts.description: A SQL join that keeps rows without a match: left, right or full outer joins return all rows of one or both tables, filling missing columns with NULL.
concepts.example: Customers LEFT JOIN orders keeps every customer. Ann with two orders gets two rows, while Bob, with none, still appears once with NULL in the order columns.

concepts.name: Platform as a Service
concepts.description: Platform as a Service: a cloud model where the provider manages servers and runtime so developers just deploy their applications, e.g. Heroku or Google App Engine.
concepts.example: With Heroku-style PaaS you push your Flask app's code and the platform installs dependencies, runs it and handles scaling. You never patch an operating system or configure a server.

concepts.name: Package Manager
concepts.description: A tool that installs, upgrades and removes software libraries and resolves their dependencies, such as pip, conda or npm.
concepts.example: Typing pip install requests downloads the requests library and also its dependencies like urllib3 and certifi at compatible versions, so the import just works.

concepts.name: pandas
concepts.description: The standard Python library for tabular data analysis, offering DataFrame and Series objects for loading, cleaning, transforming, grouping and joining data.
concepts.example: df = pd.read_csv('sales.csv') loads a spreadsheet-like table; df.groupby('region')['revenue'].sum() then gives total revenue per region in one line.

concepts.name: Series (pandas)
concepts.description: A one-dimensional labeled array in pandas: a column of values with an index, the building block of a pandas DataFrame.
concepts.example: pd.Series([3, 7, 5], index=['Mon', 'Tue', 'Wed']) holds daily sales. s['Tue'] gives 7 and s.mean() gives 5. Each column of a DataFrame is one such Series.

concepts.name: Parallel Computing
concepts.description: Doing many computations at the same time on multiple processor cores, GPUs or machines to solve problems faster.
concepts.example: Rendering a 100-frame animation on one core takes 100 minutes; splitting the frames across 4 cores, each rendering 25 at once, finishes in about 25 minutes.

concepts.name: Parameter (Computer Programming)
concepts.description: A named variable in a function definition that receives a value (the argument) when the function is called.
concepts.example: In def greet(name): return 'Hi ' + name, 'name' is the parameter. Calling greet('Ana') passes the argument 'Ana', so name holds 'Ana' during that call.

concepts.name: Paxos
concepts.description: A classic consensus algorithm that lets a group of unreliable machines agree on a single value through proposers, acceptors and majority quorums, even when some fail.
concepts.example: Five servers must agree on which of two clients' writes comes first. A proposer gets promises from a majority (3 of 5), then has them accept its value; any two majorities overlap, so they can never settle on different values.

concepts.name: pip (Package Manager)
concepts.description: The standard package installer for Python, which downloads and installs libraries from the Python Package Index (PyPI) along with their dependencies.
concepts.example: pip install pandas==2.2.0 fetches that exact version from PyPI, and pip freeze > requirements.txt records everything installed so a teammate can recreate it with pip install -r requirements.txt.

concepts.name: Pivot Table
concepts.description: A summary table that reshapes data by grouping rows into categories along rows and columns and aggregating a value, such as total sales per region per month.
concepts.example: A sales list with columns region, month and revenue becomes a grid: regions as rows, months as columns, and each cell the total revenue for that region and month.

concepts.name: Plotly
concepts.description: A Python (and JavaScript) library for creating interactive, web-based charts such as zoomable line plots, maps and 3D plots.
concepts.example: px.scatter(df, x='gdp', y='life_exp', hover_name='country') draws a chart where hovering a dot shows the country's name, and you can drag to zoom into one cluster.

concepts.name: Polars (Software)
concepts.description: A fast DataFrame library written in Rust with a Python API, using columnar memory, multithreading and lazy query optimization as an alternative to pandas.
concepts.example: pl.scan_csv('big.csv').filter(pl.col('year') == 2024).select('price').mean() builds a plan, reads only the needed columns and rows, and runs across all CPU cores when you call .collect().

concepts.name: Polymorphism (Computer Science)
concepts.description: The ability of one interface or method name to work with objects of different types, each providing its own behaviour, e.g. different classes overriding the same method.
concepts.example: A list holds a Cat and a Dog; calling animal.speak() on each prints 'Meow' then 'Woof'. The calling code is identical, and each object supplies its own version.

concepts.name: PostgreSQL
concepts.description: A powerful open-source relational database known for standards-compliant SQL, ACID transactions and extensions like PostGIS and pgvector.
concepts.example: An app stores users in PostgreSQL and also a JSONB column of preferences; one SQL query can join users to orders and filter on a key inside the JSON, all inside an ACID transaction.

concepts.name: Prefect
concepts.description: A Python workflow orchestration tool for defining, scheduling, retrying and monitoring data pipelines as decorated Python functions.
concepts.example: Decorate three Python functions with @task, call them inside an @flow, and Prefect runs them nightly, retries the download step three times if the API times out, and shows each run in a dashboard.

concepts.name: Trino (SQL Query Engine)
concepts.description: A distributed SQL query engine that runs fast interactive queries over large data in data lakes and other sources without moving the data.
concepts.example: An analyst writes one SQL query that joins Parquet files of clicks in S3 with a customers table in PostgreSQL. Trino splits the work across 20 workers and returns the answer in seconds without copying data.

concepts.name: Primary Key
concepts.description: A column or set of columns whose values uniquely identify each row of a database table and cannot be NULL.
concepts.example: In a students table, student_id 1001 belongs to exactly one row. Two students can share the name 'Sam Lee', but never the same student_id, so the ID reliably identifies a row.

concepts.name: Primitive Data Type
concepts.description: A basic built-in data type of a language, such as integer, float, boolean or character, from which more complex types are built.
concepts.example: In Java, int age = 30, double price = 9.99, boolean done = false and char grade = 'A' are primitives. A String or a list of students is built up from such basic pieces.

concepts.name: Procedural Programming
concepts.description: A programming style that structures code as a sequence of procedures (functions) that run step by step and change program state.
concepts.example: A payroll script calls read_hours(), then compute_pay(), then print_payslips() in order, each procedure updating shared data step by step, like following a recipe from top to bottom.

concepts.name: Process (Computing)
concepts.description: A running instance of a program with its own memory space and resources, managed by the operating system; multiprocessing runs several at once.
concepts.example: Opening two browser windows and a music player starts separate processes. If the music player crashes, the browser keeps running because each process has its own private memory.

concepts.name: Computer Programming
concepts.description: Writing instructions in a programming language that a computer can execute to solve problems, covering variables, control flow, functions and data structures.
concepts.example: To find the largest of 3 numbers, you write: set max to the first number; for each other number, if it is bigger, replace max. The computer follows those exact steps every time.

concepts.name: Programming Paradigm
concepts.description: A style or way of organizing programs, such as imperative, procedural, object-oriented, functional or declarative programming.
concepts.example: Summing a list can be done imperatively (a loop adding to a total), functionally (reduce with +, no changing variables) or declaratively (SELECT SUM(x) in SQL). Same result, different styles of thinking.

concepts.name: Protocol Buffers
concepts.description: Google's language-neutral format for serializing structured data into compact binary messages defined by a schema, widely used with gRPC.
concepts.example: You define message Person { string name = 1; int32 age = 2; }. Ann, 30 encodes into about 7 bytes instead of about 25 as JSON, and Java and Python code generated from the schema both read it.

concepts.name: Publish–Subscribe Pattern
concepts.description: A messaging pattern where publishers send messages to topics and all subscribers of a topic receive them, decoupling senders from receivers.
concepts.example: A 'price-changed' topic gets one message when a product's price drops; the search index, the email alerts service and the analytics service each receive their own copy, and the publisher doesn't know any of them exist.

concepts.name: Pull Request
concepts.description: A request to merge changes from one branch into another on a platform like GitHub, where teammates review, discuss and test the code before merging.
concepts.example: You fix a login bug on branch fix-login and open a pull request to main. A teammate comments on line 42, you push a correction, the tests pass, and they click Merge.

concepts.name: Pure Function
concepts.description: A function whose output depends only on its inputs and which has no side effects, so calling it with the same arguments always gives the same result.
concepts.example: add(2, 3) always returns 5 and changes nothing else, so it is pure. A function that adds to a global counter or prints to the screen is not, because it has side effects.

concepts.name: PySpark
concepts.description: The Python API for Apache Spark, letting you write distributed data processing and machine learning jobs on clusters using Python.
concepts.example: df = spark.read.parquet('s3://logs/') then df.groupBy('country').count().show() counts 10 billion log rows across 100 machines, written in a few lines of Python.

concepts.name: Python (Programming Language)
concepts.description: A popular, readable high-level programming language with dynamic typing and a huge ecosystem, dominant in data science and machine learning.
concepts.example: Printing the even numbers from 1 to 10 takes one readable line: print([n for n in range(1, 11) if n % 2 == 0]), which outputs [2, 4, 6, 8, 10].

concepts.name: PyTorch
concepts.description: An open-source deep learning framework with GPU tensors, automatic differentiation and dynamic computation graphs, widely used in research and production.
concepts.example: x = torch.tensor(3.0, requires_grad=True); y = x**2; y.backward() makes x.grad equal 6, the derivative 2x at x=3, computed automatically. The same code trains huge networks on GPUs.

concepts.name: Quantization (Neural Networks)
concepts.description: Representing neural network weights and activations with low-precision numbers like 8-bit or 4-bit integers instead of 32-bit floats, to cut memory and speed up inference.
