concepts.example: A weight of 0.4137 stored as a 32-bit float takes 4 bytes; mapping the range -1 to 1 onto 256 integer levels stores it as one 8-bit integer (about 0.41 after decoding), shrinking the model 4x with little accuracy loss.

concepts.name: Query Optimization
concepts.description: How a database chooses the cheapest plan to execute a query, e.g. join order and index use, based on relational algebra rewrites and cost estimates; EXPLAIN shows the plan.
concepts.example: For a query joining a 10-row departments table and a 10-million-row employees table filtered to one department, the optimizer chooses to filter first and use an index on dept_id instead of scanning everything.

concepts.name: R (Programming Language)
concepts.description: A programming language and environment built for statistics and data analysis, with rich packages for modeling and plotting.
concepts.example: In R, t.test(scores_a, scores_b) runs a two-sample t-test in one line, and lm(price ~ size, data = houses) fits a linear regression whose coefficients and p-values summary() prints.

concepts.name: Raft (Algorithm)
concepts.description: A consensus algorithm designed to be understandable: servers elect a leader that replicates a log of commands to followers so all agree on the same state.
concepts.example: Five servers elect one leader. A client's 'set x=5' goes to the leader, which copies it to followers; once 3 of 5 have it, it's committed. If the leader crashes, the others hold a new election.

concepts.name: RAPIDS (Software)
concepts.description: NVIDIA's suite of GPU-accelerated data science libraries, such as cuDF for pandas-like DataFrames and cuML for machine learning.
concepts.example: Swapping import pandas for import cudf lets df.groupby('user').sum() on 100 million rows run on a GPU in under a second instead of tens of seconds on the CPU.

concepts.name: Rate Limiting
concepts.description: Restricting how many requests a client can make to a service in a time window, protecting it from overload and abuse, e.g. 100 API calls per minute.
concepts.example: An API allows 100 requests per minute per key. Your 101st request in that minute gets HTTP 429 Too Many Requests, and you must wait for the window to reset.

concepts.name: Resilient Distributed Dataset
concepts.description: Resilient Distributed Dataset, Spark's original abstraction: an immutable collection partitioned across a cluster that is recomputed from its lineage if a node fails.
concepts.example: sc.parallelize([1, 2, 3, 4]).map(lambda x: x * 2) creates a new RDD [2, 4, 6, 8] split across machines. If a machine dies, Spark recomputes the lost part by replaying the map from the original data.

concepts.name: Redis
concepts.description: An in-memory key-value data store used as a fast cache, message broker and database, supporting strings, lists, hashes and sorted sets.
concepts.example: A news site caches the front page in Redis under key 'home' for 60 seconds. Thousands of visitors get it from memory in under a millisecond instead of each triggering slow database queries.

concepts.name: Fold (Higher-Order Function)
concepts.description: A higher-order function that combines all elements of a collection into one value by repeatedly applying a binary function, e.g. summing a list.
concepts.example: reduce(lambda a, b: a + b, [1, 2, 3, 4]) computes ((1+2)+3)+4 = 10. Swap in max and the same pattern finds the largest element.

concepts.name: Regular Expression
concepts.description: A compact pattern language for matching text, such as \d{3}-\d{4} for phone numbers, used to search, validate and extract parts of strings.
concepts.example: The pattern \d{3}-\d{4} matches '555-1234' but not '55-1234', because \d means any digit and {3} means exactly three of them.

concepts.name: Relational Algebra
concepts.description: A formal language of operations on relations (tables), such as selection, projection, join, union and difference, that underlies SQL and query optimization.
concepts.example: To get names of students in course 'CS101': join Students with Enrollments on student id, select rows where course = 'CS101', then project only the name column. SQL queries compile into steps like these.

concepts.name: Relational Database
concepts.description: A database that stores data in tables with rows and columns linked by keys, following the relational model and queried with SQL.
concepts.example: An Orders table stores customer_id 7 instead of copying the customer's name and address; a join with Customers on id 7 retrieves them, so updating an address means changing one row.

concepts.name: Relational Model
concepts.description: Codd's model of data as relations (tables of tuples) with keys and constraints, where queries are expressed through set-based operations.
concepts.example: A relation Students(id, name) holds tuples like (1, 'Ana') and (2, 'Ben'). Their order doesn't matter, duplicates aren't allowed, and id is a key that identifies each tuple.

concepts.name: Replication (Computing)
concepts.description: Keeping copies of the same data on multiple machines so a system stays available and durable when some fail, and can serve more reads.
concepts.example: A database keeps the same data on servers in three data centers. When one data center loses power, reads switch to another copy and users notice nothing.

concepts.name: REST
concepts.description: An architectural style for web APIs where resources are addressed by URLs and manipulated with standard HTTP methods like GET, POST, PUT and DELETE, typically using JSON.
concepts.example: GET /books/42 returns book 42 as JSON, PUT /books/42 updates it, and DELETE /books/42 removes it. The URL names the thing; the HTTP verb says what to do to it.

concepts.name: Return Statement
concepts.description: The return statement ends a function and sends a value back to the caller, which can then store or use that result.
concepts.example: def area(w, h): return w * h. Then x = area(3, 4) stores 12 in x. Code after the return line in the function never runs.

concepts.name: Row-Oriented vs Column-Oriented Format
concepts.description: The contrast between storing a table row by row (good for transactions) and column by column (good for analytic scans and compression).
concepts.example: Averaging one 'price' column over 1 billion 50-column rows: a row format must read all 50 columns, while a columnar format reads just the price column, about 1/50th of the data.

concepts.name: Rust (Programming Language)
concepts.description: A systems programming language that guarantees memory safety without garbage collection through its ownership and borrowing rules, while matching C++ speed.
concepts.example: In Rust, let a = vec![1, 2]; let b = a; then using a again fails to compile, because ownership of the vector moved to b. That rule stops use-after-free bugs before the program runs.

concepts.name: Software as a Service
concepts.description: Software as a Service: applications delivered over the internet on a subscription basis and run by the provider, such as Gmail or Salesforce.
concepts.example: Using Gmail or Slack in a browser is SaaS: you pay a monthly fee per user, and the provider runs the servers, installs updates and backs up your data.

concepts.name: Scala (Programming Language)
concepts.description: A JVM programming language that blends object-oriented and functional programming; it is the native language of Apache Spark.
concepts.example: In Scala, List(1, 2, 3).map(_ * 2) gives List(2, 4, 6) in functional style, yet you can also define classes with methods. Spark's own engine is written in Scala.

concepts.name: Schema Evolution
concepts.description: Changing a data schema over time, like adding or renaming fields, while keeping old and new data and readers compatible.
concepts.example: A user record gains an optional 'phone' field with default empty. New readers handle old files by filling in the default, and old readers simply ignore the new field, so nothing breaks.

concepts.name: scikit-learn
concepts.description: The standard Python library for classical machine learning, offering a consistent fit/predict API for models, preprocessing, model selection and metrics.
concepts.example: model = RandomForestClassifier(); model.fit(X_train, y_train); model.predict(X_test). Swapping in LogisticRegression changes just the first line, since every model shares fit and predict.

concepts.name: scikit-learn Pipeline
concepts.description: A scikit-learn object that chains preprocessing steps and a final estimator into one model, so the same transformations apply in training, cross-validation and prediction.
concepts.example: Pipeline([('scale', StandardScaler()), ('clf', LogisticRegression())]) learns scaling from the training data only, then applies the identical scaling at prediction time, avoiding leaks from test data.

concepts.name: SciPy
concepts.description: A Python library built on NumPy for scientific computing, with modules for optimization, integration, interpolation, linear algebra, signal processing and statistics.
concepts.example: scipy.optimize.minimize(lambda x: (x - 3)**2, x0=0) finds the minimum at x = 3, and scipy.integrate.quad(np.sin, 0, np.pi) returns 2.0, the area under one hump of the sine curve.

concepts.name: Scope (Computer Science)
concepts.description: The region of a program where a name such as a variable is visible and usable, e.g. local variables inside a function versus global variables.
concepts.example: x = 10 at the top of a file is global. Inside def f(): x = 5, a new local x exists only during f's call, so after calling f(), printing x still shows 10.

concepts.name: Seaborn (Software)
concepts.description: A Python statistical plotting library built on Matplotlib that makes attractive plots like histograms, box plots and heat maps directly from pandas DataFrames.
concepts.example: sns.boxplot(data=tips, x='day', y='total_bill') draws one box per weekday from a pandas DataFrame, with styled colours and labels, in a single line.

concepts.name: Second Normal Form
concepts.description: A table is in 2NF when it is in 1NF and every non-key column depends on the whole primary key, not just part of a composite key.
concepts.example: A table keyed on (order_id, product_id) also stores product_name, which depends only on product_id. Moving product_name into a separate Products table fixes this and gives 2NF.

concepts.name: SELECT (SQL)
concepts.description: The SQL statement that retrieves data, choosing columns from one or more tables and optionally filtering, grouping and sorting the rows.
concepts.example: SELECT name, age FROM people WHERE age > 30 returns just the name and age columns for people over 30, leaving the table itself unchanged.

concepts.name: Self Join
concepts.description: A join of a table with itself using aliases, used to compare rows within one table, such as pairing employees with their managers.
concepts.example: An employees table has a manager_id column. Joining employees e to employees m on e.manager_id = m.id lists each worker next to their manager's name, both from the same table.

concepts.name: Serialization
concepts.description: Converting in-memory objects into a byte or text format (JSON, pickle, protobuf) so they can be saved or sent, and rebuilding them later by deserialization.
concepts.example: A Python dict {'name': 'Ann', 'age': 30} becomes the text '{"name": "Ann", "age": 30}' with json.dumps, so it can be saved to a file or sent over a network, then rebuilt with json.loads.

concepts.name: Serverless Computing
concepts.description: A cloud model where you deploy small functions that run on demand and scale automatically, paying per execution without managing servers, e.g. AWS Lambda.
concepts.example: A function that resizes uploaded photos runs only when a photo arrives. With 3 uploads a day you pay for 3 short runs; with 3 million, the provider runs thousands of copies at once automatically.

concepts.name: Set Operations (SQL)
concepts.description: SQL operators UNION, INTERSECT and EXCEPT that combine the results of two queries with compatible columns as set union, intersection or difference.
concepts.example: SELECT email FROM customers UNION SELECT email FROM newsletter gives every distinct email in either list; INTERSECT gives only emails in both; EXCEPT gives customers not subscribed.

concepts.name: Shard (Database Architecture)
concepts.description: Splitting a database horizontally into shards, each holding a subset of rows on a separate server, so data and load scale across machines.
concepts.example: A user database with 100 million rows is split by user_id: IDs 0-25M on server A, 25-50M on B, and so on. A lookup for user 30M goes straight to server B.

concepts.name: Shuffle (Distributed Computing)
concepts.description: Redistributing data across machines in a distributed job so records with the same key end up together, as between map and reduce stages; often the costliest step.
concepts.example: Counting words over 100 machines: each machine counts its own pages, then the shuffle sends every 'apple' count to machine 7, every 'banana' count to machine 12, so each word can be totalled in one place.

concepts.name: Single Instruction, Multiple Data
concepts.description: Single instruction, multiple data: CPU or GPU instructions that apply the same operation to many data elements at once, such as adding eight floats in one step.
concepts.example: Adding two arrays of 8 numbers each: a SIMD instruction adds all 8 pairs in one go, where ordinary code would issue 8 separate additions.

concepts.name: Slowly Changing Dimension
concepts.description: Techniques for handling dimension attributes that change over time in a data warehouse, e.g. overwrite (type 1) or keep history with new rows (type 2).
concepts.example: A customer moves from Boston to Denver. Type 1 overwrites the city, losing history; type 2 adds a new row for Denver with a start date and marks the Boston row as ended, so old sales still report Boston.

concepts.name: Snowflake (Data Warehouse)
concepts.description: A cloud data warehouse that separates storage from compute, letting teams run SQL analytics on scalable virtual warehouses.
concepts.example: The finance team runs heavy month-end reports on a large virtual warehouse while the marketing team queries the same tables on a small one. Neither slows the other, and each warehouse can pause when idle to stop billing.

concepts.name: Snowflake Schema
concepts.description: A data warehouse schema like a star schema but with dimension tables normalized into several related tables, forming a snowflake shape.
concepts.example: In a star schema, a product dimension holds category_name directly. In a snowflake schema, product only holds category_id, which points to a separate Category table, saving repetition but adding a join.

concepts.name: Spark DataFrame
concepts.description: Spark's distributed table abstraction with named columns, queried through a DataFrame API or Spark SQL and optimized by the Catalyst query planner.
concepts.example: spark.read.csv('sales.csv').groupBy('region').sum('revenue') looks like pandas, but the table is split across 50 machines and Spark's optimizer plans the job before running it.

concepts.name: Spark Structured Streaming
concepts.description: Spark's stream processing engine that treats a live data stream as an unbounded table, letting you write streaming jobs with the same DataFrame and SQL API.
concepts.example: You write clicks.groupBy('page').count() as if over a normal table; Spark keeps the counts updated as new click events arrive every second from Kafka.

concepts.name: SQL
concepts.description: Structured Query Language, the standard language for defining, querying and modifying data in relational databases.
concepts.example: SELECT name FROM employees WHERE salary > 50000 ORDER BY name; says what you want, names of well-paid employees in alphabetical order, and the database works out how to fetch it.

concepts.name: SQLite
concepts.description: A lightweight, serverless relational database engine stored in a single file, embedded in apps, phones and browsers.
concepts.example: A phone's contacts app keeps everything in a single file, contacts.db. The app opens it with the SQLite library and runs SQL directly, with no separate database server to install or start.

concepts.name: Star Schema
concepts.description: A data warehouse design with a central fact table of measurements linked to surrounding dimension tables, giving simple, fast analytic queries.
concepts.example: A sales fact table holds rows like (date_id, store_id, product_id, amount). Around it sit Date, Store and Product dimension tables, so 'revenue by store city in March' is one join per dimension.

concepts.name: Static Typing
concepts.description: Checking variable and expression types at compile time, before the program runs, as in Java or Rust, catching type errors early.
concepts.example: In Java, int count = "five"; is rejected by the compiler before the program ever runs, while in Python the equivalent mistake only blows up when that line executes.

concepts.name: statsmodels
concepts.description: A Python library for statistical modeling, offering regression, generalized linear models, time series analysis and hypothesis tests with detailed result summaries.
concepts.example: smf.ols('price ~ size + rooms', data=df).fit().summary() prints a regression table with coefficients, standard errors, p-values and R-squared, much like R's output.

concepts.name: Stored Procedure
concepts.description: A named set of SQL statements saved in the database that can be called with parameters, keeping logic close to the data.
concepts.example: A bank defines a procedure transfer(from_id, to_id, amount) inside the database. The app just calls CALL transfer(1, 2, 100), and the procedure does both updates and checks the balance in one place.

concepts.name: Stream Processing
concepts.description: Processing data continuously as events arrive, with low latency, instead of in periodic batches; used for real-time analytics and alerts.
concepts.example: A card company checks each payment within 50 milliseconds of it happening, flagging a card used in Paris and Tokyo five minutes apart, instead of waiting for a nightly batch report.

concepts.name: Subquery
concepts.description: A SQL query nested inside another query, for example in a WHERE or FROM clause, whose result is used by the outer query.
concepts.example: SELECT name FROM employees WHERE salary > (SELECT AVG(salary) FROM employees) first computes the average, say 60,000, and then returns everyone earning more.

concepts.name: Table (Database)
concepts.description: A database structure that organizes data in rows (records) and columns (fields); in relational theory a table is called a relation.
concepts.example: A Books table has columns title, author and year. Each row is one book, like ('Dune', 'Herbert', 1965), and every row has the same three fields.

concepts.name: TensorFlow
concepts.description: Google's open-source machine learning framework for building and training neural networks with tensors, automatic differentiation and deployment tools.
concepts.example: With tf.keras you stack Dense layers, call model.fit(x, y, epochs=5), and TensorFlow computes the gradients and updates the weights; the trained model can then run on a phone with TensorFlow Lite.

concepts.name: Test-Driven Development
concepts.description: A software practice of writing a failing automated test first, then the minimal code to pass it, then refactoring, in short repeated cycles.
concepts.example: You first write test: assert add(2, 3) == 5, run it and watch it fail because add doesn't exist. Then write the simplest add that passes, run green, and tidy the code with the test as a safety net.

concepts.name: Third Normal Form
concepts.description: A table is in 3NF when it is in 2NF and no non-key column depends on another non-key column (no transitive dependencies).
concepts.example: An employees table stores dept_id and dept_name. dept_name depends on dept_id, not on the employee, so it moves to a Departments table; renaming a department then changes one row.

concepts.name: Thread (Computing)
concepts.description: The smallest unit of execution within a process; threads in one process share memory, letting a program do several tasks concurrently.
concepts.example: A word processor uses one thread to handle your typing and another to spell-check in the background. Both read the same document in shared memory, so the check sees your latest text.

concepts.name: Tidy Data
concepts.description: A standard layout for tabular data where each variable is a column, each observation is a row and each type of observational unit is a table.
concepts.example: A table with columns country, 2020, 2021 is messy because years are spread across columns. The tidy version has columns country, year, cases, with one row per country per year.

concepts.name: Tidyverse
concepts.description: A collection of R packages such as dplyr and ggplot2 that share a consistent design for importing, tidying, transforming and visualizing data.
concepts.example: df %>% filter(year == 2024) %>% group_by(region) %>% summarise(total = sum(sales)) reads like a sentence, and ggplot(df, aes(region, total)) + geom_col() then charts the result.

concepts.name: Tensor Processing Unit
concepts.description: Google's custom chip for machine learning that accelerates the large matrix multiplications in neural networks using a systolic array.
concepts.example: Inside a TPU, a 128x128 grid of multiply-add units passes numbers to its neighbours each clock tick, so one chip performs tens of thousands of multiplications per cycle for a neural network layer.

concepts.name: Triton (Programming Language)
concepts.description: A Python-based language and compiler from OpenAI for writing fast GPU kernels at the level of blocks of data, easier than raw CUDA.
concepts.example: A Triton softmax kernel loads a block of 1,024 values with one tl.load, computes max, exponentials and sum on the whole block, and writes it back, while the compiler handles threads and memory coalescing that CUDA makes you write by hand.

concepts.name: Tuple
concepts.description: An ordered, usually immutable collection of a fixed number of elements, such as a coordinate pair (x, y).
concepts.example: point = (3, 4) holds an x and y coordinate. You can read point[0] to get 3, but point[0] = 5 raises an error in Python because tuples can't be changed.

concepts.name: Type Hints
concepts.description: Optional annotations in dynamically typed languages like Python that declare expected types of variables and function arguments, checked by tools like mypy.
concepts.example: def area(w: float, h: float) -> float: tells readers and tools like mypy that area takes two floats and returns one. Python still runs area('a', 2) without complaint; only the checker flags it.

concepts.name: Type System
concepts.description: A language's rules for assigning types to values and expressions and checking that operations are used on compatible types.
concepts.example: Adding 3 + 'apples' is rejected in Python with a TypeError, while JavaScript turns it into the string '3apples'. Each language's type system decides which operations make sense for which kinds of values.

concepts.name: Unit Testing
concepts.description: Writing automated tests that check small, isolated pieces of code, such as single functions, behave as expected.
concepts.example: def test_add(): assert add(2, 2) == 4 checks one small function. If someone later breaks add, running pytest immediately shows test_add failing and points to the culprit.

concepts.name: Variable (Computer Science)
concepts.description: A named storage location in a program that holds a value which can be read and changed while the program runs.
concepts.example: score = 0 creates a box named score holding 0; after score = score + 10, the box holds 10. The name stays the same while its contents change.

concepts.name: Vector Database
concepts.description: A database built to store embedding vectors and quickly find the most similar ones using approximate nearest neighbor indexes, used for semantic search and RAG.
concepts.example: Each of 1 million product descriptions is stored as a 384-number embedding. A search for 'cozy winter jacket' is embedded too, and the database returns the 10 nearest vectors in milliseconds, even ones without those exact words.

concepts.name: Vectorization
concepts.description: Replacing explicit loops with whole-array operations, as in NumPy, so computations run in optimized compiled code and are much faster.
concepts.example: Instead of looping for i in range(n): c[i] = a[i] + b[i], you write c = a + b with NumPy, which runs the loop in compiled C and can be 50 to 100 times faster.

concepts.name: Version Control
concepts.description: Systems that record changes to files over time so you can review history, revert mistakes and collaborate on code, e.g. Git.
concepts.example: You change 3 files, commit with the message 'fix login', and a week later find it broke signup. git log shows exactly what changed, and git revert undoes just that commit.

concepts.name: View (SQL)
concepts.description: A saved SQL query that acts like a virtual table; a materialized view also stores its result for faster reads.
concepts.example: CREATE VIEW active_customers AS SELECT * FROM customers WHERE active = 1. Afterwards SELECT * FROM active_customers works like a table, but always reflects the current data.

concepts.name: Virtual Environment
concepts.description: An isolated Python environment with its own interpreter and installed packages, so each project can use its own dependency versions.
concepts.example: Project A needs Django 3 and project B needs Django 5. python -m venv .venv gives each project its own folder of packages, so installing Django 5 in B doesn't break A.

concepts.name: Virtual Machine
concepts.description: A software emulation of a complete computer that runs its own operating system on shared physical hardware via a hypervisor.
concepts.example: On a Mac you run a Windows VM: Windows boots in a window believing it has its own CPU, 8 GB RAM and disk, while a hypervisor quietly maps those onto the Mac's real hardware.

concepts.name: Virtualization
concepts.description: Creating virtual versions of hardware such as CPUs, memory and storage so one physical machine can run several isolated environments.
concepts.example: One physical server with 64 cores and 256 GB RAM is carved into 8 virtual machines of 8 cores and 32 GB each, each running its own operating system, isolated from the others.

concepts.name: Web Scraping
concepts.description: Automatically downloading web pages and extracting data from their HTML, typically with Python libraries like requests and BeautifulSoup.
concepts.example: A script downloads a bookshop page with requests, parses the HTML with BeautifulSoup, and collects every <span class='price'> into a list of 20 book prices.

concepts.name: WHERE Clause
concepts.description: The SQL clause that filters rows by a condition, keeping only those for which the condition is true.
concepts.example: SELECT * FROM orders WHERE total > 100 AND country = 'FR' keeps only French orders above 100; every other row is dropped from the result.

concepts.name: While Loop
concepts.description: A loop that keeps repeating a block of code as long as a condition stays true.
concepts.example: Doubling money until it passes 1,000: start with 100; while money < 1000, double it. It goes 200, 400, 800, 1600, then the condition is false and the loop stops after 4 rounds.

concepts.name: Windowing (Stream Processing)
concepts.description: Grouping an unbounded stream into finite windows, such as fixed tumbling or overlapping sliding time windows, so aggregates can be computed.
concepts.example: A 1-minute tumbling window counts clicks 12:00-12:01, then 12:01-12:02, with no overlap. A 5-minute sliding window moving every minute overlaps, so each click counts in 5 windows.

concepts.name: Workflow Orchestration
concepts.description: Automating the scheduling, ordering, retrying and monitoring of dependent tasks in data or ML pipelines, typically defined as DAGs in tools like Airflow.
concepts.example: A nightly job must download data, then clean it, then train a model, then email a report. An orchestrator runs these in order at 2 a.m., retries the download if it fails and skips training if cleaning broke.

concepts.name: XLA
concepts.description: Accelerated Linear Algebra, a compiler that optimizes machine learning computation graphs, e.g. by fusing operations, for CPUs, GPUs and TPUs; used by JAX and TensorFlow.
concepts.example: In y = relu(x * w + b), XLA fuses multiply, add and relu into one GPU kernel, so the intermediate results never get written to and read back from memory.

concepts.name: XML
concepts.description: Extensible Markup Language, a text format that represents structured data as nested, tagged elements, used for documents and data exchange.
concepts.example: <book id="42"><title>Dune</title><author>Herbert</author></book> describes a book with nested tags. Any program with an XML parser can read the title without knowing the app that wrote it.

concepts.name: YAML
concepts.description: A human-readable data serialization format using indentation for nesting, commonly used for configuration files.
concepts.example: A config file reads: server: then indented port: 8080 and debug: true. It is the same data as the JSON {"server": {"port": 8080, "debug": true}}, but with indentation instead of braces.

concepts.name: Apache Hadoop YARN
concepts.description: Hadoop's resource manager that allocates cluster CPU and memory to applications and schedules jobs such as MapReduce and Spark.
concepts.example: A cluster has 100 nodes. YARN gives a Spark job 40 containers and a MapReduce job 30, and queues the third job until resources free up.

concepts.name: Advantage Actor-Critic
concepts.description: A synchronous actor-critic algorithm that runs several environment copies in parallel and updates the policy using advantage estimates (return minus the critic's value) to reduce gradient variance.
concepts.example: Sixteen copies of a game run side by side. After every 5 steps, all of them pause, their experience is pooled into one batch, the actor and critic are updated once, and all copies continue with the same new policy.

concepts.name: Asynchronous Advantage Actor-Critic
concepts.description: An actor-critic algorithm in which many workers interact with their own environment copies in parallel and asynchronously push gradient updates to shared parameters, stabilizing training without replay.
concepts.example: Sixteen CPU threads each play their own copy of a game, compute gradients locally and push them to a shared network whenever ready, without waiting for each other, then pull the latest weights.

concepts.name: Actor-Critic with Experience Replay
concepts.description: An off-policy actor-critic algorithm that adds experience replay using truncated importance sampling with bias correction, Retrace targets and an efficient trust-region update.
concepts.example: An Atari agent stores past episodes and reuses each one several times. Because old actions came from an older policy, ACER reweights them by importance ratios, but caps each ratio, say at 10, so one rare action can't blow up the update.

concepts.name: Action Space
concepts.description: The set of all actions an agent can choose from in an environment; it may be discrete, like game buttons, or continuous, like joint torques of a robot.
concepts.example: In Pong the action space is discrete: up, down or stay. For a robot arm it is continuous: three joint torques, each any real number between -1 and 1.

concepts.name: Action-Value Function
concepts.description: A function Q(s, a) giving the expected total discounted reward from taking action a in state s and then following a given policy; acting greedily on Q gives better policies.
concepts.example: In a maze, Q(junction, left) = 8 and Q(junction, right) = 3 means turning left there and then following your policy is expected to earn 8 points versus 3, so left is the better move.

concepts.name: Actor-Critic Method
concepts.description: A family of RL methods that learn both a policy (the actor) that chooses actions and a value function (the critic) that evaluates them, using the critic's estimates to reduce policy gradient variance.
concepts.example: A player (actor) chooses moves while a coach (critic) predicts how well things should go from each position. If a move turns out better than the coach predicted, the actor makes it more likely next time; the coach also refines its predictions.

concepts.name: Advantage Function
concepts.description: The difference A(s, a) = Q(s, a) - V(s), measuring how much better an action is than the policy's average behavior in that state; used to lower variance in policy gradients.
concepts.example: If a state is worth V = 10 on average and taking 'jump' there is worth Q = 13, the advantage of jumping is +3. An action with Q = 8 has advantage -2, worse than usual.

concepts.name: Adversarial Bandit
concepts.description: A multi-armed bandit setting where rewards may be chosen by an adversary rather than drawn from fixed distributions, so algorithms like EXP3 use randomized strategies to bound regret.
concepts.example: Each day you choose one of 3 ad slots, but a competitor sees your past choices and can lower the payoff of whatever you favour. Algorithms like Exp3 randomize choices so the adversary can't exploit you.

concepts.name: Intelligent Agent
concepts.description: An entity that perceives its environment through sensors and acts on it to achieve goals; in reinforcement learning, the learner that chooses actions to maximize cumulative reward.
concepts.example: A thermostat senses the room temperature and turns heating on or off to keep 21 degrees. A chess program senses the board and picks moves to win. Both perceive and act toward a goal.

concepts.name: Agent57
concepts.description: A DeepMind agent that was the first to outperform the human baseline on all 57 Atari games, combining R2D2-style distributed recurrent learning with intrinsic exploration and a meta-controller choosing exploration levels.
concepts.example: On Pitfall, where rewards are extremely rare, Agent57 uses a bandit to pick, per episode, how exploratory to be and how far ahead to look, so it scores in hard games while staying strong in easy ones.

concepts.name: Alpha–Beta Pruning
concepts.description: An optimization of minimax search that skips branches that cannot affect the final decision by tracking the best values each player can guarantee, letting game engines search much deeper.
concepts.example: Exploring a game tree, you find a move guaranteeing you a score of 5. In the next branch, the opponent's first reply already holds you to 3, so you skip that branch's remaining replies: it can't beat 5.

concepts.name: AlphaGo
concepts.description: DeepMind's Go program that first beat a world champion, combining policy and value networks trained by supervised learning and self-play with Monte Carlo tree search.
concepts.example: In 2016 AlphaGo beat Lee Sedol 4-1. Its policy network suggested a few promising moves, its value network judged positions, and tree search combined them to look ahead.

concepts.name: AlphaGo Zero
concepts.description: A version of AlphaGo trained entirely by self-play from random play without human games, using a single residual network for policy and value guided by MCTS; it surpassed the original AlphaGo.
concepts.example: Starting from random moves with only the rules of Go, AlphaGo Zero played itself millions of times; within three days it beat the version that defeated Lee Sedol 100 games to 0.

concepts.name: AlphaStar
concepts.description: DeepMind's StarCraft II agent that reached Grandmaster level using a Transformer- and LSTM-based policy trained by imitation learning and then multi-agent reinforcement learning in a league of competing agents.
concepts.example: AlphaStar first copied human StarCraft replays, then trained in a league of agents, including exploiters built to find weaknesses in the main agents, reaching Grandmaster level on the public ladder.

concepts.name: AlphaZero
concepts.description: A general game-playing algorithm that masters chess, shogi and Go from scratch by self-play, using one neural network for policy and value and Monte Carlo tree search, with no domain knowledge beyond rules.
concepts.example: Given only the rules of chess, AlphaZero trained by self-play for about 9 hours and then beat Stockfish, a top chess engine, using the same algorithm that also mastered shogi and Go.

concepts.name: Amortized Inference
concepts.description: Training a neural network to map each observation directly to the parameters of its approximate posterior, so inference for new data is a single forward pass instead of a separate optimization.
concepts.example: Instead of running a separate optimization for each of 10,000 images to find its latent code, a VAE's encoder learns once to map any image straight to its posterior mean and variance in one forward pass.

concepts.name: Ancestral Sampling
concepts.description: Drawing a sample from a directed graphical model by sampling each variable in topological order, conditioned on the already sampled values of its parents.
concepts.example: For Cloudy -> Rain -> WetGrass: first flip Cloudy (say true), then sample Rain given Cloudy (say true), then WetGrass given Rain. Parents always come before children, giving one full sample.

concepts.name: Ape-X
concepts.description: A distributed deep RL architecture in which many actors generate experience in parallel into a shared prioritized replay buffer, while a single learner trains a DQN-style network from it.
concepts.example: Hundreds of actors play Atari, each exploring with a different noise level, and send experiences to a shared replay buffer; one GPU learner trains on the most surprising samples and periodically sends new weights back.

concepts.name: Apprenticeship Learning
concepts.description: Learning a policy from expert demonstrations by inferring a reward function under which the expert's feature expectations are matched, then optimizing for that reward.
concepts.example: Watching an expert driver who keeps centred and slows near pedestrians, the algorithm guesses reward weights for those features, finds a policy for that reward, and repeats until its driving features match the expert's.

concepts.name: Approximate Inference
concepts.description: Methods that estimate posterior distributions or marginals when exact computation is intractable, mainly sampling approaches like MCMC and optimization approaches like variational inference.
concepts.example: Computing exactly whether a patient has one of 50 diseases given 200 symptoms would mean summing over a huge number of combinations, so you instead draw samples or fit a simpler distribution that's close enough.

concepts.name: Asynchronous Dynamic Programming
concepts.description: Dynamic programming methods for MDPs that update state values in any order, one state at a time, rather than sweeping all states, which can speed up convergence and focus computation.
concepts.example: Instead of sweeping all 1 million states each round, you repeatedly update just the states near the robot's current position. Values still converge as long as every state keeps getting updated eventually.

concepts.name: Arcade Learning Environment
concepts.description: The Arcade Learning Environment, a platform exposing dozens of Atari 2600 games as RL tasks with pixel observations, the standard benchmark for deep RL since DQN.
concepts.example: An agent sees 210x160 pixel frames of Breakout, chooses joystick actions, and gets the game score as reward. The same agent is then tested on Pong, Space Invaders and dozens more without changes.

concepts.name: Baseline (Policy Gradient)
concepts.description: Subtracting a baseline, often a learned state value estimate, from returns in the policy gradient; it leaves the gradient unbiased while substantially reducing its variance.
concepts.example: Episode returns are 100, 102 and 98. Without a baseline, every action gets pushed up hugely. Subtracting a baseline of 100 leaves 0, +2 and -2, a much clearer signal of which actions were better.

concepts.name: Bayes by Backprop
concepts.description: A method for training Bayesian neural networks that learns a Gaussian distribution over each weight by maximizing a variational lower bound with the reparameterization trick and ordinary backpropagation.
concepts.example: Each weight is a Gaussian, say mean 0.3 and standard deviation 0.05. Each training step samples weights, computes the loss and backpropagates to adjust both means and spreads.

concepts.name: Recursive Bayesian Estimation
concepts.description: A recursive algorithm that tracks a belief over a hidden state by alternating a prediction step using a motion model and an update step applying Bayes' theorem to each new measurement.
concepts.example: A robot believes it's 50/50 at door 1 or 2. It moves one door right, so the prediction shifts its belief; then its camera sees a door, and the update raises probability on positions next to doors.

concepts.name: Bayesian Inference
concepts.description: Updating beliefs about unknown quantities by combining a prior distribution with the likelihood of observed data via Bayes' theorem to obtain a posterior distribution.
concepts.example: You think a coin is probably fair. After seeing 8 heads in 10 flips, your belief shifts toward a heads-biased coin, though less than if you'd seen 80 heads in 100 flips.

concepts.name: Bayesian Model Selection
concepts.description: Choosing among competing models by comparing their marginal likelihoods (evidence), often via Bayes factors, which automatically penalizes unnecessary complexity.
concepts.example: To decide if a coin is fair or biased, compare how well each model predicted the observed 6 heads in 10 averaged over its parameters. The fair model wins here, since the flexible one spreads its predictions thin.

concepts.name: Bayesian Nonparametrics
concepts.description: The field of Bayesian models with infinitely many parameters whose effective complexity grows with the data, using priors such as Dirichlet processes and Gaussian processes.
concepts.example: Clustering news articles without fixing the number of topics: with 100 articles the model might use 5 clusters, and with 10,000 it may grow to 40, letting the data decide.

concepts.name: Batch-Constrained Q-Learning
concepts.description: An offline RL algorithm that limits the policy to actions similar to those in the dataset, using a generative model of the batch's actions, to avoid errors from out-of-distribution actions.
concepts.example: From a fixed dataset of driving logs, BCQ only considers actions similar to what drivers actually did there, so it never picks an untested move like swerving hard that the Q-function might wrongly rate as great.

concepts.name: Behavior Policy
concepts.description: In off-policy RL, the policy that actually generates the experience, as opposed to the target policy being learned or evaluated; importance sampling corrects for the difference.
concepts.example: A robot explores randomly 30% of the time while collecting data; that exploratory policy is the behavior policy. Q-learning uses the data to learn the greedy target policy it would actually deploy.

concepts.name: Behavioral Cloning
concepts.description: Imitation learning by plain supervised learning: train a policy to predict the expert's action from each observed state in a dataset of demonstrations.
concepts.example: Record 10 hours of a person driving with the camera image and steering angle each frame, then train a network to predict the steering angle from the image, exactly like an image classification task.

concepts.name: Belief Propagation
concepts.description: A message-passing algorithm that computes marginal probabilities in graphical models by having nodes exchange summaries of their beliefs with neighbors; exact on trees.
concepts.example: In a chain A - B - C, A sends B a message summarizing what A knows, C does the same, and B multiplies them with its own evidence to get its exact marginal, without enumerating all combinations.

concepts.name: Belief State
concepts.description: A probability distribution over the possible hidden states of a partially observable environment, summarizing everything the agent knows; planning over belief states turns a POMDP into a belief MDP.
concepts.example: In a card game you can't see the opponent's hand, but after they pass twice you estimate 70% they hold a weak hand. That probability over possible hands is your belief state, and you choose moves based on it.

concepts.name: Bellman Operator
concepts.description: An operator that maps a value function to a new one by a one-step look-ahead using rewards and transition probabilities; it is a contraction whose fixed point is the true value function.
concepts.example: Start with a guess that every state is worth 0. Applying the Bellman operator once gives each state its immediate reward plus discounted next-state guesses. Applying it repeatedly converges to the true values.

concepts.name: Bellman Optimality Equation
concepts.description: The recursive equation stating that the optimal value of a state equals the best achievable immediate reward plus the discounted optimal value of the next state, the basis of value iteration and Q-learning.
concepts.example: If going left earns 1 then lands in a state worth 10, and going right earns 5 then lands in a state worth 2, with discount 0.9 the optimal value is max(1 + 9, 5 + 1.8) = 10.

concepts.name: Best Arm Identification
concepts.description: A bandit problem focused on finding the arm with the highest mean reward using as few pulls as possible, rather than maximizing total reward along the way.
concepts.example: A company tests 5 headline versions and needs to name the winner with 95% confidence. It keeps sampling the closest contenders and drops clear losers early, stopping once the top headline's interval separates from the rest.

concepts.name: Black-Box Variational Inference
concepts.description: Variational inference that works for almost any model by estimating ELBO gradients with Monte Carlo samples, using the score function or reparameterization gradients, without model-specific derivations.
concepts.example: For a custom model with no convenient math, you sample 10 values from the approximate posterior, score each with the model's log probability, and average to estimate the ELBO gradient, then take a step.

concepts.name: Bootstrapping (Reinforcement Learning)
concepts.description: Updating a value estimate using other current value estimates, such as using the estimated value of the next state, instead of waiting for the full actual return; the basis of TD learning.
concepts.example: After moving from state A to B and getting reward 1, you update V(A) toward 1 + 0.9 * V(B), using your current guess for B instead of waiting to see the whole episode.

concepts.name: Burn-In (MCMC)
concepts.description: The initial portion of an MCMC run that is discarded because the chain has not yet reached its stationary distribution, so early samples are biased by the starting point.
concepts.example: An MCMC sampler starts at a random guess of 1000 when the true values are near 5. The first 500 draws drift down toward 5, so you discard them and keep only later samples.

concepts.name: C51
concepts.description: A distributional DQN that models the full distribution of returns as probabilities over 51 fixed atoms, trained with a projected distributional Bellman update and cross-entropy loss.
concepts.example: Rather than predicting 'this move is worth 7 points', C51 predicts a histogram over 51 possible values from -10 to 10, such as 30% chance of 0 and 70% of 10, capturing risk as well as the mean.

concepts.name: Coordinate Ascent Variational Inference
concepts.description: A variational inference algorithm for mean-field approximations that updates each factor in turn to its optimal form given the others, increasing the ELBO at every step.
concepts.example: With a mean-field approximation q(a)q(b), fix q(b) and solve exactly for the best q(a), then fix q(a) and solve for q(b), and repeat. Each step can only raise the ELBO.

concepts.name: Centralized Training with Decentralized Execution
concepts.description: A multi-agent RL paradigm in which agents are trained with access to global information such as other agents' observations, but act at test time using only their own local observations.
concepts.example: In a robot soccer team, during training a critic sees all robots' positions and actions; at game time each robot acts only from its own camera, using its own learned actor.

concepts.name: Potential Function
concepts.description: A non-negative function over the variables of a clique in an undirected graphical model that scores how compatible their joint values are; the product of potentials defines the distribution up to normalization.
concepts.example: In an image model, neighbouring pixels A and B form a clique; a potential gives score 5 if both are 'sky' and 1 if they differ, so smooth labelings get higher probability after normalizing.

concepts.name: Conditional Probability Table
concepts.description: A table listing the probability of each value of a discrete variable for every combination of its parents' values, used to specify a Bayesian network.
concepts.example: For WetGrass with parents Rain and Sprinkler, the table has 4 rows: e.g. P(wet | rain, sprinkler) = 0.99 and P(wet | no rain, no sprinkler) = 0.01, one row for every parent combination.

concepts.name: Constrained Markov Decision Process
concepts.description: A Markov decision process with extra cost signals whose expected totals must stay below limits, solved with Lagrangian or linear programming methods; a core model for safe RL.
concepts.example: A delivery robot maximizes deliveries but must keep collisions below 1 per 1,000 trips. A Lagrange multiplier turns collisions into a penalty, raised whenever the limit is exceeded.

concepts.name: Contextual Bandit
concepts.description: A bandit problem where the learner sees a context (features) before choosing an arm, so the best arm depends on the context; used in personalized recommendation and ads.
concepts.example: A news site picks which of 5 headlines to show, but first sees the reader's age and location, so sports wins for some readers and politics for others. It learns a model from features to the best article.

concepts.name: Count-Based Exploration
concepts.description: Exploration that gives agents a bonus reward for visiting rarely seen states, based on visit counts or, in large spaces, pseudo-counts from a density model.
concepts.example: An agent gets a bonus of 1/sqrt(n) for visiting a state seen n times: 1 the first time, 0.5 on the fourth visit. Rarely seen rooms stay attractive until explored.

concepts.name: Counterfactual Regret Minimization
concepts.description: An iterative algorithm for imperfect-information games that minimizes regret separately at each information set using counterfactual values; its average strategy converges to a Nash equilibrium, powering poker bots.
concepts.example: In poker, at each decision point CFR asks how much better calling would have done than its mixed strategy, accumulates these regrets over millions of self-play hands, and plays actions in proportion to positive regret.

concepts.name: Compounding Error
concepts.description: In imitation learning, the problem that small mistakes lead a cloned policy into states the expert never visited, where it errs more, so errors compound quadratically with the horizon.
concepts.example: A cloned driving policy drifts 10 cm off centre, a situation never seen in expert data, so it makes a bigger error, drifts further, and errors snowball until it leaves the road.

concepts.name: Conservative Q-Learning
concepts.description: An offline RL algorithm that adds a regularizer pushing down Q-values of actions not in the dataset and up on dataset actions, learning conservative estimates that avoid overestimation.
concepts.example: From a fixed dataset, CQL pushes down Q-values for actions never tried, like 'brake hard at 100 km/h', so the learned policy sticks to choices backed by evidence rather than optimistic guesses.

concepts.name: Cross-Entropy Method
concepts.description: A derivative-free optimization method that samples candidate solutions from a distribution, keeps the best-performing elite fraction, and refits the distribution to them, repeating until convergence.
concepts.example: To tune 2 parameters, sample 100 guesses from a Gaussian, keep the best 10, fit a new Gaussian to those 10, and repeat. The cloud of guesses shrinks onto the best region.

concepts.name: DAgger
concepts.description: An imitation learning algorithm that repeatedly runs the current policy, asks the expert to label the visited states with correct actions, and retrains on the aggregated dataset to fix compounding errors.
concepts.example: A learner drives, drifts off-centre, and the expert labels what they would have done in those off-centre spots. Adding these to the training set teaches recovery, unlike cloning only perfect drives.

concepts.name: Deep Deterministic Policy Gradient
concepts.description: An off-policy actor-critic algorithm for continuous actions that learns a deterministic policy and a Q-function, using replay buffers and target networks as in DQN.
concepts.example: A simulated robot arm outputs exact joint torques like 0.37; a critic estimates Q for that torque, and the actor is nudged in the direction that raises Q, learning from a replay buffer of past moves.

concepts.name: Deadly Triad
concepts.description: The observation that combining function approximation, bootstrapping and off-policy learning can make value estimates diverge, explaining instability in algorithms like Q-learning with neural networks.
concepts.example: Off-policy Q-learning with a neural network and bootstrapped targets can see values grow to infinity: the network over-generalizes, the inflated estimate feeds its own target, and unvisited states never correct it.

concepts.name: Decentralized POMDP
concepts.description: A model of cooperative multi-agent decision making where several agents with private partial observations act to maximize a shared reward; finding optimal policies is very hard (NEXP-complete).
concepts.example: Two warehouse robots must deliver a box together, each seeing only its own camera and unable to talk. Both are rewarded jointly, so each must guess what the other likely sees and does.

concepts.name: Decision Transformer
concepts.description: An approach that treats RL as sequence modeling: a causal Transformer is trained on offline trajectories of returns-to-go, states and actions, then generates actions conditioned on a desired return.
concepts.example: Feed the model 'return-to-go 90, state, action, return-to-go 85, state...' from logged games. At test time ask for return 100, and it generates actions that tend to achieve a high score.

concepts.name: Deep Q-Network
concepts.description: The algorithm that learned to play Atari games from pixels by approximating Q-values with a CNN, stabilized by experience replay and a periodically updated target network.
concepts.example: DQN looks at the last 4 Breakout frames, a CNN outputs a Q-value for each joystick action, and it takes the highest. Training samples random past moves from memory and uses a slowly updated copy of the network for targets.

concepts.name: Deep Reinforcement Learning
concepts.description: The combination of reinforcement learning with deep neural networks, which act as function approximators for policies, value functions or models so agents can learn from raw, high-dimensional inputs like images.
concepts.example: A robot learns to grasp objects directly from camera images: a deep network maps pixels to motor commands, and rewards for successful grasps gradually improve it over thousands of attempts.

concepts.name: Deterministic Policy
concepts.description: A policy that maps each state to exactly one action, rather than a probability distribution over actions; common in continuous-control methods such as DDPG and TD3.
concepts.example: A thermostat policy 'if below 20 degrees, heat; else, off' always gives the same action in the same state. A stochastic policy might heat 80% of the time at 19 degrees.

concepts.name: Deterministic Policy Gradient
concepts.description: A policy gradient method for deterministic continuous-action policies, where the gradient is computed by chaining the critic's action-value gradient with the gradient of the policy's output.
concepts.example: A policy outputs steering 0.2. The critic says raising steering raises Q at slope 3 there, so the actor's weights move to increase the output slightly, following the chain rule from Q through the action.

concepts.name: Dirichlet-Multinomial Model
concepts.description: A compound model where category probabilities are drawn from a Dirichlet prior and counts are drawn from a multinomial; integrating out the probabilities gives a closed-form distribution for overdispersed counts.
concepts.example: Different authors favour different words. Draw each author's word probabilities from a Dirichlet, then draw word counts from a multinomial; the counts vary more across authors than a single fixed multinomial would allow.

concepts.name: Discount Factor
concepts.description: A number gamma between 0 and 1 that weights future rewards less than immediate ones when computing a return, keeping infinite sums finite and expressing how far ahead an agent cares.
concepts.example: With gamma = 0.9, a reward of 10 now is worth 10, one step later 9, two steps later 8.1. An endless stream of reward 1 per step sums to 1/(1-0.9) = 10 instead of infinity.

concepts.name: Distributional Reinforcement Learning
concepts.description: An approach to reinforcement learning that learns the full probability distribution of returns for each state-action pair, instead of only its expected value, using a distributional Bellman operator.
concepts.example: Two slot machines both pay 5 on average, but one always pays 5 while the other pays 0 or 10. Distributional RL learns the whole spread of payouts, so the agent can tell these risky and safe options apart.

concepts.name: Distributional Shift (Offline RL)
concepts.description: The mismatch between the data-collecting behavior policy and the policy being learned in offline RL, which makes value estimates for unseen actions unreliable and causes extrapolation error.
concepts.example: A driving dataset contains only careful drivers who never swerve. A learned policy that tries swerving gets a Q-value the data never checked, may wrongly rate it great, and then crashes when deployed.

concepts.name: Double DQN
concepts.description: A variant of DQN that reduces overestimation of Q-values by selecting the next action with the online network but evaluating it with the target network.
concepts.example: Plain DQN asks the same network to pick the best next action and to score it, so lucky noise gets picked and trusted. Double DQN lets the online network pick the action and the target network give its score.

concepts.name: Double Q-Learning
concepts.description: A Q-learning variant that keeps two independent value estimates, using one to choose the best action and the other to evaluate it, which removes the upward maximization bias.
concepts.example: If ten equally good actions each have a noisy estimate, the maximum of the noisy estimates is too high. Using table A to choose the best action and table B to score it cancels that optimistic bias.

concepts.name: Dreamer
concepts.description: A model-based RL agent that learns a latent world model from images and trains an actor-critic entirely on imagined trajectories in that latent space; DreamerV3 works across many domains with fixed settings.
concepts.example: Like a player rehearsing moves in their head, Dreamer learns a compact model of the game from pixels, then imagines thousands of short futures in that model and trains its policy on those dreams.

concepts.name: Deep Recurrent Q-Network
concepts.description: A Deep Q-Network that replaces a fully connected layer with an LSTM so the agent can integrate information over time and act in partially observable environments.
concepts.example: In Pong shown one frame at a time, you cannot tell which way the ball moves. DRQN's LSTM remembers earlier frames, so it can infer the ball's direction and still choose good actions.

concepts.name: Dueling Network Architecture
concepts.description: A Q-network architecture with two streams, one estimating the state value and one estimating each action's advantage, which are combined into Q-values to learn state values more efficiently.
concepts.example: In a driving game with an empty road, every action is worth about the same. Dueling DQN learns 'this state is good' once in a value stream and only small per-action differences in an advantage stream.

concepts.name: Dyna
concepts.description: An architecture that integrates learning, planning and acting: real experience updates both the value function and a learned model, and simulated experience from the model provides extra Q-learning updates.
concepts.example: After one real walk through a maze, the agent remembers 'left at the first door leads to the hallway'. It then replays 50 imagined steps from that memory to update values without moving again.

concepts.name: Dynamic Bayesian Network
concepts.description: A Bayesian network that models variables evolving over time by repeating a network slice per time step and linking consecutive slices; HMMs and Kalman filters are special cases.
concepts.example: To track weather and umbrella sightings over days, copy a small network (rain causes umbrella) for each day and add an arrow from yesterday's rain to today's rain.

concepts.name: Effective Sample Size
concepts.description: An estimate of how many independent samples a set of correlated MCMC draws or weighted importance samples is worth, used to judge the precision of Monte Carlo estimates.
concepts.example: 1000 MCMC draws that are highly correlated might carry the same information as only 50 independent draws, so the effective sample size is 50 and your error bars should reflect that.

concepts.name: Eligibility Trace
concepts.description: A short-term memory vector that marks recently visited states or features, decaying by gamma times lambda each step, so a TD error can update many past states at once.
concepts.example: A dog gets a treat after sit, stay, roll over. Traces remember all three tricks, with the most recent one marked strongest, so the treat strengthens each trick in proportion to how recently it happened.

concepts.name: Empirical Bayes
concepts.description: An approach that estimates the hyperparameters of a prior from the data itself, usually by maximizing the marginal likelihood, and then performs Bayesian inference with that fitted prior.
concepts.example: To rate 500 baseball batters with few at-bats, estimate the league-wide prior of batting averages from all players, then shrink each player's average toward it.

concepts.name: Entropy Regularization (Reinforcement Learning)
concepts.description: Adding a bonus proportional to the entropy of the policy's action distribution to the RL objective, which discourages premature convergence to deterministic behavior and encourages exploration.
concepts.example: A policy that picks 'left' 99% of the time gets a small entropy bonus, while one that splits 60/40 gets more. The bonus keeps the agent trying both options until it is truly sure which is better.

concepts.name: Environment (Reinforcement Learning)
concepts.description: Everything outside the agent in reinforcement learning: it receives the agent's actions, changes its state, and returns observations and rewards.
concepts.example: In chess, the environment is the board and the opponent: the agent moves a piece, and the environment answers with a new position and, at the end, a win, loss or draw.

concepts.name: Episode (Reinforcement Learning)
concepts.description: One complete run of agent-environment interaction from a start state to a terminal state, recorded as a sequence of states, actions and rewards (a trajectory or rollout).
concepts.example: One game of tic-tac-toe is an episode: it starts from an empty board, goes through moves and positions, and ends in a win, loss or draw before the next game resets everything.

concepts.name: Episodic and Continuing Tasks
concepts.description: The distinction between RL tasks that break into finite episodes ending in terminal states and tasks that go on forever, which require discounting or average reward to define a finite return.
concepts.example: A game of chess ends, so it is episodic; a thermostat controlling a building runs forever, so it is continuing and needs discounting to keep its total reward finite.

concepts.name: Epistemic and Aleatoric Uncertainty
concepts.description: Two sources of predictive uncertainty: epistemic uncertainty comes from limited knowledge and shrinks with more data, while aleatoric uncertainty is inherent noise in the data that cannot be reduced.
concepts.example: A weather model unsure about a region it has rarely seen has epistemic uncertainty that more data fixes; a fair coin flip has aleatoric uncertainty that stays 50/50 no matter how much data you collect.

concepts.name: Epsilon-Greedy
concepts.description: An exploration rule that picks the action with the highest estimated value most of the time but chooses a random action with small probability epsilon.
concepts.example: With epsilon = 0.1, a diner orders their favourite dish 9 nights out of 10 and on the 10th picks a random dish from the menu, sometimes discovering a new favourite.

concepts.name: Evolution Strategies
concepts.description: Black-box optimization methods that sample a population of perturbed parameter vectors, evaluate them, and move the search distribution toward better ones; CMA-ES also adapts the covariance. Used as a scalable RL alternative.
concepts.example: Jiggle a robot's 1000 weights in 50 random directions, test each version, then nudge the weights toward the directions that walked farthest, and repeat; no gradients through the robot needed.

concepts.name: Exact Inference (Graphical Models)
concepts.description: Computing posterior marginals or the most probable assignment in a graphical model exactly, by methods such as variable elimination or the junction tree, which can be exponential in treewidth.
concepts.example: In a tiny network with Rain, Sprinkler and Wet Grass, you can compute P(Rain | wet grass) exactly by summing over the sprinkler's two values; no sampling or approximation needed.

concepts.name: EXP3
concepts.description: An algorithm for adversarial multi-armed bandits that keeps exponential weights over arms, samples from them mixed with uniform exploration, and updates using importance-weighted reward estimates.
concepts.example: Against an adversary who changes ad payoffs each day, EXP3 picks ads at random with weights, then boosts the shown ad's weight by its reward divided by the chance it was shown.

concepts.name: Expectation Propagation
concepts.description: An approximate Bayesian inference algorithm that approximates each factor of the posterior with an exponential-family term and refines them iteratively by matching moments.
concepts.example: To approximate a messy posterior, replace each data point's factor with a simple Gaussian bump, then revisit each bump in turn and adjust it so the overall approximation matches the true moments better.

concepts.name: Expected SARSA
concepts.description: A TD control algorithm like SARSA, but its target uses the expected value of the next state's Q-values under the policy instead of the single sampled next action, which lowers variance.
concepts.example: If the next state's actions are worth 10 and 0 and the policy picks each half the time, Expected SARSA uses 5 as the next value instead of whichever one random sample happened to pick.

concepts.name: Experience Replay
concepts.description: Storing past transitions in a buffer and training on random mini-batches drawn from it, which breaks correlations between consecutive samples and lets each experience be reused many times.
concepts.example: Instead of learning only from the last few seconds of play, the agent saves 1 million past moves in a buffer and studies random handfuls of them, like reviewing shuffled flashcards.

concepts.name: Explaining Away
concepts.description: A reasoning pattern in Bayesian networks where observing a common effect makes two independent causes dependent, so confirming one cause lowers the probability of the other.
concepts.example: Grass can be wet from rain or the sprinkler. Seeing wet grass makes both more likely, but then learning the sprinkler was on makes rain less likely, because the sprinkler already explains it.

concepts.name: Exploration–Exploitation Tradeoff
concepts.description: The dilemma of choosing between exploiting actions already known to give good reward and exploring other actions that might turn out better.
concepts.example: Going to your favourite restaurant guarantees a good meal (exploit), but trying a new place might find an even better one or a bad one (explore); you must balance the two.

concepts.name: Extended Kalman Filter
concepts.description: A version of the Kalman filter for nonlinear systems that linearizes the dynamics and measurement functions around the current estimate using their Jacobians.
concepts.example: Tracking a robot that turns in arcs: the motion is nonlinear, so the EKF approximates it with a straight-line slope at the current estimate and then applies the usual Kalman update.

concepts.name: Factor Graph
concepts.description: A bipartite graph with variable nodes and factor nodes that shows how a joint distribution or function factorizes into local terms; it is the natural setting for message passing.
concepts.example: P(a,b,c) = f1(a,b) times f2(b,c) becomes a graph with variable circles a, b, c and factor squares f1 and f2, each square linked to the variables it uses.

concepts.name: Feudal Reinforcement Learning
concepts.description: A hierarchical RL approach where a manager sets goals for lower-level workers, which are rewarded for reaching them; FeUdal Networks implement this with directional goals in a learned latent space.
concepts.example: A manager tells a worker 'go to the kitchen'; the worker is rewarded for getting there, not for the overall goal, while the manager is rewarded when the household task gets done.

concepts.name: First-Visit Monte Carlo
concepts.description: A Monte Carlo prediction method that estimates a state's value by averaging returns that follow only the first visit to that state in each episode; every-visit MC averages after all visits.
concepts.example: If state A is visited at steps 2 and 7 of an episode, first-visit MC records only the return from step 2 and averages such returns over many episodes to estimate A's value.

concepts.name: Fitted Q-Iteration
concepts.description: A batch RL algorithm that repeatedly fits a regression model, such as trees or a neural network, to Bellman targets computed from a fixed dataset of transitions.
concepts.example: From a fixed log of 10,000 transitions, compute targets r + gamma times the max of the current Q-model, fit a random forest to them, and repeat 50 rounds to get better and better Q-values.

concepts.name: Forward Algorithm
concepts.description: A dynamic programming algorithm for hidden Markov models that computes the probability of an observation sequence by summing over hidden state paths step by step.
concepts.example: For an HMM of weather and ice-cream sales, you can get the probability of seeing sales 3, 1, 3 by passing running totals forward day by day, rather than listing all 8 weather sequences.

concepts.name: Function Approximation (Reinforcement Learning)
concepts.description: Representing value functions or policies with a parameterized function, such as a linear model or neural network, instead of a table, so learning generalizes across large or continuous state spaces.
concepts.example: Backgammon has about 10^20 positions, too many for a table. A neural network instead takes board features and outputs a value, so lessons from one position carry over to similar ones.

concepts.name: Generative Adversarial Imitation Learning
concepts.description: An imitation learning method that trains a policy to fool a discriminator distinguishing its state-action pairs from an expert's, matching expert behavior without explicitly recovering a reward.
concepts.example: A policy tries to drive like an expert while a discriminator guesses 'expert or imitator?' for each move. The policy is rewarded for fooling it, until its driving is indistinguishable.

concepts.name: Game Tree
concepts.description: A tree whose nodes are game positions and whose edges are moves, with leaves at terminal positions; it is the structure explored by game-playing search algorithms.
concepts.example: In tic-tac-toe, the root is the empty board, it has 9 children for the first move, each of those has 8 children, and so on down to finished games at the leaves.

concepts.name: Gaussian Process Classification
concepts.description: Classification with a Gaussian process prior over a latent function that is passed through a sigmoid; since the posterior is not Gaussian, it is approximated with Laplace, EP or variational methods.
concepts.example: To label points as spam or not, a GP draws a smooth hidden score over inputs and squashes it through a sigmoid into a probability; the non-Gaussian result is approximated, for example with Laplace.

concepts.name: Generalized Advantage Estimation
concepts.description: A method for estimating advantages as an exponentially weighted sum of multi-step TD errors, with lambda trading bias against variance in policy gradient methods.
concepts.example: With lambda = 0, the advantage is just the one-step TD error (low variance, more bias); with lambda = 1 it is the full Monte Carlo return minus the value; 0.95 blends them.

concepts.name: Generalized Policy Iteration
concepts.description: The general idea of letting policy evaluation and policy improvement interact, fully or partially, until both stabilize at the optimal policy; most RL methods fit this pattern.
concepts.example: Like a coach and player: the coach evaluates how the current game plan is doing, the player adjusts the plan to the evaluation, and they keep alternating until no change helps.

concepts.name: Generative vs. Discriminative Models
concepts.description: The distinction between models that learn the joint distribution of inputs and labels, such as naive Bayes, and models that learn the label given the input directly, such as logistic regression.
concepts.example: To tell cats from dogs, a generative model learns what cats look like and what dogs look like; a discriminative model only learns the boundary that separates them.

concepts.name: Gittins Index
concepts.description: A result showing that for discounted bandit problems with independent arms, the optimal strategy is to always play the arm with the highest index, computed separately for each arm.
concepts.example: Each slot machine gets a single score computed from its own history; with discounting, always pulling the machine with the highest score is provably optimal, so a hard joint problem splits into easy pieces.

concepts.name: Go-Explore
concepts.description: An exploration algorithm that keeps an archive of interesting states, returns to a promising one, and explores from there; it solved hard-exploration Atari games like Montezuma's Revenge.
concepts.example: In a maze game, save a snapshot each time you reach a new room. Later, reload a promising snapshot and explore onward from there, instead of starting over from the entrance every time.

concepts.name: Goal-Conditioned Reinforcement Learning
concepts.description: Reinforcement learning where policies and value functions take a goal as extra input, so one agent learns to reach many different goals; universal value function approximators are an example.
concepts.example: Instead of training one robot arm policy for 'put the cup at A' and another for 'at B', train one policy that takes the target location as input and can place the cup anywhere.

concepts.name: Gradient Temporal Difference Learning
concepts.description: TD methods such as GTD and TDC that perform true stochastic gradient descent on a projected Bellman error, so they stay stable with off-policy learning and linear function approximation.
concepts.example: Ordinary TD with off-policy data and linear features can blow up to infinity. GTD instead follows a true gradient of a projected error, so the weights converge even in such cases.

concepts.name: Gymnasium
concepts.description: A Python library, the successor to OpenAI Gym, that provides a standard API and a collection of environments for developing and benchmarking reinforcement learning agents.
concepts.example: env = gymnasium.make('CartPole-v1'); obs, info = env.reset(); then repeatedly call env.step(action) to get the next observation, reward and done flags until the pole falls.

concepts.name: Hammersley–Clifford Theorem
concepts.description: A theorem stating that a positive distribution satisfies the Markov properties of an undirected graph exactly when it factorizes into a product of potentials over the graph's cliques.
concepts.example: In a chain A - B - C, the theorem says A and C being independent given B is equivalent to P(a,b,c) factoring as f(a,b) times g(b,c), as long as all probabilities are positive.

concepts.name: Hierarchical Bayesian Model
concepts.description: A Bayesian model with several levels where parameters of individual groups are drawn from shared higher-level distributions, so groups borrow statistical strength from each other.
concepts.example: Estimating pass rates for 20 schools, some with just 5 students: each school's rate is drawn from a shared district distribution, so small schools borrow strength and avoid extreme estimates.

concepts.name: Hierarchical Reinforcement Learning
concepts.description: The area of RL that breaks a task into a hierarchy of subtasks or temporally extended actions, with higher levels choosing subgoals or skills and lower levels executing them.
concepts.example: To make breakfast, a high-level policy picks subtasks like 'boil water' and 'toast bread', and lower-level policies handle the individual hand movements for each.

concepts.name: Hindsight Experience Replay
concepts.description: A replay technique for goal-conditioned agents that relabels failed episodes as if the goal had been the state actually reached, turning sparse-reward failures into useful training signal.
concepts.example: A robot meant to push a puck to spot A pushes it to spot B instead. HER also stores the episode as 'goal was B, success', so the robot learns something useful from the miss.

concepts.name: Planning Horizon
