concepts.description: The number of future time steps an agent considers when making decisions; tasks can have a finite horizon or an infinite horizon, usually handled with discounting.
concepts.example: A chess program that looks 3 moves ahead has a horizon of 3; an investor with gamma = 0.99 effectively cares about roughly the next 100 steps.

concepts.name: Imitation Learning
concepts.description: Learning to act by imitating demonstrations from an expert, either by copying actions directly with supervised learning or by inferring the expert's goals.
concepts.example: A self-driving car records 100 hours of a human driving and learns to output the same steering for the same camera images, much as an apprentice copies a master.

concepts.name: IMPALA
concepts.description: A scalable distributed actor-critic architecture where many actors generate experience for a central learner, with the V-trace importance-weighting correction compensating for policy lag.
concepts.example: Hundreds of actor machines play games and send trajectories to one learner GPU. Since actors run slightly old policies, V-trace re-weights their data to correct for the lag.

concepts.name: Independent Q-Learning
concepts.description: A multi-agent approach in which each agent runs its own Q-learning and treats the other agents as part of the environment; simple, but the environment becomes non-stationary.
concepts.example: Two robots learning to pass a ball each run their own Q-learning and see the other as just part of the world; as both change, each one's world keeps shifting.

concepts.name: Indian Buffet Process
concepts.description: A Bayesian nonparametric prior over binary matrices with unbounded columns, letting each object have a potentially infinite set of latent features, of which only finitely many are active.
concepts.example: Customers enter a buffet with endless dishes: each tries popular dishes in proportion to how many before took them, then a few new ones. Each customer is an object and each dish a hidden feature.

concepts.name: Intrinsic Curiosity Module
concepts.description: A curiosity method that rewards the agent by the error of a learned forward dynamics model, predicting in a feature space trained with an inverse dynamics model to ignore irrelevant details.
concepts.example: An agent predicts what happens after pressing a button; if its prediction is badly wrong, it gets a curiosity reward, so it seeks out situations it does not yet understand.

concepts.name: Intrinsic Motivation
concepts.description: Reward generated by the agent itself, for example for novelty, surprise or learning progress, to drive exploration when external rewards are sparse.
concepts.example: A child plays with a new toy without any outside prize, just because it is novel. An RL agent can likewise earn self-made rewards for visiting rarely seen states.

concepts.name: Inverse Reinforcement Learning
concepts.description: The problem of inferring the reward function that an expert is optimizing from observations of its behavior, which can then be used to train a policy.
concepts.example: Watching a taxi driver avoid highways even when faster, IRL infers the driver's reward puts a high cost on tolls, then plans new routes using that inferred reward.

concepts.name: Implicit Q-Learning
concepts.description: An offline RL algorithm that learns values with expectile regression over dataset actions only, never querying unseen actions, and then extracts a policy by advantage-weighted regression.
concepts.example: From a dataset of driving logs, IQL estimates how good the best actions seen in the data are, using a high expectile, and then copies those actions more strongly the larger their advantage.

concepts.name: Implicit Quantile Networks
concepts.description: A distributional RL method that learns a network mapping sampled quantile fractions to return quantiles, giving a continuous model of the full return distribution.
concepts.example: Ask the network 'what is the 10th-percentile return?' or 'the 90th?' by feeding in 0.1 or 0.9, and it answers; any quantile can be queried, giving a smooth picture of all outcomes.

concepts.name: Ising Model
concepts.description: A model of binary spins on a lattice with pairwise interactions; in machine learning it is a classic pairwise Markov random field used to study inference and phase transitions.
concepts.example: Picture a grid of magnets each pointing up or down; neighbours prefer to align. The model gives each arrangement a probability, with aligned patterns being more likely.

concepts.name: Junction Tree Algorithm
concepts.description: An exact inference algorithm that converts a graphical model into a tree of cliques and passes messages along it to compute all marginals, with cost exponential in the largest clique.
concepts.example: A loopy graph A-B-C-D-A is turned into a tree of clusters {A,B,D} and {B,C,D}; messages passed between clusters then give exact marginals for every variable.

concepts.name: Rauch–Tung–Striebel Smoother
concepts.description: An algorithm that refines Kalman filter estimates using all observations, including future ones, by running a backward pass after the forward filtering pass.
concepts.example: Tracking a car, the filter's estimate at noon uses only data up to noon; the smoother revises the noon estimate after seeing where the car was at 12:05, making it more accurate.

concepts.name: λ-Return
concepts.description: A target that averages all n-step returns with weights decaying geometrically by lambda, interpolating between one-step TD (lambda = 0) and Monte Carlo (lambda = 1).
concepts.example: With lambda = 0.5, the target averages the 1-step return with weight 0.5, the 2-step with 0.25, the 3-step with 0.125, and so on; lambda = 1 gives the full Monte Carlo return.

concepts.name: Leapfrog Integration
concepts.description: A numerical method for simulating Hamiltonian dynamics that alternates half-step momentum updates with full-step position updates; it is time-reversible and volume-preserving, which makes it ideal for HMC.
concepts.example: To simulate a ball rolling on a surface: half a step of velocity change, a full step of position, then another half step of velocity. Repeating this keeps the energy nearly constant over long runs.

concepts.name: Least-Squares Temporal Difference
concepts.description: A TD method for linear function approximation that solves for the fixed-point weights directly with least squares instead of incremental updates; LSPI wraps it inside policy iteration.
concepts.example: Rather than nudging weights a little after each transition, LSTD collects all transitions, builds a small matrix equation from their features, and solves it once to get the TD fixed-point weights.

concepts.name: Linear-Chain CRF
concepts.description: A conditional random field whose labels form a chain, modelling the probability of a label sequence given the input; used for tagging tasks like NER and decoded with the Viterbi algorithm.
concepts.example: For the sentence 'Paris is lovely', a CRF scores whole tag sequences like CITY-VERB-ADJ using word features and tag-to-tag transitions, then picks the most likely sequence given the sentence.

concepts.name: Linear Function Approximation
concepts.description: Approximating a value function as a weighted sum of state features, which is simple to update with gradient methods and has well-understood convergence properties.
concepts.example: Estimate a house-cleaning robot's value as 2 times battery level minus 3 times dirt remaining; learning just adjusts the two weights 2 and -3 from experience.

concepts.name: Linear Programming for MDPs
concepts.description: Solving an MDP by writing the Bellman optimality conditions as a linear program over values, or its dual over state-action occupancy measures.
concepts.example: Find the smallest values V(s) such that each V(s) is at least every action's reward plus gamma times expected next V; an LP solver handles these inequalities and returns V*.

concepts.name: LinUCB
concepts.description: A contextual bandit algorithm that models each arm's expected reward as linear in the context and picks the arm with the highest upper confidence bound from a ridge-regression estimate.
concepts.example: A news site sees a user's age and interests, predicts each article's click rate with a linear model, and adds a bonus for articles whose prediction is still uncertain before picking the highest.

concepts.name: Loopy Belief Propagation
concepts.description: Applying belief propagation's message-passing updates to graphs with cycles; it gives approximate marginals and often works well in practice, for example in turbo decoding.
concepts.example: In image denoising, each pixel talks to its neighbours on a grid full of loops. Running ordinary message passing anyway, round after round, usually settles on good approximate pixel beliefs.

concepts.name: MADDPG
concepts.description: A multi-agent extension of DDPG where each agent has a centralized critic that sees all agents' observations and actions during training, while each actor acts on its own observations.
concepts.example: Two drones learning to cooperate: during training each drone's critic sees both drones' positions and actions, but at flight time each drone acts only on its own camera.

concepts.name: MAPPO
concepts.description: Proximal Policy Optimization adapted to cooperative multi-agent settings, typically with shared parameters and a centralized value function; a strong and simple multi-agent baseline.
concepts.example: Five robots share one PPO policy network for acting on their own views, while a shared critic sees the whole map during training; this simple setup does surprisingly well in StarCraft tasks.

concepts.name: Markov Blanket
concepts.description: The set of a node's parents, children and children's other parents in a Bayesian network; given its Markov blanket, the node is conditionally independent of all other variables.
concepts.example: In a family tree of genes, a person's blanket is their parents, their children and their children's other parent; once those are known, no other relative tells you more about them.

concepts.name: Markov Decision Process
concepts.description: A mathematical model of sequential decision making with states, actions, transition probabilities, rewards and a discount factor, where the next state depends only on the current state and action.
concepts.example: A robot vacuum is in a room (state), chooses to move or clean (action), ends up in a new room with some probability, and gets +1 for dust collected; the next step depends only on where it is now.

concepts.name: Markov Random Field
concepts.description: An undirected graphical model in which the joint distribution factorizes into potentials over cliques, and a variable is independent of the rest given its neighbors.
concepts.example: For an image, each pixel's label depends only on its four neighbours; the probability of a labelling is a product of neighbour-agreement scores, normalized to sum to one.

concepts.name: Markov Reward Process
concepts.description: A Markov chain with a reward attached to each state and a discount factor; it describes the value of states without any decisions and is a stepping stone to MDPs.
concepts.example: A student moves between Class, Pub and Sleep with fixed probabilities, earning -2 in class and +1 at the pub; with no choices to make, we can compute how good each place is to be in.

concepts.name: Max-Product Algorithm
concepts.description: A variant of belief propagation that replaces sums with maximizations (sums of logs in max-sum) to find the most probable joint assignment in a graphical model.
concepts.example: To find the single most likely sequence of hidden weather, replace the sums in message passing with max; for a chain this reduces to the Viterbi algorithm.

concepts.name: Maximization Bias
concepts.description: The systematic overestimation that occurs when the maximum of noisy value estimates is used as an estimate of the maximum true value, as in Q-learning targets.
concepts.example: Ten coins each truly land heads 50% of the time, but after 10 flips each, the best-looking coin might show 80%. Picking the max of noisy estimates overstates the true best.

concepts.name: Maximum Entropy Inverse Reinforcement Learning
concepts.description: An inverse RL method that models the expert as choosing trajectories with probability proportional to exponentiated reward and fits the reward by maximum likelihood, resolving ambiguity among rewards.
concepts.example: If an expert takes route A 70% of the time and route B 30%, MaxEnt IRL finds rewards where better routes are exponentially more likely but no unexplained preferences are assumed.

concepts.name: Maximum Entropy Reinforcement Learning
concepts.description: A reinforcement learning framework where the agent maximizes expected reward plus the entropy of its policy, yielding stochastic, robust policies and soft versions of Bellman equations.
concepts.example: Two paths reach the goal equally well; a max-entropy agent keeps choosing both at random instead of locking onto one, so if one gets blocked it already knows the other.

concepts.name: Model-Based Policy Optimization
concepts.description: A model-based RL algorithm that learns an ensemble of dynamics models and uses short model rollouts branched from real states to generate extra data for a Soft Actor-Critic learner.
concepts.example: A robot learns several dynamics models from real runs, then starts short 5-step imagined rollouts from real states it visited and trains SAC on that extra imagined data.

concepts.name: Mean-Field Approximation
concepts.description: A variational inference approach that approximates a complex posterior with a fully factorized distribution where each variable is independent, optimized by coordinate updates.
concepts.example: Approximating the joint posterior of a person's height and weight as if they were independent: fit a separate simple distribution to each, then update each in turn using the other's average.

concepts.name: Meta-Reinforcement Learning
concepts.description: Reinforcement learning methods that learn how to learn across a distribution of tasks, so the agent can adapt to a new task from only a few episodes of experience.
concepts.example: After training on hundreds of different mazes, an agent can solve a brand-new maze in a few tries, because it has learned a fast way to explore and adapt rather than a single route.

concepts.name: Minimax
concepts.description: A decision rule for two-player zero-sum games that searches the game tree, assuming the opponent always picks the move worst for you, and chooses the move with the best guaranteed outcome.
concepts.example: In tic-tac-toe, you look at each move, assume the opponent then picks the reply worst for you, and choose the move whose worst case is best, like a cautious player.

concepts.name: Model-Based Reinforcement Learning
concepts.description: Reinforcement learning methods that learn or use a model of the environment's dynamics and rewards, and use it to plan or to generate simulated experience, often improving sample efficiency.
concepts.example: A chess player who understands the rules can think 'if I move here, they will move there' before acting; a model-based agent likewise learns how the world responds and plans with that.

concepts.name: Model-Free Reinforcement Learning
concepts.description: Reinforcement learning methods that learn value functions or policies directly from experience without building a model of the environment's transitions, such as Q-learning and policy gradients.
concepts.example: A child learns which playground slide is most fun by trying them and remembering how each felt, without working out the physics of slides; model-free RL learns values the same way.

concepts.name: Model Predictive Control
concepts.description: A control method that at each step solves an optimization over a short future horizon using a dynamics model, applies only the first action, and then re-plans.
concepts.example: Driving a car, plan the next 3 seconds of steering that best follows the road, turn the wheel for just the first 0.1 second, then re-plan from the new position.

concepts.name: Monte Carlo Methods in Reinforcement Learning
concepts.description: RL methods that estimate values by averaging complete returns observed after visiting states or actions in sampled episodes, without bootstrapping or a model.
concepts.example: To estimate a blackjack hand's value, play 10,000 games from that hand and average the final winnings; no step-by-step bootstrapping, just complete outcomes.

concepts.name: Monte Carlo Tree Search
concepts.description: A search algorithm that incrementally builds a game tree by repeatedly selecting a path, expanding a node, running a random playout and backing up the result, focusing effort on promising moves.
concepts.example: In Go, from the current position try a promising move, play the rest of the game randomly, record win or loss, and repeat thousands of times, steering more tries toward moves that win often.

concepts.name: Moral Graph
concepts.description: Turning a Bayesian network into an undirected moral graph by connecting all parents of each node and dropping edge directions, a step used before building a junction tree.
concepts.example: If Rain and Sprinkler both point to Wet Grass, moralization 'marries' the two parents with a new edge and then drops all arrows, giving an undirected triangle.

concepts.name: Maximum a Posteriori Policy Optimization
concepts.description: An off-policy actor-critic algorithm that frames policy improvement as inference, alternating an EM-like step that reweights actions by Q-values with a KL-constrained fit of the new policy.
concepts.example: MPO first reweights candidate actions by how good the critic says they are, forming a better target distribution, then moves the policy toward it while a KL limit stops it changing too much.

concepts.name: MuJoCo
concepts.description: A fast physics engine for simulating articulated bodies with contacts, widely used as a benchmark suite for continuous-control and robotics reinforcement learning.
concepts.example: In MuJoCo's HalfCheetah task, the agent controls 6 joint torques of a 2D cheetah and is rewarded for running forward; thousands of physics steps run per second on a laptop.

concepts.name: Multi-Agent Reinforcement Learning
concepts.description: The study of several learning agents acting in a shared environment, cooperatively or competitively, where each agent's environment is non-stationary because the others are also learning.
concepts.example: Several self-driving cars learning at a busy junction: each car's best move depends on what the others learn, so the world keeps changing from every car's point of view.

concepts.name: MuZero
concepts.description: A DeepMind agent that combines Monte Carlo tree search with a learned model predicting rewards, values and policies in a latent space, mastering Go, chess, shogi and Atari without being given the rules.
concepts.example: MuZero is never told the rules of chess. It learns a hidden model that predicts rewards, values and good moves, and runs tree search inside that model to choose each move.

concepts.name: n-Step TD
concepts.description: TD methods whose update target sums n actual rewards and then bootstraps from the value estimate n steps later, spanning the range between one-step TD and Monte Carlo.
concepts.example: With n = 3, the target is the next 3 actual rewards plus the discounted value estimate 3 steps later, e.g. 1 + 0.9 times 0 + 0.81 times 2 + 0.729 times V(s3).

concepts.name: Nash Equilibrium
concepts.description: A combination of strategies, one per player, where no player can do better by changing only their own strategy; every finite game has at least one in mixed strategies.
concepts.example: In rock-paper-scissors, both players choosing each option one-third of the time is a Nash equilibrium: given the other's strategy, neither can win more by switching.

concepts.name: Natural Policy Gradient
concepts.description: A policy gradient method that rescales the gradient by the inverse Fisher information matrix, so updates follow the steepest direction in policy-distribution space rather than parameter space.
concepts.example: Two parameter changes of the same size can change a policy a lot or barely at all. The natural gradient measures step size by change in behavior, using Fisher information, so steps are consistent.

concepts.name: Noisy Networks
concepts.description: An exploration method that adds learnable, parameterized noise to a network's weights, so the agent learns how much randomness to use instead of relying on epsilon-greedy.
concepts.example: Instead of epsilon-greedy dice rolls, each network weight gets a learnable noise knob; the agent can keep randomness high where unsure and turn it down where it has learned what to do.

concepts.name: Normal-Inverse-Gamma Distribution
concepts.description: A joint distribution over a normal mean and variance that is the conjugate prior for a normal likelihood with both parameters unknown, giving closed-form Bayesian updates.
concepts.example: Measuring an unknown machine's output with unknown spread, start with a normal-inverse-gamma prior; after each batch of readings, you simply update four numbers to get the posterior.

concepts.name: Observation (Reinforcement Learning)
concepts.description: The information an agent receives from the environment at each step; it may reveal the full state or only part of it, as in partially observable problems.
concepts.example: In poker, the full state includes everyone's cards, but your observation is only your hand and the shared cards; you must decide using that partial view.

concepts.name: Off-Policy Evaluation
concepts.description: The problem of estimating how well a target policy would perform using only data collected by a different behavior policy, typically via importance sampling, model-based or doubly robust estimators.
concepts.example: Before switching a recommendation system to a new policy, reweight last month's logs: clicks on items the new policy would show more often count extra, estimating its click rate without deploying it.

concepts.name: Off-Policy Learning
concepts.description: Learning about a target policy, such as the greedy policy, from data generated by a different behavior policy; Q-learning is the classic example.
concepts.example: A student learns the best chess strategy by studying games played by beginners; the games were made by one policy, but the lessons are about another, better one.

concepts.name: Offline Reinforcement Learning
concepts.description: Reinforcement learning from a fixed, previously collected dataset with no further interaction with the environment, useful where exploration is costly or unsafe.
concepts.example: A hospital wants a better treatment policy but cannot experiment on patients, so it learns only from years of existing patient records.

concepts.name: On-Policy Learning
concepts.description: Learning the value of, or improving, the same policy that is being used to choose actions and collect data; SARSA and PPO are examples.
concepts.example: A tennis player improves by reviewing their own matches with their current style, then adjusting; after changing style, old matches are no longer the right evidence.

concepts.name: OpenAI Five
concepts.description: OpenAI's system that defeated world champions at Dota 2, training five LSTM-based agents with large-scale PPO and self-play over months of simulated game time.
concepts.example: Five neural network agents played Dota 2 against copies of themselves for the equivalent of 45,000 years of games, learning teamwork that beat the world champion team in 2019.

concepts.name: Optimal Policy
concepts.description: A policy whose expected return is at least as high as every other policy's from every state; every finite MDP has at least one deterministic optimal policy.
concepts.example: In a grid world where reaching the goal gives +1, an optimal policy takes the shortest path from every square; no other policy gets a higher expected return anywhere.

concepts.name: Optimal Value Function
concepts.description: The largest value achievable from each state (V*) or state-action pair (Q*) under any policy; acting greedily with respect to Q* gives an optimal policy.
concepts.example: In a grid world with gamma = 0.9 and +1 at the goal, a square two moves away has V* = 0.9; that is the best any policy can do from there.

concepts.name: Optimistic Initial Values
concepts.description: Setting initial value estimates higher than any realistic return so that an agent tries untested actions, which disappoint it, encouraging systematic early exploration.
aliases: optimism in the face of uncertainty
concepts.example: Start every slot machine's estimate at 10 when real payouts are around 1. Each pull disappoints, lowering that estimate, so the agent naturally tries every machine before settling.

concepts.name: Options Framework
concepts.description: A formalism for temporally extended actions, where an option has an initiation set, an internal policy and a termination condition; options turn an MDP into a semi-MDP.
concepts.example: 'Go to the door' is an option: it can start anywhere in the room, follows its own walking policy, and ends when the door is reached; a higher policy chooses among such options.

concepts.name: Parameter Learning (Graphical Models)
concepts.description: Estimating the numerical parameters of a graphical model with known structure, such as conditional probability tables, from data by maximum likelihood, Bayesian estimation or EM when data are missing.
concepts.example: Given 100 days of data on rain and wet grass and a known graph, estimate P(wet | rain) as the fraction of rainy days with wet grass; with missing values, use EM instead of counting.

concepts.name: Partially Observable Markov Decision Process
concepts.description: An extension of an MDP in which the agent cannot see the true state and instead receives observations, so it must act on a belief, a probability distribution over states.
concepts.example: A robot in a corridor with identical doors cannot tell which door it is at, so it keeps probabilities like 60% door 1, 40% door 3 and updates them after each move and sensor reading.

concepts.name: Particle Filter
concepts.description: A sequential Monte Carlo method that tracks the hidden state of a dynamic system with a set of weighted samples, propagating, reweighting by observations and resampling them over time.
concepts.example: To track a lost hiker, scatter 1000 guess points, move each according to walking speed, keep more copies of guesses that match a new phone-tower signal, and repeat.

concepts.name: Partition Function (Statistics)
concepts.description: The normalizing constant that makes an unnormalized probability distribution sum or integrate to one; computing it is often intractable in graphical and energy-based models.
concepts.example: If three outcomes have unnormalized scores 2, 3 and 5, the partition function is 10, and dividing gives probabilities 0.2, 0.3 and 0.5.

concepts.name: Probabilistic Ensembles with Trajectory Sampling
concepts.description: A model-based RL method that learns an ensemble of probabilistic neural network dynamics models and plans actions with model predictive control by sampling trajectories through them.
concepts.example: PETS learns 5 neural network models of a robot's physics, simulates many candidate action sequences through them, keeps the best ones, and executes only the first action before re-planning.

concepts.name: PILCO
concepts.description: A highly data-efficient model-based policy search method that learns a Gaussian process dynamics model and computes analytic policy gradients while propagating model uncertainty.
concepts.example: PILCO learned to swing up and balance a real cart-pole in about 7 trials by modelling the physics with a Gaussian process and computing exact policy gradients through predicted outcomes.

concepts.name: Planning (Reinforcement Learning)
concepts.description: Using a model of the environment to compute or improve a policy or value function by simulating outcomes, rather than learning only from real experience.
concepts.example: Before moving a chess piece, imagine the next few moves on a mental board and pick the line that ends best; the board in your head is the model you plan with.

concepts.name: Policy (Reinforcement Learning)
concepts.description: The agent's rule for choosing actions: a mapping from each state to an action, or to probabilities of taking each possible action in that state.
concepts.example: A thermostat policy: if temperature is below 20 degrees, turn heat on; otherwise turn it off. A stochastic policy might instead turn heat on 80% of the time at 19 degrees.

concepts.name: Policy Evaluation
concepts.description: Computing the value function of a given policy, for example by iterating its Bellman expectation equation until the values converge.
concepts.example: For a random-walking robot in a 4x4 grid, start all values at 0 and repeatedly set each square's value to the average of reward plus next-square value until the numbers stop changing.

concepts.name: Policy Gradient Method
concepts.description: A family of RL methods that parameterize the policy directly and adjust its parameters by gradient ascent on expected return, estimated from sampled trajectories.
concepts.example: A robot arm tries a throw; if the throw scored well, increase the probability of the motions it used, if poorly, decrease it, repeating over thousands of throws.

concepts.name: Policy Gradient Theorem
concepts.description: A theorem giving the gradient of expected return with respect to policy parameters as an expectation of the action-value times the gradient of the log-policy, without differentiating the dynamics.
concepts.example: If an action led to return 10 and its log-probability gradient points up, nudge parameters that way, scaled by 10; averaging such terms gives the true gradient of expected return.

concepts.name: Policy Improvement Theorem
concepts.description: A theorem stating that acting greedily with respect to a policy's action values gives a new policy that is at least as good as the old one in every state.
concepts.example: If your current route says 'turn left' but evaluation shows turning right then following the old route is better, switching to always turning right there can only help.

concepts.name: Policy Iteration
concepts.description: A dynamic programming algorithm that alternates full policy evaluation with greedy policy improvement until the policy stops changing, which yields an optimal policy.
concepts.example: Start with a random grid-world policy; compute its values exactly, switch every square to the best action under those values, and repeat; it typically finishes in a handful of rounds.

concepts.name: Potential-Based Reward Shaping
concepts.description: A result that adding a shaping reward of the form gamma times Phi(next state) minus Phi(state) for some potential function Phi changes learning speed but provably not the optimal policy.
concepts.example: In a maze, give a bonus of gamma times (minus distance to goal at the next square) minus (minus distance now); moving closer pays, but the best path stays exactly the same.

concepts.name: Principle of Optimality
concepts.description: Bellman's principle that an optimal policy's remaining decisions must themselves be optimal for the state reached, so optimal solutions are built from optimal subsolutions.
concepts.example: If the fastest route from Paris to Rome passes through Milan, then its Milan-to-Rome part must be the fastest route from Milan to Rome too.

concepts.name: Prioritized Experience Replay
concepts.description: A replay scheme that samples transitions with probability related to their TD error, so surprising experiences are replayed more often, with importance weights correcting the bias.
concepts.example: If most replayed moments are boring but one move led to a huge surprise, replay that surprising transition more often, like re-studying the questions you got most wrong.

concepts.name: Prioritized Sweeping
concepts.description: A model-based planning method that keeps a priority queue of states whose values would change most and propagates updates backward to their predecessors first.
concepts.example: When the agent finds the goal value changed, it updates the states leading into it first, then their predecessors, always handling the biggest pending change next.

concepts.name: Probabilistic Graphical Model
concepts.description: A framework that represents a joint probability distribution with a graph whose nodes are random variables and whose edges encode dependencies, including Bayesian networks and Markov random fields.
concepts.example: Draw circles for Rain, Sprinkler and Wet Grass and arrows for causes; the picture tells you the joint probability splits into three small tables instead of one big one.

concepts.name: Probabilistic Machine Learning
concepts.description: An approach to machine learning that treats models, parameters and predictions as probability distributions and uses probabilistic inference to learn and quantify uncertainty.
concepts.example: Instead of predicting tomorrow's temperature as exactly 21 degrees, a probabilistic model says '21 plus or minus 2', and it keeps uncertainty over its own parameters too.

concepts.name: Probabilistic Programming
concepts.description: Writing probabilistic models as ordinary programs with random variables, and letting a general inference engine such as MCMC or variational inference compute the posterior automatically.
concepts.example: Write a few lines: 'bias = uniform(0,1); flips ~ bernoulli(bias); observe flips = 7 heads of 10', and the engine returns the posterior over bias automatically.

concepts.name: PUCT
concepts.description: A tree-search selection rule, used in AlphaGo and AlphaZero, that adds to each action's value an exploration bonus scaled by a learned policy prior and the visit counts.
concepts.example: If a move has average value 0.5 but the policy network gives it prior 0.4 and it has been tried only twice, PUCT adds a big bonus, so search tries it before a 0.55 move already explored 100 times.

concepts.name: PyMC
concepts.description: A Python library for Bayesian modeling and probabilistic programming that lets users specify models in code and fit them with MCMC samplers such as NUTS or with variational inference.
concepts.example: In a few lines of Python, declare 'rate = Exponential(1); visits = Poisson(rate, observed=data)', call pm.sample(), and get posterior draws for the rate from the NUTS sampler.

concepts.name: Pyro
concepts.description: A probabilistic programming language built on PyTorch, with NumPyro as its JAX-based sibling, focused on scalable stochastic variational inference and deep probabilistic models.
concepts.example: Write a PyTorch model with pyro.sample statements for latent variables, write a guide for the approximate posterior, and fit both with SVI on mini-batches, even for big neural models.

concepts.name: Q-Learning
concepts.description: An off-policy TD control algorithm that updates the value of each action toward the reward plus the discounted maximum Q-value of the next state, converging to the optimal action values.
concepts.example: A robot at a crossroads goes left, gets -1, and sees the best next action is worth 10. With gamma 0.9 the target is -1 + 9 = 8, and Q(crossroads, left) moves part way from its old value toward 8.

concepts.name: QMIX
concepts.description: A cooperative multi-agent Q-learning method that combines per-agent Q-values into a joint value with a mixing network kept monotonic, so each agent's greedy action stays consistent with the team.
concepts.example: Three StarCraft units each estimate their own Q-values; a mixing network combines them into a team value that only rises when any unit's value rises, so each unit's greedy choice stays team-optimal.

concepts.name: Quantile Regression DQN
concepts.description: A distributional RL algorithm that represents the return distribution with a fixed set of quantiles learned by quantile regression, using a Wasserstein-friendly loss.
concepts.example: Instead of saying 'this action is worth 5', QR-DQN outputs 10 numbers, like 1, 2, 3, ..., 9, 10, marking the return's 5th, 15th, ... 95th percentiles, and learns them with quantile regression.

concepts.name: Recurrent Replay Distributed DQN
concepts.description: A distributed DQN agent that trains recurrent LSTM Q-networks from prioritized replay of stored sequences, using burn-in to reconstruct hidden states; it set strong Atari results.
concepts.example: Many actors store long 80-step game sequences; the learner replays them through an LSTM Q-network, first running 40 burn-in steps to warm up its memory before learning from the rest.

concepts.name: Rainbow DQN
concepts.description: An agent that combines six DQN improvements, namely double Q-learning, dueling networks, prioritized replay, multi-step returns, distributional C51 and noisy nets, to get much better Atari performance.
concepts.example: Rainbow is like a car built from the best parts of six other cars: each DQN improvement helps alone, and putting them together gave a big jump in Atari scores.

concepts.name: Random Network Distillation
concepts.description: An exploration bonus equal to the error of a network trained to predict the outputs of a fixed, randomly initialized network; the error is high on novel states.
concepts.example: A frozen random network maps each screen to a fingerprint, and a second network learns to copy it. Screens seen often are copied well; a brand-new screen gives a big error, which becomes the curiosity reward.

concepts.name: REINFORCE
concepts.description: The basic Monte Carlo policy gradient algorithm, which samples full episodes and increases the log-probability of each action in proportion to the return that followed it.
concepts.example: After an episode that earned return 20, raise the log-probability of every action taken by an amount proportional to 20; after an episode earning 2, raise them much less.

concepts.name: Resampling (Particle Filter)
concepts.description: The step in particle filtering that draws a new set of particles in proportion to their weights, discarding low-weight particles and duplicating high-weight ones to avoid weight degeneracy.
concepts.example: Out of 100 particles, one has weight 0.5 and many have nearly 0. Resampling draws a fresh 100, about half of them copies of the heavy one, and drops most of the near-zero ones.

concepts.name: Retrace(λ)
concepts.description: An off-policy multi-step return algorithm that weights traces by truncated importance ratios, giving low variance and guaranteed convergence for any behavior policy.
concepts.example: Learning from old replay data, Retrace multiplies each step of the trace by min(1, target prob / behavior prob), so it cuts the trace when actions are unlikely under the new policy but never blows it up.

concepts.name: Return (Reinforcement Learning)
concepts.description: The total reward an agent collects from a time step onward, usually the discounted sum of future rewards; RL agents try to maximize its expected value.
concepts.example: Rewards 1, 0, 2 with gamma 0.5 give a return of 1 + 0.5 times 0 + 0.25 times 2 = 1.5 from the first step.

concepts.name: Reward Hypothesis
concepts.description: The idea that every goal or purpose an agent might have can be expressed as maximizing the expected cumulative sum of a scalar reward signal.
concepts.example: Even a complex goal like 'win at chess' can be written as +1 for a win, -1 for a loss, 0 otherwise; the hypothesis claims every goal can be reduced to some such number to maximize.

concepts.name: Reward Shaping
concepts.description: Adding extra reward signals to guide an agent toward good behavior faster, such as rewards for progress toward a goal; done carelessly it can change what the agent learns.
concepts.example: A robot only rewarded for scoring a goal may never stumble on one, so give small rewards for moving toward the ball; careless bonuses, though, might make it circle the ball forever.

concepts.name: Reward Signal
concepts.description: The scalar number the environment sends to the agent after each action, indicating how good the immediate outcome was; it defines the goal in reinforcement learning.
concepts.example: In a video game, the score change after each move is the reward: +10 for a coin, -100 for losing a life, 0 otherwise.

concepts.name: Soft Actor-Critic
concepts.description: Soft Actor-Critic, an off-policy maximum-entropy actor-critic algorithm for continuous control that uses twin Q-networks and a reparameterized stochastic policy, and is known for stability and sample efficiency.
concepts.example: A robot arm learning to grasp keeps its actions as random as possible while still succeeding, uses two critics and takes the smaller estimate to avoid overoptimism, and reuses old data from a replay buffer.

concepts.name: Safe Reinforcement Learning
concepts.description: The area of reinforcement learning concerned with learning policies that respect safety constraints or avoid catastrophic outcomes during both training and deployment.
concepts.example: A delivery robot must maximize deliveries but keep collisions below one per 1000 trips; safe RL treats collisions as a constraint rather than just another penalty.

concepts.name: Sample Efficiency
concepts.description: How much data or how many environment interactions a learning algorithm needs to reach a given level of performance; a key weakness of many deep RL methods.
concepts.example: A person learns Pong in a few minutes, while early DQN needed about 10 million frames, many days of play; the human is far more sample-efficient.

concepts.name: SARSA
concepts.description: An on-policy TD control algorithm that updates Q(s, a) toward the reward plus the discounted value of the next state-action pair actually chosen; SARSA(lambda) adds eligibility traces.
concepts.example: The agent in state S takes A, gets reward 1, lands in S2 and actually chooses A2 with Q = 4; with gamma 0.9 the target is 1 + 3.6 = 4.6, so Q(S, A) moves toward 4.6.

concepts.name: Score Function Estimator
concepts.description: A way to estimate the gradient of an expectation by writing it as the expectation of the function times the gradient of the log-probability; it underlies REINFORCE and black-box VI.
concepts.example: To tune a coin's bias to get more heads, sample flips; for each one, nudge the bias along the gradient of log P(that flip), scaled by its reward. On average this equals the true gradient.

concepts.name: Self-Play
concepts.description: Training an agent by having it play against copies or past versions of itself, providing an ever-improving opponent; central to AlphaGo Zero and TD-Gammon.
concepts.example: AlphaGo Zero started knowing only the rules and played millions of games against itself; every time it improved, its opponent improved too, keeping the challenge just right.

concepts.name: Semi-Gradient Methods
concepts.description: TD methods with function approximation that update weights using the gradient of the current estimate only, ignoring how the bootstrapped target depends on the weights.
concepts.example: In TD with a neural network, the target r + gamma times V(s') also depends on the weights, but semi-gradient methods treat it as a fixed number and only differentiate V(s).

concepts.name: Semi-Markov Decision Process
concepts.description: A generalization of an MDP in which actions can take a variable, random amount of time, used to model temporally extended actions such as options.
concepts.example: A taxi decision 'drive to the airport' might take 20 or 40 minutes, so the model must handle actions lasting random amounts of time, discounting rewards by how long they took.

concepts.name: Sequential Monte Carlo
concepts.description: A family of methods that approximate a sequence of probability distributions with weighted samples, moved forward by importance sampling and resampling steps.
concepts.example: To follow a moving object through 100 video frames, carry a cloud of weighted guesses from frame to frame, reweight them by each frame's evidence, and resample when weights become lopsided.

concepts.name: Stochastic Gradient Langevin Dynamics
concepts.description: A scalable Bayesian sampling method that adds properly scaled Gaussian noise to stochastic gradient updates, so the parameter iterates approximately sample from the posterior.
concepts.example: Train a network with ordinary mini-batch updates but add a bit of random noise, matched to the step size, at every step; the weights then wander around good regions like posterior samples.

concepts.name: Sim-to-Real Transfer
concepts.description: Transferring policies trained in simulation to real robots, often using domain randomization, which trains over many randomized simulator settings so reality looks like one more variation.
concepts.example: Train a robot hand in simulation with randomly varied friction, weights and lighting; the real world then looks like just another variation, and the policy works on the physical hand.

concepts.name: Slice Sampling
concepts.description: An MCMC method that samples by drawing a random height under the density and then sampling uniformly from the horizontal slice where the density exceeds that height.
concepts.example: Standing at x on a bumpy density curve, pick a random height under the curve there, then pick a new x uniformly among points where the curve is above that height, and repeat.

concepts.name: Soft Q-Learning
concepts.description: A maximum-entropy version of Q-learning where the hard max in the Bellman backup is replaced by a log-sum-exp, giving a Boltzmann-like optimal policy over actions.
concepts.example: Next-state Q-values of 2 and 1 give a hard max of 2 but a soft value of log(e^2 + e^1), about 2.31; the soft version rewards having several good options rather than just one.

concepts.name: Boltzmann Exploration
concepts.description: Choosing actions with probabilities given by a softmax of their estimated values, with a temperature controlling how random the choices are; better actions are tried more often.
concepts.example: With action values 2 and 1 and temperature 1, choose the first with probability e^2/(e^2 + e) = 0.73; at high temperature choices become nearly 50/50, at low temperature nearly always the best.

concepts.name: Sparse Gaussian Process
concepts.description: Approximating a Gaussian process with a small set of inducing points that summarize the data, reducing cost from cubic in the dataset size; SVGP trains them with stochastic variational inference.
concepts.example: Instead of using all 100,000 training points, summarize them with 200 inducing points placed across the input space; predictions cost about the same but run thousands of times faster.

concepts.name: Sparse Reward Problem
concepts.description: The difficulty arising when an agent receives nonzero reward only rarely, such as only on reaching a goal, so random exploration seldom finds any learning signal.
concepts.example: A robot gets +1 only when a key ends up in a lock and 0 for everything else, so random flailing almost never earns any reward to learn from.

concepts.name: Stable-Baselines3
concepts.description: A Python library of reliable PyTorch implementations of standard deep RL algorithms such as PPO, SAC, DQN and TD3, with a simple API compatible with Gymnasium environments.
concepts.example: model = PPO('MlpPolicy', 'CartPole-v1'); model.learn(total_timesteps=10000) trains a working agent in two lines, with tested defaults.

concepts.name: Stan
concepts.description: A probabilistic programming language and platform for Bayesian statistical modeling that compiles models to C++ and fits them mainly with the No-U-Turn Hamiltonian Monte Carlo sampler.
concepts.example: Write a Stan model with data, parameters and model blocks for a hierarchical regression; Stan compiles it to C++ and draws posterior samples with NUTS, reporting diagnostics like R-hat.

concepts.name: State (Reinforcement Learning)
concepts.description: A description of the current situation of the environment that the agent uses to make decisions; the set of all possible states is the state space.
concepts.example: In a maze, the state might be the agent's grid coordinates (3, 5); in chess, it is the position of every piece plus whose turn it is.

concepts.name: State-Value Function
concepts.description: A function giving the expected return when starting in a state and following a given policy thereafter; it measures how good it is to be in each state.
concepts.example: If from a given chess position following your usual strategy wins 70% of the time with +1 for a win and 0 otherwise, that position's value under your policy is 0.7.

concepts.name: Stochastic Bandit
concepts.description: A multi-armed bandit where each arm's rewards are drawn independently from a fixed but unknown distribution, and the goal is to minimize regret relative to the best arm.
concepts.example: Three slot machines pay out with fixed hidden chances of 20%, 35% and 50%; each pull is independent, and you want to find and play the 50% one as quickly as possible.

concepts.name: Stochastic Game
concepts.description: A multi-player generalization of an MDP in which the state transitions and each player's reward depend on the joint action of all players; also called a Markov game.
concepts.example: In robot soccer, the next game state and each team's reward depend on what all players do at once; a stochastic game models this as a shared MDP with joint actions.

concepts.name: Stochastic Policy
concepts.description: A policy that outputs a probability distribution over actions in each state and samples the action from it, enabling exploration and the use of policy gradient methods.
concepts.example: In rock-paper-scissors, a policy that plays each move with probability 1/3 cannot be exploited, while any fixed move can; randomness here is the point.

concepts.name: Stochastic Variational Inference
concepts.description: Scaling variational inference to large datasets by optimizing the evidence lower bound with noisy gradients computed on random mini-batches of data.
concepts.example: To fit a topic model on 1 million documents, estimate the ELBO gradient from 100 random documents at a time, scaled up by 10,000, and take small steps, instead of passing over all data each update.

concepts.name: Structure Learning
concepts.description: The problem of learning the graph of a probabilistic graphical model from data, by score-based search such as BIC or by constraint-based independence tests.
concepts.example: Given data on smoking, cancer and coughing, try different arrow layouts and keep the one with the best BIC score, perhaps smoking to cancer to coughing.

concepts.name: Successor Representation
concepts.description: A representation of each state as the expected discounted future occupancy of all other states; values become a dot product with rewards, so they adapt quickly when rewards change.
concepts.example: If from home you expect to visit the cafe about 3 discounted times in future, and the cafe's reward changes to 2, home's value updates instantly by 3 times 2 without relearning.

concepts.name: Tabular Reinforcement Learning
concepts.description: RL methods that store a separate value for every state or state-action pair in a table; they are exact and well understood but only feasible for small, discrete problems.
concepts.example: In a 4x4 grid world with 4 actions, keep a 16 x 4 table of Q-values, one cell per state-action pair, and update cells directly; this would be impossible for chess.

concepts.name: Target Network
concepts.description: A periodically or slowly updated copy of the value network used to compute bootstrap targets, which keeps the targets stable and prevents divergence in deep Q-learning.
concepts.example: Chasing a target that moves every time you step is hard. DQN freezes a copy of the network and uses it for targets, updating the copy only every 10,000 steps.

concepts.name: Twin Delayed DDPG
concepts.description: Twin Delayed DDPG, which improves DDPG for continuous control by taking the minimum of two critics, updating the actor less often, and smoothing target actions with noise.
concepts.example: Two critics value a robot's move as 8 and 6; TD3 trusts 6, updates the actor only every second step, and adds a little noise to target actions so it cannot exploit sharp errors in the critics.

concepts.name: TD Error
concepts.description: The difference between a bootstrapped target, the reward plus the discounted value of the next state, and the current value estimate; it drives TD learning updates.
concepts.example: If V(s) = 5, the reward is 1, and V(s') = 6 with gamma 0.9, the TD error is 1 + 5.4 - 5 = 1.4: things went better than expected, so V(s) should go up.

concepts.name: TD-Gammon
concepts.description: Gerald Tesauro's backgammon program that learned to play at world-class level using TD(lambda) and a neural network trained by self-play, an early landmark of RL.
concepts.example: In 1992 a neural network played 1.5 million backgammon games against itself, learning position values with TD(lambda), and reached near world-champion level, even changing expert opening play.

concepts.name: TD(λ)
concepts.description: A TD learning algorithm that uses eligibility traces to blend one-step TD and Monte Carlo updates, with lambda controlling how far credit is assigned back in time.
concepts.example: With lambda = 0.8, when a reward arrives, the most recent state gets the full TD update, the one before gets 0.8 times gamma as much, and so on, spreading credit backward along the path.

concepts.name: Temporal Difference Learning
concepts.description: A family of RL methods that learn value estimates from each step by moving them toward the reward plus the discounted estimate of the next state, combining Monte Carlo sampling with bootstrapping.
concepts.example: Predicting your drive home: at the office you guess 30 minutes; after 10 minutes in heavy traffic you now guess 25 more, so you update your first guess toward 35 without waiting to arrive.

concepts.name: Thompson Sampling
concepts.description: A bandit strategy that keeps a posterior distribution over each arm's reward, samples one value per arm from it, and plays the arm with the highest sample.
concepts.example: For two ads with 3/10 and 30/100 clicks, sample a plausible click rate for each from its posterior; the uncertain first ad sometimes draws high and gets shown, so it is explored naturally.

concepts.name: Tile Coding
concepts.description: A feature construction method for linear function approximation that covers the state space with several offset grids (tilings) and represents a state by the tiles it falls into.
concepts.example: For a car's position from 0 to 1, overlay 4 grids each shifted slightly; a position activates one tile in each grid, giving 4 active binary features that generalise to nearby positions.

concepts.name: Transfer Learning in Reinforcement Learning
concepts.description: Reusing knowledge such as policies, value functions, representations or models learned on source tasks to learn faster or better on a new target task in reinforcement learning.
concepts.example: A robot that has learned to open drawers can learn to open cupboard doors faster by starting from its drawer-opening policy instead of from scratch.

concepts.name: State Transition Function
concepts.description: The part of an environment model that gives the probability of reaching each next state after taking a given action in a given state.
concepts.example: On icy ground, taking 'move right' from square 4 lands on square 5 with probability 0.8 and slips to square 3 with probability 0.2.

concepts.name: Trust Region Policy Optimization
concepts.description: A policy optimization algorithm that maximizes a surrogate objective subject to a KL-divergence trust region on the policy change, using conjugate gradient to approximate the natural gradient step.
concepts.example: TRPO improves the policy as much as possible while keeping the new policy's average KL divergence from the old one below about 0.01, so one bad update cannot ruin a working policy.

concepts.name: Upper Confidence Bounds Applied to Trees
concepts.description: A version of Monte Carlo tree search that chooses which child to explore using the UCB1 formula, balancing a move's average result against how rarely it has been tried.
concepts.example: A move that won 6 of 10 playouts and a move that won 1 of 2 get scores of their win rate plus a bonus for few tries; the less-tested move may be explored next despite its lower rate.

concepts.name: Uncertainty Quantification
concepts.description: The study of measuring and communicating how uncertain a model's predictions are, using tools such as Bayesian methods, ensembles, calibration and conformal prediction.
concepts.example: A medical model that says '80% likely benign, but I am unsure because this scan looks unusual' is more useful than a bare 'benign', because doctors know when to double-check.

concepts.name: Unscented Kalman Filter
concepts.description: A nonlinear Kalman filter that passes a small, deterministic set of sigma points through the true nonlinear functions to estimate the mean and covariance, avoiding Jacobians.
concepts.example: Instead of using a derivative, pick 5 carefully spaced points around the current estimate, push each through the true nonlinear motion, and compute the mean and spread of where they land.

concepts.name: Upper Confidence Bound
concepts.description: A bandit strategy that picks the arm with the highest optimistic estimate, its average reward plus a bonus that shrinks as the arm is tried more, achieving logarithmic regret.
concepts.example: Arm A averages 0.6 after 100 pulls and arm B averages 0.5 after 3 pulls; B's bonus for being barely tried is large, so UCB picks B to check it is not actually better.

concepts.name: Value Iteration
concepts.description: A dynamic programming algorithm that repeatedly applies the Bellman optimality update to all states until values converge, then reads off the greedy optimal policy.
concepts.example: In a grid world, start all values at 0 and repeatedly set each square's value to the best reward plus gamma times next value over actions; values spread outward from the goal until they stop changing.

concepts.name: Variable Elimination
concepts.description: An exact inference algorithm for graphical models that sums out variables one at a time, multiplying and marginalizing factors; its cost depends heavily on the elimination order.
concepts.example: To get P(C) in a chain A to B to C, first sum out A to get a factor over B, then sum out B, avoiding the full A-B-C table entirely.

concepts.name: Weighted Importance Sampling
concepts.description: An importance sampling estimator that divides by the sum of the importance weights rather than the sample count, trading a small bias for much lower variance.
concepts.example: Three samples with weights 3, 0.5, 0.5 and values 10, 0, 0: ordinary IS gives 30/3 = 10, while weighted IS divides by the total weight 4, giving 7.5, and it can never exceed the largest observed value.

concepts.name: World Model
concepts.description: A learned model of how the environment evolves in response to actions, and often of rewards, that an agent can use to predict, plan or train on imagined experience.
concepts.example: A model that predicts 'if I push the cup to the left, it will slide off the table' lets an agent imagine outcomes before acting, like rehearsing in its head.

concepts.name: World Models (Ha and Schmidhuber)
concepts.description: Ha and Schmidhuber's agent that compresses frames with a VAE, predicts future latents with an MDN-RNN, and trains a small controller with CMA-ES, even inside its own dream.
concepts.example: To learn car racing, a VAE shrinks each frame to 32 numbers, an RNN predicts the next 32 numbers, and a tiny controller tuned by evolution steers using those predictions; it can even train in its own 'dream'.
